1. Variable & Value

Your Notes: In JS, value and variable are fundamental concepts that form the basis of programming.

1.1 Q. What is a Variable?

Your Notes:
  • A variable is a container or storage location to store/hold a value.
  • It has a name and can be used to store and manipulate data in a program.
  • So containers are locations in memory used to store values. A container is also a reserved space in the computer's memory (RAM) allocated to store data.
  • A JS variable is just the name of a storage location in memory.
Definition: A variable is a named reference to a location in memory that stores a value, which the program can read and change.
Variable म्हणजे memory (RAM) मधील एक डबा (container), ज्याला आपण नाव देतो. त्या नावाने आपण value साठवतो, वाचतो आणि बदलतो. JS मध्ये variable हे फक्त memory location चे नाव (label) आहे.
Extra Details:
  • Primitive values (number, string, boolean…) are stored directly. Objects and arrays live in heap memory, and the variable holds a reference (address) to them.
  • Naming rules: a name can contain letters, digits, _ and $; it cannot start with a digit; it cannot be a reserved word (let, class…); it is case-sensitive (age ≠ Age).
  • Convention: use camelCase, e.g. userName, totalPrice.
Figure 1: A variable is a named box in memory, and the value is what is stored inside it.
let userName = "Vishal";   // variable 'userName' stores the value "Vishal"
userName = "Rahul";        // the same container now holds a new value
console.log(userName);     // Rahul
  • What happens: let creates a box called userName holding "Vishal"; assigning again puts a new value in the same box.
  • Output: Rahul.
  • ✅ Variables let you store data once and reuse/update it by name.

1.2 Q. What is a Value?

Your Notes:
  • A value is a piece of information that a program works with. It can be a number, text, true/false or more complex data.
Value म्हणजे प्रत्यक्ष माहिती (data), उदा. number, text, true/false किंवा object/array सारखा complex data. Variable हा डबा आहे आणि value ही त्या डब्यात ठेवलेली वस्तू आहे.
Extra Details: JS has 2 kinds of values.
  • Primitive (7): Number, String, Boolean, undefined, null, BigInt, Symbol.
  • Non-primitive (reference): Object, Array, Function.
let age = 25;              // Number
let name = "Vishal";       // String
let isLoggedIn = true;     // Boolean
let nothing = null;        // null
let big = 123n;            // BigInt
let user = { id: 1 };      // Object
let list = [1, 2, 3];      // Array
  • What happens: one variable per data type; JS works out the type from the value.
  • Output: (no output).

1.3 Note: Dynamic Typing

Your Notes:
  • In JS, a variable's type is changed or checked at runtime, so it is a dynamically typed language (it allows you to change the variable type at runtime).
  • JavaScript is a dynamically typed language, meaning variable types are checked at runtime. This allows you to assign any type of value to a variable and change it later.
    • let myVar = 30; // Initially a Number
    • myVar = "Vishal"; // Reassigned to a String (totally valid in JavaScript)
JS मध्ये variable चा type आधी लिहावा लागत नाही. Program चालू असताना (runtime) type ठरतो आणि नंतर बदलूही शकतो. म्हणून JS ला dynamically typed language म्हणतात. Java/C++ मध्ये type आधी fix करावा लागतो (statically typed).
let myVar = 30;
console.log(typeof myVar);  // "number"
myVar = "Vishal";
console.log(typeof myVar);  // "string"
  • What happens: the same variable first holds a number, then a string; typeof shows the current type.
  • Output: "number", "string".
  • ✅ Flexible (dynamically typed).
  • ⚠ The type can change by accident; TypeScript or careful naming helps.

1.4 Anatomy of a Declaration

Your Notes: 
var myName = 'Vishal';
    └─ var      => Keyword (declares the variable name in scope)
    └─ myName   => Identifier / Variable Name (acts as the pointer/reference)
    └─ 'Vishal' => Value (the actual data stored in memory)
  • What happens: This diagram breaks down the parts of a variable declaration. `var` is the keyword, `myName` is the identifier, and `'Vishal'` is the value stored in memory.
  • Output: (no output).
var/let/const हा keyword, myName हे variable चे नाव (identifier) आणि 'Vishal' ही memory मध्ये साठवलेली value आहे.

2. Q. What is the Variable Life Cycle?

Your Notes: The variable life cycle contains:

2.1 Declaration

Your Notes:
  • Declaration: the JavaScript compiler registers the variable identifier in its enclosing scope (global, function or block). No value is bound yet.
  • let x; // Declaring 'x'

2.2 Initialization

Your Notes:
  • The variable is allocated memory and bound to an initial value (either explicitly or by default undefined).
  • var is automatically initialized to undefined when hoisted.
  • let is initialized to undefined, or to a specified value, only when the declaration statement is executed.
  • const must be initialized immediately at declaration.
  • let x = 10; // Initializing 'x' with the value 10 (declaration + first value together) ✔ after let x; runs, x is already initialized to undefined, so a later x = 10; is the first assignment. Initialization with a value is written as let x = 10;.let x; चालल्यावर x ला आधीच undefined मिळते. म्हणून नंतरचे x = 10 हे पहिले assignment आहे, initialization नाही. value सोबत initialization म्हणजे let x = 10; असे एकाच line मध्ये लिहिणे.
  • x = 20; // Re-assigning 'x' to 20

2.3 Assignment

Your Notes:
  • Assignment (re-assignment): binding a new value to an already declared and initialized variable.
1. Declaration: variable चे नाव scope मध्ये नोंदवणे (अजून value नाही).
2. Initialization: memory देऊन पहिली value bind करणे (दिली नसेल तर undefined).
3. Assignment: आधीपासून असलेल्या variable ला नवीन value देणे.
Figure 2: The variable life cycle.
let x;          // 1. Declaration (+ initialized to undefined when this line runs)
console.log(x); // undefined
x = 10;         // 2/3. First value assigned
x = 20;         // 3. Re-assignment
let y = 5;      // Declaration + Initialization in one line
const z = 1;    // const: declaration + initialization MUST be together
  • What happens: let x creates the variable (value undefined); then it gets a value and later a new one. const must get its value on the same line.
  • Output: undefined.
  • ✅ Declaring first and assigning later is fine for let.
  • ⚠ const z; without a value → SyntaxError.

3. Q. How Many Ways to Define a Variable in JS?

Your Notes: There are 3 ways to define a variable in JS:
  1. var → Function-scoped or Globally-scoped
  2. let → Block-scoped
  3. const → Block-scoped
Figure 3: Nested scopes. var belongs to the function, while let and const belong to the block.
JS मध्ये variable बनवण्याचे 3 मार्ग आहेत: var (function scope), let (block scope) आणि const (block scope, value बदलता येत नाही).

4. Q. Differences between var vs let vs const

Featurevarletconst

ScopeFunction scopeBlock scope ({})Block scope ({})
Can be used outside a {} block?✅ Yes❌ No❌ No
Can declare without a value?✅ Yes✅ Yes❌ No, a value is required
Default value if not assignedundefinedundefinedNot possible
Can access before declaration?✅ Yes, but the value is undefined❌ No, gives ReferenceError❌ No, gives ReferenceError

5. var

Your Notes (every point):
  • var keyword: function scope / global scope.
  • Variables declared with var are scoped to the enclosing function.
  • They ignore block boundaries (like if, for, while blocks) and spill out into the parent function or global scope.
  • Introduced in: var has existed since the very first version of JavaScript (ES1, 1997) and was still the standard in ES5 (older JavaScript). Before ES6, it was the only way to declare variables. ✔ "introduced in ES5" → var exists since ES1.var ES5 मध्ये introduce झाला नाही. तो ES1 (1997) पासून आहे. ES6 आधी variable बनवण्याचा तो एकमेव मार्ग होता.
  • Scope: var is function-scoped. If it is declared inside a function, it can only be used inside that function. If declared outside any function, it becomes a global variable.
  • Accessible outside a block ({}): Yes. var ignores block scope. If you declare it inside an if, for or while block, it can still be accessed outside the block.
  • Initialization required? No. You can declare a var variable without assigning a value.
  • Default value: If no value is assigned, JavaScript automatically sets it to undefined.
  • Access before declaration: Yes. Because of hoisting, you can access it before the declaration, but the value will be undefined.
  • Hoisting: The declaration is moved to the top of its scope during compilation. Only the declaration is hoisted, not the assignment.
  • Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ): var does not have a Temporal Dead Zone.
  • Re-declaration: Allowed. You can declare the same variable multiple times in the same scope.
  • Reassignment: Allowed. You can change its value anytime.
  • Loop behavior: In a for loop, all iterations share the same variable, which may cause problems with asynchronous code like setTimeout().
  • Global object (window): If declared globally in a browser, var becomes a property of the window object.
  • Memory allocation: Memory is allocated during the creation phase and initialized with undefined.
  • Best use case: Mainly found in old JavaScript code. Rarely used in modern applications.
  • Recommendation: Avoid var in modern JavaScript because function scope and hoisting can cause unexpected bugs.
var हा function-scoped आहे. तो if/for/while च्या block ला मानत नाही आणि बाहेर "सांडतो" (spill होतो). var पुन्हा declare करता येतो, value बदलता येते आणि hoisting मुळे declaration आधी वापरल्यास undefined मिळते. Global var हा window चा property बनतो. या सगळ्यामुळे bugs होतात, म्हणून var टाळा.

Example (your code)

// Variables declared with var are scoped to the enclosing function. They ignore
// block boundaries (like if, for, while blocks) and spill out into the parent
// function or global scope.
function varDemo() {
  var z; // declared without initialization → default value undefined
  var x = 20;
  console.log("var z inside the block :", z);   // undefined
  console.log("var x inside the block ", x);    // 20
  if (true) {
    var x = 40; // redeclares/updates x in the same function
    var y = 20; // var is NOT block-scoped, so y leaks/spills outside this block
    console.log("var x inside block:", x); // 40
    console.log("var y inside block:", y); // 20
  }
  console.log("var y outside block:", y); // 20 (accessible outside block!)
  console.log("var z value:", z);         // undefined (accessed without initialization)
}
varDemo();
  • What happens: var belongs to the whole FUNCTION, not the if-block: var x = 40 inside the block overwrites the same x, and y is visible after the block. z was declared but never assigned → undefined.
  • Output: undefined, 20, 40, 20, 20, undefined.
  • ⚠ Block leaks and silent re-declaration are why var causes bugs; prefer let/const.
Extra Details: Notice that after the if block, x is 40 outside it too, because the block's var x = 40 overwrote the function's x. This is the main danger of var.

6. let

Your Notes (every point):
  • let keyword: block scope.
  • Variables declared with let are scoped to the nearest block ({}) in which they are declared.
  • They do not ignore block boundaries. They can only be accessed inside the block where they are declared.
  • Introduced in: let was introduced in ES6 (2015) to solve the problems caused by var.
  • Scope: let is block-scoped. If declared inside an if, for, while or any {} block, it is accessible only within that block.
  • Accessible outside a block ({}): No. Variables declared with let cannot be accessed outside the block where they are declared.
  • Initialization required? No. You can declare a let variable without assigning a value.
  • Default value: If no value is assigned, JavaScript automatically sets it to undefined after the declaration is executed.
  • Access before declaration: No. Accessing a let variable before its declaration throws a ReferenceError because of the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ).
  • Hoisting: let is hoisted, but it is not initialized until the declaration is reached.
  • Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ): Yes. The variable exists in memory but cannot be accessed from the beginning of the block until its declaration.
  • Re-declaration: Not allowed. You cannot declare the same let variable again in the same scope.
  • Reassignment: Allowed. You can change the value of a let variable anytime.
  • Loop behavior: In a for loop, let creates a new variable for each iteration, avoiding closure issues with asynchronous code like setTimeout().
  • Global object (window): If declared globally in a browser, let does not become a property of the window object.
  • Memory allocation: Memory is allocated during the creation phase, but the variable remains uninitialized until the declaration executes.
  • Best use case: Use let when the variable's value needs to change during program execution.
  • Recommendation: Use let whenever a variable needs to be reassigned. It is safer than var because it is block-scoped.
let हा block-scoped आहे, म्हणजे तो फक्त त्याच {} मध्ये वापरता येतो. value बदलता येते, पण त्याच scope मध्ये पुन्हा declare करता येत नाही. let hoist होतो, पण declaration line येईपर्यंत TDZ मध्ये राहतो. त्याआधी वापरल्यास ReferenceError येतो.

Example (your code)

// Variables declared with let are block-scoped, meaning they are only accessible
// within the block {} in which they are defined.
function letDemo() {
  if (true) {
    let x = 20;
    let u; // declared without initialization (defaults to undefined inside scope)
    console.log("let x inside block:", x); // 20
    x = 40; // updating is allowed
    // let x = 40; // SyntaxError: Identifier 'x' has already been declared
    console.log("let x after update:", x); // 40
    console.log("let u initialized default:", u); // undefined
  }
  // console.log(x); // ReferenceError: x is not defined (cannot access outside block)
}
letDemo();
  • What happens: let lives only inside its { } block. It can be updated (x = 40) but not declared again in the same block; outside the block it doesn't exist.
  • Output: 20, 40, undefined.
  • ✅ Each block keeps its own variables → fewer accidental clashes.

7. const

Your Notes (every point):
  • const keyword: block scope.
  • Variables declared with const are scoped to the nearest block ({}) in which they are declared.
  • They do not ignore block boundaries and cannot be accessed outside the block where they are declared.
  • Introduced in: const was introduced in ES6 (2015) to declare variables whose reference should not change.
  • Scope: const is block-scoped. It is accessible only inside the block where it is declared.
  • Accessible outside a block ({}): No. Variables declared with const cannot be accessed outside the block.
  • Initialization required? Yes. A const variable must be initialized when it is declared.
  • Default value: Not applicable. Since initialization is mandatory, there is no default value.
  • Access before declaration: No. Accessing a const variable before its declaration throws a ReferenceError because of the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ).
  • Hoisting: const is hoisted, but it is not initialized until the declaration is reached.
  • Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ): Yes. The variable exists in memory but cannot be accessed until its declaration.
  • Re-declaration: Not allowed. You cannot declare the same const variable again in the same scope.
  • Reassignment: Not allowed. Once a value is assigned, it cannot be reassigned. Attempting to do so throws a TypeError.
  • Loop behavior: In for...of and for...in loops, const creates a new binding for each iteration, and the variable cannot be reassigned inside the loop. In a classic for (const i = 0; i < 3; i++) loop, const throws a TypeError because i++ tries to reassign it. ✔ const does not work as the counter of a classic for loop.for (const i = 0; i < 3; i++) मध्ये i++ हे const ची value बदलण्याचा प्रयत्न करते, म्हणून TypeError येतो. const फक्त for...of आणि for...in loop मध्ये चालतो.
  • Global object (window): If declared globally in a browser, const does not become a property of the window object.
  • Memory allocation: Memory is allocated during the creation phase, but the variable remains uninitialized until the declaration executes.
  • Best use case: Use const for variables whose value should not be reassigned, such as configuration values, API URLs or constants.
  • Objects and arrays: Although a const variable cannot be reassigned, the properties of objects and the elements of arrays can still be modified, because only the reference is constant.
  • Recommendation: Use const by default. Only use let when you know the variable's value will change later.
for (const item of [1, 2, 3]) console.log(item);   // ✅ 1 2 3
// for (const i = 0; i < 3; i++) {}                // ❌ TypeError: Assignment to constant variable
  • What happens: for...of creates a fresh const for every item, so const works. A classic for loop must do i++, which re-assigns a const → TypeError.
  • Output: 1 2 3.
  • ✅ Use const in for...of / for...in by default.
  • ⚠ Use let in classic for (let i = 0; …) loops.
const ला declare करतानाच value द्यावी लागते आणि नंतर ती बदलता येत नाही (TypeError). पण object/array असेल तर त्याच्या आतील data बदलता येतो, कारण फक्त reference (पत्ता) constant असतो. Default म्हणून नेहमी const वापरा.

Example (your code)

// Variables declared with const are block-scoped, must be initialized upon
// declaration, and their reference cannot be updated or reassigned.
function constDemo() {
  // const name; // SyntaxError: Missing initializer in const declaration
  const name = "x";
  console.log("const name:", name);  // x
  // name = "vishal"; // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.
}
constDemo();
  • What happens: const must be initialized and can't be re-assigned.
  • Output: const name: x.
  • ✅ Signals "this binding never changes" and prevents accidental re-assignment.

8. Hoisting

8.1 Q. What is Hoisting in JS?

Your Notes:
  • Hoisting is a JavaScript mechanism, or default behavior, in which variable and function declarations are moved to the top of their scope before code execution.
  • Hoisting is JavaScript's default behavior of moving declarations to the top of their current scope during the compilation phase.
Extra Details: Nothing physically "moves". During the memory creation phase, the engine allocates memory for all declarations before running any code, so it behaves as if they were moved to the top.
Hoisting म्हणजे code चालण्याआधीच JS सर्व declarations साठी memory राखून ठेवते, जणू ते scope च्या सर्वात वर हलवले आहेत. फक्त declaration वर जाते, value (initialization) नाही.

8.2 var Hoisting

Your Notes:
  • var hoisting: the declaration is hoisted to the top and initialized with the default value of undefined.
  • Variables declared with var are hoisted to the top of their enclosing function or global scope.
  • However, only the declaration is hoisted, not the initialization.
  • This means that if you try to access a var variable before its declaration, it will return undefined instead of throwing an error.
console.log(a); // undefined (due to hoisting)
var a = 10;     // Declaration is hoisted, but initialization happens here

      Memory Creation Phase (Hoisting)
      ───────────────────────────────────────────
      aVar
      │
      ├── Memory is reserved
      └── Initialized with undefined

      Execution Phase
      ───────────────────────────────────────────
      console.log(aVar);   ✅ undefined

      var aVar = 10;
              └── Value becomes 10

      console.log(aVar);   ✅ 10
  • What happens: var a is hoisted and set to undefined before any code runs, so reading it early gives undefined, not an error.
  • Output: undefined.
  • ⚠ Hides bugs: you read a variable before giving it a value and get no error.

8.3 let & const Hoisting

Your Notes:
  • let and const are also hoisted to the top of their block scope, but they are not initialized.
  • let & const hoisting: the variables are hoisted but not initialized. They enter the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ).
  • This means that if you try to access a let or const variable before its declaration, it will throw a ReferenceError.
  • This period between the start of the block and the declaration is known as the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ).
  • During this time, the variable exists in memory but cannot be accessed.
  Memory Creation Phase (Hoisting)
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────
  aVar
  │
  ├── Memory is reserved for aVar
  ├── NOT initialized
  └── Value = <uninitialized>

  Execution Phase
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────
  Start of Block Scope
          │
          ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)                   │
  │   console.log(aVar);                         │
  │   ❌ ReferenceError                          │
  │   Cannot access 'aVar' before initialization │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          │
          ▼
  let aVar = 10;
          ├── Variable gets initialized
          └── TDZ Ends
          │
          ▼
  console.log(aVar);   ✅ 10
  • What happens: The diagram shows how let behaves during execution. During the memory phase, aVar is uninitialized (in TDZ). In the execution phase, accessing aVar before initialization throws a ReferenceError. After let aVar = 10; executes, the TDZ ends and the variable holds the value 10.
  • Output: ReferenceError (if accessed early), then 10.
Figure 4: The two phases of hoisting. var gets undefined, let/const stay uninitialized, and functions are hoisted with their full body.
var hoist होताना undefined ने initialize होतो, म्हणून आधी वापरल्यास undefined मिळते. let/const hoist होतात पण initialize होत नाहीत, म्हणून आधी वापरल्यास ReferenceError येतो.
Extra Details: function hoisting 
greet();                                  // ✅ "Hi": function declarations are fully hoisted
function greet() { console.log("Hi"); }

// sayHi();                               // ❌ TypeError: sayHi is not a function
var sayHi = function () {};               // only 'var sayHi' is hoisted (undefined)
  • What happens: function declarations are hoisted with their body, so greet() works before the line. With var sayHi = function…, only the variable is hoisted (undefined), so calling it early is a TypeError.
  • Output: Hi.
  • ⚠ Function expressions/arrow functions can't be called before their line.

9. Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)

9.1 Q. What is the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)?

Your Notes:
  • The Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) is a behavior in JavaScript that occurs with variables declared using let and const.
  • It refers to the time between the start of a block and the point where the variable is declared, during which the variable exists in memory but cannot be accessed.
  • If you try to access a let or const variable before its declaration, it will throw a ReferenceError.
  • The TDZ is the region of code / period of time from the start of the block scope until the line where the variable is officially declared and initialized. Accessing the variable inside the TDZ throws a ReferenceError.
  • Example:
{
  // TDZ starts here
  // name exists, but cannot be accessed
  console.log(name); // ❌ Error
  let name = "Vishal";
  // TDZ ends here
  console.log(name); // ✅ Vishal
}
  • What happens: from the start of the block until let name runs, name is in the Temporal Dead Zone: it exists but can't be read.
  • Output: ReferenceError at the first log; Vishal after the declaration.
  • ✅ TDZ turns "used too early" bugs into a clear error instead of a silent undefined.
  • The Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) is the time between entering a block scope and the execution of a let or const declaration. During this time, the variable is hoisted but remains uninitialized, and accessing it throws a ReferenceError.
Figure 5: TDZ timeline, from the start of the block until the let/const line executes.
TDZ म्हणजे block सुरू झाल्यापासून let/const ची declaration line execute होईपर्यंतचा काळ. या काळात variable memory मध्ये असतो पण "मृत" (dead) असतो, म्हणजे तो वापरता येत नाही. वापरल्यास ReferenceError येतो. TDZ मुळे declaration आधी variable वापरण्याची चूक लगेच पकडली जाते.
Extra Details: The TDZ is about time (execution order), not the position of the code: 
function show() { console.log(v); }  // uses v
// show();   // ❌ called here → v is still in TDZ → ReferenceError
let v = 5;
show();      // ✅ 5 (called after initialization)
  • What happens: TDZ is about TIME, not position: show() may be written above let v, but it must be CALLED after let v has run.
  • Output: 5.
  • ⚠ Calling a function that uses a let variable too early still throws.

9.2 Notes: Hoisting vs TDZ

Your Notes:
  • Hoisting means JavaScript allocates memory for declarations before executing the code.
  • The TDZ is the period during execution from the start of a block until a let or const variable is initialized. During this period the variable is hoisted but uninitialized, so accessing it throws a ReferenceError.
  • Hoisting is the process of allocating memory before execution begins.
  • The TDZ is the runtime period during execution where a hoisted let or const variable exists but cannot be accessed until its declaration is executed.
  • Hoisting is a compile-time behavior where JavaScript allocates memory for declarations before execution.
  • The Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) is a runtime period during execution where a hoisted let or const variable exists but remains uninitialized, so accessing it before its declaration results in a ReferenceError.

9.3 Q. Does a let variable default to undefined if it is declared without initialization? If yes, how is it different from var?

Your Notes:
  • Both var and let default to undefined when declared without an initializer.
  • The difference is that var is initialized to undefined during the hoisting (memory creation) phase,
  • whereas let is initialized to undefined only when execution reaches its declaration.
  • Before that point, a let variable is in the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ), so accessing it throws a ReferenceError.
console.log(a); // undefined        (var: initialized during hoisting)
var a;
// console.log(b); // ReferenceError (let: still in TDZ)
let b;
console.log(b); // undefined        (let: initialized when the declaration ran)
  • What happens: var a is undefined from the start; let b throws before its line, but after `let b;` it is initialized to undefined.
  • Output: undefined, undefined.
  • ✅ Interview point: let IS hoisted, just not initialized (TDZ).
दोघांचीही default value undefined आहे. फरक एवढाच की var ला undefined hoisting वेळीच मिळते, तर let ला declaration line चालल्यावरच मिळते. त्याआधी let TDZ मध्ये असतो.

9.4 Q. Difference between Hoisting and the TDZ in JavaScript

FeatureHoistingTemporal Dead Zone (TDZ)
DefinitionJavaScript moves declarations into memory before execution starts.The time between entering a block scope and initializing a let or const variable.
When it happensDuring the Memory Creation (Compilation) phase.During the Execution phase.
PurposeAllocates memory for variables and functions before code execution.Prevents access to let and const variables before they are initialized.
Applies tovar, let, const, function declarations and classes.Only let, const and classes.
Initializationvar is initialized to undefined; let and const are hoisted but remain uninitialized.The variable remains uninitialized until its declaration statement executes.
Access before declarationvar can be accessed (undefined); let/const cannot.Accessing a variable in the TDZ throws a ReferenceError.
ErrorNo error for var; let/const are still hoisted but cannot be accessed because of the TDZ.ReferenceError: Cannot access 'x' before initialization.
ScopeWorks according to the variable's scope (global, function or block).Exists only within the block scope of let and const.

10. Variable Shadowing

10.1 Introduction & Types

Your Notes:
  • Shadowing means an inner scope declares a variable with the same name as a variable in an outer scope.
  • The inner variable hides (shadows) the outer variable within its own scope.
  • There are two types:
    1. Legal shadowing: the inner variable hides the outer variable only inside its own block.
    2. Illegal shadowing: a var declaration inside a block conflicts with an outer let or const.

10.2 Q. What is variable shadowing in JavaScript?

Your Notes:
  • Variable shadowing occurs when a variable declared within a certain scope (e.g. a function or block) has the same name as a variable declared in an outer scope.
  • In such cases, the inner variable "shadows" or overrides the outer variable within its scope, making the outer variable inaccessible in that inner scope.
  • This can lead to confusion and bugs if not managed carefully, because it may not be immediately clear which variable is being referenced.
  • Variable shadowing occurs when an inner scope declares a variable with the same name as one in the outer scope.
  • The inner variable shadows (hides) the outer variable within its block.
  • Shadowing does not cross scope boundaries; once we exit the inner scope, the outer variable becomes accessible again with its original value. The inner and outer variables are separate, so changing the inner one never changes the outer one. ✔ the original said the outer value is "overridden by the inner variable's value if it was modified". That is wrong; the outer value is never changed.आतला आणि बाहेरचा variable हे दोन वेगळे variables आहेत. आतला बदलल्याने बाहेरच्याची value कधीच बदलत नाही.
Figure 6: Legal vs illegal shadowing.
Shadowing म्हणजे आतल्या scope मध्ये बाहेरच्या variable च्याच नावाचा नवीन variable बनवणे. आतल्या scope मध्ये आतला variable बाहेरच्याला "झाकतो" (सावली). हे दोन वेगळे variables असतात, त्यामुळे आतला बदलल्याने बाहेरचा बदलत नाही. बाहेर आल्यावर बाहेरचा variable पुन्हा दिसतो.

10.3 Q. How does variable shadowing work in JavaScript?

Your Notes:
  • When a variable is declared in an inner scope with the same name as a variable in an outer scope, the inner variable takes precedence within that inner scope.
  • The outer variable is still present in memory, but it is not accessible while inside the inner scope.
  • Once execution leaves the inner scope, the outer variable becomes accessible again.
  • Example:
var x = 10; // Outer variable
function example() {
  var x = 20; // Inner variable shadows outer variable
  console.log(x); // 20 (inner variable)
}
console.log(x); // 10 (outer variable)
  • What happens: the inner var x is a different variable that hides (shadows) the outer x inside the function.
  • Output: 10 (outer log; example() isn't called — it would print 20).
  • ⚠ Shadowing makes it unclear which x you mean; prefer different names.
  • In this example, the inner variable x (20) shadows the outer variable x (10) within the function example.
  • When console.log(x) is called inside the function, it refers to the inner variable, not the outer one.
  • Once the function execution is complete, the outer variable x (10) remains unchanged and accessible outside the function.
Extra Details: JS looks up a name through the scope chain: it checks the current scope first, then its parent, and so on up to global. The first match wins, which is why the inner x hides the outer one. Also note that example() must be called for "20" to print; the original example never calls it.

10.4 Q. What is illegal shadowing in JavaScript?

Your Notes:
  • Illegal shadowing occurs when a var declared in an inner block attempts to shadow a variable declared with let or const in the outer (enclosing function or global) scope. ✔ the original said any inner variable shadowing an outer let/const is illegal. Only an inner var causes it; an inner let/const is legal.बाहेरच्या let/const ला आतल्या let/const ने shadow करणे legal आहे. Error फक्त आतल्या block मध्ये var वापरल्यावरच येतो.
  • Since let and const cannot be redeclared in the same scope, and var is hoisted out of the block into that same scope, ✔ added why var reaches the outer scope (hoisting).var block ला मानत नाही आणि hoisting मुळे function च्या scope मध्ये जातो. तिथे त्याच नावाचा let/const असल्यामुळे clash होतो.
  • declaring a var with the same name inside the block results in a SyntaxError. Declaring an inner let/const with the same name is legal shadowing. ✔ "a variable with the same name in an inner scope" → "a var with the same name in the block".SyntaxError "कोणताही variable" मुळे नाही, तर block मधील त्याच नावाच्या var मुळे येतो.
  • Example:
let x = 10;
function example() {
  let x = 20; // Legal shadowing
  console.log(x); // 20 (inner variable)
}
  • What happens: let inside a function may shadow an outer let: legal.
  • Output: (no output: example() isn't called).
  • In this example, the inner variable x (20) legally shadows the outer variable x (10) within the function example.
  • However, if we tried to declare another let or const variable with the same name in the same scope, it would result in a SyntaxError.
  • Illegal shadowing occurs when a var declaration tries to shadow a let or const variable,
  • but because var is function-scoped, it gets hoisted to the enclosing function scope and conflicts with the existing let/const declaration.
  • Example:
function illegalShadowingDemo() {
  let name = "Vishal";
  if (true) {
    // ❌ SyntaxError
    var name = "Shinde";
  }
}
// SyntaxError: Identifier 'name' has already been declared
  • What happens: var name inside the block is hoisted to the function, where let name already exists → duplicate declaration.
  • Output: SyntaxError (the whole file fails).
  • ⚠ This error is raised while parsing, so nothing in the file runs.
Illegal shadowing म्हणजे block मध्ये var वापरून बाहेरच्या let/const च्या नावाचा variable बनवणे. var block ला मानत नाही आणि function च्या वर hoist होतो. तिथे आधीच त्याच नावाचा let/const असल्यामुळे duplicate declaration होऊन SyntaxError येतो. let/const ने let/const ला shadow करणे मात्र legal आहे.

10.5 Q. Comparison

ScenarioAllowed?Reason
var → let (inner block)✅ YesDifferent scopes (function vs block).
let → let (inner block)✅ YesThe inner let shadows the outer let.
const → const (inner block)✅ YesThe inner const shadows the outer const.
let → var (same function after hoisting)❌ Novar is hoisted to the function scope and conflicts with the existing let.
const → var (same function after hoisting)❌ NoSame reason as above.
Extra Details: let → var is legal if the var is inside a nested function, because var stays inside that function and doesn't reach the outer let: 
let a = 1;
function inner() { var a = 2; console.log(a); } // ✅ 2 (legal)
  • What happens: var inside a function shadowing an outer let is legal, because the var stays inside the function.
  • Output: 2 (when inner() is called).

10.6 Q. Differences between Legal Shadowing vs Illegal Shadowing

FeatureLegal ShadowingIllegal Shadowing
DefinitionAn inner scope declares a variable with the same name as an outer scope without causing an error.A var declaration conflicts with an existing let or const in the same function scope after hoisting.
Allowed?✅ Yes❌ No

ReasonThe variables exist in different scopes.var is hoisted to the function scope and clashes with let/const.

10.7 Code Examples (your code)

Example 1
let x = 10; // Outer variable
function example() {
  let x = 20; // Inner variable shadows outer variable
  console.log(x); // 20 (inner variable)
}
console.log(x); // 10 (outer variable)
  • What happens: let x inside example() hides the global x only inside the function.
  • Output: 10 (example() isn't called).
Legal shadowing
// # Legal shadowing
function demo() {
  var name = "vishal";
  if (true) {
    let name = "shinde"; // Shadows outer variable
    console.log(name);   // shinde
  }
  console.log(name);     // vishal
}
demo();
  • What happens: let inside the block shadows the function's var only inside the block.
  • Output: shinde, vishal.
  • ✅ Legal: inner let/const may shadow outer var/let/const.
Illegal shadowing
// # Illegal shadowing
// A var declaration inside a block conflicts with an outer let & const
function demo1() {
  let age = 90;       // ✔ was commented out, so no error happened
  if (true) {
    var age = 30;     // ❌ var hoists to function scope → clashes with let age
    console.log(age);
  }
  console.log(age);
}
demo1();
// Uncaught SyntaxError: Identifier 'age' has already been declared
// (Note: a SyntaxError stops the WHOLE file from running, so keep this
//  example commented out in real files. With let commented out it prints 30, 30.)
// WHY?
// - var ignores the block and is hoisted to the enclosing function scope.
// JS treats it like:
function demo1() {
  var age;          // hoisted
  let age = 90;     // ❌ Duplicate declaration   ✔ was 'name', now 'age'
}
  • What happens: var age is hoisted to demo1's scope where let age exists → clash.
  • Output: SyntaxError: Identifier 'age' has already been declared (prints 30, 30 if let is removed).
  • ⚠ Illegal shadowing: var inside a block can't shadow an outer let/const in the same function.
तुमच्या demo1 मध्ये let age = 90; comment केलेले होते, त्यामुळे error येत नव्हता (30, 30 print होते). आता ते uncomment केले आहे. "JS treats it like" मध्ये name ऐवजी age हवे होते. SyntaxError पूर्ण file थांबवतो, म्हणून असे example real file मध्ये comment करून ठेवा.

11. Q. Can You Change the Properties of an Object Declared with const?

Your Notes:
  • Yes.
  • const guarantees that the variable reference (the memory address stored in the stack) will not change.
  • It does not make the properties of the object in heap memory immutable.
  • To make the object immutable, you can use Object.freeze(obj). It is shallow: it freezes only the top-level properties, so for complete immutability every nested object must also be frozen (deep freeze). ✔ "completely immutable" → Object.freeze() is shallow, and nested objects can still change.Object.freeze() फक्त पहिल्या level ला lock करतो. आतले (nested) object अजूनही बदलता येतात. पूर्ण lock साठी deep freeze लागतो.
const obj = { age: 30 };
obj.age = 31;        // Allowed
// obj = { age: 32 }; // Throws TypeError
  • What happens: const protects the variable, not the object: changing a property is fine, re-assigning the whole object is not.
  • Output: (no output).
  • ⚠ const ≠ immutable; use Object.freeze for that.
const frozen = Object.freeze({ a: 1, inner: { b: 2 } });
frozen.a = 99;        // ignored (TypeError in strict mode)
frozen.inner.b = 99;  // ✅ still changes → freeze is shallow
console.log(frozen);  // { a: 1, inner: { b: 99 } }

function deepFreeze(o) {
  Object.values(o).forEach(v => typeof v === "object" && v !== null && deepFreeze(v));
  return Object.freeze(o);
}
  • What happens: freeze blocks changes to frozen's own properties, but the nested object is still changeable. deepFreeze freezes every level.
  • Output: { a: 1, inner: { b: 99 } }.
  • ✅ Protect configuration objects.
  • ⚠ freeze is shallow.
Figure 7: A const object. The reference in the stack is fixed, but the data in the heap can still change.
const फक्त reference (stack मधील पत्ता) fixed करतो, heap मधील object चे data नाही. म्हणून obj.age बदलता येते, पण obj = नवीन object केल्यास TypeError येतो. Object.freeze() फक्त पहिल्या level ला lock करतो.

12. Q. What Happens if You Declare a Variable Without Any Keyword (e.g. x = 10)?

Your Notes:
  • If declared without var, let or const, it becomes a property of the global object (window in browsers, global in Node.js) in non-strict mode.
  • In strict mode ("use strict"), it throws a ReferenceError because implicit global variable creation is forbidden.
newVar = 10;                  // ✔ was 'x = 10', but x was already declared
console.log('newVar....:', newVar);   // 10 → accidental global
console.log(window.newVar);          // 10 (browser)
  • What happens: assigning to an undeclared name in sloppy mode creates a global variable (window.newVar).
  • Output: 10, 10.
  • ⚠ Accidental globals leak memory and collide with other scripts.
✔ in your file, let x = 10 was declared earlier, so x = 10 was only a re-assignment, not an implicit global. A never-declared name is needed to show it.तुमच्या file मध्ये x आधीच let ने declare केला होता, म्हणून x = 10 हे फक्त नवीन value देणे होते, global variable नाही. Implicit global दाखवण्यासाठी कधीच declare न केलेले नाव (newVar) वापरावे लागते.
"use strict";                    // must be the first statement of the file/function
another = 10;                    // ❌ ReferenceError: another is not defined
// Note: ES modules and class bodies are always in strict mode.
  • What happens: in strict mode the same assignment is an error.
  • Output: ReferenceError.
  • ✅ Catches typos and accidental globals early.
keyword शिवाय (var/let/const न लिहिता) value दिल्यास तो चुकून global variable बनतो, जे धोकादायक आहे. "use strict" mode मध्ये असे केल्यास ReferenceError येतो.

13. Q. Why is var Shadowing let Illegal?

Your Notes:
  • var is function-scoped, while let is block-scoped.
  • var ignores block boundaries and is hoisted to the enclosing function scope.
  • If a let variable with the same name already exists in that function scope, the hoisted var declaration creates a duplicate declaration.
  • Since JavaScript does not allow a var and a let with the same name in the same scope, it throws a SyntaxError.
function demo() {
  let age = 25;
  if (true) {
    var age = 30; // ❌ SyntaxError
  }
}
  • What happens: same clash as before: var age hoists to the function where let age exists.
  • Output: SyntaxError.
  • JavaScript internally treats it like this after hoisting:
function demo() {
  var age;      // Hoisted to function scope
  let age = 25; // ❌ Duplicate declaration
}
  • What happens: how the engine sees it: var age hoisted, then let age = duplicate.
  • Output: SyntaxError.
  • var shadowing let is illegal because var is function-scoped and gets hoisted to the enclosing function scope, where it conflicts with the existing let declaration of the same name, resulting in a SyntaxError.
var block मधून बाहेर पडून function च्या top ला जातो. तिथे आधीच let age असल्यामुळे एकाच scope मध्ये दोन age होतात, म्हणून SyntaxError येतो.

14. Q. Explain the Difference between Global, Function and Block Scope

Your Notes:
  1. Global scope: Variables declared outside any function or block {}. They are accessible from anywhere in the file/application.
  2. Function scope: Variables declared with var, let or const inside a function. They are only accessible within that function.
  3. Block scope: Variables declared with let or const inside curly braces {} (e.g. an if block, loops, switch). They cannot be accessed outside that block.
let g = "global";              // Global scope
function fn() {
  var f = "function";          // Function scope
  if (true) {
    let b = "block";           // Block scope
    var leak = "var leaks";    // var ignores block → function scope
    console.log(g, f, b);      // ✅ all accessible
  }
  console.log(leak);           // ✅ "var leaks"
  // console.log(b);           // ❌ ReferenceError
}
fn();
// console.log(f);             // ❌ ReferenceError
  • What happens: g is global, f belongs to the function, b only to the if-block; var leak escapes the block.
  • Output: global function block, var leaks.
  • ✅ Shows all three scopes in one place.
Scope म्हणजे variable कुठपर्यंत वापरता येतो ती हद्द. Global म्हणजे सगळीकडे, Function म्हणजे फक्त त्या function मध्ये आणि Block म्हणजे फक्त त्या {} मध्ये (let/const साठी). var block ला मानत नाही.

15. Q. How Do let and const Protect Against Accidental Variable Overrides in Loops?

Your Notes:
  • let and const prevent accidental variable overrides because they are block-scoped, whereas var is function-scoped.
  • With var, a variable declared inside a loop is not limited to the loop.
  • After the loop finishes, the variable still exists in the surrounding function or global scope, which can accidentally overwrite or interfere with other variables.
  • With let and const, the variable exists only inside the loop block. Once the loop ends, the variable is no longer accessible, reducing the risk of accidental modification.
var i = 100;                              // some other code uses i
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {}
console.log(i);                           // 3 → the old value 100 was overwritten!

for (var k = 0; k < 3; k++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log(k), 0);   // 3 3 3 (one shared k)
}
for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log(j), 0);   // 0 1 2 (new j per iteration)
}
// console.log(j);                        // ❌ ReferenceError (j stays inside loop)
  • What happens: var i is ONE variable for the whole script, so the loop overwrites 100. With var k all three timers share the final k (3). With let j each iteration gets its own j.
  • Output: 3, then 3 3 3, then 0 1 2.
  • ✅ let in loops fixes the classic closure bug.
  • ⚠ Famous interview question: setTimeout inside a var loop.
Figure 8: In a loop with setTimeout, var shares one variable, while let creates a new binding per iteration.
var loop च्या बाहेरही राहतो आणि बाहेरच्या त्याच नावाच्या variable ला overwrite करतो. सर्व फेऱ्यांसाठी एकच var असल्यामुळे setTimeout मध्ये 3 3 3 मिळते. let प्रत्येक फेरीसाठी नवीन variable बनवतो (0 1 2) आणि loop संपल्यावर नष्ट होतो.

16. Extra Interview Questions (Detailed Answers)

Q1. Are let and const hoisted? Prove it.
  • Yes. If they were not hoisted, the code below would print the outer a (1). It throws an error instead, because the inner a is already hoisted and sitting in its TDZ.
let a = 1;
{
  console.log(a);  // ❌ ReferenceError (not 1!)
  let a = 2;
}
  • What happens: the inner let a shadows the outer one for the WHOLE block, so the first line reads the inner a while it is still in the TDZ.
  • Output: ReferenceError (not 1).
  • ⚠ Tricky output question.
Q2. Is a global let/const a property of window?
  • No. A global var x creates window.x. Global let/const are stored in a separate "script scope" (declarative environment), so window.x is undefined for them.
Q3. typeof on an undeclared variable vs a variable in the TDZ?
console.log(typeof notDeclared); // "undefined" (no error)
// console.log(typeof t);        // ❌ ReferenceError (t is in TDZ)
let t = 1;
  • What happens: typeof on a name that was never declared gives "undefined", but typeof on a let in its TDZ throws.
  • Output: "undefined".
  • ⚠ typeof is not a safe check during the TDZ.
Q4. Why was let/const introduced if var already existed?
  • var had problems: no block scope, silent re-declaration, reading undefined before declaration, leaking loop variables, and polluting window. let/const fix all of these with block scope, the TDZ and a no-re-declaration rule.
Q5. Output-based questions
// (a)
console.log(a); var a = 5;                 // undefined
// (b)
console.log(b); let b = 5;                 // ReferenceError (TDZ)
// (c)
var c = 1; var c = 2; console.log(c);      // 2
// (d)
const e = [1]; e.push(2); console.log(e);  // [1, 2]
// (e)
var f = 1; if (true) { var f = 2; } console.log(f);   // 2
// (f)
let g = 1; if (true) { let g = 2; } console.log(g);   // 1
// (g)
function h() { return typeof k; var k = 1; } console.log(h()); // "undefined"
  • What happens: seven classic output questions: (a) var hoisting → undefined; (b) let TDZ → error; (c) var can be redeclared → 2; (d) const array can be pushed → [1, 2]; (e) var ignores the block → 2; (f) let respects the block → 1; (g) var k is hoisted inside h → typeof gives "undefined".
  • Output: undefined, ReferenceError, 2, [1, 2], 2, 1, "undefined".
  • ✅ Revise these before every interview.
Q6. Which should you use by default?
  • Use const by default because it signals intent and blocks accidental re-assignment. Use let only when the value must change. Avoid var.

17. Quick Revision Summary

ConceptOne-line Summary
VariableNamed memory location that holds a value
ValueThe data itself (primitive or reference)
Dynamic typingType is checked at runtime and can change
Life cycleDeclaration → Initialization → Assignment
varFunction scope, hoisted as undefined, re-declarable, window property
letBlock scope, TDZ, re-assignable, not re-declarable
constBlock scope, TDZ, must initialize, not re-assignable, contents mutable
HoistingCompile-time memory allocation for declarations
TDZRuntime period in which a hoisted let/const cannot be accessed
Legal shadowingInner scope hides an outer variable, no error
Illegal shadowingA block var clashes with an outer let/const → SyntaxError
Implicit globalNo keyword creates a global; strict mode throws a ReferenceError
थोडक्यात: नेहमी const वापरा, value बदलायची असेल तर let वापरा आणि var टाळा. Hoisting म्हणजे आधी memory मिळणे. TDZ म्हणजे let/const declaration आधी वापरता न येणे. block मधील var ने बाहेरच्या let/const ला shadow केल्यास SyntaxError येतो.

1. Q. What is a Data Type?

Your Notes:
  • A data type defines what kind of data can be stored and manipulated within a variable.
  • It classifies the data so the interpreter understands how to perform operations on it.
  • A data type defines which type of data is stored in a variable.
  • A data type is a classification of data that tells the programming language how to store, interpret and manipulate a value.
  • A data type specifies the kind of value a variable can hold.
Definition: A data type is a classification of a value that tells JavaScript how to store it and which operations can be performed on it. In JS the type belongs to the value, not the variable, so the same variable can hold different types.
Data type म्हणजे value कोणत्या प्रकारची आहे (number, text, true/false, object...) हे सांगणारे वर्गीकरण. त्यावरून JS ठरवते की value कशी साठवायची आणि तिच्यावर कोणती operations करता येतील. JS मध्ये type हा value चा असतो, variable चा नाही.

2. Q. What are the Types of Data?

Your Notes: JavaScript Data Types 
                          JavaScript Data Types
                                  │
          ┌───────────────────────┴────────────────────────┐
          ▼                                                ▼
  Primitive Data Types                         Reference (Non-Primitive)
    (Stores Value)                              (Stores Address)

  🔢 Number    → 10, 20.5, -5, Infinity, NaN     📦 Object   → { name: "Vishal", age: 26 }
  📝 String    → "Hello", 'JavaScript', `ES6`    📚 Array    → ["Apple", "Mango", "Banana"]
  ✅ Boolean   → true / false                    📅 Date     → new Date()
  ❓ Undefined → undefined                       ⚙️ Function → function greet() {}
  🚫 Null      → null                            🗺️ Map      → new Map()
  🔢 BigInt    → 12345678901234567890n           🧩 Set      → new Set([1, 2, 3])
  🔑 Symbol    → Symbol("id"), Symbol()
  • What happens: This diagram classifies JavaScript data types into Primitive (stores value directly) and Reference (stores a memory address). Examples of primitives are Number, String, Boolean, Undefined, Null, BigInt, and Symbol. Examples of reference types are Object, Array, Date, Function, Map, and Set.
  • Output: (no output).
Primitive (Stores Value)
  • 🔢 Number → stores numeric values (integers and decimals).
  • 📝 String → stores text (a sequence of characters) enclosed in single quotes, double quotes or backticks (template literals). ✔ added backticks (`ES6`), which your own diagram uses.String फक्त ' ' आणि " " मध्येच नाही, तर backtick (` `) मध्ये सुद्धा लिहिता येते. त्याला template literal म्हणतात.
  • ✅ Boolean → stores logical values (true or false).
  • ❓ Undefined → a variable declared but not assigned a value. It represents the absence of a value, or an uninitialized variable.
  • 🚫 Null → represents an intentionally empty or missing value (it is often used to explicitly indicate that a variable or object property has no assigned value).
  • 🔢 BigInt → stores very large integers beyond Number limits (it represents integers of arbitrary precision). Available since ES2020.
    let bigNumber = 123456789012345678901234567890n; (add n at the end)
  • 🔑 Symbol → stores a unique and immutable identifier.
Reference (Stores Address)
  • 📦 Object → stores data as key-value pairs.
  • 📚 Array → stores an ordered collection of values.
  • 📅 Date → stores and manipulates dates and times.
  • ⚙️ Function → stores reusable blocks of code.
  • 🗺️ Map → stores key-value pairs with keys of any data type.
  • 🧩 Set → stores a collection of unique values.
✔ technically JS has 8 data types: 7 primitives + Object. Array, Date, Function, Map and Set are all special kinds of Object, which is why typeof [] === "object".JS मध्ये खरे 8 data types आहेत: 7 primitive आणि 1 Object. Array, Date, Function, Map, Set हे सगळे Object चेच प्रकार आहेत. म्हणून typeof [] "object" देतो.
Figure 9: The JavaScript data types: 7 primitives plus Object, with all its sub-kinds.
Primitive types (Number, String, Boolean, Undefined, Null, BigInt, Symbol) प्रत्यक्ष value साठवतात. Reference types (Object, Array, Function, Date, Map, Set) value चा memory address (पत्ता) साठवतात.

3. Primitive Data Types

Your Notes:
  • Fundamental data types.
  • Built into JavaScript.
  • Fixed size (the size and type of the value are known). Strings are the exception: they can be any length, but once created they never change. ✔ strings do not have a fixed size; what is fixed is that the value itself cannot change.String ची लांबी कितीही असू शकते, म्हणून "fixed size" पूर्ण बरोबर नाही. पण एकदा बनलेली primitive value बदलत नाही.
  • Immutable (an immutable value cannot be changed after it is created).
  • Stored by value (call by value).
  • Primitives have no methods of their own, but JS temporarily wraps them in an object (String, Number, Boolean) so methods like "hi".toUpperCase() still work (auto-boxing). ✔ "it has no additional method". Primitives can still call methods through their temporary wrapper objects.Primitive कडे स्वतःच्या methods नसतात, पण JS तात्पुरता wrapper object बनवतो. म्हणून "hello".toUpperCase() चालते (auto-boxing).
  • Think of primitive values as small individual items.
  • Changing one doesn't affect the other.
Primitive Value
  100
   │
   ▼
+--------------+
| Variable Box |
+--------------+

! Copying
let a = 10
let b = a
a ───► 10
b ───► 10
Independent copies: changing one doesn't affect the other.
  • What happens: The diagram shows how primitive values are stored and copied by value. When let b = a executes, b gets an independent copy of the value 10. Changing b won't affect a.
  • Output: (no output).
Definition: A primitive is a single, immutable value that is not an object. When copied or passed to a function, the value itself is copied.
let a = 10;
let b = a;   // copy of the value 10
b = 20;
console.log(a, b);           // 10 20 → independent
console.log("hello".toUpperCase()); // "HELLO" (auto-boxing)
  • What happens: b gets a COPY of 10, so changing b doesn't touch a. "hello".toUpperCase() works because JS wraps the primitive in a temporary String object (auto-boxing).
  • Output: 10 20, HELLO.
  • ✅ Primitives are safe to pass around: nobody can change your copy.
Primitive म्हणजे साधी, एकच value. ती copy केल्यावर पूर्ण नवीन copy बनते, त्यामुळे एक बदलली तरी दुसरी बदलत नाही. Primitive value immutable असते, म्हणजे ती आतून बदलता येत नाही.

4. Non-Primitive (Reference) Types

Your Notes:
  • Derived types, built from other values. Some are built in (Object, Array, Date, Map, Set) and some are user-defined (your own objects and classes). ✔ "user defined data type". Array, Date, Map and similar types are built in, not user-defined.Array, Date, Map हे JS मध्ये आधीच असलेले (built-in) आहेत. आपण स्वतः बनवलेले objects/classes हे user-defined आहेत.
  • Dynamic size (the size and type of the data are not fixed).
  • Mutable (a mutable object is something whose content can be changed after it is created).
  • Stored by reference (call by reference; more precisely, call by sharing).
  • Instead of storing the actual data, variables store a reference (address) to where the data lives.
  • Both variables point to the same object. If one changes the object, the change is visible through the other.
Figure 10: Copying a primitive creates a new value; copying a reference shares the same heap object.
Reference type मध्ये variable मध्ये object नसतो, तर object चा पत्ता (address) असतो. person2 = person1 केल्यावर पत्त्याची copy होते, object ची नाही. त्यामुळे दोघेही एकाच object कडे बोट दाखवतात, आणि एकातून बदल केला तर दुसऱ्यातही दिसतो.
Your Notes: easy rule to remember
  • Primitive = stores the value itself 📦
  • Reference (non-primitive) = stores the address of the value 🏠➡️📦

5. Primitive vs Non-Primitive

5.1 Quick Comparison

FeaturePrimitiveNon-Primitive
StoresActual valueMemory reference (address)
SizeFixedDynamic
Mutable❌ No (immutable)✅ Yes (mutable)
CopyIndependent copyShared reference
ExamplesNumber, String, Boolean, Null, Undefined, BigInt, SymbolObject, Array, Date, Function, Map, Set

5.2 Primitive vs Non-Primitive (Summary)

PrimitiveNon-Primitive
Stores valueStores reference (address)
Simple dataComplex data
ImmutableMutable
Compared by valueCompared by reference
Independent copyShared reference
Less memoryMore memory
Faster accessSlightly slower access

5.3 Q. Primitive vs Non-Primitive (Reference) Data Types

FeaturePrimitive Data TypesNon-Primitive (Reference) Data Types
DefinitionStore a single, simple value.Store collections of values or complex data.
Stored inThe value is stored directly in the variable (typically in stack memory).The reference (address) is stored in the variable (stack), while the actual data is stored in heap memory.
MutabilityImmutable: values cannot be changed. Any modification creates a new value.Mutable: object contents can be changed without creating a new object.
ComparisonCompared by value.Compared by reference (memory address).
Copy behaviorCopying creates a new independent value.Copying creates a new reference pointing to the same object.
Memory usageUses less memory.Uses more memory.
PerformanceFaster, because the value is accessed directly.Slightly slower, because JavaScript follows the reference to reach the actual data.
ExamplesNumber, String, Boolean, undefined, null, BigInt, SymbolObject, Array, Function, Date, Map, Set, RegExp
Extra Details: compared by reference 
console.log(10 === 10);         // true  (same value)
console.log({} === {});         // false (two different objects, two addresses)
const a = [1]; const b = a;
console.log(a === b);           // true  (same address)
  • What happens: primitives compare by value; objects compare by address. Two {} are two different objects; a and b point to the same array.
  • Output: true, false, true.
  • ⚠ To compare object contents, compare fields or JSON.stringify (simple cases).
"Stack vs heap" is a mental model. Real engines (V8) can store long strings on the heap too, but the behavior (copy by value vs shared reference) is exactly as described.
Primitive ची तुलना value ने होते (10 === 10 true). Object ची तुलना पत्त्याने होते, म्हणून दिसायला सारखे असले तरी दोन वेगळे objects {} === {} false देतात.

6. Call by Value & Call by Reference

Your Notes: Q. What is call by reference and call by value?
  • JavaScript always passes arguments by value,
  • but for objects, arrays and functions, the value being copied is the reference (memory address), not the object itself.
  • Therefore the most accurate term is call by sharing or call by value of reference, although many people informally call it call by reference.

6.1 Call by Value

Your Notes:
  • Call by value is a parameter-passing mechanism in which a copy of the original value is passed to the function.
  • The function works only with this copied value. Any changes made inside the function do not affect the original variable.
  • A copy of the variable's value is passed to the function. Changing the copied value does not change the original variable.
  • Definition:
    • A copy of the original value is passed to the function.
    • The original variable and the function parameter become two completely separate values.
    • If the function changes the parameter, the original variable is NOT affected.
Call by Value म्हणजे मूळ (original) value ची एक copy function ला दिली जाते. त्यामुळे function मध्ये केलेले बदल फक्त त्या copy वर होतात, मूळ variable वर नाही.
function changeValue(num) {
  num = 100;
}
let x = 10;
changeValue(x);
console.log(x);   // 10   ✔ removed stray backticks (`) that broke the code
  • What happens: num receives a copy of 10; changing num doesn't change x.
  • Output: 10.
तुमच्या code मध्ये } आणि console.log(x) च्या आसपास चुकून backticks (`) होते, त्यामुळे code चालला नसता. ते काढले. उत्तर 10 येते.

6.2 Call by Reference (Reference Value)

Your Notes:
  • In JavaScript, when an object, array or function is passed as an argument, the reference (memory address) is copied, not the actual object.
  • Both the original variable and the function parameter refer to the same object in memory, so modifying its properties affects the original object.
  • Technically, JavaScript is not true call by reference. It copies the reference value, which is why this behavior is more accurately called call by sharing.
  • Definition: instead of copying the entire object, JavaScript copies the memory address (reference).
    • Both variables point to the same object.
    • Changing object properties affects everyone using that object.
  • A copy of the reference (memory address) is passed to the function. Both variables point to the same object, so changing the object's contents affects the original object.
Object किंवा Array function ला दिल्यावर object ची copy जात नाही, तर त्याच्या memory address (reference) ची copy जाते. त्यामुळे दोन्ही variables एकाच object कडे निर्देश करतात. म्हणून object च्या properties मध्ये केलेले बदल original object मध्येही दिसतात.
function changePerson(person) {
  person.name = "Rahul";
}
let user = { name: "Vishal" };
changePerson(user);
console.log(user.name);   // "Rahul"
  • What happens: person receives a copy of the ADDRESS, so changing person.name changes the same object user points to.
  • Output: Rahul.
  • ⚠ Functions can mutate objects you pass in; copy first ({...obj}) if that's not wanted.
Figure 11: Call by value copies the value; call by sharing copies the address, so both names reach one object.
Extra Details: proof that JS is NOT true call by reference Re-assigning the parameter does not change the original, because only the local copy of the address changes: 
function reassign(obj) {
  obj = { name: "New" };   // obj now points to a NEW object
}
let u = { name: "Vishal" };
reassign(u);
console.log(u.name);       // "Vishal" → unchanged!
  • What happens: obj = {…} only makes the LOCAL obj point to a new object; u still points to the old one.
  • Output: Vishal.
  • ✅ Interview point: JS is always pass-by-value; for objects the value is a reference.
In true call by reference (like C++ &), this would print "New".
Parameter ला पूर्ण नवीन object दिला (obj = {...}) तर original बदलत नाही, कारण फक्त local पत्ता बदलतो. पण obj.name बदलल्यास original बदलते. म्हणूनच JS ला "call by sharing" म्हणतात, खरे "call by reference" नाही.

6.3 Comparison

Call by ValueCall by Reference (Reference Value)
Primitive data typesNon-primitive data types
Copies the actual valueCopies the reference (address)
Changes don't affect the originalProperty changes affect the original
Independent variablesShared object
Examples: Number, String, BooleanExamples: Object, Array, Function

Call by Value vs Call by Reference

FeatureCall by ValueCall by Reference (Reference Value)
DefinitionA copy of the actual value is passed to the function.A copy of the reference (memory address) is passed to the function.
Original valueRemains unchanged when the parameter is modified inside the function.Can change if the object's properties are modified inside the function.
Memory allocationA new independent copy of the value is created.Both variables point to the same object in memory.
Data typesPrimitive data typesNon-primitive (reference) data types
Copy behaviorIndependent copyShared reference
ComparisonCompared by valueCompared by reference
ExamplesNumber, String, Boolean, null, undefined, BigInt, SymbolObject, Array, Function, Date, Map, Set

6.4 Examples & Interview Answer

Your Notes (your code):
Example 1: call by value (primitive)
// EX: call by value
function updateValue(num) {
  num = 100;
  console.log("Inside Function:", num); // 100
}
let number = 10;
updateValue(number);
console.log("Outside Function:", number); // 10
// Explanation:
// 'number' is a primitive. A copy of 10 is passed to 'updateValue'.
// Changing the parameter 'num' does not modify 'number' in the calling scope.
  • What happens: a copy of 10 goes into the function.
  • Output: Inside Function: 100, Outside Function: 10.
Example 2: "call by reference" (object)
// EX: call by reference
function updateObject(obj) {
  obj.name = "Rahul";
}
let person = { name: "Vishal" };
updateObject(person);
console.log(person.name); // "Rahul"
// Explanation:
// 'person' is an object. The function receives a copy of its memory reference.
// Both 'obj' and 'person' point to the same object in the heap.
// Modifying 'obj.name' mutates the heap object, affecting the original reference.
  • What happens: the function gets a copy of the reference, so mutating the object is visible outside.
  • Output: Rahul.
  • ⚠ Strictly it is "pass by sharing": re-assigning obj inside wouldn't affect person (see Example 8 above).
Interview perspective answer:
  • Call by value: a copy of the original value is passed to the function. Any changes made to the parameter do not affect the original variable.
  • Call by reference (JavaScript behavior): JavaScript does not use true call by reference. When objects, arrays or functions are passed to a function, JavaScript copies the reference (memory address). Both variables refer to the same object, so changes to the object's properties are visible outside the function. This behavior is more accurately called call by sharing or call by value of reference.

7. typeof Operator

Your Notes: Def: the typeof operator returns a string indicating the data type of the operand. 
// 1.
let str = "vishal";
console.log(typeof str);     // "string"

// 2.
const pi = 3.14;
console.log(typeof pi);      // "number"

// 3.
const obj = ['apple', 'mango', 'banana'];
console.log(typeof obj);     // "object" (arrays are objects!)

// 4.
const today = new Date();
console.log(today);          // e.g. 2026-10-01T10:30:00.000Z (current date & time)
console.log(typeof today);   // "object"
  • What happens: typeof for a string, a number, an array and a Date. Arrays and Dates are objects.
  • Output: "string", "number", "object", the current date, "object".
  • ⚠ typeof can't tell arrays apart; use Array.isArray.
✔ output comments added. Note that typeof cannot tell an array from an object; use Array.isArray(obj) → true.तुमच्या examples मध्ये output नव्हते, ते जोडले. typeof array साठी सुद्धा "object" देतो, म्हणून array तपासायला Array.isArray() वापरा.
Extra Details: complete typeof table
ValuetypeofValuetypeof
10, NaN, Infinity"number"null"object" ⚠ (bug)
"hi""string"{}, [], new Date()"object"

undefined / undeclared"undefined"Symbol()"symbol"
10n"bigint"class A {}"function"
Array.isArray([])               // true  → correct array check
