  • What happens: the correct checks: Array.isArray for arrays, === null for null; typeof always returns a string, so typeof typeof 1 is "string".
  • Output: true, (check), "string".
typeof कोणत्याही value चा type string मध्ये सांगतो. लक्षात ठेवा: typeof null = "object" (जुना bug), typeof [] = "object", typeof function = "function", typeof NaN = "number".

8. Division by Zero & Arithmetic Edge Cases

Your Notes: A. Non-zero numbers divided by zero
  • Dividing a positive number by 0 yields Infinity.
  • Dividing a negative number by 0 yields -Infinity.
B. Zero divided by non-zero numbers
  • Dividing 0 by a positive number yields 0.
  • Dividing 0 by a negative number yields -0.
C. Zero divided by zero (0 / 0)
  • Yields NaN (Not a Number).
  • Mathematical background: when 0 is divided by 0, JavaScript returns NaN (Not a Number).
  • 0 ÷ 0 is an indeterminate mathematical expression because there is no single unique answer.
Q1. Non-zero numbers divided by zero
// Q1. Non-zero numbers divided by zero
let num = 7;
console.log(num / 0);  // Infinity
// कोणत्याही शून्य नसलेल्या (non-zero) संख्येला 0 ने divide केल्यास → Infinity
console.log(-7 / 0);   // -Infinity
// संख्या नकारात्मक (negative) असेल तर → -Infinity
  • What happens: dividing a non-zero number by 0 gives Infinity (or -Infinity), not an error.
  • Output: Infinity, -Infinity.
  • ⚠ Check the divisor yourself if Infinity is not acceptable.
Q2. Zero divided by non-zero numbers
// Q2. Zero divided by non-zero numbers
console.log(0 / 7);    // 0
// कोणत्याही शून्य नसलेल्या (non-zero) संख्येने 0 ला भागले, तरी उत्तर नेहमी 0 येते.
console.log(0 / -8);   // -0
// पण JavaScript IEEE 754 Floating-Point Standard वापरते, ज्यामध्ये +0 आणि -0 असे दोन
// प्रकारचे शून्य असतात. 0 ला नकारात्मक (negative) संख्येने भागले, तर JavaScript -0 दाखवते.
  • What happens: 0 divided by a number is 0; by a negative number it is -0 (JS has +0 and -0).
  • Output: 0, -0.
  • ⚠ -0 === 0 is true; use Object.is(x, -0) to detect it.
Q3. Zero divided by zero (0 / 0)
// Q3. Zero divided by zero (0 / 0)
console.log(0 / 0);    // NaN
// शून्याला शून्याने भागले (0 / 0) तर उत्तर NaN येते.
// 0 / 0 चे उत्तर NaN का येते?
// NaN (Not a Number) म्हणजे वैध संख्यात्मक उत्तर मिळू शकले नाही.
  • What happens: 0 / 0 has no meaningful answer, so the result is NaN.
  • Output: NaN.
Figure 12: Division edge cases. JS never throws an error when dividing by zero.
Extra Details: dividing by zero never throws an error in JS. -0 and 0 look equal (-0 === 0 → true), but Object.is(-0, 0) → false and 1 / -0 → -Infinity.

9. Type Conversion: String ↔ Number

Your Notes: 1. Convert a string to a number. There are three main ways:
  1. Unary + operator: implicitly coerces the value.
  2. Number() function: explicit conversion (called without new). ✔ "Number() Constructor: explicit wrapper conversion". Number("5") is used as a function and returns a primitive; new Number("5") would create a wrapper object, which should be avoided.Number("5") हे function म्हणून वापरले की primitive number मिळतो. new Number("5") वापरल्यास object बनतो, जो वापरू नये.
  3. parseInt() / parseFloat(): parse characters left to right until they hit a non-numeric character.
2. Number to string. The easiest ways to convert a number to a string are:
  1. concatenating it with an empty string "", or
  2. calling String() / toString().
Q1. Convert a String → Number
// ✔ heading said "number into string"

// ─── ✅ Successful conversions ─────────────────────────
let numberStr = "10";

console.log(typeof +numberStr);           // → "number"   (unary +)
console.log(typeof parseInt(numberStr));  // → "number"   (parseInt)
console.log(typeof Number(numberStr));    // → "number"   (Number)


// ─── ❌ Unsuccessful conversions ───────────────────────
let nameStr = "vishal";

console.log(+nameStr);                    // → NaN
console.log(parseInt(nameStr));           // → NaN
console.log(Number(nameStr));             // → NaN
// ✔ was "NaNa"
  • What happens: unary +, parseInt and Number all turn "10" into a number; text that isn't a number gives NaN.
  • Output: number ×3, then NaN ×3.
  • ✅ Number() is strict (whole string must be numeric); parseInt reads leading digits.
Q2. Convert a Number → String
let digit = 100;

console.log(typeof (digit + ""));         // → "string"   (concat with "")
console.log(typeof String(digit));        // → "string"   (String())
  • What happens: adding "" or calling String() converts a number to text.
  • Output: "string", "string".
Q3. Tricky Questions
console.log("null converted into number", +null);           // → 0
console.log("undefined converted into number", +undefined); // → NaN
  • What happens: null converts to 0, undefined to NaN.
  • Output: 0, NaN.
  • ⚠ Classic trap: null + 1 = 1 but undefined + 1 = NaN.
Input+xNumber(x)parseInt(x)
"10"101010
"vishal"NaNNaNNaN
null00NaN
undefinedNaNNaNNaN
पहिल्या example चे heading "number into string" होते, पण code string → number करतो, म्हणून heading बदलले. "NaNa" ही typo होती, बरोबर output NaN आहे.
Extra Details: 
parseInt("12.5px")   // 12    (integer only, stops at ".")
parseFloat("12.5px") // 12.5
Number("12.5px")     // NaN   (whole string must be valid)
(100).toString(2)    // "1100100" (to binary)
String(null)         // "null" ← null.toString() would throw TypeError
  • What happens: parseInt stops at the first non-digit (and ignores decimals), parseFloat keeps decimals, Number rejects any junk. toString(2) gives binary. String(null) is safe where null.toString() throws.
  • Output: 12, 12.5, NaN, "1100100", "null".
String → Number साठी +value, Number() आणि parseInt()/parseFloat() वापरतात. parseInt सुरुवातीचे अंक वाचतो आणि पहिल्या अक्षरावर थांबतो. Number() ला पूर्ण string valid लागते. Number → String साठी value + "" किंवा String() वापरतात.

10. Deep Dive: NaN (Not a Number)

10.1 Q. What is NaN?

Your Notes:
  • NaN stands for Not-a-Number.
  • NaN (Not-a-Number) is a special numeric value in JavaScript that indicates the result of an invalid mathematical operation or a failed numeric conversion. It belongs to the number data type.
  • Definition: NaN represents a value that cannot be represented as a valid number, usually because an invalid mathematical operation or numeric conversion was attempted.
  • It is a special value in JavaScript that represents the result of an invalid or undefined mathematical operation.
  • Scope: it is a property of the global object (accessible in the global scope).
  • NaN does not have a "default" or "initial" value. It is simply a predefined global constant.
  • Type: typeof NaN returns "number".
  • The isNaN() function checks whether a value is NaN after converting it to a number. It returns true if the resulting value is NaN; otherwise it returns false.
Q. What is NaN? (short answer)
  • NaN stands for Not-a-Number.
  • It is a special numeric value in JavaScript that represents the result of an invalid mathematical operation or a failed numeric conversion.
  • It belongs to the number data type.
  • typeof NaN returns "number".
  • NaN is a property of the global object.
  • Number.isNaN() checks whether a value is the special NaN value.
  • The global isNaN() first converts the value to a number and then checks whether the result is NaN.

10.2 Q. Why do we need NaN?

Your Notes:
  • Imagine JavaScript is asked to perform a mathematical operation, but the result is impossible.
  • Example: "Hello" - 10 (can you subtract 10 from "Hello"?)
  • It is not possible, so instead of crashing, JavaScript returns NaN.
NaN म्हणजे "हे number नाही", पण गंमत म्हणजे त्याचा type "number" आहे. चुकीचे math (उदा. "Hello" - 10) केल्यावर program crash होण्याऐवजी JS NaN देतो.

10.3 Q. What is Number.isNaN() (Recommended)?

Your Notes:
  • It checks whether a value is actually the special NaN value.
console.log(Number.isNaN(NaN));      // true
console.log(Number.isNaN(10));       // false
console.log(Number.isNaN("Hello"));  // false
  • What happens: Number.isNaN is true only for the real NaN value; it does not convert.
  • Output: true, false, false.
  • ✅ The reliable NaN check.
  • In the example above, the output is false, even though you might think it should return true because "Hello" is not a number. Here's why it returns false.
  • Q. What is "Hello"? The type of "Hello" is string, so "Hello" is a string, not the special NaN value.
  • Q. What does Number.isNaN() check?
    • Number.isNaN() does not ask: "Is this value a number?"
    • Instead it asks: "Is this value exactly the special NaN value?"
    • Since "Hello" is a string, the answer is no.
    • Therefore the code below returns false, because "Hello" is not the actual NaN value.
Example 1
console.log(Number.isNaN("Hello"));  // false
  • What happens: "Hello" is a string, not the NaN value.
  • Output: false.
Q. Check with the actual NaN value
// Q. Check with the actual NaN value
console.log(Number.isNaN(NaN));      // true, because NaN is the actual NaN value
  • What happens: the actual NaN value.
  • Output: true.
Q. Then why does isNaN("Hello") return true?
// Q. Then why does isNaN("Hello") return true?
console.log(isNaN("Hello"));         // true
// It returns true because isNaN() first converts the value to a number.
// For isNaN("Hello"), JS internally does Number("Hello"), which returns NaN.
  • What happens: the old global isNaN first converts "Hello" to a number (NaN) and then checks.
  • Output: true.
  • ⚠ So isNaN("Hello") is true even though it isn't NaN; prefer Number.isNaN.
Interview answer:
  • Number.isNaN("Hello") returns false because Number.isNaN() does not perform type conversion.
  • It only returns true if the value is exactly the special NaN value.
  • Since "Hello" is a string and not NaN, the result is false.
  • In contrast, the global isNaN() first converts "Hello" to a number, which results in NaN, so isNaN("Hello") returns true.
Example 1
// 1.
var name1 = "vishal";
var num2 = 200;
console.log("check it is number or not :", isNaN(name1), isNaN(num2)); // true false
  • What happens: isNaN converts: "vishal" → NaN → true; 200 → false.
  • Output: true false.
2. Because NaN is not equal to any value, you must check for it using isNaN() or Number.is
// 2. Because NaN is not equal to any value, you must check for it using isNaN() or Number.isNaN().
let x = "vishal";
console.log(isNaN(x));   // true (not a number)
let sum = 90;
console.log(isNaN(sum)); // false (it is a valid number)
  • What happens: same checks with other values.
  • Output: true, false.
Figure 13: The global isNaN() converts first; Number.isNaN() checks the exact value without converting.
isNaN() आधी value ला number मध्ये बदलतो, म्हणून "Hello" साठी true देतो. Number.isNaN() काहीही बदलत नाही आणि फक्त "ही value खरोखर NaN आहे का?" एवढेच विचारतो, म्हणून "Hello" साठी false देतो. नेहमी Number.isNaN() वापरा.

10.4 Q. Mathematical Operations with NaN

Your Notes:
  • With strings (using +): NaN is coerced to the string "NaN" and concatenated.
  • With numbers: any mathematical operation involving NaN results in NaN.
var word = "vishal";
var word1 = NaN;
console.log(word + word1); // "vishalNaN" (concatenation)

var no1 = 30;
var no2 = NaN;
console.log(no1 + no2); // NaN
console.log(no1 - no2); // NaN
  • What happens: with a string, + concatenates ("vishalNaN"); in math, NaN spreads into every result.
  • Output: vishalNaN, NaN, NaN.
NOTE: performing any arithmetic operation (+, -, *, /, %) between a number and NaN returns NaN.

10.5 Q. Why is NaN not equal to itself?

Your Notes:
  • According to the IEEE 754 standard, NaN is never equal to any value, including itself.
  • The self-equality trap (NaN === NaN is false): NaN is the only value in JavaScript that is not equal to itself.
console.log(NaN == NaN);  // false
console.log(NaN === NaN); // false
  • What happens: NaN is the only value not equal to itself.
  • Output: false, false.
  • ⚠ Never write x === NaN; it is always false.
  • Why? Consider parsing two invalid inputs. Both return NaN, but their origins are completely different, so they do not represent the same value. This is the reasoning behind the IEEE 754 rule, and JS applies it to every NaN. ✔ the "different origins" idea is only the intuition. The actual rule is IEEE 754, so even the same NaN compared with itself is false (let n = NaN; n === n → false)."वेगवेगळ्या ठिकाणाहून आले" हे फक्त समजण्यासाठी कारण आहे. खरे कारण IEEE 754 चा नियम आहे. त्यामुळे एकच NaN स्वतःशी तुलना केला तरी false येतो.
Example 1
let val1 = parseInt("abc"); // NaN
let val2 = parseInt("xyz"); // NaN
console.log(val1 === val2); // false
  • What happens: two NaN results are still not equal.
  • Output: false.
Q. How to check for NaN?
// Q. How to check for NaN?
console.log(Number.isNaN(NaN)); // true
console.log(Number.isNaN(10));  // false
  • What happens: Number.isNaN is the correct way to test.
  • Output: true, false.
NaN stands for Not-a-Number. It is a special numeric value that represents the result of an invalid mathematical operation or a failed numeric conversion.
Extra Details: all the ways to detect NaN 
Number.isNaN(v)    // ✅ best
Object.is(v, NaN)  // ✅
v !== v            // ✅ true only for NaN (self-inequality trick)
isNaN(v)           // ⚠ converts first
[NaN].includes(NaN) // true  (includes uses SameValueZero)
[NaN].indexOf(NaN)  // -1    (indexOf uses ===)
  • What happens: all the ways to detect NaN: Number.isNaN, Object.is, the v !== v trick; isNaN converts first. includes finds NaN but indexOf can't.
  • Output: see the comments.
  • ⚠ [NaN].indexOf(NaN) is -1: a favourite output question.

11. null & undefined

Your Notes: A. The null value
  • Represents the intentional absence of any object value.
  • The programmer explicitly assigns null.
  • typeof null returns "object".
  • This is a historic, unfixed bug in JavaScript. Objects were marked with type tag 0.
  • Since null was represented as a null pointer (all zeros), the engine read it as type tag 0 and returned "object".
  • Meaning: "I intentionally want this variable to have no value."
B. The undefined value
  • Represents an unassigned default state (a variable declared but not assigned a value).
  • Automatically initialized by the JS engine.
  • typeof undefined returns "undefined".
  • Meaning: "Value not assigned yet."
  • JavaScript automatically gives a variable the value undefined if you declare it but don't assign anything.
console.log(+null);               // 0
console.log(Number(null));        // 0
console.log(parseInt(null));      // NaN (converts null to "null" first, fails on 'n')
console.log("" + null);           // "null" (string conversion)
console.log(+undefined);          // NaN
console.log(Number(undefined));   // NaN
console.log(parseInt(undefined)); // NaN
  • What happens: null → 0 for + and Number(), but parseInt reads it as the text "null" → NaN. undefined → NaN everywhere.
  • Output: 0, 0, NaN, "null", NaN, NaN, NaN.

11.1 Q. null vs undefined (Detailed Comparison)

Featurenullundefined
DefinitionA value intentionally assigned by the programmer to indicate "no value" or an empty reference.A value automatically assigned by JavaScript when a variable is declared but not initialized.
Meaning"No value" / "empty value" / "nothing, intentionally"."Value has not been assigned yet."
Assigned byProgrammer (explicitly)JavaScript engine
TypePrimitive data typePrimitive data type
typeof result"object" (historical JavaScript bug)"undefined"
Numeric conversionConverts to 0Converts to NaN
Loose equality (==)null == undefined → trueundefined == null → true
Strict equality (===)null === undefined → falseundefined === null → false
Examplelet user = null;let user;
Figure 14: null is an intentional empty value; undefined means no value has been assigned yet.
null म्हणजे programmer ने मुद्दाम "रिकामे" ठेवलेले (value नाही). undefined म्हणजे JS ने स्वतः दिलेले "अजून value दिलेली नाही". typeof null = "object" हा JS चा जुना bug आहे. null → 0 आणि undefined → NaN होतो.
Extra Details: where undefined appears automatically 
let a;                       // declared, not assigned → undefined
function f() {}  f();        // no return → undefined
function g(p) { return p; }  g(); // missing argument → undefined
({}).missing                 // missing property → undefined
[1,2][10]                    // out-of-range index → undefined
  • What happens: the five common ways to get undefined: not assigned, no return, missing argument, missing property, out-of-range index.
  • Output: undefined in every case.
Correct null check: value === null. To check "null or undefined": value == null or value ?? "default".

12. Deep Dive: Infinity

Your Notes:
  • Represents a value greater than any other number (and -Infinity is smaller than any other number).
  • typeof Infinity returns "number".
console.log(Infinity / Infinity); // NaN
console.log(Infinity - Infinity); // NaN
console.log(Infinity + Infinity); // Infinity
console.log(Infinity % Infinity); // NaN
  • What happens: Infinity math: some operations are undefined mathematically → NaN.
  • Output: NaN, NaN, Infinity, NaN.
Extra Details: 
Number.MAX_VALUE * 2      // Infinity (overflow)
Infinity * 0              // NaN
isFinite("12")            // true  (converts)
Number.isFinite("12")     // false (no conversion) ✅
Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER   // 9007199254740991 → above this use BigInt
  • What happens: too big → Infinity; Infinity × 0 → NaN; isFinite converts "12" first, Number.isFinite does not; above MAX_SAFE_INTEGER integers lose precision.
  • Output: Infinity, NaN, true, false, 9007199254740991.
  • ✅ Use BigInt (123n) for very large integers.
Infinity म्हणजे कोणत्याही संख्येपेक्षा मोठी value, आणि तिचा type number आहे. Infinity - Infinity आणि Infinity / Infinity चे उत्तर ठरवता येत नाही, म्हणून NaN येते.

13. Truthy and Falsy Values

Your Notes: Definition: JavaScript automatically converts values into either true or false when they are used in Boolean contexts such as:
  • if
  • while
  • for
  • logical operators (&&, ||, !)
  • the ternary operator (? :)
This process is called Boolean coercion. 
// Falsy values
console.log(Boolean(false));      // false
console.log(Boolean(0));          // false
console.log(Boolean(-0));         // false
console.log(Boolean(0n));         // false
console.log(Boolean(""));         // false
console.log(Boolean(null));       // false
console.log(Boolean(undefined));  // false
console.log(Boolean(NaN));        // false

// Truthy values
// Every value other than the 8 falsy values is truthy.
console.log(Boolean(true));       // true
console.log(Boolean(10));         // true
console.log(Boolean(-5));         // true
console.log(Boolean("Hello"));    // true
console.log(Boolean("0"));        // true
console.log(Boolean("false"));    // true
console.log(Boolean(" "));        // true
console.log(Boolean([]));         // true
console.log(Boolean({}));         // true
  • What happens: Boolean(x) shows how a value behaves in an if. Exactly 8 values are falsy; everything else (even "0", "false", " ", [], {}) is truthy.
  • Output: 8 × false, then 9 × true.
  • ✅ Memorise the 8 falsy values: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN.
Q2: Is an empty object truthy or falsy?
  • Empty objects are truthy.
  • Important interview note: [] → truthy, {} → truthy.
  • Many interview questions intentionally test this concept.
  • Example:
if ({}) {
  console.log("Executed");   // "Executed"
}
  • What happens: an empty object is truthy, so the if runs.
  • Output: Executed.
  • ⚠ Check emptiness with Object.keys(obj).length.
if, while, for, &&, ||, !, ?: मध्ये JS value ला true/false मध्ये बदलते. फक्त 8 values falsy आहेत: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN. बाकी सगळे truthy आहेत, अगदी [], {}, "0" आणि "false" सुद्धा. (Chapter 3 मधील Figure 18 पहा.)

14. Mutability vs Immutability

Your Notes: Definition: JavaScript values can be divided into:
  1. Mutable
  2. Immutable
Understanding this concept is important because it explains why objects behave differently from primitive values.

14.1 Mutable Values (Non-Primitive Data Types)

Your Notes:
  • Mutable means the original value can be modified after creation.
  • Non-primitive values are mutable. These include: Object, Array, Function.
  • They are stored in heap memory.
  • Variables contain a reference (memory address) pointing to the heap object.
// Example 1
let arr = [1, 2, 3];
arr.push(4);
console.log(arr);   // [1, 2, 3, 4]

// Example 2
// let person = { name: "Vishal", age: 25 };
// person.age = 26;
// console.log(person);   // { name: "Vishal", age: 26 }
  • What happens: arrays (and objects) are mutable: push changes the same array.
  • Output: [1, 2, 3, 4].
✔ Note: Example 2 is correctly commented out. In the same file, person is already declared with let (section 6.4), so declaring it again would cause "SyntaxError: Identifier 'person' has already been declared". Use a different name (e.g. person3) to run it.हाच file मध्ये person आधीच let ने declare आहे, म्हणून पुन्हा let person लिहिल्यास SyntaxError येईल. चालवायचे असेल तर वेगळे नाव वापरा. Explanation: the variable still points to the same object in memory. Only the object's internal data changes. The reference remains the same; the object's content changes. 
// Reference example
let obj1 = { city: "Pune" };
let obj2 = obj1;
obj2.city = "Mumbai";
console.log(obj1.city); // Mumbai
console.log(obj2.city); // Mumbai
  • What happens: obj2 = obj1 copies the reference, so both names point to one object.
  • Output: Mumbai, Mumbai.
  • ⚠ Use { ...obj1 } or structuredClone(obj1) for a real copy.
Explanation: obj1 and obj2 point to the same object in heap memory. Changing the object through one reference is visible through the other. ✔ "changing one reference affects the other". The reference itself is not changed; the shared object is changed.reference (पत्ता) बदलत नाही, तर दोघांचा एकच object बदलतो. म्हणून obj2 मधून केलेला बदल obj1 मध्येही दिसतो.

14.2 Immutable Values (Primitive Data Types)

Your Notes:
  • Immutable means the original value cannot be changed.
  • Primitive values are immutable. These include: String, Number, Boolean, BigInt, Symbol, Undefined, Null.
  • They are stored directly in stack memory (conceptually).
// Example 1
let original = "Hello";
let copy = original;
original = original + " World";
console.log(original); // Hello World
console.log(copy);     // Hello
  • What happens: strings are immutable: original + " World" creates a new string; copy keeps the old one.
  • Output: Hello World, Hello.
Explanation: the string "Hello" is never modified. Instead, JavaScript creates a completely new string "Hello World" and assigns it to original. The variable copy still holds the old value. 
// Example 2
// let num1 = 10;
// let num2 = num1;
// num1 = 20;
// console.log(num1); // 20
// console.log(num2); // 10
  • What happens: (commented out) numbers are copied by value, so num2 keeps 10.
  • Output: would print 20, 10.
✔ Note: keep Example 2 commented out, or rename it. num2 is already declared with var in section 10.3, so let num2 would cause a SyntaxError.num2 आधीच var ने declare आहे, म्हणून let num2 लिहिल्यास SyntaxError येईल. Explanation: changing num1 creates a new value. num2 remains unchanged because primitive values are copied by value.
Figure 15: Immutable values are replaced with new values; mutable objects are edited in place.
Extra Details: string immutability proof 
let s = "Hello";
s[0] = "J";          // silently ignored (TypeError in strict mode)
console.log(s);      // "Hello"
s.toUpperCase();     // returns a NEW string "HELLO"; s is still "Hello"
  • What happens: you can't change one character of a string; s[0] = "J" is ignored. Methods return new strings.
  • Output: Hello.
  • ⚠ To change a character build a new string: "J" + s.slice(1).
Immutable (primitive) value बदलता येत नाही. "बदल" केल्यासारखे वाटले तरी JS पूर्ण नवीन value बनवतो. Mutable (object/array) मध्ये तोच object आतून बदलतो, म्हणून त्याच object कडे पाहणाऱ्या सर्व variables ना बदल दिसतो.

15. Memory Representation

Your Notes: 
# Primitive (Immutable)
Stack
-----
num = 10
num = 20
A new value is created.
Old value is untouched.
-----------------------------
# Non-Primitive (Mutable)
Stack                  Heap
-----                  --------------------
obj  ----------->      { name: "John" }
! Changing:
obj.name = "David"
Heap becomes:
{ name: "David" }
Reference remains same.
Object data changes.
  • What happens: Primitives are stored in the stack and are immutable; changing a primitive creates a new value. Objects are stored in the heap with a reference in the stack; changing an object modifies the data in the heap while the reference stays the same.
  • Output: (no output).
Quick Comparison
PropertyPrimitiveNon-Primitive
Mutable?NoYes
Immutable?YesNo
Stored inStackHeap
Copied byValueReference
Can modify original?NoYes
ExamplesString, NumberObject, Array
Q1: Why doesn't changing one string affect another? Strings are immutable. Changing a string creates a brand-new string instead of modifying the original.
Q2: Why does changing one object affect another variable? Because both variables store the same object reference. They point to the same object in heap memory.
Q3: Which data types are mutable? Object, Array, Function.
Q4: Which data types are immutable? String, Number, Boolean, Null, Undefined, Symbol, BigInt.

NOTE: for objects, arrays and functions:
  • The actual object/value is stored in heap memory.
  • The reference (memory address) to that object is stored in stack memory (as the variable's value).
Stack Memory                    Heap Memory
------------                   ------------------
user  ───────────────┐          { name: "Vishal" }
                     │
                     └──────────► Object
  • What happens: The variable user is stored in the stack, holding a memory address (reference) that points to the actual object { name: "Vishal" } stored in the heap.
  • Output: (no output).
  • user (the variable) is stored in the stack.
  • The stack stores the reference (memory address).
  • The actual object { name: "Vishal" } is stored in the heap.
Primitive values (Number, String, Boolean, null, undefined, Symbol, BigInt) are stored directly as the variable's value. Conceptually: 
let a = 10;
let b = a;
b = 20;
Stack
------
a = 10
b = 20
  • What happens: primitives: b = a copies 10; then b gets 20 without affecting a.
  • Output: (no output).
Stack मध्ये variables आणि primitive values असतात. Object/array चा खरा data heap मध्ये असतो आणि stack मध्ये फक्त त्याचा पत्ता असतो. (Chapter 1 मधील Figure 7 पहा.)

16. Interview Questions (Detailed)

Q1. How many data types does JavaScript have?
  • 8: seven primitives (Number, String, Boolean, Undefined, Null, BigInt, Symbol) plus Object. Arrays, functions, dates, maps and sets are all objects.
Q2. Is JavaScript pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?
  • It is always pass-by-value. For objects, the value that is passed is a reference, which is called call by sharing. Mutating the object's properties inside a function is visible outside, but reassigning the parameter is not.
Q3. Why does typeof null return "object"?
  • It is a bug from the first version of JavaScript. Values carried a type tag, and objects used tag 0. null was the null pointer (all zeros), so it read as tag 0, "object". Fixing it would break old websites, so it was never fixed.
Q4. Difference between null and undefined?
  • undefined means "not assigned yet" and is set automatically by JS. null means "intentionally empty" and is set by the programmer. typeof: "undefined" vs "object". Number(): NaN vs 0. null == undefined is true, but === is false.
Q5. How do you check if a value is an array?
  • Array.isArray(value). typeof returns "object" for arrays, so it cannot distinguish them.
Q6. How do you copy an object without sharing the reference?
const a = { x: 1, inner: { y: 2 } };
const shallow = { ...a };             // new top level, inner still shared
const deep = structuredClone(a);      // fully independent copy
shallow.inner.y = 99;  console.log(a.inner.y); // 99 (shared!)
deep.inner.y = 5;      console.log(a.inner.y); // 99 (unchanged)
  • What happens: spread copies only the top level (inner object is shared); structuredClone copies every level.
  • Output: 99, 99.
  • ✅ Use structuredClone for nested data.
Q7. What is auto-boxing?
  • When you call a method on a primitive ("hi".length), JS temporarily wraps it in a wrapper object (String, Number, Boolean), calls the method, and throws the wrapper away. The primitive itself never changes.
Q8. Why use BigInt? Can you mix BigInt and Number?
  • Number is safe only up to 2^53 − 1 (Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER), and beyond that precision is lost. BigInt stores integers of any size. You cannot mix them directly: 10n + 1 throws a TypeError, so convert explicitly: 10n + BigInt(1).
Q9. What is Symbol used for?
  • It creates a unique identifier, mostly used for object property keys that won't clash with other keys: Symbol("id") === Symbol("id") → false.
Q10. Output-based questions
console.log(typeof NaN);            // "number"
console.log(typeof null);           // "object"
console.log(typeof []);             // "object"
console.log(typeof function(){});   // "function"
console.log(typeof typeof 1);       // "string"
console.log(null == 0);             // false
console.log(null + 1);              // 1
console.log(undefined + 1);         // NaN
console.log(0 / 0, 1 / 0, -1 / 0);  // NaN Infinity -Infinity
console.log(NaN === NaN);           // false
console.log([] === []);             // false
console.log(Number.isNaN("abc"), isNaN("abc")); // false true
console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3);     // false (0.30000000000000004, floating point)
  • What happens: a set of typeof and coercion traps.
  • Output: number, object, object, function, string, false, 1, NaN, NaN Infinity -Infinity, false, false, false true, false.
  • ✅ Great last-minute revision list.

1. Type Conversion (Type Coercion) in JavaScript

Your Notes:
  • Def: Type Coercion is the automatic or implicit conversion of values from one data type to another (e.g. converting a string to a number, or a boolean to a string) when performing operations.
  • Type Conversion means converting a value from one data type to another,
  • e.g. converting a string to a number.
  • Since JavaScript is a dynamically typed language, it performs type coercion automatically at runtime when operations are applied to values of mismatched types.
Definition: Type Conversion is the general term for changing a value from one data type to another. It is either implicit (done automatically by JS, called Type Coercion) or explicit (done manually by the programmer, also called Type Casting).
Type Conversion म्हणजे एका data type ची value दुसऱ्या data type मध्ये बदलणे (उदा. "5" string → 5 number). JS स्वतः आपोआप बदलते तेव्हा त्याला Type Coercion (implicit) म्हणतात. आपण Number(), String() सारख्या functions ने स्वतः बदलतो तेव्हा त्याला Explicit Conversion / Type Casting म्हणतात.
Extra Details: JS can convert values to only 3 primitive types: String, Number and Boolean. Every coercion rule in this chapter ends in one of these three.

2. Two Types of Conversion

Your Notes (your diagram):
Figure 16: Implicit vs explicit type conversion.

2.1 Implicit Type Coercion

Your Notes:
  • Implicit coercion is performed automatically by the JavaScript engine whenever different data types are used together in an expression.
  • The programmer does NOT manually convert the values. JavaScript decides how to convert them.
  • Flow: Different data types → JavaScript engine → automatically converts → returns result.
console.log(5 + "5");    // "55"  (number → string)
console.log("10" - 2);   // 8     (string → number)
console.log(true + 1);   // 2     (boolean → number)
if ("hello") { }         // "hello" → true (string → boolean)
  • What happens: JS converts automatically: + with a string joins text; -, * and / turn strings into numbers; true becomes 1; in an if, any non-empty string is true.
  • Output: "55", 8, 2.
  • ⚠ + is the trap: it prefers strings.
Implicit coercion मध्ये आपण काहीही करत नाही. वेगवेगळ्या types एकत्र वापरल्या की JS engine स्वतः ठरवते कोणती value कोणत्या type मध्ये बदलायची.

2.2 Explicit Coercion (Manual Type Conversion)

Your Notes:
  • Explicit coercion is performed manually by the programmer using JavaScript's built-in conversion functions.
  • Flow: Original value → programmer chooses a conversion → Number() / String() / Boolean() / BigInt() → converted value.
Number("42")      // 42
Number("abc")     // NaN
String(100)       // "100"
Boolean(0)        // false
BigInt("10")      // 10n
parseInt("42px")  // 42   (reads digits until the first invalid character)
parseFloat("3.5kg") // 3.5
(123).toString()  // "123"
`${123}`          // "123" (template literal)
  • What happens: explicit conversions with functions; you choose the type.
  • Output: 42, NaN, "100", false, 10n, 42, 3.5, "123", "123".
  • ✅ Clear intent; easier to read than implicit tricks.
Extra Details: Number() vs parseInt() Number("42px") → NaN (the whole string must be numeric), but parseInt("42px") → 42 (it stops at the first non-digit). Always pass the radix: parseInt("08", 10).
Explicit conversion मध्ये programmer स्वतः Number(), String(), Boolean(), BigInt() वापरून value बदलतो. यामुळे code वाचणाऱ्याला लगेच कळते की conversion होत आहे, म्हणून हा मार्ग जास्त सुरक्षित आहे.

3. String Coercion

Your Notes:
  • String coercion is triggered when the binary + operator is used and at least one of the operands is a string.
  • In this case JavaScript performs string concatenation rather than addition.
  • Example:
console.log(1 + "2");          // "12"
console.log('Hello' + true);   // "Hellotrue"
console.log(null + 'value');   // "nullvalue"
console.log(undefined + 'Hi'); // "undefinedHi"
console.log(NaN + 'Yes');      // "NaNYes"
  • What happens: if either side of + is a string, the other is converted to a string and joined.
  • Output: "12", "Hellotrue", "nullvalue", "undefinedHi", "NaNYes".
✔ output comments added (the original examples had none).तुमच्या examples मध्ये output लिहिलेले नव्हते. प्रत्येक line चे output comment मध्ये जोडले आहे.
Figure 17: How the + operator decides between concatenation and addition.
+ operator च्या दोन्ही बाजूंपैकी एक जरी string असेल तर JS बेरीज (addition) न करता string जोडते (concatenation). म्हणून 1 + "2" = "12". null, undefined, true, NaN सुद्धा string बनून जोडले जातात.
Extra Details: Evaluation goes left to right, so the position of the string matters: 
console.log(1 + 2 + "3");   // "33"  (1+2=3 first, then 3+"3")
console.log("1" + 2 + 3);   // "123" (string from the start)
console.log([] + 1);        // "1"   ([] → "")
  • What happens: + is evaluated left to right: 1 + 2 = 3, then 3 + "3" = "33"; "1" + 2 = "12", + 3 = "123"; [] becomes "".
  • Output: "33", "123", "1".
  • ⚠ Order of operands changes the result.

4. Numeric Type Coercion

4.1 Triggers

Your Notes: Numeric coercion is triggered by:
  1. Mathematical operations: subtraction (-), multiplication (*), division (/), modulus (%)
  2. Comparison operators: <, >, <=, >= (when both operands are strings, they are compared alphabetically as strings instead, with no numeric conversion) ✔ added the exception. "10" < "9" is true, because two strings are compared character by character.दोन्ही बाजूला string असेल तर < > number मध्ये बदलत नाहीत, तर अक्षरानुसार (dictionary order) तुलना करतात. म्हणून "10" < "9" हे true आहे.
  3. Unary + operator (e.g. +val)
Also: the binary + operator when neither operand is a string (e.g. true + 1), and loose equality ==. ✔ added the missing triggers used in your own examples (true + 1, false + 3).दोन्हीपैकी कोणीही string नसेल तर + सुद्धा number मध्ये बदलतो (true + 1 = 2). == सुद्धा numeric conversion करतो. ही triggers यादीत नव्हती.

4.2 Standard Conversion Mapping to Numbers

Your Notes:
#ValueNumber
1true1
2false0
3null0
4undefinedNaN
5"" (empty string)0
6Numeric string ("42")42
7Non-numeric string ('Vishal')NaN
Extra Details: more mappings
ValueNumberWhy
" " / "\n" (whitespace only)0whitespace is trimmed → ""
" 42 "42spaces trimmed
[]0[] → "" → 0
[5]5[5] → "5" → 5
[1,2]NaN→ "1,2" → NaN
{}NaN→ "[object Object]" → NaN
Symbol()TypeErrorsymbols cannot be converted
String नसलेल्या math operations (-, *, /, %), comparison (<, >) आणि unary + मध्ये JS value ला number मध्ये बदलते. true=1, false=0, null=0, ""=0, undefined=NaN आणि non-numeric string=NaN हे नियम पाठ करा.

4.3 Examples

Your Notes (your code, outputs corrected): 
console.log("5" - 2);          // 3   (string coerced to number 5)
console.log("10" * "20");      // 200 (both strings coerced to numbers)   ✔ was "20"
console.log("10" / "3");       // 3.3333333333333335 (both strings coerced to numbers)
console.log(true + 1);         // 2   (true coerced to 1)
console.log(false + 3);        // 3   (false coerced to 0)
console.log(undefined + 8);    // NaN (undefined coerced to NaN)
console.log(null - 8);         // -8  (null coerced to 0)
console.log(+"42");            // 42  (unary + coerces "42" to number 42)
                               // ✔ was console.log("430"), which just prints the string "430"
console.log(+'vishal shinde'); // NaN (non-numeric string coerced to NaN)
  • What happens: -, *, / always convert to numbers; booleans → 1/0; undefined → NaN; null → 0; unary + converts to number.
  • Output: 3, 200, 3.3333333333333335, 2, 3, NaN, -8, 42, NaN.
✔ "10" * "20" is 200, not 20. The unary + example must use +"42"; console.log("430") has no + and no coercion."10" * "20" चे उत्तर 200 आहे, 20 नाही. console.log("430") मध्ये + नाही, म्हणून conversion होत नाही आणि फक्त "430" string print होते. unary + चे बरोबर example +"42" → 42 आहे.
Extra Details: NaN rules 
typeof NaN          // "number"   (NaN is a special number value)
NaN + 5             // NaN        (any math with NaN gives NaN)
Number.isNaN("abc") // false      (safe check: is the value itself NaN?)
isNaN("abc")        // true       (global isNaN coerces first → misleading)
  • What happens: NaN is of type number; any math with it gives NaN; Number.isNaN doesn't convert, isNaN does.
  • Output: "number", NaN, false, true.

5. Boolean Coercion

Your Notes:
  • Boolean coercion occurs in a logical context where a boolean value is expected,
  • such as an if statement, a loop condition, the ternary operator, or the logical operators &&, ||, !
  1. Falsy values (evaluate to false): false, zero (0, -0, 0n), "" (empty string), null, undefined, NaN
  2. Truthy values (evaluate to true): all other values, including the empty array [] and the empty object {}.
  • Double negation (!!) operator trick: developers frequently use !! to explicitly convert a value into its boolean equivalent.
  • Example:
console.log(!!"Hello"); // true  (truthy string)
console.log(!![]);      // true  (empty array is truthy)
console.log(!!null);    // false (null is a falsy value)
console.log(!!0);       // false (0 is falsy)
console.log(!!{});      // true  (empty object is a truthy value)
  • What happens: !! converts any value to its boolean.
  • Output: true, true, false, false, true.
Figure 18: Falsy vs truthy. Memorise the 8 falsy values; everything else is truthy.
if, loop, &&, ||, ! अशा ठिकाणी JS value ला true/false मध्ये बदलते. फक्त 8 values falsy आहेत: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN. बाकी सर्व truthy आहेत, अगदी [] आणि {} सुद्धा. !! वापरून कोणतीही value boolean मध्ये बदलता येते.
Extra Details: traps 
Boolean("0")       // true  (non-empty string!)
Boolean("false")   // true  (non-empty string!)
Boolean(" ")       // true  (a space is not empty)
[] == false        // true  (== converts [] → "" → 0) BUT
if ([]) { }        // runs, because [] is truthy
  • What happens: non-empty strings are always true; [] is truthy in an if, but [] == false is true because == converts [] → "" → 0.
  • Output: true, true, true, true, (runs).
  • ⚠ Never compare with == false; just use if (value).
&& and || return an operand, not true/false: 
"a" || "b"    // "a"   (first truthy value)
0 || "default" // "default"
"a" && "b"   // "b"   (last value if all truthy)
null && "b"   // null  (first falsy value)
0 ?? "x"       // 0     (?? only skips null/undefined)
  • What happens: || returns the first truthy value, && the first falsy (or the last value), ?? only skips null/undefined.
  • Output: "a", "default", "b", null, 0.
  • ✅ Use ?? for defaults when 0 or "" are valid values.

6. Loose Equality vs Strict Equality

Your Notes: The most important topic is how comparison operators behave under the type coercion rules.

6.1 Strict Equality (===)

Your Notes:
  • Rule: compares both the value and the type,
  • so no type coercion is performed.
  • Exception: NaN === NaN is false.
  • Example:
console.log(5 === "5");          // false (strict equality checks the type as well as the value)
console.log(true === 1);         // false (it compares boolean vs number, so types differ)
console.log(null === undefined); // false (different types: null vs undefined)
  • What happens: === never converts, so different types are never equal.
  • Output: false, false, false.
  • ✅ Use === by default.
✔ "return becase it check boolean vs number" → "returns false because it compares boolean vs number".true === 1 हे false देते, कारण एक boolean आणि दुसरा number आहे. === type सुद्धा तपासतो.
Definition: The strict equality operator (===) returns true only if both operands have the same type and the same value, without converting either one.
Extra Details: the two exceptions of === 
NaN === NaN         // false → use Number.isNaN(x)
+0 === -0           // true
Object.is(NaN, NaN) // true  (Object.is fixes both cases)
Object.is(+0, -0)   // false
{} === {}           // false (objects compare by reference, not content)
  • What happens: === has two odd cases (NaN, ±0); Object.is fixes them. Objects are compared by reference.
  • Output: false, true, true, false, false.

6.2 Loose Equality (==)

Your Notes:
  • Definition: the loose equality (==) operator compares two values after performing automatic type conversion (type coercion) if the operands have different data types.
  • It compares the values after converting them to a common type; the original data types are allowed to differ. ✔ "compares only the values, not the data types" → it does look at the types, and uses them to decide how to convert.== type कडे दुर्लक्ष करत नाही. तो type पाहूनच ठरवतो की कोणती value कशात बदलायची, आणि मग तुलना करतो.
  • Rule: compare only values, after performing type coercion if the types are different.
  • Loose equality coercion steps:
  • Comparing Number and String: converts the string to a number.
    5 == "5" → "5" is converted to 5 → 5 == 5 (returns true).
  • Comparing Boolean and other types: converts the boolean to a number (true to 1, false to 0).
    true == "1" → true becomes 1, "1" becomes 1 → 1 == 1 (returns true).
  • Comparing null and undefined: special case, null == undefined is hard-coded to return true.
  • They do not coerce to numbers under == comparison; they only equal each other or themselves.
  • Comparing Objects and Primitives: converts the object to a primitive using valueOf() or toString().
console.log(5 == "5");          // true (string coerced to number)
console.log(true == 1);         // true (boolean true coerced to 1)
console.log(null == undefined); // true (specifically defined equality)
console.log(false == "");       // true (false → 0, "" → 0)
console.log(0 == "");           // true (0 → 0, "" → 0)
console.log(0 == "0");          // true (0 → 0, "0" → 0)
  • What happens: == converts both sides to numbers (mostly) before comparing; null == undefined by special rule.
  • Output: true × 6.
  • ⚠ These conversions are why == is avoided.
Figure 19: The steps the == operator follows before comparing.
=== type आणि value दोन्ही तपासतो, कोणतेही conversion करत नाही. == आधी दोन्ही values एकाच type मध्ये बदलतो (string → number, boolean → number, object → primitive) आणि मग तुलना करतो. null == undefined नेहमी true, पण null == 0 false. Interview आणि real code मध्ये नेहमी === वापरा.
Extra Details: famous == traps 
null == 0         // false (null only equals undefined)
null >= 0         // true  (relational operators DO convert null → 0!)
undefined == 0    // false
NaN == NaN        // false
"" == 0           // true
"0" == false      // true
"" == "0"         // false (both strings → compared as strings)
[] == ![]         // true  (![] → false → 0; [] → "" → 0)
  • What happens: null equals only undefined with ==, but >= converts null to 0. "" and "0" are both 0 as numbers, but as two strings they differ. [] == ![] is true.
  • Output: false, true, false, false, true, true, false, true.
  • ✅ Top interview output questions.

6.3 == vs === (Comparison Table)

FeatureLoose Equality (==)Strict Equality (===)
Checks type?No, converts firstYes
Type coercion✅ Yes❌ No
5 == "5" / 5 === "5"truefalse
null vs undefinedtruefalse
0 vs falsetruefalse
NaN vs NaNfalsefalse
Predictable?❌ Many traps✅ Yes
RecommendedOnly for x == null (checks null OR undefined)✅ Use by default

7. Tricky Questions

Q1. What is the output of [] + [] and why?
Your Notes: Answer: "" (an empty string).
Explanation: the + operator triggers string coercion. Since arrays are non-primitive, they are converted to primitives using toString(). [].toString() returns "". Thus, "" + "" results in "".
console.log([] + []);         // ""
console.log(typeof ([] + [])); // "string"
  • What happens: [] + [] → "" + "" → "".
  • Output: "", "string".
Q2. What is the output of [] + {} and why?
Your Notes: 
console.log([] + {});   // "[object Object]"
  • What happens: [] → "", {} → "[object Object]".
  • Output: "[object Object]".
Answer: "[object Object]" (as a string).
Explanation: the + operator triggers coercion. The empty array [] is converted to the primitive string "", and the empty object {} is converted to the primitive string "[object Object]". Concatenating them gives "" + "[object Object]" = "[object Object]".
Q3. What is the output of {} + []?
Your Notes: Answer: it depends on how it is executed! 
console.log({} + []);   // "[object Object]"
  • What happens: same inside console.log (in the console's statement position {} + [] would be 0).
  • Output: "[object Object]".
  • As a statement at the start of a line (e.g. a script line {} + []; or older browser consoles): it returns 0. The {} is treated as an empty code block (which does nothing), followed by + [] (unary + on an empty array). +[] coerces [] to "", and +"" gives the number 0. ✔ modern Chrome/Edge consoles wrap the input as an expression, so typing {} + [] there now shows "[object Object]". The 0 result appears when {} is parsed as a block.नवीन Chrome/Edge console मध्ये {} + [] टाइप केल्यास "[object Object]" मिळते. 0 फक्त तेव्हाच मिळते जेव्हा {} ला code block समजले जाते.
  • Inside an expression (e.g. console.log({} + [])): it returns "[object Object]". The {} is treated as an object literal, coerces to "[object Object]", and concatenates with "" from the array.
Q4. Explain the result of "5" + 3 vs "5" - 3.
Your Notes: Answer: "5" + 3 results in "53" (string concatenation), whereas "5" - 3 results in 2 (numeric subtraction).
Explanation: the + operator has a dual purpose: string concatenation and numeric addition. If one operand is a string, it prioritises concatenation. The - operator is strictly mathematical, so it coerces "5" to the number 5 before subtracting.
Figure 20: + concatenates when a string is involved; - always does math.
+ ला दोन कामे आहेत (जोडणे आणि बेरीज). string असेल तर तो जोडतो ("53"). - ला फक्त math येते, म्हणून तो "5" ला 5 करून वजाबाकी करतो (2). [] → "" आणि {} → "[object Object]" हे लक्षात ठेवा.

8. Interview Questions

8.1 Your Notes

Q1. What is Type Coercion?
Type Coercion is the automatic conversion of one data type into another, performed by the JavaScript engine.
Q2. What is Type Casting?
Type Casting is the manual conversion of one data type into another using functions like Number(), String() and Boolean().
Q3. Which operators usually perform implicit coercion?
+, -, *, /, %, ==, <, >, <=, >=, &&, ||, !, unary + ✔ added ! and unary +. Note that && and || coerce only to decide which operand to return; they return the original operand, not true/false.यादीत ! आणि unary + नव्हते, ते जोडले. && आणि || true/false परत करत नाहीत, तर मूळ value (operand) परत करतात.
Q4. Which built-in functions perform explicit coercion?
Number(), String(), Boolean(), BigInt() ✔ also parseInt(), parseFloat(), .toString() and template literals (`${x}`).Number(), String(), Boolean(), BigInt() शिवाय parseInt(), parseFloat(), .toString() आणि template literal ने सुद्धा explicit conversion होते.

8.2 Extra Interview Questions (Detailed)

Q5. What is the difference between == and ===? Which should you use?
  • == converts the operands to a common type and then compares them. === compares type and value with no conversion. Use === by default because it is predictable. The one accepted use of == is x == null, which is true for both null and undefined.
Q6. Why is typeof NaN "number"? How do you check for NaN?
  • NaN ("Not a Number") is a special value of the Number type that represents an invalid numeric result. NaN is not equal to anything, including itself, so check it with Number.isNaN(x) (or Object.is(x, NaN)). The global isNaN("abc") returns true because it coerces first, which is misleading.
Q7. List all falsy values in JavaScript.
  • false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN. That is 8 values; everything else, including "0", "false", [], {} and functions, is truthy.
Q8. Why is null == 0 false but null >= 0 true?
  • Equality (==) has a special rule: null is equal only to undefined, and it is not converted to a number. Relational operators (>=, <) always convert to numbers, so null becomes 0, and 0 >= 0 is true.
Q9. Difference between Number() and parseInt()?
  • Number() converts the whole value and returns NaN if any part is invalid (Number("12px") → NaN). parseInt() reads digits from the start and stops at the first invalid character (parseInt("12px") → 12). Number("") is 0, but parseInt("") is NaN.
Q10. How does JS convert an object to a primitive?
  • It calls Symbol.toPrimitive if it exists. Otherwise, for a "number" hint it tries valueOf() then toString(); for a "string" hint (e.g. template literals) it tries toString() then valueOf(). Plain objects give "[object Object]", and arrays give their elements joined by commas.
const price = { valueOf() { return 100; } };
console.log(price + 1);   // 101
  • What happens: for +, the object is converted with valueOf(), which returns 100.
  • Output: 101.
Q11. Output-based questions
console.log("3" * "4");       // 12
console.log("3" + 4 + 5);     // "345"
console.log(3 + 4 + "5");     // "75"
console.log("10" - "4" - "3"); // 3
console.log(true + true);     // 2
console.log([] == 0);         // true
console.log([1] == 1);        // true
console.log([1,2] == "1,2");  // true
console.log(null + 1);        // 1
console.log(undefined + 1);   // NaN
console.log("b" + "a" + +"a" + "a"); // "baNaNa"
console.log(!!"false");       // true
console.log(1 < 2 < 3);       // true  (true < 3 → 1 < 3)
console.log(3 > 2 > 1);       // false (true > 1 → 1 > 1)
  • What happens: a mix of all coercion rules; note "b" + "a" + +"a" + "a" where +"a" is NaN, and comparison chains evaluate left to right (1 < 2 is true → true < 3 → 1 < 3).
  • Output: 12, "345", "75", 3, 2, true, true, true, 1, NaN, "baNaNa", true, true, false.

9. Quick Revision Summary

ConceptOne-line Summary

थोडक्यात: + ला string दिसली की जोडतो, बाकी math operators number बनवतात. 8 falsy values पाठ करा. == conversion करतो, === करत नाही, म्हणून नेहमी === वापरा. Explicit conversion (Number(), String()) वापरणे सर्वात सुरक्षित आहे.

1. What is a String?

Your Notes (string/string-basic.js):
  • Strings in JS are a fundamental data type that represents a sequence of characters, useful for holding data represented in text form.
  • The string data type.
  • Strings are zero-index based.
  • In JavaScript, a string is a primitive data type used to represent text.
  • You can create strings using single quotes ('), double quotes ("), or backticks (`).
  • Strings in JavaScript are immutable, meaning you cannot change individual characters directly.
What are the properties of a string? How do you find the length of a string? 1. length: a property that returns the length of the string (i.e. the number of UTF-16 code units, which is the number of characters for normal text).
Definition: A string is an immutable, ordered sequence of UTF-16 code units. Every string method RETURNS A NEW STRING; none changes the original. Primitives get methods through temporary String wrapper objects ("auto-boxing"), which is why "abc".toUpperCase() works.
String म्हणजे अक्षरांची क्रमवार मालिका (text). JS मध्ये string primitive आणि immutable आहे: एकदा बनलेली string बदलता येत नाही; प्रत्येक method नवीन string परत करतो. index 0 पासून सुरू होतो.
Example 1: String length property
let str = "vishal shinde";
// To find the length of the string, use the length property
console.log("length:", str.length);   // → length: 13
  • What happens: The length property returns the total number of characters in the string, including spaces.
  • Output: length: 13.

2. How to Create a String

  1. string literal
  2. String constructor
Example 2: Using a string literal
// 1. using a string literal
let firstName = "vishal";
let lastName = "shinde";
console.log("fullname:", firstName + lastName);   // → fullname: vishalshinde (no space was added)
  • What happens: Two string literals are created and concatenated together.
  • Output: fullname: vishalshinde.
  • ✅ Best practice for creating strings.
Example 3: Using the String constructor
// using the String constructor
let newStr = new String("vishal shinde");
console.log("string constructor:", newStr);       // → string constructor: [String: 'vishal shinde']
  • What happens: The `new` keyword is used with the String constructor, which returns an object rather than a primitive string.
  • Output: string constructor: [String: 'vishal shinde'].
  • ⚠ Avoid this; it creates an object and slows down execution.
✔ Note: new String() creates a String OBJECT, not a primitive: typeof newStr → "object", and new String("a") === new String("a") → false. Prefer literals; String(x) (without new) converts to a primitive.new String() ने string object बनतो, primitive नाही (typeof "object"). नेहमी literal ("...") वापरा; String(x) (new शिवाय) ने primitive string मिळते.

3. How to Find an Individual Character from a Given String

There are 2 ways:

  1. the charAt() method;
  2. array-like access, where individual characters correspond to numerical indexes.

Example 4: Using charAt()
// 1. using the charAt() method
const string = "vishal shinde";
const index = string.charAt(6);   // indexing starts from zero
console.log(index);               // → " " (index 6 is the SPACE)
  • What happens: `charAt(6)` returns the character at the 6th index of the string.
  • Output: " " (a space).
Example 5: Array-like access
// using array-like access, where individual characters correspond to numerical indexes
const as = string[0];             // fixed reference from str to string
console.log(as);                  // → v
  • What happens: Bracket notation is used to access the character at index 0.
  • Output: v.
  • ✅ Modern and cleaner syntax.

4. Comparing Strings

Use the less-than or greater-than operators to compare strings (they compare character by character, by UTF-16 code unit):

CharacterUnicode / ASCII Value
"a"97
"b"98

So b is greater than a.

const a = "a";
const b = "b";
if (a < b) {
  console.log("${a} is less then ${b}");   // → ${a} is less then ${b}   (literally!)
} else if (a > b) {
  console.log("${a} is Grater then ${b}");
} else {
  console.log("${a} are equal ${b}");
}
// ✔ ${...} only works inside BACKTICKS. With double quotes it prints "${a}" literally (verified).
//    Use `${a} is less than ${b}` → "a is less than b"
${} फक्त backticks (`) मध्ये चालते. double quotes मध्ये ते जसेच्या तसे छापले जाते. Watch out: "Z" < "a" is true (uppercase codes 65–90 come before lowercase 97–122), and "10" < "9" is true (string comparison, character by character). Use localeCompare for human sorting (Chapter 7).

5. Escape Characters

In JavaScript, escape characters let you include special characters in your strings.

  1. The backslash (\) escape character turns a special character into a string character; if you want double quotes inside double quotes, you have to use escape characters.
  2. Single quote.
  3. Double quotes.

EscapeMeaningExample
\'Single quote'It\'s fine' → It's fine
\"Double quote"She said, \"Hello\""
\\Backslash'C:\\Users\\Vishal'
\nNew line'Line1\nLine2'
\tTab'Hello\tWorld'
\rCarriage return'Hello\rWorld': moves the cursor back to the beginning of the current line, without moving to a new line
Example 7: Escape Characters
let s = 'hey, hi, how are you? " \n I \t am fine and you "';
console.log(s);
// → hey, hi, how are you? "
//    I 	 am fine and you "
  • What happens: The string contains a newline (`\n`) and a tab (`\t`) escape sequence, which format the output text when printed.
  • Output: Two lines, with the second line indented by a tab.
(Also: \u0041 → "A" (Unicode escape), \` inside template literals.)

6. Property Access (Bracket Notation)

Your Notes (property-access.js): syntax: string[index]
  • Property access using bracket notation [] is used to access a character at a specified index in a string.
  • String indexing starts from 0. E.g. 0 1 2 3 4 → H e l l o
  • It returns the character at the specified index.
  • Bracket notation does not support negative indexing.
  • If the index is out of range, it returns undefined.
  • That is different from charAt(), which returns an empty string for an invalid index.
  • Strings are immutable: you can read characters using bracket notation, but you cannot modify individual characters.
let str = 'Hello word'
// access the first character
console.log(str[0])                // → H
// access the last character
console.log(str[str.length - 1]);  // → d
// an out-of-range index returns undefined
console.log(str[10])               // → undefined
// negative indexes are not supported; they also return undefined.
console.log(str[-9]);              // → undefined
// using a variable as the index
let digit = 2
console.log(str[digit]);           // → l
// loop through the string
for (let i = 0; i < str.length; i++) {
  console.log(str[i])              // → H e l l o   w o r d (one per line)
}
// strings are immutable: you can't modify an individual character of a string
console.log(str[0] = 10);          // → 10 (the assignment expression's value)…
console.log(str)                   // → Hello word   …but the string is unchanged (TypeError in strict mode)
// if you want to change it, build a new string:
console.log('10' + str.slice(1))   // → 10ello word

// character access with charAt() and property access are both used to access characters, but they behave differently
console.log(str.charAt(0));        // → H
// if the index is out of bounds, charAt() returns '' (an empty string)
console.log(str.charAt(100))       // → ""

// property access with a numeric string:
// JavaScript converts the numeric property key appropriately.
console.log(str['1']);             // → e
  • What happens: Strings can be accessed using bracket notation (like an array) or charAt(). Because strings are immutable, attempting to change a character (e.g. str[0] = 10) fails silently or throws an error in strict mode.
  • Output: l, H, e, l, l, o, , w, o, r, d (from loop), 10, Hello word, 10ello word, H, "", e.
charAt() vs property access: with an invalid index, property access returns undefined, while charAt() returns an empty string.
Property access vs at(): property access gets the character at the specified index but doesn't support negative indexes; at() also gets the character at the specified index, and it supports negative indexes (str.at(-1) → "d").

7. Template Literals

Your Notes (template-literals.js), definition:
  • Template literals are a modern way to create strings in JavaScript.
  • They are written using backticks (``) instead of single quotes ('') or double quotes ("").
  • Template literals support: string interpolation (${} interpolation only works inside BACKTICKS); embedded expressions; multi-line strings; tagged templates.
  • Syntax: `text`, `${expression}` ✔ the syntax note said `{expression}`; it needs the dollar sign: `${expression}`.expression साठी ${...} लिहावे लागते; $ विसरू नका.
  • Template literals let us embed variables and expressions directly inside a string using ${expression}.
ex 1
// ex 1
let name = 'vishal';
let firstName = 'shinde';
console.log(`my name is ${name}  ${firstName}`)   // → my name is vishal  shinde

// embedded expressions, including mathematical operations
console.log(`sum of ${10 + 20}`)                  // → sum of 30

// a function call inside the template literal
function dispalyName(name) {
  console.log(name);
}
console.log(`${dispalyName('vishal')}`)
// → vishal       (printed inside the function)
// → undefined    (the function returns nothing, so ${…} inserts "undefined"); use return name;
  • What happens: Template literals (using backticks) allow embedding variables and expressions with ${}. The function call inside ${} executes, but since it returns nothing, "undefined" is inserted into the string.
  • Output: my name is vishal shinde, sum of 30, vishal, undefined.
template literals allow multi-line strings without using \n
// # template literals allow multi-line strings without using \n
let result = `vishal
    shinde
    at post
    wadgaon sahani,
    tel junnar, dist pune

`
console.log(result)   // the line breaks AND the leading spaces are kept exactly
  • What happens: Template literals support multi-line strings naturally. Line breaks and indentation within the backticks are preserved exactly in the resulting string.
  • Output: vishal (and subsequent lines with indentation).
the expression is evaluated: anything inside ${} is evaluated as JS
// # the expression is evaluated: anything inside ${} is evaluated as JS
let age = 23;
console.log(`next Year age is ${age + 1}`)                       // → next Year age is 24
// you can also use the ternary operator (a conditional expression)
let isLoggned = true;
console.log(`user is ${isLoggned ? 'user login in ' : 'log out'} `)   // → user is user login in
  • What happens: Any valid JavaScript expression, including arithmetic and ternary operators, can be evaluated inside ${}.
  • Output: next Year age is 24, user is user login in.
object property access
// # object property access
let user = { name: 'vishal', age: 25 }
console.log(`${user.name} and ${user.age}`)   // → vishal and 25
  • What happens: Object properties can be directly accessed and embedded within the template literal.
  • Output: vishal and 25.
array access
// # array access
const language = ['java', 'js', 'sql'];
console.log(`${language[0]}`)                 // → java
  • What happens: Array elements can be accessed by their index inside the template literal.
  • Output: java.
escaping backticks
// # escaping backticks
// if you want to use a backtick inside a template literal, use a backslash.
const text = `This is a \'vishal shinde\'`
console.log(text)                             // → This is a 'vishal shinde'
// ✔ this escapes SINGLE QUOTES (which don't even need escaping here). A backtick example:
//    `use \`npm i\` to install` → use `npm i` to install
  • What happens: The backslash (\) is used to escape characters, allowing you to include quotes or backticks inside the string without breaking the syntax.
  • Output: This is a 'vishal shinde'.
Summary:
  • backtick (``) + ${expression}
  • template literals = string + variables + expressions + multi-line support. They support variables, mathematical expressions, function calls, object properties, array access and multi-line strings
  • expressions inside ${} are evaluated.

8. Tagged Templates & String.raw()

Tagged template literals: a template literal can also be passed to a function; this is called a tagged template literal. 
function tab(string, ...values) {
  console.log(string);   // → ['my name is ', ' and my age is ', '']   (the static parts)
  console.log(values)    // → ['vishal', 25]                           (the ${} values)
}
const username = 'vishal';
const usrAge = 25;
tab`my name is ${username} and my age is ${usrAge}`;
// the strings array always has ONE MORE item than values (here the last part is '')
  • What happens: A tagged template literal passes the string parts as an array and the interpolated values as subsequent arguments to a function, allowing custom parsing.
  • Output: ['my name is ', ' and my age is ', ''], ['vishal', 25].
String.raw() (31-raw.js): syntax: String.raw`templateString` or String.raw({ raw: [...] }, ...substitutions)
  • String.raw() is a static method of the String object,
  • commonly used as a TAG function with template literals.
  • It returns the raw string representation of a template literal.
  • Raw means escape sequences such as \n, \t, \\ are not interpreted in the returned string; instead they are treated as normal characters.
  • It is used as String.raw(); incorrect: 'Hello'.raw();
  • Escape sequences are kept as raw text: \n is returned as two characters, \ and n, instead of creating a new line; \t is returned as \ and t instead of a tab.
  • It returns a new string.
  • It is especially useful when working with file paths, regular expressions, backslashes and escape sequences.
✔ syntax "String.raw(callstate, ...substitute)" → String.raw(callSite, ...substitutions), where callSite is an object with a raw array.दुसऱ्या syntax मध्ये पहिला argument callSite ({ raw: [...] }) असतो.
Example 1
const normalString = `Hello\nWorld`;
// \n is interpreted as a newline character
console.log(normalString)   // → Hello
                            //   World
  • What happens: In a normal template literal, escape sequences like \n are processed normally, inserting an actual newline.
  • Output: Hello (newline) World.
ex. String.raw()
// ex. String.raw()
const rawString = String.raw`Hello\nword`;
// not interpreted as a newline character
console.log(rawString)      // → Hello\nword

// Note: String.raw() preserves the raw template text, but template expressions are still evaluated (replaced):
const who = "vishal";
String.raw`C:\new\folder ${who}`;   // → "C:\new\folder vishal"   (\n stays, ${who} is replaced)
// ⚠ careful (verified): String.raw`C:\new\${who}` → "C:\new\${who}": a backslash right before $ escapes it, so no interpolation
String.raw`\d+\.\d+`;          // → "\d+\.\d+" handy for new RegExp(...)
  • What happens: String.raw returns the exact characters written inside the template literal without processing escape sequences like \n, though ${} interpolations are still evaluated.
  • Output: Hello\nword, C:\new\folder vishal, \d+\.\d+.

9. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. Are strings mutable in JavaScript?
  • No. str[0] = "X" is ignored (a TypeError in strict mode); every method returns a new string. To "change" a string, build a new one (slice + concat, replace).
Q2. Literal vs new String()?
  • A literal is a primitive (typeof "string"); new String() is a wrapper object (typeof "object"), compared by reference. Methods work on both, because primitives are auto-boxed.
Q3. str[i] vs charAt(i) vs at(i)?
  • Out of range: undefined vs "" vs undefined. Negative index: undefined vs "" vs counts from the end (at(-1) = last char).
Q4. What can you do with template literals that you can't with quotes?
  • Interpolation ${expr}, multi-line text without \n, and tagged templates (custom processing, e.g. escaping HTML, styled-components, String.raw).
Q5. Output-based questions
console.log("5" + 3, "5" - 3);           // → 53 2
console.log("abc"[5], "abc".charAt(5));  // → undefined ""
console.log(`${[1, 2]}${{}}`);           // → 1,2[object Object]
console.log("B" < "a", "10" < "9");     // → true true
let s = "hi"; s[0] = "H"; console.log(s); // → hi
console.log(typeof new String("x"), typeof String(5));   // → object string
  • What happens: Shows various string coercion and access rules: + concatenates while - converts to numbers. Arrays and objects are converted to strings via their toString() methods. "B" < "a" compares Unicode values. new String() creates an object wrapper, while String() performs primitive conversion.
  • Output: 53 2, undefined "", 1,2[object Object], true true, hi, object string.
TopicRemember
Create'…', "…", `…` (prefer literals)
lengthA property (no parentheses)
ImmutableMethods return new strings
Accessstr[i] / charAt(i) / at(-1)
Template literal`${expr}`, multi-line, tagged
String.rawKeeps \n etc. as text
थोडक्यात: string immutable आहे; methods नवीन string देतात. ${} फक्त backticks मध्ये चालते. str[i] बाहेरच्या index वर undefined देतो, charAt "" देतो, आणि at(-1) शेवटचे अक्षर देतो. String.raw escape sequences जसेच्या तसे ठेवतो.
Chapter 5: Strings II: SearchingindexOf · lastIndexOf · search · match · matchAll · includes · startsWith · endsWith · regex basics
CHAPTER 5 INDEX
  1. indexOf()
  2. lastIndexOf()
