6. charCodeAt() & codePointAt()

Your Notes (14-charAtCode.js): syntax: string.charCodeAt(position)
  • The charCodeAt() method returns an integer representing the UTF-16 code unit of the character at the specified index.
  • The returned value is generally between 0 and 65535.
  • JavaScript strings use zero-based indexing; valid indexes are 0 to string.length - 1.
  • If the index is out of range, charCodeAt() returns NaN; negative indexes also return NaN.
  • The position argument is optional: if omitted, the default position is 0.
  • charCodeAt() doesn't modify the original string.
  • IMPORTANT: charCodeAt() returns a UTF-16 CODE UNIT, not necessarily the complete Unicode code point.
Example 1: basic usage
// Example 1: basic usage
const str = "Hello, World!";
console.log(str.charCodeAt(0));               // → 72
console.log(str.charCodeAt(7));               // → 87
  • What happens: charCodeAt returns the number (UTF-16 code unit) of the character: H = 72, W = 87.
  • Output: 72, 87.
  • ✅ Useful for comparisons, simple ciphers and checking character ranges.
Example 2: default position (no argument means "Hello".charCodeAt(0))
// Example 2: default position (no argument means "Hello".charCodeAt(0))
console.log("Hello".charCodeAt());            // → 72
  • What happens: If no position is provided, charCodeAt defaults to index 0, which corresponds to the first character "H".
  • Output: 72.
Example 3: negative index
// Example 3: negative index
console.log(str.charCodeAt(-1));              // → NaN
  • What happens: no negative indexing; invalid index gives NaN (a number type!).
  • Output: NaN.
  • ⚠ Check with Number.isNaN(code), not code === NaN.
Example 4: out of range
// Example 4: out of range
console.log(str.charCodeAt(100));             // → NaN
  • What happens: index 100 doesn't exist.
  • Output: NaN.
Example 5: last character
// Example 5: last character
console.log(str.charCodeAt(str.length - 1));  // → 33
  • What happens: "!" has code 33.
  • Output: 33.
Example 6: loop through a string
// Example 6: loop through a string
let word = "JavaScript";
for (let i = 0; i < word.length; i++) {
  console.log(word[i], word.charCodeAt(i));   // → J 74, a 97, v 118, … t 116
}
  • What happens: prints each character with its code.
  • Output: J 74, a 97, v 118, a 97, S 83, c 99, r 114, i 105, p 112, t 116.
  • ✅ Notice: capital letters (65–90) have smaller codes than small letters (97–122).
Example 7: decimal index: 1.9 is converted to 1 → the character at index 1 = e → UTF-16 co
// Example 7: decimal index: 1.9 is converted to 1 → the character at index 1 = e → UTF-16 code unit 101
console.log("Hello".charCodeAt(1.9));         // → 101
  • What happens: 1.9 → 1 → "e" → 101.
  • Output: 101.
Example 8: NaN as the position is converted to 0.
Example 8: NaN as the position
// Example 8: NaN as the position is converted to 0.
console.log("Hello".charCodeAt(NaN));         // → 72
  • What happens: NaN is treated as 0 → "H" → 72.
  • Output: 72.
Example 9: charAt() vs charCodeAt()
// charAt() vs charCodeAt()
const str2 = "A";
console.log(str2.charAt(0));        // charAt() → returns the character as a string → A
console.log(str2.charCodeAt(0));    // charCodeAt() → returns the UTF-16 numeric code unit → 65
// out of range
console.log(str2.charAt(100));      // charAt() out of range → ""
console.log(str2.charCodeAt(100));  // charCodeAt() out of range → NaN
  • What happens: charAt gives the character, charCodeAt its number; out of range they give "" and NaN.
  • Output: A, 65, "", NaN.
charAt() vs charCodeAt() vs codePointAt():
// # charAt() vs charCodeAt() vs codePointAt():
//   charAt() → returns the character as a string; charCodeAt() → returns the UTF-16 code unit;
//   codePointAt() → returns the Unicode code point
const value = "A";
console.log(value.charAt(0));       // → A
console.log(value.charCodeAt(0));   // → 65
console.log(value.codePointAt(0));  // → 65
  • What happens: for a normal letter, charCodeAt and codePointAt give the same number.
  • Output: A, 65, 65.
Important Unicode / emoji difference: for normal English characters, charCodeAt() usually 
// # Important Unicode / emoji difference: for normal English characters, charCodeAt() usually works as expected.
const letter = "A";
console.log(letter.charCodeAt(0));  // → 65
// However, some Unicode characters such as emojis use TWO UTF-16 code units.
const emoji = "😀";
console.log(emoji.length);          // → 2
console.log(emoji.charCodeAt(0));   // → 55357
console.log(emoji.charCodeAt(1));   // → 56832
// The emoji is represented by two UTF-16 code units (a surrogate pair), so charCodeAt() gives separate values.
// codePointAt() returns the complete Unicode code point
console.log(emoji.codePointAt(0));  // → 128512

const emoji2 = "😀";
console.log(emoji2.charCodeAt(0));  // → 55357
console.log(emoji2.codePointAt(0)); // → 128512
  • What happens: 😀 is stored as two code units (55357, 56832 = a surrogate pair). charCodeAt reads one half; codePointAt(0) combines both into the real code point 128512.
  • Output: 65, 2, 55357, 56832, 128512, 55357, 128512.
  • ✅ Use codePointAt for emoji and rare scripts.
out-of-range comparison
// # out-of-range comparison
const str5 = "Hello";
// charAt(100) → ""; charCodeAt(100) → NaN; codePointAt(100) → undefined
  • What happens: three different "not found" values for the same bad index.
  • Output: "", NaN, undefined.
  • ⚠ Popular output question: remember "" / NaN / undefined.
Practical example: character comparison
// # Practical example: character comparison
const char = "A";
if (char.charCodeAt(0) >= 65 && char.charCodeAt(0) <= 90) {
  ```
  console.log("Uppercase letter");
  ```;
}
// ✔ (verified in Node) the markdown ``` fences were pasted INTO the code. JS reads ``` as an empty
//    template literal `` used as a TAG on another template → TypeError: "" is not a function, and the file
//    stops here. Remove the fences: if (…) { console.log("Uppercase letter"); } → Uppercase letter
  • What happens: A–Z have codes 65–90, so the condition detects an upper-case letter. The pasted ``` fences break the code (see the note).
  • Output: TypeError as written; Uppercase letter after removing the fences.
  • ⚠ Simpler today: /[A-Z]/.test(char) or char === char.toUpperCase().
code मध्ये markdown चे ``` राहिले आहेत. JS त्यांना template literal समजतो आणि "is not a function" TypeError येतो. ``` काढून टाका. charCodeAt() vs codePointAt(): charCodeAt() returns a UTF-16 code unit and works on UTF-16 units, so an emoji may produce two separate values; codePointAt() returns the Unicode code point, which is better for handling emoji and characters outside the BMP.
Interview quick points:
  1. charCodeAt() returns a number;
  2. a UTF-16 code unit;
  3. valid index: 0 to string.length - 1; negative index → NaN; out-of-range index → NaN;
  4. default index → 0;
  5. decimal indexes are converted to integers;
  6. it doesn't modify the original string.
  • charAt() returns a character
  • charCodeAt() returns a numeric UTF-16 code unit
  • codePointAt() is better for complete Unicode code points such as emoji.

NOTE: charCodeAt() returns the UTF-16 code unit at the specified index. For characters represented by surrogate pairs, such as many emojis, codePointAt() is more appropriate for retrieving the complete Unicode code point.

7. String.fromCharCode()

Your Notes (26-from-char-code.js): syntax: String.fromCharCode(num1, num2, num3, ...)
  • String.fromCharCode() is a STATIC method of the String object.
  • It creates a string from one or more UTF-16 code units: it converts numeric character codes into characters, and returns a NEW string.
  • Since it is a static method, it is called on String: String.fromCharCode(65).
  • It can accept multiple numeric arguments; each argument represents a UTF-16 code unit, and the resulting string contains the corresponding characters.
Example 1: basic usage
// # Example 1: basic usage
console.log(String.fromCharCode(65));    // → A
console.log(String.fromCharCode(66));    // → B
console.log(String.fromCharCode(67));    // → C
  • What happens: fromCharCode is called on String itself (static) and turns a code into a character.
  • Output: A, B, C.
Example 2: multiple character codes: each number is converted into its character.
// # Example 2: multiple character codes: each number is converted into its character.
console.log(String.fromCharCode(65, 66, 67));                // → ABC
  • What happens: every argument becomes one character, joined in order.
  • Output: ABC.
Example 3: creating "Hello"
// # Example 3: creating "Hello"
const str = String.fromCharCode(72, 101, 108, 108, 111);
console.log(str);                                            // → Hello
  • What happens: 72 H, 101 e, 108 l, 108 l, 111 o.
  • Output: Hello.
Example 4: special characters
// # Example 4: special characters
console.log(String.fromCharCode(189, 43, 190, 61));          // → ½+¾=
  • What happens: 189 = ½, 43 = +, 190 = ¾, 61 = =.
  • Output: ½+¾=.
Example 5: the space character
// # Example 5: the space character
console.log(String.fromCharCode(72, 105, 32, 33));           // → "Hi !"
  • What happens: 32 is the space.
  • Output: "Hi !".
Example 6: no arguments → an empty string.
// # Example 6: no arguments → an empty string.
console.log(String.fromCharCode());                          // → ""
  • What happens: nothing to convert.
  • Output: "".
Example 7: the relation with charCodeAt()
// # Example 7: the relation with charCodeAt()
const text = 'Hello';
console.log(text.charCodeAt(0));           // → 72
console.log(String.fromCharCode(72));      // → H
// charCodeAt(): character → UTF-16 code unit;  fromCharCode(): UTF-16 code unit → character
  • What happens: charCodeAt and fromCharCode are opposites.
  • Output: 72, H.
charCodeAt() vs fromCharCode(): charCodeAt() string → character code; fromCharCode() chara
// # charCodeAt() vs fromCharCode(): charCodeAt() string → character code; fromCharCode() character code → string
// # Example 8: round-trip conversion
const character = 'A';
const code = character.charCodeAt(0);
console.log(code);                         // → 65
const convertedCharacter = String.fromCharCode(code);
console.log(convertedCharacter);           // → A
  • What happens: round trip: character → 65 → character.
  • Output: 65, A.
  • ✅ Basis of simple Caesar-cipher programs: String.fromCharCode(c.charCodeAt(0) + 1).
Important: it works with UTF-16 code units (common range 0 to 65535). For characters outsi
// # Important: it works with UTF-16 code units (common range 0 to 65535). For characters outside the BMP, such as
//   many emojis, use String.fromCodePoint()
// # Example 9: the emoji problem: this does NOT correctly represent 😀, because 128512 is outside a single UTF-16
//   code unit's range; for full Unicode code points use fromCodePoint()
console.log(String.fromCharCode(128512));  // → "" (U+F600: 128512 % 65536 = 62976, a private-use char; verified)
console.log(String.fromCodePoint(128512)); // → 😀
  • What happens: fromCharCode keeps only the low 16 bits (128512 % 65536 = 62976), producing a wrong private-use character. fromCodePoint understands the full value.
  • Output: "" (wrong char), 😀.
  • ⚠ Always use fromCodePoint for emoji.
fromCharCode() vs fromCodePoint()
// # fromCharCode() vs fromCodePoint()
// String.fromCharCode() → works with UTF-16 code units.
console.log(String.fromCharCode(65));      // → A
// String.fromCodePoint(128512) works with full Unicode code points.
console.log(String.fromCodePoint());       // → ""
// ✔ the comment says fromCodePoint(128512) but the code passes NO argument → "" (empty string)
  • What happens: 65 → A; fromCodePoint with no argument returns "" (the comment expected an emoji).
  • Output: A, "".
Important interview points:
  1. fromCharCode() is a STATIC String method;
  2. it is called as String.fromCharCode();
  3. it converts numeric UTF-16 code units into characters;
  4. it can accept multiple numbers;
  5. it returns a new string;
  6. String.fromCharCode(65) returns "A";
  7. the opposite operation is charCodeAt();
  8. charCodeAt() converts character → UTF-16 code unit;
  9. fromCharCode() converts UTF-16 code unit → character;
  10. fromCharCode() works with UTF-16 code units, not arbitrary Unicode code points;
  11. for full Unicode code points and emojis, String.fromCodePoint() is generally more appropriate;
  12. calling fromCharCode() with no arguments returns an empty string.

Quick memory trick: charCodeAt(): character → number; fromCharCode(): number → character.

8. String.fromCodePoint()

Your Notes (29-fromCodePoint.js): String.fromCodePoint(num1, num2, num3, ...)
  • String.fromCodePoint() is a STATIC method of String.
  • It returns a string created from the specified sequence of Unicode CODE POINTS; it can accept one or more code points.
  • Each code point must be an integer in the valid Unicode range: 0 to 0x10FFFF (decimal: 0 to 1,114,111).
  • Unlike String.fromCharCode(), fromCodePoint() can handle Unicode code points greater than 65535.
  • This makes fromCodePoint() suitable for characters such as emoji and other characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP).
  • String.fromCodePoint() returns a NEW string; it does NOT modify anything.
Example 1: basic, emoji and multiple code points
// BASIC EXAMPLE: 9731 is the Unicode code point of the snowman character.
console.log(String.fromCodePoint(9731));              // → ☃
// EMOJI EXAMPLE
console.log(String.fromCodePoint(0x1F601));           // → 😁
// MULTIPLE CODE POINTS: each code point is converted into its corresponding character.
console.log(String.fromCodePoint(0x1F600, 0x1F602));  // → 😀😂
// CHARACTER USING A DECIMAL CODE POINT
console.log(String.fromCodePoint(65));                // → A
console.log(String.fromCodePoint(66));                // → B
console.log(String.fromCodePoint(65, 66, 67));        // → ABC
// CHARACTER USING A HEXADECIMAL CODE POINT (hexadecimal notation is common for Unicode code points)
console.log(String.fromCodePoint(0x41));              // → A
console.log(String.fromCodePoint(0x1F600));           // → 😀
// CODE POINT GREATER THAN 65535: 128512 > 65535, but fromCodePoint() supports it (the main difference from fromCharCode())
console.log(String.fromCodePoint(128512));            // → 😀
// fromCharCode() works with UTF-16 CODE UNITS (0 to 65535); fromCodePoint() with Unicode CODE POINTS (0 to 0x10FFFF)
console.log(String.fromCharCode(65));                 // → A
console.log(String.fromCodePoint(128512));            // → 😀
  • What happens: each argument is a Unicode code point (decimal or hex 0x…) and becomes one character, even above 65535.
  • Output: ☃, 😁, 😀😂, A, B, ABC, A, 😀, 😀, A, 😀.
  • ✅ The correct way to build emoji and any Unicode character from numbers.
Example 2: invalid values → RangeError
// INVALID STRING VALUE: "-" can't be converted to a valid numeric code point.
console.log(String.fromCodePoint("-"));               // ❌ RangeError: Invalid code point NaN
// ✔ (verified in Node) this line THROWS, and an uncaught error stops the file, so none of the
//    following examples ever run. Wrap each invalid case in try { … } catch (e) { console.log(e.name) }.
// STRING "INFINITY": "infinity" is a string that can't be converted to a number (IMPORTANT: "infinity" ≠ Infinity)
console.log(String.fromCodePoint("infinity"));        // ❌ RangeError
// ACTUAL INFINITY: not a valid Unicode code point.
console.log(String.fromCodePoint(Infinity));          // ❌ RangeError
// NEGATIVE CODE POINT: Unicode code points can't be negative.
console.log(String.fromCodePoint(-1));                // ❌ RangeError
// DECIMAL VALUE: code points must be INTEGERS; 3.14 isn't.
console.log(String.fromCodePoint(3.14));              // ❌ RangeError
// ZERO: "\u0000" (0 is a valid Unicode code point).
console.log(String.fromCodePoint(0));
// MAXIMUM VALID CODE POINT: 0x10FFFF
console.log(String.fromCodePoint(0x10FFFF));          // → "􏿿"
// ABOVE THE MAXIMUM: 0x110000 > 0x10FFFF
console.log(String.fromCodePoint(0x110000));          // ❌ RangeError
  • What happens: "-" and "infinity" become NaN, and NaN, Infinity, negatives, decimals and anything above 0x10FFFF are not valid code points, so each throws RangeError. 0 and 0x10FFFF are the valid limits.
  • Output: RangeError for each invalid line; the FIRST one stops the file.
  • ⚠ Validate or wrap in try...catch when the number comes from user input.
Example 3: no argument, numeric string, more emoji
// NO ARGUMENT: no code points supplied, so an empty string is returned.
console.log(String.fromCodePoint());                  // → ""
// NUMERIC STRING: a numeric string can be converted to a number.
console.log(String.fromCodePoint("65"));              // → A
// EMOJI EXAMPLES
console.log(String.fromCodePoint(0x1F600));           // → 😀
console.log(String.fromCodePoint(0x1F602));           // → 😂
console.log(String.fromCodePoint(0x1F44D));           // → 👍
  • What happens: no code points → ""; "65" is converted to the number 65.
  • Output: "", A, 😀, 😂, 👍.
Example 4: the opposite methods (and a ReferenceError)
// fromCodePoint() + charCodeAt(): charCodeAt() character → UTF-16 code unit
console.log("A".charCodeAt(0));                       // → 65
fromCharCode()   // UTF-16 code unit → character
// ✔ a bare fromCharCode() is a ReferenceError (it only exists as String.fromCharCode)
console.log(String.fromCharCode(65));                 // → A
// fromCodePoint(): Unicode code point → character
console.log(String.fromCodePoint(65));                // → A
  • What happens: charCodeAt reads a code; String.fromCharCode / String.fromCodePoint create a character. The bare fromCharCode() line throws ReferenceError (see the note).
  • Output: 65, ReferenceError, A, A.
Example 5: code point vs code unit
// UNICODE CODE POINT vs UTF-16 CODE UNIT
// IMPORTANT: a Unicode code point identifies a Unicode character; a UTF-16 code unit is a 16-bit unit used by
// JavaScript strings; characters above 0xFFFF are represented by TWO UTF-16 code units in JavaScript strings.
const emoji = "😀";
console.log(emoji.length);           // → 2
console.log(emoji.codePointAt(0));   // → 128512
  • What happens: one code point (128512) needs two code units, so length is 2.
  • Output: 2, 128512.
"-" सारखा चुकीचा code point दिल्यास RangeError येऊन file तिथेच थांबते, म्हणून पुढची उदाहरणे कधीच चालत नाहीत. प्रत्येक चुकीचे उदाहरण try/catch मध्ये लिहा. तसेच String. शिवाय fromCharCode() लिहिल्यास ReferenceError येतो. Important interview points:
  1. fromCodePoint() is a STATIC String method;
  2. syntax: String.fromCodePoint(num1, num2, ...);
  3. it converts Unicode CODE POINTS into a string;
  4. valid range 0 to 0x10FFFF;
  5. it supports code points greater than 65535;
  6. it can create emoji and other supplementary characters;
  7. an invalid code point → RangeError;
  8. a negative number → RangeError;
  9. Infinity → RangeError;
  10. a fractional number → RangeError;
  11. a number greater than 0x10FFFF → RangeError;
  12. no arguments → "";
  13. numeric strings are converted: String.fromCodePoint("65") → "A";
  14. fromCodePoint() doesn't modify the original data.

Golden rule: fromCharCode(): UTF-16 CODE UNIT → CHARACTER (a 16-bit code unit); fromCodePoint(): UNICODE CODE POINT → CHARACTER (the full Unicode code point).

9. Unicode: Code Units vs Code Points (summary)

"😀".length;                  // 2  (two UTF-16 code units = a surrogate pair)
[..."😀"].length;             // 1  (spread / for…of iterate by CODE POINT)
"a😀b".split("");             // ['a', '\ud83d', '\ude00', 'b']   ✗ breaks the emoji
[..."a😀b"];                  // ['a', '😀', 'b']                ✓
"😀".charCodeAt(0);           // 55357 (high surrogate)
"😀".codePointAt(0);          // 128512 (the full code point, 0x1F600)
// reversing a string with emoji: [...str].reverse().join("") rather than str.split("").reverse().join("")
  • What happens: JavaScript handles strings using 16-bit code units. Emojis require two units (surrogate pairs), so string methods like length or charCodeAt may miscount them. Spreading strings ([...str]) correctly iterates over Unicode code points instead.
  • Output: 2, 1, ['a', '\\ud83d', '\\ude00', 'b'], ['a', '😀', 'b'], 55357, 128512.
JS string UTF-16 code units मध्ये साठवली जाते. emoji सारखी अक्षरे दोन units घेतात, म्हणून length 2 येते आणि charAt/charCodeAt अर्धेच अक्षर देतात. पूर्ण अक्षरासाठी codePointAt, String.fromCodePoint आणि [...str] (spread) वापरा.

10. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. slice vs substring vs substr?
  • slice: negative indexes from the end, start > end → "". substring: negative → 0, swaps start/end. substr(start, length): deprecated. All exclude the end and return new strings.
Q2. How do you get the last character of a string?
  • str.at(-1) (modern), str[str.length - 1], str.slice(-1), str.charAt(str.length - 1).
Q3. charCodeAt vs codePointAt; fromCharCode vs fromCodePoint?
  • The *CharCode* methods work with 16-bit UTF-16 code units (0–65535); the *CodePoint* methods with full Unicode code points (up to 0x10FFFF), so they handle emoji correctly.
Q4. Why is "😀".length 2, and how do you count real characters?
  • The emoji is a surrogate pair (two code units). Count code points with [...str].length (or Intl.Segmenter for grapheme clusters like 👍🏽 or family emoji).
Q5. Output-based questions
console.log("Hello word".slice(-5), "Hello word".slice(5, -1));   // → " word" " wor"
console.log("Hello word".substring(8, 3), "Hello word".slice(8, 3) === "");   // → "lo wo" true
console.log("Hello".at(), "Hello".at(-6));                         // → H undefined
console.log("abc".codePointAt(100), "abc".charCodeAt(100));        // → undefined NaN
console.log(String.fromCharCode(72, 105));                         // → Hi
  • What happens: slice handles negative indices by counting from the end. substring swaps arguments if start > end. at() retrieves the first character by default but returns undefined for invalid negatives. Character code methods return raw characters or numbers based on valid index ranges.
  • Output: " word" " wor", "lo wo" true, H undefined, undefined NaN, Hi.

थोडक्यात: slice negative index मागून मोजतो, substring negative ला 0 करतो आणि उलटे indexes swap करतो. शेवटचा index नेहमी वगळला जातो. at(-1) शेवटचे अक्षर देते. emoji साठी codePointAt/fromCodePoint आणि [...str] वापरा.
Quick Revision Summary:
ConceptKey Point
slice(a, b) vs substring(a, b)Both extract parts of a string. `slice` supports negative indices (counts from end). `substring` treats negatives as 0 and swaps arguments if start > end.
at() vs charAt()Both get a character. `at()` supports negative indices (e.g. `at(-1)` for the last char), `charAt()` does not.
Code Units vs Code PointsJS strings use 16-bit code units. `charCodeAt`/`length` count units (emoji=2). `codePointAt`/`...str` count true characters.

मराठी सारांश: JS मध्ये String चा भाग काढण्यासाठी slice आणि substring वापरतात. slice मध्ये negative index चालतो, पण substring मध्ये तो 0 मानला जातो. string चे शेवटचे अक्षर मिळवण्यासाठी `at(-1)` हा सर्वात सोपा मार्ग आहे. Emoji सारखी अक्षरे दोन code units घेतात, त्यामुळे त्यांची अचूक लांबी मोजण्यासाठी `[...str].length` वापरावे.

1. replace()

Your Notes (11-replace.js): syntax: string.replace(searchValue, replacement)
  • The replace() method replaces a specified value or pattern with a new value in a string.
  • It returns a NEW string; the original string remains unchanged, because strings are immutable.
  • searchValue (the pattern) can be a string or a regular expression (RegExp); the replacement can be a string or a function.
  • If searchValue is a normal string, only the FIRST occurrence is replaced. To replace all occurrences, use a global RegExp (/g) or replaceAll().
  • By default, replace() is case-sensitive.
  • If the search value is not found, it returns the original string (content).
Example 1: basic replacement
// Example 1: basic replacement
const text = "Hello World";
const newText = text.replace("World", "JavaScript");
console.log(newText);   // "Hello JavaScript"
console.log(text);      // "Hello World"
  • What happens: replace finds "World" and returns a NEW string with "JavaScript" in its place; text itself is untouched.
  • Output: Hello JavaScript, Hello World.
  • ✅ Simple find-and-replace on fixed text.
  • ⚠ Strings are immutable: you must store the result (text = text.replace(...)).
Example 2: only the first occurrence is replaced
// Example 2: only the first occurrence is replaced
const text1 = "Hello World World";
console.log(text1.replace("World", "JavaScript"));   // → Hello JavaScript World
  • What happens: with a STRING pattern, replace changes only the first match and stops.
  • Output: Hello JavaScript World.
  • ⚠ Most common bug: expecting all matches to change. Use replaceAll or /World/g.
Example 3: replace all using a global RegExp
// Example 3: replace all using a global RegExp
const text2 = "Hello World World";
console.log(text2.replace(/World/g, "JavaScript"));  // → Hello JavaScript JavaScript
  • What happens: the g flag makes the regex global, so every match is replaced.
  • Output: Hello JavaScript JavaScript.
  • ✅ Works in every browser (older than replaceAll).
Example 4: case-sensitive by default
// Example 4: case-sensitive by default
const text3 = "Hello hello HELLO";
console.log(text3.replace("hello", "Hi"));           // → Hello Hi HELLO
  • What happens: "hello" matches only the lowercase word; "Hello" and "HELLO" are different.
  • Output: Hello Hi HELLO.
Example 5: case-insensitive replacement
// Example 5: case-insensitive replacement
const text4 = "Hello hello HELLO";
console.log(text4.replace(/hello/i, "Hi"));          // → Hi hello HELLO
  • What happens: i = ignore case, so the first match in any case ("Hello") is replaced.
  • Output: Hi hello HELLO.
Example 6: case-insensitive + global
// Example 6: case-insensitive + global
const text5 = "Hello hello HELLO";
console.log(text5.replace(/hello/gi, "Hi"));         // → Hi Hi Hi
  • What happens: g + i: every match, in any case.
  • Output: Hi Hi Hi.
  • ✅ Typical for censoring words or normalising text.
Example 7: pattern not found
// Example 7: pattern not found
const text6 = "Hello World";
console.log(text6.replace("Java", "Python"));        // → Hello World
  • What happens: no match → the string comes back unchanged (no error).
  • Output: Hello World.
  • ⚠ You can't tell from the result alone whether something was replaced; compare with the original if needed.
Example 8: empty search string: an empty string matches at the beginning, so the replaceme
// Example 8: empty search string: an empty string matches at the beginning, so the replacement is prepended.
console.log("xxx".replace("", "_"));                 // → _xxx
  • What happens: "" matches at position 0, so the replacement is inserted at the start.
  • Output: _xxx.
  • ⚠ replaceAll("", x) inserts everywhere instead (see replaceAll Example 7).
Example 9: using a regular expression
// Example 9: using a regular expression
const price = "The price is $100.";
const newPrice = price.replace(/$100/, "$150");
console.log(newPrice);   // → The price is $100.   ✗ nothing replaced (verified)
// ✔ in a RegExp, $ means "END OF STRING", so /$100/ can never match. Escape it: /\$100/ → "The price is
//    $150." (In the REPLACEMENT string, "$1" would refer to group 1; with no groups it stays literal, and "$$" is the
//    safe way to write a literal $: "$$150".)
  • What happens: $ in a regex means "end of string", so /$100/ can never match and nothing changes.
  • Output: The price is $100. (unchanged).
  • ⚠ Escape special regex characters: /\$100/. In the replacement, write $$ for a literal $.
Example 10: replace numbers
// Example 10: replace numbers
const data = "My number is 12345";
console.log(data.replace(/\d+/g, "XXXXX"));          // → My number is XXXXX
  • What happens: \d+ = one or more digits; g replaces each number.
  • Output: My number is XXXXX.
  • ✅ Mask phone numbers, IDs etc.
Example 11: replace spaces
// Example 11: replace spaces
const sentence = "Hello World JavaScript";
console.log(sentence.replace(/ /g, "-"));            // → Hello-World-JavaScript
  • What happens: / /g matches every single space.
  • Output: Hello-World-JavaScript.
  • ✅ Build URL slugs: title.toLowerCase().replace(/\s+/g, "-").
  • ⚠ / /g replaces each space separately; use /\s+/g to collapse several spaces into one dash.
Example 12: a replacement function
// Example 12: a replacement function
const numbers = "10 20 30";
const result = numbers.replace(/\d+/g, (match) => {
  return Number(match) * 2;
});
console.log(result);                                 // → 20 40 60
  • What happens: instead of a fixed text, a function receives each match and returns its replacement (here the number doubled; the returned number is converted to a string).
  • Output: 20 40 60.
  • ✅ Lets each match be replaced by a calculated value.
Example 13: capturing groups
// Example 13: capturing groups
const name = "Vishal Shinde";
const result1 = name.replace(/(\w+) (\w+)/, "$2 $1");
console.log(result1);                                // → Shinde Vishal
/* (\w+) → first capturing group, (\w+) → second capturing group, $1 → first group, $2 → second group */
  • What happens: (\w+) (\w+) captures first and last name; "$2 $1" puts them back in swapped order.
  • Output: Shinde Vishal.
  • ✅ Reorder parts of text without splitting and joining.
Example 14: replace using a callback: capitalize each word
// Example 14: replace using a callback: capitalize each word
const text7 = "hello world";
const result2 = text7.replace(/\b\w/g, (char) => {
  return char.toUpperCase();
});
console.log(result2);                                // → Hello World
  • What happens: \b\w matches the first letter of every word; the callback upper-cases it.
  • Output: Hello World.
  • ✅ Classic "capitalize each word" interview answer in one line.
Example 15: replace() vs replaceAll() with a string
// Important: replace() vs replaceAll()
const str = "apple apple apple";
console.log(str.replace("apple", "orange"));         // → orange apple apple   (by default replaces the first occurrence)
console.log(str.replaceAll("apple", "orange"));      // → orange orange orange (replaces all occurrences)
  • What happens: a string pattern: replace changes the first match, replaceAll changes all.
  • Output: orange apple apple, orange orange orange.
Example 16: special replacement patterns ($&)
// Important replacement patterns:
// $& → the entire matched substring; $1 → the first captured group; $2 → the second captured group;
// $` → the text before the matched substring; $' → the text after the matched substring
const example = "Hello World";
console.log(example.replace("World", "[$&]"));       // → Hello [World]
  • What happens: inside the replacement text, $& means "the whole matched text", so "[$&]" wraps the match in brackets.
  • Output: Hello [World].
  • ✅ Highlight search terms: text.replace(/js/gi, "$&").
  • ⚠ Because $ is special here, user-provided replacement text containing $ can behave unexpectedly; use a function to insert raw text.
Example 17: the original string is unchanged
// Does NOT modify the original string
const original = "Hello World";
const replaced = original.replace("World", "JavaScript");
console.log(original);   // "Hello World"
console.log(replaced);   // "Hello JavaScript"
  • What happens: replace returns a new string; original keeps its value.
  • Output: Hello World, Hello JavaScript.
replace() vs replaceAll():
  • replace(): replaces the first occurrence by default
  • can use a RegExp
  • supports a replacement function. replaceAll(): replaces all occurrences
  • supports string patterns
  • supports only GLOBAL RegExps
  • supports a replacement function.

Interview points:
  1. replace() returns a new string.
  2. The original string is not modified.
  3. Strings are immutable in JavaScript.
  4. searchValue can be a string or RegExp.
  5. The replacement can be a string or a function.
  6. A string pattern replaces only the first occurrence.
  7. The /g flag replaces all occurrences.
  8. The /i flag performs case-insensitive matching. 9. /gi performs global + case-insensitive matching. 10.

If no match is found, the original string is returned. 11. An empty search string inserts the replacement at the beginning. 12. replace() supports capturing groups using $1, $2, etc. 13. replace() supports callback functions. 14. Use replaceAll() when you simply want to replace all occurrences.
replace() string pattern असल्यास फक्त पहिला match बदलतो; सगळे बदलायचे असल्यास /g regex किंवा replaceAll() वापरा. replacement मध्ये $1, $2 (groups) आणि $& (पूर्ण match) वापरता येतात, किंवा function देता येतो. regex मध्ये $ म्हणजे शेवट, म्हणून "$100" शोधताना \$ लिहावे लागते.

2. replaceAll()

Your Notes (12-replaceAll.js): syntax: string.replaceAll(searchValue, replacement)
  • The replaceAll() method replaces ALL occurrences of a specified substring or pattern in a string.
  • It returns a NEW string; the original string remains unchanged, because strings are immutable.
  • searchValue can be a string or a regular expression (RegExp); the replacement can be a string or a function.
  • If searchValue is a STRING, all occurrences are replaced automatically.
  • If searchValue is a REGULAR EXPRESSION, it MUST use the global (/g) flag; otherwise replaceAll() throws a TypeError.
  • If the search value is not found, the original string is returned unchanged.
Example 1: replace all string occurrences
// Example 1: replace all string occurrences
const text = "Hello World World";
const newText = text.replaceAll("World", "JavaScript");
console.log(newText);                                    // → Hello JavaScript JavaScript
  • What happens: replaceAll with a string replaces every occurrence, no regex needed.
  • Output: Hello JavaScript JavaScript.
  • ✅ Clearer than replace(/…/g) and no need to escape special characters.
Example 2: the original string remains unchanged
// Example 2: the original string remains unchanged
console.log(text);                                       // → Hello World World
  • What happens: the original text was not changed by replaceAll.
  • Output: Hello World World.
Example 3: pattern not found
// Example 3: pattern not found
console.log("Hello World".replaceAll("Java", "Python")); // → Hello World
  • What happens: nothing to replace → same text.
  • Output: Hello World.
Example 4: using a regular expression
// Example 4: using a regular expression
console.log("abc".replaceAll(/b/g, "."));                // → a.c
// IMPORTANT: the RegExp MUST have /g
// console.log("abc".replaceAll(/b/, "."));
// TypeError: String.prototype.replaceAll called with a non-global RegExp argument
// Correct:
console.log("abc".replaceAll(/b/g, "."));                // "a.c"
  • What happens: a regex is allowed only with g; without g replaceAll throws a TypeError (on purpose, to avoid confusion).
  • Output: a.c, a.c.
  • ⚠ "abc".replaceAll(/b/, ".") → TypeError.
Example 5: case-sensitive
// Example 5: case-sensitive
const str = "Hello hello HELLO";
console.log(str.replaceAll("hello", "Hi"));              // → Hello Hi HELLO
  • What happens: string patterns are case-sensitive.
  • Output: Hello Hi HELLO.
Example 6: case-insensitive using a RegExp
// Example 6: case-insensitive using a RegExp
console.log(str.replaceAll(/hello/gi, "Hi"));            // → Hi Hi Hi
  • What happens: use a regex with g and i for case-insensitive replace-all.
  • Output: Hi Hi Hi.
Example 7: empty string
// Example 7: empty string
console.log("abc".replaceAll("", "-"));                  // → -a-b-c-
/* Unlike replace("", value): replace() inserts the replacement only at the first empty position;
   replaceAll() replaces every empty-string position. */
  • What happens: "" matches before every character and at the end, so "-" is inserted 4 times.
  • Output: -a-b-c-.
  • ⚠ replace("", "-") would give only "-abc".
Example 8: a replacement function
// Example 8: a replacement function
const numbers = "10 20 30";
const result = numbers.replaceAll(/\d+/g, (match) => {
  return Number(match) * 2;
});
console.log(result);                                     // → 20 40 60
  • What happens: the callback receives each matched number and returns it doubled.
  • Output: 20 40 60.
Example 9: replace() vs replaceAll() vs replace(/g)
// replace() vs replaceAll()
const value = "apple apple apple";
console.log(value.replace("apple", "orange"));           // → orange apple apple
console.log(value.replaceAll("apple", "orange"));        // → orange orange orange
// replace() with a global regex
console.log(value.replace(/apple/g, "orange"));          // → orange orange orange
  • What happens: replace(string) → first only; replaceAll(string) → all; replace(/apple/g) → all as well.
  • Output: orange apple apple, orange orange orange, orange orange orange.
  • ✅ Interview summary: replaceAll(str) = replace(/escapedStr/g).
replace() vs replaceAll(): replace():
  1. replaces only the FIRST occurrence when searchValue is a string;
  2. can replace all occurrences using a RegExp with /g;
  3. the RegExp does NOT require the global flag. replaceAll(): 1. replaces ALL occurrences automatically when searchValue is a string; 2. a RegExp MUST have the global (/g) flag; 3. returns a new string;
  4. the original string remains unchanged.
CallResult
replace("apple", "orange")Only the first occurrence
replace(/apple/g, "orange")All occurrences
replaceAll("apple", "orange")All occurrences
replaceAll(/apple/g, "orange")All occurrences
replaceAll(/apple/, "orange")TypeError (missing /g)

3. toLowerCase() & toUpperCase()

Your Notes (16-toLowerCase.js): syntax: string.toLowerCase()
  • The toLowerCase() method converts all uppercase characters in a string into lowercase characters.
  • It returns a NEW string; it does NOT modify the original string, because JavaScript strings are immutable.
  • Characters that are already lowercase remain unchanged; numbers, spaces and special characters are not affected.
  • toLowerCase() takes no arguments.
  • It is useful for case-insensitive comparisons.
Example 1: basic toLowerCase()
// # Example 1: basic usage
let str = "VISHal Shinde";
const newStr = str.toLowerCase();
console.log("New String:", newStr);          // → New String: vishal shinde
console.log("Original String:", str);        // → Original String: VISHal Shinde
  • What happens: every upper-case letter becomes lower case; the original variable keeps its value.
  • Output: New String: vishal shinde, Original String: VISHal Shinde.
Example 2: already lowercase
// # Example 2: already lowercase: it remains unchanged.
const str1 = "hello world";
console.log(str1.toLowerCase());             // "hello world"
  • What happens: nothing to change, the same text comes back.
  • Output: hello world.
Example 3: numbers and symbols stay the same
// # Example 3: numbers and special characters remain unchanged.
const str2 = "HELLO 123! @JavaScript";
console.log(str2.toLowerCase());             // → hello 123! @javascript
  • What happens: only letters have a case; digits and symbols are copied as they are.
  • Output: hello 123! @javascript.
Example 4: case-insensitive comparison
// # Example 4: case-insensitive comparison
const input = "HELLO";
const expected = "hello";
console.log(input.toLowerCase() === expected.toLowerCase());   // → true
  • What happens: lower-case both sides, then compare.
  • Output: true.
  • ✅ Standard way to compare user input (emails, usernames).
  • ⚠ For non-English text use localeCompare with sensitivity: "base".
Example 5: search ignoring case
// # Example 5: search ignoring case
const text = "Hello JavaScript";
console.log(text.toLowerCase().includes("javascript".toLowerCase()));   // → true
  • What happens: lower-case both the text and the search word before includes.
  • Output: true.
Example 6: the original is not modified + toLocaleLowerCase
// # the original string is not modified
const original = "HELLO";
const lower = original.toLowerCase();
console.log(original);   // → HELLO
console.log(lower);      // → hello
// # toLowerCase() vs toLocaleLowerCase(): toLowerCase() → converts to lowercase using the default Unicode rules;
//   toLocaleLowerCase() → converts based on locale-specific rules. For normal use, toLowerCase() is commonly used.
  • What happens: toLowerCase returns a new string. toLocaleLowerCase follows language rules (e.g. Turkish "I" → "ı").
  • Output: HELLO, hello.
Interview points:
  1. toLowerCase() converts uppercase characters to lowercase;
  2. returns a new string;
  3. doesn't modify the original string;
  4. strings are immutable in JavaScript;
  5. numbers and special characters are unaffected;
  6. takes no arguments;
  7. commonly used for case-insensitive comparison.

Your Notes (17-toUpperCase.js): syntax string.toUpperCase(): converts all lowercase characters in a string into uppercase characters; returns a NEW string; doesn't modify the original string (strings in JavaScript are immutable); characters that are already uppercase remain unchanged; numbers, spaces and special characters are not affected; takes no arguments; commonly used for case-insensitive comparisons.
Example 1: basic usage
// # Example 1: basic usage
let str = "vishal shinde";
const newStr = str.toUpperCase();
console.log("New String:", newStr);        // → New String: VISHAL SHINDE
console.log("Original String:", str);      // → Original String: vishal shinde
  • What happens: every lower-case letter becomes upper case; str is unchanged.
  • Output: New String: VISHAL SHINDE, Original String: vishal shinde.
Example 2: mixed case
// # Example 2: mixed case
const str1 = "JavaScript Is Awesome!";
console.log(str1.toUpperCase());           // → JAVASCRIPT IS AWESOME!
  • What happens: mixed case text becomes fully upper case.
  • Output: JAVASCRIPT IS AWESOME!.
Example 3: numbers and special characters remain unchanged.
// # Example 3: numbers and special characters remain unchanged.
const str2 = "hello 123! @javascript";
console.log(str2.toUpperCase());           // → HELLO 123! @JAVASCRIPT
  • What happens: digits, spaces and symbols have no case, so only letters change.
  • Output: HELLO 123! @JAVASCRIPT.
Example 4: already uppercase (it remains unchanged)
// # Example 4: already uppercase (it remains unchanged)
const str3 = "HELLO WORLD";
console.log(str3.toUpperCase());           // → HELLO WORLD
  • What happens: already upper case → same text.
  • Output: HELLO WORLD.
Example 5: case-insensitive comparison
// # Example 5: case-insensitive comparison
const input = "hello";
const expected = "HELLO";
console.log(input.toUpperCase() === expected.toUpperCase());   // → true
  • What happens: upper-case both sides, then compare.
  • Output: true.
  • ✅ Works the same as lower-casing both sides.
the original string is not modified
// # the original string is not modified
const original = "hello";
const upper = original.toUpperCase();
console.log(original);   // → hello
console.log(upper);      // → HELLO
  • What happens: toUpperCase returns a new string.
  • Output: hello, HELLO.
toUpperCase() vs toLocaleUpperCase(): toUpperCase() → converts characters using the default Unicode rules; toLocaleUpperCase() → converts characters based on locale-specific rules (e.g. Turkish "i" → "İ"). For normal use, toUpperCase() is commonly used.
Interview points:
  1. toUpperCase() converts lowercase characters to uppercase;
  2. returns a new string;
  3. doesn't modify the original string;
  4. strings are immutable in JavaScript;
  5. numbers and special characters remain unchanged;
  6. takes no arguments;
  7. commonly used for case-insensitive comparisons.
MethodPurpose
toLowerCase()Converts the string to lowercase
toUpperCase()Converts the string to uppercase
toLocaleLowerCase()Locale-specific lowercase conversion
toLocaleUpperCase()Locale-specific uppercase conversion

4. trim(), trimStart(), trimEnd()

Your Notes (18-trim.js): syntax: string.trim()
  • The trim() method removes whitespace characters from the beginning and end of a string: it removes leading and trailing whitespace.
  • Whitespace includes spaces, tabs (\t), newlines (\n) and other whitespace characters (e.g. the non-breaking space).
  • trim() does NOT remove spaces between characters or words.
  • It returns a NEW string; it doesn't modify the original string, because strings are immutable in JavaScript.
  • It is commonly used for cleaning user input or external data.
Example 1: basic usage
// # Example 1: basic usage
let str = "         vishal shinde at post wadGaon sahani        ";
console.log("Length of original string:", str.length);    // → 53
const newStr = str.trim();
console.log("New String:", newStr);                       // → vishal shinde at post wadGaon sahani
console.log("Length of trimmed string:", newStr.length);  // → 36
  • What happens: trim removes spaces at both ends; length shows how many were removed (53 → 36).
  • Output: 53, the text without outer spaces, 36.
  • ✅ Always trim form input before validating or saving.
Example 2: spaces inside the string are not removed: trim() only removes whitespace from t
// # Example 2: spaces inside the string are not removed: trim() only removes whitespace from the beginning ← and
//   the end →; it does NOT remove spaces in the middle.
const text = "   Hello     World   ";
console.log(text.trim());       // → "Hello     World"
  • What happens: only leading and trailing whitespace is removed; inner spaces stay.
  • Output: "Hello World".
  • ⚠ To collapse inner spaces: .replace(/\s+/g, " ").
Example 3: tabs and newlines
// # Example 3: tabs and newlines
const value = "\n\t   Hello World   \t\n";
console.log(value.trim());      // → "Hello World"
  • What happens: trim also removes tabs (\t) and newlines (\n), not just spaces.
  • Output: "Hello World".
Example 4: the original string is not modified
// # Example 4: the original string is not modified
const original = "   JavaScript   ";
const trimmed = original.trim();
console.log(original);          // → "   JavaScript   "
console.log(trimmed);           // → "JavaScript"
  • What happens: trim returns a new string.
  • Output: " JavaScript ", "JavaScript".
Example 5: a string with only whitespace
// # Example 5: a string with only whitespace
const spaces = "      ";
console.log(spaces.trim());           // → ""
console.log(spaces.trim().length);    // → 0
  • What happens: a string of only spaces becomes "".
  • Output: "", 0.
  • ✅ Check for empty input with if (!value.trim()).
Example 6: empty string
// # Example 6: empty string
console.log("".trim());               // → ""
  • What happens: nothing to remove.
  • Output: "".
Example 7: no whitespace: if there's no leading or trailing whitespace, trim() returns the
// # Example 7: no whitespace: if there's no leading or trailing whitespace, trim() returns the same content in a new string value
const word = "JavaScript";
console.log(word.trim());             // → JavaScript
  • What happens: no outer whitespace → same content.
  • Output: JavaScript.
trimStart() and trimEnd()
// # trimStart() and trimEnd()
// trimStart() ==> removes whitespace only from the beginning
const startExample = "   Hello World   ";
console.log(startExample.trimStart());   // → "Hello World   "
// trimEnd() ==> removes whitespace only from the end
const endExample = "   Hello World   ";
console.log(endExample.trimEnd());       // → "   Hello World"
  • What happens: trimStart removes only the leading spaces, trimEnd only the trailing ones.
  • Output: "Hello World ", " Hello World".
Practical example: user input
// # Practical example: user input
const userInput = "   [vishal@example.com](mailto:vishal@example.com)   ";
const cleanInput = userInput.trim();
console.log(cleanInput);   // → [vishal@example.com](mailto:vishal@example.com)
// ✔ note: the value contains a markdown link that was copy-pasted from a chat/markdown view; the intended input
//    is just "   vishal@example.com   " → "vishal@example.com"
  • What happens: cleaning an e-mail typed with extra spaces (the value here accidentally contains a markdown link).
  • Output: the trimmed value.
  • ✅ Prevents " a@b.com" and "a@b.com" being treated as different users.
Comparison:
  • trim() → removes whitespace from both the start and the end
  • trimStart() → only from the start
  • trimEnd() → only from the end.

Important interview points:
  1. trim() removes leading whitespace.
  2. trim() removes trailing whitespace.
  3. It doesn't remove whitespace between words.
  4. It returns a new string.
  5. The original string remains unchanged.
  6. Strings are immutable in JavaScript.
  7. It removes spaces, tabs, newlines and other whitespace characters.
  8. If a string contains only whitespace, trim() returns an empty string.
  9. trimStart() removes whitespace from the beginning.
  10. trimEnd() removes whitespace from the end.

Golden rule:
  • trim() → remove whitespace from BOTH sides
  • trimStart() → from the START
  • trimEnd() → from the END.

Your Notes (19-trimEnd.js): syntax string.trimEnd(): trimEnd() removes whitespace characters from the END (right side) of a string; returns a NEW string; doesn't modify the original string (strings are immutable); removes trailing whitespace such as spaces, tabs (\t), newlines (\n) and other whitespace characters; doesn't remove whitespace from the beginning of the string; doesn't remove whitespace between words; if there is no whitespace at the end, the returned string has the same content; trimRight() is an alias of trimEnd().
Example 1: basic usage
// # Example 1: basic usage
let str = "         vishal shinde at post wadGaon sahani        ";
console.log("Length of original string:", str.length);   // → 53
const newStr = str.trimEnd();
console.log("New String:", newStr);                      // → "         vishal shinde at post wadGaon sahani"
console.log("Length of trimmed string:", newStr.length); // → 45
  • What happens: trimEnd removes only the trailing spaces (53 → 45); the leading ones stay.
  • Output: 53, the text with leading spaces, 45.
Example 2: only the end whitespace is removed: the beginning spaces remain
// # Example 2: only the end whitespace is removed: the beginning spaces remain
const text = "   Hello World   ";
console.log(text.trimEnd());     // → "   Hello World"
  • What happens: only the end is cleaned.
  • Output: " Hello World".
Example 3: internal spaces are not removed: the spaces between Hello and World remain unch
// # Example 3: internal spaces are not removed: the spaces between Hello and World remain unchanged.
const text1 = "Hello     World     ";
console.log(text1.trimEnd());    // → "Hello     World"
  • What happens: inner spaces are never touched.
  • Output: "Hello World".
Example 4: tabs and newlines
// # Example 4: tabs and newlines
const text2 = "Hello World   \t\n";
console.log(text2.trimEnd());    // → "Hello World"
  • What happens: trailing tab and newline are whitespace too.
  • Output: "Hello World".
Example 5: no whitespace at the end: there is nothing to remove.
// # Example 5: no whitespace at the end: there is nothing to remove.
const text3 = "Hello World";
console.log(text3.trimEnd());    // → "Hello World"
  • What happens: nothing at the end to remove.
  • Output: "Hello World".
Example 6: the original string is not modified
// # Example 6: the original string is not modified
const original = "Hello World   ";
const result = original.trimEnd();
console.log(original);           // → "Hello World   "
console.log(result);             // → "Hello World"
  • What happens: trimEnd returns a new string.
  • Output: "Hello World ", "Hello World".
trim(), trimStart(), trimEnd()
// # trim(), trimStart(), trimEnd()
// 1. trim() → removes whitespace from BOTH the beginning and the end.
// 2. trimStart() → removes whitespace from the BEGINNING.
// 3. trimEnd() → removes whitespace from the END.
const value = "   Hello World   ";
console.log(value.trim());       // → "Hello World"
console.log(value.trimStart());  // → "Hello World   "
console.log(value.trimEnd());    // → "   Hello World"
  • What happens: one string, three methods: both ends, start only, end only.
  • Output: "Hello World", "Hello World ", " Hello World".
trimRight() ==> trimRight() is an alias of trimEnd() ==> both produce the same resul
// # trimRight() ==> trimRight() is an alias of trimEnd() ==> both produce the same result.
const value1 = "Hello World   ";
console.log(value1.trimEnd());   // → "Hello World"
console.log(value1.trimRight()); // → "Hello World"
  • What happens: trimRight is the old name of trimEnd (and trimLeft of trimStart); they behave the same.
  • Output: "Hello World" twice.
  • ⚠ Prefer the standard names trimStart/trimEnd in new code.
Important interview points (trimEnd):
  1. trimEnd() removes trailing whitespace.
  2. Trailing means whitespace at the END / RIGHT side.
  3. It returns a new string.
  4. It doesn't modify the original string.
  5. Strings are immutable.
  6. It doesn't remove whitespace from the beginning.
  7. It doesn't remove whitespace between words.
  8. trimRight() is an alias of trimEnd().
  9. trimEnd() can remove spaces, tabs, newlines and other whitespace characters from the end.
  10. If there is no whitespace at the end of the string, trimEnd() returns the same string content unchanged.

5. padEnd() & padStart()

Your Notes (21-padEnd.js): syntax: string.padEnd(targetLength [, padString])
  • padEnd() adds padding characters to the END (right side) of a string until the string reaches the specified targetLength.
  • It returns a NEW string; it doesn't modify the original string, because strings are immutable.
  • targetLength specifies the DESIRED FINAL LENGTH of the string; padString specifies the string/characters used for padding.
  • If padString is not provided, a SPACE (" ") is used by default.
  • padString can be repeated multiple times if required; if padString is longer than the remaining required length, it is truncated to make the final string exactly targetLength.
  • If targetLength is less than or equal to the current string length, no padding is added and the string is returned unchanged.
  • Padding is always added at the END / RIGHT side of the string.
Example 1: basic padding: "Hello" length = 5, targetLength = 10, required padding = 10 - 5
// # Example 1: basic padding: "Hello" length = 5, targetLength = 10, required padding = 10 - 5 = 5
const str = "Hello";
console.log(str.padEnd(10));          // → "Hello     "
console.log(str.padEnd(10, "!"));     // → Hello!!!!!
  • What happens: padEnd adds characters at the END until the length is 10 (5 needed). Default pad is a space.
  • Output: "Hello ", Hello!!!!!.
  • ✅ Fixed-width columns in console/text output.
Example 2: padding with a specific string
// # Example 2: padding with a specific string
const str1 = "123";
console.log(str1.padEnd(8, "0"));     // → 12300000
console.log(str1.padEnd(8, "abc"));   // → 123abcab
/* "123" length = 3, targetLength = 8, required padding = 8 - 3 = 5, padString = "abc" is repeated: abcabc…;
   only 5 characters are required: abcab; therefore "123" + "abcab" → "123abcab" */
  • What happens: the pad string is repeated and cut to fit: 5 characters needed → "00000" or "abcab".
  • Output: 12300000, 123abcab.
Example 3: targetLength less than the string length
// # Example 3: targetLength less than the string length
const str2 = "Hello, World!";
console.log(str2.padEnd(5));          // → Hello, World!
/* current string length = 13, targetLength = 5: since targetLength is less than the current string length, no padding is
   added; the string is returned unchanged. */
  • What happens: targetLength (5) is smaller than the length (13), so nothing is added and nothing is cut.
  • Output: Hello, World!.
  • ⚠ padEnd never shortens a string; use slice for that.
Example 4: targetLength equal to the string length ==> current length 5, targetLength 5
// # Example 4: targetLength equal to the string length ==> current length 5, targetLength 5, no padding is required.
const str3 = "Hello";
console.log(str3.padEnd(5, "!"));     // → Hello
  • What happens: already at the target length.
  • Output: Hello.
Example 5: default padString: if padString isn't provided, a SPACE (" ") is used by defaul
// # Example 5: default padString: if padString isn't provided, a SPACE (" ") is used by default.
const str4 = "Hello";
console.log(str4.padEnd(8));          // → "Hello   "
  • What happens: no padString → spaces.
  • Output: "Hello ".
Example 6: padString is longer than required
// # Example 6: padString is longer than required
const str5 = "Hello";
console.log(str5.padEnd(7, "abc"));   // → Helloab
  • What happens: only 2 characters are needed, so "abc" is cut to "ab".
  • Output: Helloab.
Example 7: the original string is not modified: padEnd() returns a NEW string.
// # Example 7: the original string is not modified: padEnd() returns a NEW string.
const original = "Hello";
const result = original.padEnd(10, "!");
console.log(original);                // → Hello
console.log(result);                  // → Hello!!!!!
  • What happens: padEnd returns a new string.
  • Output: Hello, Hello!!!!!.
Example 8: formatting data: padEnd() can align text and create table-like output.
// # Example 8: formatting data: padEnd() can align text and create table-like output.
const items = [
  { name: "apple", price: 1.25 },
  { name: "banana", price: 0.75 },
  { name: "cherry", price: 2.50 }
];
for (const item of items) {
  const name = item.name.padEnd(10, " ");
  const price = item.price.toFixed(2).padEnd(5, " ");
  console.log(`${name} ${price}`);    // → "apple      1.25 " / "banana     0.75 " / "cherry     2.50 "
}
  • What happens: padEnd(10) makes every name exactly 10 characters wide, so the prices line up in a column.
  • Output: aligned rows.
  • ✅ Simple text tables, receipts, CLI output.
padStart() vs padEnd(): padStart() → adds padding at the BEGINNING / LEFT; padEnd() → at t
// # padStart() vs padEnd(): padStart() → adds padding at the BEGINNING / LEFT; padEnd() → at the END / RIGHT.
const value = "123";
console.log(value.padStart(5, "0"));  // → 00123
console.log(value.padEnd(5, "0"));    // → 12300
console.log("Hello".padEnd(10, "ab"));   // → Helloababa
// current length = 5, target length = 10, required padding = 5, "ab" → "ababa", final result "Helloababa"
  • What happens: padStart adds on the left, padEnd on the right; "ab" is repeated to fill 5 characters.
  • Output: 00123, 12300, Helloababa.
Important interview points (padEnd):
  1. padEnd() adds padding to the END / RIGHT side.
  2. targetLength represents the DESIRED FINAL LENGTH, not the number of characters to add.
  3. It returns a new string.
  4. It doesn't modify the original string.
  5. Strings are immutable.
  6. If targetLength is less than or equal to the current string length, no padding is added.
  7. If padString is not provided, a SPACE (" ") is used.
  8. padString can be repeated when more padding is required.
  9. If padString is longer than the remaining required length, it is truncated.
  10. padEnd() is useful for formatting and aligning text.

Note: targetLength is converted to a number; if targetLength is 0 or negative, no padding is added; if targetLength is NaN, it is treated like 0; if targetLength is a decimal, it is converted to an integer; if padString is an empty string, no padding is added; if padString is omitted or undefined, spaces are used; null as padString is converted to "null"; padEnd() works with multi-character strings, not just a single character; Unicode/emoji edge case: targetLength is based on JavaScript string length (UTF-16 code units), not necessarily what a user sees as characters; padString is repeated as many times as necessary and truncated if required to reach exactly targetLength; targetLength is NOT the number of padding characters, it is the final length of the entire string: padEnd(targetLength, padString) → final length, what to add.
Quick memory trick: padStart() → padding → start/left; padEnd() → padding → end/right. Important difference: targetLength → the final desired length of the string; padString → the character/string used to fill the remaining space.
Your Notes (22-padStart.js): syntax string.padStart(targetLength [, padString]): padStart() adds padding characters to the START (left side) of a string until the string reaches the specified targetLength; it returns a NEW string; it doesn't modify the original string (strings are immutable); targetLength specifies the DESIRED FINAL LENGTH of the string; padString specifies the string/characters used for padding; if padString is not provided, a SPACE (" ") is used by default; padString can be repeated multiple times if required; if padString is longer than the remaining required length, it is truncated to make the final string exactly targetLength; if targetLength is less than or equal to the current string length, no padding is added and the string is returned unchanged; padding is always added at the START / LEFT side of the string; both padStart() and padEnd() are non-mutating methods.
Example 1: basic padding
// # Example 1: basic padding

console.log(str.padStart(3, "0"));           // → 005
console.log(str.padStart(5, "x"));           // → xxxx5
  • What happens: padStart adds characters at the START until the target length.
  • Output: 005, xxxx5.
  • ✅ Leading zeros: invoice numbers, dates, times.
Example 2: targetLength less than the string length
// # Example 2: targetLength less than the string length
let st = "Hello";
let paddedStr = st.padStart(3, "*");
console.log(paddedStr);                      // → Hello
/* current string length = 5, targetLength = 3: since targetLength is less than the current string length, no padding is
   added; the original string content is returned unchanged. */
  • What happens: target 3 < length 5 → unchanged.
  • Output: Hello.
Example 3: default padding: if padString is not provided, a SPACE (" ") is used by default
// # Example 3: default padding: if padString is not provided, a SPACE (" ") is used by default.
const str1 = "hello";
console.log(str1.padStart(10));              // → "     hello"
  • What happens: default pad is a space → right-aligned text.
  • Output: " hello".
  • ✅ Right-align numbers in a column.
Example 4: targetLength equal to the string length: current length = 5, targetLength = 5, 
// # Example 4: targetLength equal to the string length: current length = 5, targetLength = 5, no padding is required.
const str2 = "Hello";
console.log(str2.padStart(5, "*"));          // → Hello
  • What happens: already 5 long.
  • Output: Hello.
Example 5: a multi-character padding string
// # Example 5: a multi-character padding string
const str4 = "123";
console.log(str4.padStart(10, "abcdef"));    // → abcdefa123
/* current length = 3, targetLength = 10, required padding = 10 - 3 = 7, padString = "abcdef" repeated: abcdefabcdef…;
   only 7 characters are required: abcdefa; final result: "abcdefa" + "123" → "abcdefa123" */
  • What happens: 7 characters needed: "abcdef" + "a".
  • Output: abcdefa123.
Example 6: padString is longer than required
// # Example 6: padString is longer than required
const str5 = "Hello";
console.log(str5.padStart(7, "abc"));        // → abHello
/* current length = 5, targetLength = 7, required padding = 2, padString = "abc": only 2 characters are required, so
   "abc" is truncated to "ab"; final result: "ab" + "Hello" → "abHello" */
  • What happens: only 2 needed, "abc" is cut to "ab".
  • Output: abHello.
Example 7: an empty padString (can't pad)
// # Example 7: an empty padString (can't pad)
const str6 = "Hello";
console.log(str6.padStart(10, ""));          // → Hello
/* an empty string can't add padding, so the original string content is returned unchanged. */
  • What happens: an empty pad string can't fill anything, so the string is returned as is.
  • Output: Hello.
Example 8: the original string is not modified
// # Example 8: the original string is not modified
const original = "123";
const result = original.padStart(5, "0");
console.log(original);                       // → 123
console.log(result);                         // → 00123
/* padStart() returns a NEW string; the original string remains unchanged. */
  • What happens: padStart returns a new string.
  • Output: 123, 00123.
Example 9: a useful real-world example
// # Example 9: a useful real-world example
const hour = "9";
const minute = "5";
const time = `${hour.padStart(2, "0")}:${minute.padStart(2, "0")}`;
console.log(time);                           // → 09:05
/* padStart() is commonly used for: formatting time, formatting dates, adding leading zeros, formatting IDs, and masking
   sensitive information (e.g. card.slice(-4).padStart(card.length, "*")) */
  • What happens: each part is padded to 2 digits, giving a clock format.
  • Output: 09:05.
  • ✅ Also for masking: card.slice(-4).padStart(card.length, "*") → ************1234.
padStart() vs padEnd()
// # padStart() vs padEnd()
const value = "123";
console.log(value.padStart(5, "0"));         // → 00123
console.log(value.padEnd(5, "0"));           // → 12300
  • What happens: same value, padded on different sides.
  • Output: 00123, 12300.
Edge cases: decimal, negative, NaN, undefined, empty pad
// targetLength is converted to an integer
console.log("Hello".padStart(8.9, "0"));     // "000Hello"
// negative targetLength → no padding
console.log("Hello".padStart(-5, "0"));      // "Hello"
// NaN → effectively no padding
console.log("Hello".padStart(NaN, "0"));     // "Hello"
// undefined padString → the default space
console.log("Hi".padStart(5, undefined));    // "   Hi"
// empty-string padString → no padding: if padString is an empty string, no padding is added.
console.log("Hi".padStart(5, ''));           // → "Hi"
// ✔ the comment said "   Hi"; an EMPTY padString adds nothing, so the result is "Hi" (verified)
  • What happens: 8.9 → 8; negative and NaN targets mean "no padding"; undefined pad → default space; "" pad → nothing added.
  • Output: 000Hello, Hello, Hello, " Hi", "Hi".
  • ⚠ These odd inputs never throw, so bugs stay silent; validate numbers first.
Important interview points (padStart):
  1. padStart() adds padding to the START / LEFT side.
  2. targetLength represents the DESIRED FINAL LENGTH, not the number of characters to add.
  3. It returns a new string.
  4. It doesn't modify the original string.
  5. Strings are immutable.
  6. If targetLength is less than or equal to the current string length, no padding is added.
  7. If padString is not provided, a SPACE (" ") is used.
  8. padString can be repeated when more padding is required.
  9. If padString is longer than the remaining required length, it is truncated.
  10. If padString is an empty string, no padding is added.
  11. padStart() and padEnd() are non-mutating methods.
  12. padStart() is commonly used for adding leading zeros.
  • targetLength → the final desired length of the complete string
  • padString → the character/string used to fill the remaining space.

6. split()

Your Notes (23-split.js): syntax: string.split(separator, limit)
  • The split() method divides a string into an array of substrings based on a specified separator.
  • It returns a NEW array containing the separated substrings; it doesn't modify the original string, because strings are immutable.
  • The separator is optional and can be a string or a regular expression.
  • limit is optional and specifies the maximum number of elements returned in the resulting array.
  • If no separator is provided, the entire string is returned as a single element inside an array.
  • If the separator is not found in the string, the entire string becomes the first and only element of the array.
  • split("") splits the string into individual UTF-16 code units.
  • split() can use regular expressions as separators.
Example 1: split a string into characters
// # Example 1: split a string into characters
const str = "vishal shinde";
const word = str.split("");
console.log(word);                // → ['v','i','s','h','a','l',' ','s','h','i','n','d','e']
  • What happens: split("") breaks the string into single characters (including the space).
  • Output: 13 characters.
  • ⚠ Breaks emoji into halves; use [...str] for Unicode-safe splitting.
Example 2: no separator: the entire string becomes one element of an array.
// # Example 2: no separator: the entire string becomes one element of an array.
const strCopy = str.split();
console.log(strCopy);             // → ['vishal shinde']
  • What happens: no separator → the whole string becomes one array item.
  • Output: ['vishal shinde'].
Example 3: basic usage with a string separator
// # Example 3: basic usage with a string separator
let str1 = "apple,banana,orange";
let result = str1.split(",");
console.log(result);              // → ['apple', 'banana', 'orange']
  • What happens: cuts the string at every comma.
  • Output: ['apple', 'banana', 'orange'].
  • ✅ Parse CSV-like data or tags.
Example 4: using a space as the separator
// # Example 4: using a space as the separator
let sentence = "Hello world!";
let words = sentence.split(" ");
console.log(words);               // → ['Hello', 'world!']
  • What happens: split on a space gives the words.
  • Output: ['Hello', 'world!'].
Example 5: using a limit: limit = 3, so at most 3 elements are returned.
// # Example 5: using a limit: limit = 3, so at most 3 elements are returned.
let str2 = "a,b,c,d,e";
let result2 = str2.split(",", 3);
console.log(result2);             // → ['a', 'b', 'c']
  • What happens: the second argument limits how many items are returned (the rest is dropped).
  • Output: ['a', 'b', 'c'].
  • ⚠ Unlike other languages, the remaining text is NOT kept in the last item.
Example 6: limit = 0: an empty array is returned.
// # Example 6: limit = 0: an empty array is returned.
console.log("a,b,c".split(",", 0));    // → []
  • What happens: limit 0 → empty array.
  • Output: [].
Example 7: a limit greater than the available elements: all available elements are returne
// # Example 7: a limit greater than the available elements: all available elements are returned.
console.log("a,b,c".split(",", 10));   // → ['a', 'b', 'c']
  • What happens: a limit bigger than the number of parts has no effect.
  • Output: ['a', 'b', 'c'].
Example 8: a regular expression as the separator: \d → digit, + → one or more, so the stri
// # Example 8: a regular expression as the separator: \d → digit, + → one or more, so the string is split
//   wherever one or more digits are found.
let strr = "apple123banana456orange";
let resultr = strr.split(/\d+/);
console.log(resultr);             // → ['apple', 'banana', 'orange']
  • What happens: a regex separator: any run of digits splits the string.
  • Output: ['apple', 'banana', 'orange'].
  • ✅ Split on several different separators at once.
Example 9: separator not found: since "," isn't found, the entire string is returned as a 
// # Example 9: separator not found: since "," isn't found, the entire string is returned as a single element.
const data = "Hello World";
console.log(data.split(","));     // → ['Hello World']
  • What happens: separator not found → one item with the whole string.
  • Output: ['Hello World'].
Example 10: an empty-string separator splits the string into individual characters.
// # Example 10: an empty-string separator splits the string into individual characters.
let text = "Hello";
console.log(text.split(""));      // → ['H', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o']
  • What happens: "" separator → individual characters.
  • Output: ['H', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o'].
Example 11: an empty string with a non-empty separator ==> the original string is empty
// # Example 11: an empty string with a non-empty separator ==> the original string is empty; since separator "a"
//   doesn't exist, the result contains the original empty string.
const emptyString = "";
console.log(emptyString.split("a"));   // → ['']
  • What happens: an empty string split by any non-empty separator still gives one (empty) item.
  • Output: [''].
  • ⚠ So "".split(",").length is 1, not 0. Filter empty items if needed.
Example 12: an empty string without a separator ==> the entire (empty) string is return
// # Example 12: an empty string without a separator ==> the entire (empty) string is returned as one array element.

  • What happens: no separator → the whole (empty) string as one item.
  • Output: [''].
Example 13: string and separator both empty ==> special case: an empty string split by 
// # Example 13: string and separator both empty ==> special case: an empty string split by an empty string → [].
console.log("".split(""));             // → []
  • What happens: special case: empty string AND empty separator → empty array.
  • Output: [].
Example 14: consecutive separators create an empty-string element.
// # Example 14: consecutive separators create an empty-string element.
const fruits = "apple,,banana";
console.log(fruits.split(","));        // → ['apple', '', 'banana']
  • What happens: two commas in a row → an empty item between them.
  • Output: ['apple', '', 'banana'].
  • ⚠ Use .filter(Boolean) to drop empty items.
Example 15: a separator at the beginning → the first element is an empty string.
// # Example 15: a separator at the beginning → the first element is an empty string.
console.log(",apple,banana".split(","));   // → ['', 'apple', 'banana']
  • What happens: a separator at the start → an empty first item.
  • Output: ['', 'apple', 'banana'].
Example 16: a separator at the end → the last element is an empty string.
// # Example 16: a separator at the end → the last element is an empty string.
