  • What happens: a separator at the end → an empty last item.
  • Output: ['apple', 'banana', ''].
Example 17: multiple spaces: split(" ") treats every individual space as a separator; for 
// # Example 17: multiple spaces: split(" ") treats every individual space as a separator; for one or more whitespace
//   characters, use a regular expression.
const sentence1 = "Hello    World    JavaScript";
console.log(sentence1.split(" "));     // → ['Hello', '', '', '', 'World', '', '', '', 'JavaScript']
console.log(sentence1.split(/\s+/));   // → ['Hello', 'World', 'JavaScript']
  • What happens: split(" ") creates empty items for every extra space; /\s+/ treats a whole run of spaces as one separator.
  • Output: 9 items with empties, then ['Hello', 'World', 'JavaScript'].
  • ✅ Word counting: text.trim().split(/\s+/).length.
Example 18: the original string is not modified
// # Example 18: the original string is not modified
const original = "apple,banana,cherry";
const newArray = original.split(",");
console.log(original);                 // "apple,banana,cherry"
console.log(newArray);                 // → ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']
  • What happens: split returns a new array; the string is unchanged.
  • Output: apple,banana,cherry and the array.
Example 19: a practical example
// # Example 19: a practical example
const fullName = "Vishal Shinde";
const nameParts = fullName.split(" ");
console.log(nameParts);                // → ['Vishal', 'Shinde']
console.log(nameParts[0]);             // → Vishal
console.log(nameParts[1]);             // → Shinde
// Technically split("") splits into UTF-16 code units, which can behave unexpectedly with some emojis:
console.log("😀".split(""));           // ["\uD83D", "\uDE00"]  two UTF-16 code units → use [..."😀"]
  • What happens: split the full name and take the parts by index. The emoji line shows split("") breaking a surrogate pair.
  • Output: ['Vishal', 'Shinde'], Vishal, Shinde, two broken halves.
  • ⚠ Names with middle names or extra spaces need more care (trim + /\s+/).
Important interview points:
  1. split() converts a string into an array.
  2. It returns a NEW array.
  3. It doesn't modify the original string.
  4. The separator can be a string or a regular expression.
  5. If no separator is provided, the entire string is returned as one array element.
  6. If the separator isn't found, the entire string is returned as one array element.
  7. split("") splits the string into individual UTF-16 code units.
  8. limit specifies the maximum number of elements in the array.
  9. limit = 0 returns an empty array.
  10. Consecutive separators can create empty-string elements.
  11. A separator at the beginning creates an empty first element.
  12. A separator at the end creates an empty last element.
  13. Regular expressions can be used for powerful splitting.

Common interview question: what is the difference between split("") and split()? split("") → splits into individual characters ("Hello".split("") → ['H','e','l','l','o']); split() → doesn't split the string ("Hello".split() → ["Hello"]). 
// extra (verified): capturing groups in the separator are KEPT in the result
"a1b2".split(/(\d)/);          // → ['a', '1', 'b', '2', '']
"a-b_c d".split(/[-_ ]/);      // → ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']
// reverse a string: split + reverse + join
"Hello".split("").reverse().join("");   // → "olleH"
  • What happens: capturing groups in the separator are kept in the result; a character class splits on several symbols; split + reverse + join reverses a string.
  • Output: ['a','1','b','2',''], ['a','b','c','d'], olleH.

7. concat()

Your Notes (25-concat.js): syntax: string.concat(string1, string2, ..., stringN)
  • The concat() method in JavaScript combines (concatenates) two or more strings into a single string.
  • It appends the provided values to the end of the original string and returns a NEW string containing the concatenated result.
  • concat() does NOT modify the original string, because strings are immutable in JavaScript.
  • concat() can accept multiple arguments; the arguments are converted to strings before concatenation (concat() accepts values, not only strings).
  • With no arguments, it returns a string with the same content.
  • + and template literals are more commonly used in modern JavaScript.
  • Be careful: "" + null / concat(null) produces "null" (a string), not actual null.
Example 1: basic usage
// # Example 1: basic usage
const str1 = 'Hello';
const str2 = 'World';
const result = str1.concat(', ', str2, '!');
console.log(result);                    // → Hello, World!
  • What happens: concat joins all arguments to the original string in order.
  • Output: Hello, World!.
Example 2: multiple strings
// # Example 2: multiple strings
const greeting = 'Hello';
const name = 'Alice';
const punctuation = '!';
const message = greeting.concat(', ', name, punctuation);
console.log(message);                   // → Hello, Alice!
  • What happens: several pieces joined in one call.
  • Output: Hello, Alice!.
Example 3: multiple arguments
// # Example 3: multiple arguments
let firstName = 'Vishal';
const newStr = firstName.concat(' ', 'Shinde', ' ', 'Pune');
console.log(newStr);                    // → Vishal Shinde Pune
  • What happens: any number of arguments.
  • Output: Vishal Shinde Pune.
Example 4: the original string is not modified: concat() creates and returns a new string.
// # Example 4: the original string is not modified: concat() creates and returns a new string.
const original = 'Hello';
const newString = original.concat(' World');
console.log(original);                  // → Hello
console.log(newString);                 // → Hello World
  • What happens: concat returns a new string.
  • Output: Hello, Hello World.
Example 5: using an array with the spread operator: the spread operator (...) passes every
// # Example 5: using an array with the spread operator: the spread operator (...) passes every array element as a
//   separate argument, equivalent to "".concat("hello", " ", "Vishal", "!");
const greet = ['hello', ' ', 'Vishal', '!'];
console.log(''.concat(...greet));       // → hello Vishal!
  • What happens: spread passes each array item as a separate argument.
  • Output: hello Vishal!.
  • ✅ Same as greet.join(""), which is more common.
Example 6: concat() with no arguments returns a new string with the same content.
// # Example 6: concat() with no arguments returns a new string with the same content.
const text = 'Hello';
console.log(text.concat());             // → Hello
  • What happens: no arguments → a copy of the same text.
  • Output: Hello.
Example 7: numbers are converted into strings.
// # Example 7: numbers are converted into strings.
console.log(''.concat(4, 5));           // → "45" (not 9)
console.log('Age: '.concat(25));        // → Age: 25
  • What happens: numbers are turned into text and joined, not added.
  • Output: "45", Age: 25.
  • ⚠ Interview trap: ''.concat(4, 5) is "45", not 9.
Example 8: booleans are converted to strings: true → "true", false → "false"
// # Example 8: booleans are converted to strings: true → "true", false → "false"
console.log('Value: '.concat(true));    // → Value: true
console.log('Value: '.concat(false));   // → Value: false
  • What happens: booleans become "true"/"false".
  • Output: Value: true, Value: false.
Example 9: concat(null) does NOT return actual null: null is converted to the string "null
// # Example 9: concat(null) does NOT return actual null: null is converted to the string "null"
console.log(''.concat(null));           // → "null"
  • What happens: null becomes the text "null".
  • Output: "null".
  • ⚠ Watch out when joining values that may be null; use ?? "" first.
Example 10: undefined is converted into the string "undefined".
// # Example 10: undefined is converted into the string "undefined".
console.log(''.concat(undefined));      // → "undefined"
  • What happens: undefined becomes the text "undefined".
  • Output: "undefined".
Example 11: a normal object is converted to its string representation.
// # Example 11: a normal object is converted to its string representation.
console.log(''.concat({}));             // → [object Object]
  • What happens: a plain object becomes "[object Object]".
  • Output: [object Object].
  • ⚠ Use JSON.stringify(obj) to see its contents.
Example 12: arrays are converted into strings ([].toString())
// # Example 12: arrays are converted into strings ([].toString())
console.log(''.concat([]));             // → ""
console.log(''.concat([1, 2, 3]));      // → 1,2,3
  • What happens: arrays are turned into comma-separated text ([] → "").
  • Output: "", 1,2,3.
Example 13: concat() vs the + operator: both produce the same result: first.concat(second)
// # Example 13: concat() vs the + operator: both produce the same result: first.concat(second) / first + second
const first = 'Hello';
const second = ' World';
console.log(first.concat(second));      // → Hello World
console.log(first + second);            // → Hello World
  • What happens: concat and + give the same result.
  • Output: Hello World twice.
  • ⚠ + is faster and more common; concat throws if called on null/undefined.
Example 14: concat() vs template literals: modern JavaScript commonly prefers template lit
// # Example 14: concat() vs template literals: modern JavaScript commonly prefers template literals when variables are involved.
const firstName1 = 'Vishal';
const city = 'Pune';
const usingConcat = firstName1.concat(' lives in ', city);
console.log(usingConcat);               // → Vishal lives in Pune
const usingTemplateLiteral = `${firstName1} lives in ${city}`;
console.log(usingTemplateLiteral);      // → Vishal lives in Pune
  • What happens: both build the same sentence; the template literal is easier to read.
  • Output: Vishal lives in Pune twice.
  • ✅ Prefer template literals in modern code.
Important note: concat() does NOT mutate the original string.
// # Important note: concat() does NOT mutate the original string.
const str = 'Hello';
const result1 = str.concat(' World');
console.log(result1);                   // → Hello World
// concat() means: CONCATENATE: JOIN STRINGS: RETURN A NEW STRING
  • What happens: concat never changes str.
  • Output: Hello World.
concat() vs + vs template literal:
  • "Hello".concat(" ", "World") → "Hello World"
  • "Hello" + " " + "World" → "Hello World"
  • `${"Hello"} ${"World"}` → "Hello World".

Important interview points:
  1. concat() combines two or more strings.
  2. It returns a NEW string.
  3. It doesn't modify the original string.
  4. Strings are immutable in JavaScript.
  5. concat() accepts multiple arguments.
  6. Arguments are converted to strings.
  7. concat() with no arguments returns the same string content.
  8. concat() can concatenate numbers, booleans, null, undefined, objects and arrays after converting them to strings.
  9. concat(null) returns "null", not actual null.
  10. concat(undefined) returns "undefined".
  11. concat() can be replaced by the + operator in most cases.
  12. Template literals are often preferred in modern JavaScript for readability.

8. repeat()

Your Notes (28-repet.js): str.repeat(count)
  • The repeat() method returns a new string containing the specified number of copies of the string, concatenated together; the original string is NOT modified.
  • count specifies how many times the string should be repeated.
  • If count is 0, repeat() returns an empty string.
  • If count is a negative number, repeat() throws a RangeError; if count is Infinity or -Infinity, repeat() throws a RangeError.
  • If count is NaN, it is treated as 0, so repeat() returns an empty string; if count is undefined, it is treated as 0.
  • If count is a decimal number, it is converted to an integer by truncating the decimal part.
  • count can be a value that converts to a number, such as a numeric string.
  • If the requested repeated string would be too large, repeat() throws a RangeError.
✔ file name "repet" → repeat.file चे नाव "repet" नसून repeat आहे.
Example 1: repeat(3), repeat(0), repeat(1), repeat(2)
// BASIC EXAMPLE
const str = 'abc';
console.log(str.repeat(3));            // → abcabcabc
// REPEATING WITH ZERO: count = 0, therefore an empty string is returned.
const str1 = 'abc';
console.log(str1.repeat(0));           // → ""
// REPEATING WITH ONE: the original string content is returned.
console.log('abc'.repeat(1));          // → abc
// REPEATING WITH TWO
console.log('abc'.repeat(2));          // → abcabc
  • What happens: repeat(n) joins n copies; 0 gives "", 1 gives the same text.
  • Output: abcabcabc, "", abc, abcabc.
Example 2: invalid and unusual counts
// NEGATIVE COUNT
// console.log('abc'.repeat(-1));      // RangeError: negative count is not allowed.
// INFINITY
// console.log('abc'.repeat(Infinity));   // RangeError: Infinity would create an infinitely large string.
// NaN is treated as 0.
console.log('abc'.repeat(NaN));        // → ""
// UNDEFINED is converted to 0.
console.log('abc'.repeat(undefined));  // → ""
// DECIMAL COUNT: the decimal part is removed, 2.9 becomes 2.
console.log('abc'.repeat(2.9));        // → abcabc
// NUMERIC STRING: "3" is converted to the number 3.
console.log('abc'.repeat('3'));        // → abcabcabc
  • What happens: negative or Infinity → RangeError (commented out). NaN and undefined → 0; 2.9 → 2; "3" → 3.
  • Output: "", "", abcabc, abcabcabc.
  • ⚠ Interview trap: repeat(-1) throws, repeat(NaN) does not.
Example 3: empty string, original unchanged, multi-character
// EMPTY STRING: repeating an empty string still produces an empty string.
console.log(''.repeat(5));             // → ""
// THE ORIGINAL STRING IS NOT MODIFIED
const str2 = 'abc';
const result = str2.repeat(3);
console.log(result);                   // → abcabcabc
console.log(str2);                     // → abc
// MULTI-CHARACTER STRING: the complete string is repeated each time.
console.log('Hello '.repeat(3));       // → "Hello Hello Hello "
  • What happens: repeating "" is still ""; repeat returns a new string; the whole text (including the space) is repeated.
  • Output: "", abcabcabc, abc, "Hello Hello Hello ".
Example 4: practical use, too large, repeat vs concat
// PRACTICAL EXAMPLES: useful for creating separators.
console.log('-'.repeat(10));           // → ----------
console.log('*'.repeat(5));            // "*****"
// RANGEERROR FOR A VERY LARGE RESULT
// console.log('abc'.repeat(1e10));    // RangeError: the resulting string would be too large.
// REPEAT() vs CONCAT()
console.log('abc'.repeat(3));             // → abcabcabc   used when the SAME string needs to be repeated
console.log('abc'.concat('abc', 'abc'));  // → abcabcabc   used to combine strings/values
  • What happens: build separators/star patterns; a huge result throws RangeError; repeat copies the SAME text while concat joins different values.
  • Output: ----------, *****, abcabcabc, abcabcabc.
  • ✅ Star-pattern programs: for (let i = 1; i <= 3; i++) console.log("*".repeat(i)).
Important interview points:
  1. repeat() returns a NEW string.
  2. repeat() doesn't modify the original string.
  3. count = 0 → "".
  4. A negative count → RangeError.
  5. count = Infinity → RangeError.
  6. count = NaN → treated as 0.
  7. count = undefined → treated as 0.
  8. A decimal count is truncated.
  9. Numeric strings are converted to numbers.
  10. Very large results can cause a RangeError.

Golden rule:
  • repeat(count): count = 0 → ""
  • count >
  • 0 → the repeated string
  • a negative count → RangeError
  • Infinity → RangeError
  • NaN → ""
  • a decimal → truncated
  • a huge result → RangeError. repeat() = "COPY THIS STRING N TIMES".

9. valueOf()

Your Notes (24-valueOf.js): syntax: value.valueOf()
  • The valueOf() method in JavaScript returns the primitive value of an object.
  • valueOf() is primarily useful during the automatic type conversion of objects into primitive values.
  • It is available on many built-in objects such as String, Number, Boolean, Date, Object and Array.
  • For primitive values, valueOf() generally returns the value itself.
  • valueOf() does NOT modify the original value.
Example 1: String valueOf(): for a string primitive, valueOf() returns the string itself.
// # Example 1: String valueOf(): for a string primitive, valueOf() returns the string itself.
let str = "Hello, World!";
console.log(str.valueOf());                // → Hello, World!
console.log(typeof str.valueOf());         // → string
  • What happens: for a primitive string, valueOf just gives the same string.
  • Output: Hello, World!, string.
Example 2: Number valueOf() returns the primitive number value
// # Example 2: Number valueOf() returns the primitive number value
let num = 100;
console.log(num.valueOf());                // → 100
console.log(typeof num.valueOf());         // → number
  • What happens: number.valueOf() returns the number.
  • Output: 100, number.
Example 3: Boolean valueOf()
// # Example 3: Boolean valueOf()
let bool = true;
console.log(bool.valueOf());               // → true
console.log(typeof bool.valueOf());        // → boolean
  • What happens: boolean.valueOf() returns the boolean.
  • Output: true, boolean.
Example 4: String object vs string primitive: new String("Hello") creates an OBJECT; value
// # Example 4: String object vs string primitive: new String("Hello") creates an OBJECT; valueOf() extracts the
//   primitive string value from that object.
let primitiveString = "Hello";
console.log(primitiveString.valueOf());    // → Hello
let stringObject = new String("Hello");
console.log(stringObject);                 // → [String: 'Hello']
console.log(stringObject.valueOf());       // → Hello
console.log(typeof stringObject);          // → object
console.log(typeof stringObject.valueOf());   // → string
  • What happens: new String() creates a wrapper OBJECT; valueOf() unwraps it back to a primitive.
  • Output: Hello, [String: 'Hello'], Hello, object, string.
  • ⚠ Avoid new String/Number/Boolean: new Boolean(false) is an object and therefore TRUTHY.
Example 5: Number object
// # Example 5: Number object
let numberObject = new Number(100);
console.log(typeof numberObject);          // → object
console.log(numberObject.valueOf());       // → 100
console.log(typeof numberObject.valueOf());   // → number
  • What happens: same idea for Number objects.
  • Output: object, 100, number.
Example 6: Boolean object
// # Example 6: Boolean object
let booleanObject = new Boolean(true);
console.log(typeof booleanObject);         // → object
console.log(booleanObject.valueOf());      // → true
console.log(typeof booleanObject.valueOf());  // → boolean
  • What happens: same idea for Boolean objects.
  • Output: object, true, boolean.
Example 7: Array valueOf() does NOT convert the array into a primitive value: it returns t
// # Example 7: Array valueOf() does NOT convert the array into a primitive value: it returns the array object itself.
let arr = [1, 2, 3];
console.log(arr.valueOf());                // → [1, 2, 3]
console.log(arr.valueOf() === arr);        // → true
  • What happens: for arrays, valueOf returns the very same array (not a primitive).
  • Output: [1, 2, 3], true.
Example 8: for normal objects, Object.valueOf() returns the object itself.
// # Example 8: for normal objects, Object.valueOf() returns the object itself.
let obj = { name: "Vishal", age: 25 };
console.log(obj.valueOf());                // → { name: 'Vishal', age: 25 }
console.log(obj.valueOf() === obj);        // → true
  • What happens: for plain objects, valueOf returns the object itself.
  • Output: the object, true.
Example 9: Date valueOf() returns the timestamp in milliseconds; the exact value depends o
// # Example 9: Date valueOf() returns the timestamp in milliseconds; the exact value depends on the time zone /
//   time representation. Date.valueOf() is useful because it converts a Date object into its numeric timestamp.
let date = new Date("2026-01-01");
console.log(date.valueOf());               // → 1767225600000
console.log(typeof date.valueOf());        // → number
  • What happens: for a Date, valueOf returns the milliseconds since 1 Jan 1970 UTC.
  • Output: 1767225600000, number.
  • ✅ Compare/subtract dates: date2 - date1 uses valueOf automatically.
Example 10: automatic type conversion: JavaScript internally converts the Number object in
// # Example 10: automatic type conversion: JavaScript internally converts the Number object into its primitive value.
let numObj = new Number(10);
console.log(numObj + 5);                   // → 15
  • What happens: + needs primitives, so JavaScript calls valueOf() on the Number object (10) and adds 5.
  • Output: 15.
Example 11: a custom valueOf(): here we override valueOf(). When JavaScript converts the o
// # Example 11: a custom valueOf(): here we override valueOf(). When JavaScript converts the object into a primitive
//   value, user.valueOf() returns 25, therefore 25 + 10 = 35
let user = {
  name: "Vishal",
  age: 25,
  valueOf() {
    return this.age;
  }
};
console.log(user.valueOf());               // → 25
console.log(user + 10);                    // → 35
  • What happens: our own valueOf returns age, so user + 10 uses 25.
  • Output: 25, 35.
  • ✅ Control how your objects behave in math (e.g. a Money object).
  • ⚠ Surprising for readers; prefer explicit methods like user.getAge().
valueOf() vs toString(): valueOf() → used to get the primitive value; toString() → used to
// # valueOf() vs toString(): valueOf() → used to get the primitive value; toString() → used to get the string representation.
let number = 123;
console.log(number.valueOf());             // → 123
console.log(number.toString());            // → "123"
console.log(typeof number.valueOf());      // → number
console.log(typeof number.toString());     // → string
  • What happens: valueOf keeps the number; toString turns it into text.
  • Output: 123, "123", number, string.
Primitive values include String, Number, Boolean, BigInt, Symbol, Undefined and Null. For wrapper objects such as new String(), new Number() and new Boolean(), valueOf() returns the corresponding primitive value.
Important interview points:
  1. valueOf() returns the primitive value of an object.
  2. It is commonly involved in automatic type conversion.
  3. String.valueOf() returns the string value.
  4. Number.valueOf() returns the number value.
  5. Boolean.valueOf() returns the boolean value.
  6. Date.valueOf() returns the timestamp in milliseconds.
  7. Array.valueOf() returns the array itself.
  8. Object.valueOf() returns the object itself by default.
  9. valueOf() can be overridden in custom objects.
  10. valueOf() doesn't modify the original object/value.
  11. valueOf() is particularly useful for converting wrapper objects into their primitive values. valueOf() means: "Give me the actual primitive value used by JavaScript during type conversion." (See Chapter 3 for ToPrimitive.)

10. localeCompare()

Your Notes (27-to-local-compare.js): syntax: string.localeCompare(compareString [, locales [, options]])
  • localeCompare() compares two strings in a locale-sensitive manner: it compares the reference string (the string on which localeCompare() is called) with compareString.
  • It returns a NUMBER indicating the relative sort order of the two strings: whether the reference string comes before, is equal to, or comes after compareString.
  • The exact numeric value is NOT guaranteed to be -1 or 1. The important results are: a negative number → the reference string comes BEFORE compareString; 0 → EQUAL; a positive number → it comes AFTER compareString.
  • localeCompare() is commonly used for sorting strings.
  • IMPORTANT: don't depend on exactly -1 or 1; use result < 0, result === 0, result > 0.
Example 1: basic comparison: negative: "apple" comes before "banana"; positive: "banana" c
// # Example 1: basic comparison: negative: "apple" comes before "banana"; positive: "banana" comes after "apple";
//   "apple" and "apple" are equal.
const str1 = 'apple';
const str2 = 'banana';
console.log(str1.localeCompare(str2));       // → -1 (negative)
console.log(str2.localeCompare(str1));       // → 1  (positive)
console.log(str1.localeCompare('apple'));    // → 0
  • What happens: localeCompare returns <0 if the first string comes before, >0 after, 0 if equal.
  • Output: -1, 1, 0.
Example 2: using the result correctly
// # Example 2: using the result correctly
const result = 'apple'.localeCompare('banana');
if (result < 0) {
  console.log('apple comes before banana');
}
// Don't write result === -1, because localeCompare() doesn't guarantee that the result will be exactly -1.
  • What happens: check the sign (< 0), not an exact value.
  • Output: apple comes before banana.
  • ⚠ Never write === -1; other engines may return other negative numbers.
Example 3: case sensitivity: the result can depend on the locale and comparison options, s
// # Example 3: case sensitivity: the result can depend on the locale and comparison options, so don't assume a fixed
//   positive or negative value.
const str3 = 'apple';
const str4 = 'Apple';
console.log(str3.localeCompare(str4));       // → -1 (in en: lowercase sorts first)
  • What happens: in the English locale, lower case sorts before upper case.
  • Output: -1.
Example 4: sensitivity "base" ignores differences in case and accents: apple and Apple are
// # Example 4: sensitivity "base" ignores differences in case and accents: apple and Apple are considered equal
console.log('apple'.localeCompare('Apple', undefined, { sensitivity: 'base' }));   // → 0
  • What happens: sensitivity "base" ignores case (and accents), so they count as equal.
  • Output: 0.
  • ✅ Case-insensitive equality that also works for other languages.
Example 5: accent comparison: with sensitivity "base", accent differences are ignored.
// # Example 5: accent comparison: with sensitivity "base", accent differences are ignored.
console.log('resume'.localeCompare('résumé', undefined, { sensitivity: 'base' }));     // → 0
console.log('resume'.localeCompare('résumé', undefined, { sensitivity: 'accent' }));   // → -1
// with sensitivity "accent", the accent difference is considered.
  • What happens: "base" ignores accents; "accent" counts them.
  • Output: 0, -1.
Example 6: ignorePunctuation: true → punctuation characters are ignored during comparison.
// # Example 6: ignorePunctuation: true → punctuation characters are ignored during comparison.
const value1 = 'Hello, World';
const value2 = 'Hello World';
console.log(value1.localeCompare(value2, undefined, { ignorePunctuation: true }));   // → 0
  • What happens: the comma is ignored, so both strings compare equal.
  • Output: 0.
Example 7: numeric sorting: numeric: true compares numeric parts of strings numerically
// # Example 7: numeric sorting: numeric: true compares numeric parts of strings numerically
//   (without it, lexicographic ordering gives '1', '10', '2').
const numbers = ['2', '10', '1'];
numbers.sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b, undefined, { numeric: true }));
console.log(numbers);                        // → ['1', '2', '10']
  • What happens: numeric: true compares digit sequences as numbers, so "2" < "10".
  • Output: ['1', '2', '10'].
  • ✅ Natural sorting of file names: file2 before file10.
Example 8: locale: the second argument specifies the locale; "de" → the German locale (dif
// # Example 8: locale: the second argument specifies the locale; "de" → the German locale (different locales can have
//   different sorting rules).
const word1 = 'ä';
const word2 = 'z';
console.log(word1.localeCompare(word2, 'de'));   // → -1 (in German, ä sorts with a, before z)
  • What happens: in German rules "ä" sorts like "a", before "z".
  • Output: -1.
Example 9: sorting an array of strings with locale-sensitive rules
// # Example 9: sorting an array of strings with locale-sensitive rules
const fruits = ['banana', 'Apple', 'cherry', 'apple'];
fruits.sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b));
console.log(fruits);                         // → ['apple', 'Apple', 'banana', 'cherry']
// (the default sort() compares UTF-16 codes: ['a','B','c'].sort() → ['B','a','c']; localeCompare → ['a','B','c'])
  • What happens: sort with localeCompare gives dictionary order (apple, Apple, banana, cherry).
  • Output: ['apple', 'Apple', 'banana', 'cherry'].
  • ⚠ Default sort() would put "Apple" first because capital letters have smaller codes.
sensitivity options:
sensitivitya vs A (case)a vs á (accent)
baseequalequal
accentequaldifferent
casedifferentequal
variant (default for sort)differentdifferent
✔ your list was missing the "case" label: the line "Base characters and case are considered, but accents are ignored" describes sensitivity: "case" (verified: "a" vs "A" → -1, "a" vs "á" → 0), and the quote in "a" and "á was unclosed."Base characters आणि case तपासतो, accents दुर्लक्षित करतो" हे sensitivity: "case" चे वर्णन आहे; ते नाव list मध्ये राहिले होते. localeCompare() vs ===: === checks whether two strings have exactly the same value ("apple" === "apple" → true); localeCompare() compares the relative sorting order ("apple".localeCompare("banana") → a negative number). localeCompare() is NOT simply an equality operator.
localeCompare() vs indexOf(): indexOf() → finds the position of a substring ("Hello World".indexOf("World") → 6); localeCompare() → compares two strings according to sorting order.
Important interview points:
  1. localeCompare() compares two strings.
  2. It performs a locale-sensitive comparison.
  3. It returns a number.
  4. A negative number → the reference string comes before compareString. 5. 0 → the strings are considered equal. 6.

A positive number → the reference string comes after compareString. 7. Don't assume the result is exactly -1 or 1. 8. localeCompare() is useful for sorting strings. 9. The locales argument can specify language/locale-specific comparison rules. 10. The options argument allows customization of the comparison. 11. sensitivity controls how case and accents are handled. 12. ignorePunctuation can ignore punctuation. 13. numeric: true can be used for numeric comparison inside strings. 14. localeCompare() doesn't modify the original strings.
Common options:
  • "base" → ignores case and accents
  • "accent" → considers accents but ignores case
  • "case" → considers case but ignores accents
  • "variant" → considers base characters, accents and case
  • ignorePunctuation: true → ignore punctuation
  • numeric: true → compare numeric portions numerically. localeCompare(): string → compare → number
  • negative → BEFORE, zero → EQUAL, positive → AFTER.

11. normalize()

Your Notes (30-normalize.js): syntax: string.normalize() / string.normalize(form)
  • The normalize() method returns a new string containing the Unicode normalization form of the original string.
  • Unicode allows some characters to be represented in multiple ways. For example, é can be represented as a single character "é" (code point é), or as two Unicode characters, "e" + a combining accent (e ́).
  • Even though both look visually identical, JavaScript considers them different strings; normalize() converts them into a standard Unicode form.
  • normalize() returns a NEW string; it doesn't modify the original string, because strings are immutable.
  • normalize() helps convert equivalent Unicode representations into a consistent format.
  • The default normalization form is NFC. normalize() supports four Unicode normalization forms: NFC, NFD, NFKC, NFKD.
  • If an invalid normalization form is provided, normalize() throws a RangeError.
Example 1: why normalize() is needed
// Example 1: why normalize() is needed
const str1 = 'é';
const str2 = 'é';
console.log(str1);                 // → é
console.log(str2);                 // → é
// they look the same visually, but this is false, because internally they have different Unicode representations.
console.log(str1 === str2);                             // → false
// after normalization, both strings have the same Unicode representation.
console.log(str1.normalize() === str2.normalize());     // → true
  • What happens: the two é look the same but one is a single character and the other is "e" + an accent mark, so === is false. After normalize() both have the same form.
  • Output: é, é, false, true.
  • ✅ Always normalize before comparing user text (names, search).
Example 2: default normalize(): the default normalization form is NFC.
// Example 2: default normalize(): the default normalization form is NFC.
const text = 'é';
console.log(text.normalize());                          // → é
console.log(text.normalize() === text.normalize("NFC"));   // → true
  • What happens: normalize() without an argument uses NFC.
  • Output: é, true.
1. NFC (Normalization Form Canonical Composition) combines characters when possible.
// # 1. NFC (Normalization Form Canonical Composition) combines characters when possible.
const nfc = 'é';
console.log(nfc.normalize("NFC"));                      // → é (1 code unit)
  • What happens: NFC composes "e + accent" into one character.
  • Output: é (1 code unit).
2. NFD (Normalization Form Canonical Decomposition) separates combined characters.
// # 2. NFD (Normalization Form Canonical Decomposition) separates combined characters.
const nfd = 'é';
console.log(nfd.normalize("NFD"));                      // → é (2 code units: e + ◌́)
// visually it looks similar, but internally it is decomposed.
  • What happens: NFD splits é into "e" + a combining accent.
  • Output: é (2 code units).
  • ✅ Remove accents: str.normalize("NFD").replace(/\p{M}/gu, "") → "e".
NFC vs NFD: NFC combines characters when possible; NFD separates combined characters.
// # NFC vs NFD: NFC combines characters when possible; NFD separates combined characters.
const value = 'é';
console.log(value.normalize("NFC"));
console.log(value.normalize("NFD"));
  • What happens: same value printed in both forms; they look identical, but their lengths differ (1 vs 2).
  • Output: é, é.
3. NFKC / 4. NFKD
// # 3. NFKC (Normalization Form Compatibility Composition) performs compatibility normalization and composition: it
//   converts compatibility characters into their standard equivalents.
// # 4. NFKD (Normalization Form Compatibility Decomposition) performs compatibility normalization and decomposition.
//   ✔ added examples (verified): "ﬁ".normalize("NFKC") → "fi" (ligature → 2 letters); "①".normalize("NFKC") → "1";
//   NFC leaves "ﬁ" unchanged. "a".normalize("X") → RangeError.
  • What happens: compatibility forms also turn look-alike special characters into plain ones (ligature "ﬁ" → "fi", "①" → "1").
  • Output: see the comments.
  • ✅ Useful for search and usernames, to treat look-alikes as the same.
Example: comparing Unicode strings
// # Example: comparing Unicode strings
const name1 = "José";
const name2 = "José";
console.log(name1 === name2);                           // → false
console.log(name1.normalize() === name2.normalize());   // → true
  • What happens: "José" typed two different ways is not ===, but becomes equal after normalize().
  • Output: false, true.
the original string is not modified: normalize() returns a new normalized string.
// # the original string is not modified: normalize() returns a new normalized string.
const original = 'é'
const normalized = original.normalize();
console.log(original);
console.log(normalized);
  • What happens: normalize returns a new string; original is unchanged (both print as é).
  • Output: é, é.
normalize() एकाच दिसणाऱ्या पण वेगळ्या Unicode रूपातल्या strings (é = एक code point, किंवा e + accent) एका standard रूपात आणतो, म्हणून त्यांची तुलना === ने बरोबर होते. NFC जोडतो, NFD वेगळे करतो, आणि NFKC/NFKD "ﬁ" सारखी compatibility अक्षरे साध्या "fi" मध्ये बदलतात.

12. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. How do you replace all occurrences of a substring?
  • str.replaceAll("a", "b"), or str.replace(/a/g, "b") (escape regex special characters), or str.split("a").join("b") (the old way).
Q2. How do you reverse a string? Capitalize words? Check a palindrome?
  • Reverse: [...s].reverse().join(""). Capitalize: s.replace(/\b\w/g, c => c.toUpperCase()). Palindrome: const c = s.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]/g, ""); c === [...c].reverse().join("").
Q3. padStart/padEnd: what is targetLength?
  • The FINAL length of the result (not how many characters to add); padString is repeated/truncated to fit, and "" adds nothing.
Q4. Why use localeCompare for sorting instead of sort()?
  • The default sort compares UTF-16 codes ("B" < "a", "10" < "2"); localeCompare follows language rules and supports options like numeric and sensitivity.
Q5. Output-based questions
console.log("a-b-c".replace("-", "+"), "a-b-c".replaceAll("-", "+"));   // → a+b-c a+b+c
console.log("x".padStart(3, "ab"), "x".padEnd(0, "y"));                 // → abx x
console.log("a,,b".split(","), "".split(","));                          // → ['a', '', 'b'] ['']
console.log("ab".repeat(2.7), "ab".concat(1, null));                    // → abab ab1null
console.log(["10", "9", "1"].sort(), ["10", "9", "1"].sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b, undefined, { numeric: true })));
// → ['1', '10', '9'] ['1', '9', '10']
  • What happens: `replace` only replaces the first instance, while `replaceAll` replaces all. `padStart/padEnd` fill up to the target length. `split` splits on every match. `repeat` duplicates strings and `concat` converts nulls to strings. `localeCompare` naturally sorts numbers as strings (e.g., 9 before 10) instead of ASCII order (where 10 comes before 9).
  • Output: 'a+b-c' 'a+b+c', 'abx' 'x', ['a', '', 'b'] [''], 'abab' 'ab1null', ['1', '10', '9'] ['1', '9', '10'].
MethodReturnsWatch out
replace / replaceAllNew stringreplace(string) = first only; replaceAll(regex) needs g
toLowerCase / toUpperCaseNew stringUse for case-insensitive compare
trim / trimStart / trimEndNew stringInner spaces stay
padStart / padEndNew stringtargetLength = final length
splitAn ARRAYsplit("") breaks emoji; limit; empty items
concat / repeatNew stringValues become strings; repeat(-1) → RangeError
localeCompareA number (<0, 0, >0)Don't test === -1
normalizeNew stringCompare Unicode text after normalizing
थोडक्यात: string बदलणारे सगळे methods नवीन string देतात (split array देतो). replace एकदा, replaceAll सगळीकडे बदलतो. trim आतल्या spaces ना हात लावत नाही. padStart/padEnd मध्ये targetLength म्हणजे अंतिम लांबी. sorting साठी localeCompare, आणि Unicode तुलनेसाठी normalize वापरा.
Quick Revision Summary:
ConceptKey Point
replace & replaceAll`replace()` changes the first match (unless you use regex with `/g`). `replaceAll()` replaces all occurrences safely using a string.
trim & pad`trim()` removes spaces from ends. `padStart`/`padEnd` add padding until the string reaches the target length.
split & sort`split()` converts string to array. The default array `.sort()` sorts alphabetically; use `localeCompare({numeric: true})` to sort numbers inside strings correctly.

मराठी सारांश: Strings मध्ये बदल करण्यासाठी replace/replaceAll वापरतात. trim सुरुवातीची आणि शेवटची मोकळी जागा काढतो. padStart/End ने string ला ठराविक लांबीपर्यंत वाढवता येते. split ने string चे तुकडे करून array बनतो, आणि localeCompare ने संख्यांचे योग्य sorting करता येते.

PDF Export Ready HTML File: js_string_cheat_sheet.html (file:///d:/IMP/FULL-JS/js_string_cheat_sheet.html) ✔ that HTML file is not in the folder any more; this chapter replaces it inside the master PDF.ती HTML file आता folder मध्ये नाही; हा chapter तिची जागा घेतो.

1. String Basics & Creation

#1. length
  • 📖 Exact Definition: a read-only data property reflecting the number of UTF-16 code units (16-bit units) present in the string.
  • ⚙️ Parameters: none (property access). ↩️ Return Value: Number (a non-negative integer count, e.g. 0, 5).
"Hello".length; // 5
"😀".length;    // 2 (a surrogate pair uses 2 units)
  • What happens: length counts UTF-16 units; an emoji uses 2.
  • Output: 5, 2.
⚡ Edge Cases: "".length ➔ 0; undefined.length | null.length ➔ 💥 TypeError. Read-only property! Assignment fails silently, or throws a TypeError in strict mode (verified: h.length = 10 → still 5; strict mode → TypeError).

#2. Property access []
  • 📖 Exact Definition: accesses the character at a zero-based numeric index using bracket notation. Read-only, because strings are immutable primitives.
  • ⚙️ Parameters: index (coerced to a string property key). ↩️ Return Value: a single-character String if the index is valid; undefined if negative or out of bounds.
"Hello"[0];   // "H"
"Hello"[100]; // undefined
  • What happens: bracket access; missing index → undefined.
  • Output: "H", undefined.
⚡ Edge Cases: ""[0] ➔ undefined; "abc"[-1] | "abc"[100] ➔ undefined; "abc"[undefined] ➔ undefined (looks up the property "undefined").

#3. String() (global conversion)
  • 📖 Exact Definition: the global constructor invoked as a function to perform explicit primitive string coercion on any given value.
  • ⚙️ Parameters: value (any JavaScript value). ↩️ Return Value: a primitive String representation.
String(123);  // "123"
String(null); // "null"
  • What happens: String() converts any value safely.
  • Output: "123", "null".
⚡ Edge Cases: String("") ➔ ""; String(undefined) ➔ "undefined"; String(null) ➔ "null"; String(Symbol("id")) ➔ "Symbol(id)" (does NOT throw, unlike "" + Symbol()).

#4. toString()
  • 📖 Exact Definition: an Object prototype method that returns the string representation of a value; overridden by the primitive wrappers.
  • ⚙️ Parameters: for numbers, an optional radix (base 2..36). ↩️ Return Value: a primitive String.
(255).toString(16); // "ff" (hexadecimal)
  • What happens: number.toString(radix) converts to another base.
  • Output: "ff".
⚡ Edge Cases: "".toString() ➔ ""; null.toString() | undefined.toString() ➔ 💥 TypeError.

#5. Template literals
  • 📖 Exact Definition: strings enclosed in backticks (`) allowing embedded expression interpolation, multi-line strings, and tagged templates.
  • ⚙️ Parameters: expressions inside ${}. ↩️ Return Value: a primitive String.
`Hello ${name}`;   // "Hello Vishal"  (when const name = "Vishal")
`Sum: ${10 + 20}`; // "Sum: 30"
  • What happens: ${} inserts any expression's value.
  • Output: "Hello Vishal", "Sum: 30".
length हा property आहे (method नाही) आणि तो UTF-16 units मोजतो, म्हणून emoji ची length 2 येते. [] ने चुकीचा index दिला तर undefined मिळतो. String() कोणतीही value (null, undefined, Symbol सुद्धा) सुरक्षितपणे string मध्ये बदलतो, पण null.toString() error देतो.

2. Searching Methods

#6. indexOf(): 📖 searches the calling string forward, starting from fromIndex, to locate the first occurrence of searchString. ⚙️ searchString (substring), fromIndex (start index, default 0). ↩️ Number (the 0-based index of the first match; -1 if not found). 
"Hello World".indexOf("o"); // 4
  • What happens: first position of "o".
  • Output: 4.
⚡ Edge Cases: "Hello".indexOf("") ➔ 0 | "Hello".indexOf("", 3) ➔ 3; a negative fromIndex is treated as 0; "Hello".indexOf("e", Infinity) ➔ -1.

#7. lastIndexOf(): 📖 searches the calling string backward, starting from fromIndex, to locate the last occurrence of searchString. ⚙️ searchString, fromIndex (default +Infinity). ↩️ Number (the 0-based forward index of the match; -1 if not found). 
"Hello Hello".lastIndexOf("Hello"); // 6
  • What happens: last position where "Hello" starts.
  • Output: 6.
⚡ Edge Cases: a negative fromIndex is treated as 0 (searches index 0 only); "Hello".lastIndexOf("") ➔ 5 (the string length).

#8. search(): 📖 executes a search for a match between a regular expression and the calling string. ⚙️ regexp (a RegExp object, or a string implicitly converted to a RegExp). ↩️ Number (the 0-based index of the first match; -1 if no match is found). 
"Hello World".search(/World/); // 6
  • What happens: index of the first regex match.
  • Output: 6.
⚡ Edge Cases: ignores the global /g flag; no fromIndex parameter; "Hello".search("") ➔ 0.

#9. includes(): 📖 determines whether the calling string contains the specified searchString, starting the search from position. ⚙️ searchString, position (default 0). ↩️ Boolean (true if found, false otherwise). 
"Hello World".includes("World"); // true
  • What happens: true/false contains check.
  • Output: true.
⚡ Edge Cases: case-sensitive; passing a RegExp throws 💥 TypeError; "Hello".includes("") ➔ true; a negative position is treated as 0.

#10. startsWith(): 📖 determines whether the calling string begins with the characters of searchString at the specified position. ⚙️ searchString, position (default 0). ↩️ Boolean. 
"Hello".startsWith("He"); // true
  • What happens: prefix check.
  • Output: true.
#11. endsWith(): 📖 determines whether the calling string ends with searchString, considering characters up to length. ⚙️ searchString, length (the max length to consider, default str.length). ↩️ Boolean. 
"Hello".endsWith("lo"); // true
  • What happens: suffix check.
  • Output: true.

3. Regex Matching Methods

#12. match(): 📖 retrieves the result of matching a string against a regular-expression pattern. ⚙️ regexp (a RegExp object or a string). ↩️ Without /g: a match Array with details; with /g: an Array of match strings; no match: null. 
"test1 test2".match(/test\d/g); // ["test1", "test2"]
  • What happens: with g: all matched strings.
  • Output: ["test1", "test2"].
#13. matchAll(): 📖 returns an iterator of all matching results, including the capturing groups for every match. ⚙️ regexp (a RegExp object MUST have the /g flag). ↩️ a RegExp String Iterator yielding detailed match arrays. 
const res = "t1 t2".matchAll(/t(\d)/g);
console.log([...res]);   // → [['t1','1'], ['t2','2']] (each with index, input, groups)
  • What happens: all matches with their groups, as an array via spread.
  • Output: [['t1','1'], ['t2','2']].
indexOf/lastIndexOf/search index (number) देतात, includes/startsWith/endsWith true/false देतात. match /g शिवाय तपशील देतो, /g सोबत फक्त सगळे matches; matchAll ला regex असेल तर /g आवश्यक आहे.

4. Extracting & Accessing Methods

#14. slice(): 📖 extracts a section of a string from start to end (exclusive) and returns it as a new string without modifying the original. ⚙️ start (0-based index), end (exclusive end index, default str.length). ↩️ a new extracted String. 
"Hello World".slice(0, 5); // "Hello"
"Hello World".slice(-5);   // "World"
  • What happens: start included, end excluded; negative from the end.
  • Output: "Hello", "World".
#15. substring(): 📖 extracts the characters between start and end (exclusive), automatically swapping the parameters if start > end. ⚙️ start, end (default str.length). ↩️ a new extracted String. 
"Hello World".substring(5, 0); // "Hello" (swaps arguments)
  • What happens: substring swaps reversed arguments.
  • Output: "Hello".
#16. charAt(): 📖 returns the UTF-16 code unit character at the specified 0-based index. ⚙️ index (default 0). ↩️ a single-character String if valid; "" (empty string) if out of bounds or negative. 
"Hello".charAt(1);  // "e"
"Hello".charAt(99); // ""
  • What happens: character or "".
  • Output: "e", "".
#17. charCodeAt(): 📖 returns an integer between 0 and 65535 representing the UTF-16 code unit at the given index. ⚙️ index (default 0). ↩️ Number (a 0..65535 code unit) or NaN (out of range). 
"A".charCodeAt(0); // 65
  • What happens: UTF-16 code.
  • Output: 65.
#18. codePointAt(): 📖 returns a non-negative integer that is the Unicode code point value at the position (handles emojis/Unicode beyond 16 bits). ⚙️ pos (0-based position index). ↩️ Number (the Unicode code point) or undefined. 
"😀".codePointAt(0); // 128512 (0x1F600)
  • What happens: full code point of the emoji.
  • Output: 128512.
✔ "handles 32-bit emojis" → code points go up to 21 bits (0x10FFFF); the point is that codePointAt reads the whole surrogate pair, while charCodeAt reads only one 16-bit half.codePointAt पूर्ण surrogate pair वाचतो; charCodeAt फक्त 16-bit चा एक भाग वाचतो.
#19. at() (ES2022): 📖 a modern ES2022 method returning the character at an index, natively supporting relative negative indexing from the end. ⚙️ index (positive or negative). ↩️ a single-character String if valid; undefined if out of bounds. 
"Hello".at(-1); // "o" (last character)
  • What happens: negative index from the end.
  • Output: "o".

5. Modifying & Replacing Methods

#20. replace(): 📖 replaces the first match (or all matches if a /g regex is used) of searchValue with a replacement string or function. ⚙️ searchValue (string/RegExp), replacement (string/function). ↩️ a new replaced String. 
"Hello Hello".replace("Hello", "Hi"); // "Hi Hello"
  • What happens: string pattern → first match only.
  • Output: "Hi Hello".
#21. replaceAll(): 📖 returns a new string with all occurrences of searchValue replaced by the replacement. ⚙️ searchValue (a string, or a global RegExp with /g), replacement. ↩️ a new replaced String. 
"Hello Hello".replaceAll("Hello", "Hi"); // "Hi Hi"
  • What happens: every match.
  • Output: "Hi Hi".
#22. concat(): 📖 combines the text of one or more string arguments with the calling string and returns a new string. ⚙️ str1, ..., strN (strings, or values coerced to string). ↩️ a new concatenated String. 
"Hello".concat(" ", "World"); // "Hello World"
  • What happens: joins strings.
  • Output: "Hello World".
#23. repeat(): 📖 constructs and returns a new string containing count copies of the calling string concatenated together. ⚙️ count (a non-negative number). ↩️ a new repeated String. 
"abc".repeat(3); // "abcabcabc"
  • What happens: n copies.
  • Output: "abcabcabc".

6. Case, Whitespace, Padding & Splitting

#24. toLowerCase() | #25. toUpperCase(): 📖 converts the string to lowercase or uppercase according to the host locale. "HELLO".toLowerCase(); // "hello" ✔ toLowerCase()/toUpperCase() do NOT use the host locale; they use the default Unicode mapping, the same everywhere. Locale rules are only in the toLocale… versions (verified: "I".toLowerCase() → "i", "I".toLocaleLowerCase("tr") → "ı").toLowerCase locale पाहत नाही; locale चे नियम फक्त toLocaleLowerCase/toLocaleUpperCase मध्ये असतात.
#26. toLocaleLowerCase() | #27. toLocaleUpperCase(): 📖 convert the string to lowercase or uppercase respecting language-specific rules (e.g. Turkish i/İ: "i".toLocaleUpperCase("tr") → "İ").
#28. trim() | #29. trimStart() | #30. trimEnd(): 📖 remove whitespace from both ends, the start only (trimLeft), or the end only (trimRight).
#31. padStart() | #32. padEnd(): 📖 pad the string from the start or end with padString until the target length is reached. "5".padStart(3, "0"); // "005"
#33. split(): 📖 divides the string into an ordered array of substrings by searching for the separator boundary. "a,b,c".split(","); // ["a", "b", "c"]
#34. valueOf(): 📖 returns the primitive string value of a String object or primitive.

7. Static & Modern Methods

#35. String.fromCharCode() | #36. String.fromCodePoint() | #37. String.raw(): 📖 static methods for generating strings from code units, code points (emojis), or raw template literals.
#38. isWellFormed() (ES2023) | #39. toWellFormed() (ES2023): 📖 modern ES2023 methods to test or repair Unicode strings containing lone surrogate units. 
"ab\uD800".isWellFormed();   // false (lone surrogate)
"ab\uD800".toWellFormed();   // "ab�" (replaced with U+FFFD)
  • What happens: a lone surrogate (half an emoji) makes a string "not well formed"; toWellFormed replaces it with �.
  • Output: false, "ab�".
  • ✅ Clean text before sending it to APIs that need valid UTF-16 (e.g. encodeURIComponent).
#40. localeCompare(): 📖 compares two strings in a locale-sensitive order, for sorting algorithms.
#1 ते #40 चे सार: वाचणारे methods (indexOf, includes, at…) number/boolean/char देतात; बदलणारे methods (replace, trim, pad, repeat…) नेहमी नवीन string देतात कारण string immutable आहे. Static methods (String.fromCharCode, String.raw) String वरच call होतात, string value वर नाही.

8. Master Return Values & Edge Case Matrix

MethodExact Return TypeNormal ReturnNot Found / Invalid ReturnPassed undefined / null
indexOf()NumberIndex (0..len-1)-1Searches the string "undefined" / "null"
lastIndexOf()NumberIndex (0..len-1)-1Searches the string "undefined" / "null"
search()NumberIndex (0..len-1)-1Converts to /undefined/ / /null/ ✔ undefined → an EMPTY regex, so it returns 0; only null becomes /null/ (verified: "abc".search(undefined) → 0).
includes()BooleantruefalseChecks "undefined" / "null"
match()Array / NullMatch ArraynullMatches an empty regex at the start ✔ that is for undefined (→ [""]); null becomes /null/.
matchAll()IteratorMatch IteratorEmpty IteratorMust be a global RegExp ✔ the /g rule is only for RegExp arguments (a non-global regex → TypeError); undefined/null/strings are turned into a new global regex.
charAt()StringChar string"" (empty string)Index 0 ➔ first char
at()String / UndefinedChar stringundefinedIndex 0 ➔ first char
charCodeAt()NumberUTF-16 code unitNaNIndex 0 ➔ first code unit

search(undefined) रिकामा regex बनतो म्हणून 0 देतो; match(undefined) [""] देतो; matchAll चा /g नियम फक्त RegExp argument साठी आहे.
Created for Complete Interview Revision.
Figure 25: Grouping all string methods by what they return.

9. Interview Programs, Questions & Revision

Common string programs (all verified in Node):
Program 1: reverse a string
const rev = s => [...s].reverse().join("");                 // rev("hello") → "olleh", rev("a😀b") → "b😀a"
  • What happens: spread splits into characters (emoji-safe), reverse flips the array, join makes a string again.
  • Output: "olleh", "b😀a".
  • ✅ split("") would break the emoji; [...s] doesn't.
Program 2: palindrome check
const isPal = s => { const c = s.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]/g, ""); return c === rev(c); };
isPal("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama");                      // → true
  • What happens: lower-case, remove everything that isn't a letter/digit, then compare with its reverse.
  • Output: true.
Program 3: count vowels
const vowels = s => (s.match(/[aeiou]/gi) || []).length;     // vowels("Hello World") → 3
  • What happens: match all vowels (g + i); || [] handles "no match" (null).
  • Output: 3.
Program 4: character frequency
const freq = s => [...s].reduce((m, c) => (m[c] = (m[c] || 0) + 1, m), {});   // freq("hello") → { h:1, e:1, l:2, o:1 }
  • What happens: reduce builds an object where each character's count goes up by 1.
  • Output: { h:1, e:1, l:2, o:1 }.
Program 5: anagram check
const anagram = (a, b) => [...a.toLowerCase()].sort().join("") === [...b.toLowerCase()].sort().join("");
anagram("Listen", "Silent");                                  // → true
  • What happens: sort the letters of both words; equal sorted strings = anagrams.
  • Output: true.
  • ⚠ Sorting is O(n log n); a frequency map is O(n).
Program 6: capitalize each word
const cap = s => s.split(" ").map(w => w.charAt(0).toUpperCase() + w.slice(1)).join(" ");
cap("hello js world");                                        // → "Hello Js World"
  • What happens: split into words, upper-case the first letter, add the rest, join back.
  • Output: "Hello Js World".
Program 7: longest word
const longest = s => s.split(" ").reduce((a, w) => w.length > a.length ? w : a, "");
longest("I love javascript a lot");                           // → "javascript"
  • What happens: reduce keeps the longer of the current best and each word.
  • Output: "javascript".
Program 8: first non-repeating character
const firstUnique = s => [...s].find(c => s.indexOf(c) === s.lastIndexOf(c));   // firstUnique("aabbcdd") → "c"
  • What happens: a character appears once when its first and last positions are the same.
  • Output: "c".
  • ⚠ O(n²) because of indexOf inside find; use a frequency map for long strings.
Program 9: string compression
const compress = s => s.replace(/(.)\1*/g, m => m[0] + m.length);              // compress("aaabccdddd") → "a3b1c2d4"
  • What happens: (.)\1* matches a character followed by repeats of itself; replace it with the char + count.
  • Output: "a3b1c2d4".
Q1. Which string methods mutate the original string?
  • None. Strings are immutable; every method returns a new value. Even s[0] = "x" and s.length = 0 are ignored (TypeError in strict mode).
Q2. charAt vs at vs [] for a bad index?
  • charAt → "" ; at → undefined (and at supports negative indexes) ; [] → undefined (no negative support: "abc"[-1] → undefined).
Q3. Why does "😀".length give 2, and how do you count real characters?
  • length counts UTF-16 code units, and an emoji is a surrogate pair. Use [...str].length or Array.from(str).length to count code points.
Q4. String(x) vs x.toString()?
  • String() works for every value (null → "null", undefined → "undefined", Symbol → "Symbol(id)"); x.toString() throws a TypeError for null/undefined.
Q5. Output-based questions
console.log("Hello".indexOf(""), "Hello".lastIndexOf(""), "Hello".search(""));   // → 0 5 0
console.log("abc".charAt(9), "abc".at(9), "abc".charCodeAt(9));                 // → "" undefined NaN
console.log("abc".search(undefined), "abc".match(undefined));                   // → 0 ['']
console.log("abc".repeat(undefined) === "", "Hello".substring(5, 0));           // → true Hello
console.log((255).toString(16), String(Symbol("id")), "😀".codePointAt(0));     // → ff Symbol(id) 128512
  • What happens: `indexOf("")` matches at every position including ends. Missing indexes in `charAt` return `""`, but `undefined` in `at` and `[]`. `search(undefined)` looks for string `"undefined"`. `.repeat(undefined)` acts like `.repeat(0)`. `.substring` swaps arguments if `start > end`. `toString(16)` converts to hex, and `String()` safely converts symbols.
  • Output: 0 5 0, "" undefined NaN, 0 [''], true 'Hello', 'ff' 'Symbol(id)' 128512.
GroupMethodsReturns
Basicslength, [], String(), toString(), template literalsNumber / String

Regexmatch, matchAllArray or null / Iterator
Extractslice, substring, charAt, charCodeAt, codePointAt, atString / Number
Transformreplace, replaceAll, concat, repeat, case, trim, pad, normalizeNew string
Convertsplit, valueOfArray / primitive
Static / modernfromCharCode, fromCodePoint, raw, isWellFormed, toWellFormed, localeCompareString / Boolean / Number
थोडक्यात: string कधीच बदलत नाही, प्रत्येक method नवीन value देतो. चुकीच्या index वर charAt "" देतो, at आणि [] undefined देतात. emoji ची length 2 असते, म्हणून खरे characters मोजायला [...str] वापरा. reverse, palindrome, anagram, frequency हे programs interview मध्ये नेहमी विचारले जातात.
Quick Revision Summary:
ConceptKey Point
String ImmutabilityEvery string method returns a new string or a different type (like Array/Boolean/Number). The original string never changes.
length vs Emoji`.length` counts UTF-16 code units (Emojis count as 2). Use `[...str].length` to get the true visual character count.
ConversionUse `String(value)` as it safely converts `null`, `undefined`, and `Symbol()`, whereas `.toString()` throws errors on null/undefined.

मराठी सारांश: Strings कधीही बदलत नाहीत (Immutable); सर्व methods नवीन व्हॅल्यू देतात. Emojis ची length 2 येते, म्हणून खरी अक्षरे मोजायला [...str] वापरावे. null किंवा undefined ला string मध्ये बदलताना String() सुरक्षित आहे, toString() error देतो.
Chapter 9: Regular Expressions (Regex)creating regex · flags · character classes · quantifiers · anchors · groups & named groups · lookahead/lookbehind · greedy vs lazy · lastIndex trap · real validations
CHAPTER 9 INDEX
  1. What is a regex? Creating one & flags
  2. test() and match()
  3. Building blocks: classes, quantifiers, anchors
  4. Groups, named groups & replace
  5. Lookahead & lookbehind
  6. Greedy vs lazy & the lastIndex trap
  7. Real-world validations
  8. Unicode (u flag)
  9. Interview Questions & Revision

1. What is a regex? Creating one & flags

Definition: A regular expression is a pattern that describes text. It is used to search, test, extract and replace text. In JavaScript it is a RegExp object, written as a literal /pattern/flags or created with new RegExp("pattern", "flags").
Example 1: literal vs constructor, and flags
console.log(new RegExp("a+", "g").flags);   // → g
console.log(/x/gimsuy.flags);               // → gimsuy
What happens: both create a RegExp. Use the constructor when the pattern comes from a variable (user input); then backslashes must be doubled ("\\d").
Flags: g = global (all matches) · i = ignore case · m = multiline (^ and $ per line) · s = dotAll (. matches \n) · u = unicode · y = sticky · d = match indices.
⚠ Trap: building a regex from user input without escaping special characters (. * + ? ( ) [ ] $ ^) changes its meaning.
Regex म्हणजे text चा नमुना (pattern). त्याने text शोधणे, तपासणे, काढणे आणि बदलणे सोपे होते. /pattern/flags असे लिहितात; g सगळे matches, i case ignore.

2. test() and match()

Example 2: test() returns true/false
console.log(/cat/.test("concatenate"));    // → true   (found anywhere)
console.log(/^cat/.test("concatenate"));   // → false  (^ = must START with cat)
console.log(/cat/i.test("CAT"));           // → true   (i = ignore case)
What happens: test() checks whether the pattern occurs anywhere, unless anchors (^ $) pin it to the start/end.
✅ Fastest way to validate input (yes/no).
⚠ For full-string validation you MUST use ^…$, otherwise "abc123xyz" passes /\d+/.
Example 3: match() with and without g
console.log("a1b22c333".match(/\d+/g));   // → ['1', '22', '333']
console.log("a1b22c333".match(/\d/));     // → ['1', index: 1, input: 'a1b22c333', groups: undefined]
What happens: with g you get all matched strings; without g you get only the first match plus details (index, groups).
⚠ No match returns null, not [], so write (str.match(re) || []).length.

3. Building blocks: classes, quantifiers, anchors

TokenMeaningTokenMeaning
\d / \Ddigit / non-digit*0 or more
\w / \Wword char [A-Za-z0-9_] / not+1 or more
\s / \Swhitespace / not?0 or 1 (optional)
.any char except newline{n} {n,} {n,m}exactly n / n+ / n to m
[abc] [^abc] [a-z]one of / none of / range^ $start / end
a|ba or b\bword boundary
Example 4: escaping the dot
console.log("a.b".split("."));            // → ['a', 'b']   (split with a STRING: literal dot)
console.log("a.b".replace(/./g, "x"));    // → xxx          (. in regex = ANY character)
console.log("a.b".replace(/\./g, "x"));   // → axb          (\. = a real dot)
What happens: in a regex, . is a wildcard; escape it as \. to mean a literal dot.
⚠ Classic bug: /$100/ never matches "$100", because $ means "end"; write /\$100/ (see Chapter 7).
Example 5: collapse multiple spaces
console.log("  many   spaces  ".trim().replace(/\s+/g, " "));   // → "many spaces"
What happens: \s+ matches every run of whitespace; g replaces all of them with one space.
✅ Very common cleanup for user input and search terms.

4. Groups, named groups & replace

Example 6: capture groups in replace
console.log("2026-10-02".replace(/(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})/, "$3/$2/$1"));   // → 02/10/2026
What happens: each ( ) captures a part; in the replacement $1, $2, $3 refer to them.
✅ Reformat dates, swap names, etc. in one line.
Example 7: named groups (?<name>…)
const m = "2026-10-02".match(/(?<y>\d{4})-(?<mo>\d{2})-(?<d>\d{2})/);
console.log(m.groups.y, m.groups.d);   // → 2026 02
What happens: named groups are available on match.groups by name.
✅ Much more readable than m[1], m[3]; also usable in replace as $<y>.
Example 8: matchAll and a replace callback
console.log([..."x1y2".matchAll(/([a-z])(\d)/g)].map(m => m[1] + "=" + m[2]));   // → ['x=1', 'y=2']
console.log("hello world".replace(/\b\w/g, c => c.toUpperCase()));              // → Hello World
What happens: matchAll gives every match WITH its groups; a function as replacement computes each new piece.
✅ \b\w = the first letter of each word, the classic "capitalize words" answer.

5. Lookahead & lookbehind

Example 9: match only if followed / preceded by something
console.log("price: 100rs, 250rs".match(/\d+(?=rs)/g));   // → ['100', '250']  positive lookahead
console.log("$5 €7".match(/(?<=\$)\d/g));                 // → ['5']           positive lookbehind
console.log("abc1".match(/[a-z](?!\d)/g));                // → ['a', 'b']      negative lookahead
What happens: (?=X) "followed by X", (?!X) "not followed by X", (?<=X) "preceded by X", (?<!X) "not preceded by X". They check without including X in the match.
✅ Extract numbers without the unit; essential for password rules (Example 13).

6. Greedy vs lazy & the lastIndex trap

Example 10: greedy .* vs lazy .*?
const html = "<b>x</b><b>y</b>";
console.log(html.match(/<b>.*<\/b>/)[0]);    // → <b>x</b><b>y</b>   (greedy: as MUCH as possible)
console.log(html.match(/<b>.*?<\/b>/)[0]);   // → <b>x</b>            (lazy: as LITTLE as possible)
What happens: quantifiers are greedy by default; adding ? makes them lazy.
⚠ Don't parse real HTML with regex; use the DOM (DOMParser) instead.
Figure 26: Greedy vs lazy matching on the same text.
Example 11: the lastIndex trap with g + test()
const re = /a/g;
console.log(re.test("aa"), re.lastIndex);   // → true 1
console.log(re.test("aa"), re.lastIndex);   // → true 2
console.log(re.test("aa"));                 // → false   (!) starts searching at index 2
What happens: a regex with g (or y) remembers where the last match ended in lastIndex, and the next test()/exec() continues from there; after failing it resets to 0.
⚠ Famous bug: reusing one /…/g regex to validate several inputs gives alternating true/false. Don't use g with test(), or reset re.lastIndex = 0.

7. Real-world validations

Example 12: email and Indian mobile number
const email = /^[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]+$/;
console.log(email.test("vishal.s@gmail.com"), email.test("bad@com"));   // → true false
const mobile = /^[6-9]\d{9}$/;
console.log(mobile.test("9876543210"), mobile.test("1234567890"));     // → true false
What happens: email = name chars, @, domain, a dot, extension. mobile = starts with 6–9, then exactly 9 more digits (10 in total).
✅ Good enough for quick front-end checks.
⚠ Perfect email validation by regex is impossible; the real check is sending a confirmation mail. Always validate again on the server.
Example 13: strong password with lookaheads
const strong = /^(?=.*[A-Z])(?=.*\d)(?=.*[^\w\s]).{8,}$/;
console.log(strong.test("Pass@1234"), strong.test("password"));   // → true false
What happens: each (?=.*X) checks "somewhere there is X" (an upper-case letter, a digit, a symbol) without consuming text; .{8,} then requires length ≥ 8.
✅ Each rule is independent, so it's easy to add/remove a rule.

8. Unicode (u flag)

Example 14: emoji and Indian scripts
console.log("😀".match(/./)[0].length);    // → 1   (half of the surrogate pair!)
console.log("😀".match(/./u)[0].length);   // → 2   (u: the whole emoji)
console.log(/^\p{L}+$/u.test("मराठी"));     // → false (!)
What happens: without u, regex works on UTF-16 code units, so . grabs half an emoji. \p{L} = any letter, but Devanagari vowel signs (ा ी ्) are MARKS (\p{M}), not letters.
Fix: /^[\p{L}\p{M}]+$/u matches Marathi/Hindi words.
✅ Always use the u flag when text can contain emoji or non-English scripts.
Regex मध्ये \d digit, \w word char, \s space, + एक किंवा जास्त, ^ $ सुरुवात/शेवट. ( ) group बनवतो, (?=…) पुढे काय आहे ते तपासतो. g flag सोबत test() वापरल्यास lastIndex मुळे उत्तर बदलते. मराठी text साठी u flag आणि [\p{L}\p{M}] वापरा.

9. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. test() vs match() vs exec()?
  • test → boolean; match → array (all with g, first + details without g) or null; exec → one detailed match at a time (loops with g via lastIndex).
Q2. Greedy vs lazy?
  • Greedy (*, +) takes as much as possible; lazy (*?, +?) as little as possible.
Q3. Why does a /g regex give alternating true/false with test()?
  • lastIndex keeps the position after each match; the next call starts there. Remove g or reset lastIndex.
Q4. What is a lookahead?
  • (?=X) asserts that X follows without including it in the match; (?!X) asserts it doesn't.
Q5. Output-based questions
console.log("a-b_c".replace(/[-_]/g, " "));             // → a b c
console.log("aaa".match(/a+?/)[0], "aaa".match(/a+/)[0]); // → a aaa
console.log(/^\d{3}$/.test("1234"), /\d{3}/.test("1234")); // → false true
console.log("x".match(/y/));                              // → null
  • What happens: replace(/[-_]/g, " ") replaces all hyphens and underscores with spaces. match(/a+?/) is lazy (matches one "a"), while /a+/ is greedy (matches "aaa"). ^\\d{3}$ strictly matches exactly 3 digits (fails on "1234"), while \\d{3} matches 3 digits anywhere (succeeds on "123"). "x".match(/y/) fails and returns null.
  • Output: a b c, a aaa, false true, null.
NeedRegex
Only digits/^\d+$/
Trim inner spaces/\s+/g → " "
Capitalize words/\b\w/g
10-digit mobile/^[6-9]\d{9}$/
Strong password/^(?=.*[A-Z])(?=.*\d)(?=.*[^\w\s]).{8,}$/
थोडक्यात: validation साठी नेहमी ^…$ वापरा, dot escape करा (\.), test() सोबत g टाळा, आणि Unicode text साठी u flag वापरा.

ConceptKey Point
Regex Flagsg (global), i (case-insensitive), m (multiline), u (Unicode).
Greedy vs Lazy*, + match as much as possible. Adding ? (e.g. *?) makes them match as little as possible.
test() vs match()test() returns a boolean. match() returns an array of matches or null.

मराठी सारांश: Regular Expressions (Regex) हे string मधील pattern शोधण्यासाठी वापरले जातात. test() true/false देते, तर match() मिळालेला result array मध्ये देते. ^ आणि $ वापरून अचूक validation करता येते. Greedy patterns जास्तीत जास्त match करतात, तर lazy patterns कमीत कमी.
