1. Scope

Your Notes:
  • Scope determines the accessibility and visibility of variables.
  • Scope is a certain region of the program where a defined variable exists and can be recognized; beyond it, the variable cannot be recognized. So scope determines the accessibility and visibility of variables in the program.
  • Scope in JS refers to the context in which variables are declared and accessed, so it determines the visibility and lifetime of variables.
  • Scope is the region of a program where variables, functions and classes are accessible.
  • Scope determines:
    1. Visibility (where variables can be accessed)
    2. Accessibility (who can use them)
  • Scope is the accessibility boundary of variables, functions and classes in JavaScript.
Definition: Scope is the region of code in which a variable, function or class is visible and can be accessed. In JavaScript, scope is lexical: it is decided by where the code is written.
Scope म्हणजे code मधील अशी हद्द जिथे variable "दिसतो" आणि वापरता येतो. हद्दीबाहेर तो variable JS ला ओळखता येत नाही. Scope वरून variable कुठे दिसेल (visibility), कोण वापरू शकेल (accessibility) आणि तो किती काळ राहील (lifetime) हे ठरते.

2. Types of Scope

Your Notes:
  1. Functional scope (local scope)
  2. Block scope
  3. Global scope
  4. Module scope (for variables inside ES6 modules)
Figure 27: Nested scopes (global → script/module → function → block). Inner scopes can see outer ones, never the reverse.
JS मध्ये 4 मुख्य scopes आहेत: Global, Function (Local), Block आणि Module. ते एकमेकांच्या आत असतात. आतला scope बाहेरचे variables पाहू शकतो, पण बाहेरचा scope आतले variables पाहू शकत नाही.

3. Global Scope

Your Notes:
  • When the JS engine executes a script, it creates the Global Execution Context and assigns to it the variables that you defined outside any function.
  • So these variables have global scope and are called global variables.
  • A global variable can be accessed anywhere in the program.
  • Variables declared outside every function and block belong to the global scope. They are created inside the Global Execution Context.
let a = "Hi"; // global variable defined outside the function
function Hi() {
  console.log("say", a);   // "say Hi"
}
Hi();
console.log(a); // "Hi" → accessible anywhere in the program
  • What happens: a is declared outside every function, so it is global and readable both inside Hi() and outside.
  • Output: say Hi, Hi.
  • ✅ Shared values (config, constants) can live globally.
  • ⚠ Too many globals clash with other scripts; keep them few.
कोणत्याही function किंवा block च्या बाहेर declare केलेला variable global असतो. तो program मध्ये कुठूनही वापरता येतो. JS script सुरू करताना Global Execution Context बनवते आणि global variables तिथे ठेवते.
Extra Details: Too many global variables are risky. Any code can change them, and names can clash between files ("global namespace pollution"). Prefer function, block or module scope.

4. Local Scope (Function Scope)

Your Notes:
  • Variables declared inside a function have function scope, also called local scope.
  • Variables declared inside a function using let, const and var are confined to that function.
  • They cannot be accessed outside the function.
  • Every function creates a new scope. Variables declared inside a function cannot be accessed outside that function.
  • Inside a function, var, let and const are all local to that function.
function say() {
  var mes = "Hi,"; // declared inside the function, so it has function (local) scope;
                   // it is accessible only within the function
  console.log(mes);  // "Hi,"
}
// console.log(mes); // Uncaught ReferenceError: mes is not defined
//                   // (cannot be accessed outside the function)
say();
  • What happens: mes is declared inside say(), so it exists only while say runs and only inside it.
  • Output: Hi, (the outside log would be a ReferenceError).
  • ✅ Functions keep their working data private.
✔ the commented line used msg, but the variable is mes. With msg, the error would happen only because msg was never declared anywhere, which doesn't demonstrate function scope.तुमच्या comment मध्ये msg लिहिले होते, पण variable चे नाव mes आहे. function scope दाखवण्यासाठी console.log(mes) हवे, तेव्हाच "mes is not defined" error येतो.
Function मध्ये declare केलेले var, let, const सगळे त्या function पुरतेच (local) असतात. Function संपल्यावर ते बाहेरून वापरता येत नाहीत. प्रत्येक function स्वतःचा नवीन scope बनवतो.

5. Block Scope

Your Notes:
  • The let and const keywords allow you to declare block-scoped variables.
  • Whenever you see curly brackets {}, that is a block. It can be the area of an if, else or switch condition, or a for, do or while loop.
  • Variables declared with let and const inside a block ({}) are only accessible within that block.
  • var does not support block scope and leaks into the surrounding function or global scope.
function block() {
  let b = "Hello";
  if (true) {
    let c = "bye";
    console.log(b + c);    // "Hellobye"
  }
  // console.log(b + c); // Uncaught ReferenceError: c is not defined, because c has
  //                     // block scope and cannot be accessed outside the block
}
block();
  • What happens: c lives only in the if-block; b lives in the whole function. Inside the block both are visible.
  • Output: Hellobye.
  • ✅ Block scope keeps temporary variables from leaking.
Extra Details: var leaks, let doesn't 
if (true) { var v = 1; let l = 2; }
console.log(v);   // 1  (var leaked out of the block)
// console.log(l); // ❌ ReferenceError
  • What happens: var ignores the { } block and belongs to the surrounding scope; let stays inside.
  • Output: 1 (l → ReferenceError).
  • ⚠ var leaking out of if/for blocks is a common bug source.
{ } (if, else, switch, for, while) म्हणजे block. let/const ने declare केलेले variables फक्त त्या block मध्येच वापरता येतात. var block ला मानत नाही आणि बाहेर (function/global मध्ये) सांडतो.

6. Q. What are Global Scope and Script Scope in the Browser?

6.1 Global Scope in the Browser

Your Notes:
  • Variables declared with var, and function declarations, outside any function are attached to the global window object. Anything declared outside every function or block is global, but let/const are NOT attached to window. ✔ the original said every variable or function you define is attached to window. Only var and function declarations are; let/const go into the script scope.सगळे global variables window ला जोडले जात नाहीत. फक्त var आणि function declarations window चा property बनतात. let/const script scope मध्ये राहतात.
  • If you define a variable with var outside a function, it creates a global variable in the browser (a property of window).
  • When a browser loads JavaScript using a <script> tag, it creates an environment to run that code.
  • The browser has a global object called window. Anything attached to window can be accessed anywhere in the page.
var city = "Pune";
console.log(window.city);   // "Pune"
// Because a var declared outside a function becomes a property of window.
  • What happens: a top-level var in a classic browser script becomes a property of window.
  • Output: Pune.
  • ⚠ It can overwrite built-ins like window.name or window.status.
✔ the example used var name = "John". window.name is a special built-in browser property (it always stores a string), so it is a misleading example. Use another name, like city.window.name हा browser चा आधीपासून असलेला खास property आहे, म्हणून name हे नाव example साठी गोंधळात टाकणारे आहे. त्याऐवजी city सारखे दुसरे नाव वापरा.

6.2 Script Scope (specific to browser environments)

Your Notes:
  • If you declare a variable using let or const at the top level of a script, it is stored in the script scope, not on the window (global) object.
  • They are global variables, but they are NOT added to window, because let and const create a script scope instead of a window property.
  • (The script tag is how JS files are loaded into an HTML document.)
  • If you create a variable using const or let, it is located in the script scope in the browser (another kind of global scope).
  • The script scope is shared by all classic <script> tags on the same page. A top-level let/const in one script file is accessible in the other script files loaded after it. ✔ the original said "script scope is specific to each JS file" and "each script has its own scope". That is wrong: all classic scripts on a page share ONE script scope. Only ES modules get a private scope per file.प्रत्येक script file चा वेगळा scope नसतो. एका page वरील सगळ्या साध्या <script> tags चा एकच script scope असतो, म्हणून a.js मधील let b.js मध्ये वापरता येतो. प्रत्येक file चा खाजगी scope फक्त module (type="module") मध्ये असतो.
  • Because the scope is shared, declaring the same let/const name in two scripts gives "SyntaxError: Identifier has already been declared". ✔ the original said a script's variables and functions are only available within that script. They are available to every script on the page.दोन script files मध्ये एकाच नावाचा let असल्यास SyntaxError येतो, कारण दोघांचा scope एकच आहे.
  • Think of script scope as a shared global area for let/const, separate from the window object (it is not private to each file). ✔ "a private area created for each <script> file" → a shared area that is separate from window.Script scope हा प्रत्येक file चा खाजगी भाग नाही, तर let/const साठी window पासून वेगळा पण सगळ्या scripts चा सामायिक भाग आहे.
let m = "Hi";        // script scope (global, but not on window)
var d = "GoodBye";   // global scope → window.d
function display() {
  const n = "Hello";
  let s = "bye";
  if (true) {
    console.log(m + n + s);  // "HiHellobye"
  }
  console.log(m + d);        // "HiGoodBye"
}
display();
  • What happens: m (let) is global but stored in the Script scope, d (var) on window. display() can read both, plus its own n and s.
  • Output: HiHellobye, HiGoodBye.
Figure 28: In the browser, var and functions go on window; top-level let/const go into one script scope shared by all classic scripts.
Browser मध्ये बाहेर declare केलेला var आणि function window object ला जोडले जातात. बाहेर declare केलेले let/const "script scope" मध्ये जातात. ते global आहेत, पण window.m ने मिळत नाहीत. हा script scope सगळ्या scripts चा एकच असतो.

7. Module Scope (ES Modules)

Your Notes:
  • Used with <script type="module"> or import/export.
  • Top-level variables belong only to that module.
  • They are NOT added to the global scope.
  • They can only be shared using export/import.
// module.js
export const moduleScopedVar = "I am module-scoped";

// main.js
import { moduleScopedVar } from "./module.js";
console.log(moduleScopedVar); // "I am module-scoped" → accessible here
  • What happens: variables at the top of a module are private to that file unless exported; main.js imports it explicitly.
  • Output: I am module-scoped.
  • ✅ No accidental globals; dependencies are visible in the import lines.
  • ⚠ Modules need type="module" (browser) or ESM in Node.
✔ Note: these lines must be in two separate module files. In your notes file, which is a normal script, export/import cause "SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module" and stop the whole file. Keep them commented out there.export/import फक्त module file मध्ये चालतात. साध्या script file मध्ये ते लिहिल्यास पूर्ण file SyntaxError देऊन थांबते, म्हणून notes file मध्ये त्या lines comment करून ठेवा.
Extra Details: Modules are automatically in strict mode, have their own top-level scope, run only once even if imported many times, and their top-level this is undefined.
Module मधील प्रत्येक file चा स्वतःचा खाजगी scope असतो. त्यातील variables global बनत नाहीत. दुसऱ्या file मध्ये वापरायचे असतील तर export करून import करावे लागतात.

8. Summary & Strict Mode

Your Notes: Summary
  1. Global scope: variables declared outside any function are accessible anywhere in the script.
  2. Local/function scope: variables declared inside a function are accessible only within that function.
  3. Block scope (ES6, let and const): variables declared inside a block {} are only accessible within that block.
Strict mode: in strict mode, assigning to an undeclared variable throws a ReferenceError instead of silently creating a global variable, which makes your code more secure. (Top-level var declarations still become global.)
Example: "use strict"; ✔ the original said strict mode restricts var declarations that leak into the global scope. It doesn't; it blocks accidental globals created without any keyword.strict mode var ला थांबवत नाही. तो keyword शिवाय value दिल्यामुळे (x = 10) चुकून बनणारे global variables थांबवतो आणि ReferenceError देतो.
"use strict";
function f() {
  total = 5;    // ❌ ReferenceError: total is not defined (no var/let/const)
}
f();
  • What happens: in strict mode, assigning to an undeclared name throws instead of creating a global.
  • Output: ReferenceError: total is not defined.
  • ✅ Catches typos early.

9. Differences between Scope and Lexical Scope

Your Notes: Scope
  1. Refers to the region or context where variables and functions are accessible.
  2. Determines variable accessibility and visibility (e.g. global, local, block).
  3. The scope structure is fixed when the code is written; the scope environments (memory for the variables) are created at runtime, when execution enters a function or block. ✔ the original said "scope is defined at runtime and depends on how and when code is executed". In JS, which variables are visible is decided by where the code is written; only the memory is created at runtime.JS मध्ये कोणता variable कुठे दिसेल हे code कुठे लिहिला यावर ठरते, runtime ला नाही. फक्त त्या variables साठी memory (environment) code चालताना बनते.
  4. The environments are managed by execution contexts.
  5. Variables are declared using var, let and const.
  6. Dynamic in terms of entering or exiting during execution (a scope's environment is created on entry and can be removed on exit).
Your Notes: Lexical scope
  1. Lexical scope is also known as static scope.
  2. Scope is determined by the position of variables and functions in the source code.
  3. Defined at compile time, not runtime.
  4. Inner functions can access the variables of their outer functions.
  5. Controlled by code structure and closures.
  6. Predictable, and does not change based on how functions are called.
FeatureScope (General Concept)Lexical Scope (Specific Type of Scope)
DefinitionThe overall concept that controls variable accessibility in JSA type of scope based on where code is physically written
Scope typesGlobal, Function, Block (ES6+), ModuleLexical: defined at write time based on nesting
When definedEnvironments are created at runtime, but visibility follows the code structure (JS scope is lexical) ✔ "created at runtime depending on how code is executed"फक्त memory runtime ला बनते, visibility चे नियम code च्या रचनेवरूनच ठरतात.Determined at compile time (code structure)
Determines what?Where variables can be accessed or referencedWhich outer variables a function can "see"
How it's usedGeneral rule in JS variable resolutionUsed to form closures and determine variable access in nested functions
Dynamic or static?Can refer to dynamic behaviors (like with, eval, both of which should be avoided)Always static: fixed at code definition
Examplevar, let and const follow block/function/global scope rulesInner functions accessing variables from outer functions
Extra Details: JS has no dynamic scope. In a dynamically scoped language, a function would see the variables of whoever called it. JS never does this: every function (and every let/const) uses lexical scope. Only this depends on how a function is called, and this is not a scope.
Scope ही मोठी संकल्पना आहे (variable कुठे वापरता येतो). Lexical scope म्हणजे JS चा नियम: variable कुठून येईल हे function code मध्ये कुठे लिहिले आहे यावरून ठरते, कुठून call केले यावरून नाही. JS मधील सगळे scopes lexical आहेत.

10. Closures

Your Notes:
  • Definition: a closure is a function bundled together with its lexical environment.
  • It allows an inner function to remember variables from its outer function even after the outer function has finished execution.
function outer() {
  let count = 0;
  return function () {
    count++;
    console.log(count);
  };
}
const increment = outer();
increment();   // 1
increment();   // 2
increment();   // 3
  • What happens: the returned inner function keeps a link to count in outer's scope, so each call increases the same count.
  • Output: 1, 2, 3.
  • ✅ Private state without classes or globals.
Figure 29: A closure. outer() has finished, but the returned function carries its lexical environment (count) with it.
Closure म्हणजे function + त्याचा lexical environment (बाहेरचे variables). outer() चालून संपला तरी आतले function count ला "लक्षात ठेवते", जणू ते पाठीवर बॅग (backpack) घेऊन फिरते. म्हणून increment() प्रत्येक वेळी 1, 2, 3 देतो.
Extra Details: where closures are used
  • Data privacy / encapsulation: count can't be changed from outside, only through the returned function.
  • Function factories: const add5 = makeAdder(5).
  • Event handlers, setTimeout callbacks, memoization, and once()/debounce()/throttle().
  • The classic loop bug (var in a loop with setTimeout) is a closure problem; let fixes it (see Chapter 1, Figure 8).
function makeAdder(x) {
  return function (y) { return x + y; };   // closes over x
}
const add5 = makeAdder(5);
console.log(add5(10));   // 15

const c1 = outer(), c2 = outer();
c1(); c1(); c2();        // 1 2 1 → each call to outer() creates a NEW count
  • What happens: makeAdder(5) remembers x = 5. Each outer() call creates a NEW count, so c1 and c2 count separately.
  • Output: 15, then 1 2 1.
  • ✅ Function factories: create many functions with different saved settings.
Each closure keeps its own copy of the environment, and variables are kept alive in memory as long as the closure exists. Many long-lived closures can therefore increase memory use.

11. Scope Chain

Your Notes: JavaScript searches for variables in this order: 
Current Scope
      ↓
Parent Scope
      ↓
Grandparent Scope
      ↓
Global Scope
      ↓
ReferenceError
  • What happens: [TODO: Explanation required]
  • Output: [TODO: Output required]
let globalVar = 1;
function one() {
  let parentVar = 2;
  function two() {
    let childVar = 3;
    console.log(globalVar);  // 1 (found in global scope)
    console.log(parentVar);  // 2 (found in parent scope)
    console.log(childVar);   // 3 (found in current scope)
  }
  two();
}
one();
  • What happens: two() looks for each variable in its own scope, then one(), then the global scope (the scope chain).
  • Output: 1, 2, 3.
Figure 30: The scope chain. Lookup always goes from the inner scope outward, and the first match wins.
Variable शोधताना JS आधी current scope मध्ये पाहते, नसेल तर parent, मग grandparent, आणि शेवटी global मध्ये. कुठेच सापडला नाही तर ReferenceError येतो. ही साखळी (chain) function कुठे लिहिले आहे यावरून ठरते, आणि शोध नेहमी आतून बाहेर होतो.

12. Lexical Scope

Your Notes:
  • Lexical scope is nothing but static scope.
  • Lexical scope means JavaScript resolves variables based on WHERE THE FUNCTION IS DEFINED, NOT WHERE THE FUNCTION IS CALLED. This is also called static scope.
  • Lexical scope is the rule JavaScript uses to resolve variables based on the physical (lexical) location where functions are defined in the source code.
  • The golden rule: JavaScript looks at where a function is defined (written), NOT where it is called.
  • Lexical scope (also called static scope) means that JavaScript determines where a variable comes from based on where the code (functions and variables) is written, not where the function is called.
let x = 10;
function first() {
  console.log(x);
}
function second() {
  let x = 20;
  first();
}
second();   // 10 (first was defined in global scope, so it sees global x)
  • What happens: first() was WRITTEN in the global scope, so it reads the global x = 10, even though it is CALLED inside second() where x = 20.
  • Output: 10.
  • ✅ Lexical scope: what a function can see is fixed by where it is written.
  • ⚠ Interview favourite: answer is 10, not 20.
Q. Why is it called "lexical"?
  • The word lexical means related to the written source code.
  • JavaScript decides the parent scope by looking at where functions are physically written. It does not depend on where they execute.
// 1.
let value = 10;
function first2() {          // ✔ renamed from first → first2
  console.log(value);
}

// 2.
function second2() {         // ✔ renamed from second → second2
  let value = 20;
  first2();
}
second2();   // 10
  • What happens: same rule with renamed functions.
  • Output: 10.
✔ in your file, first and second were declared twice. Function declarations are hoisted and the last one wins, so the earlier second() call ran the second version, which reads value before let value = 10 executes, giving "ReferenceError: Cannot access 'value' before initialization" (verified in Node). Renaming them fixes it.तुमच्या file मध्ये first आणि second दोनदा declare केले होते. Hoisting मुळे शेवटचे declaration जिंकते, म्हणून पहिल्या second() call वेळी नवीन version चालले आणि value TDZ मध्ये असल्यामुळे ReferenceError आला (Node मध्ये तपासले). नावे बदलल्याने (first2, second2) प्रश्न सुटतो.
Figure 31: Lexical scope. first() looks where it was defined (global x = 10), not where it was called (second's x = 20).
Lexical scope चा golden rule: function कुठे लिहिले आहे (defined) ते महत्त्वाचे, कुठून call केले ते नाही. first() global मध्ये लिहिले आहे, म्हणून तो global x = 10 पाहतो. second() मधील x = 20 त्याला कधीच दिसत नाही. म्हणून उत्तर 10 येते.

13. Interview Questions (Detailed)

Q1. What is scope? What types of scope does JavaScript have?
  • Scope is the region of code where a variable is visible. JS has global scope, function (local) scope, block scope (let/const), module scope, and, in browsers, the script scope for top-level let/const. All of them are lexical.
Q2. What is lexical scope?
  • Variables are resolved based on where functions are written in the source code, not where they are called. A nested function can access the variables of its outer functions.
Q3. What is a closure? Give a practical use.
  • A closure is a function together with the lexical environment in which it was created. It can use outer variables even after the outer function has returned. Common uses are private counters, function factories, memoization, event handlers and debounce/throttle.
function createBank() {
  let balance = 0;                         // private
  return {
    deposit(n) { balance += n; return balance; },
    getBalance() { return balance; }
  };
}
const acc = createBank();
acc.deposit(100);
console.log(acc.getBalance());  // 100
console.log(acc.balance);       // undefined → truly private
  • What happens: balance is only reachable through the returned methods, so it is truly private.
  • Output: 100, undefined.
  • ✅ Module/encapsulation pattern before #private fields existed.
Q4. What is the scope chain?
  • It is the ordered list of scopes JS searches to resolve a variable: current → parent → … → global. If the variable is not found anywhere, JS throws a ReferenceError. The chain is fixed when the function is written (lexical).
Q5. Are let/const at the top of a script added to window?
  • No. Only top-level var and function declarations become window properties. Top-level let/const live in the script scope, which is still global but separate from window.
Q6. Does JavaScript have dynamic scope?
  • No, JavaScript scope is always lexical. this depends on how a function is called, which is why it can feel dynamic, but this is a binding and not a scope. eval and with can change scope at runtime and should be avoided.
Q7. Output-based questions
// (a)
var a1 = 1;
function f1() { console.log(a1); var a1 = 2; }
f1();                       // undefined (local a1 hoisted, shadows global)

// (b)
let b1 = 1;
{ let b1 = 2; }
console.log(b1);            // 1

// (c)
function makeCounter() { let c = 0; return () => ++c; }
const k1 = makeCounter(), k2 = makeCounter();
console.log(k1(), k1(), k2()); // 1 2 1

// (d)
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i)); // 3 3 3
for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) setTimeout(() => console.log(j)); // 0 1 2

// (e)
let name = "global";
function show() { console.log(name); }
function run() { let name = "local"; show(); }
run();                      // "global" (lexical scope)
  • What happens: five classic output questions on hoisting, block scope, closures, loops and lexical scope.
  • Output: undefined, 1, 1 2 1, 3 3 3 and 0 1 2, global.
  • ✅ Revise these before interviews.

Lexical Scope: The Core Difference

1. What is Scope?

Definition: Scope determines the accessibility and visibility of variables, functions, and objects in certain regions of your code during runtime.
  • Analogy: scope represents the boundary lines of your code. Inside the boundary, variables are recognized and alive; outside the boundary, they can't be seen or accessed.
  • In JavaScript, scope controls both the visibility (where a variable can be used) and the lifetime (how long it exists in memory) of a variable.
JavaScript scope types:
  1. Global scope: declared outside any function/block; accessible everywhere.
  2. Local / function scope: declared inside a function; accessible only within that function.
  3. Block scope (ES6+): declared with let/const inside {}; accessible only inside those braces.
  4. Module scope: scoped strictly to a module; imported/exported explicitly.
Figure 32: Nested scopes: lookup goes from the inside outward, never inward.
Scope म्हणजे variable कुठे दिसतो आणि किती वेळ जिवंत राहतो याची सीमा. JS मध्ये 4 प्रकार आहेत: global, function, block (let/const) आणि module. आतल्या scope मधून बाहेरचे variables दिसतात, बाहेरून आतले दिसत नाहीत.

2. Deep Dive: Types of Scope

A. Global scope: variables declared outside of any function or block have global scope.
  • When the JavaScript engine runs a script, it creates a Global Execution Context and allocates these variables there.
  • They are accessible from anywhere in your program.
let a = "Hi";            // global variable, defined outside any function or block
function Hi() {
  console.log("say", a); // accessible inside functions → say Hi
}
Hi();
console.log(a);          // accessible in the global scope → Hi
  • What happens: a global variable is visible inside functions and outside.
  • Output: say Hi, Hi.
B. Local / function scope: variables declared inside a function are function-scoped (or locally scoped).
  • Whether declared using var, let, or const, they are confined to that function's execution context.
  • They can't be accessed from outside the function.
function say() {
  var mes = "Hi,";       // 'mes' is function-scoped (local)
  console.log(mes);      // → Hi,
}
say();
// attempting to access 'mes' outside results in a ReferenceError
// console.log(mes);     // Uncaught ReferenceError: mes is not defined
  • What happens: mes exists only inside say().
  • Output: Hi,
C. Block scope (introduced in ES6): a block is defined by a pair of curly braces {}. This includes code blocks inside if statements, else branches, switch cases, and loops (for, while, do-while).
  • Variables declared with let and const inside a block are block-scoped and can't be accessed outside the block.
  • var does NOT support block scope: it ignores curly braces and leaks (spills) into the enclosing function or global scope.
function block() {
  let b = "Hello";
  if (true) {
    let c = "bye";
    console.log(b + c);   // outputs: "Hellobye" (both are visible here)
  }
  // console.log(b + c);  // throws ReferenceError: c is not defined
}
block();
  • What happens: c is block-scoped to the if; b to the function.
  • Output: Hellobye.
D. Browser-specific: global scope vs script scope. In browser environments, there is a distinct separation between variables attached directly to the global window object and variables that stay in script scope.
Scope typeBrowser global / window scopeScript scope
DeclarationVariables declared with var, or functions declared at the top level outside functionsVariables declared with let or const at the top level outside functions
Window objectAttached as properties on the global window object (e.g. window.myVar)Not attached to the global window object
AccessibilityGlobally accessible by any script loaded on the pageGlobally accessible by any script loaded on the page
PollutionPollutes the global window namespace (risking name collisions)Keeps the window object clean
// run at the top level of a browser script:
let m = "Hi";
var d = "GoodBye";
console.log(window.d);   // "GoodBye" (var goes to the Global/Window scope)
console.log(window.m);   // undefined (let stays in Script scope)
function display() {
  const n = "Hello";
  let s = "bye";
  if (true) {
    console.log(m + n + s);   // "HiHellobye" (accessing script-scoped 'm')
  }
  console.log(m + d);         // "HiGoodBye"
}
display();
  • What happens: top-level var → window.d; top-level let → Script scope, not on window. display() sees all of them.
  • Output: GoodBye, undefined, HiHellobye, HiGoodBye.
  • ⚠ Run in a browser; in Node there is no window (ReferenceError).
✔ the comment said "HiHelloScale"; m + n + s = "Hi" + "Hello" + "bye" = "HiHellobye" (verified).m + n + s चे उत्तर "HiHellobye" आहे, "HiHelloScale" नाही.
E. Module scope: in modern ES6 JavaScript modules (<script type="module"> or files using import/export), variables declared at the top level are scoped to that module file only.
  • They don't pollute the global scope or script scope.
  • They can only be accessed in other files if explicitly exported and imported.
// module.js
export const moduleScopedVar = "I am module-scoped";
// main.js
import { moduleScopedVar } from "./module.js";
console.log(moduleScopedVar);   // "I am module-scoped"
  • What happens: module scope: shared only via export/import.
  • Output: I am module-scoped.
Browser मध्ये top-level var आणि function window object वर जातात; top-level let/const "Script" scope मध्ये राहतात, सगळीकडे दिसतात पण window.m undefined असतो. Module मधले variables फक्त त्या file पुरते असतात, export/import केल्याशिवाय बाहेर दिसत नाहीत.

3. Advanced Scope Concepts

A. Variable hoisting
  • var hoisting: declarations are hoisted to the top of their scope and initialized with undefined.
  • let & const hoisting: declarations are hoisted but not initialized. They are in the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ); accessing them before initialization throws a ReferenceError.
console.log(name);   // var is hoisted, outputs: undefined
var name = "vishal";
// console.log(lastName); // throws ReferenceError: Cannot access 'lastName' before initialization
let lastName = "shinde";
  • What happens: var name is hoisted with undefined; let lastName is in the TDZ before its line.
  • Output: undefined (ReferenceError for the commented line).
  • ⚠ In a browser, a global var name is window.name (always a string), so it would print "".
✔ Note: in a browser, avoid "name" as a demo variable: a top-level var name is window.name, which is always a STRING ("" at first), so values get converted (var name = 5 → "5").Browser मध्ये name हे window.name आहे आणि ते नेहमी string असते, म्हणून demo साठी दुसरे नाव वापरा.
B. Closures: a closure is the combination of a function bundled together with references to its surrounding state (the lexical environment). In other words, a closure gives an inner function access to the outer function's scope even after the outer function has finished executing. 
function outerFunction(outerVariable) {
  return function innerFunction(innerVariable) {
    console.log('Outer Variable: ' + outerVariable);
    console.log('Inner Variable: ' + innerVariable);
  }
}
const newFunction = outerFunction('outside');
newFunction('inside');   // still remembers 'outerVariable'! → Outer Variable: outside / Inner Variable: inside
  • What happens: innerFunction remembers outerVariable after outerFunction has returned.
  • Output: Outer Variable: outside, Inner Variable: inside.
C. Strict mode ("use strict"): strict mode restricts certain JavaScript behaviors to make your code more secure and prevent bugs.
  • Implicit globals: without strict mode, assigning a value to an undeclared variable (e.g. x = 10) implicitly creates a global variable. In strict mode, this throws a ReferenceError.

4. Scope vs Lexical Scope: The Core Difference

A. The basic definitions
  • Scope: the actual runtime environment or box where a variable is stored and can be accessed.
  • Lexical scope (static scope): the ruleset that dictates how nested scopes look up variables. "Lexical" means "relating to the written source code". Therefore, lexical scope means variable access is decided by where variables and functions are physically written in the code, not where they are executed.
B. The "one-way mirror" analogy: think of nested functions as a series of nested rooms with one-way mirrors:
  1. Looking outward (allowed): if you are in the innermost room (inner function), you can look out through the mirror and see the variables in the outer rooms (parent functions and global scope).
  2. Looking inward (blocked): someone in the outer room (global/parent scope) can't look into the inner room.

They can't see or access the variables inside the inner function. Diagram: Global Scope (outer room): let globalVal = 100; → Parent Function Scope (middle room): let parentVal = 200; → Inner Function Scope (innermost room): let childVal = 300; console.log(globalVal, parentVal, childVal) → works! (looks outward). In the global room: console.log(childVal) → throws ReferenceError! (can't look inward).

C. The ultimate interview test: "written place" vs "called place". To understand lexical scope, look at the classic interview question below. Try to predict what is printed: 
let x = 10;
function first() {
  console.log(x);
}
function second() {
  let x = 20;
  first();   // calling first() from inside second()
}
second();    // → 10
  • What happens: first() reads x from where it was written (global), not from second().
  • Output: 10.
What is printed: 10 or 20?
  • Answer: 10.
  • Why? JavaScript uses lexical scope (static scope). When the JS engine looks for x inside the first() function, it doesn't care where first() was called (inside second()). It only cares where first() was defined (written).
  • Since first() was defined in the global scope, its parent scope is the global scope, where x is 10.
Lexical structure (definition/write time): Global Scope (let x = 10) → first() (parent is the Global Scope) and second() (let x = 20). Runtime resolution flow: second() is invoked → calls first() → runs console.log(x) inside first() → looks up the scope chain of first's definition (Global) → finds x = 10 (global), outputs: 10. It does NOT look at the calling environment (second).
If JavaScript had dynamic scope (which it does not!), the engine would resolve x based on where the function was called, printing 20. Because it uses lexical scope, it resolves x based on where it was defined, printing 10.
Figure 33: Lexical scope: first() reads x from where it was written (Global), not from where it was called (second).
D. Detailed comparison table
FeatureScope (general concept)Lexical scope (specific ruleset)
What is it?The boundary/box containing variables at runtimeThe lookup rules based on where the code was written
When is it set?Activates and is instantiated at runtime when code executesFixed at compile time (when you write the code)
Dynamic or static?Can have dynamic variables inside active context framesAlways static. The nesting hierarchy never changes.
DirectionHolds local variablesDictates that lookup goes outward (inner to outer)
How it's usedManages memory execution contextsAllows the creation of closures (functions remembering parent variables)
✔ (wording) "compile time (when you write the code)" mixes two moments: the nesting is decided by where you WRITE the code (author time), and the engine reads it when it PARSES the code, before running it. Either way it never depends on where the function is called.Lexical scope code कुठे लिहिला यावर ठरतो, आणि engine तो code चालवण्याआधी parse करताना ओळखतो; function कुठे call झाला यावर तो अवलंबून नसतो.
Lexical scope चा नियम: function variable शोधताना ज्या ठिकाणी तो लिहिला आहे तिथून बाहेर शोधतो, जिथे call झाला तिथे नाही. म्हणून first() 10 छापतो. याच नियमामुळे closures शक्य होतात.

5. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. Scope vs lexical scope?
  • Scope is the box where variables live at runtime; lexical scope is the rule that the lookup chain follows the place where code was written (inner → outer).
Q2. Why does window.m give undefined for a top-level let m?
  • Top-level let/const live in the Script scope (a declarative record), not as properties of the global object; only var and function declarations become window properties.
Q3. Does JavaScript use dynamic scope?
  • No. Variable lookup is lexical. (Only this behaves "dynamically": it depends on how a function is called.)
Q4. What happens with x = 10 (no declaration) with and without strict mode?
  • Sloppy mode creates an implicit global (window.x); strict mode throws ReferenceError: x is not defined.
Q5. Output-based questions
let x = 1; function f() { console.log(x); } function g() { let x = 2; f(); } g();   // → 1
function h() { if (true) { var v = "var"; let l = "let"; } console.log(v, typeof l); } h();   // → var undefined
console.log(typeof t); let t = 5;            // → ReferenceError (TDZ; typeof doesn't help)
const add = a => b => a + b; console.log(add(2)(3));   // → 5 (closure)
  • What happens: four output questions: lexical scope (1), var leaks / let doesn't (var undefined), typeof in TDZ throws, curried closure (5).
  • Output: 1, var undefined, ReferenceError, 5.
ScopeCreated byVisible
Global / windowtop-level var, functioneverywhere, as window.x
Scripttop-level let / consteverywhere, not on window
Functionvar / let / const inside a functiononly inside the function
Blocklet / const inside {}only inside the braces
Moduletop-level of a moduleonly via export / import
थोडक्यात: scope = variable ची सीमा, lexical scope = लिहिलेल्या जागेवरून शोधण्याचा नियम. var block ला मानत नाही, let/const मानतात. Strict mode मध्ये undeclared variable ला value दिल्यास ReferenceError येतो. "Written place, not called place" हे interview चे सूत्र लक्षात ठेवा.
Quick Revision Summary:
ConceptKey Point
Scope vs Lexical ScopeScope is the active runtime memory box where variables live. Lexical Scope is the rule that determines variable lookup based on where the code is physically written, not where it is called.
Lexical Lookup (One-way mirror)Inner functions can access variables from outer functions (looking outward), but outer functions cannot access inner variables (looking inward).
Dynamic vs Static ScopeJavaScript uses Static (Lexical) Scope. Variable access is determined at definition time. The only exception is this, which acts dynamically based on the calling context.

मराठी सारांश: Scope म्हणजे runtime मधील जागा जिथे variables असतात. Lexical Scope म्हणजे variable शोधण्याचा नियम, जो code कुठे लिहिला आहे यावर ठरतो, कुठे कॉल केला यावर नाही. Inner function ला बाहेरील variables मिळतात, पण बाहेरील function ला आतले variables मिळत नाहीत. JavaScript मध्ये scope नेहमी static असतो (फक्त this डायनॅमिक आहे).

In this chapter every "error" example is shown separately, with the result each one gives on its own.functionHoisting.js मध्ये sayHi एकदा var ने आणि नंतर let ने declare केले आहे. त्यामुळे file parse होतानाच SyntaxError येतो आणि एकही line चालत नाही. variableHoisting.js मध्ये मुद्दाम दिलेल्या ReferenceError मुळे file तिथेच थांबते आणि showTDZ() चालतच नाही. म्हणून इथे प्रत्येक error example वेगळा चालवून त्याचा निकाल दाखवला आहे. शिकताना असे error examples comment करून ठेवा किंवा वेगळ्या file मध्ये लिहा.

1. Q. What is Hoisting in JavaScript?

Your Notes (variableHoisting.js):
  1. Hoisting in JavaScript is the default behavior (mechanism) in which, during the creation phase, the JavaScript engine "moves" your variable and function declarations to the top of their scope before executing the code. This is known as hoisting.
  2. It is the process in which, during the creation (compilation) phase, the JavaScript engine moves variable and function declarations to the top of their containing scope (either local or global) before code execution. This is known as hoisting.
  3. This means that no matter where functions and variables are declared, they are moved to the top of their scope, regardless of whether that scope is global or local.
✔ Note: nothing is physically moved. During the creation phase the engine allocates memory for every declaration first; the code then behaves AS IF the declarations were at the top (see Chapter 1).code प्रत्यक्ष वर हलवला जात नाही. creation phase मध्ये सर्व declarations साठी आधी memory राखून ठेवली जाते, म्हणून ते "वर गेल्यासारखे" वागतात.
Definition: Hoisting is the result of JavaScript's two-phase execution: in the creation (memory) phase the engine registers every declaration in its scope (var → undefined, let/const/class → uninitialized, function declarations → the whole function); in the execution phase the code runs line by line.
Figure 34: Hoisting is the creation phase registering declarations before the execution phase runs the code.
Hoisting म्हणजे code चालण्याआधी (creation phase) JS सर्व declarations ची नोंद करते: var ला undefined, let/const/class ला "uninitialized" (TDZ), आणि function declaration ला पूर्ण function. मग execution phase मध्ये code वरून खाली चालतो.

2. Variable Hoisting with var

Your Notes (your code): 
console.log(count);   // → undefined
var count;

// Here we reference the variable before its declaration.
// The first line doesn't cause an error, because the JavaScript engine registers the variable declaration
// at the top of its scope and initializes it with the special value undefined.
console.log("myName :", myName);   // → myName : undefined
var myName;
myName = "vishal shinde";
// ✔ the log said "myName" but the variable was called "name". In a BROWSER, a global var name
//    IS window.name (a built-in string property, normally ""), so it would print "" instead of undefined.
  • What happens: both var declarations are moved (hoisted) to the top of the scope and set to undefined before the code runs, so logging them early gives undefined.
  • Output: undefined, myName : undefined.
  • ⚠ No error means the bug (using a value too early) goes unnoticed.
comment मध्ये myName लिहिले होते, पण variable चे नाव name होते. browser मध्ये global var name म्हणजे window.name (आधीपासून असलेली string), म्हणून undefined ऐवजी "" येईल. त्यामुळे myName हे नाव वापरले.

So this is what the code looks like in the execution phase: during the creation phase of the global execution context, the JavaScript engine places the variable myName in memory and initializes its value with undefined.

3. let & const Hoisting and the Temporal Dead Zone

Your Notes: Q. So var variables are hoisted, but what about let and const?
  1. Variables declared with let and const are also hoisted to the top of their scope, but they are not initialized.
  2. They remain in a temporal dead zone (TDZ) from the start of the block until the declaration is encountered. (The TDZ starts at the beginning of the scope and ends at initialization.)
  3. Accessing them before their declaration results in a ReferenceError.
  4. let and const are hoisted, but not initialized. They stay in the TDZ until initialization.
console.log(counter);   // ❌ ReferenceError: Cannot access 'counter' before initialization
let counter;            // a variable declared with let/const is hoisted, but stays in the TDZ until this line
// ⚠ an uncaught error STOPS the rest of the script, so keep this commented out in your file
  • What happens: let is hoisted too, but stays uninitialized (TDZ) until its line, so reading it early throws.
  • Output: ReferenceError.
  • ✅ Turns early use into a clear error.
Q. What is the temporal dead zone?
  1. The temporal dead zone is a concept in JavaScript that refers to the time period between the start of a block scope and the point at which the declared variable is initialized.
  2. The TDZ is the time period between the start of the block scope and the initialization of a let or const variable. 
    {
  // TDZ starts here
  console.log(x);   // ❌ ReferenceError
  let x = 5;        // TDZ ends here
}
    • What happens: the TDZ runs from the start of the block to the let line.
    • Output: ReferenceError.
  3. The temporal dead zone is the term used to describe the state where variables are in scope but cannot be accessed yet, until they are initialized.
  4. The TDZ starts at the beginning of the block where the variable is declared and ends when the variable is initialized.
Q. Write a function that demonstrates the temporal dead zone
function showTDZ() {
  console.log("Function started");
  try {
    console.log(counter);   // ❌ ReferenceError (TDZ), caught below
  } catch (e) {
    console.log("Error accessing 'counter' before declaration:", e.message);
  }
  let counter = 10;         // TDZ ends here
  console.log("After initialization, counter =", counter);   // ✅ 10
}
showTDZ();
// → Function started
// → Error accessing 'counter' before declaration: Cannot access 'counter' before initialization
// → After initialization, counter = 10
  • What happens: try/catch lets us see the TDZ error without stopping the program; after let counter = 10 it works.
  • Output: the three lines shown.
  • ✅ Good interview demo of the TDZ.
let/const सुद्धा hoist होतात, पण त्यांना value मिळत नाही. block सुरू झाल्यापासून declaration line पर्यंत ते TDZ मध्ये असतात, आणि त्या काळात वापरल्यास ReferenceError येतो. try...catch ने हा error पकडून दाखवता येतो (showTDZ). (Chapter 1, Figure 5 पहा.)

4. Function Hoisting

Your Notes (functionHoisting.js): Q. What is function hoisting?
  1. Def: hoisting is the default behavior (mechanism) in JavaScript in which the engine "moves" variable and function declarations to the top of their surrounding scope. This is known as hoisting.
  2. Functions are hoisted, but differently from normal variables.
  3. Functions are hoisted completely: a var variable is hoisted as undefined, but for a function the complete function is registered in the surrounding scope. So it doesn't matter whether you call the function before or after its declaration; it still works.
  4. Function hoisting is a behavior in JavaScript where function declarations are moved to the top of their containing scope during the creation phase, before the code is executed. This means you can call a function before it is defined in the code.
  5. When a function declaration is hoisted, its entire definition (including the body) is moved to the top of its containing scope during the creation phase.
1. Function + var inside it + global var
display();
console.log("a", a);

function display() {
  console.log(x);         // → undefined   (local var x is hoisted inside display)
  var x = 20;
  console.log("hello");   // → hello
}
var a = 10;
// → undefined
// → hello
// → a undefined
  • What happens: display() works before its line (function hoisting). Inside it, var x is hoisted locally → undefined. a is undefined when logged because var a = 10 runs later.
  • Output: undefined, hello, a undefined.
2
var myVar;
console.log(myVar);   // → undefined   (the variable is also hoisted)
greet();              // → "welcome"   (called before the function declaration)
myVar = 10;
function greet() {
  console.log("welcome");
}
  • What happens: var myVar is undefined at first; greet() works before its declaration.
  • Output: undefined, welcome.
3
sayHello();           // → "sayHello"
function sayHello() {
  console.log("sayHello");
}
  • What happens: a function declaration is fully hoisted.
  • Output: sayHello.
4
functionName();       // → "hi"
function functionName() {
  console.log("hi");
}
console.log(s);       // → undefined   (because of hoisting; no error like with let/const)
var s = 10;
console.log(s);       // → 10
  • What happens: function declaration hoisted; var s undefined until assigned.
  • Output: hi, undefined, 10.
Key points about function hoisting:
  1. The entire function declaration is hoisted (not just its name), so you can call the function anywhere within the scope (i.e. the entire function is available before the place where it is defined; the complete function is put into the scope).
  2. Like variables, the JavaScript engine also hoists function declarations: it registers them at the top of the script. During the creation phase of the execution context, the JavaScript engine stores the function object in heap memory and puts a reference to it in the scope.
Extra Details: two traps
1. A function declaration and a var with the same name: the function wins during hoisting,
// 1. A function declaration and a var with the same name: the function wins during hoisting,
//    then the var ASSIGNMENT overwrites it when that line runs
console.log(typeof foo);   // → "function"
var foo = 1;
function foo() {}
console.log(typeof foo);   // → "number"
  • What happens: during hoisting the function declaration wins over the var with the same name; then the line var foo = 1 replaces it with a number.
  • Output: "function", then "number".
  • ⚠ Never reuse a name for a variable and a function.
2. A function declared inside a block ({ }) is block-scoped in modern JS:
// 2. A function declared inside a block ({ }) is block-scoped in modern JS:
console.log(typeof blockFn);   // → "undefined"   (not hoisted out of the block yet)
{ function blockFn() {} }
console.log(typeof blockFn);   // → "function"    (sloppy mode copies it out after the block runs)
  • What happens: in modern JS a function declared in a block belongs to that block; sloppy mode also copies it out once the block has run.
  • Output: "undefined", then "function".
  • ⚠ Behaviour differs in strict mode (stays block-scoped); avoid functions inside blocks.

5. Output-Based Question

Your Notes: 
var x = 21;
var fun = function () {
  console.log(x);   // → undefined
  var x = 20;
};
fun();
  • What happens: inside fun, the local var x is hoisted and shadows the global x, so the log reads the local one before it is assigned.
  • Output: undefined.
  • ⚠ Classic trap: people expect 21.
Explanation of the code above:
  1. Basically, hoisting happens in 2 steps here:
    1. the global code is set up (global execution context), and
    2. the local scope is set up when the function is called (function execution context).
  2. First the global scope is created: x is registered (then becomes 21) and fun is registered (then gets the function).
  3. Then, when fun() runs, a separate execution context is created for that function (the local scope), and it has its own creation phase: the local x is hoisted to the top of the function scope and set to undefined, but it is present in the local scope.
Note: when a variable is present in the current scope, JS does not check the parent or global scope; it always prefers the current scope. (So the local x, hoisted as undefined, shadows the global x = 21, and undefined is printed.)
Figure 35: Each function call gets its own creation phase, so a hoisted local var shadows the global variable.
fun() call झाल्यावर त्याचे स्वतःचे execution context बनते आणि त्यात local x आधीच undefined म्हणून hoist होतो. console.log(x) ला current scope मध्येच x सापडतो (undefined), म्हणून तो global x = 21 पर्यंत जातच नाही.

6. Rest Parameter Rule

Your Notes: 
// ex.
// const fn = (x, y, ...num, z, a) => {
//   console.log(x, y);
// };
// ❌ Uncaught SyntaxError: Rest parameter must be last formal parameter
// fn(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7);
// ✔ the commented call was "fun(1, 2, …)" (a different function)

// solution: the rest parameter goes LAST
const fn1 = (x, y, z, ...num) => {
  console.log(x, y, z, num);   // → 1 2 3 [4, 5, 6, 7]
};
fn1(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7);
// ✔ the comment on this working line said "show error like … Rest parameter must be last";
//    this is the FIXED version, and it runs fine
  • What happens: a rest parameter must be the LAST parameter; putting it in the middle is a SyntaxError. With ...num last, the extra arguments are collected into an array.
  • Output: 1 2 3 [4, 5, 6, 7].
दुरुस्त केलेल्या (solution) line वर error ची comment चुकून राहिली होती; ती line व्यवस्थित चालते. rest parameter (...num) नेहमी शेवटी हवा, नाहीतर SyntaxError येतो.

7. Q. Are Function Expressions Hoisted?

Your Notes:
  1. Function expressions are not hoisted like function declarations.
  2. For function declarations, the entire function (its name and body) is hoisted.
  3. But for function expressions, only the variable is hoisted, not the function assignment.
What happens during hoisting:
  1. In the creation phase, JavaScript scans your code and sets up memory for variable and function declarations.
  2. For the line var sayHi = function(){}, only the sayHi variable declaration is hoisted, not the function itself.
During the creation phase: var sayHi; // initialized as undefined
Execution phase:
  1. When JS reaches the line where the function is assigned, it sets sayHi to the anonymous function.
  2. Before that line runs, sayHi is just undefined.
  3. When you do console.log(sayHi); → it prints undefined (the variable is declared but not assigned).
  4. When you do sayHi(); before the assignment → you get "TypeError: sayHi is not a function", because you're trying to call undefined.
console.log(sayHi(10, 20));   // ❌ TypeError: sayHi is not a function
var sayHi = function (a, b) {
  return a + b;
};
  • What happens: only var sayHi is hoisted (undefined); calling undefined as a function is a TypeError.
  • Output: TypeError: sayHi is not a function.
  • ⚠ Function expressions must be defined before they are called.

8. Q. Are Arrow Functions Hoisted?

Your Notes:
  1. Arrow functions are also not hoisted.
  2. Arrow functions, like function expressions, are treated as variables.
  3. Arrow functions are not hoisted in a way that lets you call them before their declaration; they behave like function expressions, not function declarations.
Arrow function hoisting: arrow functions are not hoisted like function declarations. Like function expressions, arrow functions are assigned to variables, and only the variable is hoisted, not the function definition.
What happens during hoisting:
  1. In the creation phase, JavaScript scans the code and sets up memory for variable and function declarations.
  2. For the line var sayHi = () => {}, only the sayHi variable declaration is hoisted, not the arrow function assignment.
During the creation phase: var sayHi; // initialized as undefined
Execution phase:
  1. When JavaScript reaches the line where the arrow function is assigned, it sets sayHi to the arrow function.
  2. Before that line runs, sayHi is just undefined.
  3. When you do console.log(sayHi); → it prints undefined (the variable exists but isn't assigned yet).
  4. When you do sayHi(); before the assignment → you get "TypeError: sayHi is not a function", because you're calling undefined.
Arrow function with var (each example run on its own)
console.log(sayHi);   // → undefined
sayHi();              // ❌ TypeError: sayHi is not a function
var sayHi = () => {
  console.log("hello");
};
  • What happens: same with an arrow function stored in var.
  • Output: undefined, then TypeError.
Arrow function with let (separate file / scope)
sayHi();              // ❌ ReferenceError: Cannot access 'sayHi' before initialization
let sayHi = () => {
  console.log("hello");
};
// ✔ in your file this let sayHi was in the SAME script as "var sayHi" above →
//    SyntaxError: Identifier 'sayHi' has already been declared, and the whole file stopped
  • What happens: with let the variable is in the TDZ, so the error is a ReferenceError instead.
  • Output: ReferenceError.
Internal implementation (what the engine effectively does)
var sayHi;             // hoisted → undefined
console.log(sayHi);    // → undefined
sayHi(10, 20);         // ❌ TypeError: sayHi is not a function
sayHi = function (a, b) {
  return a + b;
};
  • What happens: what the engine effectively does with var + function expression.
  • Output: undefined, then TypeError.
If declared with let or const: ✔ heading typo "i# f declared" → "If declared".heading मधील typo दुरुस्त केला.
  1. The variable is hoisted but not initialized → the TDZ (temporal dead zone) applies.
  2. Accessing it before the declaration → ReferenceError.
  3. They are hoisted too, but not initialized.
  4. The time between the start of the block and the actual declaration is called the temporal dead zone (TDZ).
  5. Any access during the TDZ throws a ReferenceError.
console.log(sayHi);   // ❌ ReferenceError: Cannot access 'sayHi' before initialization
sayHi();              // ❌ won't even reach this line
let sayHi = function () {
  console.log("sayHi");
};
  • What happens: let function expression: even reading it early throws.
  • Output: ReferenceError.
Note:
  1. Function expressions / arrow functions → only the variable name is hoisted (set to undefined with var until the assignment). 
    console.log(multiply(2, 3));   // ❌ TypeError: multiply is not a function
var multiply = (a, b) => a * b;
    • What happens: var + arrow function → undefined at call time.
    • Output: TypeError: multiply is not a function.
  2. Only var multiply; is hoisted (initialized to undefined); the function assignment happens later.
Why are function expressions and arrow functions not hoisted? (see the explanation above): they are VALUES assigned to variables, and only the variable declaration is hoisted.
Figure 36: The three outcomes of calling a function before its line: declaration ✅, var expression TypeError, let/const ReferenceError.
function declaration पूर्णपणे hoist होते, म्हणून आधी call करता येते. var ने बनवलेले function expression किंवा arrow function आधी undefined असते, म्हणून TypeError येतो. let/const ने बनवलेले TDZ मध्ये असते, म्हणून ReferenceError येतो.

9. Uses of Hoisting & Summary Table

Your Notes:
  1. Hoisting lets us call function declarations before they are defined, and read var variables (as undefined) before their line, without getting an error. let/const/class still throw a ReferenceError in the TDZ. ✔ "hoisting enables us to extract the value of variables and functions even before initialization". That is true only for function declarations (full value) and var (just undefined); let/const throw.आधी value मिळणे फक्त function declaration (पूर्ण function) आणि var (फक्त undefined) साठी खरे आहे. let/const आधी वापरल्यास ReferenceError येतो.
  2. This happens without an error because the first phase of an execution context is the creation phase.

10. Interview Questions (Detailed)

Q1. What is hoisting?
  • During the creation phase of an execution context, JS registers all declarations in their scope before running any code: var as undefined, let/const/class as uninitialized (TDZ), and function declarations with their full body. Nothing is physically moved.
Q2. Are let and const hoisted?
  • Yes, but they are not initialized, so accessing them before the declaration line throws a ReferenceError (TDZ). Proof: an inner let x makes an outer x unreachable before its line.
Q3. Why can you call a function declaration before it is defined, but not a function expression?
  • The declaration's whole function is stored in the creation phase. A function expression is just a value assigned to a variable when the line runs; before that the variable is undefined (var → TypeError) or in the TDZ (let/const → ReferenceError).
Q4. What is the difference between "undefined" and "not defined"?
  • undefined means the variable exists (e.g. a hoisted var) but has no value yet. "not defined" (ReferenceError) means no such variable exists in any reachable scope.
Q5. Are classes hoisted?
  • Yes, but like let they stay in the TDZ: new P(); class P {} → ReferenceError: Cannot access 'P' before initialization.
Q6. Output-based questions
console.log(a1); var a1 = 5;                  // → undefined
console.log(typeof f1); function f1() {}       // → "function"
console.log(typeof f2); var f2 = () => {};    // → "undefined"
var v = 1; function t() { console.log(v); var v = 2; } t();   // → undefined
var w = 1; function u() { console.log(w); } u();               // → 1
console.log(typeof foo); var foo = 1; function foo() {}        // → "function"
  • What happens: six hoisting output questions in one place.
  • Output: undefined, "function", "undefined", undefined, 1, "function".
  • ✅ Revise before interviews.

varHoisted as undefined
let / const / classHoisted but uninitialized → TDZ → ReferenceError
Function declarationHoisted with its body → callable before its line
Function expression / arrowOnly the variable is hoisted → TypeError (var) / ReferenceError (let/const)
Every function callHas its own creation phase → local vars shadow outer ones
Best practiceDeclare before use; prefer const/let; keep error examples out of runnable files
