1. Closure

Your Notes (closure.js):
  1. A closure is the combination of a function bundled together (enclosed) with references to its surrounding state (its lexical scope, or environment).
  2. In other words, a closure gives you access to an outer function's scope from an inner scope.
  3. JavaScript closures are created every time a function is created, at function creation time.
  4. This allows the inner function to access variables defined in the outer function's scope even after the outer function has finished executing.
  5. A closure is nothing but the ability of a function to access variables and functions that are lexically outside its own scope (so the inner function holds references to its outer function's variables).
Basic closure
function makeFunc() {
  var name = "vishal";
  function displayName() {
    console.log(name);
  }
  return displayName;
}
var myName = makeFunc();
// makeFunc returns displayName, the inner function, so myName can now print the name
console.log(myName);   // → [Function: displayName]   (the function itself)
myName();              // → "vishal"   (makeFunc has finished, but name is still remembered)
  • What happens: makeFunc returns displayName; even after makeFunc has finished, displayName still remembers name. That remembered environment is the closure.
  • Output: [Function: displayName], vishal.
  • ✅ Lets a function keep data between calls.
  • In JavaScript, every time we create a new function, it binds itself to its environment (lexical scope). So it doesn't matter whether you call it directly where it is or return it from the function: it still has access to its parent scope (and the global scope).
  • i.e. you can return displayName; and call it later, or call displayName() directly instead of returning it.
So what is the use of this syntax?
  1. Closures make it possible for a function to have private variables.

JavaScript closures are used to control what is and is not in the scope of a particular function, and which variables are shared between sibling functions in the same scope.
Definition: A closure is a function plus a live reference to the lexical environment in which it was created. Because of it, an inner function can read and update the outer function's variables even after the outer function has returned.
Figure 37: A closure. The returned function keeps a reference to the environment where it was created, so name survives after makeFunc() ends.
Closure म्हणजे function + तो जिथे बनला त्या जागेचे (lexical environment) variables. बाहेरचे function संपले तरी आतले function त्या variables ला "लक्षात ठेवते" आणि वापरू शकते. makeFunc() संपल्यानंतरही myName() ला "vishal" मिळते.

2. When is a Closure Created?

Your Notes:
  1. In JavaScript, closures are created every time a function is created, at function creation time. Closures are created at function creation time, not execution time, and they allow inner functions to "remember" the variables of their outer functions.
  2. Because in JavaScript, every time we create a new function, it binds itself to its environment (lexical scope).
  3. So a closure in JavaScript is a function that retains access to the variables and functions in its outer (enclosing) scope, even after the outer function has finished executing.
  4. Closures let you create private data and encapsulate functionality within a function, which makes them a powerful and essential concept in JavaScript.
  5. Closures are a key feature of JavaScript, enabling powerful patterns like data encapsulation, currying, memoization and function factories. They are essential for asynchronous operations (like callbacks, promises and event handlers).
How closures are formed:
  1. When a function is defined inside another function, it gets access to the outer function's variables. Even when the outer function has finished executing,
  2. the inner function retains access to those variables, creating a closure.
How closures are formed (again): when a function is defined inside another function, the inner function automatically gets access to the outer function's variables. Even if the outer function has returned, the inner function still has access; this retained access is the closure.
Note: technically every JS function is a closure (even a top-level function closes over the global scope). It only becomes interesting when the function outlives the scope it was created in (returned, stored, or used as a callback).

3. Purpose of a Closure in JavaScript

Your Notes: briefly, what is the purpose of a closure, and how is it defined?
  1. A closure is a function that lets you remember and access variables from its outer scope in the inner scope, even after the outer function has executed (i.e. a closure gives you access to an outer function's scope from an inner scope).
It helps in:
  1. Data encapsulation (data hiding): hiding variables from the global scope. (Data privacy / encapsulation with private variables.) JavaScript didn't have built-in private variables like some other languages; closures let you create variables that are hidden from the outside world but accessible to inner functions. Encapsulation = hiding internal details and exposing only what's necessary.
  2. Maintaining state: preserving values across function calls (preserving scope/context, keeping data alive between calls). Maintaining state in asynchronous code: in callbacks, event listeners, promises and async functions, closures help you remember the variables you need.
  3. Creating private variables (hiding data): preventing direct access to internal data.
  4. Stateful functions: turning a normal function into a stateful function.
  5. Memoization & caching: closures let you store results (like in a cache) and reuse them later. The cache lives in the function's lexical scope.
In short, the purpose of a closure is to:
  • keep variables alive even after the outer function has returned
  • provide data privacy (like private variables)
  • enable powerful patterns like memoization, currying and function factories
  • and make async code and callbacks work with remembered state.
Use CaseBenefit
Private variablesEncapsulation
Custom function generatorsFlexibility
Async operationsPreserve scope/context
Stateful functionsMemory without global variables
Currying/partial applicationClean, reusable function logic
Are there other mechanisms in JS for data hiding?
  1. Yes! In addition to closures, JavaScript provides several other mechanisms for data hiding and encapsulation:
  2. IIFE (Immediately Invoked Function Expressions): a traditional pattern for creating scoped/private data.
  3. Modules (ES6 modules): when you export only what's needed, everything else inside a module is private by default.
  4. Private fields (#) in classes (ES2022+): JavaScript classes now support true private fields using #.
Closure चे उपयोग: (1) private variables (data hiding), (2) function calls दरम्यान state लक्षात ठेवणे, (3) memoization/cache, (4) function factories आणि currying, (5) callbacks/async मध्ये value लक्षात ठेवणे. data hiding साठी IIFE, ES modules आणि class चे #private fields हे इतर मार्ग आहेत.

4. What are Function Factories?

Your Notes:
  • A function factory is a function that creates and returns other functions.
  • It usually takes some parameters (configuration).
  • It uses closures to "remember" those parameters.
  • Each returned function is customized based on the input.
function multiplier(factor) {
  // factory function
  return function (x) {
    return x * factor;   // the closure remembers 'factor'
  };
}
const double = multiplier(2);   // creates a "double" function
const triple = multiplier(3);   // creates a "triple" function
console.log(double(5));         // → 10
console.log(triple(5));         // → 15
  • What happens: each call to multiplier creates a new function that remembers its own factor.
  • Output: 10, 15.
  • ✅ Function factories.
Note: multiplier is the factory. It produces new functions (double, triple) that each remember their own factor. This works because of closures.

5. How a Closure is Defined

Your Notes:
  1. A closure is created when an inner function is returned from an outer function and the inner function retains access to the outer function's variables.
function outerFunction(outerVariable) {
  return function innerFunction(innerVariable) {
    // innerFunction is the closure function
    console.log(`Outer: ${outerVariable}, Inner: ${innerVariable}`);
  };
}
const closureFunction = outerFunction("Hello");
closureFunction("World");   // → Outer: Hello, Inner: World
// innerFunction forms a closure by remembering outerVariable, even after outerFunction has executed.
  • What happens: closureFunction remembers outerVariable = "Hello".
  • Output: Outer: Hello, Inner: World.

6. Closure Output Questions

Your Notes:
Output-based question
let count = 0;
(function printCount() {
  if (count === 0) {
    let count = 1;        // a NEW block-scoped count (shadows the outer one)
    console.log(count);   // → 1
  }
  console.log(count);     // → 0   (back to the outer count)
})();
  • What happens: the let count inside the if is a new variable that exists only in that block; outside it, count is the outer 0.
  • Output: 1, 0.
✔ the second log had an empty output comment; it prints 0.दुसऱ्या console.log चे output 0 आहे: if block मधील let count फक्त त्या block पुरता होता.
2. Write a function that allows you to do this: var addSix = createBase(6); addSix(10); addSix(21);
function createBase(num) {
  return function (num1) {
    console.log(num + num1);
  };
}
var addSix = createBase(6);
addSix(10);   // → 16
addSix(21);   // → 27
  • What happens: createBase(6) returns a function that remembers num = 6.
  • Output: 16, 27.

7. Time Optimisation Question

Your Notes:
Example 6a: the slow version
function find(index) {
  let a = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < 100000; i++) {
    a[i] = i * i;            // the heavy work runs on EVERY call
  }
  console.log(a[index]);
}
console.time("6");
find(6);                     // → 36
console.timeEnd("6");        // → e.g. 6: 2.6ms
console.time("12");
find(12);                    // → 144
console.timeEnd("12");       // → e.g. 12: 1.3ms
  • What happens: find builds a 100 000-item array on EVERY call, then reads one value.
  • Output: 36, 144 (each call takes milliseconds).
  • ⚠ Repeating expensive work on every call wastes time.
Example 6b: optimised with a closure
// optimise the function above using a closure
// solution:
function find1() {
  let a = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < 100000; i++) {
    a[i] = i * i;            // the heavy work runs ONCE
  }
  return function (index) {
    console.log(a[index]);   // the closure reuses the same array
  };
}
let closure = find1();
console.time("6");
closure(6);                  // → 36
console.timeEnd("6");        // → e.g. 6: 0.07ms
console.time("12");
closure(12);                 // → 144
console.timeEnd("12");       // → e.g. 12: 0.01ms   (timings vary by machine; measured in Node)
  • What happens: find1 builds the array ONCE and returns a function that remembers it; each later call only reads from it.
  • Output: 36, 144, much faster.
  • ✅ Closures can cache expensive setup (same idea as memoization).
  • ⚠ The array stays in memory as long as closure exists.
पहिल्या version मध्ये प्रत्येक call वेळी 1 लाख elements चा array पुन्हा बनतो. closure version मध्ये array एकदाच बनतो आणि returned function तोच array वारंवार वापरतो, म्हणून ते खूप वेगवान आहे (2.6ms → 0.07ms). हा memoization/caching चा पाया आहे.

8. Block Scope and setTimeout: What Is Logged?

Your Notes: 
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log(i);   // → 3, 3, 3
  }, 1000);
}
  • What happens: var i is ONE variable shared by all callbacks; when they run (after 1 s) the loop has finished and i is 3.
  • Output: 3, 3, 3.
  • ⚠ Most famous closure interview question.
  • var has function scope. On the first iteration the value is 0, but it is not printed right away, because the setTimeout callbacks run only after all the synchronous code has finished. The callbacks keep a reference to the variable i in memory, and by the time they run, the current value of i is 3. ✔ the sentence ended with "the current value of the i is e" (garbled) → "is 3".वाक्य अर्धवट/चुकीचे होते: callbacks चालतात तेव्हा i ची value 3 असते.
  • The loop runs quickly and completes before any of the setTimeout callbacks execute.
  • When the callbacks finally run after 1000 ms, they all access the same i, which is now 3 (because the loop has finished).
  • Because var is function-scoped, all 3 setTimeout callbacks share the same variable i, and by the time they run, i = 3.
StepWhat happens
1st iteration, i = 0i is declared with var (available globally). A setTimeout callback is scheduled to run after 1000 ms. The closure remembers the reference to i (not the value, but the variable).
2nd iteration, i = 1i is updated to 1. Another callback is registered for 1000 ms. All closures still point to the same i.
3rd iteration, i = 2i becomes 2. Another callback is added for 1000 ms.
After the loop endsThe loop has finished and i has become 3. All 3 callbacks are waiting to run, and all of them see i = 3, because they refer to the same variable.
If you are not allowed to use let, solve it with a closure, like an IIFE:
Fix 1: use let
// let creates a new block-scoped i on each iteration → each setTimeout gets a different i
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log(i);   // → 0, 1, 2
  }, 1000);
}
  • What happens: let creates a new i for every iteration, so each callback remembers its own value.
  • Output: 0, 1, 2.
  • ✅ Simplest fix.
Fix 2: use an IIFE (before let existed)
// and using an IIFE:
// it captures the value of i during that iteration and saves it as the local variable j inside the function scope.
// Each setTimeout now uses its own copy of j, not the shared i.
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  (function (j) {
    setTimeout(() => {
      console.log(j);   // → 0, 1, 2
    }, 1000);
  })(i);
}
  • What happens: the IIFE runs immediately with the current i and stores it as its own parameter j; each callback closes over a different j.
  • Output: 0, 1, 2.
  • When using var, the variable i is hoisted and shared across all iterations, so all callbacks access the final value of i.
  • Using let creates a new i for each iteration (block scope), so each setTimeout captures the correct value of i.
  • An IIFE can be used to create a new scope for each iteration and pass in the current value of i.
  • Here a new scope is created on every iteration, and j is a local variable inside the function, rather than coming from the outer scope.
Figure 38: Closures capture VARIABLES, not values. var shares one i; let and an IIFE give each callback its own.

9. Private Counter & Run-Only-Once

Your Notes:
How will you use a closure to create a private counter?
function counter() {
  let _counter = 0;
  // the leading _ is a convention meaning "private"
  function add(increment) {
    _counter = _counter + increment;
  }
  function retrieve() {
    return _counter;
  }
  return {
    add,
    retrieve,
  };
}
// from outside you can't reach _counter directly; you access it through the closures
let c = counter();
c.add(8);
c.add(8);
console.log(c.retrieve());   // → 16
console.log(c._counter);     // → undefined   (truly private)
  • What happens: _counter lives in counter()'s scope; only add and retrieve can reach it.
  • Output: 16, undefined.
  • ✅ Real data privacy.
Example 10a: a normal function runs every time
let view;
function likeTheVideo() {
  view = "vishal shinde";
  console.log("like to ", view);
}
likeTheVideo();              // → "like to  vishal shinde"
  • What happens: likeTheVideo just runs whenever called.
  • Output: like to vishal shinde.
Example 10b: run only once using a closure flag
let hi;
function likeTheVideo1() {
  let called = 0;
  return function () {
    if (called > 0) {
      console.log("function already called");
    } else {
      hi = "vishal shinde";
      console.log("like to", hi);
      called++;
    }
  };
}
let done = likeTheVideo1();
done();                      // → "like to vishal shinde"
done();                      // → "function already called"
  • What happens: called lives in the closure; after the first call it is 1, so later calls only print a message.
  • Output: like to vishal shinde, function already called.
  • ✅ Prevent double-submits, one-time initialisation.
Generic implementation: run only once
function once(fun) {
  let run = false;
  return function (...args) {
    if (run) {
      console.log("already run this function ");
      return;
    } else {
      run = true;
      return fun(...args);
    }
  };
}
let run = once(likeTheVideo);
run();   // → "like to  vishal shinde"
run();   // → "already run this function "
run();   // → "already run this function "
  • What happens: once wraps ANY function: the closure variable run records whether it has been called; ...args forwards the arguments.
  • Output: like to vishal shinde, already run this function ×2.
  • ✅ Reusable helper (lodash has _.once).
private counter मध्ये _counter फक्त add/retrieve या closures मधूनच बदलता/वाचता येतो, बाहेरून नाही. once() मध्ये run नावाचा flag closure मध्ये लक्षात राहतो, म्हणून function फक्त पहिल्यांदाच चालते.

10. Closure vs Scope · Closures & Garbage Collection

Your Notes: what is the difference between closure and scope?
Closure:
  1. Whenever you create a function inside another function, the inner function is a closure function that can access all the variables and functions of the outer function, even when the outer function is lexically out of scope.
  2. Definition: a closure is a function that remembers and can access variables from its lexical scope (the scope in which it was created) even after that outer scope is no longer active.
  3. Key feature: closures "close over" their environment, meaning they capture the variables and functions of their enclosing scope.
  4. Scopes in a closure: local scope (variables declared inside the closure), outer function scope (variables from the function where the closure is defined), global scope (variables accessible globally).
Scope:
  1. Scope defines which variables you can access.
  2. Definition: scope refers to the accessibility and visibility of variables and functions in a specific part of the program.
  3. Key feature: scope determines where you can access a variable or function. Types of scope: local scope (variables defined within a specific function or block), global scope (variables accessible throughout the program), block scope (introduced with let and const; variables confined to a block, e.g. inside an if or for block).
How do closures affect garbage collection?
  1. Closures can affect garbage collection by extending the lifetime of variables in JS.
  2. A closure keeps a reference to variables from its outer function, even after the outer function has finished executing. This can prevent JavaScript from garbage-collecting those variables.
function createClosure() {
  let largeArray = new Array(1000).fill("data");
  return function () {
    console.log(largeArray.length);
  };
}
// the closure is created
let closureFn = createClosure();
// Here largeArray is NOT garbage-collected: when a closure captures variables,
// those variables stay in memory as long as the closure exists.
// Normally, after createClosure() runs, largeArray would be removed,
// but the inner function (closure) still has a reference to largeArray.
// Since closureFn keeps the function alive, largeArray stays in memory.
  • What happens: the returned function uses largeArray, so it can't be garbage-collected while closureFn exists.
  • Output: (no output).
  • ⚠ Closures holding big data are a common memory leak.
How to avoid memory leaks with closures 
// 1. if you no longer need the closure, remove the reference to free up memory
closureFn = null;   // the reference is removed, so largeArray can be garbage-collected
  • What happens: setting the only reference to null lets the GC free the function and largeArray.
  • Output: (no output).
  • ✅ Release closures you no longer need.
Does a closure prevent garbage collection? Yes, closures can prevent garbage collection in JavaScript by keeping references to variables in their outer scope, even after the outer function has finished executing. This can lead to memory leaks if not handled properly.
How closures affect garbage collection: in JavaScript, garbage collection removes variables that are no longer needed. However, if a closure retains a reference to an outer function's variables, they won't be collected. When a closure captures variables, those variables stay in memory as long as the closure exists.
Extra Details: common closure memory leaks: event listeners that are never removed (removeEventListener), long-running setInterval callbacks, and caches that only grow. Clear timers, remove listeners, and limit cache size (or use a WeakMap keyed by objects).

11. Closure Scope Chain

Your Notes (ClosureScopeChain.js):
  1. The closure scope chain is the mechanism JavaScript uses to find variable references by searching a series of nested scopes (starting from the innermost scope and going outward).
  2. The closure and the scope chain are fundamental concepts in JavaScript that determine how variables and functions are accessed in nested environments.
  3. The scope chain is the hierarchy of variable scopes that JavaScript uses to resolve variable references.
  4. Every time a function is invoked, a new scope is created. When a function is executed, JavaScript first looks for the variable within the local scope. If the variable is not found there, it looks in the outer scope, and then continues looking in the next outer scopes until it reaches the global scope.
Every closure has (at least) three scopes:
  1. Local scope (its own scope)
  2. Outer function scope(s)
  3. Global scope
✔ "every closure have three scope" → AT LEAST three: with deeper nesting (like sum below) there are several outer function scopes, plus any block scopes."फक्त तीन scope" नाही, तर किमान तीन. खालील sum example मध्ये अनेक बाहेरचे function scopes आहेत (a, b, c) आणि त्यानंतर global.
Nested closures (currying)
let e = 10;
function sum(a) {
  return function (b) {
    return function (c) {
      return function (d) {
        return a + b + c + d + e;   // d: own · c, b, a: outer scopes · e: global
      };
    };
  };
}
console.log(sum(1)(2)(3)(4));   // → 20
  • What happens: each returned function remembers the argument of the one before it; the last one adds all four plus the global e.
  • Output: 20.
  • ✅ Currying: pass arguments one at a time.
Local → outer → global
// global scope
var userName = 'vishal';
function makeFum() {
  // outer function scope
  var name = 'welcome';
  function displayName(num) {
    // local scope (own scope)
    console.log(name, num, userName);
  }
  return displayName;
}
// makeFum()(26)
// can also be written this way:
const fun = makeFum();
fun(26);   // → welcome 26 vishal
  • What happens: displayName sees its own num, the outer function's name and the global userName.
  • Output: welcome 26 vishal.
When displayName is executed, it has access to the variables in its local scope (num). If a variable is not found in the local scope, JavaScript looks in the outer scope (name). If it's not found there either, JavaScript continues searching in the global scope (userName).
Figure 39: The closure scope chain in sum(1)(2)(3)(4). Each inner function can reach every outer scope.
Scope chain म्हणजे variable शोधण्याची साखळी: आधी स्वतःचा scope, मग बाहेरचे function scopes, आणि शेवटी global. sum(1)(2)(3)(4) मध्ये सर्वात आतले function a, b, c (बाहेरचे) आणि e (global) सगळे वापरू शकते, म्हणून 20 मिळते.

12. Lexical Scope

Your Notes (lexicalScope.js):
  1. Lexical scope refers to the current context of your code; it can be local, global or block scope.
  2. Lexical scope in JavaScript means that a variable defined outside a function is accessible inside another function defined in that scope, but the opposite is not true, i.e. a variable defined inside a function is not accessible outside it. In other words, lexical scope is the ability of an inner function scope to access variables or functions from its parent scope (but not vice versa). ✔ "defined after the variable declaration". The order of writing doesn't matter; what matters is that the function is written INSIDE the scope that owns the variable (and, for let/const, that it runs after the declaration line, because of the TDZ).variable आधी की नंतर लिहिला हे महत्त्वाचे नाही; function त्या variable च्या scope च्या आत लिहिलेले आहे की नाही हे महत्त्वाचे आहे. let/const साठी function चालताना TDZ संपलेला असावा.
  3. Lexical scope means that the scope of variables is determined by the physical placement of the code, i.e. where functions and variables are written in the source code.
  4. Lexical scope is also known as static scope.
  5. The term "lexical" means that the scope is determined by the physical placement of the code in the source.
  6. Lexical scope is a way of managing variable access in JavaScript based on the physical structure of the code, i.e. it is the process that defines the scope of variables and functions by their position in the source code.
How does lexical scope work? A variable defined outside a function is accessible inside the functions written in that scope, but the opposite is not true: a variable defined inside a function is not accessible outside it.
When is the lexical environment created? Whenever an execution context is created, a lexical environment is created with it. 
var useName = "vishal";
// global scope
function local() {
  // local scope
  console.log(useName);
}
local();   // → "vishal"
  • What happens: a function can read global variables.
  • Output: vishal.

In the example above, useName is defined outside the function, so we can access it inside another function because of lexical scope. In the following example, however, we cannot access a variable defined inside the function from outside it:

function local1() {
  let name1 = "vishal";
}
local1();
// console.log("name", name1);   // ❌ ReferenceError: name1 is not defined
// We can't access variables inside the function; we can only access variables outside this local scope.
// ✔ the comment said "userName is not defined"; the real message is "name1 is not defined".
//    Also, this uncaught error stopped the rest of lexicalScope.js, so it is commented out here.
  • What happens: variables inside a function can't be read from outside.
  • Output: (ReferenceError if uncommented).
Lexical scope:
  1. Lexical scope refers to the current context of your code, i.e. it is the process of determining the scope of variables and functions based on their position in the source code.
    Definition: lexical scope refers to the region of code where a variable is accessible, based on the position of the code in the source file.
    Static / fixed: it is static (decided when the code is written, not at runtime).
  2. Lexical scope is the region of the source code where a variable is accessible (it is a static scope, determined when writing the code).
  3. Lexical scope is determined by the physical code structure, i.e. the nesting of functions.
  4. Variable lifetime: normally, variables are discarded after a function finishes executing (unless preserved by a closure).
  5. When it happens: it is set at the time of writing/defining the code.
  6. Purpose: used for basic variable visibility and scoping rules.
  7. Nature: static, determined at compile time.
function outer() {
  let a = 10;            // 'a' is in outer's lexical scope
  function inner() {
    console.log(a);      // inner has access because of lexical scope → 10
  }
  inner();
}
outer();
  • What happens: inner is written inside outer, so it can use a.
  • Output: 10.
Closure:
  1. Definition: a closure is a function that retains access to its lexical scope even after the outer function has finished executing, i.e. a function that keeps access to its outer scope after the outer function has finished.
    Access: inner functions can continue to access outer variables even after the outer function has returned.
  2. Access: inner functions can access variables from the outer scope even after the outer function has completed.
    Persistence: a returned function (closure) remembers the variables of its parent's scope.
  3. A returned function (closure) can still access a variable from its parent function even after the parent has finished executing.
  4. Closures are based on lexical scope, but persist after the outer function's execution.
  5. Variable lifetime: variables are retained (kept alive) by the closure, not discarded.
  6. When it happens: closures are formed at function creation time, but their usefulness is seen at execution/return.
  7. Purpose: used for data privacy, function factories, memoization and async callbacks.
  8. Nature: WHICH variables a closure can see is fixed lexically (static); their VALUES are read live at runtime, and the environment is kept alive at runtime. ✔ "nature are dynamic determine at runtime". A closure does not choose its variables at runtime; only the lifetime and the current values are runtime matters.closure कोणते variables पाहू शकतो हे code लिहितानाच (lexically) ठरते. runtime ला फक्त त्यांच्या सध्याच्या values वाचल्या जातात आणि environment जिवंत ठेवले जाते.
function outer() {
  let counter = 0;   // stays alive because of the closure
  return function inner() {
    counter++;
    return counter;
  };
}
const fn = outer();
console.log(fn());   // → 1
console.log(fn());   // → 2
console.log(fn());   // → 3
  • What happens: counter survives between calls because the returned inner function keeps it alive.
  • Output: 1, 2, 3.
Differences between lexical scope and closure

Example of lexical scope
// global scope
function subscribed() {
  // inner scope 2
  var name = "vishal shinde";
  // inner scope
  function displayName() {
    // displayName is a closure: a function plus its ability to remember variables in the outer scope
    // inner scope 1
    console.log(name);   // → "vishal shinde"
    alert(name);         // the inner function accesses the 'name' variable of its outer function (browser only)
  }
  displayName();
}
subscribed();
  • What happens: displayName reads name from its parent subscribed().
  • Output: vishal shinde (and an alert in the browser).
  • ⚠ alert exists only in browsers (ReferenceError in Node).
Example 2
let a = "hello ";
const first = () => {
  // console.log(c);   // the parent function can't access the child function's variable
  let b = "How are you";
  const second = () => {
    let c = "i am fine thank you !";
    console.log(a + " " + b + " " + c);   // → "hello  How are you i am fine thank you !"
  };
  second();
};
first();
  • What happens: second can see c (own), b (parent) and a (global); first can't see c.
  • Output: hello How are you i am fine thank you !.
  • Lexical scoping describes how the JavaScript engine uses the location of a variable in the code to determine where that variable is available.
  • A closure is the combination of a function and its ability to remember variables in its outer scope.
  • Using a closure gives access to the outer scope's variables and functions after the outer function's execution is complete.
  • Lexical scope refers to the rule (mechanism) that determines the visibility and lifetime of variables based on their physical location in the source code.
FeatureLexical Scope 🟦Closure 🟩

LifetimeVariables discarded after the function endsVariables retained as long as the closure exists

Lexical scope = variable कुठे दिसेल हे code कुठे लिहिला यावरून ठरणे (static). Closure = त्याच lexical scope चे variables, बाहेरचे function संपल्यानंतरही जिवंत ठेवणे. Lexical scope हा नियम आहे, आणि closure हा त्या नियमाचा परिणाम आहे जो memory मध्ये टिकतो.

13. Interview Questions (Detailed)

Q1. What is a closure? Explain with an example.
  • A function together with references to the variables of the scope it was created in. function counter() { let c = 0; return () => ++c; }: the returned arrow keeps c alive and private between calls.
Q2. Why does a var loop with setTimeout print 3 3 3, and how do you fix it?
  • All callbacks close over the SAME function-scoped i, which is 3 when they run. Fix with let (a new binding per iteration), an IIFE that passes i as a parameter, or setTimeout(fn, 1000, i) (extra setTimeout arguments are passed to the callback).
Q3. What are practical uses of closures?
  • Private state (counters, the module pattern), function factories and currying, memoization/caching, once/debounce/throttle, event handlers and async callbacks that remember values.
Q4. Can closures cause memory leaks? How do you prevent them?
  • Yes. Captured variables stay alive as long as the closure is reachable. Remove event listeners, clear intervals, set references to null and bound caches when they are no longer needed.
Q5. What is the difference between scope, lexical scope and closure?
  • Scope = where a variable is visible. Lexical scope = the rule that visibility comes from where the code is written. Closure = a function keeping access to its lexical scope after that scope's function has returned.
Q6. Do two calls of a factory share state?
  • No. Each call creates a new lexical environment: const a = counter(), b = counter(); a(); a(); b(); → 1, 2, 1.
Q7. Output-based questions
function make() { let x = 0; return { inc: () => ++x, get: () => x }; }
const m = make(); m.inc(); m.inc();
console.log(m.get());                          // → 2   (both closures share x)

const fns = [];
for (var k = 0; k < 3; k++) fns.push(() => k);
console.log(fns.map(f => f()));                // → [3, 3, 3]

const add = a => b => a + b;
console.log(add(2)(3));                        // → 5

let v = 1;
function show() { console.log(v); }
v = 2;
show();                                        // → 2   (closures read the CURRENT value)
  • What happens: closures share variables (inc and get use one x); var in a loop is shared → [3, 3, 3]; curried add; a closure reads the variable's CURRENT value, not the value at creation time.
  • Output: 2, [3, 3, 3], 5, 2.
  • ✅ Revise before interviews.

2. Phase 1: the Parsing Phase

  1. When you run the code, it goes into the parsing phase.
  2. Parsing has different steps:
    1. Lexical analysis (tokenization), also known as the lexer:
      1. breaks your code into tokens, e.g. let a = 10; → let, a, =, 10, ;
      2. tokens are the basic building blocks (keywords, identifiers, symbols/operators, literals);
      3. once the tokens are created, they are passed to the syntax parser (syntax analysis).
    2. Syntax analysis (parsing) (checks the syntax and generates the AST, the Abstract Syntax Tree):
      1. the syntax analyser (parser) takes the stream of tokens from the lexer;
      2. it checks whether the code's syntax is correct, e.g. whether let a = 10; is valid; if the syntax is correct, it builds a tree structure called the AST: 
        VariableDeclaration (let)
└── VariableDeclarator
    ├── Identifier (a)
    └── Literal (10)
        • What happens: [TODO: Explanation required]
        • Output: [TODO: Output required]
      3. once the AST (abstract syntax tree) is created, it is passed on to the compiler/interpreter.
✔ Important consequence (verified in Node): a script is PARSED COMPLETELY before any line runs. With console.log('first'); let x = ;, nothing is printed at all; the SyntaxError stops the whole script. This is why the earlier chapters' files with a SyntaxError (duplicate let/const, raw HTML) printed nothing. JS चालवण्यापूर्वी संपूर्ण script parse होते. कुठेही SyntaxError असेल तर पहिली ओळ सुद्धा चालत नाही. म्हणूनच मागच्या files मध्ये duplicate let/const असताना काहीच print झाले नाही.

3. Phase 2: Compilation (Just-In-Time Compilation, JIT)

(Step 3: the JIT compiler compiles the AST to machine code just before execution.)
  1. The AST is passed on (in V8, first to the Ignition interpreter, which turns it into bytecode).
  2. The engine converts the code to bytecode, and the JIT compiler turns frequently used ("hot") parts into machine code.
  3. It happens just before / while running the code (hence "Just in Time").
  4. Optimization is done based on how your code behaves at runtime (types seen, functions called often).
  5. Then the created bytecode/machine code goes to the execution phase.
✔ Clarified: the AST isn't compiled straight to machine code up front. Modern engines first INTERPRET bytecode (fast start), profile it, and JIT-compile only hot functions to optimized machine code; if their assumptions break (e.g. a variable changes type), they DE-optimize back to bytecode.engine आधी bytecode चालवतो (लगेच सुरुवात), आणि वारंवार चालणाऱ्या functions नाच optimized machine code मध्ये बदलतो. type बदलल्यास तो optimization रद्द करतो (deoptimize).

4. Phase 3: the Execution Phase

  1. Once the bytecode is ready, the engine executes it (and the compiled machine code).
  2. The code is executed and the result is displayed.

5. Execution Context, Memory Heap & Call Stack

Once the code is compiled, the JS engine creates an execution context to start executing the code. So everything in JavaScript happens inside an execution context.
What happens when you run a JavaScript program?
  1. When the JavaScript program runs, an execution context is created.
  2. This execution is not possible without 2 major components of the JavaScript engine:
    1. the memory heap;
    2. the call stack.

1. Memory heap

  1. This is the place where memory is stored (objects, arrays, functions, closures).
  2. This memory is constantly in sync with the call stack and the garbage collector.
  3. So the memory heap is the space where variables and functions are allocated memory (primitives in a frame may live on the stack; objects always live on the heap).
  4. Heap memory is where dynamically allocated memory resides.
  5. Heap memory holds the data that is referenced by the execution contexts.

What is the call stack?

The call stack is the mechanism that keeps track of all the function calls.

  1. The JavaScript engine uses the call stack to keep track of execution contexts: when a function is called, a new frame is added to the call stack, and when the function completes, its frame is removed (basically it works Last In, First Out, LIFO).
  2. The execution phase uses the call stack.
  3. The call stack holds the execution contexts (each with its own creation and execution phases); the heap is separate and holds the objects those contexts refer to. ✔ "inside the call stack we have creation phase, execution context, and heap memory". The call stack contains EXECUTION CONTEXTS (frames); creation/execution are PHASES of each context; the heap is a separate memory area.call stack मध्ये फक्त execution contexts (frames) असतात. creation आणि execution हे प्रत्येक context चे टप्पे (phases) आहेत, आणि heap ही वेगळी memory आहे.
  4. Hoisting and the scope chain are set up in the CREATION phase. ✔ "hoisting and scope chain are created in execution phase" → in the CREATION (memory) phase, before any line runs; that's exactly why hoisting works.hoisting आणि scope chain creation phase मध्ये तयार होतात (code चालण्याआधी), म्हणूनच hoisting काम करते.
  5. In order to manage execution contexts, the JavaScript engine uses a call stack.
  6. The call stack is a data structure that keeps track of the currently executing function in a program.
  7. It operates on the Last In, First Out (LIFO) principle, meaning that the last function added to the stack is the first one to be completed and removed.
function one() { two(); }
function two() { console.log(new Error().stack); }   // stack: two ← one ← global (verified)
one();
function rec() { rec(); }
rec();   // RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded (stack overflow)
  • What happens: each call pushes a frame on the call stack: one() → two(); the error's stack trace shows that order. A function that calls itself forever keeps pushing until the stack is full.
  • Output: a stack trace two ← one, then RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded.
  • ✅ Reading stack traces tells you exactly which calls led to an error.
  • ⚠ Recursion always needs a base case.

6. When You Run JS Code for the First Time, the Global Execution Context Is Created

The JavaScript engine goes through the creation phase before executing any code. During this phase it sets up the global execution context; the global execution context is the first one to be created and pushed onto the call stack. This happens when the JavaScript engine starts executing the code.

The global execution context has 2 phases:
  1. Creation phase (also known as the memory creation phase):
    1. creates the global object (window in browsers, global in Node.js) and sets up the this reference;
    2. JS allocates (reserves) memory for all the variables and functions: variables get a special value like undefined, and for function declarations it literally stores the whole code of the function in this memory space;
    3. this is where variables and functions are hoisted.
    I.e. function declarations are stored fully in memory, meaning the entire function is available for use before the code executes. Variables (var, let, const) are also registered in memory: var variables are initialized with undefined; let and const are declared but not initialized (they remain in the temporal dead zone (TDZ) until the code assigning them a value is executed). ✔ Note: only function DECLARATIONS are stored whole. A function expression/arrow stored in a var is undefined in this phase (calling it early → TypeError: … is not a function), and in let/const it's in the TDZ.फक्त function declaration पूर्ण साठवले जाते. var मधले function expression/arrow undefined असते, आणि let/const मधले TDZ मध्ये. 
    console.log(a, typeof sq, typeof expr);   // → undefined function undefined  (verified)
var a = 10;
function sq(n) { return n * n; }
var expr = function () {};
console.log(b);   // ❌ ReferenceError: Cannot access 'b' before initialization (TDZ)
let b = 2;
    • What happens: in the creation phase var a and var expr get undefined, function sq gets its whole body; let b stays in the TDZ.
    • Output: undefined function undefined, then ReferenceError.
  2. Code execution phase (where the code is actually run):
    1. after memory allocation, the code starts executing line by line;
    2. variables are assigned their values, and if a function is invoked, an altogether NEW execution context is created (and pushed onto the call stack). This function execution context also has 2 components:
      1. memory creation phase: memory is allocated in the first phase for the variables and functions inside this function (including its parameters and arguments);
      2. code execution phase: once memory is allocated, the function executes and does the calculation; when it encounters the special keyword return, return tells the function that it is done with its work and returns control back to the execution context where the function was invoked;
      3. then the whole execution context for that instance of the function is deleted (popped off the call stack).
  1. When JS is done with all its work and the program finishes, the global execution context is also removed (deleted, popped off).
  2. To manage all of this (execution-context creation, deletion and control), the engine maintains a stack: this is called the call stack.
  3. So execution contexts are managed by the call stack.
Figure 41: An execution context has a memory component (creation phase) and a code component (execution phase); each function call pushes a new context onto the call stack.
Program सुरू झाल्यावर Global Execution Context बनतो. त्याचे 2 टप्पे: (1) creation/memory phase: variables ना undefined, function declarations ना पूर्ण code (हेच hoisting); (2) execution phase: ओळीने code चालतो. function call झाल्यावर त्याचा नवीन context call stack वर जातो, return नंतर तो काढला जातो (LIFO).

7. What is an Execution Context?

  1. The execution context is the environment in which JavaScript code is evaluated and executed.
  2. So the execution context is a big box or container in which the whole JS code is executed.
The execution context is a container with two components:
  1. Memory component (memory creation phase), also known as the variable environment:
    1. this is the place where all the variables and functions are stored as key-value pairs, like key: value, a: 10, fn: {…};
    2. it is the environment in which all these variables and functions are stored as key-value pairs.
  2. Code component (code execution phase), also known as the thread of execution:
    1. this is the place where code is executed, one line at a time.
(Each context also gets a this binding and a reference to its OUTER lexical environment, which forms the scope chain, Chapter 10.)

8. What are an Interpreter and a Compiler in JS?

1. Interpreter

  1. An interpreter takes your code, translates it and executes it line by line.
  2. An interpreter runs slower overall, because it interprets every line at runtime.
  3. But it STARTS faster, because it doesn't wait to compile; it starts executing immediately, line by line. ✔ your points 2 and 3 said both "slower" and "faster". Both are true in different senses: faster to START, slower to RUN.interpreter सुरुवात लवकर करतो (start fast), पण एकूण चालण्यात हळू असतो (run slow). दोन्ही वाक्ये वेगवेगळ्या अर्थाने बरोबर आहेत.
  4. It stops at the first error it encounters (runtime errors; in JS, SyntaxErrors are caught for the whole script before running, §2).
  5. An interpreter does not produce a separate file.
  6. It cannot optimize as effectively.

2. Compiler

  1. Translates (compiles) the entire code before execution, creating optimized machine code, and then execution starts; i.e. it translates the whole source code into machine code.
  2. Faster execution (because the code is already compiled).
  3. Runs after full compilation.
  4. Shows all errors after compiling.
  5. Generates a separate machine-code file, e.g. .exe.
  6. Can optimize code before execution.
Differences between a compiler and an interpreter
FeatureCompilerInterpreter
📜 DefinitionTranslates the entire source code at once into machine codeTranslates and executes code line by line
⚡ SpeedFaster execution (the code is already compiled)Slower (interprets every line at runtime)
🕒 When Code RunsRuns after full compilationRuns immediately, line by line
🧠 Error DetectionShows all errors after compilingStops at the first error it encounters
📦 OutputGenerates a separate machine-code file (e.g. .exe)Does not produce a separate file
🔁 Code OptimizationCan optimize code before executionCannot optimize as effectively
🔧 Used InC, C++, Java (with JVM), RustJavaScript (in browsers), Python, Ruby
✔ modern JavaScript is NOT purely interpreted: engines like V8 (Chrome/Node), SpiderMonkey (Firefox) and JavaScriptCore (Safari) use an interpreter + JIT compiler. Java is also a hybrid (javac → bytecode, then the JVM's JIT).आजची JavaScript फक्त interpreted नाही: V8 सारखे engines interpreter + JIT compiler दोन्ही वापरतात. Java सुद्धा bytecode + JVM JIT असा hybrid आहे.

9. What is a JIT Compiler?

  1. Just-In-Time compiler.
  2. It is a combination of a compiler and an interpreter, used in modern JavaScript engines (like V8 in Chrome) to boost performance.
  3. The JIT approach does both:
    1. it starts running code immediately (like an interpreter);
    2. the compiler's job is to compile hot code into optimized machine code at runtime.
  4. The JIT compiler is used to compile while running ("just in time"), i.e. to optimize your code for high performance.
  5. The JIT compiler makes your code more optimized so it runs very fast.
Tip from how JITs work: keep object shapes and variable types consistent (don't add properties in random order or switch a variable from number to string), so the engine can keep its optimized code.

10. Garbage Collector & Engine Optimizations

Garbage collector:
  1. Garbage collection tries to free up memory whenever possible, e.g. objects that can no longer be reached (a function's local objects after it returns, a callback after you clear its timeout); it collects all the garbage and sweeps it, using the mark-and-sweep algorithm.
  2. Garbage collection does the job of collecting garbage and optimizing the memory space used by the JavaScript engine.
Mark-and-sweep: start from the roots (the global object, the current call stack), MARK everything reachable through references, then SWEEP (free) everything unmarked. Unreachable objects are collected even if they reference each other (cycles). Memory leaks happen when you KEEP references by mistake (global variables, forgotten timers/listeners, big closures).
The JavaScript engine uses optimization techniques like:
  1. inlining (replacing a function call with the function's body)
  2. hidden classes / shapes (fast property access for objects with the same structure)
  3. inline caching (remembering where a property was found at a call site)
✔ "copy elision" is a C++ compiler optimization, not a JS-engine technique; the usual JS trio is inlining, hidden classes and inline caching."copy elision" हे C++ चे optimization आहे, JS engine चे नाही. JS मध्ये inlining, hidden classes आणि inline caching वापरतात.

11. The JS Runtime Environment Contains the Following

  1. JS engine: JS has three phases:
    1. parsing: lexical analysis (tokenization) and syntax analysis (parsing), which creates the AST;
    2. the compilation phase;
    3. the execution phase. (The engine = memory heap + call stack.)
  2. Web APIs (setTimeout, DOM, fetch…: provided by the browser; libuv/C++ APIs in Node).
  3. Event loop.
  4. Callback queues:
    1. the macrotask queue (timers, events);
    2. the microtask queue (promise callbacks, queueMicrotask). (Chapter 62 shows the order.)
    ✔ "ca;;back queue" → callback queue."ca;;back" नाही, callback queue.
Is JS a synchronous, single-threaded language?
  1. Single-threaded means JS can only execute one command at a time; and synchronous single-threaded means JS executes one command at a time, in a specific order, so it can only go to the next line once the current line has finished executing. (The asynchronous behaviour comes from the RUNTIME around the engine: Web APIs + queues + the event loop.)
JS runtime = JS engine (heap + call stack) + Web APIs (setTimeout, DOM, fetch) + event loop + callback queues (micro आणि macro). engine स्वतः single-threaded आणि synchronous आहे; async काम browser/Node च्या मदतीने होते.

12. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. What happens when JS code runs?
  • Parse (tokens → AST; a SyntaxError stops everything) → bytecode is interpreted → hot code is JIT-compiled → execution inside execution contexts on the call stack, with objects in the heap; async work goes through Web APIs, queues and the event loop.
Q2. What is an execution context and what are its phases?
  • The environment where code runs: a memory/variable environment + a thread of execution, a this binding and an outer-scope reference. Creation phase (hoisting: var → undefined, function declarations whole, let/const in the TDZ), then execution phase (line by line).
Q3. Is JavaScript interpreted or compiled?
  • Both: it is JIT-compiled. Engines parse the whole script, interpret bytecode for a fast start, and compile hot paths to optimized machine code at runtime.
Q4. What is the call stack and what is a stack overflow?
  • A LIFO stack of execution contexts (frames). Infinite or too-deep recursion exceeds its limit → RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded.
Q5. Output-based questions
console.log(x); var x = 1;           // → undefined (creation phase)
console.log(f());  function f() { return "ok"; }   // → ok (declaration stored whole)
console.log(g);    var g = () => 1;  // → undefined
// g();  before its line             // TypeError: g is not a function
console.log(1); let y = ;            // → nothing prints: SyntaxError at parse time
function a() { b(); } function b() { throw new Error("x"); } a();   // stack trace: b ← a ← global
  • What happens: creation-phase rules in one block; the broken `let y = ;` line is a SyntaxError found while parsing, so in a real file NOTHING would print.
  • Output: undefined, ok, undefined, (SyntaxError).
  • ⚠ A single syntax error stops the whole file before any line runs.
TermMeaning
Lexer / ParserCode → tokens → AST
Interpreter / JITBytecode runs now; hot code → machine code
Execution contextMemory (variable env) + code (thread of execution)
Creation phaseHoisting: var → undefined, functions whole, let/const TDZ
Call stackLIFO list of contexts
Memory heapObjects/functions; cleaned by mark-and-sweep GC
RuntimeEngine + Web APIs + event loop + queues
थोडक्यात: code → tokens → AST → bytecode → (hot) machine code. प्रत्येक run साठी execution context बनतो: आधी memory phase (hoisting), मग execution phase. contexts call stack वर LIFO पद्धतीने येतात-जातात, objects heap मध्ये राहतात, आणि GC mark-and-sweep ने memory मोकळी करतो. JS JIT-compiled आहे, फक्त interpreted नाही.

1. Expression & Operator

1.1 Q. What is an Expression?

Your Notes:
  • Definition: an expression is a combination of operators and operands, and it returns a result as a single value. A single value or variable on its own (like 5 or num) is also an expression. ✔ added that an expression doesn't need an operator. A literal or a variable alone also produces a value.Expression साठी operator असणे गरजेचे नाही. फक्त 5 किंवा फक्त num हे सुद्धा expression आहेत, कारण ते value देतात.
  • Operands are evaluated from left to right, but the order of operations is decided by operator precedence and associativity (e.g. * before +, and ** and = group right to left). ✔ "expressions are always executed left to right" is not always true. 2 + 3 * 4 = 14 (not 20), and 2 ** 3 ** 2 = 512 (right to left).expression नेहमी डावीकडून उजवीकडे चालत नाही. आधी precedence (उदा. * आधी, + नंतर) आणि associativity पाहिली जाते. 2 + 3 * 4 = 14 आणि 2 ** 3 ** 2 = 512 (उजवीकडून).
  • A combination of operands (variables, literals) and operators that is evaluated to resolve to a single value.

1.2 Q. What is an Operator?

Your Notes:
  • An operator is a special character or symbol that represents a specific mathematical or logical action.
  • A special character or symbol that represents a specific mathematical, comparison or logical action.
Ex. expression = operands + operators
// num, num1 and num2 are operands; * and / are operators
let num  = 20;
let num1 = 30;
let num2 = 5;

let result = (num * num1) / num2;
console.log("result", result);      // → result 120   (600 / 5)
  • What happens: an expression combines operands (values/variables) with operators and produces a value: 20 * 30 = 600, then / 5.
  • Output: result 120.
  • ✅ Brackets make the order explicit and readable.
Figure 42: An expression. Operands combined with operators always produce a single value.
Expression म्हणजे operands (values/variables) आणि operators (+, *, / ...) यांचा संच, जो शेवटी एकच value देतो. Operator म्हणजे विशिष्ट काम (गणित, तुलना, logic) दाखवणारे चिन्ह.

1.3 Q. How to Check Truthy and Falsy Values

Your Notes: using an if…else condition:
Truthy check
let name = "vishal";

if (name) {
  console.log("this is truthy value");   // → runs ("vishal" is truthy)
} else {
  console.log("this is falsy value");
}
  • What happens: the if converts "vishal" to boolean; a non-empty string is truthy.
  • Output: this is truthy value.
Condition check
var score = 99;

if (score === 0) {
  console.log("OMG WE LOST THE GAME...!");
}
// If the CONDITION is false, the else block runs.
else {
  console.log("WE WIN THE GAME..");      // → runs (99 === 0 is false)
}
// ✔ comment said "if you give a falsy value, it always goes to else"
  • What happens: 99 === 0 is false, so the else block runs.
  • Output: WE WIN THE GAME..
✔ here the condition is score === 0, not the truthiness of score. The else block runs because the condition is false, not because score is falsy (99 is truthy). Also fixed "GAGE" → "GAME" and "LOSS" → "LOST".इथे condition score === 0 आहे, म्हणजे score truthy/falsy आहे की नाही हे तपासले जात नाही. condition false झाली म्हणून else चालतो. 99 स्वतः truthy आहे.

Note: when working with floating-point numbers in JavaScript, consider using methods like toFixed(2) when a precise decimal representation is necessary.

console.log(0.1 + 0.2);             // → 0.30000000000000004
console.log((0.1 + 0.2).toFixed(2)); // → "0.30"  (toFixed returns a STRING)
  • What happens: 0.1 and 0.2 can't be stored exactly in binary, so the sum has a tiny error. toFixed rounds for display and returns a string.
  • Output: 0.30000000000000004, "0.30".
  • ⚠ For money, calculate in paise/cents (integers) or use Number(x.toFixed(2)); compare with Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON.
Assignment operator उजवीकडील value डावीकडील variable मध्ये ठेवतो. x += 5 म्हणजे x = x + 5, आणि बाकीचे (-=, *=, /=, %=, **=) याच प्रकारे. decimal गणितात 0.1 + 0.2 हे अचूक 0.3 येत नाही, म्हणून toFixed() वापरा.

4. Arithmetic Operators

Your Notes: Definition
  • Arithmetic operators take numerical values (either literals or variables) as their operands and return a single numerical value.
Operator NameActionSymbolExampleOutput
AdditionAdds two values+20 + 3050
SubtractionSubtracts right from left-30 - 2010
MultiplicationMultiplies two values*20 * 30600
DivisionDivides left by right/30 / 201.5
ModulusReturns the remainder%20 % 3020
ExponentiationRaises a value to a power**5 ** 3125
Notes:
  • (+) Addition → adds two numbers.
  • (-) Subtraction → subtracts the second number from the first.
  • (*) Multiplication → multiplies two numbers.
  • (/) Division → returns the quotient.
  • (%) Modulus → returns the remainder after division.
  • (**) Exponentiation → raises the left operand to the power of the right operand.
Example: 5 ** 3 = 5 × 5 × 5 = 125
Interview notes:
  • ✔ Division (/) returns the quotient.
  • ✔ Modulus (%) returns the remainder.
  • ✔ Exponentiation (**) was introduced in ES2016 (ES7).
Extra Details: 
-7 % 3          // → -1   (% keeps the sign of the LEFT operand; it is a remainder, not a mathematical modulo)
7 % -3          // → 1
2 ** 3 ** 2     // → 512  (** is right-associative: 2 ** 9)
(2 ** 3) ** 2   // → 64
// -2 ** 2      // ❌ SyntaxError → write (-2) ** 2 = 4
10 / 3          // → 3.3333333333333335   Math.floor(10 / 3) → 3
  • What happens: % keeps the sign of the left number; ** works right-to-left; -2 ** 2 is not allowed without brackets.
  • Output: -1, 1, 512, 64, 3.3333333333333335.
  • ⚠ Use ((n % m) + m) % m for a true positive modulo.
+, -, *, / हे साधे गणित आहे. % भागाकारानंतरची बाकी देतो, आणि ** घात (power) देतो (5 ** 3 = 125). % चे उत्तर डावीकडील संख्येच्या चिन्हानुसार (sign) येते: -7 % 3 = -1.

5. String Operators

Your Notes: Definition
  • String operators are used to concatenate (join) two or more strings.
  • In JavaScript, the (+) operator is overloaded. It performs both numeric addition and string concatenation, depending on the operands.
String operators table
Operator NameSymbolPurpose
String Concatenation+Joins two or more strings
String Concatenation Assignment+=Appends a string to an existing string
Coercion rules
ExpressionOperation
String + AnythingString Concatenation
Number + NumberNumeric Addition
String - NumberNumeric Subtraction
String * NumberNumeric Multiplication
String / NumberNumeric Division
String % NumberNumeric Modulus
Implicit string coercion
  • The (+) operator behaves differently depending on the operand types.
  • Rule 1 → if either operand is a STRING, JavaScript converts the other operand into a STRING and performs concatenation.
  • Rule 2 → operators like -, *, /, %, ** do NOT perform string concatenation. Instead, JavaScript converts the string into a NUMBER and performs arithmetic.
Syntax (1)
// 1. Concatenation (+) : string1 + string2
let firstName = "Vishal", lastName = "Shinde";
let fullName = firstName + " " + lastName;
console.log(fullName);         // → "Vishal Shinde"
  • What happens: + between strings joins them.
  • Output: Vishal Shinde.
2. Concatenation assignment (+=) : string += anotherString
// 2. Concatenation assignment (+=) : string += anotherString
let greeting = "Hello, ";
greeting += "Vishal";
console.log(greeting);         // → "Hello, Vishal"
  • What happens: += appends text to an existing string.
  • Output: Hello, Vishal.
  • ⚠ In big loops, push parts into an array and join once (cleaner).
+ ला एक जरी string मिळाली तर तो जोडतो (concatenation). -, *, /, % string ला number बनवून गणित करतात. += string च्या शेवटी नवीन string जोडतो. (Chapter 3, Figure 17 पहा.)

6. 1's Complement & 2's Complement (Interview Notes)

Your Notes: Q. What is 1's complement?
  • Definition: 1's complement means flipping (inverting) every bit of a binary number.
  • Rule: 0 → 1, 1 → 0.
  • Formula: 1's complement = flip all bits.
Example
Decimal : 5
Binary  : 00000101
1's Complement : 11111010

Explanation:
  00000101
  ↓↓↓↓↓↓↓↓
  11111010
- Every 0 becomes 1.
- Every 1 becomes 0.
  • What happens: [TODO: Explanation required]
  • Output: [TODO: Output required]
Q. What is 2's complement?
  • Definition: 2's complement = 1's complement + 1, OR flip every bit and then add 1.
  • Formula: 2's complement = (~n) + 1 (in JS, ~n + 1 gives -n).
Example
Decimal : 5
Binary  : 00000101

Step 1 : Take 1's complement
  00000101
  ↓
  11111010

Step 2 : Add 1
   11111010
 + 00000001
 ----------
   11111011

Result: 11111011 = -5
  • What happens: [TODO: Explanation required]
  • Output: [TODO: Output required]
Q. Why do computers use 2's complement?
  • If computers used only 1's complement, there would be TWO representations of zero:
    1. Positive zero → 00000000
    2. Negative zero → 11111111
  • Having two representations of zero makes arithmetic operations more complicated.
  • 2's complement solves this problem: positive zero → 00000000, and the 2's complement of zero is also 00000000, so only ONE representation of zero exists.
Advantages of 2's complement
  • Only one representation of zero.
  • Easier addition and subtraction.
  • Faster CPU implementation.
  • Easier overflow detection.
  • Used by almost every modern computer.
Q. Difference between 1's complement and 2's complement
Feature1's Complement2's Complement
RuleFlip all bitsFlip all bits + add 1
Formula~n~n + 1
Represents negativeHistoricallyYes
Zero representation+0 and -0Only one 0
Used todayNoYes
Used by CPUsNoYes
Examples
DecimalBinary1's Complement2's Complement
5000001011111101011111011 (-5)
6000001101111100111111010 (-6)
10000010101111010111110110 (-10)
JavaScript relation
  • The bitwise NOT (~) operator performs ONLY the 1's complement (it flips all bits).
  • Example: ~5 → binary 00000101 → 11111010.
  • JavaScript interprets the resulting bit pattern as a 32-bit signed integer using two's complement representation. Therefore ~5 = -6.
  • Formula: ~x = -(x + 1)
~0   // → -1
~1   // → -2
~5   // → -6
~10  // → -11
  • What happens: ~n flips every bit, which in two's complement equals -(n + 1).
  • Output: -1, -2, -6, -11.
  • ✅ Remember the formula ~n = -(n + 1).
Interview tips
  • 1's complement → flip every bit.
  • 2's complement → flip every bit + add 1.
  • Modern computers store all negative integers using 2's complement representation.
1's complement म्हणजे सर्व bits उलटे करणे (0→1, 1→0). 2's complement म्हणजे bits उलटे करून 1 मिळवणे, आणि याच पद्धतीने computer negative numbers साठवतो (उदा. -5 = 11111011). JS चा ~ फक्त bits उलटतो, म्हणून ~x = -(x + 1), उदा. ~5 = -6.

7.8 >> vs >>>

Your Notes (positive number): 
5 >> 1    // → 2
5 >>> 1   // → 2
  • What happens: for positive numbers >> and >>> both shift right by one bit (≈ divide by 2, rounded down).
  • Output: 2, 2.
  • दोन्हींचा output 2 येतो, कारण 5 हा positive number आहे आणि त्याचा sign bit = 0 आहे.
  • कधी फरक पडतो? फरक फक्त negative numbers मध्ये दिसतो:
-5 >> 1    // → -3
-5 >>> 1   // → 2147483645
// ✔ first line was written "5 >> 1 // -3" (missing minus sign)
  • What happens: >> keeps the sign bit (stays negative); >>> fills with 0, turning a negative number into a huge positive one.
  • Output: -3, 2147483645.
  • ⚠ >>> on negative numbers is a frequent output-question trap.
पहिल्या line मध्ये "5 >> 1 // -3" लिहिले होते. 5 >> 1 चे उत्तर 2 येते; -3 हे -5 >> 1 चे उत्तर आहे.
  • >> = signed right shift → डावीकडे sign bit (0 किंवा 1) कॉपी होतो.
  • >>> = unsigned right shift → डावीकडे नेहमी 0 भरला जातो. त्यामुळे negative संख्या मोठ्या positive संख्येत बदलू शकते.

After  : 00000000 00000000 00000000 00000010

7.10 Shift Summary

Your Notes: one-line rules to remember
  1. << (left shift): shift bits left, fill the right with 0, discard the leftmost bit.
  2. >> (signed right shift): shift bits right, fill the left with the sign bit (0 for positive, 1 for negative), discard the rightmost bit.
  3. >>> (unsigned right shift): shift bits right, always fill the left with 0, discard the rightmost bit. Negative numbers become large positive integers.
Comparison
OperatorExampleBeforeAfterFilled WithResult
<<5 << 10000010100001010Right → 010
>>5 >> 10000010100000010Left → 0 (sign bit)2
>>-5 >> 11111101111111101Left → 1 (sign bit)-3
>>>5 >>> 10000010100000010Left → 02
>>>-5 >>> 1111110110111…1101 (32-bit)Left → 02147483645
✔ the -5 >>> 1 "After" value was shown as 8 bits (01111101 = 125). It only makes sense as 32 bits (0x7FFFFFFD), which is why the result is 2147483645.-5 >>> 1 चा result फक्त 8 bits मध्ये दाखवला तर 125 दिसतो. खरे उत्तर 32 bits वरून येते (0x7FFFFFFD = 2147483645).
Extra Details: practical bitwise tricks 
n & 1          // → 1 if odd, 0 if even
~~4.7          // → 4   (drops decimals, like Math.trunc for 32-bit values)
x | 0          // → converts to a 32-bit integer
!!~"abc".indexOf("b")   // → true  (old trick: ~(-1) is 0)
  • What happens: common bit tricks: n & 1 checks the last bit (odd/even); ~~ and | 0 cut decimals; ~indexOf turns -1 into 0 (falsy).
  • Output: 1/0, 4, integer, true.
  • ⚠ These tricks only work for 32-bit integers and hurt readability; prefer % 2, Math.trunc and includes().

8. Comparison Operators

Your Notes: Definition
  • Comparison operators compare two operands and return a Boolean value (true or false).
  • Operands can be numbers, strings, booleans, objects or other values.
  • Strings are compared lexicographically (dictionary order), based on their Unicode values.
  • Comparison operators are commonly used with: if...else, loops, the ternary operator and conditional statements.
Operator NameSymbolPurpose
Loose Equal==Compares values after type coercion
Strict Equal===Compares value and data type
Loose Not Equal!=Checks inequality after type coercion
Strict Not Equal!==Checks value and type without coercion
Greater Than>Left value is greater than right
Less Than<Left value is less than right
Greater Than or Equal>=Left value is greater than or equal
Less Than or Equal<=Left value is less than or equal
All comparison operators
let a = 10;
let b = 20;

console.log("Loose Equal (==):",          a == "10");   // → true
console.log("Strict Equal (===):",        a === "10");  // → false
console.log("Loose Not Equal (!=):",      a != b);      // → true
console.log("Strict Not Equal (!==):",    a !== "10");  // → true
console.log("Greater Than (>):",          a > b);       // → false
console.log("Less Than (<):",             a < b);       // → true
console.log("Greater Than or Equal (>=):", a >= b);      // → false
console.log("Less Than or Equal (<=):",    a <= b);      // → true
  • What happens: == converts types first, === does not; >, <, >=, <= compare numbers.
  • Output: true, false, true, true, false, true, false, true.
  • ✅ Use === and !== by default.
String comparison (Unicode)
// Strings are compared character by character using their Unicode values.
console.log("A" < "a");        // → true   ("A" = 65, "a" = 97)
console.log("cat" > "car");    // → true   ("t" > "r")
  • What happens: strings compare character by character by code: "A" (65) < "a" (97); "cat" vs "car" differ at t > r.
  • Output: true, true.
  • ⚠ "10" < "9" is true as strings! Convert to numbers first.

JavaScript compares the strings character by character from left to right:

Position"cat""car"Result
1ccSame
2aaSame
3trDifferent → compare Unicode values (t = 116 > r = 114)
Equality with coercion
console.log(true == 1);            // → true
console.log(null == undefined);    // → true
console.log(null === undefined);   // → false
console.log(5 == "5");             // → true
console.log(5 === "5");            // → false
// ✔ was "console.log(5 === "5"); false", a stray "false" statement outside the comment
console.log(false == 0);   // → true   type coercion happens: false is converted to the number 0
console.log(false === 0);  // → false  strictly type-checked: false is boolean, 0 is number
console.log("10" > 5);     // → true   "10" → 10 > 5
console.log("apple" > "Apple");  // → true  lowercase letters have higher Unicode values than uppercase
  • What happens: == converts types (true → 1, "5" → 5); null == undefined by a special rule; === needs the same type.
  • Output: true, true, false, true, false, true, false, true, true.
5 === "5" नंतर false हा शब्द comment च्या बाहेर लिहिला होता, त्यामुळे तो एक वेगळा (निरुपयोगी) statement बनत होता. तो // comment मध्ये नेला. == vs === (most asked interview question)
Feature=====
Type conversionYesNo
Checks valueYesYes
Checks data typeNo (converts first)Yes
RecommendedNoYes
Interview preferenceAvoidPreferred
Extra Details: trap "10" > "9" → false. When both sides are strings, JS compares them character by character ("1" < "9"), not as numbers. Convert first: Number("10") > Number("9") → true.
Comparison operators नेहमी true/false देतात. == आधी type बदलतो, === बदलत नाही, म्हणून नेहमी === वापरा. strings अक्षरानुसार, Unicode value ने तुलना होतात: "A" (65) < "a" (97), आणि "cat" > "car" कारण t > r.

9. Logical Operators

Your Notes: Definition
  • Logical operators are used to perform logical (Boolean) operations.
  • They usually work with boolean values (true or false).
  • However, in JavaScript they can also return non-boolean values because of short-circuit evaluation.
  • Logical operators: (1) logical AND (&&), (2) logical OR (||), (3) logical NOT (!).
Operator NameSymbolPurpose
Logical AND&&Returns first falsy value or last truthy
Logical OR||Returns first truthy value or last falsy
Logical NOT!Reverses Boolean value

9.1 Logical AND (&&)

Your Notes: Definition
  • Logical AND is also called logical conjunction.
  • With booleans, it returns true only when ALL operands are true. With other values, it returns the last operand when all are truthy (not necessarily true). ✔ "returns true" → it returns the last operand's actual value, e.g. "Hello" && 100 → 100.&& नेहमी true परत करत नाही. सगळे truthy असल्यास तो शेवटची value (operand) परत करतो, उदा. "Hello" && 100 = 100.
  • If any operand is falsy, it immediately stops execution and returns that falsy value.
Truth Table
ABA && B
falsefalsefalse
falsetruefalse
truefalsefalse
truetruetrue
Short-circuit evaluation (&&) 
           a && b
              │
              ▼
      Is "a" truthy?
        /          \
      No            Yes
      │              │
      ▼              ▼
 Return "a"     Evaluate "b"
 (stop here)    Return "b"
Rule: if the first operand is falsy, JavaScript never evaluates the second operand.

9.2 Logical OR (||)

Your Notes: Definition
  • Logical OR is also called logical disjunction.
  • Returns true if at least one operand is truthy (with non-boolean values it returns that truthy value itself).
  • If the first operand is truthy, JavaScript immediately returns it.
Truth Table

 Return "a"     Evaluate "b"
 (stop here)    Return "b"
