Chapter 31: Arrow Functions=> syntax · implicit return · lexical this · no arguments / prototype / new
CHAPTER 31 INDEX
  1. What is an Arrow Function?
  2. Normal Function → Arrow Function
  3. Syntax Rules (one expression, one parameter, no parameters, multiple statements)
  4. Key Characteristics (implicit return, lexical this, no constructor, no arguments, no prototype)
  5. Arrow Function vs Normal Function
  6. Examples: arguments, this binding, new
  7. Why Arrow Functions Cannot be Constructors
  8. Interview Questions & Revision

1. Arrow Function

Your Notes:
  • An arrow function is a shorter syntax for writing function expressions, introduced in ES6.
  • It uses the => syntax, does not have its own this, arguments or prototype, supports implicit return for single expressions, and cannot be used as a constructor with the new keyword.
  • The arrow function is a type of function introduced in ES6 (ECMAScript 2015) that provides a shorter, cleaner and more concise syntax for defining functions in JS.
  • It uses the (fat arrow) => syntax and is especially useful for creating small, inline functions (i.e. arrow functions are useful for small, one-time-use functions and are commonly used in callbacks and array methods).
  • It uses the arrow (=>) syntax and is commonly used for:
    • small functions
    • callback functions
    • array methods
    • situations where you want to inherit this from the surrounding scope
  • Arrow functions are always function expressions; they are never function declarations.
Definition: An arrow function ((params) => expression, ES6) is a compact function expression. It has no own this, arguments, super, new.target or prototype. These come from the surrounding (lexical) scope, and it cannot be called with new.
Arrow function (=>) हा function लिहिण्याचा छोटा प्रकार (ES6) आहे. त्याचा स्वतःचा this, arguments, prototype नसतो; this तो बाहेरच्या (lexical) scope मधून घेतो. new सोबत तो वापरता येत नाही. callbacks आणि array methods साठी तो खूप उपयोगी आहे.

2. Normal Function → Arrow Function

Your Notes (your code): 
// normal function
function sum(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
sum(4, 5);    // → 9

// this function converted into an arrow function
const sumArrow = (a, b) => {
  console.log(a + b);
  return a + b;
};
sumArrow(10, 20);    // → logs 30, returns 30
// ✔ was "const sum = …" → SyntaxError: Identifier 'sum' has already been declared.
//    The whole arrowFunction.js (the file index.html loads) did not run at all.
  • What happens: the same addition written as a normal function and as an arrow function.
  • Output: 9, then 30 (logged and returned).
  • ✅ Shorter syntax.
function sum आणि const sum एकाच नावाने declare केल्यामुळे SyntaxError येत होता आणि arrowFunction.js मधील एकही line चालत नव्हती (Node मध्ये तपासले). index.html हीच file load करते. म्हणून arrow version चे नाव sumArrow केले.
Figure 76: Turning a normal function into an arrow function, step by step.

3. Syntax Rules

Your Notes:
1–2. If the function body is only one expression
// If the function body contains only one expression, you may omit {} and return.
// If the body consists of a single expression, the braces {} and the return keyword are omitted.
const sum1 = (a, b) => console.log(a + b);
sum1(2, 3);    // → 5
// ✔ was sum1() with no arguments → undefined + undefined → NaN
  • What happens: one-expression body: no braces, no return (implicit return).
  • Output: 5.
3. Only one parameter
// If there is only one parameter, the parentheses () around it can be omitted (they are optional).
let add = (a) => `the value of a ${a}`;     // same as: a => `…`
console.log(add(5));    // → "the value of a 5"
// ✔ was add() with no argument → "the value of a undefined"
  • What happens: one parameter: brackets are optional.
  • Output: the value of a 5.
4. No parameters
// If there are no parameters, use an empty set of parentheses.
const sum2 = () => `if no parameter add empty set of parenthesis`;
console.log(sum2());    // → "if no parameter add empty set of parenthesis"
// ✔ was console.log(sum2) without () → prints the function itself: [Function: sum2]
  • What happens: no parameters: empty brackets are required.
  • Output: if no parameter add empty set of parenthesis.
Multiple statements (braces are required)
const multiply = (a, b) => {
  console.log('multiply');
  return a * b;
};
console.log(multiply(3, 4));   // → "multiply", then 12
  • What happens: several statements need braces and an explicit return.
  • Output: multiply, 12.
sum1() आणि add() ला arguments दिले नव्हते, त्यामुळे NaN आणि undefined येत होते. console.log(sum2) मध्ये () नव्हते, त्यामुळे function चालण्याऐवजी function स्वतःच print होत होते. हे सर्व दुरुस्त केले.
Extra Details: returning an object literal needs ( ) 
const makeUser = (name) => ({ name });   // → { name: "…" }
const wrong    = (name) => { name };     // → undefined  ({ } is read as a function BODY)
  • What happens: to return an object literal, wrap it in ( ); otherwise { } is read as the function body.
  • Output: { name }, undefined.
  • ⚠ Classic arrow-function bug.

4. Key Characteristics of Arrow Functions

Your Notes:
  1. Short syntax: arrow function syntax is cleaner and shorter than regular functions. 
    function square(x) {
  return x * x;
}
    • What happens: normal function form.
    • Output: (no output).
  2. Implicit return: for single-expression functions, the return is implicit (automatic). 
    const double = n => n * 2;
    • What happens: the same idea as an arrow.
    • Output: (no output).
  3. Lexical this: this is the most important feature. Arrow functions do not create their own this; they inherit this from the surrounding (lexical) scope. 
    const person = {
  name: "Vishal",
  normalFunction() {
    console.log(this.name);
  },
  arrowFunction: () => {
    console.log(this.name);
  }
};
person.normalFunction();   // → "Vishal"      (this = person)
person.arrowFunction();    // → undefined     (this = outer scope, NOT person; "" in a browser, where this = window)
    • What happens: a normal method gets this = the object before the dot; an arrow function takes this from the surrounding code (not the object).
    • Output: Vishal, undefined.
    • ⚠ Don't use arrow functions as object methods that need this.
  4. No this binding: arrow functions do not have their own this; they inherit it from their enclosing context (lexical scope).
  5. Arrow functions cannot be used as constructors: they cannot be used with new. 
    const Person = (name) => {
  this.name = name;
};
// new Person("Vishal");   // ❌ TypeError: Person is not a constructor
    • What happens: arrow functions can't be constructors.
    • Output: TypeError if called with new.
    Arrow functions don't have a prototype, constructor behavior, or their own this.
  6. No arguments object: arrow functions do not have their own arguments object. In some environments, arguments may refer to an outer function's arguments if one exists. The key point is that arrow functions do not create their own arguments object. 
    const test = () => {
  console.log(arguments);     // ❌ ReferenceError in a browser (no own arguments)
};

// Instead, use rest parameters:
const test2 = (...args) => {
  console.log(args);
};
test2(1, 2, 3);               // → [1, 2, 3]
// ✔ the rest-parameter version was written INSIDE the first test function and re-used
//    the name "test"; it is now separate (test2)
    • What happens: arrow functions have no own arguments object; use rest parameters.
    • Output: [1, 2, 3].
  7. No prototype.
rest parameter चे example पहिल्या test function च्या आत आणि त्याच नावाने लिहिले होते, जे चालणार नाही. ते वेगळे (test2) केले. person.arrowFunction() मध्ये this हा person नसतो, म्हणून undefined येते; browser मध्ये this = window असल्यामुळे window.name ("") येते.
Figure 77: Lexical this. A normal method gets this from the call (person.); an arrow function takes this from the outer scope.
Extra Details: where lexical this HELPS 
const timer = {
  v: 1,
  later() {
    setTimeout(() => console.log(this.v), 0);   // → 1  (arrow uses later()'s this = timer)
    // with function () {…} here, this would be window/undefined → wrong value
  }
};
timer.later();
  • What happens: the arrow callback inside setTimeout uses later()'s this (timer), so this.v works.
  • Output: 1.
  • ✅ The main reason arrows exist: callbacks keep the outer this.
Rule of thumb: use a normal function for object methods and an arrow function inside methods (callbacks).

5. Q. Differences between Arrow Functions and Normal Functions

Your Notes: 1. Arrow function:
  1. Arrow function syntax is shorter and cleaner. (They are anonymous function expressions, but they take the variable's name when assigned.)
  2. this binding in arrow functions is lexical: it inherits this from the surrounding scope where the arrow function is defined.
  3. Arrow functions do not have their own arguments object (use a rest parameter, ...rest, to access the arguments).
  4. For a single-line expression, they return the value implicitly without the return keyword.
  5. Arrow functions cannot be used with the new keyword and do not have a prototype property.
  6. Suitable for callbacks, one-line expressions, and scenarios where inheriting this is needed.
2. Normal function:
  1. Uses the function keyword, making it more verbose than an arrow function (it can be either a named or an anonymous function).
  2. this binding is dynamic: it depends on how the function is called (as a method, globally, or with call, apply and bind).
  3. Normal functions have an arguments object that contains all passed arguments.
  4. Explicit return: in all cases you must use the return keyword to return a value.
  5. Normal functions can be used with the new keyword to create new objects.
  6. Suitable for methods, object definitions, and scenarios where dynamic this binding is required.
Arrow FunctionNormal Function
Introduced in ES6Available since the beginning of JavaScript
Shorter syntaxMore verbose syntax
Always a function expressionCan be a function declaration or a function expression
Does not have its own thisHas its own this based on how it is called
Does not have its own argumentsHas its own arguments object
Supports implicit return for single expressionsRequires return to return a value
Cannot be used with newCan be used as a constructor
Has no prototypeHas a prototype property
Best for callbacks, array methods and lexical thisBest for object methods, constructors and dynamic this

6. Examples

Your Notes (your code, corrected):
arguments: arrow vs normal
let sayHi = () => {
  // console.log(arguments); // ❌ ReferenceError: arguments is not defined (browser)
  console.log("hi");
};
sayHi(1, 2, 3);              // → "hi"
// ✔ the arguments line is commented out; in the browser it stopped the rest of the file

function normalFunction() {
  console.log(arguments);
}
normalFunction(1, 2, 3);     // → [Arguments] { '0': 1, '1': 2, '2': 3 }
  • What happens: arrow: no arguments; normal function: has arguments.
  • Output: hi, [Arguments] { '0': 1, '1': 2, '2': 3 }.
Example of a normal function
// a normal function uses the function keyword
function squareNormal(num) {
  // a normal function has the arguments object, containing all passed arguments
  console.log(arguments);    // → [Arguments] { '0': 40 }
  // explicit return (you must use the return keyword)
  return num * num;
}
console.log(squareNormal(40));   // → 1600
// ✔ parameter "num" was missing → ReferenceError: num is not defined;
//    also renamed from "square", which clashed with "const square" below (SyntaxError)
  • What happens: a normal function has arguments and needs return.
  • Output: [Arguments] { '0': 40 }, 1600.
Example of an arrow function (1)
// arrow function syntax: no function keyword and no function name; it uses the fat arrow
const square = (num) => {
  return num * num;
};
  • What happens: arrow version with braces and return.
  • Output: (no output).
2. implicit return
// 2. implicit return
const abc = (num) => num + num;
  • What happens: implicit return.
  • Output: (no output).
3. no arguments object
// 3. no arguments object
const ab = (...nums) => {
  console.log(nums);         // no arguments object, so use a REST parameter to get the arguments
};
ab(1, 2);                    // → [1, 2]
// ✔ comment said "use spread operator"; collecting arguments is the REST parameter (...args)
  • What happens: rest parameter instead of arguments.
  • Output: [1, 2].
this binding
// a normal function has its own (dynamic) this binding
let user = {
  name: "vishal shinde",
  // the arrow function refers to its lexical scope, because it does not have its own this
  rc1: () => {
    console.log(this.name);
  },
  // the normal function has its own dynamic this binding
  rc2() {
    console.log(this.name);
  },
};
user.rc1();   // → undefined   (browser: "" → window.name)
user.rc2();   // → "vishal shinde"
  • What happens: rc1 (arrow) uses the outer this; rc2 (method) uses user.
  • Output: undefined, vishal shinde.
new: arrow ❌ vs normal ✅
// 2. Arrow function (❌ cannot be used with new)
const PersonArrow = (name, age) => {
  this.name = name;
  this.age = age;
};
// const user2 = new PersonArrow("Sara", 30); // ❌ TypeError: PersonArrow is not a constructor
// ✔ commented out, because the TypeError stopped the file before the next example ran

// Normal function (constructor function)
function Person(name, age) {
  this.name = name;
  this.age = age;
  this.sayHello = function () {
    console.log(`Hi, I'm ${this.name}, ${this.age} years old.`);
  };
}
const user1 = new Person("Vishal", 25);
user1.sayHello();   // → "Hi, I'm Vishal, 25 years old."
  • What happens: arrows can't be used with new; constructor functions can.
  • Output: Hi, I'm Vishal, 25 years old.
square() मध्ये num parameter नव्हता (ReferenceError), आणि function square व const square एकाच नावाचे होते (SyntaxError). "spread" हा शब्द बदलून "rest" केला: ...args ने arguments गोळा करणे म्हणजे rest parameter. arguments आणि new PersonArrow या errors मुळे पुढचा code चालत नव्हता, म्हणून त्या lines comment केल्या.

7. Why Arrow Functions Cannot be Used as Constructors

Your Notes:
  1. They do not have their own this, arguments, prototype, super or new.target.
  2. They inherit this from their surrounding (lexical) scope.
  3. So you cannot use new with an arrow function.

8. Interview Questions (Detailed)

Q1. What are the main differences between arrow functions and regular functions?
  • Arrow functions have no own this (lexical this), no arguments object, no prototype, can't be used with new, can't be generators, and support implicit return. Regular functions have dynamic this, arguments, prototype and work as constructors.
Q2. Why does an arrow function used as an object method give undefined for this.name?
  • Because the arrow takes this from the scope where the object literal is written (global/module), not from the object before the dot.
Q3. Can call/apply/bind change the this of an arrow function?
  • No. They can pass arguments, but this stays lexical (whatever it was where the arrow was created).
Q4. When should you NOT use an arrow function?
  • Avoid arrow functions for object methods that use this, for constructors (new), for prototype methods, when you need arguments, and for DOM event handlers that rely on this being the element.
Q5. Output-based questions
const f = x => x * 2;                 console.log(f(4));            // → 8
const g = () => ({ a: 1 });           console.log(g().a);           // → 1
const h = () => { a: 1 };             console.log(h());             // → undefined
console.log(typeof (() => {}));                                     // → "function"
console.log((() => {}).prototype);                                  // → undefined
const o = { n: "o", m() { return [1].map(() => this.n); } };
console.log(o.m());                                                 // → ["o"]
  • What happens: six output questions: implicit return, returning objects, label trap, typeof, no prototype, lexical this in map.
  • Output: 8, 1, undefined, function, undefined, ["o"].
ConceptSummary
Syntax(a, b) => a + b; one param: a => …; none: () => …
Implicit returnSingle expression, no { }; wrap objects in ( )
thisLexical (from the outer scope), never its own
Noarguments, prototype, new, super, new.target
Use forCallbacks, array methods, keeping the outer this
Avoid forObject methods, constructors
थोडक्यात: arrow function म्हणजे छोटे function expression. त्याचा स्वतःचा this नाही (तो बाहेरचा this घेतो), arguments नाही (…rest वापरा), prototype नाही आणि new नाही. callbacks साठी उत्तम, पण object methods साठी normal function वापरा.

Chapter 32: IIFE (Immediately Invoked Function Expression)(function () { … })() · private scope · module pattern · async IIFE
CHAPTER 32 INDEX
  1. What is an IIFE? (Syntax)
  2. Why are Parentheses Used?
  3. Examples (basic, with parameters)
  4. Why Do We Use IIFEs? (5 uses)
  5. IIFE vs Normal Function
  6. Advantages & Disadvantages
  7. Function Declaration vs IIFE
  8. Output-Based Question & the ASI Trap
  9. Key Points & Revision

1. Q. What is an IIFE (Immediately Invoked Function Expression)?

Your Notes:
  • An IIFE (immediately invoked function expression) is a JavaScript function that is defined and executed immediately after it is created.
  • Unlike a normal function, an IIFE does not need to be called separately. It is a JavaScript function that runs as soon as it is defined (as soon as JavaScript reaches it).
  • Syntax:
(function () {
  // code inside IIFE
})();

// or

(() => {
  // code
})();
// ✔ first syntax was written "})())" (one extra ")")
  • What happens: two IIFE syntaxes: function or arrow wrapped in ( ) and called with ().
  • Output: (no output).
  • It is a self-contained block of code.
  • An immediately invoked function expression is a JavaScript function that is defined and executed immediately after its creation.
  • It is a way to create a self-contained block of code that doesn't interfere with the surrounding code, and it executes immediately.
  • It is used to create a scope for variables, avoiding polluting the global variables.
  • The final () executes it immediately after defining it.
  • It is also known as a self-executing anonymous function.
Definition: An IIFE is a function expression that is called in the same statement it is created, as in (function () { … })(). Its variables live in their own function scope, so nothing leaks into the surrounding (global) scope.
IIFE म्हणजे असे function जे बनताच लगेच चालते, त्याला वेगळा call करावा लागत नाही. त्याचे variables त्याच्या आतच राहतात, त्यामुळे global scope खराब (pollute) होत नाही.

2. Q. Why are Parentheses Used?

Your Notes:
  • Normally, function greet() {} is a function declaration. To execute it immediately, JavaScript must first treat it as a function expression, so
  • wrapping it in parentheses converts it into a function expression.
(function () {
  console.log("Hello");
})();
  • What happens: defined and called immediately.
  • Output: Hello.
  • The last () immediately invokes (calls) the function.
Figure 78: Anatomy of an IIFE: wrap it (expression), call it (), and end with ; to avoid the ASI trap.

3. Examples

Your Notes (your code):
Example 1
(function () {
  console.log('This function run immediately..');   // → "This function run immediately.."
})();
  • What happens: runs once, right away.
  • Output: This function run immediately..
Example 2: with parameters
(function (name) {
  console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`);                   // → "Hello, Alice!"
})("Alice");
  • What happens: arguments go in the final ().
  • Output: Hello, Alice!.

4. Why Do We Use IIFEs?

Your Notes:
  1. To avoid polluting the global namespace or scope: it creates a private scope (avoids global namespace pollution).
  2. To execute code immediately (used for initialization logic).
  3. To encapsulate variables: variables inside the IIFE are not accessible from outside.
  4. Module pattern (before ES6 modules): before import and export, developers used IIFEs to create private and public members.
  5. Async IIFE: useful when you want to use await without creating a separate async function.
1. Avoid global namespace pollution
// variables declared inside the IIFE cannot be accessed outside it
(function () {
  let count = 0;
  console.log(count);    // → 0
})();
// console.log(count);   // ❌ ReferenceError: count is not defined → the IIFE creates a private scope
  • What happens: variables inside the IIFE stay private.
  • Output: 0 (count → ReferenceError outside).
  • ✅ Avoids polluting the global scope.
2. Execute code immediately (initialization code that should run only once)
(function () {
  console.log('Application started....');
})();
  • What happens: one-time startup code.
  • Output: Application started....
3. Encapsulate variables
(function () {
  let password = '123';
})();
// console.log(password);   // ❌ ReferenceError (variables defined inside the IIFE are not accessible outside)
  • What happens: password can't be read from outside.
  • Output: (ReferenceError if uncommented).
4. Module pattern (before ES6 import/export, for private and public members)
const Module = (function () {
  let privateVar = 'i am private';
  function privateMethod() {
    console.log(privateVar);
  }
  return {
    getPrivateVar() {
      return privateVar;
    },
    show() {
      privateMethod();
    }
  };
})();

console.log(Module.getPrivateVar());   // → "i am private"
Module.show();                         // → "i am private"
console.log(Module.privateVar);        // → undefined (truly private, thanks to closure)
  • What happens: the IIFE returns an object with public methods; privateVar stays hidden in the closure (module pattern).
  • Output: i am private, i am private, undefined.
  • ✅ Pre-ES6 way to make modules.
5. Async IIFE (use await without creating a separate named async function)
(async function () {
  const data = await Promise.resolve('Hello');
  console.log(data);                   // → "Hello"
})();
  • What happens: an async IIFE lets you use await without naming a function.
  • Output: Hello.
  • ✅ Top-level await alternative in scripts.
Figure 79: The module pattern. The IIFE keeps data private and exposes only the returned public methods (through closures).
IIFE चे 5 उपयोग: global scope स्वच्छ ठेवणे, code लगेच एकदा चालवणे, variables खाजगी (private) ठेवणे, module pattern (private data + public methods), आणि async IIFE मध्ये await वापरणे. Module pattern मध्ये closure मुळे बाहेरचे methods आतला private data वापरू शकतात.

5. IIFE vs Normal Function

Your Notes:
FeatureNormal FunctionIIFE (Immediately Invoked Function Expression)
DefinitionA function that is declared and called whenever needed.A function that is defined and executed immediately after it is created.
Syntaxfunction greet() {}(function(){})();
ExecutionExecutes only when explicitly called.Executes automatically as soon as it is defined.
Function callMust be called separately using greet().No separate function call is required.
ReusabilityCan be called multiple times.Normally executes only once.
HoistingFunction declarations are fully hoisted.An IIFE is a function expression, so it is not hoisted.
ScopeCreates a local scope only when it is called.Creates a private/local scope immediately upon execution.
Global namespaceMay pollute the global namespace if global variables are used.Helps avoid global namespace pollution by keeping variables private.
ParametersParameters are passed when the function is called.Parameters are passed immediately during execution.
Return valueReturns a value when called.Can also return a value immediately.
Typical use casesReusable business logic, utility functions, calculations, event handlers.Initialization code, one-time execution, creating private scope, module pattern.
Modern usageVery common in all JavaScript applications.Less common today because let, const and ES6 modules provide better scoping, but still useful and frequently asked in interviews.
Examplefunction greet(){ console.log("Hello"); } greet();(function(){ console.log("Hello"); })();

6. Advantages & Disadvantages

Advantages of IIFE
  1. Prevents global variable pollution
  2. Creates a private scope
  3. Executes code immediately
  4. Used for one-time initialization
  5. Supports the module pattern
  6. Can be asynchronous using an async IIFE
Disadvantages
  1. Cannot be reused after execution
  2. May reduce readability if overused
  3. Less necessary today because of let, const and ES6 modules
Interview: an IIFE (Immediately Invoked Function Expression) is a function expression that is created and executed immediately after its definition. It is mainly used to create a private scope, avoid polluting the global namespace, execute initialization code once, and implement the module pattern.

7. Differences between Function Declaration & IIFE

Your Notes: 
// Function declaration: the function is declared first and called later
function hi() {
  console.log('Hello');
}
hi();                           // → "Hello"

// IIFE (immediately invoked function expression): the function is created and executed immediately
(function () {
  console.log('Hello');         // → "Hello"
})();
  • What happens: declaration: define now, call later; IIFE: define and call at once.
  • Output: Hello, Hello.

8. Output-Based Question & the ASI Trap

Your Notes: 
(function (x) {
  return (function (y) {
    // x is looked up in the inner scope first; if it's not found there, JS looks in the parent
    // scope, where x exists. This happens because of closure.
    console.log(x);   // → 1   (the inner function first looks for x in its own scope)
  })(2);
})(1);
// This happens because of lexical scope and closure.
  • What happens: nested IIFEs: the inner function doesn't declare x, so it uses the outer x (1).
  • Output: 1.
Closure: a closure is the combination of a function and the lexical environment in which it was created. It allows the function to access variables from its outer (enclosing) scope even after the outer function has finished executing. ✔ in your file, the IIFE just before this question ended with })() and no semicolon. JavaScript joined the two lines into one expression, (…)()(function(x){…})(1), and threw "TypeError: (intermediate value)(...) is not a function" (verified in Node), so this question never ran. Always end an IIFE with ;.या question च्या आधीच्या IIFE च्या शेवटी ; नव्हता. त्यामुळे JS ने दोन्ही lines एकच expression समजल्या: आधीच्या IIFE चा result (undefined) पुढच्या (function…) ने call करायचा प्रयत्न केला आणि TypeError आला (Node मध्ये तपासले). म्हणून IIFE नेहमी ; ने संपवा, किंवा ;(function(){…})() असे सुरुवातीला ; लावा.
Figure 80: The ASI trap. A line starting with ( continues the previous line unless it ended with ;.
(x) चा शोध आधी आतल्या function मध्ये होतो, तिथे नसल्यामुळे बाहेरच्या function मधील x = 1 मिळतो. हे lexical scope आणि closure मुळे होते. ( ने सुरू होणारी line आधीच्या line शी जोडली जाते, म्हणून आधीच्या statement नंतर ; अनिवार्य आहे.

9. Key Points

Your Notes:
  • IIFE: Immediately Invoked Function Expression.
  • It runs immediately after being defined. ✔ "it return immediately after being defined" → "it runs (executes) immediately".IIFE "return" होत नाही तर लगेच "run" (चालते) होते. return value देणे हे वेगळे आहे.
  • It creates a private/local scope.
  • It helps avoid global namespace pollution.
  • It was commonly used before ES6 modules.
  • Today, let, const and ES6 modules have reduced the need for IIFEs, but they are still useful.

10. Interview Questions (Detailed)

Q1. What is an IIFE and why use one?
  • A function expression that runs immediately: (function(){ … })();. Used to create a private scope, avoid global pollution, run one-time initialisation, build the module pattern and use await via an async IIFE.
Q2. Why must the function be wrapped in parentheses?
  • A line starting with function is parsed as a declaration, which can't be invoked immediately (and needs a name). The parentheses turn it into an expression. !function(){}() or void function(){}() also work.
Q3. How do IIFEs relate to closures?
  • Functions returned from an IIFE keep access to the IIFE's variables after it finishes (closure). That is how the module pattern keeps data private.
Q4. Are IIFEs still needed today?
  • Less often: block scope (let/const in { }) and ES modules give private scope. They are still used for async IIFEs, one-off initialisation and older codebases/libraries.
Q5. Why can a missing semicolon break an IIFE?
  • A line beginning with ( continues the previous line, so a()\n(function(){})() becomes a()(function(){})() → TypeError. End statements with ; or start the IIFE with ;(.
Output-based questions
const r = (function (a, b) { return a + b; })(2, 3);
console.log(r);                               // → 5
console.log(typeof (function () {})());       // → "undefined"  (no return value)
var counter = (function () { let c = 0; return () => ++c; })();
console.log(counter(), counter());            // → 1 2
  • What happens: an IIFE can return a value; with no return it gives undefined; an IIFE-built counter keeps private state.
  • Output: 5, "undefined", 1 2.
  • ⚠ Start a line with ; before ( when not using semicolons (ASI trap).
ConceptSummary
IIFE(function(){…})();: define and run immediately
Why ( )Turns a declaration into an expression that can be called
UsesPrivate scope, one-time init, module pattern, async IIFE
TrapAlways end the previous statement with ;
TodayOften replaced by let/const blocks and ES modules

Chapter 33: First-Class FunctionsFunctions as values: assign · pass · return · store
CHAPTER 33 INDEX
  1. What is a First-Class Function?
  2. What does "First-Class Citizen" mean?
  3. The 4 Abilities (with examples)
  4. Why are First-Class Functions Important?
  5. Interview Definition, Key Points & Technical Note
  6. Interview Questions & Revision

1. Q. What is a First-Class Function in JS?

Your Notes: Definition
  • A first-class function (also called a first-class citizen) is a feature of JavaScript where functions are treated like any other value (such as numbers, strings, booleans or objects).
  • Since functions are values, they can be:
    1. assigned to variables,
    2. passed as arguments to other functions,
    3. returned from other functions,
    4. stored inside arrays or objects (stored in data structures like arrays or objects).
  • If a language allows functions to be used anywhere a normal value can be used, then functions are called first-class functions, and the language supports first-class functions.
  • A first-class citizen is also known as a first-class object or first-class function.
  • First-class function refers to an entity that can be treated as a value, in the same way as other types like strings, numbers and objects.
  • First-class function means that a function can be treated like a value or variable; such a function is known as a first-class function.
  • A function can be assigned to a variable, passed as an argument to another function, manipulated, and returned from functions. Basically, everything a variable can do, a function can also do. (A language has first-class functions when functions in that language are treated like any other value.)
  • In such a language, functions can be treated as variables: a function can be passed as an argument to another function, manipulated and returned. Whatever a variable can do, a function can do.
  • First-class function means a programming language where functions can be treated like variables or values; such functions are called first-class citizens.
First-class function म्हणजे function ला number, string सारखी एक साधी value समजणे. म्हणजे function variable मध्ये ठेवता येते, दुसऱ्या function ला argument म्हणून देता येते, function मधून return करता येते, आणि array/object मध्ये साठवता येते.

2. What does "First-Class Citizen" mean?

Your Notes:
  • A first-class citizen is any entity in a programming language that can be used and manipulated just like any other value.
  • In JavaScript, functions are first-class citizens because they can be:
    1. stored in variables
    2. passed to functions
    3. returned from functions
    4. stored in objects and arrays
  • So "first-class citizen" is a term that describes a language feature: a particular entity is treated as equal to other entities in how it can be manipulated and used within the language.
Figure 81: The four things that make functions first-class in JavaScript.

3. The 4 Abilities

Your Notes (your code, corrected):
1. A function can be assigned to a variable
function displayName(name) {
  console.log("name", name);
}
// here the FUNCTION ITSELF is assigned to the variable (no parentheses!)
const calledFunction = displayName;
calledFunction("vishal");      // → "name vishal"
// ✔ was "const calledFunction = displayName("vishal")". With (), the function is CALLED
//    and only its return value (undefined) is stored, so no function was assigned.
  • What happens: assigning a function WITHOUT () stores the function itself; it can then be called through the new name.
  • Output: name vishal.
  • ⚠ With (), you'd store the result (undefined), not the function.
Also assigned to a variable (function expression)
const myFunction = function (name) {
  console.log(name);
};
myFunction("shinde");          // → "shinde"
  • What happens: a function expression is a value in a variable.
  • Output: shinde.
2. A function can be passed as an argument to another function
function operation(fun, a, b) {
  return fun(a, b);
}
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
// here the add function is passed as an argument to the operation function
const newFun = operation(add, 10, 20);
console.log(newFun);           // → 30
  • What happens: add is passed as an argument and called inside operation.
  • Output: 30.
  • ✅ Basis of callbacks and higher-order functions.
3. A function can be returned from another function
function multiply(factor) {
  return function (number) {
    const result = number * factor;
    console.log(result);
  };
}
// const doneMultiply = multiply(10);
// doneMultiply(6);            // → 60
// can also be written as:
multiply(10)(8);               // → 80
  • What happens: multiply returns a function that remembers factor.
  • Output: 80.
4. A function can be stored in a data structure
// you can also store functions in data structures like arrays or objects
function square(num) {
  return num * num;
}
function displaySquare(fn) {
  console.log("square are " + fn(5));
}
displaySquare(square);         // → "square are 25"
// ✔ was fn() with no argument → square(undefined) → "square areNaN"

const operations = [
  function () {
    console.log("Add");
  },
  function () {
    console.log("Subtract");
  }
];
operations[0]();               // → "Add"
operations[1]();               // → "Subtract"

// Functions can be stored inside objects
const calculator = {
  add: function (a, b) {
    return a + b;
  }
};
console.log(calculator.add(10, 20));   // → 30
  • What happens: functions passed as values, stored in arrays and in objects.
  • Output: square are 25, Add, Subtract, 30.
displayName("vishal") मध्ये () असल्यामुळे function लगेच चालते आणि त्याचा return (undefined) variable मध्ये जातो; function स्वतः assign होत नाही. function assign करण्यासाठी () शिवाय displayName लिहा. displaySquare मध्ये fn() ला argument नव्हता, म्हणून NaN येत होते; fn(5) केल्यावर 25 येते (Node मध्ये तपासले). "let num = 10" हा variable वापरला जात नव्हता.
Extra Details: a higher-order function is a function that takes a function as an argument or returns a function (like operation and multiply above, or map/filter/setTimeout). Higher-order functions are possible because functions are first-class.

4. Why are First-Class Functions Important?

Your Notes:
  • Because they make JavaScript powerful and flexible.
  • Many important JavaScript concepts depend on first-class functions, such as:
    1. Callbacks
    2. Higher-order functions
    3. Closures
    4. Promises
    5. Async/await
    6. Event handling
    7. Functional programming

5. Interview Definition, Key Points & Technical Note

Interview definition: a first-class function is a function that is treated like any other value in JavaScript. It can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments, returned from other functions, and stored in data structures such as arrays and objects.

Key points
  • JavaScript treats functions as values.
  • Functions are objects in JavaScript.
  • Functions can be assigned, passed, returned and stored.
  • The feature is called first-class functions, or functions as first-class citizens.
A small technical note
  • "First-class function" and "first-class citizen" are closely related but not exactly the same.
  • First-class citizen is a general language concept (any value with full capabilities),
  • while first-class function means that functions are first-class citizens in JS.
Q1. What makes functions first-class in JavaScript?
  • They can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments, returned from functions and stored in arrays/objects, exactly like numbers or strings.
Q2. What is the difference between passing add and add() as an argument?
  • add passes the function itself (to be called later, as a callback); add() calls it immediately and passes its RETURN value.
Q3. Give real examples that depend on first-class functions.
  • Callbacks (setTimeout, addEventListener), array methods (map/filter/reduce), closures and function factories, promises (.then(fn)), middleware, currying and memoization.
Q4. First-class function vs higher-order function?
  • First-class is a property of the language: functions are values. A higher-order function is a specific function that takes or returns another function, which is only possible because functions are first-class.
Output-based question
const fns = { double: x => x * 2, inc: x => x + 1 };
const apply = (fn, v) => fn(v);
console.log(apply(fns.double, 5), apply(fns.inc, 5));   // → 10 6
const f = Math.max;
console.log(f(3, 9, 4));                                // → 9
  • What happens: functions in an object picked by name; built-in functions like Math.max can be stored too.
  • Output: 10 6, 9.
AbilityExample
Assignconst f = add; (no parentheses)
Passoperation(add, 1, 2)
Returnmultiply(10)(8)
Store[fn1, fn2], { add: fn }
EnablesCallbacks, HOFs, closures, promises, events
थोडक्यात: JS मध्ये function ही value आहे. ती assign, pass, return आणि store करता येते. function assign करताना () लावू नका: f = add म्हणजे function, तर f = add() म्हणजे त्याचा result.

Chapter 34: Pure & Impure FunctionsDeterministic · side effects · predictable vs unpredictable
CHAPTER 34 INDEX
  1. What is a Pure Function?
  2. Characteristics of a Pure Function
  3. Why Determinism Matters (6 reasons)
  4. What is an Impure Function?
  5. Pure vs Impure (tables)
  6. Deterministic vs Non-Deterministic
  7. Predictable vs Unpredictable
  8. Interview Questions & Revision

1. Pure Function & Impure Function

Your Notes:
  • Pure and impure functions are concepts in JS used to differentiate functions based on their behavior and side effects.
Q. What is a pure function?
  • A pure function always returns the same output for the same input, no matter how many times it's called.
  • A pure function is a function that always returns the same output for the same input and does not produce any side effects. Its result depends only on its input arguments.
  • A pure function in JavaScript is a function that always produces the same output for the same input (i.e. given an input, the function always produces the same output).
  • It does not have any side effects (i.e. it does not modify any external state or variable outside the function).
  • It also does not modify any external state or interact with the outside world (i.e. no API call, no DOM manipulation, no changing global variables).
  • A pure function is deterministic: its behavior is predictable and depends only on its input arguments.
Definition: A pure function (1) always returns the same output for the same input, and (2) has no side effects: it doesn't change anything outside itself, including its arguments, and doesn't read changing outside data. A side effect is any observable change or interaction outside the function (globals, DOM, network, console, storage, time, random).
Figure 82: A pure function depends only on its inputs; an impure function reads or changes things outside it.
Pure function म्हणजे असे function जे (1) एकाच input साठी नेहमी तेच output देते, आणि (2) बाहेरच्या कशातही बदल करत नाही (global variable, DOM, API, console काहीच नाही). त्याचा result फक्त त्याच्या arguments वर अवलंबून असतो.

2. Characteristics of a Pure Function

Your Notes:
  • Always returns the same output for the same input.
  • Deterministic.
  • Depends only on its parameters.
  • Does not modify external variables.
  • Does not perform DOM manipulation.
  • Does not make API calls.
  • Does not read/write files.
  • Does not access the current time (Date.now()).
  • Does not generate random values (like Math.random()).
  • It does not modify the input data (it does not mutate its arguments).
  • It does not rely on or modify external state (i.e. it has no side effects like changing global variables or DOM manipulation).
  • There's no randomness, no time dependency, and no reliance on external state.
Extra Details: "does not mutate its arguments", the most common hidden impurity: 
// ❌ impure: changes the array that was passed in
function addItemBad(arr, item) { arr.push(item); return arr; }

// ✅ pure: returns a NEW array, the original stays the same
function addItem(arr, item) { return [...arr, item]; }

const list = [1, 2];
const list2 = addItem(list, 3);
console.log(list, list2);   // → [1, 2] [1, 2, 3]
  • What happens: push changes the caller's array (impure); spread builds a new array (pure).
  • Output: [1, 2] [1, 2, 3].
  • ✅ Pure functions are predictable and easy to test; React state updates need them.

3. Why Does Determinism Matter in Pure Functions?

Your Notes: Definition
  • A deterministic function is a function that always produces the same output for the same input, no matter how many times you execute it.
  • In simple words: same input → same output (always).
  • A deterministic function's result depends only on its input arguments, not on external factors such as time, random numbers or global variables.
Why does determinism matter in pure functions? A deterministic function always produces the same output for the same input. This makes pure functions reliable, predictable and easier to work with.
  1. Predictable behavior: a deterministic function always behaves the same way. 
    function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
console.log(add(2, 3));   // → 5
console.log(add(2, 3));   // → 5
console.log(add(2, 3));   // → 5
    • What happens: same input always gives the same output, no side effects.
    • Output: 5, 5, 5.
    Every time you pass 2 and 3, the result is always 5, so it is easy to understand, easy to predict the output, and has no unexpected behavior.
  2. Easier to debug and test: since the output never changes for the same input, testing becomes very simple. 
    function square(num) {
  return num * num;
}
square(4);   // → 16
square(4);   // → 16
square(4);   // → 16
    • What happens: always 16 for 4.
    • Output: 16 ×3.
    If a test fails, you know the problem is in the function itself, not in some external state. So: easier unit testing, easier debugging, fewer bugs.
  3. No side effects: pure functions do not modify anything outside the function. 
    function multiply(a, b) {
  return a * b;
}
    • What happens: a pure function.
    • Output: (no output).
    The function does not change global variables, does not modify objects, does not call APIs, and does not manipulate the DOM; it simply returns a value. So it is safe to reuse, causes no accidental changes to application state, and is easier to maintain.
  4. Great for functional programming: functional programming relies heavily on pure functions. Because they are deterministic, results are predictable, functions can be composed together, and code becomes easier to understand.
  5. Safe for memoization (caching): since the same input always produces the same output, JS can cache the result. This improves performance and avoids unnecessary calculations.
  6. Safe for parallel execution: because pure functions don't share or modify external state, multiple copies can run simultaneously without interfering with each other. This gives better performance, no race conditions, and easier concurrent programming.
Determinism is important in pure functions because it guarantees that the same input always produces the same output. This makes functions predictable, easier to test, easier to debug, free from side effects, reusable, suitable for functional programming, and enables performance optimizations such as memoization and safe parallel execution.
Your code
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
console.log(add(2, 3));   // → 5
console.log(add(5, 6));   // → 11   (it always produces the same result for the same inputs)
// ✔ was add(5.6), a dot instead of a comma → ONE argument 5.6 → 5.6 + undefined = NaN
  • What happens: deterministic results.
  • Output: 5, 11.
add(5.6) मध्ये comma ऐवजी dot लिहिला होता, त्यामुळे 5.6 हा एकच argument गेला आणि b = undefined झाल्यामुळे NaN आले (Node मध्ये तपासले). add(5, 6) केल्यावर 11 येते.
Deterministic म्हणजे एकाच input ला नेहमी तेच output. त्यामुळे function चा result आधीच सांगता येतो, testing आणि debugging सोपे होते, result cache (memoization) करता येतो, आणि अनेक copies एकाच वेळी सुरक्षितपणे चालवता येतात.

4. What is an Impure Function in JS?

Your Notes:
  • An impure function is a function that either produces side effects or depends on external state, instead of depending only on its input arguments.
  • An impure function in JS is a function that violates one or more principles of a pure function.
  • An impure function relies on and/or modifies external state.
  • An impure function has side effects (i.e. it modifies external state or interacts with the outside world: makes API calls, changes global variables, manipulates the DOM, performs I/O operations).
  • Impure functions may be non-deterministic: they can return a different value each time.
    • An impure function may be non-deterministic, but it is considered impure if it has side effects or depends on external state.
Why is an impure function impure?
  • It may return different outputs for the same input.
  • It may depend on external state.
  • It may modify global variables.
  • It may modify objects or arrays passed as arguments.
  • It may perform API calls.
  • It may manipulate the DOM.
  • It may perform file or database operations.
  • It has one or more side effects:
    1. it performs a side effect;
    2. it modifies external state, like a global variable, or depends on external state;
    3. its output does not depend only on the input; it depends on the current state, not just the input to the function.
Impure: depends on and changes a global
let counter = 0;
function increment() {
  counter++;
  return counter;
}
console.log(increment());   // → 1
console.log(increment());   // → 2   (same call, different output → impure)
  • What happens: increment changes a variable outside itself, so the same call gives different results.
  • Output: 1, 2.
  • ⚠ Hidden shared state causes hard-to-find bugs.
Extra Details: making it pure 
const incrementPure = (n) => n + 1;   // the state comes IN as an argument, the new value goes OUT
let c = 0;
c = incrementPure(c);   // → 1
c = incrementPure(c);   // → 2   (the caller manages the state; the function stays pure)
  • What happens: make it pure by passing the state in and returning the new value; the caller stores it.
  • Output: 1, 2.

5. Differences between Pure and Impure Functions

Your Notes:
FeaturePure FunctionImpure Function
DefinitionAlways returns the same output for the same input and has no side effects.Produces side effects or depends on external state.
OutputSame output for the same input.May or may not return the same output for the same input.
Depends onOnly input arguments.Input arguments and/or external state.
Deterministic✅ Yes❌ Not necessarily.
Side effects❌ No✅ Yes
Modifies global variables❌ No✅ May modify them.
API calls❌ No✅ Yes
DOM manipulation❌ No✅ Yes
Random values❌ No✅ May use Math.random().
Current time❌ No✅ May use Date.now().
Easy to test✅ Yes❌ Harder
Easy to debug✅ Yes❌ Harder
Reusable✅ High❌ Lower
Why prefer pure functions
ReasonExplanation
Easier to debugDepends only on input, making bugs easier to locate.
PredictableSame input always produces the same output.
ReusableCan be used anywhere because it has no side effects.
Easy to testProduces consistent results, making unit testing straightforward.
No side effectsDoesn't modify global variables, objects or external state.
Functional programmingWorks well with map(), filter(), reduce() and other functional programming concepts.
MemoizationResults can be cached for improved performance.
Parallel executionCan safely execute concurrently because there is no shared mutable state.

6. Differences between Deterministic vs Non-Deterministic

Your Notes:
FunctionDeterministicPureReason
add(a,b)✅✅Same input → same output, no side effects
square(x)✅✅Depends only on input
console.log(name)✅❌Same output but has a side effect (writes to the console)
Math.random()❌❌Output changes every time
Date.now()❌❌Depends on the current time
fetch()❌❌Depends on the server response
database.get()❌❌Depends on database state
increment() using a global variable❌❌Depends on and modifies external state
DeterministicNon-Deterministic
Same input → same outputSame input → different output
Depends only on inputDepends on input + external factors
PredictableUnpredictable
Easy to testHarder to test
Usually pureUsually impure

A non-deterministic function is a function that does not always return the same output for the same input. Its result depends not only on its input arguments but also on external factors such as time, random values, global state, user input, APIs, databases or other changing data sources.

  • Pure function: a function that always returns the same output for the same input and has no side effects.
  • Impure function: a function that has side effects or depends on external state instead of only its input arguments.

7. Differences between Predictable vs Unpredictable

Your Notes:
PredictableUnpredictable
Same input → same outputSame input may produce different outputs
Easy to know the resultDifficult to know the result
DeterministicNon-deterministic
Easier to testHarder to test
Usually pureOften impure

Predictable means that a function always behaves consistently. For the same input, it always produces the same output, making its behavior easy to understand, test and debug.

A non-predictable function may produce different outputs for the same input because its behavior depends on changing external conditions rather than only on its input arguments.

Deterministic असणे पुरेसे नाही: console.log(name) नेहमी तेच दाखवते, पण console मध्ये लिहिणे हा side effect आहे, म्हणून ते impure आहे. Pure होण्यासाठी दोन्ही अटी लागतात: (1) same input → same output, आणि (2) कोणताही side effect नाही.

8. Interview Questions

Q1. Is a function that uses console.log pure?
  • No. Writing to the console is a side effect, even if the return value is always the same.
Q2. Is Array.prototype.map pure? Is sort?
  • map, filter and slice return new arrays and do not mutate the original, so with a pure callback they are pure. sort, push, splice and reverse mutate the array in place, so they are impure. toSorted() (ES2023) is the non-mutating version of sort.
Q3. What is a side effect? Give examples.
  • Any observable change or interaction outside the function: changing a global/outer variable, mutating an argument object/array, DOM updates, network calls (fetch), console.log, writing to localStorage/files, timers. Reading changing external data (Date.now(), Math.random()) also makes a function impure.
Q4. How do you make an impure function pure?
  • Pass everything it needs as arguments and return a new value instead of changing outside state: const add = (cart, item) => [...cart, item] instead of cart.push(item); inject time/randomness as parameters (makeId(now, rand)); keep side effects (API, DOM) in a separate thin layer that calls pure functions.
Q5. Why are pure functions important in React/Redux?
  • Reducers must be pure so state changes are predictable and can be compared by reference; components should render the same output for the same props/state. Pure functions also make memoization (React.memo, useMemo) and testing reliable.
Q6. Output-based question
let total = 10;
const addToTotal = (x) => total + x;      // impure: reads external state
console.log(addToTotal(5));               // → 15
total = 20;
console.log(addToTotal(5));               // → 25   (same input, different output!)
  • What happens: reading an outside variable is also impure: the result changes when total changes.
  • Output: 15, 25.
ConceptSummary
PureSame input → same output + no side effects
ImpureSide effects and/or depends on outside state
Side effectsGlobals, DOM, API, console, files, mutating arguments
Non-deterministic sourcesMath.random(), Date.now(), network, user input
Why pureTestable, predictable, cacheable (memoization), parallel-safe
थोडक्यात: pure = same input, same output आणि बाहेर काहीही बदल नाही. impure = बाहेरचे state वाचते किंवा बदलते (global, DOM, API, random, time). शक्य तिथे pure functions लिहा, आणि side effects (API, DOM) वेगळ्या ठिकाणी ठेवा.

Chapter 35: MemoizationCache expensive results · memoize polyfill · Map vs object · pitfalls
CHAPTER 35 INDEX
  1. What is Memoization?
  2. Why Use Memoization?
  3. How Memoization Works
  4. Disadvantages
  5. Implementing memoize (polyfill) with an object
  6. memoize with a Map
  7. memoize with call()
  8. Cache-key pitfalls & memoized recursion (Fibonacci)
  9. Interview Questions (Detailed)
  10. Quick Revision Summary

1. Q. What is Memoize?

Your Notes (memoize.js):
  1. Memoization is an optimization technique
  2. in programming that involves storing the results of expensive function calls and reusing those cached results when the same inputs occur again.
  3. It helps improve performance by avoiding redundant computations.
  4. In JavaScript, memoization is often implemented by wrapping a function in another function that maintains a cache of previously computed results.
Definition: Memoization caches a function's return value per input. The next call with the same arguments returns the stored result instead of recomputing it. It is built on a closure (the cache lives in the wrapper's lexical scope, Chapter 13) and is safe only for pure functions (Chapter 34).
Figure 83: How a memoized call works. Look up the argument key; compute only on a cache miss (timings measured in Node).
Memoization म्हणजे महाग (वेळखाऊ) function चा result त्याच्या input सोबत cache मध्ये ठेवणे. पुन्हा तोच input आला तर पुन्हा calculate न करता लगेच cache मधून result देणे. यासाठी closure वापरतात, आणि हे फक्त pure functions साठीच सुरक्षित आहे.

2. Why Use Memoization?

Your Notes:
  • Improves performance: reduces repeated computations for the same inputs.
  • Ideal for expensive operations: useful for operations involving recursion, heavy calculations or API calls.
  • Saves time: trades a small amount of memory (for caching) for significant computation time.

3. How Memoization Works

Your Notes:
  • A cache (usually a Map or an object) is used to store results.
  • Before executing the function:
  • check whether the result for the given inputs already exists in the cache.
  • If it exists, return the cached result.
  • If not, compute the result, store it in the cache, and then return it.

4. Disadvantages

Your Notes:
  1. Memory usage: it stores results in memory, which can grow significantly for many unique inputs.
  2. Limited use case: not useful for functions with side effects or inputs that change frequently.
Extra Details: more limits
  • Impure functions give wrong answers: if the result depends on time, randomness or outside state, a cached value becomes stale.
  • Key cost: JSON.stringify on big arguments can cost more than the function itself.
  • Unbounded growth: use an LRU (limit the size) or a WeakMap (for object keys) in long-running apps.

5. Implement a Caching memoize Function (Polyfill of memoize)

Your Notes (your code): 
function calculations(a, b) {
  for (let i = 0; i < 100000; i++) {}   // simulate heavy work
  return a + b;
}

// This defines a function named memoize that takes two parameters:
//   fun: the function you want to memoize (i.e. cache the result of)
//   context: an optional context (this value) in which to execute fun
// ✔ the comment said "myMemoize"; the function is named memoize
function memoize(fun, context) {
  // initialize a cache object to store the computed results for specific arguments
  let cache = {};
  // return a new function that acts as the memoized version of the provided function
  return function (...args) {
    // convert the arguments into a string key that uniquely identifies the combination of arguments
    // (this serialized string is used as the key to store the result in the cache object)
    let argKey = JSON.stringify(args);

    // Check whether the result for the current arguments is already in the cache.
    // If it isn't, compute it by calling the original function, and store it in the cache.
    // 'context' specifies the this in which the function should be executed.
    if (!(argKey in cache)) {
      cache[argKey] = fun.apply(context || this, args);
    }
    // return the cached result (computed now or earlier)
    return cache[argKey];
  };
}
// ✔ was "if (!cache[argKey])". A falsy RESULT (0, "", false, null) looks "not cached", so it was
//    recomputed on EVERY call (verified in Node: a result of 0 was computed 3 times for 3 calls)

let result = memoize(calculations);
console.time("result");
result(1100, 1200);        // executes the function and caches the result → 2300
console.timeEnd("result"); // → e.g. result: 0.38ms

console.time("result");
result(1100, 1200);        // retrieves the result from the cache
console.timeEnd("result"); // → e.g. result: 0.006ms
  • What happens: memoize wraps a slow function: the arguments are turned into a key (JSON.stringify); the first call computes and stores the result, the next call with the same arguments returns it from the cache.
  • Output: 2300 both times; the second call is much faster.
  • ✅ Speeds up expensive pure functions (calculations, recursion).
  • ⚠ Only for PURE functions; the cache grows forever unless you limit it.
!cache[argKey] ही अट falsy values (0, "", false) ला "cache मध्ये नाही" असे समजते. त्यामुळे result 0 असल्यास प्रत्येक call ला पुन्हा calculation होते (Node मध्ये 3 call = 3 calculations). argKey in cache किंवा Map.has() वापरल्याने ही चूक टळते.

6. memoize Using a Map Object

Your Notes (your code): 
function memoization(fun, context) {
  // create a new Map to store cached results
  // keys = the arguments passed, values = the function's results
  let map = new Map();

  // return a new function (a closure) that wraps around the original function
  return function (...args) {
    // convert the arguments array into a string (a unique key)
    // this lets us store/retrieve results based on the input
    let argKey = JSON.stringify(args);

    // if the result for these arguments is not already cached
    if (!map.has(argKey)) {
      // call the original function with the provided context (if any) and arguments,
      // and store the result in the cache (map)
      map.set(argKey, fun.apply(context || this, args));
    }
    // return the cached result (whether newly stored or stored earlier)
    return map.get(argKey);
  };
}

let mapResult = memoization(calculations);
console.time("map");
mapResult(5000, 4000);     // → 9000 (computed)
console.timeEnd("map");    // → e.g. map: 0.096ms
console.time("map");
mapResult(5000, 4000);     // → 9000 (from cache)
console.timeEnd("map");    // → e.g. map: 0.003ms
  • What happens: same idea with a Map as the cache: has/set/get.
  • Output: 9000 computed, then 9000 from cache.
  • ✅ Map.has works correctly even when the cached result is 0/""/false.
Extra Details: Map vs object as a cache
Object {}Map
Checkkey in obj (not !obj[key])map.has(key) ✅ handles falsy results
KeysStrings onlyAny type (even objects)
Size / clearingObject.keys(obj).lengthmap.size, map.clear(), map.delete()
Prototype keysCan clash with names like "toString"No clashes

7. memoize Using the call Method

Your Notes (your code): 
function cache(fun, context) {
  let cache = {};                    // (the inner variable has the same name as the function; it works, but it's confusing)
  return function (...args) {
    let argKey = JSON.stringify(args);
    if (!(argKey in cache)) {        // ✅ "in" also works for falsy results
      cache[argKey] = fun.call(context || this, ...args);   // call takes the args spread out, apply takes an array
    }
    return cache[argKey];
  };
}
let mapResult1 = cache(calculations);

console.time("first call");
console.log(mapResult1(10000, 30000));   // → 40000   (FIRST call: computed, then cached)
console.timeEnd("first call");           // → e.g. first call: 0.09ms
// ✔ the label said "second call" / "returns cached result", but this is the first call with these
//    arguments, so it is computed. A second call with (10000, 30000) would come from the cache.
  • What happens: same with an object cache and fun.call; the in operator also handles falsy results.
  • Output: 40000 (first call, computed).
हा (10000, 30000) चा पहिलाच call आहे, म्हणून result calculate होतो; तो cache मधून येत नाही. "second call" हे label चुकीचे होते. call() ला arguments वेगवेगळे (...args) लागतात, तर apply() ला array लागतो.

8. Cache-Key Pitfalls & Memoized Recursion

Extra Details: JSON.stringify keys are not perfect (verified in Node) 
JSON.stringify([undefined])     // → "[null]"   (undefined and null get the SAME key!)
JSON.stringify([() => 1])       // → "[null]"   (functions are lost)
JSON.stringify([{ a: 1, b: 2 }]) === JSON.stringify([{ b: 2, a: 1 }])   // → false (same data, different key order)
  • What happens: JSON.stringify keys have limits: undefined and null give the same key, functions disappear, and key order matters for objects.
  • Output: "[null]", "[null]", false.
  • ⚠ For object arguments, a WeakMap keyed by the object itself is safer.
Fixes: for a single primitive argument, use it directly as a Map key; for object arguments, use a WeakMap keyed by the object; or let the caller pass a custom resolver(...args) that builds the key.
Memoized Fibonacci (recursion + closure cache)
const fib = (() => {
  const memo = {};
  const f = (n) => n < 2 ? n : (memo[n] ??= f(n - 1) + f(n - 2));
  return f;
})();
console.log(fib(50));   // → 12586269025   (instant; without memo, about 2^50 calls → effectively never finishes)
  • What happens: fib(n) stores each answer in memo, so every n is computed once instead of exponentially many times.
  • Output: 12586269025 instantly.
  • ✅ Classic interview: memoized Fibonacci is O(n).
Figure 84: Memoization turns exponential recursion (repeated subproblems) into linear work.
JSON.stringify ने बनवलेल्या key मध्ये undefined आणि null एकच दिसतात, functions गायब होतात, आणि object मधील keys चा क्रम बदलला तर key बदलते. Fibonacci सारख्या recursion मध्ये तेच subproblem पुन्हा पुन्हा येते; memoization ने प्रत्येक n एकदाच calculate होतो, म्हणून fib(50) लगेच मिळते.

9. Interview Questions (Detailed)

Q1. What is memoization, and how is it related to closures?
  • It caches function results by input. The cache is a variable in the wrapper function's scope, and the returned function keeps it alive through a closure, so the cache persists between calls but stays private.
Q2. Write a memoize polyfill.
function memoize(fn) {
  const cache = new Map();
  return function (...args) {
    const key = JSON.stringify(args);
    if (!cache.has(key)) cache.set(key, fn.apply(this, args));
    return cache.get(key);
  };
}
  • What happens: short, correct memoize using Map.has.
  • Output: (no output).
Q3. Which functions should NOT be memoized?
  • Impure functions (they depend on time, randomness or outside state, or have side effects like API writes and logging), cheap functions (caching costs more than computing), and functions called with endlessly unique inputs (the cache only grows).
Q4. What is the bug in if (!cache[key])?
  • Falsy results (0, "", false, null, NaN) are treated as "not cached", so they are recomputed every time. Use key in cache or map.has(key).
Q5. Memoization vs caching?
  • Memoization is a specific kind of caching: storing a function's output keyed by its input arguments. Caching is the general idea (HTTP caches, localStorage, CDN…).
Q6. Where is memoization used in real projects?
  • Recursive algorithms (fib, dynamic programming), expensive selectors/filters, React's useMemo/useCallback/React.memo, and caching API responses by URL.
Q7. Output-based questions
let n = 0;
const sq = memoize(x => { n++; return x * x; });
sq(4); sq(4); sq(5);
console.log(n);              // → 2   (4 computed once, 5 once)

let z = 0;
const zero = memoize(() => { z++; return 0; });
zero(); zero();
console.log(z);              // → 1 with Map.has / "in"  ·  2 with the buggy !cache[key]
  • What happens: count how many times the real function runs: 4 once, 5 once; the zero-result function runs once with Map.has.
  • Output: 2, 1.
  • ⚠ A cache check with !cache[key] recomputes falsy results.

10. Quick Revision Summary

ConceptSummary
MemoizationCache results by input; reuse them for repeated inputs
Built onA closure holding a cache (object or Map)
Checkmap.has(key) / key in obj, never !obj[key]
KeyUsually JSON.stringify(args); beware undefined/null, functions and key order
Use forPure, expensive, repeated calls (recursion, heavy calculations)
CostMemory; can grow without limit
थोडक्यात: memoization = input नुसार result cache करणे. cache closure मध्ये राहतो. फक्त pure आणि महाग functions साठी वापरा. cache तपासायला Map.has किंवा in वापरा, !cache[key] नाही (falsy result चा bug).

CHAPTER 36 INDEX
  1. What is Function Currying?
  2. How Currying is Constructed (closures / bind)
  3. Basic Examples (f1, sum)
  4. Why Use Currying?
  5. Currying with Arrow Functions & Rectangle Area
  6. Currying with bind()
