  8. Infinite Currying
  9. Partial Application vs Currying
  10. Generic curry() Function (polyfill)
  11. Interview Questions (Detailed)
  12. Quick Revision Summary
⚠ File-level note (currying.js): ✔ function multiply1 is declared TWICE (curried, then normal). Function declarations are hoisted and the LAST one wins, so multiply1(10) ran the normal version and returned NaN, and mul(3)(4) crashed with "TypeError: mul is not a function" at line 136. The bind, evaluate, infinite-currying and curry() examples after it never ran (verified in Node). The normal version is renamed multiplyN here.multiply1 दोनदा declare केले होते. hoisting मध्ये शेवटचे declaration जिंकते, त्यामुळे multiply1(10) ने NaN दिले आणि mul(3)(4) वर TypeError येऊन file थांबली. पुढचे bind, evaluate, infinite currying, curry() examples कधीच चालले नाहीत (Node मध्ये तपासले). दुसऱ्या function चे नाव multiplyN केले.

1. Q. What is Function Currying?

Your Notes:
  1. Def: currying turns a function so that it takes one argument at a time and returns a new function expecting the next argument (i.e. it converts a function callable as f(a, b) into one callable as f(a)(b)). This is known as function currying.
  2. Function currying is a technique in JavaScript for transforming a function with multiple arguments into a sequence of functions that each take a single argument.
  3. Currying creates a chain of functions, each handling a single argument.
  4. In other words: instead of taking all arguments at once, the function takes the first one and returns a new function that takes the 2nd argument and returns a new function that takes the 3rd, and so on, until all arguments have been supplied.
Definition: Currying transforms f(a, b, c) into f(a)(b)(c): a chain of unary functions. Each returned function closes over the arguments received so far (Chapter 13), and the original logic runs when the last argument arrives.
Figure 85: Currying. Each call takes one argument and returns a function that remembers the earlier ones.
Currying म्हणजे सगळे arguments एकदम न घेता एका वेळी एक argument घेणे: f(a, b, c) चे f(a)(b)(c) करणे. प्रत्येक function पुढचा argument घेणारे नवीन function परत देते, आणि closure मुळे आधीचे arguments लक्षात राहतात. शेवटचा argument आल्यावर खरे काम होते.

2. How is Currying Constructed?

Your Notes:
  1. Curried functions are constructed by chaining closures: each function immediately returns its inner function.
Function currying can be done in 2 ways:
  1. using the bind() function
  2. using the concept of closures.
✔ Note: bind() gives PARTIAL APPLICATION (it pre-fills arguments, possibly several at once), not strict one-argument-at-a-time currying. True currying is built with closures (or a curry() helper, section 10).bind() मुळे partial application होते (काही arguments आधीच भरले जातात); खरे currying (एका वेळी एक argument) closures ने किंवा curry() helper ने होते.

3. Basic Examples

Your Notes (your code):
Example 1
// this is a normal function
function f(a, b) {
  console.log(a, b);
}
f(10, 20);              // → 10 20

// the function above converted into a curried function callable as f1()()
function f1(a) {
  return function (b) {
    return a + b;
  };
}
let res = f1(4);
console.log(res(5));    // → 9
  • What happens: f takes both arguments at once; f1 takes one, returns a function that takes the next.
  • Output: 10 20, 9.
  • ✅ Currying = one argument per call.
2
// # 2
function sum(n1) {
  return function (n2) {
    return function (n3) {
      console.log(n1 + n2 + n3);
    };
  };
}
sum(10)(20)(30);        // → 60
// The inner functions access the parent functions' parameters (arguments) → this is a closure.
  • What happens: three nested functions; each remembers the earlier arguments through closures.
  • Output: 60.

4. What is the Use of Function Currying? Why Should You Use It?

Your Notes:
  1. Currying makes functions more versatile and reusable.
  2. Currying is useful when you want to use a function with some arguments fixed and provide the remaining ones later.
  3. Reusability: it lets you create specialized functions by pre-filling some arguments.
  4. Readability: it helps break a complex function down into smaller parts.
  5. It creates higher-order functions.
  6. Currying helps you avoid passing the same variable again and again.
  7. It helps keep functions small and less error-prone (each step can stay pure).
  8. It divides one function into multiple functions, so that each one handles one responsibility.
🔹 Why use function currying?
  • Reusability (function customization): you can create specialized versions of a function by fixing some arguments. Example: a multiplication function can become a "double" or "triple" function.
  • Avoid repetition (DRY principle): it helps reuse code without writing similar logic multiple times.
  • Function composition: it makes it easier to build complex functions from smaller ones.
  • Partial application: you can pass some arguments now and others later.
  • Improved readability and maintainability.

5. Currying with Arrow Functions

Your Notes (your code):
Example 3a: arrow currying and partial use
let sum1 = (a) => (b) => (c) => console.log(a + b + c);
sum1(10)(20)(30);           // → 60

// you can also apply the curried function like this:
let result = sum1(20);      // partially applied sum
result(3)(4);               // → 27
// currying is useful when a function is used with some arguments fixed and the rest provided later
  • What happens: a => b => c => … is the short arrow form; sum1(20) fixes a = 20 for later calls.
  • Output: 60, 27.
Example 3b: curried rectangle area
// now create a curried version of "calculate rectangle area"
function createRectangleArea(length) {
  return function (height) {
    return length * height;
  };
}
let area = createRectangleArea(10);
let allArea = area(10);
console.log("allArea", allArea);   // → allArea 100
  • What happens: fix length once, then pass different heights.
  • Output: allArea 100.
  • ✅ Reuse a function with a fixed setting.

6. 2nd Approach: Creating a Curried Function with bind()

Your Notes:
  1. bind() definition: the bind() method returns a new function with the specified this value and, optionally, pre-filled arguments. It does not invoke the function immediately; it returns a new function to invoke later.
  2. Using bind(), we can achieve function currying (strictly speaking, partial application).
Example 4a: normal vs curried multiply
function multiply(x, y, z) {
  return x * y * z;
}
console.log("multiplication", multiply(3, 4, 5));   // → multiplication 60

// curried version of the function above
function multiply1(x) {
  return function (y) {
    return function (z) {
      return x * y * z;
    };
  };
}
let mul = multiply1(10);
console.log("currying multiple", mul(3)(4));        // → currying multiple 120
  • What happens: multiply takes 3 arguments at once; multiply1 takes them one call at a time.
  • Output: multiplication 60, currying multiple 120.
Example 4b: a function for bind()
// using the bind() method
function multiplyN(x, y, z) {
  return x * y * z;
}
// ✔ was declared again as "function multiply1(x, y, z)", which replaced the curried multiply1
//    (hoisting) and crashed mul(3)(4) above
  • What happens: a normal 3-argument function used with bind in the next blocks.
  • Output: (no output).
  • Here we create a curried version of the function using bind(). bind() essentially creates a copy of the multiply function, and we pass some pre-filled arguments.
  • Behind the scenes it works like this: x is set to 10, and the next arguments come in the next call: 
    // let multiplyByTen = (y, z) => {
//   let x = 10;
//   return x * y * z;
// };
// multiplyByTen(3, 4);
    • What happens: (commented) an alternative: a wrapper with x fixed inside.
    • Output: (no output).
  • When we call bind, it returns a new function (a copy of the multiply function); it does not invoke it directly; we call it later.
Example 6a: partial application with bind
let multipleByTwo = multiplyN.bind(this, 10);        // x = 10
let multipleByThree = multipleByTwo.bind(this, 3);   // y = 3
console.log(multipleByThree(4));                     // → 120   (10 * 3 * 4)
  • What happens: bind returns a new function with some arguments fixed: first x = 10, then y = 3.
  • Output: 120.
  • ⚠ bind's first argument is this; pass null when this isn't used.
Example 6b: calling a curried function too early
let addition = (a) => {
  return (b) => {
    return (c) => {
      return a + b + c;
    };
  };
};
let out = addition(10);
console.log(out(4));       // → [Function (anonymous)]   (returns another function that expects the next argument)
console.log(out(4)(6));    // → 20
  • What happens: out(4) still returns a function, because one argument is missing; out(4)(6) completes it.
  • Output: [Function (anonymous)], 20.
bind(this, 10) ने x = 10 आधीच भरला जातो आणि नवीन function मिळते. ते लगेच चालत नाही, नंतर call करावे लागते. out(4) ला अजून एक argument हवा आहे, म्हणून ते function परत देते.

7. Create the Curried Function for the Following Output

Your Notes: evaluate("sum")(4)(2), evaluate("sub")(4)(2), evaluate("mul")(4)(2), evaluate("div")(4)(2) 
function evaluate(operator) {
  return function (a) {
    return function (b) {
      if (operator === "sum") {
        return a + b;
      } else if (operator === "sub") {
        return a - b;
      } else if (operator === "mul") {
        return a * b;
      } else if (operator === "div") {
        return a / b;
      } else {
        return "invalid operator ";
      }
    };
  };
}
let output = evaluate("mul");
console.log(output(10)(20));          // → 200
// evaluate("sum")(4)(2) → 6 · evaluate("sub")(4)(2) → 2 · evaluate("div")(4)(2) → 2
  • What happens: the first call picks the operation; the next two give the numbers.
  • Output: 200.
  • ✅ Create specialised functions: const multiply = evaluate("mul").

8. How to Create Infinite Currying

Your Notes: what is infinite currying?
  1. Infinite currying means you can keep passing arguments one by one, indefinitely, until you decide to stop.
  2. It's often used for flexible function calls.
  3. Infinite currying means the function keeps returning another single-argument function until you stop it (usually by calling it with no argument, or by meeting a specific condition).
  • i.e. you can pass any number of parameters: (1)(2)…
  • Write a function that accepts n parameters.
// the outer function takes one argument `a`
function infiniteCurryingAddition(a) {
  // it returns an inner function that takes another argument `b`
  return function (b) {
    // If b is provided (not undefined), recursively call infiniteCurryingAddition with the sum of a and b.
    if (b !== undefined) {
      return infiniteCurryingAddition(a + b);
    }
    // If b is not provided (undefined), return the accumulated sum a.
    return a;
  };
}
let output1 = infiniteCurryingAddition(2);
console.log(output1(4)(5)(6)());      // → 17
// ✔ the check was "if (b)". Passing 0 (falsy) ended the chain early:
//    infiniteCurryingAddition(2)(4)(0)(5) → TypeError: ...is not a function (verified in Node)
  • What happens: each call with a number adds it and returns a new function; calling with no argument ends the chain and returns the total.
  • Output: 17.
  • ✅ Popular interview question: sum(1)(2)(3)().
  • ⚠ Check b !== undefined, not if (b), or 0 breaks the chain.
if (b) मध्ये 0 हा falsy असल्यामुळे chain मधेच संपत होती, आणि पुढचा (5) call केल्यावर TypeError येत होता. b !== undefined वापरल्याने 0 सुद्धा चालतो आणि फक्त रिकामा call () थांबवतो.
  • Each call returns a new function expecting the next argument.
  • When we finally call it with no argument, (), it returns the accumulated result.
  • Infinite currying = currying where the number of arguments is not fixed and you keep calling until you stop.

9. What is the Difference between Partial Application and Currying?

Your Notes:

1. Partial application

  1. It fixes a specific number of arguments and generates a new function that expects the remaining arguments later (the new function may take several arguments at once).
  2. Partial application fixes some arguments of a function but keeps the rest open.
  3. Partial functions are useful for customization and code reuse.
  4. Partial application transforms a function into a new function that takes fewer arguments, by "pre-filling" some of the arguments.
  5. Partial application creates a function with a smaller arity (the number of arguments the function takes).
  6. Partial application refers to fixing a few arguments of a function, creating a new function with fewer parameters.
  7. This lets you "pre-fill" certain arguments and reuse the partially applied function for specific tasks.

2. Currying

  1. Currying breaks a complex function into a series of functions, each taking a single argument and returning a new function that expects the next argument.
  2. It breaks the function into a chain of unary (nested) functions.
  3. It creates a series of functions, one per argument, each always taking only one argument at a time.
Note: the number of nested functions in a curried function depends on the number of arguments it receives. 
// partial application: fixing a few arguments of a function
function sumAll(a) {
  return function (b, c) {
    return a + b + c;
  };
}
let output2 = sumAll(4);
console.log(output2(4, 5));     // → 13
// or
console.log(sumAll(4)(4, 5));   // → 13
  • What happens: partial application: fix a, give b and c together later.
  • Output: 13, 13.
  1. The number of nested functions in a curried function depends on the number of arguments. Here there are 3 arguments, but only 2 functions,
  2. so the example above is not currying; we did partial application for the sumAll function.
What does partial application do?
  1. Partial application transforms a function into another function with a smaller arity (arity means the number of arguments a function receives).
  2. Partial function application is a concept in functional programming where you fix some of a function's arguments and return a new function that takes the remaining arguments.
What factor does the number of nested curried functions depend on? The number of nested functions in a curried function depends on the number of arguments.
Real example of partial application
function applyDiscount(discount) {
  return function (price) {
    return price - price * (discount / 100);
  };
}
let res1 = applyDiscount(10);   // fix the discount at 10% for all products in a category
console.log(res1(200));         // → 180
// Suppose you want to fix a 10% discount for all products in a certain category, but still pass the price dynamically.
// (with exactly 2 one-argument steps, this is ALSO a curried function: partial application and currying overlap here)
  • What happens: fix the discount once, apply it to any price.
  • Output: 180.
  • ✅ Real-world partial application.
Figure 86: Currying (one argument per call) vs partial application (pre-fill some, pass the rest at once).

10. Write a curry Function to Convert f(a, b, c) into f(a)(b)(c)

Your Notes (your code): 
// `curry` takes a function `fun` as input and returns a curried version of it.
function curry(fun) {
  // `curried` handles the arguments in a curried manner.
  return function curried(...args) {
    console.log(args.length, fun.length);   // (debug log: collected count vs required count)
    // Check whether the number of arguments passed so far (args.length)
    // is equal to or greater than the number of arguments the original function (fun) expects.
    if (args.length >= fun.length) {
      // If we have enough arguments, call the original function
      // with the collected arguments and return the result.
      return fun(...args);
    } else {
      // If we do not have enough arguments, return a new function that collects more.
      return function (...next) {
        // This new function calls `curried` recursively,
        // combining the arguments already collected (args) with the new ones (next).
        return curried(...args, ...next);
      };
    }
  };
}

function add(a, b, c) {
  return a + b + c;
}
let res3 = curry(add);
console.log(res3(3, 4, 5));     // → logs "3 3", then 12

// partial application:
const add1 = res3(1);           // returns a new function waiting for the next arguments   (logs "1 3")
const add2 = add1(2);           // again returns a new function waiting for one more argument (logs "2 3")
const result5 = add2(3);        // now it has all three arguments, so it returns 6   (logs "3 3")
console.log("result", result5); // → result 6
  • What happens: generic curry: collect arguments until there are as many as the function expects (fun.length), then call it.
  • Output: 12, then 6 (with debug logs).
  • ✅ Turns ANY function into a curried one; works with (1)(2)(3) or (1, 2)(3).
Understanding the curry function:
  • Input function (fun): the original function that takes multiple arguments.
  • Curried function (curried): this inner function collects the arguments provided. ✔ the notes called it "curriedFun"; in the code it is named curried.notes मध्ये curriedFun नाव होते, पण code मध्ये function चे नाव curried आहे.
  • Checking the argument count: if the number of collected arguments is greater than or equal to the number of parameters the original function expects (fun.length), it calls the original function with all collected arguments.
  • Recursive call: if fewer arguments have been collected, it returns another function that keeps collecting. This allows partial application of arguments until all required arguments are collected.
Extra Details: the fun.length trap 
// fun.length stops counting at the first default parameter or rest parameter:
const g = (a, b = 2, c) => a + b + c;     // g.length is 1!
console.log(curry(g)(1));                 // → NaN   (called immediately with only a = 1 → 1 + 2 + undefined)
// Fix: let curry accept an explicit arity → curry(fn, arity = fn.length)
  • What happens: fun.length stops at the first default parameter, so curry thinks g needs only 1 argument and calls it too early.
  • Output: NaN.
  • ⚠ Pass the arity explicitly for such functions.

11. Interview Questions (Detailed)

Q1. What is currying? How is it different from partial application?
  • Currying converts f(a, b, c) into f(a)(b)(c), with exactly one argument per call. Partial application pre-fills some arguments and returns a function for the rest, which may take several at once (bind, sumAll(4)(4, 5)). Every curried call is a partial application, but not every partial application is currying.
Q2. Implement curry(fn).
const curry = fn => function c(...a) {
  return a.length >= fn.length ? fn(...a) : (...n) => c(...a, ...n);
};
curry((a, b, c) => a + b + c)(1)(2)(3);   // → 6
curry((a, b, c) => a + b + c)(1, 2)(3);   // → 6
  • What happens: a one-line curry using the same idea.
  • Output: 6, 6.
Q3. Implement sum(1)(2)(3)…() (infinite currying).
const sum = a => b => b === undefined ? a : sum(a + b);
console.log(sum(1)(2)(3)());   // → 6   (use b === undefined, not !b, so 0 works)
  • What happens: infinite currying in one line.
  • Output: 6.
Q4. Which concept makes currying possible?
  • Closures: each returned function keeps access to the arguments received by the outer calls. Functions also have to be first-class (returned as values).
Q5. Real-world uses of currying?
  • Configured helpers like const logError = log("ERROR"), event handlers with pre-set ids onClick={handle(id)}, discount/tax calculators, and composing data pipelines (map(multiply(2))).
Q6. What is the downside of currying?
  • Extra function calls and closures (small performance/memory cost), harder debugging and stack traces, and it is less readable for people who aren't used to it. It relies on fn.length, which fails with default/rest parameters.
Q7. Output-based questions
const add3 = a => b => c => a + b + c;
console.log(add3(1)(2)(3));              // → 6
console.log(typeof add3(1)(2));          // → "function"
const double = (x => y => x * y)(2);
console.log([1, 2, 3].map(double));      // → [2, 4, 6]
function m(x, y) { return x * y; }
console.log(m.bind(null, 5)(4));         // → 20   (partial application with bind)
  • What happens: five output questions: full call, partial call type, curried function in map, bind as partial application.
  • Output: 6, "function", [2, 4, 6], 20.

12. Quick Revision Summary

ConceptSummary
Curryingf(a, b, c) → f(a)(b)(c); one argument per call
Built withClosures (true currying) · bind() (partial application)
WhyReuse via pre-filled arguments, specialized functions, composition, DRY
Infinite curryingKeep returning a function; stop on () → check b === undefined
Partial applicationPre-fill some arguments; the rest can come together
curry() polyfillCollect arguments until args.length ≥ fn.length
TrapDuplicate function names (hoisting) · fn.length with default/rest parameters
थोडक्यात: currying = एका वेळी एक argument घेणाऱ्या functions ची साखळी, जी closures मुळे चालते. bind() हे partial application आहे. infinite currying मध्ये b === undefined तपासा (0 साठी). curry() polyfill fn.length पर्यंत arguments गोळा करतो.

1. this

Your Notes (16_this/this.js):
  1. this is a special keyword that refers to the context in which a function is executed. Its value depends on how and where the function is called.
  2. When a function is invoked through an object, the this keyword in that scenario points to the object the function was invoked on (simply, the object on the left side of the dot).
  3. this is used to refer to the current context object.

2. Types of Binding

Your Notes: in JS there are 2 types of binding (your notes):
  1. Explicit binding: done with the call(), apply() and bind() methods.
  2. Implicit binding: when you invoke a function in an object using . (dot) notation, the this keyword in that scenario points to the object on which the function is invoked.
✔ there are 4 rules, not 2: also new binding (this = the new object) and default binding (plain call → globalThis, or undefined in strict mode). Arrow functions ignore all four and use the lexical this.binding चे 2 नाही तर 4 नियम आहेत: new binding (new ने बनलेला object), explicit (call/apply/bind), implicit (dot च्या डावीकडचा object), आणि default (साधा call → window, strict mode मध्ये undefined). arrow function यापैकी कोणताच नियम पाळत नाही, तो बाहेरचा this घेतो.
  1. Note: this is not a variable; it is a keyword, and you cannot assign a new value to this (this = obj is a SyntaxError). ✔ "you can not change this to any object". You can't ASSIGN to this, but you CAN choose which object it points to with call/apply/bind.this = obj असे assign करता येत नाही, पण call/apply/bind ने this कोणत्या object कडे point करेल ते ठरवता येते.
  2. The this object contains the current context in which a function is executed (this is nothing but a reference to something, like an object).
  3. this can have different values depending on where it is placed.
  4. The this keyword refers to different objects depending on how it is used.
Definition: this is decided at CALL time (except in arrow functions). Priority: new > explicit (call/apply/bind) > implicit (obj.fn()) > default (fn() → globalThis, or undefined in strict mode). Arrow functions take this from the enclosing scope at DEFINITION time.
Figure 87: The 4 binding rules of this (priority from left to right) and the arrow-function exception.
this ची value function कसा call केला यावर ठरते: new ने → नवीन object; call/apply/bind ने → दिलेला object; obj.fn() ने → dot च्या डावीकडचा obj; साधा fn() → window (strict mode मध्ये undefined). arrow function चा स्वतःचा this नसतो, तो बाहेरच्या scope चा this वापरतो.

3. In an Object Method: this Refers to the Object

Your Notes:
Example 1
const obj = {
  myAge: 27,
  myName: function () {
    console.log("in object method this refer to the object :", this, this.myAge);
  },
};
obj.myName();   // → in object method this refer to the object : { myAge: 27, myName: ƒ } 27
  • What happens: called as obj.myName(), so this is obj.
  • Output: the object and 27.
  • ✅ Methods can use the object's own data through this.
in this example the greet method is defined using the method shorthand syntax,
// # in this example the greet method is defined using the method shorthand syntax,
//   a more concise way to define methods in object literals
const obj4 = {
  name: "akshu",
  greet() {
    console.log("shortHand", this);
  },
};
obj4.greet();   // → shortHand { name: 'akshu', greet: ƒ }
  • What happens: method shorthand works the same: this = the object before the dot.
  • Output: shortHand { name: 'akshu', … }.

4. Alone: this Refers to the Global Object

Your Notes: 
console.log(this);
// in the Node environment, this refers to an empty object ({} = module.exports)
// but in the browser, it refers to the window object
  • What happens: at the top level, this is {} in a Node CommonJS file and window in a browser script.
  • Output: {} / window.

5. In a Function: this Refers to the Global Object

Your Notes:
Example 1
function MyName() {
  console.log(this);   // in a function, this also refers to the global object (window), in non-strict mode
}
MyName();
  • What happens: a plain function call in sloppy mode gets the global object as this.
  • Output: window (browser) / globalThis (Node).
example 2
// example 2
let name1 = "vishal shinde";
// it returns undefined because it is defined with let, and let variables are not attached to the window object
function display() {
  console.log("this.name", this.name1);   // → this.name undefined
  // ✔ comment said "return the global object variable where we have defined it". this = window,
  //    but let/const variables are NOT window properties, so window.name1 is undefined (var would work)
}
display();
  • What happens: this is window, but let variables aren't window properties.
  • Output: this.name undefined.
  • ⚠ Only var and function declarations become window properties.
4. in a function, in strict mode: this is undefined
// 4. in a function, in strict mode: this is undefined
function strict() {
  "use strict";
  console.log("in strict mode this", this);   // → undefined
}
strict();
  • What happens: in strict mode a plain function call gets this = undefined.
  • Output: undefined.
  • ✅ Strict mode makes the mistake visible (TypeError when you use it).
साध्या function मध्ये this = window असतो. पण let ने declare केलेला variable window वर जात नाही, म्हणून this.name1 = undefined. var ने declare केल्यास तो window ची property बनतो. strict mode मध्ये this undefined असतो.

6. Arrow Functions with the this Keyword

Your Notes:
  1. this does not work the same way with arrow functions. ✔ "This function not work with the arrow function". this does exist inside an arrow function; it just isn't the arrow's OWN this, it's the outer one.arrow function मध्ये this वापरता येतो, फक्त तो स्वतःचा नसतो, बाहेरच्या scope चा असतो.
  2. In traditional functions (function keyword), the value of this is determined by how the function is called, i.e. the calling context (e.g. an object or event handler).
  3. Arrow functions do not bind their own this.
  4. Arrow functions do not have their own this. this is inherited from the parent scope (lexical scope). Instead, they inherit this from the surrounding lexical context (the scope in which they were defined).
  5. In an arrow function, the this value comes from its parent function (or the global scope if there is none).
const obj1 = {
  name: "Alice",
  greet: () => {
    console.log("using arrow function", this.name);
    // 'this' refers to the surrounding scope, not obj1. Here the surrounding scope is the global scope
    // (an object literal { } does NOT create a scope for this), and the global object has no useful name property.
  },
};
obj1.greet();
// → Node: undefined (this = {})
// → Browser: "" (empty string!)  because window.name is a built-in property whose default value is ""
// the arrow function inherits this from its lexical scope, which is the global scope in this case
// (or the outer function, if there is one). Since there is no name property in the global scope, this.name is undefined.

function chai() {
  let username = "vishal";
  console.log("this inside the function", this);   // → window (browser, non-strict) / globalThis (Node)
  // ✔ comment said "this returns undefined". In a non-strict normal function, this = global object;
  //    it is undefined only in strict mode / ES modules
}
chai();

const chai1 = function () {
  let username = "vishal";
  console.log("this inside the function", this.username);   // → undefined
  // local variables are never properties of this
};
chai1();
  • What happens: an arrow method takes this from outside the object (global), so this.name is not obj1's name. In normal functions this is the global object; local variables are never on this.
  • Output: undefined ("" in a browser), global object, undefined.
  • ⚠ Don't use arrows as object methods.
chai() मध्ये this undefined नसून window असतो (strict mode नसल्यास). username हा local variable आहे, तो this ची property नाही, म्हणून this.username undefined. browser मध्ये window.name ही built-in property "" असते, म्हणून arrow मध्ये this.name ने undefined ऐवजी रिकामी string येते. 
// here this is the global context (i.e. it refers to the window object)
this.a = 5;
console.log(a);    // → 5 (browser: window.a)  |  ❌ ReferenceError in Node (this is module.exports there)
// console.log(this)   // returns the window object

function greeting() {
  console.log(this.a);   // → 5 (browser) / undefined (Node, if the line above hadn't thrown)
}
greeting();
  • What happens: in a browser, top-level this is window, so this.a creates window.a; greeting() also sees window.
  • Output: 5, 5 (browser); ReferenceError in Node.

7. this in Nested Objects & Inner Functions

Your Notes: 
let user = {
  name: "vishal",
  age: 24,
  // this normal function refers to the current context, so it returns vishal and 24
  getData() {
    console.log(this.name, this.age);   // → vishal 24
    console.log(this);                  // this refers to its parent object (user), not the global object
  },
  getData1: () => {
    console.log(this.name, this.age);
    // here the arrow function returns undefined (browser: "" undefined) because it refers directly to the
    // window object, and window does not have (useful) name and age properties
    // an arrow function only refers to its parent function; if it has no parent function it refers to the global (window) object
    console.log(this);                  // → window / {} in Node
  },
  childObj: {
    newName: "shinde vishal",
    // so this normal function refers to childObj, not the user object
    getData2() {
      console.log(this.newName, this.name);   // → shinde vishal undefined
      console.log("this", this);              // → this { newName: 'shinde vishal', getData2: ƒ }
    },
  },
};
user.getData();
user.getData1();
user.childObj.getData2();
// Arrow functions do not have their own this.
// Instead, they use the value of this from the surrounding lexical scope.
// If there is no surrounding context, this will refer to the global object (window).
// so a normal function's this points to the object it was called on (the object immediately left of the dot)
  • What happens: normal methods use the object left of the dot (user, then childObj); the arrow uses the outer this.
  • Output: vishal 24; undefined undefined; shinde vishal undefined.
  • ✅ Rule: this = the object before the dot at CALL time.
✔ "normal function pointing to the immediate parent function" → a normal function's this is the object immediately LEFT OF THE DOT at call time (user.childObj.getData2() → childObj).normal function चा this म्हणजे call करताना dot च्या लगेच डावीकडचा object. user.childObj.getData2() मध्ये तो childObj आहे, user नाही. 
let user1 = {
  name: "vishal",
  age: 28,
  hi() {
    console.log(this.name, this.age);   // → vishal 28
    console.log(this);                  // → user1
  },
  // if you define an arrow function, it returns undefined because it refers to the window object
  h1: () => {
    console.log(this);   // refers to the window object, because an arrow has no this binding of its own; it uses the surrounding lexical scope
    console.log(this.name, this.age);   // → undefined undefined (browser: "" undefined)
  },
  get1() {
    this.newName = "akshu";
    const h2 = () => {
      console.log(this);                                   // → user1 (arrow takes this from get1)
      console.log("hello word ", this.newName, this.name); // → hello word  akshu vishal
    };
    h2();
  },
};
user1.hi();
user1.h1();
user1.get1();
// ✔ the old comment said "the newName: 'akshu'; statement does nothing because it's a standalone
//    statement". The code now uses this.newName = "akshu", which DOES add newName to user1 (verified in Node)
  • What happens: hi uses user1; h1 (arrow) uses the outer this; inside get1 the arrow h2 inherits get1's this (user1).
  • Output: vishal 28; undefined undefined; akshu vishal.
  • ✅ Arrow functions INSIDE methods are the right place for arrows.
let per = {
  name: "vishal",
  age: 30,
  getData() {
    // the normal function points to per
    console.log("getData", this);       // → getData per
    // const display = () => {
    function display() {
      console.log("display", this.name);   // → display vishal   (because of call(per))
      const getDataAll = () => {
        console.log("getDataAll", this);   // → getDataAll per   (arrow takes display's this)
      };
      getDataAll();
    }
    display.call(per);   // without .call(per), display() would get the default this (window / undefined)
  },
};
per.getData();
  • What happens: display.call(per) sets this to per; the arrow inside display inherits it.
  • Output: getData per, display vishal, getDataAll per.
get1 हा normal method आहे, म्हणून त्याचा this = user1. आतला h2 arrow असल्यामुळे तोच this वापरतो, म्हणून "akshu vishal" येते. per मध्ये display हा साधा function आहे; call(per) ने त्याचा this per केला आणि आतल्या arrow ने तोच this घेतला.

8. this Keyword in a Class

Your Notes: 
class userData {
  constructor(n) {
    this.name = n;   // this = the new object being created
  }
  getInformation() {
    console.log(this.name);
  }
}
const user5 = new userData("vishal");
console.log(user5);       // → userData { name: 'vishal' }
user5.getInformation();   // → vishal
// (class bodies are always strict: const f = user5.getInformation; f(); → TypeError, this is undefined)

const person = {
  firstName: "vishal",
  getName() {
    let firstName = "data";   // a local variable, NOT this.firstName
    return this.firstName;
  },
};
console.log("person.getName();", person.getName());   // → person.getName(); vishal
person.getName();   // returns "vishal", but nothing is printed
  • What happens: in a class, this is the new instance; a local variable with the same name is not this.firstName.
  • Output: userData { name: 'vishal' }, vishal, person.getName(); vishal.
  • ⚠ Detaching a class method loses this (TypeError).

9. Output Questions

Your Notes:
What is the result of accessing its ref? And why?
// function makeUser() {
//   return {
//     hi: "john",
//     ref: this,
//   };
// }
// let res = makeUser();
// console.log(res.ref.hi);
// → undefined (browser, non-strict): makeUser() is a plain call, so this = window, and window.hi is undefined
// → TypeError in strict mode / modules: this is undefined, so undefined.hi crashes
// An object literal { } does not change this: "ref: this" uses the this of makeUser.
  • What happens: makeUser() is a plain call, so ref: this stores window (or undefined in strict mode), not the new object.
  • Output: undefined (or TypeError in strict mode).
Then how do you fix the above example to print the name?
function makeUser() {
  return {
    hi: "john",
    // ref1: this,   // instead of that, make a function (method) which returns this
    ref1() {
      return this;
    },
  };
}
let res1 = makeUser();
console.log("ref()", res1.ref1().hi);   // → ref() john   (res1.ref1() → this = res1)
  • What happens: a method ref1() is called as res1.ref1(), so this = res1.
  • Output: ref() john.
What is the output of the following code? (1)
let user6 = {
  nav: "vishal",
  loggedMessage() {
    console.log(this.nav);
    // it returns undefined because loggedMessage is passed into setTimeout as a callback, which is called after the delay;
    // when the function is called after the delay it is no longer called on the user6 object, so this points to the
    // window object, where no nav variable is present, so it returns undefined
  },
};
setTimeout(user6.loggedMessage, 100);   // → undefined
// ✔ the comment said "after one second" but the delay here is 100 ms
  • What happens: passing user6.loggedMessage to setTimeout detaches it; later it is called without an object, so this is lost.
  • Output: undefined.
  • ⚠ Classic interview trap.
how do we fix this?
// # how do we fix this?
setTimeout(function () {
  user6.loggedMessage();   // → vishal  (called WITH the dot, so this = user6)
}, 1000);
// other fixes: setTimeout(user6.loggedMessage.bind(user6), 1000)  or  setTimeout(() => user6.loggedMessage(), 1000)
  • What happens: call it with the dot inside a wrapper (or use bind / an arrow), so this stays user6.
  • Output: vishal.
setTimeout ला फक्त function दिला जातो, object नाही. नंतर तो साधा fn() म्हणून call होतो, म्हणून this = window आणि nav undefined. wrapper function किंवा bind(user6) ने this पुन्हा user6 होतो.
What will be the output? (1)
var length = 4;
function callback() {

}
const object = {

  method(fn) {
    fn();   // a plain call → this = window
  },
};
object.method(callback);   // → 4 (browser: var length = 4 becomes window.length)  |  undefined in Node
  • What happens: fn() is a plain call → this = window; var length = 4 created window.length.
  • Output: 4 (browser), undefined (Node).
modified question: we pass more arguments; what is the output?

}
const object1 = {

  },

object1.method(callback, 3, 4);   // → 3   (arguments.length is 3; verified in Node)
  • What happens: arguments[0]() is called as a method of the arguments object, so this = arguments, and arguments.length is 3.

पहिल्यात fn() साधा call आहे, म्हणून this = window आणि window.length = 4 (var length). दुसऱ्यात arguments[0]() हा arguments object वरचा call आहे (dot किंवा bracket च्या डावीकडे arguments), म्हणून this = arguments आणि त्याची length = 3.

10. Implement Calculation (Method Chaining)

Your Notes: implement the calculation in the following way: 
const calc = {
  total: 0,
  add(a) {
    this.total += a;
    return this;
    // we return this because we need to return the whole object; only then can we access
    // the other functions defined in the object (chaining)
  },
  multiply(b) {
    this.total *= b;
    return this;
  },
  subtract(c) {
    this.total -= c;
    return this;
  },
};
const output = calc.add(10).multiply(5).subtract(10).add(10);
console.log(output.total);   // → 50   (0+10 = 10 → ×5 = 50 → −10 = 40 → +10 = 50)
  • What happens: each method changes total and returns this (the object), so the next method can be chained.
  • Output: 50.
  • ✅ Chainable APIs (like jQuery).
Extra Details: losing this & fixes 
const { getData } = user;   getData();      // this lost → default binding
const bound = user.getData.bind(user);      // fix 1: bind (permanent; a second bind is ignored)
btn.addEventListener("click", function () { this; });   // this = the element (btn)
btn.addEventListener("click", () => { this; });         // this = outer this, NOT the button
// in classes: handle = () => { … }  (class field arrow) keeps this = instance
  • What happens: ways this gets lost or fixed: destructuring a method loses it; bind fixes it permanently; a normal listener gets the element; an arrow listener keeps the outer this.
  • Output: (notes).

11. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. How is the value of this decided?
  • By the call site: new → the new object; call/apply/bind → the given object; obj.fn() → obj; plain fn() → globalThis (undefined in strict mode). Arrow functions use the enclosing scope's this.
Q2. Why shouldn't you use arrow functions as object methods?
  • An object literal doesn't create a this scope, so the arrow takes the outer (often global) this and can't see the object's properties. Use method shorthand; use arrows INSIDE methods for callbacks.
Q3. Why does this get lost in setTimeout(obj.method)?
  • Only the function reference is passed; it is later called without an object (default binding). Fix with bind, a wrapper function or an arrow wrapper.
Q4. call vs apply vs bind?
  • call(thisArg, a, b) and apply(thisArg, [a, b]) invoke immediately; bind(thisArg, …) returns a new function with this fixed permanently (even call can't override it, only new can).
Q5. What is this in a constructor / class?
  • The newly created instance. Forgetting new on a constructor function makes this the global object (or undefined in strict mode); a class throws "Class constructor cannot be invoked without 'new'".
Q6. Output-based questions
const o = { x: 1, f() { return this.x; }, g: () => typeof this };
console.log(o.f());                  // → 1
const f = o.f; console.log(f());     // → undefined (browser non-strict: window.x)
console.log(o.f.call({ x: 9 }));     // → 9
console.log(o.f.bind({ x: 2 }).call({ x: 3 }));   // → 2 (bind wins)
console.log((0, o.f)());             // → undefined (the comma operator loses the object)
  • What happens: five output questions: method call, detached call, call, bind beats call, comma operator detaches.
  • Output: 1, undefined, 9, 2, undefined.

fn()window/globalThis; undefined in strict mode
Arrow functionOuter (lexical) this
Global scopewindow (browser) / {} (Node CommonJS)
थोडक्यात: this हा function कसा call केला यावर ठरतो (arrow सोडून). dot च्या डावीकडचा object म्हणजे this. callback म्हणून पाठवल्यावर this हरवतो, तो bind ने परत मिळवा. arrow ला स्वतःचा this नाही, तो बाहेरचा this घेतो. chaining साठी method मधून return this करा.

processUserInput हे नाव दोनदा declare केले आहे. hoisting मुळे दुसरे version वापरले जाते, आणि "vishal" ला function समजून call केल्याने TypeError येतो. दुसऱ्या function ला वेगळे नाव द्या.

1. Callback

Your Notes (23_callback/callback.js):
  1. A callback function in JavaScript is a function that is passed as an argument to another function and is executed later, after some operation has been completed or at a specific point in the function's execution.
  2. A callback function is a function passed as an argument to another function, and it is executed after the completion of a (usually asynchronous) task. ✔ "after the complication of synchronous task" → after the COMPLETION of a task (often an asynchronous one). Callbacks can also run synchronously (§7)."complication" नाही, "completion" (काम पूर्ण झाल्यावर). callback synchronous सुद्धा असू शकतो.
Definition: A callback is just a function passed as an argument to another function (the higher-order function), which decides WHEN to call it: immediately (a synchronous callback, e.g. arr.map(cb)) or later (an asynchronous callback, e.g. setTimeout(cb), events, I/O). This works because functions are first-class values in JS (Chapter 33).

2. Why Callbacks?

Your Notes:
  1. Handle asynchronous operations: callbacks are commonly used in JS for handling asynchronous tasks like API requests, file reading or event handling.
  2. Code reusability: callbacks allow functions to be more generic and reusable.
  3. Event handling: they let a function execute only when a certain event occurs.
  4. A callback function is a function that is passed as an argument to another function and is intended to be executed after a certain event, operation or condition is completed.
  1. A callback function is a function passed as an argument to another function, intended to be executed after the completion of some operation, or at a specified time or condition.
  2. Callback functions are commonly used in situations where you want to ensure that certain code is executed when a particular task completes, such as reading a file, making an API request or handling a user event.
  3. So callback functions are crucial in JavaScript for handling asynchronous operations, event handling and various other scenarios where you need to control the flow of your code based on the completion of some task.
A callback is just a function. It's passed as an argument. It can be called later, synchronously or asynchronously.
Callback म्हणजे दुसऱ्या function ला argument म्हणून दिलेला function. तो कधी चालवायचा ते तो दुसरा function (higher-order function) ठरवतो: लगेच (synchronous) किंवा काम झाल्यावर नंतर (asynchronous). उपयोग: async कामे, events, आणि code reusable बनवणे.

3. First Examples

Your Notes:
Example 1a: a function with a timer returns nothing
console.log("start");
function importantAction(username) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log(username);   // → vishal (after 1 s)
  }, 1000);
}
const name = importantAction("vishal");
console.log(name);   // → undefined (importantAction returns nothing)
// ✔ the "//undefined" comment was on console.log(username), which prints "vishal" after 1 s;
//    it's console.log(name) that prints undefined
  • What happens: importantAction schedules a log and returns undefined immediately.
  • Output: start, undefined, vishal after 1 s.
Example 1b: passing a callback
function processUserInput(name, cb) {
  console.log(name);   // → vishal
  cb(name);
}
function getUser(name) {
  console.log("Hello", name);   // → Hello vishal
}
processUserInput("vishal", getUser);   // getUser is passed WITHOUT () (a reference, not a call)
  • What happens: getUser is passed WITHOUT () and called inside processUserInput.
  • Output: vishal, Hello vishal.
  • ✅ The caller decides what happens next.
console.log(username) १ सेकंदाने "vishal" दाखवतो; undefined येते ते console.log(name) मध्ये, कारण importantAction काहीच return करत नाही.

4. JavaScript Functions are First-Class Citizens: Callbacks Make Functions Reusable

Your Notes: Def: so a callback function is a function that you pass into another function as an argument for execution later. 
// example 1:
function isOdd(number) { return number % 2 != 0; }
function isEven(number) { return number % 2 === 0; }
function filtered(numbers, fu) {
  let result = [];
  for (const number of numbers) {
    if (fu(number)) {
      result.push(number);
    }
  }
  return result;
}
let numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6];
// here we pass isOdd and isEven as callback functions
console.log(filtered(numbers, isOdd));    // → [1, 3, 5]
console.log(filtered(numbers, isEven));   // → [2, 4, 6]
// The logic of filtered is the same; you can pass any function that accepts an argument and returns a
// boolean value as the second argument of the filter function.
// Instead of a separate named function, you can also pass an anonymous function to the filter function.
  • What happens: filtered contains the loop; the callback decides which numbers to keep.
  • Output: [1, 3, 5], [2, 4, 6].
  • ✅ One function, many behaviours: just pass a different callback.

5. Arrow Functions as Callbacks & an Async Example

Your Notes: you can also use an arrow function as a callback function, as shown in the following code: 
function filter(numbers, callback) {
  let data = [];
  for (const number of numbers) {
    if (callback(number)) {
      data.push(number);
    }
  }
  return data;
}
const oddNumbers = filter(numbers, (number) => number % 2 != 0);
console.log("oddNumbers", oddNumbers);   // → oddNumbers [1, 3, 5]
  • What happens: an arrow function passed inline as the callback.
  • Output: oddNumbers [1, 3, 5].
Callbacks can sometimes lead to callback hell and a deeply nested code structure when dealing with a set of (multiple) asynchronous operations. 
// example 2
function fetchData(url, callback) {
  setTimeout(function () {
    const data = { message: "Data fetch successfully" };
    callback(data);
  }, 1000);
}
function handledData(data) {
  console.log(data.message);   // → Data fetch successfully (after 1 s)
}
fetchData("www.google.com", handledData);
// In the above example, fetchData is a function that takes a URL and a callback function as arguments.
// It simulates an asynchronous operation, and after the delay calls the provided callback function with the fetched data.
// handledData is the callback function that processes the data when it is available.
  • What happens: fetchData simulates a slow request and calls the callback with the data when ready.
  • Output: Data fetch successfully after 1 s.
  • ✅ How async code worked before promises.
Classification of callback functions:
  1. synchronous callback functions;
  2. asynchronous callback functions.

A callback function is a function passed as an argument to another function, to be called back at a later time.

6. Calculator: Normal Way vs Callback + Higher-Order Function

Your Notes: the normal way, without using callback functions or higher-order functions:
Example 5a: separate functions for each operation
const add = (a, b) => { return a + b; };
console.log(add(4, 5));   // → 9
const sub = (a, b) => { return a - b; };
console.log(sub(4, 5));   // → -1
const mul = (a, b) => { return a * b; };
console.log(mul(4, 5));   // → 20
  • What happens: three independent functions.
  • Output: 9, -1, 20.
Example 5b: one higher-order calculator
// instead, use a callback function and a higher-order function, which is easier
const add1 = (a, b) => { return a + b; };
const sub1 = (a, b) => { return a - b; };
// here calculator is the higher-order function,
// and add1 and sub1 are the callback functions passed as arguments to another function, calculator
const calculator = (num1, num2, callback) => {
  return callback(num1, num2);
};
console.log(calculator(4, 5, add1));     // → 9
console.log(calculator(20, 10, sub1));   // → 10
// ✔ comment said "add1 and sub2"; the function is sub1
  • What happens: calculator receives the operation as a callback.
  • Output: 9, 10.
  • ✅ Add new operations without changing calculator.

7. Synchronous Callback Function

Your Notes:
  1. (It runs sequentially and blocks the execution of code until the callback finishes.)
  2. A synchronous callback is executed during the execution of the higher-order function that uses the callback.
  3. A synchronous callback is executed immediately within the function it is passed to, blocking further execution of code until it completes.
  4. These callbacks are executed in sequence, so the program waits for the callback to finish before moving on to the next operation.
  5. They don't let the main thread continue executing other code until they finish.
Example 1
function isOdd2(number) { return number % 2 != 0; }
function isEven2(number) { return number % 2 === 0; }
function filtered2(numbers2, fu) {
  let result = [];
  for (const number of numbers) {   // ⚠ uses the OUTER "numbers", not the parameter numbers2
    if (fu(number)) {
      result.push(number);
    }
  }
  return result;
}
let numbers2 = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6];
// here we pass isOdd and isEven as callback functions
console.log(filtered(numbers2, isOdd));    // → [1, 3, 5]
console.log(filtered(numbers2, isEven));   // → [2, 4, 6]
// ✔ you defined filtered2 / isOdd2 / isEven2 but call filtered / isOdd / isEven, so the new
//    functions are never used; and inside filtered2 the loop should be: for (const number of numbers2)
  • What happens: the new functions are never used, and filtered2 loops over the outer numbers (a bug).
  • Output: [1, 3, 5], [2, 4, 6] (from the old functions).
  • ⚠ Watch for copy-paste names and wrong variables.
1. In the above example, isOdd and isEven are examples of synchronous callbacks, because t
// 1. In the above example, isOdd and isEven are examples of synchronous callbacks, because they are executed
//    during the execution of the filter function.
// 2. A synchronous callback function executes immediately and blocks the execution of the code that follows it in the same thread.
//    It is also sometimes called a blocking callback, because it prevents the program from continuing until the callback function is finished.

// example 2
function greet(name) {
  console.log(`hello, ${name}`);
}
function processUserInput2(callback) {
  const name = "alliance";
  callback(name);
}
processUserInput2(greet);   // → hello, alliance
console.log("this run after the callbackfunction");   // → printed AFTER (synchronous)
  • What happens: a synchronous callback runs immediately inside processUserInput2, before the next line.
  • Output: hello, alliance, then the next log.
✔ renamed processUserInput to processUserInput2 to fix the hoisting crash (function was declared twice). ✔ मराठी: hoisting मुळे होणारा crash टाळण्यासाठी दुसरे function processUserInput2 असे rename केले, कारण एकाच नावाची दोन functions होती.
example 3
// example 3
function synchronousCallback() {
  console.log("start");
  function callBack() {
    console.log("callback");
  }
  callBack();
  console.log("end");
}
synchronousCallback();   // → start → callback → end
  • What happens: the callback runs in order, inside the function.
  • Output: start, callback, end.

8. Asynchronous Callback Function

Your Notes:
  1. An asynchronous callback is executed after the execution of the higher-order function that uses the callback.
  2. With an asynchronous callback, the callback function is not executed immediately; instead it is scheduled to run at a later time, often after some asynchronous operation completes. ✔ "after some synchronous operation complete" → after an ASYNCHRONOUS operation (timer, request, event) completes.asynchronous callback हा async काम (timer, API, event) पूर्ण झाल्यावर चालतो.
  3. So asynchronous callbacks are commonly used for tasks like making HTTP requests, reading files or handling user interactions that may take some time to complete. They let the main thread continue executing other code while waiting for the asynchronous operation to finish.
  4. An asynchronous callback is executed after an operation completes, but that operation doesn't block the rest of the code from running. The callback is typically invoked after a non-blocking operation, such as an API request, a timer or an event handler.
Note: asynchronous callbacks are often used in situations where you don't know how long the operation will take (e.g. fetching data from a server, reading files, etc.). 
function getData(callback) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    const data = { name: "vishal" };
    callback(data);
  }, 2000);
}
console.log("fetch data....");
getData((data) => {
  console.log(`data received ${data.name}`);
});
console.log("this running before data is received....");
// In this example, setTimeout delays the execution of the callback by 2 seconds. This makes the callback
// asynchronous, because the rest of the code continues running while the timer counts down. The console output will be:
// → fetch data.... → this running before data is received.... → data received vishal (2 s)
  • What happens: the callback is given to setTimeout, so it runs after 2 s while the rest of the code continues.
  • Output: fetch data…, this running before data is received…, data received vishal.

9. What is the Difference between a Synchronous and an Asynchronous Callback?

Your Notes: Synchronous callback: blocks the execution of the code until the callback finishes; executed immediately (during the higher-order function's execution), in sequence, before the next line of code.
Asynchronous callback: does not block the execution of the code; executed later, after some asynchronous operation is completed. 
// example of an asynchronous callback
function asynchronousCallback() {
  console.log("start");
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log("callback");
  }, 1000);   // here the callback is scheduled for after one second
  console.log("end");
}
asynchronousCallback();   // → start → end → callback (1 s)
// In the above code, setTimeout schedules the callback to execute after a one-second delay; meanwhile the
// program continues executing the code after setTimeout without waiting for the callback.
// Asynchronous means that if JavaScript has to wait for an operation to complete, it executes the rest of the code while waiting.
// NOTE
// 1. JavaScript is a single-threaded language; it carries out asynchronous operations via the callback queue and the event loop.
  • What happens: asynchronous callback: end prints before callback.
  • Output: start, end, callback.
Synchronous callbackAsynchronous callback
When it runsImmediately, inside the HOFLater, after the HOF has returned
Blocking?YesNo
Examplesmap, filter, forEach, sort, your filtered()setTimeout, addEventListener, fetch().then, fs.readFile
Orderstart → callback → endstart → end → callback
Figure 88: A synchronous callback runs inside the call; an asynchronous callback runs after the current code finishes.
Synchronous callback HOF च्या आत लगेच चालतो, आणि तो संपेपर्यंत पुढची ओळ थांबते (map, filter). Asynchronous callback नंतर चालतो (setTimeout, events, fetch), म्हणून आधी "end" आणि मग "callback" येते.

10. Example: Download & Process a Picture

Your Notes: suppose that you need to develop a script that downloads a picture from a remote server and processes it after the download completes. Downloading the picture from a remote server takes time, depending on the network speed and the size of the picture. So the following download() function uses the setTimeout() function to simulate the network request.
Example 11a: the wrong order without a callback
function downloadUrl(url) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log(`downloading the ${url}`);
  }, 1000);
}
function process(picture) {
  console.log(`processing picture ${picture} `);
}
let url = "www.google.com";
downloadUrl(url);
process(url);
// output
// processing picture www.google.com
// downloading the www.google.com
// So the above output is not what you expected, because the process function executed before the download finished.
// But the correct way is:
// first download the picture and wait for the download to complete,
// then process the picture.

// To solve this issue, you can pass the process() function to the download() function and execute process()
// inside download() once the download completes, in the following way:
  • What happens: downloadUrl's log is delayed, but process runs immediately.
  • Output: processing picture …, then downloading the …
  • ⚠ Async work doesn't block, so order must be handled with callbacks/promises.
Example 11b: callback called outside the timer (still wrong)
function download(url, callback) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log("downloading url....");
  }, 1000);
  callback(url);   // ⚠ called OUTSIDE the timer
}
let url1 = "www.google.com";
// function pressing(url){
//     console.log('processing...')
// }
// download(url1, Processing);
// you can also define the processing function as an anonymous function here
download(url, function (url) {
  console.log("processing the url");
});
// so here first "processing" and then
// "downloading url..."
  • What happens: callback(url) runs right away, not after the timer.
  • Output: processing the url, then downloading url….
  • ⚠ The callback must be called INSIDE the async completion.
✔ (verified in Node: "processing the url" prints BEFORE "downloading url....") this version does NOT fix the order, because callback(url) is called right away, outside setTimeout. Move it INSIDE the timer, after the download: 
function download(url, callback) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log("downloading url....");
    callback(url);   // ✅ runs only after the "download" finishes
  }, 1000);
}
download(url, (url) => console.log("processing the url"));   // → downloading url.... → processing the url
  • What happens: the callback is now called inside the timer, after the download.
  • Output: downloading url…., processing the url.
  • ✅ Correct sequencing with callbacks.
callback(url) setTimeout च्या बाहेर लिहिल्यामुळे तो लगेच चालतो, म्हणून "processing" आधी येते आणि क्रम सुधारत नाही. callback ला setTimeout च्या आत, download नंतर ठेवा. Define 2 callback functions (success and failure): 
function downloaded(url, success, failure) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log("downloading the url....");
  }, 1000);
  !url ? failure(url) : success(url);
}
download(
  url,
  (url) => { console.log("processing..++++"); },
  (url) => { console.log("invalid url"); }
);
// ✔ you defined downloaded() but call download() (which ignores the 3rd argument), so the
//    failure callback can never run. Call downloaded(url, …) and put the success/failure call inside the timer.
//    (Node's convention is one error-first callback: cb(err, data).)
  • What happens: success/failure callbacks; the code calls the wrong function, so failure never runs.
  • Output: processing..++++ (immediately).
  • ⚠ Node style: one error-first callback cb(err, data).

11. Example of Multiple (Nested) Callback Functions

Your Notes: if you have multiple nested callback functions: 
let uri = "example.com";
let uri1 = "test.com";
let uri2 = "testa test.com";
function fetChImage(uri, callback) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log(`download the image ${uri}`);
  }, 1000);
  callback(url);   // ⚠ passes the GLOBAL "url" (www.google.com), not uri; and outside the timer
}
fetChImage(uri, function (uri) {
  console.log(`processing url like ${uri}`);              // → processing url like www.google.com
  fetChImage(uri1, function (uri) {
    console.log(`processing url like ${uri1}`);           // → processing url like test.com
    fetChImage(uri2, function (uri2) {
      console.log(`precessing url like ${uri2}`);         // → precessing url like www.google.com
    });
  });
});
// all three "processing" lines print immediately; the three "download the image …" lines come 1 s later
// ✔ fix: callback(uri) inside the setTimeout
// so this callback strategy does not scale well when the complexity grows significantly:
// multiple callbacks are nested on top of each other (callback hell, Chapter 63)
  • What happens: nested callbacks to download three images in order; bugs: uses the global url and calls back outside the timer.
  • Output: three processing lines immediately, downloads after 1 s.
  • ⚠ Deep nesting = callback hell; promises/async-await fix it.

12. What are the Problems with Callbacks?

Your Notes: 2 main issues with callbacks:
  1. Callback hell
  2. Inversion of control (control of execution moves away from the main program)
The control of execution moves away from the main program, making it harder to predict what happens next. Inversion of control means we lose control of our program when we use callbacks. Callbacks are a common example of Inversion of Control (IoC), because when we pass a function as a callback, we give up control over when and how that function will be executed. Instead, the function is called later by another piece of code.
What can go wrong when you hand over control (that's why promises were invented) 
thirdPartyCheckout(cart, function onPaid() { chargeCard(); });
// the library might call onPaid twice (double charge!), never, too early, or swallow errors.
// Promises fix this: a promise settles ONLY ONCE, and YOU attach .then().
  • What happens: giving your callback to third-party code means trusting it to call it exactly once, at the right time (inversion of control).
  • Output: (concept).
  • ⚠ Promises solve this trust problem.

13. Higher-Order Function

Your Notes (23_callback/higherOrder.js):
  1. A higher-order function is a function that takes one or more functions as arguments, or returns a function as its result.
  2. Def: a function which takes another function as an argument (or returns one) is called a HOF (higher-order function).
  3. In JavaScript, a higher-order function is a super flexible function.
It can do two special things, so a higher-order function either:
  1. Accepts another function as an argument: just as a regular function takes a number or string as input (a parameter or argument), a higher-order function takes another function as an argument. Think of it as a function that can invite another function to the party.
  2. Returns a function: a higher-order function can also give you back a new function, i.e. it returns a new function as its result.
The most real-life examples of higher-order functions: map, filter and reduce are higher-order functions that take callback functions to process arrays.
example with the map higher-order function
// example with the map higher-order function
const number = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
function double(x) { return x * 2; }
const doubleNumbers = number.map(double);
console.log(doubleNumbers);   // → [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
  • What happens: map is a higher-order function: it calls double for every item.
  • Output: [2, 4, 6, 8, 10].
example with the filter function
// example with the filter function
function isEven(x) { return x % 2 === 0; }
const eveNum = number.filter(isEven);
console.log(eveNum);          // → [2, 4]
  • What happens: filter keeps items where the callback returns true.
  • Output: [2, 4].
  1. So a higher-order function is a function that can work with other functions, either by taking them as input or by creating a new function as output.
  2. They make your code more flexible and powerful by letting you bundle a block of logic and reuse it to solve different kinds of problems.
  3. Higher-order functions are commonly used in JavaScript for tasks such as array manipulation (e.g. map, filter), event handling, and asynchronous programming (functions like setTimeout and promises).
  4. Using higher-order functions, you write more maintainable and modular code, promote the separation of concerns, and reuse code blocks to perform specific tasks. ✔ "you wire … and prompt the separation of concern and reside te code block" → you WRITE … PROMOTE separation of concerns and REUSE code blocks.HOF मुळे code modular होतो, प्रत्येक भागाचे काम वेगळे राहते (separation of concerns), आणि code पुन्हा वापरता येतो.

14. Higher-Order Function vs Callback & Why Use HOFs

Your Notes: what is the difference between a higher-order function and a callback function?
  • Callback function: a function that is passed as an argument to another function, to be called back at a later time.
  • Higher-order function: a function that takes another function as an argument, or returns a function as its result, is called a HOF.
In number.map(double): map is the higher-order function, double is the callback.

Why use higher-order functions?

  1. Code reusability: encapsulate reusable logic in functions.
  2. Abstraction: makes code cleaner and more expressive.
  3. Functional composition: combine small functions to build more complex behaviour.
  4. Callbacks and promises: essential for asynchronous programming (e.g. setTimeout, then in Promises).
  5. Modularity and composability.
  6. They help break down complex logic into smaller, reusable pieces. Using higher-order functions, you can compose simpler functions into more complex ones, which promotes clean and modular code.
  7. Avoiding code duplication: since higher-order functions let you pass different behaviour as arguments, you can avoid repeating similar code. For example, instead of writing a custom loop each time, you can use higher-order functions like map, filter or reduce to handle collections in a consistent and declarative manner.
  8. Improved readability: using higher-order functions can improve the readability of code by expressing operations in terms of the functions they execute. This is especially true with well-named functions (e.g. filter, map, compose).
function createAdder(x) {
  // here createAdder is a higher-order function: it returns a function as its result
  return function (y) {
    return x * y;
  };
}
const data = createAdder(5);
const result = data(5);
console.log("result", result);   // → result 25
// ✔ the name says "adder" but the code MULTIPLIES (x * y → 25). For an adder use x + y → 10,
//    or rename it createMultiplier. (This returned function is also a closure over x, Chapter 13.)
  • What happens: a function that returns a function is also higher-order; the returned function remembers x.
  • Output: result 25.
Figure 89: A higher-order function takes a callback as input and/or returns a new function.
Higher-order function = जो function दुसरा function argument म्हणून घेतो किंवा function परत करतो (map, filter, calculator, createAdder). Callback = जो function argument म्हणून दिला जातो (double, isEven, add1). number.map(double) मध्ये map हा HOF आणि double हा callback आहे.

15. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. Callback vs higher-order function?
  • The HOF is the function that receives (or returns) a function; the callback is the function that is passed in. In setTimeout(fn, 1000), setTimeout is the HOF and fn is the callback.
Q2. Are all callbacks asynchronous?
  • No. map/filter/forEach/sort call their callbacks synchronously; setTimeout, events, I/O and .then call them asynchronously.
Q3. Why pass getUser and not getUser()?
  • getUser is the function reference (the HOF will call it later); getUser() calls it right now and passes its RETURN value (here undefined), which is a common bug.
Q4. What are the problems with callbacks and their fixes?
  • Callback hell (fix: named functions, promises, async/await) and inversion of control (fix: promises settle once, and the caller attaches handlers). Also scattered error handling (fix: error-first callbacks or .catch / try-catch).
Q5. Write your own HOF: a "repeat" or "once" function.
function once(fn) {
  let done = false, result;
  return (...args) => (done ? result : ((done = true), (result = fn(...args))));
}
const init = once(() => console.log("init"));
init(); init();   // → init (only once)
  • What happens: once wraps fn so it runs only the first time and then returns the saved result.
  • Output: init (once).
  • ✅ Useful for initialisation code.
Q6. Output-based questions
function hof(cb) { console.log("A"); cb(); console.log("C"); }
hof(() => console.log("B"));                      // → A B C
function later(cb) { setTimeout(cb, 0); console.log("X"); }
later(() => console.log("Y"));                    // → X Y
console.log([1, 2, 3].map((n) => n * 10));        // → [10, 20, 30]
const mult = (x) => (y) => x * y;  console.log(mult(3)(4));   // → 12
  • What happens: synchronous callback runs inside (A B C); async callback runs later (X Y); map; curried function.
  • Output: A B C, X Y, [10, 20, 30], 12.
TermRemember
CallbackA function passed as an argument
HOFTakes and/or returns a function
Sync callbackRuns inside the call (map, filter)
Async callbackRuns later (setTimeout, events)
Callback problemsCallback hell, inversion of control
थोडक्यात: callback = argument म्हणून दिलेला function; HOF = function घेणारा किंवा परत करणारा function. sync callback लगेच चालतो, async नंतर. callback ला setTimeout/async काम पूर्ण झाल्यावरच call करा, बाहेर नाही. एकाच नावाचे functions दोनदा declare करू नका.

CHAPTER 39 INDEX
  1. How to Return Multiple Values
  2. Using an Array

1. How to Return Multiple Values from a Function

Your Notes (37_returnMultiPleValue.js):
  1. A JS function returns a single value. If you want to return multiple values from a function, you can pack the return values into an array or into the properties of an object.
  2. ES6 allows destructuring assignment syntax to unpack values from the array or object. ✔ "destructuring assessment" → destructuring ASSIGNMENT (same in the NOTE below)."assessment" नाही, "assignment" (destructuring assignment).
Definition: return a, b does NOT return two values (the comma operator returns only b, Chapter 68). Return a container instead: an array (order matters → array destructuring) or an object (names matter → object destructuring, order-free, self-documenting).
JS function एकच value परत करतो. अनेक values हव्या असतील तर त्या array किंवा object मध्ये घालून परत करा, आणि destructuring ने वेगळ्या काढा. return a, b लिहिल्यास फक्त b परत येतो.

2. Using an Array

function getName() {
  let firstName = "vishal";
  let lastName = "shinde";
  return [firstName, lastName];
}
let value = getName();
console.log(value);      // → ['vishal', 'shinde']
console.log(value[0]);   // → vishal
console.log(value[1]);   // → shinde

// but to take multiple values from a function in ES6, use the destructuring syntax;
// here we use array destructuring
const [fName, lName] = getName();
console.log("fName", fName);   // → fName vishal
console.log(lName, lName);     // → shinde shinde
// ✔ prints lName twice; you probably meant console.log("lName", lName) → lName shinde
  • What happens: return an array, then read by index or destructure into variables.
  • Output: ['vishal', 'shinde'], vishal, shinde, fName vishal, shinde shinde.
  • ✅ Arrays suit short, ordered results.

3. Returning Multiple Values from a Function Using an Object

function display() {
  let name = "vishal";
  let age = 38;
  let id = 34;
  // here we return multiple values from the function and use the destructuring syntax;
  // here we use object destructuring
  return { name, age, id };   // property shorthand: { name: name, age: age, id: id }
}
const details = display();
console.log(details);            // → { name: 'vishal', age: 38, id: 34 }
const { name, age, id } = display();
console.log(name, age, id);      // → vishal 38 34

// # NOTE
// JavaScript doesn't support functions that return multiple values; you can wrap multiple values into an array or
// an object and return the array or object.
// Use the destructuring assignment syntax to unpack the values from the array and the properties from the object.
  • What happens: return an object with property shorthand, then destructure by name.
  • Output: { name, age, id }, vishal 38 34.
  • ✅ Order doesn't matter; skip what you don't need.

4. Object Properties: Shorthand (Modern JavaScript)

const name1 = "vishal";
const neaAge = 25;
// traditional way
const person5 = {
  fullName: name1,
  age: neaAge,
};
console.log(person5);   // → { fullName: 'vishal', age: 25 }

// using shorthand notation for object properties
const person6 = { name1, neaAge };
console.log(person6);   // → { name1: 'vishal', neaAge: 25 }
// instead of writing fullName: name1 and age: neaAge, you can simply write the variable names directly in the
// object literal; ⚠ but then the KEYS are the variable names (name1, neaAge), not fullName/age.
  • What happens: { name1, neaAge } uses the variable NAMES as keys.
  • Output: { fullName: 'vishal', age: 25 }, { name1: 'vishal', neaAge: 25 }.
shorthand { name1, neaAge } मध्ये key चे नाव variable च्या नावासारखेच असते (name1, neaAge). वेगळे नाव हवे असल्यास fullName: name1 असे लिहावे लागते.
Which one to choose? 
// array → short, ordered results (like React's useState): const [count, setCount] = useState(0)
// object → many values / optional values; caller picks by name, order doesn't matter:
function stats(nums) {
  return { min: Math.min(...nums), max: Math.max(...nums), avg: nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b) / nums.length };
}
const { max, avg } = stats([2, 4, 9]);   // skip what you don't need → 9 5
const [, second] = getName();            // skip with an empty slot → "shinde"
  • What happens: array vs object returns: pick by position or by name; skip values with commas or by leaving names out.
  • Output: 9 5, "shinde".

5. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. Can a JS function return multiple values?
  • Not directly; return an array or object and destructure it. return a, b returns only b (comma operator).
Q2. Array or object: which is better?
  • An array for a few positional values (a tuple style, easy renaming); an object for named, many or optional values (clearer and order-independent).
Q3. What is the property shorthand?
  • { x, y } is the same as { x: x, y: y }: the key takes the variable's name.
Q4. How do you rename or default while destructuring a returned object?
  • const { name: userName = "guest", age } = display();
Q5. Output-based questions
function f() { return 1, 2, 3; }      console.log(f());     // → 3
function g() { return [1, 2]; }       const [a, , c = 9] = g();  console.log(a, c);   // → 1 9
function h() { return { x: 1 }; }     const { x, y = 0 } = h();  console.log(x, y);   // → 1 0
const v = 5; console.log({ v });                                 // → { v: 5 }
  • What happens: return 1, 2, 3 returns only the last value (comma operator); destructuring supports skipping and defaults.
  • Output: 3, 1 9, 1 0, { v: 5 }.
  • ⚠ You can't return multiple values without an array/object.
ReturnUnpack
return [a, b]const [a, b] = f()
return { a, b }const { a, b } = f()
{ a, b }Shorthand for { a: a, b: b }
थोडक्यात: अनेक values साठी array किंवा object return करा आणि destructuring ने काढा. object जास्त स्पष्ट असतो आणि क्रम महत्त्वाचा नसतो. shorthand मध्ये key चे नाव variable चेच असते.

CHAPTER 40 INDEX
  1. What is an Array? (13 points)
  2. How to Create an Array (literal, constructor, split)
  3. Tricky Questions: Array Constructor
  4. Accessing & Modifying Elements (negative index, at())

  6. Array.isArray()
