push/pop शेवटी काम करतात (वेगवान), unshift/shift सुरुवातीला काम करतात (सगळे elements सरकावे लागतात म्हणून हळू), आणि splice कुठेही काढतो, घालतो किंवा बदलतो. हे पाचही original array बदलतात (mutating).

2. push()

Your Notes (5_push.js):
  • Used to insert elements at the end of the array.
  • Syntax: array.push(element); returns the new length of the array.
  • The push() method is one of the most commonly used array methods in JavaScript.
    • It is used to add one or more elements to the end of an array.
  • It modifies the original array and returns the new length of the array (i.e. it appends values to the array).
  • The push() method adds the specified elements at the end of the array.
  • push() is a mutating method (i.e. it modifies the original array rather than creating a new array).
  • i.e. push is a mutating method because when you push an element, it adds the new element at the end and returns the new array length, instead of creating a new array.
  • i.e. it modifies the original array, giving it the new element and a new length.
Ex.1: push one value
const num = [5, 3, 9, 1, 7, 2, 10, 4, 6, 8];
console.log(num.length);       // → 10
const newNum = num.push(30);
// push returns the new length of the array and adds the given element at the end
console.log(newNum);           // → 11
// the original array is modified, with the new element added at the end
console.log(num);              // → [5, 3, 9, 1, 7, 2, 10, 4, 6, 8, 30]
  • What happens: push adds to the END and returns the NEW LENGTH (not the array).
  • Output: 10, 11, the array with 30 at the end.
  • ✅ Fast (no shifting of other items).
  • ⚠ Mutates the original array; const x = arr.push(…) stores a number.
Ex. push multiple values
num.push(40, 50, 60);
console.log(num);              // → [… 8, 30, 40, 50, 60]
  • What happens: push accepts several values at once.
  • Output: … 8, 30, 40, 50, 60.
Ex.2: push one array into another with the spread operator
const num1 = [5, 3, 9, 1, 7, 2, 10, 4, 6, 8];
const num2 = [11, 12, 13, 14, 15];
const num3 = num1.push(...num2);
const num4 = num1.push(...num2);
console.log(num3);             // → 15
console.log(num4);             // → 20   (pushed num2 a second time)
console.log(num1);             // → [5 … 8, 11 … 15, 11 … 15]
  • What happens: spread passes every item of num2 as a separate argument; pushing twice adds them twice.
  • Output: 15, 20, the combined array.
  • ✅ Append one array into another in place.
Ex-3, 4, 5: undefined, null, empty string
// you can also add undefined to the array
num1.push(undefined);
console.log(num1);             // → [… 15, undefined]

// this adds null to the end of the array and logs the new length of the array
console.log(num1.push(null));  // → 22
// ✔ comment said "which is now 13"; num1 already had 21 elements, so the new length is 22 (verified in Node)

// it also works with an empty string
console.log(num1);
num1.push('');
console.log(num1);             // → [… undefined, null, '']
  • What happens: any value can be pushed, including undefined, null and "".
  • Output: …undefined, 22, …null, ''.
num1 मध्ये आधीच 20 elements होते (num2 दोनदा push केला) आणि undefined नंतर 21 झाले. म्हणून push(null) नंतर length 22 येते, 13 नाही.
push() with call(): push is a generic method and works on array-like objects
// you can also call push on a non-array object with call(): Array.prototype.push.call(arrayLike, 1, 2, 2)
const obj = {
  0: 'A',
  1: 'B',
  length: 2
};
Array.prototype.push.call(obj, 'c');
console.log(obj);              // → { '0': 'A', '1': 'B', '2': 'c', length: 3 }
// call() changes the this value (this = obj)
  • What happens: push is generic: with call it works on array-like objects (numbered keys + length).
  • Output: { '0': 'A', '1': 'B', '2': 'c', length: 3 }.
Q. Why is push() a mutating method? A mutating method changes the original array.
Q. Pushing one array into another
let y = [1, 2, 3];
let z = [4, 5, 6];
let ry = y.push(z);            // adds z as ONE nested element
let zy = y.push(...z);         // adds 4, 5, 6 individually
console.log(ry);               // → 4
console.log(y);                // → [1, 2, 3, [4, 5, 6], 4, 5, 6]
  • What happens: push(z) adds the whole array as ONE item (nested); push(...z) adds each value.
  • Output: 4, [1, 2, 3, [4, 5, 6], 4, 5, 6].
  • ⚠ Forgetting ... creates nested arrays.
Q. push() with the arguments object
function xyz() {
  Array.prototype.push.call(arguments, 100, 800);
  console.log(arguments);      // → [Arguments] { '0': 1, '1': 1, '2': 2, '3': 100, '4': 800 }
}
xyz(1, 1, 2);
  • What happens: push via call on the arguments object.
  • Output: [Arguments] { …, '3': 100, '4': 800 }.
Q. What is the difference between arr.push(arr2) and arr.push(...arr2)?
  • arr.push(arr2) adds arr2 as one nested array element.
  • arr.push(...arr2) adds each element of arr2 individually.
Q. What is the time complexity of push()?
  • O(1) for adding a single element at the end (amortized).
  • O(k) when adding k elements in one call.
Q. When should you use push()?
  • Use push() when you want to: add an element to the end of an array
  • add multiple elements at once
  • build an array dynamically
  • append user input
  • collect results in loops
  • merge arrays using the spread operator.
Extra Details: non-mutating alternative: const next = [...arr, item]; or arr.concat(item) create a NEW array (useful in React and other state code).

3. pop()

Your Notes (6_pop.js):
  • Syntax: array.pop()
  • The pop() method removes the last element of an array.
  • The pop() method returns the removed element.
  • pop() is a mutating method (i.e. it changes the original array and its length, rather than creating a new array).
  • The pop() method does not create a new array.
  • If the array is empty, it returns undefined, and the original array is not modified.
  • Def: it is used to remove the last element from an array. It modifies the original array and returns the removed element.
  • The pop() method removes the last element from an array, modifies the original array, and returns the removed element.
  • If the array is empty, it returns undefined.
Ex-1
const NUMBERS = [5, 3, 9, 1, 7, 2, 10, 4, 6, 8, null, undefined];
console.log(NUMBERS.length);   // → 12
// ✔ comment said 10, but null and undefined are elements too → 12

// pop returns the element removed from the array
const Remove = NUMBERS.pop();
console.log(Remove);           // → undefined   (the LAST element was undefined!)

// so it modified the original array
console.log(NUMBERS);          // → [5, 3, 9, 1, 7, 2, 10, 4, 6, 8, null]
// this returns the modified length of the array
console.log(NUMBERS.length);   // → 11
  • What happens: pop removes and returns the LAST item; here the last item is undefined.
  • Output: 12, undefined, the shortened array, 11.
  • ✅ Stack (LIFO): push + pop.
  • ⚠ Mutates the original array.
array मध्ये null आणि undefined सुद्धा elements आहेत, म्हणून length 12 आहे, 10 नाही. शेवटचा element undefined असल्यामुळे pop() ने undefined परत दिले. "array रिकामा आहे" आणि "शेवटचा element undefined आहे" या दोन्हीत pop() चे उत्तर सारखेच (undefined) येते, हे लक्षात ठेवा.
Ex-2: pop() on an empty array
// if the array is empty, pop() returns undefined and does not modify the original array
const array = [];
const removeElement = array.pop();
// this returns undefined because the array is empty
console.log(removeElement);    // → undefined
// the array is empty, so the original array is not modified
console.log(array);            // → []
  • What happens: pop on an empty array returns undefined and changes nothing.
  • Output: undefined, [].
Ex-3: removing multiple elements at a time
// removing multiple elements at once is not possible: pop() removes only one element at a time
console.log(NUMBERS.pop());    // → null
  • What happens: pop removes only one item per call.
  • Output: null.
  • ⚠ Use splice or length to remove several.
Q. Why is pop() a mutating method?
  • A mutating method changes the original array instead of creating a new array.
  • So pop is a mutating method: it modifies the original array by removing the last element.
Q. What does pop() return? The pop() method returns the element removed from the array.
Q. Time complexity
  • Removing the last element is very efficient,
  • because it reads the last element and decreases the array length; it does not shift other elements.
  • O(1)
Q. What happens if you call pop() on an empty array? Nothing is removed, the array stays empty, and undefined is returned.
Q. Can pop() remove multiple elements at once?
  • No.
  • Each call removes only one element.
  • To remove multiple elements, call pop() multiple times, or use splice(-n) (or set arr.length = arr.length - n). ✔ "or use slice()". slice() does not remove anything (it only copies); splice() removes.slice() array मधून काहीच काढत नाही, फक्त copy देतो. एकाच वेळी अनेक elements काढायचे असतील तर splice(-n) वापरा.
Q. When should you use pop()?
  • To remove the last element
  • To implement a stack (LIFO: last in, first out) ✔ "stack (lio)" → LIFO.stack म्हणजे LIFO: शेवटी आलेला आधी बाहेर जातो (push + pop).
  • To process elements from the end
  • To remove a temporary item
Q. pop() vs push()
push()pop()
Adds one or more elements at the endRemoves the last element
Parameters: one or more elementsParameters: none
Returns the new array lengthReturns the removed element
Does not create a new arrayDoes not create a new array
Time complexity O(1)Time complexity O(1)
On an empty array, it inserts the new element and returns the new lengthOn an empty array, it returns undefined and the original array is not modified
✔ the second list was titled "push()" again; it describes pop().दुसऱ्या यादीचे heading चुकून push() होते; ती यादी pop() ची आहे.
pop() also works on array-like objects (generic method, via call())
const obj = {
  0: 'A',
  1: 'B',
  2: 'c',
  length: 3
};
const removed = Array.prototype.pop.call(obj);
console.log(removed);          // → 'c'   (obj.length becomes 2)
  • What happens: pop also works on array-like objects via call.
  • Output: 'c'.
Q. pop() with arguments
function test() {
  const removed = Array.prototype.pop.call(arguments);
  console.log(removed);        // → 30
  console.log(arguments);      // → [Arguments] { '0': 10, '1': 20 }
}
test(10, 20, 30);
  • What happens: pop via call on arguments.
  • Output: 30, { '0': 10, '1': 20 }.
Figure 97: A stack (push + pop) vs a queue (push + shift).

4. unshift()

Your Notes (7_unShift.js):
  • Syntax: array.unshift(elements), i.e. array.unshift(ele1, ele2, ele3, …) ✔ "unShift" → "unshift" (method names are case-sensitive; arr.unShift is not a function).JS case-sensitive आहे: unShift() नावाचा method नाही, unshift() (सर्व छोटी अक्षरे) आहे.
  • The unshift() method inserts (adds) one or more new elements at the start (beginning) of an array, modifies the original array, and returns the new length of the array.
  • It returns the new length of the array (i.e. it inserts the given values at the beginning of the array and returns the new length).
  • unshift() is a mutating method (it modifies the original array rather than creating a new array).
  • The unshift() method is the opposite of push():
    • push() adds elements to the end of an array,
    • unshift() adds elements to the beginning of an array.
  • Like push(), unshift() modifies the original array and returns the new length of the array.
  • Elements are inserted in the same order they are passed.
Ex-1
const num = [5, 3, 9, 1, 7, 2, 10, 4, 6, 8];
// unshift returns the new length of the array and adds the given element at the BEGINNING
// ✔ comment said "at the end of the array"
console.log(num.length);       // → 10
// every existing element moves one position to the right
const newNum = num.unshift(30);
console.log(newNum);           // → 11
console.log(num);              // → [30, 5, 3, 9, 1, 7, 2, 10, 4, 6, 8]
  • What happens: unshift adds to the START and returns the new length; every other item moves one place right.
  • Output: 10, 11, [30, 5, 3, …].
  • ⚠ Slower than push on big arrays (all items shift).
Ex-2: unshift multiple values at the beginning
num.unshift(40, 50, 60);
console.log(num);              // → [40, 50, 60, 30, 5, …]   (same order as passed)
  • What happens: several values are inserted in the order given.
  • Output: [40, 50, 60, 30, 5, …].
Ex-3: unshift one array into another
const num1 = [5, 3, 9, 1, 7, 2, 10, 4, 6, 8];
const num2 = [11, 12, 13, 14, 15];
console.log(num1.unshift(num2));     // → 11   (num2 added as ONE nested array)
console.log(num1);                   // → [[11, 12, 13, 14, 15], 5, 3, …]
const num3 = num1.unshift([...num2]); // → 12   (still ONE nested array: [...num2] is a copy)
const num4 = num1.unshift(...num2);   // → 17   (spread: 5 separate elements)
console.log(num3);                   // → 12
console.log(num4);                   // → 17
console.log(num1);                   // → [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, [11…15], [11…15], 5, 3, …]
  • What happens: unshift(array) or unshift([...array]) inserts ONE nested array; unshift(...array) inserts each value.
  • Output: 11, 12, 17 and the resulting array.
Ex-4, 5, 6: undefined, null, empty string
num1.unshift(undefined);       // unshift(undefined) is possible
num1.unshift(null);            // unshift(null) is possible
console.log(num1);             // → [null, undefined, 11, …]
console.log(num1.unshift('')); // → 20   (an empty string is also possible)
console.log(num1);             // → ['', null, undefined, 11, …]
  • What happens: undefined, null and "" can all be inserted.
  • Output: [null, undefined, …], 20, ['', null, undefined, …].
Ex-7: unshift() with an object
let use = [];
use.unshift({ name: 'vishal' });
console.log(use);              // → [{ name: 'vishal' }]
  • What happens: objects can be inserted too.
  • Output: [{ name: 'vishal' }].
Ex-7: unshift() in a loop (reverses the order)
let result = [];
for (let i = 0; i < num1.length; i++) {
  result.unshift(num1[i]);     // each new element goes to the FRONT
}
console.log(result);           // → [8, 6, 4, 10, 2, … '', ]   (num1 reversed)
  • What happens: unshifting each item into a new array reverses the order.
  • Output: the reversed array.
  • ⚠ Simpler: [...arr].reverse() or arr.toReversed().
Ex-8: unshift() on an array-like object
const obj = {
  0: "B",
  1: "C",
  length: 2
};
Array.prototype.unshift.call(obj, "A");
console.log(obj);              // → { '0': 'A', '1': 'B', '2': 'C', length: 3 }
  • What happens: unshift on an array-like object via call.
  • Output: { '0': 'A', '1': 'B', '2': 'C', length: 3 }.
Q. Why is unshift() a mutating method? A mutating method changes the original array.
Q. Time complexity
  • O(n)
  • Because every element must move one position to the right before the new element can be inserted.
Q. Why is unshift() slower than push()?
  • push() adds elements at the end, so there is no need to shift elements,
  • but unshift() adds elements at the beginning, so every existing element must move one position to the RIGHT. ✔ "each element by left position" → elements move to the RIGHT (to make space at index 0).unshift मध्ये index 0 वर जागा करण्यासाठी सगळे elements उजवीकडे (right) सरकतात, डावीकडे नाही.
  • Because unshift() must shift every existing element one position to the right before inserting the new element at index 0.
Q. What is the difference between the push and unshift() methods?
  • push(): adds one or more elements at the end of the array and returns the new length of the array; elements are added after the existing ones; push is faster because it adds at the end, so nothing needs shifting.
  • unshift(): adds one or more elements at the start (beginning) of the array and also returns the new length of the array; elements are added before the existing ones; unshift() is slower because all existing elements need to shift.
Q. push vs unshift()
Featurepush()unshift()
PurposeAdds one or more elements to the end of an arrayAdds one or more elements to the beginning of an array
Modifies original array?YesYes
Return valueNew length of the arrayNew length of the array
Order of additionElements are added after existing onesElements are added before existing ones
PerformanceFaster (especially for large arrays)Slower (as it shifts all existing elements)
Q. When should you use unshift()?
  • To add items at the beginning of the array
  • To build a queue from the front
  • To insert high-priority items before existing ones
Q. What is the difference between arr.unshift(arr2) and arr.unshift(...arr2)?
  • arr.unshift(arr2) inserts arr2 as a single nested array at the beginning.
  • arr.unshift(...arr2) inserts each element of arr2 individually at the beginning.

5. shift()

Your Notes (8_shift.js):
  • Syntax: array.shift()
    • It does not accept any parameters.
    • If the array has elements, it returns the removed first element.
    • If the array is empty, it returns undefined.
  • The shift() method removes the first element of an array (so every element moves one position left).
  • The shift() method returns the element removed from the array.
  • shift() is a mutating method (it changes the length of the original array, i.e. it modifies the original array).
  • If the array is empty, shift() returns undefined and does not modify the original array.
  • The shift() method is the opposite of the pop() method:
    • pop() removes the last element,
    • shift() removes the first element.
  • Like pop(), shift() modifies the original array, but unlike pop(), it must move every remaining element one position to the left, making it slower.
  • The shift() method removes the first element from an array, modifies the original array and returns the removed element. If the array is empty, it returns undefined.
  • No new array is created by shift() (the original array is modified).
Ex-1
const NUMBERS = [5, 3, 9, 1, 7, 2, 10, 4, 6, 8];
console.log(NUMBERS.length);   // → 10
const Remove = NUMBERS.shift();
// shift returns the element removed from the array
console.log(Remove);           // → 5
console.log(NUMBERS);          // → [3, 9, 1, 7, 2, 10, 4, 6, 8]
// this returns the modified length of the array
console.log(NUMBERS.length);   // → 9
// ✔ the comments said "pop method"; this example is shift()
  • What happens: shift removes and returns the FIRST item; others move left.
  • Output: 10, 5, [3, 9, …], 9.
  • ✅ Queue (FIFO): push + shift.
  • ⚠ Mutates the original array.
Ex-2: shift() on an empty array
// if the array is empty, shift() returns undefined and does not modify the original array
const array = [];
const removeElement = array.shift();
console.log(removeElement);    // → undefined   (the array is empty)
console.log(array);            // → []          (not modified)
  • What happens: shift on an empty array returns undefined.
  • Output: undefined, [].
Example: shift() inside a while loop
// shift() used in the while condition removes the next element until the array is empty
const name = ['vishal', 'shinde', 'at', 'post'];
let i;
while (typeof (i = name.shift()) !== 'undefined') {
  console.log(i);              // → vishal, shinde, at, post
}
// ✔ added "let i". Without it, i becomes an accidental global (ReferenceError in strict mode).
// ⚠ This loop also stops early if the array CONTAINS undefined. Safer: while (name.length) { … }
  • What happens: the loop keeps shifting until shift returns undefined (array empty).
  • Output: vishal, shinde, at, post.
  • ⚠ Stops early if the array contains undefined; while (arr.length) is safer.
i ला let नव्हते, त्यामुळे तो चुकून global variable बनत होता. तसेच array मध्ये मधेच undefined असल्यास हा loop तिथेच थांबेल; while (name.length) हा जास्त सुरक्षित पर्याय आहे.
Q. Does shift() work with different data types? Yes
const arr = [100, "JavaScript", true, null, undefined, { name: "Ram" }, [1, 2, 3]];
console.log(arr.shift());      // → 100
// Arrays in JavaScript can contain any data type, and shift() always removes the first element regardless of its type.
  • What happens: shift removes the first item whatever its type.
  • Output: 100.
Q. shift() on an array-like object
// Like push() and pop(), shift() is a generic method: it works on array-like objects using call()
const obj = { 0: "A", 1: "B", 2: "C", length: 3 };
const remove = Array.prototype.shift.call(obj);
console.log(remove);           // → 'A'   (obj becomes { 0: 'B', 1: 'C', length: 2 })
  • What happens: shift on an array-like object via call.
  • Output: 'A'.
Queue example
// A queue uses:
//   push()  → insert at the rear
//   shift() → remove from the front
const queue = [];
queue.push(10);
queue.push(20);
queue.push(80);
console.log(queue);            // → [10, 20, 80]
console.log(queue.shift());    // → 10
// This is called FIFO: first in, first out.
  • What happens: queue: push adds at the back, shift takes from the front (FIFO).
  • Output: [10, 20, 80], 10.
Q. Why is shift() a mutating method?
  • A mutating method changes the original array.
  • The shift method removes the first element of an array,
  • so the original array changes. Therefore shift() is a mutating method.
Q. What does shift() return? It returns the removed element.
Q. Which is faster for removing an element, pop() or shift()?
  • pop: the pop method is faster than shift, because pop removes the last element of the array, so there is no need to shift elements.
  • shift: shift() removes the first element of the array, so all remaining elements need to shift one position to the left.
Q. What is the difference between pop() and shift()?
  • pop(): removes the last element of an array; returns the removed element; on an empty array it returns undefined and does not modify the original array; it is associated with stacks (LIFO) and removes the last element; generally pop() is fast, because removing the last element requires no shifting.
  • shift(): removes the first element of an array; returns the removed element; on an empty array it returns undefined; it is associated with queues (FIFO) and removes the element from the front; generally shift() is slower, because all remaining elements need to shift one position to the left. ✔ "shift() method are associated with linked list" → it is associated with QUEUES (FIFO); a JS array is not a linked list.shift() चा संबंध queue (FIFO) शी आहे, linked list शी नाही. JS array हा linked list नाही.
Featurepop()shift()
PurposeRemoves the last element from an arrayRemoves the first element from an array
Return valueThe removed last elementThe removed first element
Modifies original?✅ Yes✅ Yes
Position affectedEnd of the arrayBeginning of the array
Performance🔼 Faster (no re-indexing required)🔽 Slower (needs to re-index elements)
Q. When should you use shift()?
  • To remove the first element of an array
  • To implement a queue (FIFO)
  • To process items in the order they were added
  • To remove the oldest item from a list
Q. Which data structure commonly uses shift()? A queue (FIFO, first in first out) is commonly implemented using operations like push() (enqueue) and shift() (dequeue). While shift() models queue behavior, it is still an array method in JS.

6. splice()

Your Notes (9_splice.js):
  • Syntax: splice(start, deleteCount, item1, item2, …)
    • start (required): the index at which to start changing the array.
    • If start is greater than the length of the array, it is treated as array.length: nothing is removed, but any items given are added at the end. ✔ "the array will not be modified". That is true only when no items are passed; with items they are appended (your own edge case at the end shows this).start हा length पेक्षा मोठा असेल तर काहीच काढले जात नाही, पण items दिले असतील तर ते शेवटी जोडले जातात. म्हणजे array बदलू शकतो.
    • deleteCount (optional): the number of elements to remove, starting from the start index.
      • If omitted, all elements from the start index to the end of the array are removed.
      • If deleteCount is zero, nothing is removed (only insertion happens).
    • item1, item2, …: the items to add to the array, starting at the start index. If no items are specified, splice() only removes elements.
  • Definition:
    • The splice() method changes the contents of an array by removing, replacing or inserting elements at a specified index.
    • It modifies the original array and returns an array containing the removed elements.
  • The splice() method is used to modify the original array by:
    1. removing elements,
    2. inserting new elements,
    3. replacing existing elements.
  • splice() changes the original array itself.
  • The splice() method in JavaScript is used to modify an array by removing, replacing or adding elements.
    • (i.e. the splice() method of array instances changes the contents of an array by removing, replacing or adding new elements in place)
  • It directly alters the original array (splice() is a mutating method, because it inserts, removes and replaces elements in the original array).
  • Basically, the splice() method removes elements from an array and, if necessary, inserts new elements in their place (i.e. most of the time it is used to delete elements).
  • The splice() method returns an array containing only the elements that were deleted (i.e. a new array holding the removed segment).
  • The splice() method changes the contents of an array by removing or replacing existing elements and/or adding new elements. If no elements are removed, an empty array is returned.
  • A negative index counts from the end.
Figure 98: splice(start, deleteCount, …items): remove, then insert at the same place, in the original array.
Your Notes (your code, corrected):
Q. What happens when you call splice() without arguments?
// It always returns an empty array (no start index and no delete count were given)
let sub = [];
console.log(sub.splice());       // → []
  • What happens: splice with no arguments removes nothing.
  • Output: [].
ex-2
const month = ["January", "February", "March", "April", "May", "June",
               "July", "August", "September", "October", "November", "December"];
const data1 = month.splice();
console.log(data1);              // → []
  • What happens: same on the months array.
  • Output: [].
Q.2. What is the output if you give only the first argument (no second argument)?
// If you give the first argument but not the second, it deletes elements from the given start index to the last element
// const data = month.splice(1);  // deletes all elements from start index 1 to the end of the array
// console.log(data);             // returns an array containing the deleted elements

  • What happens: splice(1) would delete everything from index 1, but the line is commented, so month is unchanged.

ex-2: remove two elements
const fruits = ["Apple", "Banana", "Cherry", "Date"];
// start index is 1 and delete count is 2
const deletedFruits = fruits.splice(1, 2);
console.log(fruits);             // → ['Apple', 'Date']
// splice() returns an array containing the deleted elements
console.log(deletedFruits);      // → ['Banana', 'Cherry']
  • What happens: splice(start, deleteCount) removes items and returns them in an array.
  • Output: ['Apple', 'Date'], ['Banana', 'Cherry'].
  • ✅ One method to remove, insert or replace anywhere.
  • ⚠ Mutates the original array.
ex-3: insert without removing

  • What happens: deleteCount 0 + extra arguments = insert without removing.
  • Output: [], ['vishal', 'January', …].

  • Output: the updated month list, ['March'].

}

splice() on a sparse array: splice works with sparse arrays
const arr = [1, , 3, 4, , 5, undefined, null];
console.log(arr.splice(1, 2));   // → [<1 empty item>, 3]
console.log(arr);                // → [1, 4, <1 empty item>, 5, undefined, null]
  • What happens: splice works on sparse arrays; holes are moved/removed like normal items.
  • Output: [<1 empty item>, 3], the remaining array.
Q. How to replace an element using splice()
// To replace an element, give the delete count as the 2nd argument and the inserted element(s) as the
// 3rd argument onward (you can give multiple elements). If you don't want to add or replace anything,
// don't give a third argument.
const arr1 = [1, , 3, 4, , 5, undefined, null];
// replace 3 with the string "three"
const newOne = arr1.splice(2, 1, 'three');
console.log(arr1);               // → [1, <1 empty item>, 'three', 4, <1 empty item>, 5, undefined, null]
console.log(newOne);             // → [3]

// if you don't want to add or replace anything, don't give the 3rd argument
const newTow = arr1.splice(2, 0);
console.log(newTow);             // → []
console.log(arr1);               // → unchanged
  • What happens: replace: deleteCount 1 + the new value; deleteCount 0 with no new items does nothing.
  • Output: the array with 'three', [3], [], unchanged.
Q. Does splice() work with negative indexes?
// Yes. A negative index counts from the end of the array: -1 is the last element, -2 the second-last, and so on.
let arrx = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
// start index is -2 and delete count is 2
// remove 2 elements starting from the second-to-last element (-2)
console.log(arrx.splice(-2, 2)); // → [4, 5]
console.log(arrx);               // → [1, 2, 3]
// ✔ comment said [1, 2, 5]; removing 4 and 5 leaves [1, 2, 3]
  • What happens: a negative start counts from the end: -2 = the second-last item.
  • Output: [4, 5], [1, 2, 3].
Add an element at the end using splice
let abc = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
// const result = abc.splice(-1, 0, 'vishal');  // this inserts BEFORE the last element, not at the end
// so use this approach instead:
const result = abc.splice(abc.length, 0, 'vishal');
console.log('result', result);   // → result []
console.log(abc);                // → [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 'vishal']
  • What happens: start = length inserts at the end (-1 would insert before the last item).
  • Output: result [], [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 'vishal'].
Add an element at the beginning
let a = [1, 2, 3];
a.splice(0, 0, 'Yes');
console.log(a);                  // → ['Yes', 1, 2, 3]
  • What happens: start 0, delete 0 inserts at the front.
  • Output: ['Yes', 1, 2, 3].
Important edge cases
// start > length
console.log(a.splice(10, 1, 'A'));   // → []   (nothing removed)
console.log(a);                      // → ['Yes', 1, 2, 3, 'A']
// If start is greater than the array length, JavaScript treats it as array.length,
// so inserted items are appended to the end. Nothing is removed.

// start < -length
console.log(a.splice(-10, 1));       // → ['Yes']
// Negative indexes smaller than -arr.length are treated as zero
  • What happens: a start past the end is treated as length (append); a start below -length is treated as 0.
  • Output: [], ['Yes', 1, 2, 3, 'A'], ['Yes'].
Q. Why is splice() a mutating method? Because it changes the elements, length and order of the original array.
Q. Time complexity
  • Insert at the beginning: O(n)
  • Remove at the beginning: O(n)
  • Insert in the middle: O(n)
  • Remove in the middle: O(n)
  • Insert at the end: O(1)
  • Remove at the end: O(1)

7. Differences between splice() vs slice()

Your Notes:
splice()slice()
Used to insert, remove or replace elements in an arrayUsed to extract (copy) a portion of an array
Returns an array of the removed elementsReturns a new array containing the extracted elements
Mutating methodNon-mutating method
Does not create a new array; it modifies the original arrayDoes not modify the original array
Used for insert, delete, replaceUsed to extract or get a portion of an array
deleteCount specifies how many elements to removeThe end index is exclusive (not included)
Q. When to use splice()?
  • To insert elements
  • delete elements
  • replace elements
  • when you want to modify the original array.

When to use slice()?
  • To copy part of an array
  • to keep the original array unchanged
  • to create a shallow copy
  • to extract a range of elements.
Extra Details: ES2023 non-mutating twins 
const base = [1, 2, 3, 4];
const out = base.toSpliced(1, 2, "x");   // → [1, "x", 4]   (base is still [1, 2, 3, 4])
// also: toSorted(), toReversed(), with(index, value)
  • What happens: toSpliced (ES2023) returns a NEW array with the change; the original stays the same.
  • Output: [1, "x", 4].
  • ✅ Non-mutating versions: toSorted, toReversed, with().
splice = original array कापतो/घालतो/बदलतो आणि काढलेले elements परत देतो (mutating). slice = original न बदलता त्याचा एक भाग copy करून नवीन array देतो (non-mutating). लक्षात ठेवायची युक्ती: spliCE मध्ये "C" = Change.

8. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. What do push/pop/shift/unshift return?
  • push and unshift return the new length; pop and shift return the removed element (undefined if the array is empty).
Q2. Why is shift()/unshift() slower than pop()/push()?
  • They work at index 0, so every other element has to be re-indexed: O(n). push/pop work at the end: O(1).
Q3. splice() vs slice()?
  • splice(start, deleteCount, ...items) mutates the array (remove/insert/replace) and returns the removed elements. slice(start, end) does not mutate; it returns a shallow copy of a range (end excluded).
Q4. How do you remove an item by value?
  • Find the index first and guard it: const i = arr.indexOf(v); if (i !== -1) arr.splice(i, 1); (without the guard, splice(-1, 1) removes the last item). Non-mutating: arr.filter(x => x !== v).
Q5. How do you implement a stack and a queue with arrays?
  • Stack (LIFO): push + pop. Queue (FIFO): push + shift (or a head-index pointer for large queues to avoid O(n) shifts).
Q6. How do you insert at a specific index without mutating?
  • [...arr.slice(0, i), item, ...arr.slice(i)] or ES2023 arr.toSpliced(i, 0, item).
Output-based questions
const s = [1, 2, 3];
console.log(s.push(4), s.pop(), s.unshift(0), s.shift());   // → 4 4 4 0
console.log([].pop(), [].shift());                          // → undefined undefined
const t = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
console.log(t.splice(1, 2), t);                             // → [2, 3] [1, 4, 5]
console.log(t.splice(-1), t);                               // → [5] [1, 4]
const u = [1, 2]; u.push([3, 4]); console.log(u.length);    // → 3
  • What happens: six output questions: return values of push/pop/unshift/shift, empty arrays, splice, nested push.
  • Output: 4 4 4 0, undefined undefined, [2, 3] [1, 4, 5], [5] [1, 4], 3.
MethodReturnsRemember
push / unshiftNew lengthend / start · unshift is O(n)
pop / shiftRemoved element (undefined if empty)stack / queue
spliceArray of removed elementsremove · insert · replace · negative index OK
All fiveMutate the original array · generic (work on array-likes via call())
थोडक्यात: push/unshift नवीन length देतात, pop/shift काढलेला element देतात, आणि splice काढलेल्या elements चा array देतो. पाचही original array बदलतात. stack = push + pop, queue = push + shift.

1. Which Search Method?

Figure 99: Choosing a search method: by value, by condition, or a true/false test. None of them mutate the array.
value शोधायची असेल तर indexOf/lastIndexOf/includes, condition ने शोधायचे असेल तर find/findIndex/findLast/findLastIndex, आणि "कोणी तरी पास होतो का / सगळे पास होतात का" हे तपासायला some/every. यापैकी कोणताच method original array बदलत नाही.

2. indexOf()

Your Notes (10_indexOf.js):
  • Syntax: indexOf(searchElement, fromIndex)
    • searchElement (required): the element you want to search for.
    • fromIndex (optional): the index where the search begins. ✔ "fromElement" → "fromIndex".दुसऱ्या parameter चे नाव fromIndex आहे (index क्रमांक), fromElement नाही.
  • The indexOf() method is used to search for a specified element in an array (or a substring in a string) and returns the index of its first occurrence.
    • It searches from left to right.
    • It returns the first matching index.
    • It returns -1 if the element is not found.
    • It does not modify the original array.
  • The indexOf() method returns the first index at which a given element can be found in the array. If the element is not found (not present in the array), it returns -1.
    (i.e. it returns the first, i.e. earliest, index of a given element in the array; i.e. the index of the first occurrence of the given element.) ✔ "first (latest index)" → first = EARLIEST (lowest) index.indexOf सर्वात पहिला (सर्वात लहान) index देतो, "latest" नाही.
  • The indexOf() method searches in the forward direction (left to right).
  • The indexOf() method shows only the first matching element in a given array (if duplicates are present, it shows the first match).
  • indexOf() accepts a negative fromIndex, but handles it in a different way (explained below).
  • indexOf() is not a mutating method (it does not modify the original array; it returns the index of the first occurrence of a specified element in the array).
Basic
const NAMES = ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "Diana", "Edward", "Fiona",
               "George", "Hannah", "Ian", "Julia", "Alice" /* duplicate */];

// if the element is present, it returns the index of its first occurrence
const data = NAMES.indexOf("Alice");     // → 0
console.log(data);
// if the element is not present, indexOf() returns -1
const data1 = NAMES.indexOf("vishal");   // → -1
console.log(data1);
  • What happens: indexOf returns the index of the FIRST match (using ===), or -1.
  • Output: 0, -1.
  • ✅ Find the position of a value.
  • ⚠ Always compare with -1: if (arr.indexOf(x) !== -1).
Example 2: start from a particular index (2nd parameter)
const name = NAMES.indexOf("Alice", 5);
console.log(name);                       // → 10   (the duplicate "Alice")
  • What happens: the second argument says where to start searching.
  • Output: 10.
Example 3
const array = [2, 9, 9];
const newArray = array.indexOf(2);
console.log(newArray);                   // → 0
  • What happens: first index of 2.
  • Output: 0.
Q. Does indexOf() work with negative indices?
  • No: indexOf() does not use a negative index to search from the end.
  • When you pass a negative number as the start index, JavaScript treats it as start = array.length + start.
  • So it is adjusted to a positive index, and the search still goes left to right, not from the end.
  • If you do not provide fromIndex, it defaults to 0. If you provide a negative fromIndex, it is treated as array.length + fromIndex, and the search still proceeds forward from that calculated index.
  • Behavior with a negative fromIndex: the starting position is calculated as array.length + fromIndex. However, the search only proceeds forward from this position, not backward.
let arrr = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50];
// searching for 30 from -3 (array.length + (-3) = 5 - 3 = 2), so the starting index is 2
console.log(arrr.indexOf(30, -3));   // → 2   (index of 30)
// searching for 10 from -3
console.log(arrr.indexOf(10, -3));   // → -1  (10 is not found from index 2 onward)
// no fromIndex → starts from index 0
console.log(arrr.indexOf(30));       // → 2
  • What happens: a negative fromIndex counts from the end (5 - 3 = 2); 10 is before index 2, so not found.
  • Output: 2, -1, 2.
What if the negative index is too small? 
const arrg = [10, 20, 30];
let res = arrg.indexOf(10, -100);
console.log(res);                    // → 0
// The negative index is too small: arrg.length + (-100) = 3 + (-100) = -97.
// When the calculated index is still negative, it is treated as zero (the search starts at 0).
  • What happens: if length + fromIndex is still negative, the search starts at 0.
  • Output: 0.
  • A negative fromIndex adjusts the starting point but does not reverse the search direction.
  • If the adjusted fromIndex is out of bounds (e.g. less than 0), the search starts at 0.
example 4
// example 4
// returns -1 because 2 is not present at or after the start position
const a = array.indexOf(2, -1);      // array = [2, 9, 9] → 3 + (-1) = 2, so the start index is 2
console.log(a);                      // → -1  (index 2 holds 9, not 2)
// ✔ comment said "(5 + (-1)) = 4"; this array's length is 3, so the start is 2
  • What happens: 3 + (-1) = 2, and index 2 holds 9.
  • Output: -1.
example 4
// example 4
const b = array.indexOf(2, -3);      // 3 + (-3) = 0
console.log(b);                      // → 0
  • What happens: 3 + (-3) = 0, so the whole array is searched.
  • Output: 0.
Example 5: you can't use indexOf() to search for NaN
const arr = [2, NaN, 4];
// NaN === NaN is false, so indexOf(NaN) doesn't work. Use arr.findIndex(Number.isNaN) instead.
const c = arr.indexOf(NaN);
console.log(c);                          // → -1
// so the correct approach is:
console.log(arr.findIndex(Number.isNaN)); // → 1
console.log(arr.includes(NaN));           // → true
// ✔ was arr.indexOf(Number.isNaN), which searches for the FUNCTION itself → -1

// if fromIndex >= length, JavaScript doesn't search at all and immediately returns -1:
console.log(arr.indexOf(2, 5));          // → -1
  • What happens: indexOf uses ===, and NaN !== NaN, so it can't find NaN; findIndex(Number.isNaN) and includes can. A fromIndex beyond the end returns -1.
  • Output: -1, 1, true, -1.
  • ⚠ Use includes for yes/no checks with NaN.
arr.indexOf(Number.isNaN) मध्ये indexOf "Number.isNaN" हा function array मध्ये आहे का ते शोधतो, NaN नाही, म्हणून -1. NaN शोधायला findIndex(Number.isNaN) किंवा includes(NaN) वापरा.
Example 6: holes vs a real undefined
// you can't use indexOf() to find an EMPTY SLOT in a sparse array (indexOf skips holes)
const app = [2, , 4, , null, undefined, ""];
const dd = app.indexOf();                // no argument → searches for undefined
console.log(dd);                         // → 5   (the REAL undefined at index 5; holes 1 and 3 are skipped)

// indexOf() CAN find a real undefined value
const d = app.indexOf(undefined);
console.log(d);                          // → 5
// indexOf() returns the index of a null value
const d2 = app.indexOf(null);
console.log(d2);                         // → 4
// indexOf() returns the index of an empty string
const d3 = app.indexOf('');
console.log(d3);                         // → 6
// ✔ the comments said app.indexOf() returns -1 and that indexOf "is not able to find undefined";
//    it returns 5. Only HOLES are skipped, not real undefined values (verified in Node).
  • What happens: indexOf skips holes but finds a real undefined, null and "".
  • Output: 5, 5, 4, 6.
indexOf फक्त रिकाम्या जागा (holes) वगळतो. array मध्ये खरा undefined असेल तर तो सापडतो (index 5). indexOf() ला argument न दिल्यास तो undefined शोधतो, म्हणून सुद्धा 5 येते.
Find all occurrences and their count
const stdName = ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "Diana", "Edward", "Fiona", "George",
                 "Hannah", "Ian", "Julia", "Alice", "Bob", "Alice"];
let count = 0;
let occurrences = [];
let element = 'Alice';
let index = stdName.indexOf(element);
while (index !== -1) {
  occurrences.push(index);
  index = stdName.indexOf(element, index + 1);   // continue searching AFTER the last match
  count++;
}
console.log(occurrences);    // → [0, 10, 12]
console.log(count);          // → 3
  • What happens: search again from index + 1 after every match until -1.
  • Output: [0, 10, 12], 3.
  • ✅ Classic "all occurrences" pattern.

3. lastIndexOf()

Your Notes (11_lastIndexOf.js):
  1. lastIndexOf(searchElement, fromIndex)
  2. The lastIndexOf() method in JavaScript is used to find the last occurrence of a specified element in an array or string (i.e. it returns the last, greatest, index of an element within the array equal to the given element).
  3. It is used to find the last occurrence of a specified value in an array and returns its index; if the element is not found (not present in the array), it returns -1.
  4. It searches from last to first (backward direction, i.e. right to left).
  5. Useful when you want to find the last matching item, unlike indexOf(), which finds the first.
  6. lastIndexOf() is not a mutating method (it does not modify the original array; it returns the index of the last occurrence of a specified element).
const fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry", "date", "banana",
                "elderberry", "fig", "grape", "banana"];
const data = fruits.lastIndexOf("banana");
console.log(data);           // → 8

// lastIndexOf(searchElement, fromIndex): the 2nd argument is where the BACKWARD search starts
const fruitData = fruits.lastIndexOf("banana", 6);
console.log(fruitData);      // → 4   (starts at index 6 and searches backward → finds index 4)

// if not found, it returns -1
const data1 = fruits.lastIndexOf("main", 2);
console.log(data1);          // → -1

// ex
const animals = ["lion", "tiger", "elephant", "giraffe", "zebra", "tiger", "kangaroo", "panda"];
const lastIndex = animals.lastIndexOf("tiger");
console.log(lastIndex);      // → 5
  • What happens: lastIndexOf searches from the end; fromIndex 6 means search backward from index 6.
  • Output: 8, 4, -1, 5.
Negative indexing
Example 1
const numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70];
  • What happens: the array used by the next examples.
  • Output: (no output).
Example 1: the last occurrence of 30, without fromIndex
// Example 1: the last occurrence of 30, without fromIndex
const index = numbers.lastIndexOf(30);
console.log(index);          // → 2
// It searches backward from the last element (70) and finds 30 at index 2, its last occurrence.
  • What happens: search backward from the end.
  • Output: 2.
Example 2: the last occurrence of 20, starting from index -2
// Example 2: the last occurrence of 20, starting from index -2
const index1 = numbers.lastIndexOf(20, -2);   // 7 + (-2) = 5
console.log(index1);         // → 1
// The negative fromIndex (-2) means we start at index 5 (array.length = 7, and 7 + (-2) = 5).
// We then search backward from index 5 (value 60) and find 20 at index 1, so the method returns 1.
  • What happens: -2 → start at index 5, then search backward.
  • Output: 1.
Example 3: the last occurrence of 20, starting from index -1
// Example 3: the last occurrence of 20, starting from index -1
const index2 = numbers.lastIndexOf(20, -1);
console.log(index2);         // → 1
// -1 means start at index 6 (7 + (-1) = 6). Searching backward from index 6 (value 70),
// we find 20 at index 1, so the method returns 1 again.
  • What happens: -1 → start at index 6.
  • Output: 1.
Example 4: the element is not found
// Example 4: the element is not found
const index3 = numbers.lastIndexOf(100);      // searching for a non-existent element
console.log(index3);         // → -1   (100 is not in the array)
  • What happens: not present.
  • Output: -1.
You can't use lastIndexOf() with NaN 
const ap = [NaN];
const sdp = ap.lastIndexOf(NaN);
console.log(sdp);            // → -1
// Because NaN === NaN is false, NaN is not considered equal to any NaN, even itself.

// Solution: a workaround using findLastIndex()
const ap1 = [1, NaN, 2, NaN];
const index11 = ap1.findLastIndex(Number.isNaN);
console.log(index11);        // → 3 ✅
  • What happens: lastIndexOf can't find NaN either; findLastIndex with Number.isNaN can.
  • Output: -1, 3.
You also can't use lastIndexOf() to find empty slots in a sparse array 
const app = [1, , 3];
const a = app.lastIndexOf(undefined);
console.log(a);              // → -1   (the hole is skipped and there is no real undefined)

const ab = [2, 3, 4, 5, , 8, "", null, NaN, undefined];
// no argument passed to lastIndexOf
console.log(ab.lastIndexOf());           // → 9
// If no argument is passed, it searches for undefined, and this array HAS a real undefined at index 9.

// Searching for undefined
console.log(ab.lastIndexOf(undefined));  // → 9
// The array explicitly contains undefined at index 9 (the hole at index 4 is skipped), so it returns 9.
// ✔ the comments said lastIndexOf() returns -1 because "undefined is not found" and that the array
//    "does not explicitly contain undefined"; it does (last element), so both return 9 (verified in Node)

// Searching for null
console.log(ab.lastIndexOf(null));       // → 7   (null is at index 7)
// Searching for an empty string ('')
console.log(ab.lastIndexOf(""));         // → 6   ('' is at index 6)
// Searching for NaN
console.log(ab.lastIndexOf(NaN));        // → -1
// lastIndexOf can't find NaN, because NaN is not equal to itself in JavaScript.
// Even though NaN is in the array, it returns -1.
  • What happens: holes are skipped; a real undefined is found; NaN can't be found.
  • Output: -1, 9, 9, 7, 6, -1.
ab array च्या शेवटी खरा undefined आहे, म्हणून lastIndexOf() आणि lastIndexOf(undefined) दोन्ही 9 देतात. फक्त index 4 वरील रिकामी जागा (hole) वगळली जाते.

Q. What is the difference between indexOf() and lastIndexOf()?

indexOf():
  1. The indexOf() method finds the index position of a specified element in an array and returns the index of its first occurrence. If it matches, it returns the index of the first match.
  2. If not found, it returns -1.
  3. It searches in the forward direction (left to right, i.e. first to last).
lastIndexOf():
  1. The lastIndexOf() method returns the index of the last occurrence of the specified element. If it matches, it returns the last index of that element.
  2. If it doesn't match, it returns -1.
  3. lastIndexOf() searches from last to first (backward direction, i.e. right to left).
FeatureindexOf()lastIndexOf()
PurposeFinds the first occurrenceFinds the last occurrence
Search directionLeft → right (start to end)Right → left (end to start)
ReturnsIndex of the first match, or -1Index of the last match, or -1
When not foundReturns -1Returns -1
Default search startIndex 0Last index (array.length - 1)
Optional fromIndex paramStarts searching from fromIndexStarts searching backward from fromIndex
Supports NaN?❌ No (NaN !== NaN)❌ No (NaN !== NaN)
Strict comparison usedYes (===)Yes (===)
Example[1,2,3,2].indexOf(2) → 1[1,2,3,2].lastIndexOf(2) → 3

4. includes()

Your Notes (15_includes.js):
  1. includes(searchElement, fromIndex)
  2. The includes() method determines whether a certain element is present in the array or not.
  3. It returns true or false: true if present, otherwise false.
  4. The includes method works in the forward direction.
  5. The includes() method compares searchElement to the elements of the array using the SameValueZero algorithm (like === but NaN equals NaN).
  6. includes also checks the empty slots of a sparse array: a hole is treated as undefined (so includes(undefined) finds holes too).
  7. The includes() method works with a negative fromIndex.
// example
const empty = [1, 2, 3];
// includes returns a boolean value, true or false
const result = empty.includes(2);
console.log('result', result);   // → result true

// includes() has a second argument: the search starts from that index, going forward
// NOTE: if fromIndex is greater than or equal to the array length, false is returned
const man = [1, 2, 3];
const res = man.includes(3, 3);
console.log(res);                // → false  (there is no index 3)
// ✔ "Formal index" → "fromIndex"

// If the computed index is less than or equal to zero, the entire array is searched
const array = ["a", "b", "c"];
const search = array.includes("c", -100);
// The value to search for is "c", and fromIndex is -100.
// array.length + fromIndex = 3 + (-100) is negative, so the search starts from zero,
// i.e. the beginning of the array. "c" is present at index 2, so the method returns true.
console.log('search', search);   // → search true

const array1 = ["a", "b", "c"];
const search1 = array1.includes("c", -1);
console.log('search', search1);  // → search true
// The value to search for is "c", and fromIndex is -1.
// A negative fromIndex means the search starts at array.length + fromIndex = 3 + (-1) = 2,
// i.e. the last element. At index 2 the value is "c", which matches, so the method returns true.
  • What happens: includes returns true/false; fromIndex past the end → false; very negative → whole array; -1 → only the last item.
  • Output: result true, false, search true, search true.
  • ✅ Most readable membership check.
includes() on a sparse array: undefined, NaN, null, empty string
const ab = [2, 3, 4, 5, , 8, '', null, undefined, NaN];
console.log(ab.includes());          // → true   (searches undefined)
console.log(ab.includes(undefined)); // → true
console.log(ab.includes(null));      // → true
console.log(ab.includes(''));        // → true
console.log(ab.includes(NaN));       // → true   ✅ unlike indexOf
console.log([1, , 3].includes(undefined));   // → true   (a hole counts as undefined)
  • What happens: includes treats holes as undefined and CAN find NaN (SameValueZero).
  • Output: true ×6.
  • ⚠ Difference from indexOf: holes and NaN.
includes() फक्त "आहे का?" (true/false) सांगतो. तो SameValueZero वापरतो, म्हणून NaN सापडतो (indexOf ला सापडत नाही). तो रिकाम्या जागेला (hole) undefined समजतो. index हवा असेल तर indexOf, आणि फक्त हो/नाही हवे असेल तर includes वापरा.

5. find()

Your Notes (12_find.js):
  1. Syntax: array.find(callback(element, index, array), thisArg?). find() takes a callback function.
  2. Def: the find() method returns the first element in an array that satisfies a provided testing function. If no match is found, it returns undefined. (i.e. find() is used to find the first element in an array that satisfies a provided testing function; it returns the first matching element, or undefined if no element is found.)
  3. The find() method returns the first element in the array that satisfies a given condition (provided testing function), i.e. it returns the value of the first element in the array where the predicate is true. If no value satisfies the condition, it returns undefined.
  4. find() is a non-mutating method (it does not modify the original array; it just performs a read operation) and returns the first element in the array that satisfies the provided callback function.
  5. Even if several elements in the array satisfy the given condition, find returns only the first one.
example
// example
const array = [5, 12, 8, 130, 44];
const find = array.find((ele, index) => {
  return ele > 10;
});
// returns the first element that satisfies the given condition
console.log(find);           // → 12
  • What happens: find returns the first ITEM that passes the test.
  • Output: 12.
example: if no element satisfies the condition, it returns undefined
// example: if no element satisfies the condition, it returns undefined
const notFind = array.find((ele, index) => {
  return ele === 0;
});
console.log(notFind);        // → undefined
// ✔ was "return (ele = 0)", an ASSIGNMENT. It returns 0 (falsy) by accident and overwrites the
//    parameter; use === for comparison.
  • What happens: nothing passes → undefined.
  • Output: undefined.
  • ⚠ Use === in the callback; = assigns.
(ele = 0) ही तुलना नसून assignment आहे. ती 0 (falsy) परत देते म्हणून योगायोगाने undefined आले. तुलनेसाठी === वापरा. NOTE:
  1. The only "problem" with the find method is that it returns only one element that satisfies the condition.
  2. The find() method is used for searching. (To get ALL matching elements, i.e. filtering, use filter().) ✔ "used for the searching and filtering" → find is for searching one item; filtering is filter()'s job.find फक्त पहिला जुळणारा element देतो. सगळे जुळणारे हवे असतील (filtering) तर filter() वापरा.
Example 1
// element and index, without a condition
var demo = [10, 20, 30, 40, 56, 78, 88, 99, 48];
const data = demo.find((ele, index) => {
  console.log("element", ele);
  console.log("index", index);
});
// returns undefined because the callback returns nothing (undefined = falsy) for every element
console.log(data);           // → undefined
  • What happens: the callback returns nothing (undefined = falsy), so no item is found.
  • Output: logs, then undefined.
example
// example
const longArray = [5, 12, 8, 130, 44, 3, 15, 17, 21, 6, 28, 34, 55, 89, 144, 233, 377, 610,
                   987, 1597, 2584, 4181, 6765, 10946, 17711, 28657, 46368, 75025, 121393];
const newData = longArray.find((ele, index, array) => {
  return ele < 1000;
});
// it returns only 5, because find returns the first element that matches the condition:
// instead of returning multiple values, it returns only the first occurrence
console.log(newData);        // → 5
  • What happens: find stops at the first match, even if many match.
  • Output: 5.
  • ⚠ Need all matches? Use filter.
example: array of objects, returns the first match
// example: array of objects, returns the first match
const fruits = [
  { name: 'Apple', quantity: 10 }, { name: 'Banana', quantity: 5 },
  { name: 'Orange', quantity: 8 }, { name: 'Mango', quantity: 15 },
  { name: 'Pineapple', quantity: 3 }, { name: 'Grapes', quantity: 12 },
  { name: 'Strawberry', quantity: 6 }, { name: 'Blueberry', quantity: 20 },
  { name: 'Peach', quantity: 7 }, { name: 'Cherry', quantity: 25 }
];
const fData = fruits.find(({ name }) => {
  return name === 'Orange';
});
console.log(fData);          // → { name: 'Orange', quantity: 8 }
  • What happens: find an object by a property (destructured in the callback).
  • Output: { name: 'Orange', quantity: 8 }.
  • ✅ Look up a record by id/name.
Find the first prime number in the given array
function findPrimeNumber(number, index, arr) {
  // start checking from 2
  let start = 2;
  // loop through possible divisors from 2 up to the square root of the number
  while (start <= Math.sqrt(number)) {
    // if the number is divisible by 'start' (remainder 0), it's not prime
    if (number % start++ < 1) {
      return false;
    }
  }
  // if no divisors are found and the number is greater than 1, it's prime
  return number > 1;
}
const numbers = [4, 6, 8, 22, 29, 35];
const firstPrime = numbers.find(findPrimeNumber);
console.log(firstPrime);     // → 29
  • What happens: a prime test used as the find callback; 29 is the first prime.
  • Output: 29.
ex 5: find() on a sparse array
const arr = [0, 1, , , 5, 6];
// without a condition (no return), find returns undefined; it does NOT return the last element
let un = arr.find((ele, index) => {
  console.log(ele);          // → 0, 1, undefined, undefined, 5, 6   (holes ARE visited!)
  console.log(index);        // → 0 … 5
});
console.log(un);             // → undefined
// ✔ comment said "by default it returns the last element"; with no truthy return it returns undefined

const ne = arr.find((element, index) => {
  if (element === 0) {
    console.log('deleted element are ', arr[5]);   // → deleted element are 6
    delete arr[5];
  }
  return element;            // 0 is falsy → keep going; 1 is truthy → found
});
console.log(ne);             // → 1
  • What happens: find visits holes as undefined; returning the element itself means "find the first truthy item".
  • Output: 0 1 undefined undefined 5 6 …, undefined, deleted element are 6, 1.
Note:
  1. The .find() method stops searching the array as soon as it finds the first element that satisfies the given condition (i.e. the callback returns true).
  2. find() does NOT skip empty slots: it visits holes as undefined. ✔ "find() skips empty slots". find, findIndex, findLast and findLastIndex all visit holes (as undefined); forEach, map, filter, some, every and indexOf skip them (verified in Node: "Index: 1, Value: undefined" is printed).find रिकाम्या जागा वगळत नाही; तो त्यांना undefined समजून तपासतो. Node मध्ये "Index: 1, Value: undefined" print झाले, यावरून हे सिद्ध होते. forEach/map/filter/some/every मात्र holes वगळतात.
const sparse = [1, , , 4];
const found = sparse.find((value, index) => {
  console.log(`Index: ${index}, Value: ${value}`);
  return value === undefined;
});
// → Index: 0, Value: 1
// → Index: 1, Value: undefined   ← the hole is visited and MATCHES
console.log("Result:", found);   // → Result: undefined   (the matched "value" IS undefined)
  • What happens: the hole is visited and matches value === undefined, but the returned value is undefined too.
  • Output: Result: undefined.
  • ⚠ You can't tell "found undefined" from "not found"; use findIndex.

6. findIndex()

Your Notes (13_findIndex.js):
  1. Syntax: array.findIndex(callback(element[, index[, array]])[, thisArg])
    • callback: a function executed for each element of the array. It takes:
    • element: the current element.
    • index (optional): the index of the current element.
    • array (optional): the array being traversed.
    • thisArg (optional): the value to use as this when executing the callback.
  2. The findIndex() method of Array instances returns the index of the first element in the array that satisfies the provided testing function (i.e. the index of the first element that satisfies the condition in the callback). ✔ "TypeArray instances" → Array instances (TypedArrays also have it, but this is the Array method).हा Array चा method आहे; "TypeArray" हा शब्द इथे चुकीचा होता.
  3. If no element satisfies the testing function, -1 is returned.
  4. It returns the index of the first element in the array where the predicate is true, i.e. findIndex() returns the index of the first element that satisfies the given condition. It returns the index, not the element itself. If the condition is not satisfied, it returns -1.
Example 1
// without a condition, it returns -1
const longArray = [5, 12, 2584, 8, 130, 44, 3, 15, /* … */ 121393];
const index = longArray.findIndex((ele, index, array) => {
  console.log('element', ele);
  console.log('index', index);
  console.log(array);
});
console.log(index);          // → -1   (the callback returns nothing, so no element matches)
// ✔ comment said "return =1"
  • What happens: the callback returns nothing, so nothing matches.
  • Output: -1.
example 2
// example 2
// Condition: return elements greater than 8. Several elements are greater than 8,
// but it returns the index of 12, which is 1:
// the index of the FIRST element that satisfies the condition
const data = longArray.findIndex((element, index) => {
  return element > 8;
});
console.log("data", data);   // → data 1
  • What happens: findIndex returns the INDEX of the first match.
  • Output: data 1.
findIndex on a non-array (array-like) object
const arrayLike = {
  length: 3,
  "-1": 0.1,     // ignored: not a valid index
  0: 2,
  1: 7.3,
  2: 4
};
console.log(Array.prototype.findIndex.call(arrayLike, (x) => {
  return !Number.isInteger(x);   // first non-integer
}));                             // → 1   (7.3)
  • What happens: findIndex works on array-like objects via call; "-1" isn't an index.
  • Output: 1.

Differences between find() and findIndex()

  • find(): (1) the find method returns the first element of the array that satisfies the given test function (callback); (2) if no element satisfies the condition, it returns undefined.
  • findIndex(): (1) the findIndex() method returns the index of the first element in the array that satisfies the given condition; (2) if no element satisfies the condition, it returns -1.
Featurefind()findIndex()
DefinitionReturns the first element that satisfies the conditionReturns the index of the first element that satisfies the condition
Return typeElement (any type in the array)Number (index)
Return if not foundundefined-1
Callback parameters(element, index, array)(element, index, array)
Mutates array?❌ No❌ No
Common use caseGet the actual element valueGet the position/index of a matching element
Usage:
  1. Finding an element with a condition: findIndex is useful when you need the index of an element that meets a specific condition, rather than the element itself.
  2. Complex conditions: you can use complex conditions or check object properties.
Note:
  1. findIndex() stops searching once it finds the first element that satisfies the condition.
  2. If the array is empty, the method immediately returns -1.
  3. findIndex() does NOT skip empty slots; it visits them as undefined. ✔ "findIndex() skips empty slots". Your own example below prints all 4 indexes, including the holes.खालील example मध्ये index 1 आणि 2 (holes) सुद्धा print होतात, म्हणजे findIndex holes वगळत नाही.
const sparse = [1, , , 4];
const index4 = sparse.findIndex((value, idx) => {
  console.log(`Index: ${idx}, Value: ${value}`);
  return value === 4;
});
// → Index: 0, Value: 1
// → Index: 1, Value: undefined   ← hole visited
// → Index: 2, Value: undefined   ← hole visited
// → Index: 3, Value: 4
console.log("Result:", index4);  // → Result: 3
  • What happens: findIndex also visits holes.
  • Output: Result: 3.

7. findLast() & findLastIndex()

Your Notes (17_findLast.js):
  1. Syntax: findLast(callback(ele, index, array))
  2. The findLast() method in JavaScript returns the value of the last element in an array that satisfies the provided testing function.
  3. findLast() iterates an array in reverse order and returns the value of the first element (from the end) that satisfies the given condition or test function. ✔ "findLase" / "findindex() iterate in reverse" → findLast() (findIndex goes forward).उलट्या क्रमाने (शेवटून) शोधतो तो findLast() आहे; findIndex() पुढे (सुरुवातीपासून) शोधतो.
  4. If no element satisfies the condition, it returns undefined.
  5. Basically, it returns the first matching value when searching in reverse order, which is the last matching value in forward order.
Example 1
// Example 1
const array = [5, 12, 8, 130, 44];
const found = array.findLast(element => element > 10);
console.log(found);          // → 44   (checks 44 first, from the end)
  • What happens: findLast searches from the end and returns the item.
  • Output: 44.
Example 2
// Example 2
const users = [
  { name: 'Alice', active: false }, { name: 'Bob', active: true },
  { name: 'Charlie', active: false }, { name: 'David', active: true }
];
const lastActiveUser = users.findLast(user => user.active);
console.log(lastActiveUser); // → { name: 'David', active: true }
  • What happens: last active user.
  • Output: { name: 'David', active: true }.
  • ✅ Latest matching record without reversing.
Your Notes (14_findLastIndex.js):
  1. Syntax: findLastIndex(callback(element[, index[, array]])[, thisArg])
    • callbackFn: a function to test each element. It takes the following arguments:
    • element: the current element being processed.
    • index: the index of the current element.
    • array: the array findLastIndex was called upon.
    • thisArg (optional): the value to use as this when executing callbackFn.
  2. The findLastIndex() method returns the index of the last element in the array that satisfies a provided testing function.
  3. If no element satisfies the condition, it returns -1. It runs in reverse order and returns the index of the first element (from the end) that satisfies the given condition.
Example 1
// Example 1
const array2 = [5, 12, 8, 130, 44];
const index = array2.findLastIndex(element => element > 10);
// returns 4: the INDEX of 44, the last element greater than 10 (it iterates from the end)
console.log(index);          // → 4
// ✔ comment said "here return 44 as last index"; 44 is the VALUE, the return value is the index 4
  • What happens: findLastIndex returns the index of the last match.
  • Output: 4.
Example 2
// Example 2
const array11 = [5, 12, 8, 130, 44];
const index1 = array11.findLastIndex(element => element > 200);
console.log(index1);         // → -1
  • What happens: no match.
  • Output: -1.
Example 3
// Example 3
const arraylikeObj = {
  length: 3,
  0: 2,
  1: 7.3,
  2: 4,
  3: 3            // ignored, because length is 3
};
const num = Array.prototype.findLastIndex.call(arraylikeObj, (ele) => {
  return Number.isInteger(ele);
});
console.log(num);            // → 2   (4 is the last integer within length 3)
  • What happens: only indexes below length count.
  • Output: 2.
Use case:
  1. This method is useful when you want to locate the last occurrence of an element that satisfies a condition.
  2. If the array is empty, the method immediately returns -1.
  3. findLastIndex() also does NOT skip empty slots (it visits them as undefined). ✔ "findLastIndex() also skips empty slots". Your example below prints indexes 2 and 1 (holes).खालील example मध्ये holes (index 2, 1) सुद्धा print होतात, म्हणजे ते वगळले जात नाहीत.

✔ the "Sparse arrays" row said "Skips empty slots" for all three.तिघेही holes ला undefined समजून तपासतात, वगळत नाहीत. 
const sparse = [1, , , 4];
const lastIndex = sparse.findLastIndex((value, idx) => {
  console.log(`Index: ${idx}, Value: ${value}`);
  return value < 4;
});
// → Index: 3, Value: 4
// → Index: 2, Value: undefined   ← hole visited
// → Index: 1, Value: undefined   ← hole visited
// → Index: 0, Value: 1
console.log("Result:", lastIndex);   // → Result: 0
  • What happens: findLastIndex visits holes too.
  • Output: Result: 0.
find = पहिली जुळणारी value, findIndex = पहिल्या जुळणाऱ्याचा index, findLast = शेवटची जुळणारी value, findLastIndex = शेवटच्या जुळणाऱ्याचा index. सापडले नाही तर value वाल्यांना undefined आणि index वाल्यांना -1 मिळते. चौघेही holes ला undefined समजून तपासतात.

8. some()

Your Notes (22_some.js):
  1. Syntax: array.some(callback(element, index, array), thisArg)
    • callback: the function to test each element.
    • element: the current element being processed.
    • index (optional): the index of the current element.
    • array (optional): the array some() was called upon.
    • thisArg (optional): the value to use as this when executing the callback.
  2. The some() method tests whether at least one element in the array passes the test implemented by the provided function. It returns true if the callback returns a truthy value for any element; otherwise it returns false.
  3. true if at least one element passes the test; false if none of the elements pass the test.
  4. It is not a mutating method (it does not modify the original array).
  5. It is an iterative method: it calls a provided callback function once for each element in an array.
NOTE:
  1. The some() method stops iterating as soon as it finds an element that satisfies the condition.
  2. It doesn't check the remaining elements once the condition is met.
// check whether any even number is present in the array
const newarr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7];
const even = (element) => {
  return element % 2 === 0;
};
console.log(newarr.some(even));      // → true   (stops at 2)

// testing an array of objects
const users = [
  { name: "Alice", age: 22 },
  { name: "Bob", age: 17 },
  { name: "Charlie", age: 35 },
];
const hasAdult = users.some((user) => user.age >= 18);
console.log(hasAdult);               // → true   (Alice and Charlie are adults)

// checking for a specific value
const array = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"];
const containsBanana = array.some((fruit) => fruit === "banana");
console.log(containsBanana);         // → true   ('banana' is in the array)
  • What happens: some returns true as soon as ONE item passes.
  • Output: true, true, true.
  • ✅ Fast "is there any…?" check (stops early).
some() on a sparse array (holes are SKIPPED)
console.log([1, , 2].some((x) => {
  return x === undefined;
}));                                 // → false  (the hole is never checked)

console.log([1, , 1].some((ele) => {
  return ele !== 1;
}));                                 // → false

console.log([1, undefined, 1].some((x) => {
  return x === undefined;
}));                                 // → true   (a REAL undefined is checked)
  • What happens: some skips holes; a real undefined is checked.
  • Output: false, false, true.

9. every()

Your Notes (31_every.js):
  1. Syntax: array.every(callback(element, index, array), thisArg);
  2. The every() method in JavaScript is an array method used to test whether all elements in an array pass the specified test (the provided callback function).
  3. If all elements pass the test, it returns true; otherwise it returns false.
  4. The every() method tests whether all elements in an array pass the provided function.
  5. It returns a boolean value, true or false.
  6. every() is an iterative method.
  7. every() is a non-mutating method.
  8. every() does not modify the original array.
  9. It returns true if the predicate function returns true for every array element, and false otherwise.
Note:
  1. For an empty array, every() never runs the callback and returns true (vacuous truth). (some() on an empty array returns false.) ✔ "does not execute the callback for empty arrays". True, but the important part is the RESULT: [].every(...) → true.रिकाम्या array वर every() callback चालवत नाही आणि थेट true देतो (कोणीच नापास झाले नाही). some() मात्र false देतो. हा interview मध्ये विचारला जाणारा trap आहे.
  2. It stops executing and returns false as soon as it encounters an element that does not satisfy the condition.
Example
// Example
const isAbove40 = (currentValue) => {
  return currentValue > 40;
};
const b = [100, 340, 56, 400, 290, 45];
const value = b.every(isAbove40);
// returns true only if ALL values satisfy the condition; if even one doesn't, it returns false
console.log(value);          // → true
// ✔ renamed isBelow → isAbove40 (the function checks "> 40", i.e. ABOVE)
  • What happens: every returns true only if ALL items pass.
  • Output: true.
Example 2: check whether an array is a subset of another array
// Example 2: check whether an array is a subset of another array
const subset = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7];
const subset1 = [5, 6, 7];
const isSubset = (subset, subset1) => {
  return subset1.every((element) => {
    return subset.includes(element);
  });
};
// true, because every element of subset1 is present in subset
console.log(isSubset(subset, subset1));   // → true
  • What happens: subset check: every item of the small array is included in the big one.
  • Output: true.
Example 3
// Example 3
console.log([1, , 2].every((element) => {
  return element !== undefined;
}));                         // → true
  • What happens: every skips holes.
  • Output: true.
Example 4
// Example 4
console.log([2, , 2].every((ele) => {
  return ele === 2;
}));                         // → true
  • What happens: hole skipped, both 2s pass.
  • Output: true.
Sparse arrays 
// A sparse array is an array with "holes" (missing indices). every() skips holes
// (indices that are not initialized or have been deleted).
const sparseArray = [1, , 3];    // the second element is a "hole"
const result = sparseArray.every(num => num !== undefined);
console.log(result);             // → true
// every() skips the hole and does not call the callback for it.

console.log([].every(x => x > 100), [].some(x => x > 100));   // → true false
  • What happens: holes are skipped; an empty array gives every → true and some → false (vacuous truth).
  • Output: true, true false.
  • ⚠ Classic trick question.
When to use: use every() when you want to confirm that all elements in an array meet a condition and you need a simple true/false answer without modifying the original array.
some = "किमान एक पास?" (एक सापडला की थांबतो), every = "सगळे पास?" (एक नापास झाला की थांबतो). दोघेही holes वगळतात. रिकाम्या array वर some → false आणि every → true.

10. NaN & Holes: How Each Method Behaves

MethodFinds NaN?Empty slots (holes)Comparison
indexOf / lastIndexOf❌ NoSkipped=== (strict)
includes✅ YesTreated as undefinedSameValueZero
find / findIndex / findLast / findLastIndex✅ with Number.isNaNVisited as undefinedYour callback

11. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. includes() vs indexOf()?
  • includes returns a boolean and uses SameValueZero (finds NaN, treats holes as undefined). indexOf returns the position and uses === (can't find NaN, skips holes).
Q2. find() vs filter()?
  • find returns the FIRST matching element (or undefined) and stops early; filter returns an ARRAY of all matches (possibly empty) and always scans everything.
Q3. find() vs findIndex() vs findLast()?
  • find → value, findIndex → index (or -1), findLast/findLastIndex → same but searching from the end (ES2023).
Q4. What do [].some(fn) and [].every(fn) return?
  • some → false (no element passed), every → true (vacuous truth: no element failed).
Q5. Why does [{id: 1}].includes({id: 1}) return false?
  • Objects are compared by reference; the literal creates a NEW object. Use some(o => o.id === 1) instead.
Q6. How do you find all indexes of a value?
  • Loop with indexOf(value, lastIndex + 1) until it returns -1, or use arr.reduce((acc, v, i) => (v === x && acc.push(i), acc), []).
Output-based questions
console.log([1, 2, 3].indexOf("2"));           // → -1   (strict: "2" !== 2)
console.log([NaN].indexOf(NaN), [NaN].includes(NaN));   // → -1 true
console.log([1, 2, 3, 2].lastIndexOf(2));       // → 3
console.log([5, 12, 8].find(x => x > 100));    // → undefined
console.log([5, 12, 8].findIndex(x => x > 100));// → -1
console.log([].some(Boolean), [].every(Boolean));        // → false true
console.log([{ id: 1 }].includes({ id: 1 }));   // → false (different object reference)
  • What happens: seven search output questions: strict match, NaN, last index, find/findIndex misses, empty some/every, object references.
  • Output: -1, -1 true, 3, undefined, -1, false true, false.
NeedUse
Is it there? (simple value)includes()
Where is it? (first / last)indexOf() / lastIndexOf()
Get the object that matchesfind() / findLast()
Index of the object that matchesfindIndex() / findLastIndex()
Any / all pass?some() / every()
All matching itemsfilter() (Chapter 45)
थोडक्यात: साध्या value साठी includes/indexOf, condition साठी find-family, आणि हो/नाही साठी some/every. NaN शोधायला includes किंवा findIndex(Number.isNaN) वापरा. objects ची तुलना reference ने होते, म्हणून includes({…}) false देते.
