1. Object

Your Notes (objects.js):
  1. Objects are a fundamental part of JS; they provide a way to group related data and functions together.
  2. Non-primitive (reference) data type: objects are compared by reference.
  3. Def: a JS object is a collection of key-value pairs where each key is a string (or a Symbol) and the value can be any data type, including other objects. ✔ added Symbol; a number key is converted to a string ("1").key फक्त string नाही तर Symbol सुद्धा असू शकतो. number key आपोआप string बनतो.
  4. Objects can have properties and methods, which makes them versatile for many use cases.
  5. An object is a collection of properties, and a property is an association between a key and a value. A property value can be a function, in which case the property is called a method.
  6. In addition to the objects predefined in the browser, you can also define your own objects.
Definition: An object is an unordered-by-intent collection of properties (key → value). Keys are strings or Symbols; values can be anything, including functions (methods). Objects are reference types: variables hold a reference, copying copies the reference, and === compares references.
Object म्हणजे key-value जोड्यांचा संग्रह. key (नाव) string किंवा Symbol असते, आणि value काहीही असू शकते (number, string, array, function, दुसरा object). value function असेल तर त्याला method म्हणतात. object reference type आहे.

2. Object Literal & Accessing Values

Your Notes: Object literal
  1. An object literal is simply a key: value pair data structure.
  2. Storing variables and functions together in one container: we refer to this as an object.
To access a value from an object:
  1. using dot (.) notation
  2. using [] bracket notation

3. Notes: Enumerable vs Iterable

Your Notes:
  1. JS (plain) objects are not iterable. ✔ "not iterative" → not ITERABLE (for…of doesn't work on them)."iterative" नाही, "iterable" हा शब्द: साध्या object वर for...of चालत नाही.
  2. JS objects don't have a length property.
  3. JavaScript object properties are enumerable, so we can use the for…in loop to iterate over the keys of the enumerable properties. (Enumerable properties are the properties of an object that can be listed or iterated over with a loop or methods like Object.keys(). for…in iterates over the enumerable properties of an object.)
  4. The loop retrieves the keys (property names) of the object one at a time.
  5. When you compare 2 objects, their addresses (references) are compared, not their values (contents).
What is enumerable?
  1. Enumerable means the properties of an object can be listed (looped over) with a loop like for...in.
    1. It applies to object properties (keys).
    2. Check it with propertyIsEnumerable, Object.keys() or for...in.
What is iterable?
  1. Iterable means the entire object can be looped over with a for...of loop. It must have a Symbol.iterator method.
    1. It applies to objects like arrays, strings, sets and maps.
    2. Regular objects are not iterable unless you define Symbol.iterator.
Difference between iterable and enumerable
FeatureEnumerableIterable
What it applies toObject properties (keys)The whole object (like arrays, strings)
How to loopfor...in, Object.keys()for...of, spread [...]
Method requirementNo special method neededMust have [Symbol.iterator]()
Example typesPlain objects {}Arrays, strings, sets, maps
Enumerable = object च्या properties for...in किंवा Object.keys() ने मोजता (list) येतात. Iterable = संपूर्ण object for...of ने loop करता येतो (Symbol.iterator लागतो). साधा object enumerable आहे पण iterable नाही; array दोन्ही आहे.

4. Pass by Value vs Pass by Reference

Your Notes: 1. Pass by value
  1. Applies to: primitive types (number, string, boolean, undefined, null, symbol, bigint).
  2. Behavior: a copy of the value is passed to the function.
  3. Changes do not affect the original variable.
2. Pass by reference
  1. Applies to: non-primitive types (objects, arrays, functions).
  2. Behavior: a reference (memory address) is passed.
  3. Changes to the object's CONTENTS affect the original object (reassigning the parameter does not; see call by sharing, Chapter 2). ✔ "changes affect the original variable". Only mutations of the shared object are visible; assigning a new object to the parameter is not.object च्या आतील बदल original मध्ये दिसतात, पण parameter ला नवीन object दिल्यास original बदलत नाही (call by sharing).
AspectPass by ValuePass by Reference
Affects original?NoYes (mutations)
TypePrimitivesObjects, arrays, functions
What is passed?A copy of the valueA reference to the original
Pass by value (primitive)
// Pass by value: a copy of the primitive value is created and passed to the function (or assigned to a variable).
// Changes made to the copy do not affect the original value.
let a = 10;
function passByValue(a) {
  return (a = 20);
}
console.log("modified value", passByValue(a));   // → modified value 20
console.log("original value:", a);               // → original value: 10
  • What happens: the function gets its own copy of 10; changing it doesn't touch the outer a.
  • Output: modified value 20, original value: 10.
Assigning an object copies the reference
// Pass by reference: the reference to the memory location is passed (or assigned).
// Changes made to the object through this reference affect the original object.
const obj = {
  id: 1,
  name: "vishal",
  address: { city: "pune" },
};
console.log("obj", obj);
let object = obj;   // NOT a copy: a second reference to the SAME object
console.log(object);
object.address.country = "india";
console.log(object);
// we added a new property through "object", and it was also added to the original object
console.log(obj.address.country);      // → "india"
console.log(object.address.country);   // → "india"
// the country property shows up in both, because there is only ONE object
// ✔ comment said "create copy of the object with its references"; assignment copies only the reference
  • What happens: object = obj does NOT copy; both names point to one object, so adding country through one is visible through the other.
  • Output: india, india.
  • ⚠ Use spread/structuredClone when you need an independent copy.
let object = obj; ने object ची copy बनत नाही, फक्त त्याच object चा दुसरा reference (पत्ता) बनतो. म्हणून एकातून केलेला बदल दुसऱ्यातही दिसतो.

5. Copying Objects

Your Notes: to avoid this situation (to make an object behave like pass by value), create a copy of the object in one of these ways:
  1. Object.assign(target, ...sources) ✔ "Object.assign(targetArray, sourceArray)" → target and source OBJECTS.Object.assign ला arrays नाही, तर target object आणि source objects लागतात.
  2. using the spread operator
Object.assign(target, source…)
  1. Used to copy the properties from one or more source objects to a target object.
  2. A great way to copy or merge objects in JS.
  3. It returns the target object.
  4. If you use Object.assign() to merge objects and two sources have the same key, the later source's value wins: it overrides the earlier one.
Copy with Object.assign
const newObj = Object.assign({}, obj);
console.log("newObj", newObj);
console.log("before name", newObj.name);                  // → vishal
console.log("update the name", (newObj.name = "akshu"));  // → akshu
console.log("after updating name", newObj.name);          // → akshu
console.log("original object ", obj.name);                // → vishal   (top level copied ✅)
  • What happens: Object.assign({}, obj) copies the top-level properties into a new object; changing newObj.name doesn't change obj.
  • Output: vishal, akshu, akshu, vishal.
Copy with spread
// spread operator: 1. creates a copy of the object
const newOne = { ...obj };
console.log("newOne", newOne);
console.log("before..", newOne.name);                     // → vishal
newOne.name = "akshu sawant";
console.log("after updating", newOne.name);               // → akshu sawant
  • What happens: { ...obj } does the same shallow copy, with shorter syntax.
  • Output: vishal, akshu sawant.
  • ✅ Most common way to copy/update objects (e.g. React state).
Extra Details: both are SHALLOW copies 
const copy = Object.assign({}, obj);
copy.address.city = "X";
console.log(obj.address.city);   // → "X"   (the nested address object is SHARED)
const deep = structuredClone(obj);   // a deep copy: nested objects copied too
  • What happens: both copies are SHALLOW: the nested address object is shared, so changing it through the copy changes the original. structuredClone copies every level.
  • Output: X.
  • ⚠ Shallow-copy bugs are very common with nested data.
Object.assign({}, obj) आणि {...obj} दोन्ही shallow copy करतात: वरच्या level च्या properties नवीन होतात, पण आतले (nested) objects अजूनही shared असतात. पूर्ण स्वतंत्र copy साठी structuredClone() वापरा.

6. How to Compare Objects

Your Notes:
  1. Objects are compared by reference (i.e. two objects are equal only if they refer to the same object, the same memory location).
  2. Independent objects are not equal even if they look the same.
let obj12 = { name: "vishal", education: "BE" };
let obj123 = { name: "vishal", education: "BE" };
let obj1234 = obj123;
console.log(obj12 === obj123);   // → false (two objects are compared by reference, not by value or content)
const isEqual = obj123 === obj1234 ? true : false;
console.log("isequal", isEqual);   // → isequal true
const isEqual1 = obj12 === obj123 ? true : false;
console.log("isequal1", isEqual1); // → isequal1 false
  • What happens: objects are compared by reference: two equal-looking objects are different; two variables pointing to the same object are equal.
  • Output: false, isequal true, isequal1 false.

7. Creating Objects & Accessing Properties

Your Notes: an object created using an object literal: 
let person = {
  name: "vishu",
  age: 29,
  "it-a-feature": false,
  greet() {
    console.log("name :" + this.name);
  },
  welcome: function () {
    console.log("welcome : " + this.name);
  },
};

// to access the functions and properties of an object
console.log(person.name);   // → vishu
person.greet();             // → name :vishu
person.welcome();           // → welcome : vishu
  • What happens: dot notation reads properties and calls methods; this inside a method is the object.
  • Output: vishu, name :vishu, welcome : vishu.
How do you access a property like 'it-a-feature'?
  1. It is not possible to access this property using . (dot) notation, so you have to use [] bracket notation. ✔ "donation" → notation."donation" नाही, "notation" (लिहिण्याची पद्धत).
console.log(person["it-a-feature"]);   // → false
// What happens if you try to access it with dot notation?
// console.log(person."it-a-feature");  // ❌ SyntaxError: Unexpected string

// you can also access properties using brackets []
console.log("access property using bracket notation : ", person["name"]);   // → vishu

// how to call a function: access it with [] and then call it with () parentheses
person["welcome"]();   // → welcome : vishu
person["greet"]();     // → name :vishu
// ✔ comment said "access using the square bracket () parenthesis" → access with [ ], CALL with ( )
  • What happens: keys with special characters must use bracket notation with a string; methods can be read with [ ] and called with ( ).
  • Output: false, vishu, welcome : vishu, name :vishu.

8. An Object as a Value Inside an Object

Your Notes: i.e. one object containing another object: 
let bioData = {
  fullName: {
    firstName: "vishal",
    lastName: "shinde",
  },
  age: 45,
  getData() {
    console.log(`full-name ${this.fullName.firstName} ${this.fullName.lastName}`);
  },
};
bioData.getData();   // → full-name vishal shinde
console.log("get object data using dot notation :", bioData.fullName.firstName);   // → vishal
// you can also access it this way:
console.log("used another way", bioData.fullName["firstName"]);                   // → vishal
  • What happens: nested properties are reached step by step (dot or bracket).
  • Output: full-name vishal shinde, vishal, vishal.

9. How to Add and Modify the Properties of an Object

Your Notes: 
let name = "username";
let age = "userNameAge";
let myObj = {
  [name]: "vishal",       // computed key → "username"
  [age]: 39,              // computed key → "userNameAge"
  address: { city: "pune", country: "ind" },
  getData() {
    console.log(this.username, this.userNameAge);
  },
  getInfo: function () {
    console.log("welCome " + this.username + " from " + this.address.city);
  },
};
console.log("myObj", myObj);

// add/update properties using . (dot) notation
myObj.address.city = "mumbai";
myObj.address.zip = 412401;
myObj["getData"]();   // → vishal 39
myObj.getInfo();      // → welCome vishal from mumbai
// add new data
myObj.job = "SED1";
console.log(myObj);

// you can also add data using bracket notation
myObj.address["locality"] = "wadGaon sahani";
console.log(myObj);

// you can also add or update a function
myObj.display = function () {
  return `${this.job} ${this.username}`;
};
console.log(myObj.display());   // → SED1 vishal
myObj.getInfo();                // → welCome vishal from mumbai   (before updating the function)

myObj.getInfo = function () {
  return "thanks for updating";
};
// after updating, getInfo() looks like this:
console.log(myObj.getInfo());   // → thanks for updating
  • What happens: computed keys [name] use the variable's value; properties and methods can be added or replaced at any time with dot or bracket notation.
  • Output: vishal 39, welCome vishal from mumbai, SED1 vishal, thanks for updating.
  • ✅ Objects are dynamic; handy for building data step by step.
If you define an object this way, you can't use dot notation; you need square bracket notation: 
let my = "name";
const data = {
  "first-name": "vishal",   // a key like first-name must be written as a string, otherwise → SyntaxError
  lastName: "shinde",
  [my]: "vishu",
};
console.log(data);           // → { 'first-name': 'vishal', lastName: 'shinde', name: 'vishu' }
// accessing this property with dot notation is a SyntaxError:
// console.log(data."first-name");   // ❌ SyntaxError: Unexpected string
console.log(data["first-name"]);     // → vishal
console.log(data.lastName);          // → shinde
// ✔ the comments said "references error"; a hyphenated key without quotes (and data."x") is a SYNTAX error
  • What happens: "first-name" needs quotes as a key and bracket access; [my] is computed.
  • Output: { 'first-name': 'vishal', lastName: 'shinde', name: 'vishu' }, vishal, shinde.
Note: inside square bracket notation you can write a variable or an expression. 
console.log("fullName", data["last" + "Name"]);   // → shinde   (an expression gives "lastName")
// you can also access a property through a variable with bracket notation:
console.log(data[my]);                            // → vishu
console.log("new data", (data.age = 28));         // → new data 28   (add data with dot notation)
console.log(data);
// to add a key that isn't a valid identifier, use bracket notation:
console.log((data["last-date"] = 45));            // → 45
console.log(data);
  • What happens: bracket notation accepts any expression or variable; it can also add new keys.
  • Output: shinde, vishu, new data 28, 45.
  • ✅ Use bracket notation when the key comes from a variable.
dot notation (obj.key) फक्त valid नाव असलेल्या keys साठी चालते. "first-name" सारख्या (- किंवा space असलेल्या) keys, variable मधील key किंवा expression साठी bracket notation (obj["key"], obj[var]) वापरा. [name]: value ही computed key आहे, म्हणजे variable ची value key बनते.

10. Object.values(), Object.keys(), Object.entries()

Your Notes: these Object methods get the values, keys and entries of an object:
  1. Object.values() (ES2017)
  2. Object.keys() (ES5)
  3. Object.entries() (ES2017)
✔ "ES8 having … values, keys, entries". values/entries came in ES8 (ES2017), but Object.keys is older (ES5).Object.values आणि Object.entries ES8 (2017) मध्ये आले, पण Object.keys आधीपासून (ES5) आहे.

Object.values()

  1. This method returns an array containing all of the object's own property values, i.e.

Object.values() is a built-in JavaScript method that returns an array of the values of an object's own enumerable properties. 
// how to work with nested objects and arrays
const person1 = {
  id: 1,
  name: "Alice",
  age: 30,
  subjects: ["Math", "Science"],
  address: { street: "123 Main St", city: "Springfield", state: "IL" },
  isActive: true,
};
// normal objects and nested objects need different approaches
let value = Object.values(person1);
console.log(value);   // → [1, 'Alice', 30, ['Math', 'Science'], { street: … }, true]

// to work with nested objects and arrays, use this approach:
Object.values(person1).forEach((val) => {
  if (typeof val === "object" && val !== null) {
    Object.values(val).forEach((ele) => {
      console.log(ele);          // → Math, Science, 123 Main St, Springfield, IL
    });
  } else {
    console.log("val", val);     // → val 1, val Alice, val 30, val true
  }
});
// (note: forEach returns undefined, so storing its result, as in "let val = …forEach(…)", gives undefined)
  • What happens: Object.values gives an array of the values; for nested ones, check typeof === "object" and loop again.
  • Output: the values, then the nested items and the plain values.

Object.keys()

  1. The Object.keys() method returns an array containing all of the object's own property names (i.e. it returns the keys of the object), i.e.

Object.keys() is a built-in method that returns an array of keys (property names) from an object's own enumerable properties. 
// returns an array containing all the property names of an object
let keys = Object.keys(person1);
console.log(keys);   // → ['id', 'name', 'age', 'subjects', 'address', 'isActive']

// for nested objects, work this way:
Object.keys(person1).forEach((keys) => {
  let value = person1[keys];
  if (typeof value === "object" && value !== null) {
    Object.keys(value).forEach((key) => {
      console.log(key);          // → 0, 1 (array indexes), street, city, state
    });
  } else {
    console.log(keys);           // → id, name, age, isActive
  }
});
  • What happens: Object.keys gives the property names; nested keys need a second loop (array indexes appear as 0, 1).
  • Output: the key list, then the inner keys.

Object.entries()

  1. The Object.entries() method returns an array containing all of the object's data.
  2. Object.entries() returns each property (key and value) in a separate array.
  3. Object.entries() takes an object and returns an array of arrays, where each inner array contains two elements: the key and the value.
  4. Object.entries() returns an array of [key, value] pairs from an object's own enumerable properties.
// first, get the top-level data
// let entries = Object.entries(person1);
// console.log(entries);

// print each [key, value] array
Object.entries(person1).forEach((ele) => {
  console.log(ele);                     // → ['id', 1], ['name', 'Alice'], …
});

// you can also get each key and value separately
Object.entries(person1).forEach(([key, value]) => {
  console.log([key, value]);
  console.log(key, value);
});

// and you can go one level deeper into nested values
Object.entries(person1).forEach(([key, value]) => {
  if (typeof value === "object" && value !== null) {
    Object.entries(value).forEach(([keys, values]) => {
      console.log(keys, values);        // → 0 Math, 1 Science, street 123 Main St, …
    });
  } else {
    console.log(key, value);            // → id 1, name Alice, age 30, isActive true
  }
});
  • What happens: Object.entries gives [key, value] pairs, which can be destructured and walked one level deeper.
  • Output: the pairs and nested pairs.
Note: if you work with nested objects and want every nested property or value, you need to pass the (actual) nested value as the argument to Object.keys() or Object.entries() to get its contents, as in the examples above (shown again in your notes in two commented-out forms). For unlimited depth, use recursion.
Object.keys() = keys चा array, Object.values() = values चा array, Object.entries() = [key, value] जोड्यांचा array. हे फक्त object च्या स्वतःच्या (own) enumerable properties देतात. nested object साठी आतल्या value वर पुन्हा हेच methods वापरा (किंवा recursion).

11. Object.fromEntries()

Your Notes: ✔ the heading said "# object.entries():", but this section is about Object.fromEntries() (ES2019).heading मध्ये object.entries() लिहिले होते, पण हा भाग Object.fromEntries() बद्दल आहे.
  1. Object.fromEntries() is the reverse of Object.entries(): it takes an array of key-value pairs and converts it back into an object.
  2. Object.fromEntries(iterable)
  3. This static method transforms a list of key-value pairs (arrays) into an object.
  4. Object.fromEntries() expects an iterable of key-value pairs, such as an array of arrays where each inner array contains two elements: [key, value].
  5. So the Object.entries() method converts an object into an array of arrays; if you want to convert that array of arrays back into an object, use Object.fromEntries().
  6. Object.fromEntries() is a static method in JavaScript that transforms a list of key-value pairs (like an array of arrays, or a Map) into a plain JavaScript object.
Use cases:
  • convert a Map to an object
  • convert an array of [key, value] pairs to an object
  • transform, filter or rename keys dynamically with Object.entries() + map() + Object.fromEntries().
Example 1
// convert a Map to an object
const map = new Map([["foo", "bar"], ["baz", 42]]);
console.log(Object.fromEntries(map));   // → { foo: 'bar', baz: 42 }
  • What happens: Object.fromEntries turns a Map (or list of pairs) into an object.
  • Output: { foo: 'bar', baz: 42 }.
Array of pairs → object
// 2. convert an array to an object
// With Object.fromEntries, you can convert from an array to an object:
const arr = [["0", "a"], ["1", "b"], ["2", "c"]];
const data1 = Object.fromEntries(arr);
console.log(data1);                     // → { 0: "a", 1: "b", 2: "c" }
  • What happens: each [key, value] pair becomes a property.
  • Output: { 0: 'a', 1: 'b', 2: 'c' }.
Round trip: entries then fromEntries
// object → entries → object (round trip)
let arrayObject = Object.entries(person1);
console.log("array object", arrayObject);
let objectOfArray = Object.fromEntries(arrayObject);
console.log(objectOfArray);             // → the same shape as person1
  • What happens: entries → array of pairs; fromEntries → back to an object.
  • Output: the same shape as person1.
Extra Details: transform an object with entries → map → fromEntries 
const prices = { apple: 10, mango: 20 };
const doubled = Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(prices).map(([k, v]) => [k, v * 2]));
console.log(doubled);   // → { apple: 20, mango: 40 }
  • What happens: entries → map over pairs → fromEntries: transform every value of an object.
  • Output: { apple: 20, mango: 40 }.
  • ✅ Standard pattern for "map over an object".

12. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. Dot notation vs bracket notation?
  • Dot works only for valid identifier keys known when writing the code. Bracket works for any string (spaces, hyphens, numbers), variables and expressions: obj[key], obj["first-name"].
Q2. How do you copy an object? Shallow vs deep?
  • Shallow: {...obj}, Object.assign({}, obj): nested objects stay shared. Deep: structuredClone(obj) (or JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)), which loses functions, undefined, Dates, etc.).
Q3. Why is {a: 1} === {a: 1} false? How do you compare objects?
  • === compares references, and these are two different objects. Compare the keys/values yourself (shallow or recursive) or use a library deep-equal; JSON.stringify comparison fails when the key order differs.
Q4. Enumerable vs iterable?
  • Enumerable is a per-property flag (for…in / Object.keys list it). Iterable is an object with [Symbol.iterator] (for…of / spread work). Plain objects are enumerable but not iterable.
Q5. In what order are object keys listed?
  • Integer-like keys first, in ascending order, then string keys in insertion order (then Symbols): {b: 1, 2: 'x', a: 2, 1: 'y'} → keys ["1", "2", "b", "a"].
Q6. Output-based questions
const p = { a: 1 }; const q = p; q.a = 2;
console.log(p.a);                             // → 2
const r = { ...p }; r.a = 3;
console.log(p.a);                             // → 2
console.log({ a: 1 } == { a: 1 });            // → false
const k = "x"; console.log({ [k + 1]: 5 });   // → { x1: 5 }
console.log(Object.keys({ b: 1, 2: 0, a: 1, 1: 0 }));   // → ['1', '2', 'b', 'a']
  • What happens: five output questions: shared reference, spread copy, object equality, computed key, key order.
  • Output: 2, 2, false, { x1: 5 }, ['1', '2', 'b', 'a'].
ConceptSummary
ObjectKey → value properties; keys are strings/Symbols; a reference type
AccessDot for simple names; bracket for any string, variable or expression
Assign vs copyb = a shares; {...a} / Object.assign are shallow; structuredClone is deep
Compare=== compares references
keys / values / entries / fromEntriesObject ⇄ arrays of keys, values and [key, value] pairs
थोडक्यात: object = key-value. b = a ने copy होत नाही. {...a} shallow copy देते. === reference तपासतो. keys/values/entries ने object चे arrays मिळतात, आणि fromEntries ने array पुन्हा object बनतो.

1. How to Delete a Property from an Object

Your Notes: 
const user = { firstName: "vishal", lastName: "shinde", age: 33 };
// delete one property
console.log(user);               // → { firstName: 'vishal', lastName: 'shinde', age: 33 }
console.log(delete user.age);    // → true   (delete returns true on success)
console.log(user);               // → { firstName: 'vishal', lastName: 'shinde' }
  • What happens: delete removes a property and returns true.
  • Output: the object, true, the object without age.
  • ⚠ Setting a property to undefined keeps the key; delete removes it.
Extra: to "remove" a key without mutating, use rest destructuring: const { age, ...rest } = user;

2. Q. What are the Object.seal() and Object.freeze() Methods in JS?

Your Notes:
  1. These 2 methods are used to control how an object can be modified.
  2. Object.seal() and Object.freeze() are two methods in JS that let you control the mutability (the ability to modify) of an object.
  3. They are used to restrict changes to the structure or values of an object, but they have different levels of restriction.
  4. Both Object.seal() and Object.freeze() work only shallowly. They do not affect nested objects by default.

1. Object.seal()

  1. Object.seal() prevents adding or deleting properties, but allows modifying existing values.
  2. Object.seal() does not work on nested objects; it only affects the top-level properties (it is shallow).
  • No new properties can be added.
  • No properties can be removed.
  • Existing properties can be updated (if they are writable).
"use strict";   // (without strict mode, the forbidden changes are silently IGNORED)
const person2 = { name: "John", age: 30 };
Object.seal(person2);
person2.age = 31;          // ✅ OK, you can modify existing properties
person2.gender = "male";   // ❌ TypeError: Cannot add property gender, object is not extensible
delete person2.name;       // ❌ TypeError: Cannot delete property 'name' of #<Object>
// ✔ your code sealed person2 but then changed person1 (a different, NOT sealed object), so all
//    three lines "worked" and the seal never showed (verified in Node)
  • What happens: seal blocks adding and deleting, but existing values can change; in strict mode the forbidden actions throw.
  • Output: age changes; adding/deleting → TypeError.
  • ✅ Fix the shape of an object.
तुमच्या code मध्ये person2 ला seal केले, पण बदल person1 वर केले. person1 sealed नसल्यामुळे सगळे बदल झाले आणि seal चा परिणाम दिसलाच नाही. sealed person2 वर प्रयत्न केल्यावर (strict mode मध्ये) TypeError येतो.

2. Object.freeze(obj)

  1. Prevents adding, deleting or modifying any property. The object becomes completely read-only (shallow freeze).
  2. Additionally, it makes all existing properties immutable, meaning their values cannot be changed.
  3. But note: freeze() makes only the top level of your object immutable. If your object has nested objects, they are not frozen (unless you freeze them too).
  • No new properties can be added.
  • No properties can be removed.
  • No properties can be modified (even if they were writable).
const car = { make: "Toyota", model: "Camry" };
Object.freeze(car);
car.model = "Corolla";   // ❌ TypeError in strict mode (silently ignored otherwise): can't modify property values
car.year = 2020;         // ❌ adding new properties is not allowed
delete car.make;         // ❌ deleting properties is not allowed
console.log(Object.isSealed(person2), Object.isFrozen(car));   // → true true
  • What happens: freeze blocks changing, adding and deleting.
  • Output: true true.
  • ✅ Protect constants/config.
  • ⚠ Shallow only.
Conclusion
  • Object.seal() allows modifying existing property values, but prevents adding or deleting properties.
  • Object.seal(): prevents property addition and deletion, but allows value changes.
  • Object.freeze(): prevents property addition, deletion and modification (making the object immutable, at the top level).
  • Object.freeze() disallows all changes: no adding, no deleting and no modifying of properties.
Figure 113: Normal vs sealed vs frozen object.
seal = नवीन property जोडता येत नाही आणि delete करता येत नाही, पण असलेली value बदलता येते. freeze = काहीच बदलता येत नाही. दोन्ही shallow आहेत (nested objects बदलू शकतात), आणि strict mode नसल्यास चुकीचे बदल शांतपणे दुर्लक्षित होतात.

3. The Relational Operator (in)

Your Notes:
  1. The relational in operator is used to check whether a given property exists in an object, i.e. whether a property exists in an object (either as an own property or an inherited one).
  2. It returns true if the specified property is in the object; otherwise it returns false.
  3. The in operator checks both own properties (properties directly present on the object) and inherited properties (properties in the object's prototype chain).
  4. The in operator checks whether a key/index exists in an object or array, not values.
const person11 = {
  id: 1, name: "Alice", age: 30,
  subjects: ["Math", "Science"],
  address: { street: "123 Main St", city: "Springfield", state: "IL" },
  isActive: true,
};
console.log("present or not : ", "state" in person11.address);   // → true
console.log("...", "subjects" in person11);                      // → true
// to check whether a VALUE is present in an array, use:
console.log(person11.subjects.includes("Math"));                 // → true
console.log("isActive" in person11);                             // → true

// in also checks whether a property is present in the prototype chain
console.log("toString" in person11);   // → true (it is present in the prototype chain)
  • What happens: the in operator checks if a property exists, including inherited ones (toString); includes checks VALUES in an array.
  • Output: true, true, true, true, true.

4. hasOwnProperty()

Your Notes:
  1. This method checks whether an object has a specific property as its OWN property (not inherited from the prototype chain).
  2. hasOwnProperty() only checks whether the property exists as an own (direct) property of the object, not on its prototype.
  3. object.hasOwnProperty(property). property: a string or symbol with the name of the property to test. Returns true if the object itself contains the property, otherwise false.
console.log("hasOwnProperty", person.hasOwnProperty("toString"));   // → false
// false, because hasOwnProperty() only checks own (direct) properties, not the prototype
console.log(person.hasOwnProperty("name"));                         // → true
  • What happens: hasOwnProperty checks only the object's own properties.
  • Output: false, true.
hasOwnProperty() doesn't work when the object is created with Object.create(null). You are creating an object without a prototype, meaning it does not inherit from Object.prototype, so it does not have built-in methods like hasOwnProperty(), toString() and valueOf(). 
let stud = Object.create(null);
stud.name = "vishal";
stud.age = 88;
console.log(stud);                 // → [Object: null prototype] { name: 'vishal', age: 88 }
// When an object is created with Object.create(null), hasOwnProperty doesn't work.
// Check whether the object has the property "name":
// console.log(stud.hasOwnProperty('name'));   // ❌ TypeError: stud.hasOwnProperty is not a function
// To solve this issue, use:
console.log(Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(stud, "name"));   // → true ✅
console.log(Object.hasOwn(stud, "name"));                          // → true (ES2022, recommended)
// in operator: checks whether the property exists anywhere in the object, including its prototype chain.
  • What happens: Object.create(null) has no prototype, so it has no hasOwnProperty method; Object.hasOwn works on any object.
  • Output: the null-prototype object, true, true.
  • ✅ Prefer Object.hasOwn (ES2022).
in operator object आणि त्याची prototype chain दोन्ही तपासतो ("toString" in obj → true). hasOwnProperty फक्त object च्या स्वतःच्या properties तपासतो. Object.create(null) ने बनवलेल्या object ला prototype नसतो, म्हणून त्यावर Object.hasOwn(obj, key) वापरा.

5. Useful Object Methods in JavaScript

Your Notes:
  1. Object.keys(): returns an array containing the names of all enumerable own properties of the object.
  2. Object.values(): returns an array containing the values of all enumerable own properties of the object.
  3. Object.entries(): returns an array of [key, value] pairs for each enumerable own property of the object.
  4. obj.hasOwnProperty() / Object.hasOwn(): returns a boolean indicating whether the object has the specified property as its own property. ✔ "Object.hasOwnPopery()". hasOwnProperty is an INSTANCE method (obj.hasOwnProperty); the static version is Object.hasOwn().hasOwnProperty हा object वरचा (instance) method आहे: obj.hasOwnProperty(key). Object वरचा static method Object.hasOwn(obj, key) आहे.
  5. Object.seal(): allows modifying existing property values, but prevents adding or deleting properties.
  6. Object.freeze(): disallows all changes: no adding, no deleting, and no modifying of properties.
  7. Object.assign(target, ...sources): used to copy or merge objects (it creates a shallow copy).
  8. in (operator): checks whether a property exists in the object (it checks the object itself as well as the prototype chain).
  9. object.hasOwnProperty(): checks whether a property exists in the object (only on the object itself, not in the prototype chain).

6. Interview Programs

Your Notes (your code):
Write a function to dynamically add a property to a given object
let student = {
  name: "vishal",
  age: 28,
  grades: { math: 80, science: 85, history: 88 },
};
const addProperty = (student, property, value) => {
  let add = (student.grades[property] = value);
  console.log(add);            // → 98
};
addProperty(student, "cs", 98);
console.log(student);          // → { …, grades: { math: 80, science: 85, history: 88, cs: 98 } }
// ✔ was "let newProperty = addProperty(…); newProperty;". addProperty returns nothing (undefined),
//    and the line "newProperty;" did nothing, so both were removed
  • What happens: bracket notation with a variable adds a property dynamically.
  • Output: 98, the updated student.
Write a function that checks whether two objects are equal (shallow)
let objA = { name: "vishal", education: "BE", age: 28 };
let objB = { name: "akshu", education: "BE", age: 29 };
let objC = { name: "vishal", education: "BE", age: 28 };

function compareObject(obj1, obj2) {
  // get the keys of each object, to check whether the lengths are the same
  let key1 = Object.keys(obj1);
  let key2 = Object.keys(obj2);
  if (key1.length !== key2.length) return false;
  for (let key in obj1) {
    if (obj1[key] !== obj2[key]) {
      return false;
    }
  }
  return true;
}
let res = compareObject(objA, objB);
console.log(res);              // → false
  • What happens: shallow equality: same number of keys and every top-level value ===.
  • Output: false.
  • ⚠ Nested objects are compared by reference only; see the deep version.
How to work with deeply nested objects (deep compare)
function deepNestedObject(obj1, obj2) {
  if (
    typeof obj1 === "object" && obj1 !== null &&
    typeof obj2 === "object" && obj2 !== null
  ) {
    let key1 = Object.keys(obj1);
    let key2 = Object.keys(obj2);
    if (key1.length !== key2.length) return false;
    for (let key in obj1) {
      if (!deepNestedObject(obj1[key], obj2[key])) return false;
    }
    return true;
  } else {
    return obj1 === obj2;
  }
}
let res6 = deepNestedObject(objA, objC);
console.log("res6", res6);     // → res6 true
// ✔ the check was "typeof obj2 === 'object' && obj1 !== null" (obj1 twice). When obj2 was null,
//    Object.keys(null) crashed: deepNestedObject({a: {x: 1}}, {a: null}) → TypeError (verified in Node)
  • What happens: deep equality: recurse into nested objects; primitives are compared with ===.
  • Output: res6 true.
  • ⚠ Doesn't handle Dates, Maps or circular references.
दुसऱ्या object साठी चुकून obj1 !== null तपासले होते (obj1 दोनदा). त्यामुळे obj2 null असल्यास Object.keys(null) वर TypeError येत होता. obj2 !== null केल्यावर बरोबर चालते.
Write a function that transforms an array of objects into an object keyed by id
let inputArray = [
  { id: 1, name: "vishal" },
  { id: 2, name: "vishu" },
  { id: 3, name: "akshu" },
];
let newObj11 = {};
for (let key of inputArray) {
  console.log(key.id, key);
  newObj11[key.id] = key;
}
console.log(newObj11);
// → { '1': { id: 1, name: 'vishal' }, '2': { id: 2, name: 'vishu' }, '3': { id: 3, name: 'akshu' } }
// one-liner: Object.fromEntries(inputArray.map(o => [o.id, o]))
  • What happens: turn an array into an object keyed by id for fast lookups.
  • Output: { '1': {...}, '2': {...}, '3': {...} }.
  • ✅ obj[id] lookup is O(1) instead of searching the array.

7. What is the Difference between a Normal Object and a Map?

Your Notes:

Normal object {}

  1. A normal object is a collection of key-value pairs where keys are always strings or Symbols. If you use a non-string key (like a number or an object), it is converted into a string.
  2. Key order: integer-like keys ("1", "2") come first, in ascending numeric order; the other string keys follow in insertion order. This order is guaranteed by modern specs (ES2015+, fully ES2020); it just isn't pure insertion order. ✔ "no guarantee of order / not guaranteed in older environments". The order IS defined today: integer keys first (ascending), then strings in insertion order (verified in Node: ['1', '2', 'b', 'a']).आजच्या JS मध्ये object keys चा क्रम ठरलेला आहे: आधी integer keys (चढत्या क्रमाने), मग बाकीच्या keys insertion क्रमाने. फक्त तो पूर्णपणे insertion order नाही.
  3. Performance: not specifically optimized for frequent additions and deletions of key-value pairs. Performance can degrade with a large number of keys.
  4. Methods & properties: Object.keys(obj), Object.values(obj), Object.entries(obj); it uses generic utility methods, and you must check for inherited keys with .hasOwnProperty().
  5. Iteration: iterate with a for...in loop, Object.keys(), Object.values() or Object.entries().
  6. Prototype inheritance: inherits from Object.prototype, which includes methods like toString, hasOwnProperty, etc. This can cause issues if keys conflict with prototype properties.
  7. Serialization and parsing: easily serializable with JSON.stringify().
let ob = {};
ob[1] = "vishal";       // the key 1 is converted to the string "1"
console.log(ob);        // → { '1': 'vishal' }
for (let key in ob) {
  console.log(key, ob[key]);   // → 1 vishal   (key is the STRING "1")
}
// OR
Object.entries(ob).forEach(([key, value]) => console.log(key, value));
  • What happens: object keys are always strings: ob[1] stores the key "1".
  • Output: { '1': 'vishal' }, 1 vishal.

Map

  1. Map is a built-in object in JS that stores key-value pairs where a key can be of any type (string, number, object, function). Insertion order is preserved, and it provides fast lookups and better performance than a normal object for dynamic key-value storage.
  2. Keys are iterated in insertion order, which is always predictable (insertion order is preserved).
  3. Optimized for frequent additions and deletions of key-value pairs. It performs better in scenarios with frequent updates or large data sets.
  4. Methods and properties: built-in methods:
    • set(key, value): adds or updates a key-value pair.
    • get(key): retrieves the value associated with a key.
    • delete(key): removes a key-value pair.
    • has(key): checks whether a key exists.
    • clear(): removes all key-value pairs.
    • size: returns the number of key-value pairs.
  5. Iteration: iterate directly with for...of, map.keys(), map.values(), map.entries() or forEach().
  6. Prototype inheritance: a Map's ENTRIES never collide with inherited properties (keys live inside the Map, not as properties), so there is no risk of key conflicts with prototype properties. ✔ "Does not inherit from Object.prototype". A Map instance does inherit (Map.prototype → Object.prototype); what's true is that its stored keys can't clash with inherited names.Map object स्वतः Object.prototype पासून inherit करतो. पण त्यातील keys properties म्हणून साठवल्या जात नाहीत, म्हणून "toString" सारख्या inherited नावांशी त्यांचा संघर्ष होत नाही.
  7. Serialization and parsing: a Map cannot be serialized directly with JSON.stringify(); it requires conversion to an array or object first: const map = new Map([['key', 'value']]);
let map1 = new Map();
map1.set(1, "vishal");
console.log(map1.get(1));        // → 'vishal'   (the key is the NUMBER 1, not a string)
// ✔ comment said "Output: 'value'"
for (let [key, value] of map1) {
  console.log(key, value);       // → 1 vishal
}
// OR
map1.forEach((value, key) => console.log(key, value));   // → 1 vishal
const jsonString = JSON.stringify(Array.from(map1));
console.log(jsonString);         // → '[[1,"vishal"]]'
// ✔ comment said '[["key","value"]]'
  • What happens: a Map keeps the real key type (number 1); it is iterable; JSON needs it converted to an array first.
  • Output: vishal, 1 vishal, 1 vishal, '[[1,"vishal"]]'.
  • ✅ Use Map for non-string keys and frequent add/remove.
FeatureObjectMap
Key typesString / Symbol onlyAny type
Insertion orderInteger keys first, then insertion orderPure insertion order
PerformanceLess efficient for dynamic operationsOptimized for key operations
Built-in methodsLimited (Object.keys, etc.)Rich API (set, get, etc.)
IterationManual or utility-basedDirect with for...of
Prototype key clashesYes (can cause issues)No (cleaner)
JSON serializationDirectly worksNeeds conversion
SizeObject.keys(o).lengthmap.size
✅ Use Map when:
  • you need non-string keys
  • you care about insertion order
  • you need frequent additions/deletions
  • you need better performance.

✅ Use Object when:
  • you want simple key-value pairs with string keys
  • you need JSON support
  • you don't need insertion order or complex keys.

8. How to Convert a Map Object into a Normal Object

Your Notes: 1. Using Object.fromEntries(): Object.fromEntries() is a built-in method that transforms an iterable (like a Map) into an object. Each key-value pair in the Map becomes a key-value pair in the resulting object. 
const myMap = new Map([["a", 1], ["b", 2], ["c", 3]]);
const myObject = Object.fromEntries(myMap);
console.log(myObject);   // → { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }

// Note: you can't create a Map like this:
// const myMap1 = new Map({ name: 'vishal', age: 28 });   // ❌ TypeError: object is not iterable
  • What happens: Object.fromEntries converts a Map to an object; a plain object can't be passed to new Map.
  • Output: { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }.
2. Using forEach() with a loop: if you want to build the object manually, iterate through the Map with forEach() and assign the values to an object. 
const myObj1 = {};
myMap.forEach((value, key) => {   // Map's forEach callback receives (value, key), in THAT order
  myObj1[key] = value;
});
console.log("myObj", myObj1);    // → myObj { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }
// ✔ was "(key, value) =>" → the names were swapped, giving { '1': 'a', '2': 'b', '3': 'c' } (verified in Node)
  • What happens: Map.forEach gives (value, key), in that order.
  • Output: myObj { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }.
  • ⚠ Swapping the parameter names swaps keys and values.
Map च्या forEach ला callback मध्ये आधी value आणि मग key मिळते: (value, key). parameters (key, value) असे लिहिल्यामुळे नावे उलटी झाली आणि { '1': 'a' … } असा चुकीचा object बनला. 3. Using reduce(): you can also use reduce() to convert a Map to an object. 
console.log("myMap", myMap);                       // → Map(3) { 'a' => 1, 'b' => 2, 'c' => 3 }
console.log("spread map object like", [...myMap]); // → [['a', 1], ['b', 2], ['c', 3]]

// const ReduceData = [...myMap].reduce((acc, [key, value]) => {
//   acc[key] = value;
//   return acc;
// }, {});
// console.log('reduce data', ReduceData);

// this approach can also be used:
const ReduceData = myMap.entries().reduce((acc, [key, value]) => {
  acc[key] = value;
  return acc;
}, {});
console.log("reduce data", ReduceData);            // → reduce data { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }
// ⚠ iterator.reduce() is an Iterator Helper (ES2025): Node 22+ / modern browsers only.
//    [...myMap].reduce(…) (the commented version) works everywhere.
  • What happens: spread turns a Map into pairs; reduce builds an object (iterator.reduce is new in ES2025).
  • Output: the Map, the pairs, { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }.

9. How Many Ways Are There to Create an Object?

Your Notes:
1. using an object literal
// 1. using an object literal
// const car = { brand: "Toyota", year: 2022 };

// 2. using the Object constructor
const carNew = new Object();
carNew.brand = "Toyota";
  • What happens: object literal and new Object() both create a plain object.
  • Output: (no output).
3. using the Object.create() method
// 3. using the Object.create() method
// Object.create(proto) creates an object whose prototype is proto.
// Using Object.create(null) creates an object with no prototype, meaning it does not inherit from Object.prototype.
// let objectG = Object.create();   // ❌ TypeError: Object prototype may only be an Object or null: undefined
const objectG = Object.create(Object.prototype);   // ✅ (like {})
// ✔ Object.create() needs an argument (an object or null)
  • What happens: Object.create(proto) creates an object with the given prototype; it needs an argument.
  • Output: (no output).
4. constructor function
// 4. constructor function
function Car(brand, year) {
  this.brand = brand;
  this.year = year;
}
const car1 = new Car("Honda", 2020);
  • What happens: a constructor function called with new creates objects of a "type".
  • Output: (no output).
5. using an ES6 class
// 5. using an ES6 class
// class Car {
//   constructor(brand, year) {
//     this.brand = brand;
//     this.year = year;
//   }
// }
const car2 = new Car("Ford", 2023);
console.log('car', car2);   // → car Car { brand: 'Ford', year: 2023 }
  • What happens: creating an object with new (a class would work the same way).
  • Output: car Car { brand: 'Ford', year: 2023 }.

10. Output-Based Question

Your Notes: 
const shape = {
  radius: 20,
  diameter() {
    return this.radius * 2;
  },
  perimeter: () => 2 * Math.PI * this.radius,
};
console.log(shape.diameter());    // → 40
// ✔ was "console.log(shape.diameter()); 20" (a wrong value written as a stray statement); 20 * 2 = 40
// An arrow function doesn't have its own this binding, so it inherits this from the surrounding scope,
// where this.radius is undefined.
console.log(shape.perimeter());   // → NaN   (2 * π * undefined)
  • What happens: diameter is a normal method (this = shape); perimeter is an arrow, so this is not shape.
  • Output: 40, NaN.
  • ⚠ Don't write object methods as arrow functions.
diameter() हा normal method आहे, त्यामुळे this = shape आणि 20 * 2 = 40. ओळीच्या शेवटी लिहिलेला 20 हा चुकीचा आणि comment बाहेरचा होता. perimeter arrow function असल्यामुळे this बाहेरचा असतो, म्हणून radius undefined आणि उत्तर NaN.

11. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. Object.seal vs Object.freeze vs Object.preventExtensions?
  • preventExtensions: no new properties. seal: no add/delete, but values can change. freeze: no add/delete/modify. All three are shallow; use a recursive deepFreeze for nested objects.
Q2. in vs hasOwnProperty vs Object.hasOwn?
  • in checks own + inherited properties ("toString" in obj → true). hasOwnProperty checks only own properties, but fails on Object.create(null) objects. Object.hasOwn(obj, key) (ES2022) is the safe modern version.
Q3. When do you use a Map instead of an object?
  • When you need non-string keys (objects, numbers kept as numbers), frequent adds/deletes, an easy size, guaranteed insertion order, or no prototype key clashes. Use an object for fixed-shape records and JSON data.
Q4. Write a deep-equal function.
  • Return a === b for primitives; for two non-null objects, compare key counts and recurse on every key (handle arrays the same way). Remember to check BOTH values for null.
Q5. What does delete return? Can it remove a variable?
  • It returns true when the property is gone (or never existed), and false for non-configurable properties (TypeError in strict mode). It removes object properties, not variables declared with let/const/var.
Q6. Output-based questions
const o1 = Object.freeze({ a: { b: 1 } });
o1.a.b = 2;
console.log(o1.a.b);                       // → 2   (freeze is shallow)
console.log("length" in [1, 2]);           // → true
console.log({}.hasOwnProperty("toString"));// → false
const m = new Map([[{}, "x"]]);
console.log(m.get({}));                    // → undefined (a different object key)
console.log(typeof Object.create(null).toString);   // → "undefined"
  • What happens: five output questions: shallow freeze, in on arrays, hasOwnProperty vs inherited, Map object keys by reference, null-prototype objects.
  • Output: 2, true, false, undefined, "undefined".
ToolRemember
delete obj.kRemoves a property (returns true)
seal / freezeShallow; silent in sloppy mode, TypeError in strict mode
in / hasOwnInherited + own / own only
Object vs MapRecords & JSON / dynamic keys of any type
CreateLiteral, new Object, Object.create, constructor function, class
थोडक्यात: seal = add/delete बंद, freeze = सगळे बंद (दोन्ही shallow). in prototype सुद्धा तपासतो, Object.hasOwn फक्त स्वतःच्या properties. object keys string असतात, तर Map मध्ये कोणत्याही type ची key चालते. Map च्या forEach मध्ये (value, key) असा क्रम असतो.

Chapter 52: Object DestructuringBasic · nested · partial · dynamic keys
CHAPTER 52 INDEX
  1. Object Destructuring
  2. Nested Destructuring

1. Object Destructuring

Your Notes (objectDestructring.js):
  1. Def: object destructuring is a feature in JS used to extract (unpack) values from an object and then assign them to variables in a more concise and readable way.
  2. i.e. destructuring makes it possible to unpack properties from the object into distinct variables.
Example 1
const myBio = {
  name: "vishal",
  age: 30,
  degree: "BE",
};
  • What happens: the object used in the examples.
  • Output: (no output).
to get data the traditional way
// # to get data the traditional way
console.log(myBio.name);     // → vishal
console.log(myBio.degree);   // → BE
  • What happens: reading each property with dot notation.
  • Output: vishal, BE.
by using destructuring
// # by using destructuring
const { name, age, degree } = myBio;
console.log(name);     // → vishal
console.log(age);      // → 30
console.log(degree);   // → BE
  • What happens: { name, age, degree } = myBio creates three variables from the properties with the same names.
  • Output: vishal, 30, BE.
  • ✅ Shorter code, especially with many properties.
Definition: const { a, b: alias, c = default, ...rest } = obj; picks properties by NAME (order doesn't matter), can rename them, give defaults (used only when the value is undefined) and collect the rest.
Figure 114: Object destructuring unpacks properties into variables by name.
Destructuring म्हणजे object मधून properties काढून त्याच नावाच्या variables मध्ये एका ओळीत ठेवणे. जुळणी key च्या नावाने होते, क्रमाने नाही.

2. How to Destructure a Nested Object

Your Notes:
Example 1
const user = {
  username: "Vishal",
  address: {
    city: "Pune",
    location: { lat: 18.5204, lng: 73.8567 },
  },
  contact: {
    email: "vishal@example.com",
    phone: { home: "020-123456", mobile: "9876543210" },
  },
};

const {
  username,
  address: {
    city,
    location: { lat, lng },
  },
  contact: {
    phone: { mobile, home },
  },
} = user;
console.log(mobile);   // → 9876543210
console.log(home);     // → 020-123456
  • What happens: nested patterns pull values out of nested objects in one statement.
  • Output: 9876543210, 020-123456.
  • ⚠ Very deep patterns are hard to read; destructure in steps if needed.
you can also pick out just one particular nested object
// # you can also pick out just one particular nested object
const {
  contact: { phone },
} = user;
// You're destructuring contact, but not creating a variable named contact.
// You're only extracting phone from contact.
// So, contact is not defined in the current scope.
// console.log(contact);   // ❌ ReferenceError: contact is not defined
console.log(phone);        // → { home: '020-123456', mobile: '9876543210' }
  • What happens: only the innermost name becomes a variable; contact is just part of the path.
  • Output: the phone object (contact → ReferenceError).
nested destructuring मध्ये "address: { city }" लिहिल्यावर फक्त city हा variable बनतो, address नावाचा variable बनत नाही. दोन्ही हवे असल्यास: const { address, address: { city } } = user;

3. Dynamic Properties (Keys)

Your Notes: now we can add dynamic properties or keys (how to get dynamic data in an object).
How do you make an object key dynamic in a given object? To make a dynamic key in an object, define the key inside square brackets, as shown in the example below. In this example, the dynamic key is "Greet" (the value of name1) and its value is "how are you". ✔ the comment said the key is "vishal"; the key is the VALUE of name1, i.e. "Greet".key "vishal" नाही. [name1] मध्ये name1 ची value "Greet" key बनते. 
let name1 = "Greet";
let myData = {
  [name1]: "how are you",
  [20]: "this is my age",
};
console.log(myData);   // → { '20': 'this is my age', Greet: 'how are you' }
// integer-like key "20" is listed FIRST (key order rule, Chapter 51)
  • What happens: computed keys in an object literal; integer-like keys are listed first.
  • Output: { '20': 'this is my age', Greet: 'how are you' }.
Extra Details: rename, default, rest, dynamic destructuring 
const { name: fullName, city = "Pune", ...others } = { name: "vishal", age: 30, degree: "BE" };
console.log(fullName, city, others);   // → vishal Pune { age: 30, degree: 'BE' }
const k = "age";
const { [k]: myAge } = myBio;          // → myAge = 30
function show({ name, age = 18 } = {}) { return `${name} ${age}`; }   // destructuring in parameters
  • What happens: rename (name: fullName), default (city = "Pune"), rest (...others), computed key, and destructuring in parameters.
  • Output: vishal Pune { age: 30, degree: 'BE' }.
  • ✅ Function parameters: function f({ name, age = 18 } = {}).

4. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. Array destructuring vs object destructuring?
  • Arrays match by POSITION ([a, b] = arr); objects match by KEY NAME ({a, b} = obj), so order doesn't matter.
Q2. How do you rename and set defaults?
  • const { name: n = "guest" } = obj; The default applies only when the value is undefined (not null).
Q3. What happens when you destructure undefined or null?
  • TypeError: Cannot destructure property … of undefined. Protect it with a default: const { a } = obj ?? {}; or function f({ a } = {}).
Q4. How do you swap variables or remove a key immutably?
  • Swap: [a, b] = [b, a]. Remove a key: const { password, ...safeUser } = user;
Q5. Output-based questions
const { a = 5 } = { a: null };   console.log(a);     // → null
const { b = 5 } = {};            console.log(b);     // → 5
const { x: { y } } = { x: { y: 1 } }; // console.log(x) → ReferenceError
const { length } = "hello";      console.log(length); // → 5
  • What happens: defaults apply only to undefined, not null; nested patterns don't create the parent variable; primitives can be destructured too.
  • Output: null, 5, 5.
SyntaxMeaning
{ a }Take property a
{ a: b }Rename to b
{ a = 1 }Default if undefined
{ a: { c } }Nested (a is NOT created)
{ ...rest }Remaining own properties
{ [k]: v }Dynamic key
थोडक्यात: object destructuring नावाने जुळते, rename (a: b), default (a = 1), nested, rest आणि dynamic key [k] करता येतात. undefined/null वर destructuring केल्यास TypeError येतो.

Chapter 53: JSONJSON vs JS object · stringify / parse · replacer · what JSON drops
CHAPTER 53 INDEX
  1. What is JSON?
  2. JavaScript Object
  3. Object ⇄ JSON
  4. Differences between JSON and a JS Object
  5. JSON.stringify with a 2nd Argument
  6. JSON.stringify() vs JSON.parse()
  7. Interview Questions & Revision

1. JSON

Your Notes (Json.js):
  1. JavaScript Object Notation.
  2. JSON is a data interchange format derived from the JS object.
  3. A JSON string can easily be converted into a JS object, or a JS object into JSON. ✔ "object can easily converted into ja object": typo "ja" → JS."ja object" नाही, "JS object".
  4. JSON is a lightweight data interchange format.
  5. JSON is a string representation of data.
  6. JSON keys are written in double quotes, like "name" (single quotes do not work); values depend on the data type, but keys are always in double quotes.
  7. JSON is always in string format.
  8. JSON keys must be double-quoted strings, and values can be a string, boolean, number, array, null or another object (i.e. it supports only specific data types: strings, numbers, objects, arrays, booleans and null).
  9. JSON does not have methods; it is a data interchange format.
  10. Used primarily for data exchange over the network (APIs or server responses).
  11. Immutable in its raw form (a string); it needs to be parsed into an object for manipulation.
  12. It can be converted to a JS object using JSON.parse(json) and converted back into JSON using JSON.stringify(obj).
let person = {
  name: "vishal",
  age: 28,
  education: "BE",
};
console.log(person);
// used to convert into JSON
let json = JSON.stringify(person);
console.log(json);   // → {"name":"vishal","age":28,"education":"BE"}

// convert into a JS object (normal object)
let obj = JSON.parse(json);
console.log(obj);    // → { name: 'vishal', age: 28, education: 'BE' }
  • What happens: JSON.stringify turns an object into a JSON string; JSON.parse turns it back into an object.
  • Output: the JSON string and the object.
  • ✅ Send/store data as text (APIs, localStorage).
Definition: JSON is a text format for data: objects {}, arrays [], double-quoted strings, numbers, true/false and null. JSON.stringify converts JS → text, JSON.parse converts text → JS.
Figure 115: JSON.stringify and JSON.parse convert in opposite directions.
JSON म्हणजे data पाठवण्यासाठी (API, server) वापरला जाणारा string format. JS object → JSON साठी JSON.stringify(), आणि JSON → JS object साठी JSON.parse(). JSON मध्ये keys नेहमी double quotes मध्ये असतात आणि functions चालत नाहीत.

2. JavaScript Object

Your Notes:
  1. An object is a collection of key-value pairs in memory, used in JS code.
  2. An object in JavaScript is a collection of key-value pairs, where each key (also called a property) maps to a value.
  3. It's used to store and group related data and functionality (methods).
  4. JavaScript objects are actual objects (live data in memory).
  5. In JavaScript, object keys must be either strings, symbols, or numbers. ✔ numbers are allowed in the syntax, but they are stored as strings; the only real key types are string and Symbol (see point 9).number key लिहिता येतो, पण तो string म्हणून साठवला जातो. खरे key types फक्त string आणि Symbol आहेत.
  6. If you define a key as an identifier (e.g., keyName), JavaScript automatically treats it as a string.
  7. If you use a key with special characters (e.g., spaces or hyphens), the key must be enclosed in quotes (either single ' or double " quotes). ✔ removed "reserved words": reserved words like class, if and new are allowed as unquoted keys (obj.class works).class, if सारखे reserved words quotes शिवाय key म्हणून चालतात. quotes फक्त space, hyphen इत्यादींसाठी लागतात.
const obj = {
  "first name": "John",       // Quotes are necessary because of the space
  "1stAge": 30,               // Quotes required for keys that start with a number
  "key-with-hyphen": "value",
};
  • What happens: object keys with spaces, hyphens or a leading digit need quotes.
  • Output: (no output).
  1. JavaScript object keys are always strings (or Symbols), and if they aren't valid identifiers (i.e., they contain special characters or spaces), they must be quoted (either single or double quotes).
  2. Numbers and symbols can be used as object keys, but numbers are automatically converted to strings when used as keys (Symbols stay Symbols). ✔ Symbols are NOT converted to strings; only numbers are.फक्त number key string बनते. Symbol key Symbol च राहते.
  3. Supports any valid JavaScript data type, including functions, undefined and regular expressions.
  4. JavaScript objects can have methods (functions) associated with them.
  5. Used in JavaScript programs for creating and manipulating data structures and logic.
  6. Mutable and directly editable in JavaScript.
  7. JavaScript objects can hold Date objects natively.
How do you convert an object into JSON?
// # How do you convert an object into JSON?
const jsonObj = JSON.stringify(person);
console.log(jsonObj);    // it returns JSON format → {"name":"vishal","age":28,"education":"BE"}

  • Output: {"name":"vishal","age":28,"education":"BE"}.
How do you convert JSON into a normal JavaScript object?

  • What happens: parse → object.
  • Output: { name: 'vishal', age: 28, education: 'BE' }.

3. Differences between JSON and a JS Object

Your Notes: 1. JS object:
  1. A native data structure used to store key-value pairs.
  2. A JS object can contain functions or methods, undefined and symbols.
  3. Example: 
    const person = {
  name: "Vishal",
  age: 25,
  greet() {
    console.log("Hello");
  },
};
    • What happens: a JS object can contain methods.
    • Output: (no output).
  4. In a JS object, quotes around keys are optional.
    1. Trailing commas ARE allowed. ✔ "trailing commas are not allowed". In JS objects { a: 1, } is valid (verified in Node). Only JSON forbids them.JS object मध्ये शेवटचा comma (trailing comma) चालतो. फक्त JSON मध्ये तो चालत नाही (SyntaxError).
    2. Functions and methods are allowed.
    3. Single quotes are allowed.
  5. JS objects are normally used to manipulate and store data.
  6. A JS object is the actual data we use in code for manipulation.
2. JSON:
  1. JSON is a data format used for storing and exchanging data (usually between client and server).
  2. JSON does not have methods or functions; it only supports data.
  3. Example: 
    {
  "name": "Vishal",
  "age": 25,
  "greet": function() { console.log("Hello"); }   // ❌ Not allowed
}
    • What happens: JSON is data only: functions aren't allowed.
    • Output: (invalid JSON).
  4. In JSON, quotes around keys are required (only double quotes).
    1. Trailing commas are not allowed.
    2. Functions and methods are not allowed.
    3. Single quotes are not allowed.
  5. Used to transmit data.
  6. JSON is a string representation of data.
FeatureJS ObjectJSON
TypeLive data structureText (string)
Key quotesOptional; ' or "Required; " only
Trailing commaAllowedSyntaxError
Functions / undefined / SymbolAllowedNot allowed
UseManipulation in codeTransfer / storage

4. What is the Output: JSON.stringify with a 2nd Argument

Your Notes:
Example 1
const setting = {
  username: "vishal",
  level: 19,

};
  • What happens: the object used in the next example.

what happens if you give a 2nd argument?

  • What happens: an array as the second argument keeps only those keys.

The 2nd argument is the replacer (an array of keys to keep, or a function (key, value) ⇒ newValue). The 3rd argument is the indentation: JSON.stringify(obj, null, 2).
Extra Details: what JSON.stringify drops or changes (verified) 
JSON.stringify({ a: undefined, f() {}, s: Symbol("x"), n: NaN, d: new Date(0) });
// → '{"n":null,"d":"1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z"}'
// undefined, functions, Symbols → removed;  NaN/Infinity → null;  Date → ISO string
JSON.parse("{'a':1}");    // ❌ SyntaxError (single quotes)
JSON.parse('{"a":1,}');   // ❌ SyntaxError (trailing comma)
// Map/Set → "{}" ; circular reference → TypeError ; BigInt → TypeError
  • What happens: JSON can't represent undefined, functions or Symbols (removed), NaN (→ null), Dates (→ string); JSON.parse is strict about quotes and commas; Map/Set become {}; circular refs and BigInt throw.
  • Output: '{"n":null,"d":"1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z"}', SyntaxErrors.
  • ⚠ Why JSON deep copy is lossy.

5. What is the Difference between JSON.stringify() and JSON.parse()?

Your Notes: 1. JSON.stringify(): converts a JavaScript object/array/value 👉 into a JSON string. Use it when you want to store or send data (like to a server or to localStorage).
2. JSON.parse(): converts a JSON string 👉 back into a JavaScript object/array. Use it when you receive data (like from a server or from localStorage). ✔ the heading "what is differences between json.stringify" was missing "and JSON.parse()".heading मध्ये "JSON.stringify आणि JSON.parse मधला फरक" असे असायला हवे.
FeatureJSON.stringify()JSON.parse()
InputJavaScript object/array/valueJSON string
OutputJSON stringJavaScript object/array/value
UsageSave or send dataRead or use data

6. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. What does JSON.stringify skip?
  • Properties whose value is undefined, a function or a Symbol (in arrays they become null). NaN/Infinity become null, Dates become ISO strings, and Map/Set become {}.
Q2. Is JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) a good deep clone?
  • Only for plain data. It loses functions, undefined, Dates (they become strings), Map/Set, and fails on circular references and BigInt. Prefer structuredClone.
Q3. What are the replacer and reviver?
  • The replacer (2nd argument of stringify) filters or changes values; the reviver (2nd argument of parse) changes values while parsing, e.g. turning date strings back into Date objects.
Q4. How do you store an object in localStorage?
  • localStorage stores only strings: localStorage.setItem("u", JSON.stringify(u)), then read it with JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("u")).
Q5. Output-based questions
console.log(JSON.stringify([undefined, () => 1]));   // → [null,null]
console.log(JSON.stringify({ a: [1, { b: 2 }] }));      // → {"a":[1,{"b":2}]}
console.log(typeof JSON.stringify(5));                  // → string
console.log(JSON.parse("true"), JSON.parse("null"));    // → true null
console.log(JSON.stringify("hi"));                      // → "hi" (with quotes)
  • What happens: five output questions: undefined/functions in arrays become null, nesting, stringify returns a string, parse primitives, strings get quotes.
  • Output: [null,null], {"a":[1,{"b":2}]}, string, true null, "hi".
PointRemember
JSONText format; double-quoted keys; no functions or trailing commas
stringify(v, replacer, space)JS → string
parse(text, reviver)string → JS
Droppedundefined, functions, Symbol; NaN → null
थोडक्यात: JSON हा string format आहे. stringify ने JS → JSON, parse ने JSON → JS. JSON मध्ये double quotes, functions नाहीत, trailing comma नाही. JS object मध्ये trailing comma चालतो.
