1. Map

Your Notes (mapObject.js):
  1. A Map object is a built-in JS object used to store key-value pairs (a collection of key-value pairs) where keys and values can be any data type.
  2. In a Map, insertion order is preserved (a Map maintains the order of its entries), which means that when you iterate over the Map, entries come in the order they were inserted.
Key characteristics of Map
  1. Keys in a Map are unique.
  2. Preserves order: entries are iterated in the order they are inserted.
  3. Any data type as key: unlike objects, where keys are strings or Symbols, a Map allows keys of any data type, including objects, functions and primitives.
  4. A Map has a size property that returns the number of key-value pairs present in the Map.
Map हा key-value साठवणारा built-in object आहे. यात key कोणत्याही type ची (object, function, number) असू शकते, insertion क्रम जपला जातो, आणि size ने किती entries आहेत ते लगेच कळते.

2. How to Create a Map

Your Notes:
Example 1
let map = new Map([["1", "data"]]);
console.log(map);                      // → Map(1) { '1' => 'data' }
  • What happens: new Map([[key, value]]) creates a Map from pairs.
  • Output: Map(1) { '1' => 'data' }.
  • ✅ Any value can be a key (objects, numbers), and order is kept.
1. set values in the map
// 1. set values in the map
map.set("name", "vishal");
map.set("age", 30);
console.log(map);                      // → Map(3) { '1' => 'data', 'name' => 'vishal', 'age' => 30 }
  • What happens: set adds or updates a key.
  • Output: Map(3) {...}.
  • ✅ set returns the map, so calls can be chained.
2. get a value from the map
// 2. get a value from the map
let data = map.get("age");
console.log(data, map.get("name"));    // → 30 vishal
  • What happens: get reads by key.
  • Output: 30 vishal.
3. the has() method checks whether a specific key exists in the map
// 3. the has() method checks whether a specific key exists in the map
console.log(map.has("name"));          // → true
if (!map.has("education")) {
  map.set("education", "BE");
}
console.log(map);                      // → Map(4) { …, 'education' => 'BE' }

// // 4. remove a key-value pair by its key
// console.log(map.delete('education'))   // → true
// console.log(map);

// // 5. remove everything from the map using the clear() method
// console.log('clear', map.clear())      // → clear undefined
// console.log(map);                      // → Map(0) {}
  • What happens: has checks if a key exists; add only if missing. delete and clear (commented) remove entries.
  • Output: true, Map(4) {...}.

3. Iterating over the Map

Your Notes: we can iterate over the map using:
  1. for…of loop
  2. forEach() method
  3. map.values() method
  4. map.keys() method
  5. map.entries() method
for of loop
// # for of loop
for (let [key, value] of map) {
  console.log(key, value);             // → 1 data, name vishal, age 30, education BE
}
  • What happens: a Map is iterable; for…of gives [key, value].
  • Output: 1 data, name vishal, age 30, education BE.
iterating using forEach()
// # iterating using forEach()
map.forEach((value, key) => {
  console.log(`${key}: ${value}`);     // → 1: data, name: vishal, …
});
  • What happens: Map.forEach gives (value, key).
  • Output: 1: data, name: vishal, …
In a Map object, the methods keys(), values() and entries() are used to interact with the map's keys, values and key-value pairs, respectively. Here's how each of them works:
1. map.keys(): returns a Map Iterator of the keys in insertion order.
// # 1. map.keys(): returns a Map Iterator of the keys in insertion order.
let key = map.keys();
for (let keys of key) {
  let value = map.get(keys);
  console.log("return both", value, keys);   // → return both data 1, …
}
// console.log(key);
// console.log(key.next().value);
// console.log(key.next().value);
// console.log(key.next().value);
  • What happens: keys() iterator, then get each value.
  • Output: return both data 1, …
2. map.values(): returns a Map Iterator of the values in insertion order.
// # 2. map.values(): returns a Map Iterator of the values in insertion order.
let values = map.values();
console.log(values);                   // → [Map Iterator] { 'data', 'vishal', 30, 'BE' }
for (let val of values) {
  console.log(val);                    // → data, vishal, 30, BE
}
// console.log(values.next().value);
// console.log(values.next().value);
// console.log(values.next().value);
  • What happens: values() iterator.
  • Output: data, vishal, 30, BE.
3. map.entries(): returns a Map Iterator of the [key, value] pairs in insertion order
// # 3. map.entries(): returns a Map Iterator of the [key, value] pairs in insertion order
const entries = map.entries();
console.log("entries", entries);
console.log(
  entries.forEach((ele) => {
    console.log("ele", ele);           // → ele ['1', 'data'], ele ['name', 'vishal'], …
  })
);                                     // → undefined   (forEach returns undefined)
// ⚠ iterator.forEach is an ES2025 Iterator Helper (Node 22+ / modern browsers)
// console.log(entries.next().value);
// console.log(entries.next().value);
// console.log(entries.next().value);
  • What happens: entries() iterator; iterator.forEach is a new ES2025 helper and returns undefined.
  • Output: the pairs, undefined.
Note: an iterator can be used only once; after a loop consumes it, next() gives { value: undefined, done: true }. 
// example:
const myMap = new Map([
  ["a", 1],
  ["b", 2],
  ["c", 3],
]);
// Using keys()
for (const key of myMap.keys()) {
  console.log(key);          // Output: 'a', 'b', 'c'
}
// Using values()
for (const value of myMap.values()) {
  console.log(value);        // Output: 1, 2, 3
}
// Using entries()
for (const [key, value] of myMap.entries()) {
  console.log(`${key}: ${value}`);   // Output: 'a: 1', 'b: 2', 'c: 3'
}
  • What happens: keys(), values(), entries() with for…of.
  • Output: a b c, 1 2 3, a: 1 b: 2 c: 3.

4. Summary of Map Methods

Your Notes:
  • set(key, value): adds or updates a key-value pair.
  • get(key): retrieves the value associated with the key.
  • has(key): checks whether the Map contains the specified key.
  • delete(key): removes a key-value pair.
  • clear(): clears all key-value pairs in the Map.
  • size: returns the number of key-value pairs.
  • forEach(callback): executes a callback for each key-value pair in the Map (callback receives value, key).
  • toString(): returns a string representation of the Map, which is just "[object Map]" (not the contents).
  • keys(): returns the keys of the given Map object (an iterator).
  • values(): returns the values of the given Map object (an iterator).
  • entries(): returns the key-value pairs of the Map object (an iterator).
✔ "key()" / "value()" → keys() / values() (the singular names don't exist); toString() gives "[object Map]" (verified in Node).key() आणि value() असे methods नाहीत, keys() आणि values() आहेत. Map चा toString() फक्त "[object Map]" देतो, data दाखवत नाही.

5. How to Convert a Map Object into a Normal Object

Your Notes: 1. Using Object.fromEntries(): Object.fromEntries() is a built-in method that transforms an iterable (like a Map) into an object. Each key-value pair in the Map becomes a key-value pair in the resulting object.
Example 1
const myObject = Object.fromEntries(myMap);
console.log(myObject);   // Output: { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }
  • What happens: Object.fromEntries turns a Map into an object.
  • Output: { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }.
  • ✅ Needed before JSON.stringify (a Map becomes {}).
note: we can't define a Map like this:
// # note: we can't define a Map like this:
const myMap1 = new Map({ name: "vishal", age: 28 });
// ❌ TypeError: object is not iterable (cannot read property Symbol(Symbol.iterator))
// ✔ this line is NOT commented out in your file, so the program STOPS here and none of the code
//    below runs (verified in Node). Comment it out, or use new Map(Object.entries({ name: "vishal", age: 28 })).
  • What happens: a plain object isn't iterable, so new Map(obj) throws and stops the file.
  • Output: TypeError.
  • ⚠ Use new Map(Object.entries(obj)).
ही ओळ comment केलेली नसल्यामुळे इथे TypeError येऊन पुढचा सगळा code (forEach, reduce, Array) चालतच नाही. ती comment करा, किंवा new Map(Object.entries(obj)) वापरा. 2. Using forEach() with a loop: if you want to create the object manually, iterate through the Map with the forEach() method and assign the values to an object. 
const myObj1 = {};
myMap.forEach((value, key) => {
  myObj1[key] = value;
});
console.log("myObj", myObj1);   // → myObj { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }
// ✔ was "(key, value) =>". Map's forEach passes (value, key), so it built { '1': 'a', '2': 'b', '3': 'c' }
  • What happens: build an object from a Map with forEach (value first, then key).
  • Output: myObj { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }.
Map.forEach मध्ये क्रम (value, key) आहे. (key, value) लिहिल्याने keys आणि values उलट झाल्या. 3. Using reduce(): you can also use reduce() to convert a Map to an object. 
console.log("myMap", myMap);                        // → Map(3) { 'a' => 1, 'b' => 2, 'c' => 3 }
console.log("spread map object like", [...myMap]);  // → [['a', 1], ['b', 2], ['c', 3]]
const ReduceData = [...myMap].reduce((acc, [key, value]) => {
  acc[key] = value;
  return acc;
}, {});
console.log("reduce data", ReduceData);             // → reduce data { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }
  • What happens: spread a Map into pairs, then reduce into an object.
  • Output: the Map, [['a',1],['b',2],['c',3]], { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }.

6. How to Convert a Map to an Array

Your Notes: you can convert a Map to an array using Array.from() or the spread operator (...).
1. Array.from()
// 1. Array.from()
const entriesArray = Array.from(map);
console.log(entriesArray);
// Output: [['1', 'data'], ['name', 'vishal'], ['age', 30], ['education', 'BE']]
  • What happens: Array.from(map) gives an array of [key, value] pairs.
  • Output: the 4 pairs.
2. Using the spread operator
// 2. Using the spread operator
const spreadArray = [...map];
console.log(spreadArray);
// Output: [['1', 'data'], ['name', 'vishal'], ['age', 30], ['education', 'BE']]
// ✔ the comments said [['name', 'Alice'], ['age', 30]], but this map holds '1', name: vishal, age: 30, education: BE
  • What happens: spread does the same.
  • Output: the 4 pairs.
output मध्ये 'Alice' लिहिले होते, पण या map मध्ये '1' → data, name → vishal, age → 30, education → BE आहेत.

7. What is the Difference between Map and Set?

Your Notes: ✔ heading "map() and set()": these are the Map and Set objects (constructors), not the array map() method.इथे array चा map() method नाही, तर Map आणि Set objects आहेत.

1. Map

  1. A Map is a collection of key-value pairs.
  2. Use a Map when you need to associate values with keys.
  3. It stores key-value pairs (each key is unique, but values may be duplicated).
  4. It also maintains insertion order.
  5. Keys can be any type: object, function, primitive.
Use cases:
  1. when you need to associate values with keys;
  2. storing configuration settings, metadata or other key-value data.
// defined
const map = new Map([
  ["key1", "value1"],
  ["key2", "value2"],
]);
  • What happens: Map defined from an array of pairs.
  • Output: (no output).
Methods: set(key, value): adds or updates a key-value pair · get(key): retrieves the value associated with a key · delete(key): removes a key-value pair · has(key): checks whether a key exists · clear(): removes all key-value pairs · size: returns the number of key-value pairs.
It iterates over key-value pairs, with a for…of loop, the forEach method, and map.keys(), map.values() and map.entries(): 
for (const [key, value] of map) {
  console.log(`${key}: ${value}`);
}
  • What happens: loop over its entries.
  • Output: key1: value1, key2: value2.

2. Set

  1. A collection of unique values, i.e. a Set is a collection of unique values (no duplicates).
  2. Used when you need to store distinct items without duplicates.
  3. It stores only values.
  4. Each value must be unique.
  5. Each entry in a Set is a unique value.
Stores only values, no keys · all values are unique · maintains insertion order.
Use cases: removing duplicates from an array; checking whether an item exists in a collection. 
// initialize:
const set = new Set([1, 2, 3, 4]);
// iterates over values:
for (const value of set) {
  console.log(value);
}
  • What happens: a Set stores unique values; for…of gives each value.
  • Output: 1 2 3 4.
Methods: add(value): adds a value to the Set · delete(value): removes a value · has(value): checks whether a value exists · clear(): removes all values · size: returns the number of values.
MethodDescription
for...ofLoop over values directly
forEach()Callback for each value
values()Returns an iterator over values
entries()Returns [value, value] pairs
[...set]Spread into an array for more operations
Figure 116: Map stores key → value pairs; Set stores unique values only.
Map = key → value जोड्या (key unique). Set = फक्त unique values (duplicate आपोआप दुर्लक्षित). दोन्ही insertion क्रम जपतात आणि दोन्हीत size, has, delete, clear आहेत.

8. Set Object

Your Notes (setObject.js):
  1. A Set object is used to store unique values.
  2. A Set object in JavaScript is a collection of unique values.
  3. Unlike arrays, Set objects do not allow duplicate values.
  4. The values can be of any data type, including primitive values or object references.
Key characteristics of Set:
  1. Unique values: each value must be unique; no duplicates are allowed.
  2. Order of insertion: elements are iterated in the order they were added.
  3. Any data type: values can be of any type, including objects and primitives.
Example 1
const set = new Set();
console.log(set);           // → Set(0) {}
  • What happens: an empty Set.
  • Output: Set(0) {}.
we can also initialize a set with an iterable (like an array)
// # we can also initialize a set with an iterable (like an array)
let set1 = new Set([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]);
console.log(set1);          // → Set(6) { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 }
  • What happens: a Set from an array.
  • Output: Set(6) {...}.
adding values: using the add() method
// # adding values: using the add() method
set.add("shinde");
set.add([10, 20]);
set.add({ name: "vishal" });
console.log(set);           // → Set(3) { 'shinde', [ 10, 20 ], { name: 'vishal' } }
  • What happens: add stores any value; objects/arrays are stored by reference.
  • Output: Set(3) { 'shinde', [10, 20], { name: 'vishal' } }.
checking a value using the has() method
// # checking a value using the has() method
// The has() method checks whether a value is present in the Set.
console.log(set.has({ name: "vishal" }));   // → false  (a NEW object, a different reference)
console.log(set.has(10));   // → false
console.log(set.has(30));   // → false
// ✔ comment said "set.has(10) → true". The set holds the ARRAY [10, 20], not the number 10 (verified in Node)
  • What happens: has compares by reference/value (SameValueZero): a new {} is a different object, and 10 isn't stored (only the array [10, 20] is).
  • Output: false, false, false.
  • ⚠ Keep a reference if you need to look up an object later.
set मध्ये 10 हा number नाही, [10, 20] हा array आहे, म्हणून has(10) false. तसेच { name: "vishal" } हा नवीन object (वेगळा reference) आहे, म्हणून त्यासाठीही false. object/array साठी तोच reference (variable) वापरावा लागतो.
remove a value
// # remove a value
// The delete() method removes a specific value.
let deleted = set.delete("shinde");
console.log("deleted", deleted);   // → deleted true
console.log(set.has("shinde"));    // Output: false
  • What happens: delete removes a value and returns true if it existed.
  • Output: deleted true, false.
clearing the set
// # clearing the set
// The clear() method removes all values from the Set.
set.clear();
console.log(set.size);             // Output: 0
  • What happens: clear removes everything.
  • Output: 0.

9. Iterating over a Set

Your Notes: you can iterate over the values of a Set using for...of or the forEach() method.
Example 1
const set2 = new Set(["apple", "banana", "cherry"]);
  • What happens: a Set of fruits.
  • Output: (no output).
using a for of loop
// # using a for of loop
for (const value of set2) {
  console.log(value);    // → apple, banana, cherry
}
  • What happens: for…of in insertion order.
  • Output: apple, banana, cherry.
forEach() method
// # forEach() method
set2.forEach((ele) => {
  console.log(ele);      // → apple, banana, cherry
});
  • What happens: forEach over a Set.
  • Output: apple, banana, cherry.

10. Convert a Set into an Array / Object

Your Notes:
how to convert a set into an array
// # how to convert a set into an array
let newArray = Array.from(set2);
console.log(newArray);   // → ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']
  • What happens: Array.from turns a Set into an array.
  • Output: ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry'].
the spread operator (...)
// # the spread operator (...)
// Using the spread operator
// const spreadArray = [...mySet];
// console.log(spreadArray);   // Output: ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']
// ✔ comment said [1, 2, 3]; mySet holds the fruit names

// # how to convert a set into an object
const mySet = new Set(["apple", "banana", "cherry"]);
const obj = {};
[...mySet].forEach((value, index) => {
  obj[index] = value;
});
console.log(obj);        // → { '0': 'apple', '1': 'banana', '2': 'cherry' }
  • What happens: spread to an array, then index → value into an object.
  • Output: { '0': 'apple', '1': 'banana', '2': 'cherry' }.
using the reduce method
// # using the reduce method
const reduceSet = [...mySet].reduce((acc, ele, index) => {
  acc[index] = ele;
  return acc;
}, {});
console.log(reduceSet);  // → { '0': 'apple', '1': 'banana', '2': 'cherry' }
  • What happens: same with reduce.
  • Output: { '0': 'apple', '1': 'banana', '2': 'cherry' }.

11. Set Iterators: values() and keys()

Your Notes: using the values() method (with an iterator you have to call the next() method to get each value). The values() method returns an iterator of all the values in the Set. 
const mySet2 = new Set(["apple", "banana", "cherry"]);
const iterator = mySet2.values();
console.log("iterator", iterator);       // → iterator [Set Iterator] { 'apple', 'banana', 'cherry' }
console.log(iterator.next().value);      // Output: 'apple'
console.log(iterator.next().value);      // Output: 'banana'
// ✔ comments said true / false; next().value gives the VALUE (verified in Node)
  • What happens: values() is an iterator; next().value reads one at a time.
  • Output: the iterator, apple, banana.
The keys() method is available, but it behaves the same as the values() method. This is because a Set only contains values (without keys), and both keys() and values() return an iterator over the values. 
const keysIterator = mySet.keys();
console.log("key", keysIterator);
console.log(keysIterator.next().value);  // Output: 'apple'
console.log(keysIterator.next().value);  // Output: 'banana'
console.log(keysIterator.next().value);  // Output: 'cherry'
// ✔ comments said 1, 2, 3; mySet holds apple, banana, cherry
  • What happens: for a Set, keys() is the same as values().
  • Output: apple, banana, cherry.
next().value ने पुढची value मिळते, true/false किंवा 1, 2, 3 नाही. mySet मध्ये apple, banana, cherry आहेत, म्हणून तेच क्रमाने मिळतात. Summary of Set methods:
  1. add(value): adds a new value to the Set.
  2. delete(value): removes a value from the Set.
  3. has(value): checks whether a value exists in the Set.
  4. clear(): removes all values from the Set.
  5. size: gets the number of elements in the Set.
  6. forEach(callback): executes a callback function for each value in the Set.
  7. values(): returns an iterator object of the values in the Set.
  8. keys(): returns an iterator object of keys in the Set (same as values() in a Set).
  9. entries(): returns an iterator object of [value, value] pairs.
  10. [Symbol.iterator](): allows iteration over the Set using a for...of loop.
Extra Details (verified in Node) 
console.log([...new Set([1, 2, 2, 3])]);   // → [1, 2, 3]   (remove duplicates: the #1 interview use)
const a = new Set([1, 2, 3]), b = new Set([2, 3, 4]);
console.log([...a.intersection(b)]);       // → [2, 3]   (ES2025 Set methods: union, difference, isSubsetOf…)
// WeakMap / WeakSet: keys must be objects, held weakly (garbage-collectable), not iterable
  • What happens: [...new Set(arr)] removes duplicates; ES2025 adds set operations like intersection.
  • Output: [1, 2, 3], [2, 3].
  • ✅ Fastest dedupe in one line.
  • ⚠ Set methods are new (Node 22+).

12. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. How do you remove duplicates from an array?
  • [...new Set(arr)] or Array.from(new Set(arr)). It works for primitives; objects are compared by reference.
Q2. Why does set.has({a: 1}) return false after set.add({a: 1})?
  • Set/Map use SameValueZero: objects match only by reference. Keep the reference in a variable and use that. (NaN equals NaN in a Set.)
Q3. Map vs WeakMap?
  • WeakMap keys must be objects and are held weakly (an entry disappears when the key object is garbage-collected); a WeakMap isn't iterable and has no size. Use it for private data or caches attached to objects.
Q4. How do you convert between Object, Map and Array?
  • Object → Map: new Map(Object.entries(o)). Map → Object: Object.fromEntries(m). Map → Array: [...m]. Set → Array: [...s].
Q5. Output-based questions
const s = new Set([1, "1", 1, NaN, NaN]);
console.log(s.size);                         // → 3
const m = new Map(); m.set("a", 1).set("a", 2);
console.log(m.size, m.get("a"));             // → 1 2
console.log(new Set("hello").size);          // → 4
const k = {}; m.set(k, "obj");
console.log(m.get(k), m.get({}));            // → obj undefined
new Map().forEach((v, k) => console.log(v, k));   // (order: value, key)
  • What happens: Set treats 1 and "1" as different and NaN as equal to NaN; set on the same Map key overwrites; a string spreads into characters; object keys match only by reference.
  • Output: 3, 1 2, 4, obj undefined.

1. Copying Objects

Your Notes (shallow-deep-copy/shallow-copy.js): if you want to copy something, there are 2 types of copying for objects or arrays:
  1. shallow copy;
  2. deep copy.

Both behave differently when it comes to nested structures like arrays or objects.
Definition: A shallow copy creates a new outer object/array but copies nested objects BY REFERENCE (shared). A deep copy recursively creates new copies of every nested object/array, so the copy shares nothing with the original. Plain assignment (b = a) is NEITHER: it copies only the reference.
Shallow copy म्हणजे बाहेरचा object नवीन, पण आतले (nested) objects जुनेच (shared). Deep copy म्हणजे आत-बाहेर सगळे नवीन, मूळ object शी काहीच संबंध नाही. b = a ही copy नाहीच, फक्त त्याच object चा दुसरा पत्ता (reference) आहे.
Figure 117: Assignment vs shallow copy vs deep copy: what is shared.

2. Shallow Copy

Definition:
  • A shallow copy copies only the top-level properties of an object or array;
  • the nested arrays' or objects' properties are not copied (only their references are).
  • A shallow copy creates a new object or array, but the nested structures (arrays or objects) still share references (i.e. they still refer to the original objects).
  • I.e. the top-level object gets a new reference, but the nested objects still refer to the original objects' references.
How to create a shallow copy of an object or array?
  1. Object: a shallow copy creates a new object; the top-level values are copied into the new object; if a property contains another object or array, only its reference is copied, so if you change a nested object or array in the copy, the original object is affected too.
  2. Array: a shallow copy creates a new array; the top-level items are copied into the new array; if an item is an object or another array, its reference is copied, not the actual object/array; therefore changing a nested object in the copied array will also affect the original array.
How to create a shallow copy?
  1. Object:
    1. Object.assign({}, obj): creates a new object and copies the properties from the original object (syntax: Object.assign(target, source)).
    2. Spread operator {...obj}: creates a new object and copies the properties.
  2. Array:
    1. slice(): creates a new array containing the elements of the original array.
    2. Spread operator [...arr]: creates a new array and copies the elements. (Also Array.from(arr), arr.concat().)

3. How Objects and Arrays Work: Reference vs Copy

Assignment shares the same object
let obj = {
  name: "vishal",
  age: 25,
  mobile: 9970710108,
};
// * assign obj to obj2, so obj2 references the same object in memory
let obj2 = obj;
console.log(obj2);
console.log(obj);
// so obj2 doesn't make a copy of obj: it refers to the same object in memory, so any change made through obj or obj2
// affects both (i.e. it doesn't create a copy, both point to the same object in memory: shared state)
let address = (obj2.address = "pune");
console.log(address);   // → pune
console.log(obj);       // → { name: 'vishal', age: 25, mobile: 9970710108, address: 'pune' }
console.log(obj2);      // → the same object
  • What happens: obj2 = obj copies only the reference; adding address through obj2 shows in obj.
  • Output: pune, both show address: 'pune'.
  • ⚠ Not a copy at all.
Shallow copies of an object
// Object.assign(target, ...sources)
let newObj = Object.assign({}, obj);
// creates a new object and copies all the properties of obj
console.log(newObj);
// ✔ the comment said "Object.assign(source, destination)"; the order is (TARGET, ...SOURCES)

// spread operator
let newObje1 = { ...obj };
console.log(newObje1);
  • What happens: Object.assign({}, obj) and { ...obj } create a new object with the same top-level properties.
  • Output: two copies of obj.
Shallow copies of an array
let arr = [10, 20, 30, 50, 62, 45, 21];
// using the slice() method
let newArr = arr.slice();
console.log(newArr);
// using the spread operator
let newArr1 = [...arr];
console.log(newArr1);
  • What happens: slice() and [...arr] create new arrays with the same items.
  • Output: two copies of arr.

4. Nested Data Is Shared (Object Example)

const person = {
  name: "vishal",
  age: 25,
  address: { city: "pune", locality: "mumbial", zip: 412401 },
};
const shallowCopay = Object.assign({}, person);
console.log(shallowCopay);
// doesn't affect the original object, because age is a top-level property of the object.
shallowCopay.age = 50;
console.log(shallowCopay);   // → age 50
console.log(person);         // → age 25
// if you change a nested object's properties, it affects the original too
// (because the nested object still references the original object in memory)
shallowCopay.address.city = "mumbail";
console.log(shallowCopay);   // → city: 'mumbail'
console.log(person);         // → city: 'mumbail' too
  • What happens: the shallow copy has its own top-level properties (age), but address is the SAME object in both.
  • Output: age 50 vs 25; city 'mumbail' in both.
  • ⚠ Classic shallow-copy bug with nested data.
Array example 
let sampleArr = [1, 2, 3, { a: 10 }, ["b", "c"]];
let sampleArr2 = sampleArr.slice();
console.log(sampleArr2);
// Here, if you modify a nested array/object property, it also affects the original array, because we created a
// shallow copy, and a shallow copy copies only the top-level items of an array or properties of an object.
let newA = (sampleArr2[3].a = 100);
console.log(newA);         // → 100
console.log(sampleArr);    // → [1, 2, 3, { a: 100 }, ['b', 'c']]
console.log(sampleArr2);   // → [1, 2, 3, { a: 100 }, ['b', 'c']]
// This only affects the original array, not the shallow copy (a top-level change).
sampleArr[2] = 6;
console.log(sampleArr);    // → [1, 2, 6, …]
console.log(sampleArr2);   // → [1, 2, 3, …]
  • What happens: slice() copies the top level: changing a nested object shows in both; changing a top-level slot of the original doesn't affect the copy.
  • Output: 100, both show { a: 100 }; [1, 2, 6, …] vs [1, 2, 3, …].

5. What Happens When You Use Object.assign() with an Array?

When Object.assign() is used with an array, it copies the array's enumerable properties, including its elements (indexes), into the target array. It copies the properties/elements of arr1 into personArr. personArr is the target, so personArr is modified. It doesn't replace the entire array; only the matching indexes are overwritten. Object.assign() modifies and returns the target object.

let personArr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
let arr1 = ["a", "b", "c"];
let arrL = Object.assign([], personArr);
console.log(arrL);     // → [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]   (a shallow copy)
let newAll = Object.assign(personArr, arr1);
console.log(newAll);   // → ['a', 'b', 'c', 4, 5]   (verified; newAll === personArr)
// ✔ the comment said "copies the properties of personArr into arr1"; it's the reverse: arr1's elements
//    are copied INTO personArr (the target), overwriting indexes 0–2 (it doesn't override the entire array)
  • What happens: Object.assign([], arr) copies an array; Object.assign(target, src) copies src's indexes INTO the target (overwriting 0–2).
  • Output: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], ['a', 'b', 'c', 4, 5].
  • ⚠ The first argument is changed; pass {} or [] to avoid mutating.

6. Shallow Copy with the Spread Operator & Summary

Example 1
let data = { name: "alice", age: 45, address: { city: "mh", zip: "124512" } };
let dataObj = { ...data };
console.log(dataObj);
// Modify a property of the copied object
dataObj.age = 90;
// it is modified only in the copy and doesn't affect the original, because it's a (shallow) copy
console.log(dataObj);   // → age 90
console.log(data);      // → age 45
// If you modify the nested object, it affects the original as well
dataObj.address.mobile = "9970710102";
console.log(dataObj);   // → address has mobile
console.log(data);      // → address has mobile too (verified)
  • What happens: spread: top-level change only in the copy, nested change in both.
  • Output: age 90 vs 45; mobile in both.
spread operator with an array
// # spread operator with an array
let arr11 = [1, 2, 3, { name: "alice" }];
// creating a shallow copy of arr11
let arr2 = [...arr11];
console.log(arr2);
arr2[3].name = "vishal";
console.log(arr11);   // → [1, 2, 3, { name: 'vishal' }]
console.log(arr2);    // → [1, 2, 3, { name: 'vishal' }]
// (in Node, the first console.log(arr2) also shows "vishal": DevTools/Node print the live object)
  • What happens: spreading an array copies the references to the objects inside it.
  • Output: both show { name: 'vishal' }.
Summary:
  1. The spread operator creates a shallow copy of both objects and arrays.
  2. For top-level properties or elements, the copies are independent, so modifying one won't affect the other.
  3. For nested objects or arrays, the reference to the same object is copied, meaning that changes to the nested data affect both the original and the copied structure.
When to use it? Use the spread operator for shallow copies of objects or arrays when you don't have nested structures. If you need a deep copy (i.e. copying nested objects/arrays), use a custom copy function or another method like JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) or structuredClone.

7. Deep Copy

Your Notes (deep-copy.js), definition:
  • A deep copy recursively copies all values and the nested structure, so it is entirely independent of the original.
  • Deep copy: both the top-level and the nested objects are copied, so no references are shared between the original and the copied array or object.
  • I.e. in a deep copy of an object or array, all the nested objects and properties are recursively copied.
  • I.e. the copied object or array doesn't share any references with the original, and changes made to the copy don't affect the original object.
  • Objects and arrays are deeply copied, meaning each nested object or array gets a new reference.
  • Deep copy means recursively copying all nested structures, so no references are shared between the original and the copy.
✔ spellings: "defincation" → definition, "origional" → original, "refrences" → references."defincation/origional/refrences" या spellings definition/original/references अशा आहेत. How to create a deep copy in JS?
  1. Deep copy of an object using serialization and deserialization: JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)); common for objects and arrays, but it can only handle JSON-safe values (no functions, undefined or non-serializable data).
  2. Using libraries: _.cloneDeep(obj) from Lodash handles more complex objects (with non-JSON-safe data).
  3. structuredClone(obj): a built-in JS method used to make deep copies of objects and arrays.

8. Deep Copy with JSON (Serialization & Deserialization)

JSON deep copy of an object
const person = {
  name: 'vishal', age: 29,
  address: { city: 'pune', locality: 'junnar', village: 'wadgaon sahani', zip: 412401 },
};
// * make a deep copy using serialization & deserialization (only works with JSON-safe values: no functions, undefined)
let deepCopy = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(person));
console.log(deepCopy);
person.name = 'akshu';
console.log(person);     // → name: 'akshu'
console.log(deepCopy);   // → name: 'vishal'
// * modify the nested object
deepCopy.address.village = 'sawargaion';
// it doesn't affect the original object
console.log(deepCopy);   // → village: 'sawargaion'
console.log(person);     // → village: 'wadgaon sahani'   (verified)
  • What happens: stringify then parse builds brand-new nested objects, so changes on either side don't affect the other.
  • Output: akshu vs vishal; village differs.
  • ✅ Simple deep copy for plain data.
JSON deep copy of an array
// @ deep copy of an array using serialization & deserialization.
let arr = [1, 2, 3, { a: 10 }, ['b', 'c']];
const arrDeepCopy = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(arr));
console.log(arrDeepCopy);
arr[3].a = 'vishal';
// Here it does NOT affect the copy, because the copied object is independent
console.log(arr);           // → { a: 'vishal' }
console.log(arrDeepCopy);   // → { a: 10 }
// ✔ the comment said "Here does affect to the copied object"; it does NOT (verified)
// * modifying the copy also doesn't affect the original array
console.log(arrDeepCopy[4].push('vishal'));   // → 3 (push returns the new length)
console.log(arrDeepCopy);                     // → […, ['b', 'c', 'vishal']]
  • What happens: same for arrays: nested objects/arrays are independent.
  • Output: { a: 'vishal' } vs { a: 10 }, 3, the copy with 'vishal' pushed.
What the JSON method breaks (verified in Node) 
JSON.parse(JSON.stringify({ u: undefined, d: new Date(0), n: NaN, s: new Set([1]), f() {} }));
// → { d: '1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z', n: null, s: {} }
//   undefined & functions dropped · Date → string · NaN/Infinity → null · Map/Set → {} · class instances lose their prototype
const c = {}; c.self = c; JSON.stringify(c);   // ❌ TypeError: Converting circular structure to JSON
  • What happens: JSON copy loses undefined and functions, turns Date into a string, NaN into null, Map/Set into {}, and throws on circular references.
  • Output: { d: '1970-…', n: null, s: {} }, TypeError.
  • ⚠ Use structuredClone for real data.

9. Deep Copy with structuredClone()

structuredClone with an array
let deepCopyObj = structuredClone(arr);   // works for both objects & arrays
console.log(deepCopyObj);

let arrg = [10, 20, 30, { name: 'vishal' }, function () { console.log('Hello'); }];
console.log(arrg);
// console.log(structuredClone(arrg))   // ❌ DataCloneError: … could not be cloned (verified)
// * arrg contains a function, and structuredClone doesn't support functions (or Symbols) in an array or object;
//   so to copy the array we need to exclude those functions & symbols first; only then can we deep copy it
const filterArr = arrg.filter((ele, index) => {
  return typeof ele !== 'function' && typeof ele !== 'symbol';
});
console.log(filterArr);                   // → [10, 20, 30, { name: 'vishal' }]
console.log(structuredClone(filterArr));
  • What happens: structuredClone deep-copies most values (Dates, Maps, Sets, cycles), but throws on functions; filter them out first.
  • Output: the copy, DataCloneError for arrg, the filtered copy.
  • ✅ Built-in, correct deep copy.
Removing functions from an object before cloning
// @ structuredClone() with an object
let newObj = {
  name: 'vishal', age: 25,
  address: { city: 'pune', location: 'junnar', zip: 412401 },
  function() { console.log('Hello word'); },
};
// since structuredClone() doesn't support functions and symbols, we can exclude them before cloning.
// console.log(structuredClone(newObj));
let filterObject = Object.fromEntries(
  Object.entries(newObj).filter(([]) => {
    return typeof value !== 'function';
  })
);
console.log(filterObject);   // → still contains "function" (verified)
console.log((newObj.address.zip = 520411));
console.log(newObj);
  • What happens: the filter callback uses ([]) and checks an undefined variable `value`, so nothing is removed.
  • Output: filterObject still has the function.
  • ⚠ Write .filter(([, value]) => typeof value !== 'function').
✔ (verified in Node) the filter callback destructures nothing (([])) and then checks value, which is undefined → typeof undefined !== "function" is always true, so NOTHING is filtered and the function stays. Fix: .filter(([, value]) => typeof value !== 'function') → { name, age, address }. filter मध्ये ([]) असे लिहिल्यामुळे value नावाचा variable मिळतच नाही, म्हणून function filter होत नाही. ([, value]) असे लिहा. structuredClone keeps: Date, Map, Set, RegExp, typed arrays, circular references (verified: Date stays a Date, Map.get works). It can't clone: functions, DOM nodes, Symbols as values; and class instances lose their prototype (they become plain objects).

10. Write a Deep Copy without Built-in Methods

Write code to make a deep copy of the given object (note: don't use built-in methods), i.e. recursively copy all nested objects and arrays (ensuring no references to the original object).

function makeDeepCopy(object) {
  // check the type: object, array, or not an object / null
  // if it's a primitive (string, number, boolean, null, undefined, symbol) or a function, return it directly
  if (typeof object !== 'object' || typeof object === null) {
    return object;
  }
  // determine whether the given input is an object or an array: an array → initialize with [], an object → {}
  let copiedValue = Array.isArray(object) ? [] : {};
  // get all the keys of the object (or the array indices)
  const keys = Object.keys(object);
  console.log(keys);
  // iterate through each key in the object, or index in the array
  for (let i = 0; i < keys.length; i++) {
    copiedValue[keys[i]] = makeDeepCopy(object[keys[i]]);
    // keys[i] represents the key (property name) of the original object.
    // object[keys[i]] gives the value associated with the key
    // makeDeepCopy(object[keys[i]]) ensures that if the value is another object or array, it is also deeply copied recursively.
  }
  return copiedValue;
}
const called = makeDeepCopy(newObj);
console.log(called);
const calledArray = makeDeepCopy(arr);
console.log(calledArray);
  • What happens: a recursive deep copy: primitives are returned, objects/arrays are rebuilt key by key.
  • Output: copies of newObj and arr.
  • ⚠ typeof x === null is never true (typeof null is "object"), so null crashes Object.keys; Dates and cycles aren't handled.
✔ (verified in Node) typeof object === null is never true (typeof null is "object"), so a null VALUE passes the check and Object.keys(null) throws: makeDeepCopy({ a: null }) → TypeError: Cannot convert undefined or null to object. Use object === null. typeof null हे "object" येते, त्यामुळे typeof object === null कधीच true होत नाही. null value आल्यास Object.keys(null) मुळे TypeError येतो. object === null असे थेट तपासा. 
// ✅ improved version (null, Date, circular references)
function deepCopy(value, seen = new WeakMap()) {
  if (value === null || typeof value !== "object") return value;
  if (value instanceof Date) return new Date(value);
  if (seen.has(value)) return seen.get(value);         // circular references
  const out = Array.isArray(value) ? [] : {};
  seen.set(value, out);
  for (const key of Object.keys(value)) out[key] = deepCopy(value[key], seen);
  return out;
}
  • What happens: improved version: handles null, Dates and circular references (WeakMap remembers already-copied objects).
  • Output: (function).
  • ✅ Shows how a robust deep copy works.
Explanation of the above code (deep copy without built-in helpers):
  1. The function creates a deep copy of the object or array, i.e. recursively copies all nested objects and arrays, ensuring no references to the original object or array remain.
  2. Base case: the function first checks whether the input is not an object, or null; if true, it simply returns the input, since primitive types like number, string, boolean, null and undefined don't need deep cloning.
  3. Recursive case: if the input is an object or array, it initializes an empty object or array and retrieves all the keys of the object. It iterates through each key, recursively calling makeDeepCopy on each property of obj, and assigns the result to the corresponding key in copiedValue.
  4. Return: finally, it returns the deeply copied object or array.

11. Deep Copy vs Shallow Copy & When to Use Them

When to use deep copy & shallow copy:
  1. Shallow copy: for copying objects or arrays that have no nested structures; use the spread operator for both objects and arrays.
  2. Deep copy: if you need a deep copy (i.e. nested objects and arrays also copied), use structuredClone, JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) for JSON-safe data, or a custom function.
Shallow copyDeep copy
What is copiedOnly the first-level (top-level) properties/elementsEverything: top level AND nested objects/arrays
Nested dataShared references to the original objects in memoryNew, independent objects
Changing nested dataAffects BOTH the copy and the originalDoesn't affect the original
SpeedFaster (copies only the first level)Slower (copies everything)
HowObject.assign({}, obj), {...obj}, slice(), [...arr]structuredClone(obj), JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)), recursion, Lodash cloneDeep()
Use caseObjects with only primitive values, or you don't care about nested referencesWhen you need a completely independent clone of the object or array
(Your notes' DEEP COPY VS SHALLOW COPY list is the content of this table: shallow copies only the first level, nested elements are references to the same objects in memory, changes to nested data affect both, it's faster, made with Object.assign/spread/slice, and used when the object has only primitive values; deep copies everything, the whole copy is independent, nested changes don't affect the original, it's slower, made with JSON/structuredClone/recursion/cloneDeep, and used when you need a completely independent clone.)

12. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. Shallow vs deep copy?
  • Shallow: a new top-level container, with nested objects shared. Deep: everything recursively new. Assignment copies only the reference.
Q2. What's wrong with JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))?
  • It drops undefined/functions/Symbols, turns Dates into strings and NaN into null, loses Map/Set and prototypes, and throws on circular references.
Q3. structuredClone vs JSON vs Lodash cloneDeep?
  • structuredClone: built-in, handles Date/Map/Set/cycles, but no functions/DOM. JSON: only plain JSON data. cloneDeep: the most flexible (keeps functions by reference, custom types), but it's a dependency.
Q4. Write a deep clone. What edge cases matter?
  • null (typeof null === "object"), arrays vs objects, Date/RegExp/Map/Set, circular references (WeakMap), Symbol keys, prototypes, and getters.
Q5. Output-based questions
const a = { x: { y: 1 } };
const s = { ...a };  s.x.y = 2;            console.log(a.x.y);   // → 2
const d = structuredClone(a);  d.x.y = 3;  console.log(a.x.y);   // → 2
const j = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify({ t: new Date(0) }));
console.log(typeof j.t);                                        // → string
console.log([1, [2]].slice()[1] === [1, [2]][1]);              // → false (two different literals)
  • What happens: four output questions: spread shares nested data, structuredClone doesn't, JSON turns Date into a string, two literals are different objects.
  • Output: 2, 2, string, false.
थोडक्यात: b = a म्हणजे copy नाही. spread / assign / slice हे shallow copy करतात (nested shared). structuredClone हा deep copy साठी सर्वोत्तम built-in आहे (functions सोडून). JSON पद्धत Date, undefined, functions गमावते. स्वतःचा deep copy लिहिताना null साठी object === null तपासा.
Chapter 56: Prototypes: Zero to Hero (Basics)[[Prototype]] · function.prototype · __proto__ · prototype chain · own vs inherited · shadowing
CHAPTER 56 INDEX
  1. What is a Prototype?
  2. Why Prototypes Matter
  3. Zero: the Problem Prototypes Solve
  4. Function Prototypes
  5. The Prototype Chain (your code + fix)
  6. __proto__ vs prototype
  7. Full Example: Own vs Inherited
  8. Property Lookup, Shadowing & Live Prototypes
  9. The constructor Property
  10. Prototypes of Built-in Objects
  11. Analogy & Summary
  12. Interview Questions & Revision

1. What Is a Prototype in JavaScript?

Your Notes (22_prototype/index.js):
  1. In JavaScript, a prototype is an object
  2. that other objects can inherit properties and methods from, i.e. a prototype is an object from which other objects inherit.
  3. Every JavaScript object has a hidden internal property called [[Prototype]] (often accessed using __proto__ or through Object.getPrototypeOf()), which refers to another object: its prototype. (I.e. it helps with method sharing and inheritance.)
  4. It is an integral part of JavaScript's object-oriented programming model and facilitates inheritance.
  5. A prototype object is associated with every (normal) function, and every object has a [[Prototype]] link, by default. ✔ "associated with every function and object". Only normal functions (and classes) have a .prototype PROPERTY (arrow functions and methods don't: (() => {}).prototype → undefined). Every object has a [[Prototype]] LINK, which may be null (Object.create(null))..prototype ही property फक्त normal functions आणि classes कडे असते, arrow function कडे नसते. प्रत्येक object कडे [[Prototype]] link असते, आणि ती null सुद्धा असू शकते.
  6. It enables inheritance, allowing one object to access the properties and methods of another object.
Definition: Every object has an internal link [[Prototype]] to another object (or null). When you read a property that the object doesn't have, JS follows this link and looks there, then that object's link, and so on, until it reaches null. This linked list is the prototype chain, and it is how inheritance works in JS.
Prototype म्हणजे एक object, ज्याच्याकडून दुसरे objects properties आणि methods वारसा (inherit) घेतात. प्रत्येक object कडे [[Prototype]] नावाची लपलेली link असते, जी त्याच्या "पालक" (prototype) object कडे जाते. एखादी property object मध्ये नसेल तर JS ती या link ने पालकांमध्ये शोधतो.

2. Why Prototypes Matter

Your Notes:
  1. JavaScript is prototype-based, not class-based (though the ES6 class syntax is syntactic sugar over prototypes). This means:
  2. you can share methods across instances using prototypes;
  3. it enables inheritance between objects, and JavaScript uses a prototype chain to resolve property and method lookups.
Prototypes in JS, covering:
  1. function prototypes;
  2. the prototype chain;
  3. object creation;
  4. inheritance using Object.create;
  5. modifying prototypes with __proto__ or Object.setPrototypeOf;
  6. built-in object prototypes. (Points 3–5 are covered in detail in Chapter 57.)

3. Zero: the Problem Prototypes Solve

Start from zero: why not put methods inside the constructor? 
function Bad(n) {
  this.n = n;
  this.hi = function () {};   // a NEW function object is created for EVERY instance
}
console.log(new Bad(1).hi === new Bad(2).hi);   // → false (1000 objects = 1000 copies of hi)

function Good(n) { this.n = n; }
Good.prototype.hi = function () {};             // ONE function, shared through the prototype
console.log(new Good(1).hi === new Good(2).hi); // → true
  • What happens: methods created inside the constructor are new functions for every object; methods on the prototype are shared.
  • Output: false, true.
  • ✅ Prototype methods save memory with many instances.
Data that differs per object (name, age) goes on the instance with this; behaviour that is the same for all (methods) goes on the prototype, written once and shared by everyone. This saves memory and lets you change behaviour for all instances in one place.
method constructor मध्ये लिहिला तर प्रत्येक object साठी नवीन copy बनते. prototype वर लिहिला तर एकच copy सगळे objects share करतात. म्हणून data object वर (this) आणि methods prototype वर ठेवतात.

4. Function Prototype

Your Notes: 
function person(name) {
  this.name = name;
}
console.log(person.prototype);   // → {}   (looks empty, but it has a hidden constructor: person)
// You can attach methods to this prototype:
person.prototype.sayHello = function () {
  console.log("Hello, I am " + this.name);
};
new person("Vishal").sayHello();   // → Hello, I am Vishal
  • What happens: every function has a prototype object; methods added to it are available to all instances.
  • Output: {}, Hello, I am Vishal.
Every normal function automatically gets a prototype object: { constructor: person }. It is used only when the function is called with new: the new object's [[Prototype]] is set to person.prototype.

5. The Prototype Chain

Your Notes: it is useful when accessing a property: 
const p = new Person("Vishal");
p.sayHello();   // Looks for sayHello on p → Person.prototype → Object.prototype → null
// If it's not found on the object, JavaScript looks up the chain (called the prototype chain) until it reaches null.
  • What happens: property lookup: the object, then its prototype, then Object.prototype, then null.
  • Output: (depends on Person being defined).
✔ (verified in Node) this line CRASHES: TypeError: p.sayHello is not a function. Two reasons: (1) the method above was added to lowercase person.prototype, not Person; (2) Person.prototype.sayHello is assigned further down (line 71). The function declaration Person is hoisted, but the assignment to its prototype is NOT, so at this point Person.prototype has no sayHello. Move this call below the Person.prototype.sayHello = … line. ही ओळ TypeError देते. कारण: (1) वरचा method लहान person वर लावला, मोठ्या Person वर नाही; (2) Person.prototype.sayHello खाली (line 71) लावला आहे. function declaration hoist होते, पण prototype वरची assignment hoist होत नाही. म्हणून call त्या ओळीच्या खाली हलवा. 
// ✔ fixed order:
function Person(name, age) { this.name = name; this.age = age; }
Person.prototype.sayHello = function () { console.log(`Hi, I'm ${this.name}…`); };
const p = new Person("Vishal");
p.sayHello();   // ✅ found on Person.prototype
  • What happens: define the constructor and prototype methods BEFORE creating objects that use them.
  • Output: Hi, I'm Vishal…
Figure 118: The prototype chain of p1: each __proto__ link points up until null.

6. __proto__ vs prototype

Your Notes:
  1. __proto__: refers to the prototype of an instance object (used for lookup).
  2. prototype: a property of constructor functions, used when creating new instances.
prototype__proto__ ([[Prototype]])
Who has it(Normal) functions & classesEvery object (incl. functions)
What it isThe object that becomes the prototype of instances made with newThe link this object uses for lookup
Relationnew Person() → instance.__proto__ === Person.prototype
Modern wayFn.prototypeObject.getPrototypeOf(obj) / Object.setPrototypeOf(obj, p)
Note: __proto__ is a legacy accessor (it lives on Object.prototype, so it doesn't exist on Object.create(null) objects). Prefer Object.getPrototypeOf.
prototype = function ची property: new ने बनणाऱ्या objects चा पालक कोण असेल ते. __proto__ = प्रत्येक object ची link: माझा पालक कोण. नियम: new Person() ने बनलेल्या object चा __proto__ === Person.prototype.

7. Full Example: Own vs Inherited Properties

Your Notes: Prototypes of built-in objects: Arrays → Array.prototype; Dates → Date.prototype; Functions → Function.prototype; Objects → Object.prototype.
Example 1
// p1 (instance)
//    |
//    └──> Person.prototype
//              |
//              └──> Object.prototype
//                          |
//                          └──> null

// Constructor Function
function Person(name, age) {
  this.name = name;   // own property
  this.age = age;     // own property
}
// Add a method to the prototype
Person.prototype.sayHello = function () {
  console.log(`Hi, I'm ${this.name} and I'm ${this.age} years old.`);
};
// Add another property to the prototype
Person.prototype.species = "Human";

// Create an instance
const p1 = new Person("Vishal", 25);
// Own properties
console.log(p1.name);   // Vishal
console.log(p1.age);    // 25
// Inherited from the prototype
p1.sayHello();             // Hi, I'm Vishal and I'm 25 years old.
console.log(p1.species);   // Human

// Check the prototype link
console.log(p1.__proto__ === Person.prototype);   // true
  • What happens: own properties live on the instance; methods and shared values come from Person.prototype; __proto__ links them.
  • Output: Vishal, 25, Hi, I'm Vishal and I'm 25 years old., Human, true.
Explore the prototype chain
// Explore the prototype chain
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(p1));                 // Person.prototype → { sayHello: [Function], species: 'Human' }
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(Person.prototype));   // Object.prototype
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(Object.prototype));   // null
  • What happens: Object.getPrototypeOf walks the chain: Person.prototype → Object.prototype → null.
  • Output: the three steps.
  • Own properties go directly on the object.
  • Shared methods/properties go on the prototype.
  • __proto__ links an object to its prototype.
  • The prototype chain is used to find missing properties/methods.
How do you tell own from inherited? (verified) 
console.log(Object.keys(p1));               // → ['name', 'age']             (own only)
console.log("species" in p1);               // → true                        (own + inherited)
console.log(Object.hasOwn(p1, "species"));  // → false                       (own only)
for (const k in p1) console.log(k);         // → name, age, sayHello, species (for…in includes inherited enumerable!)
  • What happens: Object.keys/hasOwn see only own properties; in and for…in also see inherited (enumerable) ones.
  • Output: ['name', 'age'], true, false, name age sayHello species.

8. Property Lookup, Shadowing & Live Prototypes

Reading vs writing (verified in Node)
Writing creates an own property (shadowing)
// READ walks up the chain; WRITE always goes on the object itself (it "shadows")
p1.species = "Alien";         // creates an OWN property on p1
const p2 = new Person("A", 1);
console.log(p1.species, p2.species);   // → Alien Human   (p2 still reads the prototype)
  • What happens: reading looks up the chain, but assigning always creates/changes a property on the object itself.
  • Output: Alien Human.
Prototypes are live
// prototypes are LIVE: a change is seen by all existing instances
Person.prototype.species = "Homo sapiens";
console.log(p2.species, p1.species);   // → Homo sapiens Alien   (p1's own value shadows it)
  • What happens: changing the prototype affects every existing instance (unless shadowed).
  • Output: Homo sapiens Alien.
Replacing the prototype object
// but REPLACING the whole prototype object only affects instances created later
function Shape() {}
const s1 = new Shape();
Shape.prototype = { area() { return 0; } };
const s2 = new Shape();
console.log(typeof s1.area, typeof s2.area);   // → undefined function
console.log(s2.constructor === Shape);         // → false (the new object lost .constructor)
  • What happens: old instances keep the old prototype; the new object also loses .constructor.
  • Output: undefined function, false.
  • ⚠ Add methods instead of replacing Fn.prototype.
Shared mutable values (bug)
// a mutable value on the prototype is SHARED (a classic bug)
const shared = { list: [] };
const x1 = Object.create(shared), x2 = Object.create(shared);
x1.list.push(1);
console.log(x2.list);   // → [1]   put arrays/objects on the instance (this.list = []) instead
  • What happens: an array on the prototype is shared by all instances.
  • Output: [1].
  • ⚠ Put arrays/objects in the constructor (this.list = []).
property वाचताना JS chain वर चढत शोधतो, पण लिहिताना (assign) ती नेहमी object वरच नवीन (own) property बनते. हिला shadowing म्हणतात. prototype मध्ये केलेला बदल सगळ्या objects ना लगेच दिसतो, पण संपूर्ण prototype object बदलल्यास तो बदल फक्त नंतर बनलेल्या objects ना लागू होतो. prototype वर array ठेवल्यास तो सगळ्यांचा shared होतो.

9. The constructor Property

console.log(Person.prototype.constructor === Person);   // → true
console.log(p1.constructor === Person);                 // → true (inherited from the prototype)
const p3 = new p1.constructor("Copy", 1);                // create a "sibling" without knowing the class name
// ⚠ if you overwrite Fn.prototype = {...}, restore it: Fn.prototype.constructor = Fn
  • What happens: prototype.constructor points back to the function; instances inherit it.
  • Output: true, true.
  • ✅ Create a sibling object: new obj.constructor(...).

10. Prototypes of Built-in Objects

const arr = [1, 2];
Object.getPrototypeOf(arr) === Array.prototype;                // true  → arr.map, arr.push come from here
Object.getPrototypeOf(Array.prototype) === Object.prototype;   // true
function f() {}
Object.getPrototypeOf(f) === Function.prototype;               // true  → f.call, f.bind come from here
(5).toFixed === Number.prototype.toFixed;                      // true  (primitives are temporarily boxed)
"a".__proto__ === String.prototype;                            // true
Object.getPrototypeOf(Object) === Function.prototype;          // true  (Object itself is a function)
  • What happens: built-ins use the same system: arrays get map/push from Array.prototype, functions get call/bind from Function.prototype; primitives are boxed temporarily.
  • Output: true ×6.
[1,2]  → Array.prototype    → Object.prototype → null
f      → Function.prototype → Object.prototype → null
"abc"  → String.prototype   → Object.prototype → null
new Date() → Date.prototype → Object.prototype → null
  • What happens: [TODO: Explanation required]
  • Output: [TODO: Output required]
Array, String, Function, Date सगळ्यांचे methods त्यांच्या prototype वर असतात (Array.prototype.map इत्यादी). सगळ्या chains शेवटी Object.prototype आणि मग null पर्यंत जातात. primitive ("abc", 5) वर method वापरताना JS तात्पुरता wrapper object बनवतो.

11. What is __proto__? Analogy & Summary

Your Notes: __proto__ is a reference to the prototype of the object, meaning the object it inherits from.
Analogy: imagine you're a student (p1), and your teacher (Person.prototype) has notes (the sayHello() method). You don't have the notes, but you know how to find the teacher and ask. In JavaScript: p1.__proto__ → points to Person.prototype. That's how p1 gets access to sayHello(). 
p1 ---> __proto__ ---> Person.prototype ---> __proto__ ---> Object.prototype ---> null
  • What happens: [TODO: Explanation required]
  • Output: [TODO: Output required]

12. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. What is the prototype chain?
  • The chain of [[Prototype]] links from an object up to null. Property reads walk it until the property is found; if it reaches null, the result is undefined.
Q2. __proto__ vs prototype?
  • prototype is a property of functions/classes used by new; __proto__ (Object.getPrototypeOf) is every object's link to its prototype. For x = new F(): x.__proto__ === F.prototype.
Q3. Why put methods on the prototype instead of in the constructor?
  • One shared copy instead of one per instance (memory), and it can be updated for all instances at once. Per-instance data stays in the constructor.
Q4. How do you check own vs inherited properties?
  • Object.hasOwn(obj, k) / obj.hasOwnProperty(k) are own only; k in obj includes inherited; Object.keys is own enumerable; for…in includes inherited enumerable.
Q5. What does the new keyword do?
    1. Creates an empty object;
    2. links its [[Prototype]] to Fn.prototype;
    3. calls Fn with this = that object;
    4. returns it (unless Fn returns its own object).
Q6. Output-based questions
function F() {}
F.prototype.x = 1;
const a = new F();
a.x = 2;
delete a.x;
console.log(a.x);                                   // → 1 (the own property is gone, the inherited one shows)
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(Object.prototype));   // → null
console.log(typeof (() => {}).prototype);           // → undefined
console.log({}.toString === Object.prototype.toString);   // → true
  • What happens: deleting an own property reveals the inherited one; the chain ends at null; arrow functions have no prototype; {} uses Object.prototype's toString.
  • Output: 1, null, undefined, true.
TermMeaning
[[Prototype]] / __proto__An object's link to its parent object
Fn.prototypeThe parent given to objects made by new Fn()
Prototype chainLookup path up to null
Own vs inheritedObject.hasOwn vs in
ShadowingWriting creates an own property that hides the inherited one
थोडक्यात: प्रत्येक object ची [[Prototype]] link असते. property नसेल तर JS chain वर null पर्यंत शोधतो. data object वर, methods prototype वर. x.__proto__ === F.prototype. लिहिणे नेहमी object वरच होते (shadowing).

Note: your file lists "3. Object creation, 4. Inheritance using Object.create, 5. Modifying prototypes with __proto__ or Object.setPrototypeOf" but doesn't show code for them; this chapter adds that code (all verified in Node) to take the topic from basic to hero level.

1. Object Creation & Setting a Prototype

1. Object.create(proto)
const animal = {
  eats: true,
  walk() { return this.name + " walks"; },
};
// 1. Object.create(proto): a new object whose [[Prototype]] is proto (the recommended way)
const dog = Object.create(animal);
dog.name = "Tommy";
console.log(dog.eats, dog.walk());                // → true Tommy walks
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(dog) === animal);   // → true
  • What happens: dog's prototype is animal, so dog inherits eats and walk; this inside walk is dog.
  • Output: true Tommy walks, true.
  • ✅ Cleanest way to set up inheritance between plain objects.
2. Object.setPrototypeOf
// 2. Object.setPrototypeOf(obj, proto): change an EXISTING object's prototype (slow; avoid in hot code)
const cat = { name: "Kitty" };
Object.setPrototypeOf(cat, animal);
console.log(cat.walk());                          // → Kitty walks
  • What happens: changes the prototype of an existing object.
  • Output: Kitty walks.
  • ⚠ Slow; engines de-optimise objects whose prototype changes.
3. __proto__ in a literal
// 3. __proto__ in an object literal (allowed, standardised)
const lion = { __proto__: animal, name: "Lion" };
console.log(lion.walk());                         // → Lion walks

// 4. new Fn(): the prototype is Fn.prototype   5. class: the prototype is Class.prototype
  • What happens: __proto__ inside {} sets the prototype at creation.
  • Output: Lion walks.
Note: this inside an inherited method is the object BEFORE the dot (dog), not the prototype (animal); see Chapter 37. 
const base = { count: 0, inc() { this.count++; } };
const c1 = Object.create(base);
c1.inc();
console.log(c1.count, base.count, Object.hasOwn(c1, "count"));   // → 1 0 true
  • What happens: c1.inc() reads count from base (0), then WRITES count on c1 itself; base keeps 0.
  • Output: 1 0 true.
  • ⚠ Shared state on a prototype looks shared but writes create own copies.
Object.create(proto) ने दिलेल्या object ला पालक बनवून नवीन object तयार होतो; ही सर्वात चांगली पद्धत आहे. setPrototypeOf आधीच बनलेल्या object चा पालक बदलतो, पण ते हळू असते. inherited method मध्ये this म्हणजे dot च्या डावीकडचा object (dog), prototype नाही.

2. Inheritance with Constructor Functions (the pre-ES6 way)

function Animal(name) { this.name = name; }
Animal.prototype.speak = function () { return this.name + " makes a sound"; };

function Dog(name, breed) {
  Animal.call(this, name);   // step 1: inherit the OWN properties (like super(name))
  this.breed = breed;
}
Dog.prototype = Object.create(Animal.prototype);   // step 2: link the prototypes
Dog.prototype.constructor = Dog;                   // step 3: restore the constructor
Dog.prototype.bark = function () { return this.name + " barks"; };

const d = new Dog("Rex", "Lab");
console.log(d.speak(), d.bark());                    // → Rex makes a sound Rex barks
console.log(d instanceof Dog, d instanceof Animal);  // → true true
console.log(d.constructor === Dog);                  // → true
// chain: d → Dog.prototype → Animal.prototype → Object.prototype → null
  • What happens: classic ES5 inheritance: call the parent constructor for own properties, link the prototypes with Object.create, restore constructor.
  • Output: Rex makes a sound Rex barks, true true, true.
  • ✅ Shows what class/extends does behind the scenes.
Why not Dog.prototype = Animal.prototype? Then both share ONE object: adding bark to Dog would add it to every Animal. Why not Dog.prototype = new Animal()? It runs the Animal constructor needlessly and puts an unwanted name property on the prototype.
Figure 119: Constructor inheritance: d → Dog.prototype → Animal.prototype → Object.prototype → null.
जुन्या पद्धतीने inheritance साठी 3 steps: (1) Animal.call(this, name) ने properties घ्या; (2) Dog.prototype = Object.create(Animal.prototype) ने methods ची link जोडा; (3) constructor परत Dog करा. class extends हेच सगळे आपोआप करतो.

3. ES6 class = Syntactic Sugar over Prototypes

class A2 {
  constructor(n) { this.n = n; }   // own property
  hi() { return "hi " + this.n; }  // goes on A2.prototype (not on the instance)
  static s() { return 1; }         // goes on A2 itself
}
class B2 extends A2 {
  hi() { return super.hi() + "!"; }   // super.hi → A2.prototype.hi
}
const b = new B2("x");
console.log(b.hi());                                         // → hi x!
console.log(typeof A2);                                      // → function   (a class IS a function)
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(B2.prototype) === A2.prototype);   // → true (method inheritance)
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(B2) === A2);               // → true (static inheritance)
console.log(Object.hasOwn(b, "hi"));                         // → false (the method is on the prototype)
  • What happens: class syntax builds the same chain: methods on the prototype, statics on the class, extends links both; super.hi calls the parent method.
  • Output: hi x!, function, true, true, false.
What class adds on top: it must be called with new (a TypeError otherwise); the body is always strict mode; methods are non-enumerable; it is not hoisted like functions (TDZ); and it has super, static, #private fields and getters/setters.
class हा नवीन inheritance प्रकार नाही, तो prototype वर बसवलेली सोपी syntax (sugar) आहे. class मधले methods ClassName.prototype वर जातात, आणि extends दोन chains जोडतो: instances साठी prototype chain आणि static साठी constructor chain.

4. instanceof & isPrototypeOf

// x instanceof F  ⇔  F.prototype appears somewhere in x's prototype chain
d instanceof Animal;                  // true
Animal.prototype.isPrototypeOf(d);    // true (same check, without needing a constructor)
Object.prototype.isPrototypeOf(d);    // true
// replacing F.prototype breaks instanceof for old objects:
s1 instanceof Shape;                  // false (s1's prototype is the OLD Shape.prototype)
  • What happens: instanceof checks whether F.prototype is in the object's chain; isPrototypeOf asks the same from the prototype's side.
  • Output: true, true, true, false.

5. Functions are Objects too: the Function / Object Chicken-and-Egg

function f() {}
Object.getPrototypeOf(f) === Function.prototype;                  // true
Object.getPrototypeOf(Function.prototype) === Object.prototype;   // true
Object.getPrototypeOf(Object) === Function.prototype;             // true (Object is a function)
Function.__proto__ === Function.prototype;                        // true (Function is a function too)
typeof Function.prototype;                                        // "function"
// so: f.call / f.bind come from Function.prototype; f.hasOwnProperty comes from Object.prototype
  • What happens: functions are objects whose prototype is Function.prototype; Object and Function are themselves functions.
  • Output: true ×4, "function".

6. Extending Built-in Prototypes & Writing Polyfills

// a polyfill = adding a missing standard method yourself, on the built-in prototype
Array.prototype.myMap = function (cb) {
  const result = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < this.length; i++) {
    if (i in this) result[i] = cb(this[i], i, this);   // this = the array (it's on the prototype)
  }
  return result;
};
console.log([1, 2, 3].myMap((x) => x * 2));   // → [2, 4, 6]

// ⚠ danger: a method added by assignment is ENUMERABLE → it shows up in for…in over EVERY array
for (const k in [10]) console.log(k);         // → 0, myMap
// safer: Object.defineProperty(Array.prototype, "myMap", { value: fn, enumerable: false, writable: true, configurable: true })
// best practice: never modify built-in prototypes in app code ("monkey patching"); only polyfill standard
// methods, guarded by: if (!Array.prototype.flat) { … }
  • What happens: a polyfill adds a method to Array.prototype; this inside it is the array. Added by assignment, it becomes enumerable and appears in for…in.
  • Output: [2, 4, 6], 0 myMap.
  • ⚠ Don't modify built-in prototypes in app code; use defineProperty with enumerable: false for real polyfills.
Array.prototype वर method जोडल्यास सगळ्या arrays ना तो मिळतो; यालाच polyfill म्हणतात (interview मध्ये map/filter/bind चे polyfill विचारतात). पण साध्या assignment ने जोडलेला method for...in मध्ये दिसतो, आणि built-ins बदलल्याने इतर code तुटू शकतो. म्हणून फक्त standard method नसेल तेव्हाच, आणि defineProperty ने जोडा.

7. Objects without a Prototype

const dict = Object.create(null);
console.log(typeof dict.toString, Object.getPrototypeOf(dict));   // → undefined null
// a pure dictionary: keys like "toString" / "__proto__" can't clash with anything inherited
// use Object.hasOwn(dict, k), not dict.hasOwnProperty (see Chapter 51)
  • What happens: Object.create(null) makes an object with no prototype: a pure dictionary.
  • Output: undefined null.
  • ✅ Keys like "toString" can't clash with inherited ones.

8. Pitfalls & Best Practices

  1. Put methods on the prototype (or in a class body); put per-instance data (especially arrays/objects) in the constructor.
  2. Don't use arrow functions for prototype methods: Person.prototype.hi = () => this.name, because the arrow gets the outer this (Chapter 37).
  3. Add prototype methods BEFORE calling them (your crash in Chapter 56 §5).
  4. Avoid __proto__ and setPrototypeOf on existing objects (slow, legacy); use Object.create / class.
  5. When replacing Fn.prototype, restore .constructor.
  6. Long chains = slower lookups; keep hierarchies shallow and prefer composition.

9. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. Classical vs prototypal inheritance?
  • Classical: classes are blueprints and objects are copies. Prototypal: objects link directly to other objects and delegate lookups at runtime. JS classes are syntax over prototypes.
Q2. Implement inheritance without class.
  • Child calls Parent.call(this, …); Child.prototype = Object.create(Parent.prototype); Child.prototype.constructor = Child; then add the child methods.
Q3. What does Object.create(proto, descriptors) do?
  • It creates a new object with [[Prototype]] = proto (null is allowed), optionally with property descriptors. No constructor runs.
Q4. How does instanceof work? Can you fool it?
  • It walks x's chain looking for F.prototype. Changing prototypes (setPrototypeOf / replacing F.prototype) changes the result; Symbol.hasInstance can customise it.
Q5. Write a polyfill for Function.prototype.bind.
Function.prototype.myBind = function (ctx, ...pre) {
  const fn = this;
  return function (...args) { return fn.apply(ctx, [...pre, ...args]); };
};
  • What happens: a bind polyfill on Function.prototype: this is the original function; it returns a function that applies it with the saved context and arguments.
  • Output: (function).
  • ✅ Common interview task.
Q6. Output-based questions
const A = { greet() { return "A"; } };
const B = Object.create(A);
B.greet = function () { return "B+" + A.greet(); };
console.log(B.greet());                               // → B+A
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(B) === A);          // → true
class P { m() { return 1; } }
class C extends P { m() { return super.m() + 1; } }
console.log(new C().m());                             // → 2
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(C.prototype) === P.prototype);   // → true
  • What happens: an object can delegate to another (B → A); class super calls the parent method; prototypes chain.
  • Output: B+A, true, 2, true.
ToolUse
Object.create(p)A new object linked to p
Object.getPrototypeOf / setPrototypeOfRead / change the link
Parent.call + Object.createConstructor inheritance
class / extends / superThe same thing, cleaner syntax
instanceof / isPrototypeOfChain membership checks
Fn.prototype.methodShared methods & polyfills
थोडक्यात: Object.create ने link जोडा. constructor inheritance = Parent.call + Object.create + constructor fix. class/extends हे prototypes वरचे sugar आहे. instanceof prototype chain तपासतो. built-in prototypes बदलणे टाळा; फक्त polyfill साठी, काळजीपूर्वक बदला.
