Chapter 58: Classes (ES6)Constructor/prototype pattern · class declaration & expression · fields · get/set · static · #private · extends/super
CHAPTER 58 INDEX
  1. What is a Class?
  2. Before ES6: Constructor + Prototype Pattern
  3. ES6 Class Declaration
  4. Class Expressions
  5. What Happens Under the Hood
  6. Class Features: Fields, Getters/Setters, Static, #Private
  7. Inheritance: extends & super
  8. Class Rules & Gotchas
  9. Interview Questions & Revision

1. Class

Your Notes (31_class/class.js):
  1. A class is a blueprint for creating objects.
  2. A class encapsulates data and the functions that manipulate that data.
  3. JavaScript classes are syntactic sugar over prototypal inheritance. ✔ "synthetic sugar" → SYNTACTIC sugar (a nicer syntax for something that already exists)."synthetic" नाही, "syntactic" sugar: आधीपासून असलेल्या गोष्टीसाठी (prototype) सोपी लिहिण्याची पद्धत.
  4. In ES6, a class is a special function (typeof ClassName → "function").
  5. Prior to ES6, JavaScript had no class keyword; to mimic a class you often used the constructor + prototype pattern.
Definition: A class (ES2015) is a template for objects: the constructor sets per-instance data, methods go on ClassName.prototype (shared), static members go on the class itself, and extends/super set up the prototype chain for inheritance. Under the hood it is still a constructor function plus prototypes (Chapters 42–43).
Class म्हणजे objects बनवण्याचा साचा (blueprint). constructor मध्ये प्रत्येक object चा data, आणि methods prototype वर (सगळ्यांसाठी एकच copy). JS मधला class हा प्रत्यक्षात function + prototype च आहे, फक्त लिहायला सोपा (syntactic sugar).

2. How to Define a "Class" with the Constructor-Prototype Pattern

Your Notes: 1. This Person is a constructor function that contains a property, name. ✔ heading "phototype pattern" → PROTOTYPE pattern."phototype" नाही, prototype. 
function Person(name) {
  this.name = name;
}
Person.prototype.getName = function () {
  // getName() is assigned to the prototype so that it is shared by all instances of the Person type
  return this.name;
};
let per = new Person("vishal shinde");
console.log(per);             // → Person { name: 'vishal shinde' }
console.log(per.getName());   // → vishal shinde
  • What happens: constructor function + prototype method: the ES5 way of making "classes".
  • Output: Person { name: 'vishal shinde' }, vishal shinde.

3. ES6 Class Declaration

class Person1 {
  constructor(name) {
    this.name = name;
  }
  getname() {   // (camelCase convention: getName)
    return this.name;
  }
}
let per1 = new Person1("vishu");
console.log(per1);   // → Person1 { name: 'vishu' }
const name = per.getName();
console.log(name);   // → vishal shinde
// ✔ this calls per (the OLD Person instance), so it prints "vishal shinde". To test the class,
//    use per1.getname() → "vishu" (verified in Node)
  • What happens: the class version does the same; the last lines call the OLD per object.
  • Output: Person1 { name: 'vishu' }, vishal shinde.
  • ✅ Cleaner syntax for the same prototype system.
इथे per (जुना Person object) वापरला आहे, म्हणून "vishal shinde" येते. class तपासायचा असेल तर per1.getname() लिहा, उत्तर "vishu" येईल.
Constructor functionES6 class
function Person(name) { this.name = name }class Person { constructor(name) { this.name = name } }
Person.prototype.getName = function () {…}getName() {…} inside the class body
Can be called without new (bug: this = window)Must use new (TypeError otherwise)
Hoisted (function declaration)Not usable before the declaration (TDZ)
Inheritance: Parent.call + Object.createextends + super

4. JavaScript Class Expressions (Similar to Function Expressions)

  1. Classes have expressions: a class expression provides an alternative way to define a new class.
  2. A class expression doesn't require an identifier after the class keyword, and you can use a class expression in a variable declaration or pass it into a function as an argument.
// a class expression starts with the keyword class, optionally followed by the class identifier (name)
// the left side of the expression is the user variable, assigned to the class expression
let user = class {
  constructor(name, age) {
    this.name = name;
    this.age = age
  }
  display() {
    return {
      name: this.name,
      age: this.age
    }
  }
}
let per4 = new user('vishal shinde', 45)
console.log(per4);             // → user { name: 'vishal shinde', age: 45 }
console.log(per4.display());   // → { name: 'vishal shinde', age: 45 }
// (class names are PascalCase by convention: const User = class { … })
  • What happens: a class can be stored in a variable (class expression) and used with new.
  • Output: user { … }, { name: 'vishal shinde', age: 45 }.
✔ "class identification" → class IDENTIFIER (name), and "left side … is person variable" → it is the USER variable."identification" नाही "identifier" (नाव), आणि डावीकडचा variable person नाही, user आहे. 
// a NAMED class expression: the name is visible only inside the class
const U = class Named { who() { return Named.name; } };
console.log(new U().who(), U.name);   // → Named Named
  • What happens: a named class expression's name is visible inside the class and as .name.
  • Output: Named Named.

5. What Happens Under the Hood

class Person1 { constructor(name) { this.name = name; } getname() { return this.name; } }
typeof Person1;                                   // "function"
Object.getOwnPropertyNames(Person1.prototype);    // ['constructor', 'getname']  (methods on the prototype)
Object.keys(new Person1("x"));                    // ['name']  (only data is on the instance)
Object.getPrototypeOf(new Person1("x")) === Person1.prototype;   // true
  • What happens: a class is a function; methods live on the prototype; only data lives on the instance.
  • Output: "function", ['constructor', 'getname'], ['name'], true.
class मधील methods ClassName.prototype वर जातात आणि data instance वर राहतो, अगदी constructor function + prototype pattern सारखेच.

6. Class Features: Fields, Getters/Setters, Static, #Private

class A {
  #secret = 1;          // private field: only accessible inside the class
  count = 0;            // public field: created on every instance
  static total = 0;     // static field: lives on A itself, shared

  constructor(n) {
    this.n = n;
    A.total++;
  }
  get upper() { return this.n.toUpperCase(); }    // getter: read like a property
  set upper(v) { this.n = v.toLowerCase(); }      // setter: assign like a property
  #helper() { return this.#secret; }              // private method
  reveal() { return this.#helper(); }
  static create(n) { return new A(n); }           // static method: A.create(), not a.create()
}
const a = new A("vi");
a.upper = "XY";
console.log(a.n, a.upper);      // → xy XY
console.log(a.reveal());        // → 1
// a.#secret                    // ❌ SyntaxError: private field outside the class
console.log(Object.keys(a));    // → ['count', 'n']   (#secret is invisible)
console.log(A.total);           // → 1   (static: on the class, not on instances)
  • What happens: private #fields/#methods are hidden outside the class; public fields go on each instance; static members live on the class; get/set look like properties.
  • Output: xy XY, 1, ['count', 'n'], 1.
  • ✅ Real encapsulation with #private.
field = प्रत्येक object वर आपोआप बनणारी property. get/set = function असून property सारखे वापरता येतात. static = class वरच असलेले (A.total, A.create), objects वर नाही. #private = class च्या बाहेरून दिसत नाही (खरी encapsulation).

7. Inheritance: extends & super

class B extends A {
  constructor(n, r) {
    super(n);       // MUST be called before using this (it runs A's constructor)
    this.r = r;
  }
  reveal() {
    return "B:" + super.reveal();   // call the parent's version of the method
  }
}
const b = new B("vi", 2);
console.log(b.reveal());          // → B:1
console.log(b instanceof A);      // → true
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(B.prototype) === A.prototype);   // → true  (methods chain)
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(B) === A);                       // → true  (statics are inherited: B.create works)
  • What happens: extends + super(n) runs the parent constructor first; super.reveal() calls the parent method; statics are inherited too.
  • Output: B:1, true, true, true.
  • ⚠ Using this before super() → ReferenceError.
Figure 120: class B extends A builds the prototype chain b → B.prototype → A.prototype → Object.prototype.

8. Class Rules & Gotchas (verified in Node)

  1. new is required: A("x") → TypeError: Class constructor A cannot be invoked without 'new'.
  2. TDZ, not hoisted like functions: new C(); class C {} → ReferenceError: Cannot access 'C' before initialization.
  3. The class body is always strict mode: a method extracted and called alone has this = undefined (Chapter 37); use arrow-function fields or bind for callbacks: handle = () => this.n;
  4. In a subclass, this before super() → ReferenceError.
  5. Methods are non-enumerable (they don't show up in for…in), unlike Fn.prototype.x = … assignments.
  6. A class can extend built-ins: class MyArr extends Array {}.

9. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. Is a JS class a real class like in Java?
  • No. It is syntactic sugar over constructor functions and prototypes: typeof is "function", methods live on .prototype, and inheritance is a prototype chain. It adds stricter rules (new required, strict mode, TDZ) and features (#private, static blocks).
Q2. What does super do?
  • super(...) in a constructor calls the parent constructor (required before using this); super.method() calls the parent's method from an overriding method.
Q3. static vs instance members?
  • Static members belong to the class (Math-like utilities, counters, factories: A.create()); instance members belong to each object made with new. Static members are inherited by subclasses (B.create).
Q4. How do you make data private in JS?
  • #private fields/methods (true privacy, enforced by the language), or closures (a variable inside the constructor/factory), or convention _name (not really private).
Q5. Output-based questions
class P { constructor() { this.x = 1; } get double() { return this.x * 2; } static hi() { return "hi"; } }
const p = new P();
console.log(p.double);                 // → 2 (no parentheses: a getter)
console.log(P.hi(), typeof p.hi);      // → hi undefined
class Q extends P { constructor() { super(); this.x = 5; } }
console.log(new Q().double);           // → 10
console.log(typeof P);                 // → function
// P();                                // TypeError: Class constructor P cannot be invoked without 'new'
  • What happens: a getter is read without (); static methods are on the class, not on instances; the child's constructor sets x = 5; classes can't be called without new.
  • Output: 2, hi undefined, 10, function.
FeatureSyntax
Constructorconstructor(a) { this.a = a }
Method (on the prototype)greet() {}
Fieldcount = 0
Getter / setterget x() {} / set x(v) {}
Staticstatic total = 0; static create() {}
Private#secret; #helper() {}
Inheritanceclass B extends A { constructor() { super() } }
थोडक्यात: class = constructor + prototype ची सोपी syntax. new शिवाय call करता येत नाही, declaration आधी वापरता येत नाही (TDZ), body strict mode मध्ये असते. fields, get/set, static, #private ही वैशिष्ट्ये आहेत. extends + super ने inheritance होतो, आणि super() नेहमी this च्या आधी लिहा.

Chapter 59: Singleton PatternOne instance · class expression · IIFE + closure · static field · ES module singleton
CHAPTER 59 INDEX
  1. What is a Singleton Class?
  2. Singleton with a Class Expression
  3. Singleton with an IIFE + Closure (+ the crash)
  4. Better Ways (class with static field, ES module)
  5. Interview Questions & Revision

1. Singleton Class

Your Notes (38_singleToneClass.js):
  1. A singleton class is a design pattern in JS that ensures a class has only one instance and provides a global point of access to that instance.
  2. It limits the instantiation of a class to a single instance.
  3. I.e. only one instance is created throughout the code or system.
  4. A class expression can be used to create one by calling the class constructor immediately: use the new operator with the class expression and include the parentheses at the end of the class declaration.
Characteristics of a singleton class:
  1. Single instance: ensures only one instance of the class exists.
  2. Global access: provides a way to access this instance globally.
  3. Controlled instantiation: the instance is created when first accessed (lazy initialization) or immediately when the class is defined (eager initialization).
✔ spelling "singleTone" → SINGLETON (single + ton)."singleTone" नाही, "Singleton" (एकच instance).
Definition: A singleton guarantees exactly one shared instance (e.g. a config store, logger, DB connection, cache) and a single way to get it. In JS it's built with a closure (IIFE), a class with a static instance, or simply an ES module (modules are evaluated once and cached).
Singleton म्हणजे class चा फक्त एकच object (instance) संपूर्ण app मध्ये असणे, आणि तो सगळीकडून एकाच मार्गाने मिळणे. उदा. config, logger, database connection. JS मध्ये तो closure (IIFE), static field असलेला class किंवा ES module ने बनवतात.

2. Singleton with a Class Expression (eager)

// the new operator with a class expression, including the parentheses at the end;
// the class expression is used to create a singleton object
let app = new (class {
  constructor(name) {
    this.name = name;
    // # how it works:
    // the class has a constructor that accepts an argument, and also a method, start.
    // The class expression evaluates to a class, therefore you can call its constructor immediately by placing parentheses after the expression;
    // the expression returns the instance of the class, created by calling the class expression, which is assigned to app
  }
  start() {
    console.log(`starting....${this.name}`);
  }
})("vishal");
// only one instance is created throughout the system:
// the class expression creates a singleton by calling the class constructor immediately
app.start();   // → starting....vishal   (your file never calls it)
  • What happens: new (class { … })("vishal") defines a class and creates its only instance immediately; nobody else can create another (the class has no name).
  • Output: starting....vishal.
  • ✅ Quick one-off singleton.
✔ Note (verified in Node): this is only a "practical" singleton: the class has no name, but it is still reachable as app.constructor, so new app.constructor("other") creates a SECOND, different instance (app === two → false).हा पूर्ण singleton नाही: app.constructor वापरून new app.constructor("other") ने दुसरा वेगळा object बनवता येतो.

3. Singleton with an IIFE + Closure (lazy)

const singleTone = (function () {
  let instance;
  function createInstances() {
    const object = new Object('hi how are you ');
    return object
  }
  return {
    getInstances: function () {
      if (!instance) {
        instance = createInstances()
      }
      return instance
    }
  }
})
let obj = singleTone.getInstances();
const obj2 = singleTone.getInstances();
console.log(obj);
console.log(obj2);
console.log(obj == obj2);
  • What happens: this module-pattern singleton is missing the () at the end of the IIFE, so singleTone is a FUNCTION, and singleTone.getInstances is undefined.
  • Output: TypeError: singleTone.getInstances is not a function.
  • ⚠ Classic IIFE bug: the final () makes it run.
✔ (verified in Node) the function is wrapped in ( ) but never CALLED, so singleTone is the function itself → TypeError: singleTone.getInstances is not a function. Add () at the end: })();. After the fix: obj → [String: 'hi how are you '] (new Object('…') creates a String wrapper object), and obj == obj2 → true (also ===). IIFE च्या शेवटी () नाही, म्हणून function call होत नाही आणि singleTone म्हणजे फक्त function राहतो. })(); असे लिहा. नंतर दोन्ही calls तोच object देतात (true). 
// ✅ fixed
const singleton = (function () {
  let instance;                                         // private, kept alive by the closure
  return {
    getInstance() {
      if (!instance) instance = { createdAt: Date.now() };   // lazy: created on the first call
      return instance;
    },
  };
})();
singleton.getInstance() === singleton.getInstance();   // true
  • What happens: the fixed version: the IIFE runs once; instance is private and created lazily on the first call; later calls return the same object.
  • Output: true.
  • ✅ Global shared object without a global variable.
Figure 121: A closure-based singleton: every call returns the same stored instance.

4. Better Ways (verified in Node)

a) Class singleton with a private static field
// a) class with a private static field: even "new" returns the same object
class Single {
  static #instance;
  constructor() {
    if (Single.#instance) return Single.#instance;   // returning an object from a constructor replaces "this"
    Single.#instance = this;
  }
}
new Single() === new Single();   // true
  • What happens: the constructor returns the stored instance if it exists, so every new gives the same object.
  • Output: true.
  • ⚠ Surprising: new normally creates a NEW object.
b) ES-module singleton
// b) the ES-module singleton (the simplest and most common in real apps)
// config.js
const config = { apiUrl: "/api", debug: false };
export default config;           // every import gets the SAME object (modules run once, Chapter 85)
// c) freeze it if nobody should change it: export default Object.freeze(config);
  • What happens: a module runs only once; every import gets the same exported object.
  • Output: (no output).
  • ✅ The simplest and most common singleton in real apps; freeze it to prevent changes.
Pros: one shared state, controlled creation, lazy loading. Cons: hidden global state, harder unit testing (state leaks between tests), tight coupling; prefer passing dependencies explicitly when you can.

5. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. What is the singleton pattern? Give real examples.
  • One instance + one access point: an app config, logger, cache, DB pool, Redux store, toast manager.
Q2. Implement a singleton in JS (two ways).
  • IIFE + closure with getInstance() (lazy), or a class whose constructor returns the stored static #instance. A module export is a singleton by default.
Q3. Why isn't new (class {…})() a true singleton?
  • The constructor is still reachable via instance.constructor, so more instances can be made. Guard inside the constructor (static instance check) for a real one.
Q4. Lazy vs eager initialization?
  • Eager creates the instance at load time (the class-expression version); lazy creates it on the first getInstance() call, which saves work if it's never used.
Q5. Output-based questions
const S = (() => { let i; return { get: () => (i ??= { n: Math.random() }) }; })();
console.log(S.get() === S.get());               // → true
console.log(typeof (function () { return {}; }));   // → function  (without the () call: your bug)
class C { static #i; constructor() { if (C.#i) return C.#i; C.#i = this; this.x = 1; } }
const c1 = new C(); c1.x = 5;
console.log(new C().x);                         // → 5 (the same object)
  • What happens: lazy ??= singleton; without () the IIFE is just a function; the class singleton returns the same object, so x stays 5.
  • Output: true, function, 5.
WayCode ideaInit
Class expressionnew (class {…})(args)Eager
IIFE + closure(() => { let i; return { getInstance } })()Lazy
Static fieldconstructor returns Class.#instanceFirst new
ES moduleexport default objOn first import
थोडक्यात: singleton = एकच instance. IIFE + closure (शेवटी () विसरू नका), static #instance असलेला class, किंवा सर्वात सोपे ES module. class expression चा पद्धतीत constructor अजूनही मिळतो, म्हणून तो पूर्ण singleton नाही.

Chapter 60: Object Property Controlproperty descriptors · defineProperty · getters & setters · private #fields · freeze · seal · preventExtensions
CHAPTER 60 INDEX
  1. Property descriptors & defineProperty
  2. Getters & setters
  3. freeze vs seal vs preventExtensions
  4. Interview Questions & Revision

1. Property descriptors & defineProperty

Definition: Every object property has hidden settings called a property descriptor: value, writable (can it be changed?), enumerable (does it show up in for...in / Object.keys?) and configurable (can it be deleted or redefined?). Object.defineProperty() creates a property with exactly the settings you choose.
Example 1: defineProperty defaults are all false
const u = {};
Object.defineProperty(u, "id", { value: 7 });
u.id = 9;                     // silently ignored (TypeError in strict mode)
console.log(u.id);            // → 7
console.log(Object.keys(u));  // → []   (not enumerable)
console.log(Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(u, "id"));
// → { value: 7, writable: false, enumerable: false, configurable: false }
What happens: with defineProperty, every flag you don't pass defaults to false, so id is read-only, hidden from keys and undeletable. A normal assignment (u.x = 1) instead makes all flags true.
Output: 7, [] and the descriptor shown.
✅ Advantage: create constants or hidden internal properties on an object (this is how built-ins like Array.prototype.map are non-enumerable).
⚠ Trap: the failed write is SILENT in sloppy mode; you only get a TypeError with "use strict".
Figure 122: The three descriptor flags and what each one blocks.

2. Getters & setters

Example 2: a computed property with get / set
const acc = {
  first: "Vishal",
  last: "Shinde",
  get full() { return this.first + " " + this.last; },
  set full(v) { [this.first, this.last] = v.split(" "); }
};
acc.full = "Akshay Patil";          // calls the setter
console.log(acc.first, acc.full);   // → Akshay Akshay Patil
What happens: full looks like a normal property, but reading it runs get, and assigning runs set (with the assigned value as v).
Output: the setter split the name into first/last; the getter rebuilds it.
✅ Advantage: derived values that are always up to date, without calling a method (acc.full, not acc.getFull()).
⚠ Trap: inside a getter, returning this.full calls itself again → "Maximum call stack size exceeded". Store data in another field.
Example 3: a setter that validates (class + private field)
class Temp {
  #c = 0;                                       // private, can't be read from outside
  get f() { return this.#c * 9 / 5 + 32; }
  set c(v) {
    if (v < -273.15) throw new RangeError("below absolute zero");
    this.#c = v;
  }
}
const t = new Temp();
t.c = 100;
console.log(t.f);   // → 212
t.c = -300;         // → RangeError: below absolute zero
What happens: the setter checks the value before storing it in the private #c; the getter converts it to Fahrenheit on read.
✅ Advantage: invalid state can't get in (encapsulation); callers still use simple property syntax.
⚠ Disadvantage: hidden work behind an innocent-looking assignment can surprise readers; keep getters/setters fast and side-effect-free.

3. freeze vs seal vs preventExtensions

Example 4: Object.freeze() (shallow!)
const fz = Object.freeze({ a: 1, n: { b: 2 } });
fz.a = 5;           // ignored
fz.z = 1;           // ignored
delete fz.a;        // ignored
fz.n.b = 99;        // ✔ works: the nested object is NOT frozen
console.log(fz, Object.isFrozen(fz));   // → { a: 1, n: { b: 99 } } true
What happens: freeze makes every own property read-only and blocks adding/deleting, but only one level deep.
✅ Advantage: protects config objects and constants from accidental changes.
⚠ Trap: freeze is SHALLOW; for full protection freeze recursively (deepFreeze). Changes fail silently unless "use strict" (then TypeError).
Example 5: Object.seal()
const se = Object.seal({ a: 1 });
se.a = 2;           // ✔ allowed: existing props stay writable
se.b = 3;           // ignored: can't add
delete se.a;        // ignored: can't delete
console.log(se);    // → { a: 2 }
What happens: seal fixes the SHAPE (no add/delete) but values can still change.
✅ Use when an object must keep exactly its fields, e.g. a form state with a fixed set of keys.
Example 6: Object.preventExtensions()
const pe = Object.preventExtensions({ a: 1 });
pe.b = 2;           // ignored: can't add
delete pe.a;        // ✔ allowed: can delete
console.log(pe);    // → {}
What happens: it only blocks NEW properties; existing ones can be changed or deleted.
MethodAddDeleteChange valueCheck
preventExtensions✖✔✔Object.isExtensible
seal✖✖✔Object.isSealed
freeze✖✖✖Object.isFrozen
प्रत्येक property ला writable, enumerable, configurable असे flags असतात. defineProperty ने ते ठरवता येतात (default false). Getter/setter property सारखे दिसतात पण function चालवतात. freeze सगळे बंद करतो (पण shallow), seal फक्त add/delete बंद करतो, preventExtensions फक्त add बंद करतो.

4. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. Is Object.freeze deep?
  • No, it is shallow. Nested objects stay mutable; write a recursive deepFreeze for full immutability.
Q2. freeze vs seal?
  • Both block adding/deleting; seal still allows changing existing values, freeze doesn't.
Q3. What is const vs Object.freeze?
  • const blocks re-assigning the VARIABLE; freeze blocks changing the OBJECT's properties. You often need both.
Q4. Why don't built-in methods show up in for...in?
  • They are defined with enumerable: false.
Q5. Output-based questions
const o = Object.freeze([1, 2]); o.push(3);   // → TypeError: Cannot add property 2, object is not extensible
const p = {}; Object.defineProperty(p, "x", { value: 1, enumerable: true }); p.x = 2; console.log(p.x, Object.keys(p));   // → 1 ['x']
const q = { get v() { return 5; } }; q.v = 10; console.log(q.v);   // → 5 (no setter, write ignored)
  • What happens: three output questions: a frozen array can't grow, a non-writable property ignores writes, a getter without setter ignores writes.
  • Output: TypeError, 1 ['x'], 5.
ToolUse
definePropertyExact control of one property
get / setComputed / validated properties
#privateTrue privacy in classes
freeze / seal / preventExtensionsLock the object (shallow)
थोडक्यात: const variable लॉक करतो, freeze object लॉक करतो (फक्त पहिली पातळी). Getter/setter ने validation आणि computed values सोपे होतात.

Chapter 61: Proxy & Reflectnew Proxy(target, handler) · traps: get, set, has, ownKeys, apply · Reflect API · validation · default values · negative indexes · reactivity · revocable proxies
CHAPTER 61 INDEX
  1. What is a Proxy?
  2. get trap: logging & default values
  3. set trap: validation & reactivity
  4. has / ownKeys: hiding properties
  5. Arrays & functions
  6. Reflect & revocable proxies
  7. Interview Questions & Revision

1. What is a Proxy?

Definition: A Proxy wraps an object (the target) and lets you intercept basic operations on it (reading, writing, deleting, checking with in, calling…) through functions called traps in a handler object: new Proxy(target, handler). Reflect is a built-in object whose methods (Reflect.get, Reflect.set…) perform the default behaviour of each operation, so traps can call it to "do the normal thing".
Figure 123: Every operation on the proxy goes through a trap first, which may forward it to the target with Reflect.

2. get trap: logging & default values

Example 1: log every property read
const user = { name: "Vishal", age: 25 };
const logged = new Proxy(user, {
  get(target, key, receiver) {
    console.log("read", key);
    return Reflect.get(target, key, receiver);   // default behaviour
  }
});
console.log(logged.name);   // → read name, then Vishal
What happens: logged.name calls the get trap with the target and the key "name"; the trap logs and then returns the real value via Reflect.get.
✅ Advantage: debugging/tracking access without touching the original object.
⚠ Disadvantage: every access goes through a function, so proxies are slower than plain objects in hot code.
Example 2: default value for missing keys
const withDefault = new Proxy({}, {
  get: (t, k) => (k in t ? t[k] : "N/A")
});
console.log(withDefault.city);   // → N/A   (instead of undefined)
What happens: the trap returns "N/A" whenever the key doesn't exist.
✅ Advantage: safe config/translation objects with fallbacks.
⚠ Trap: it also answers for keys like "then" or "toJSON", which can confuse await and JSON.stringify; guard such keys.

3. set trap: validation & reactivity

Example 3: validation
const validated = new Proxy({}, {
  set(t, k, v) {
    if (k === "age" && (typeof v !== "number" || v < 0))
      throw new TypeError("age must be a positive number");
    t[k] = v;
    return true;               // must return true, or strict mode throws
  }
});
validated.age = 30;
validated.age = -1;            // → TypeError: age must be a positive number
console.log(validated.age);    // → 30 (the bad value was never stored)
What happens: every assignment passes through set; invalid values are rejected before reaching the target.
✅ Advantage: one central place for validation rules.
⚠ Trap: forgetting return true → TypeError "'set' on proxy: trap returned falsish" in strict code (modules/classes).
Example 4: reactivity (how Vue 3 works)
const reactive = (obj, onChange) => new Proxy(obj, {
  set(t, k, v) {
    const ok = Reflect.set(t, k, v);
    onChange(k, v);            // e.g. re-render the UI
    return ok;
  }
});
const state = reactive({ count: 0 }, (k, v) => console.log("render", k, v));
state.count++;                 // → render count 1
What happens: state.count++ reads (get) then writes (set); the set trap stores the value and notifies the listener.
✅ Advantage: automatic UI updates; Vue 3's reactive() is built on Proxy.

4. has / ownKeys: hiding properties

Example 5: hide "private" _keys
const hidden = new Proxy({ name: "a", _secret: 1 }, {
  has: (t, k) => !k.startsWith("_") && k in t,
  ownKeys: t => Reflect.ownKeys(t).filter(k => !k.startsWith("_"))
});
console.log("_secret" in hidden, Object.keys(hidden));   // → false ['name']
What happens: has intercepts the in operator; ownKeys intercepts Object.keys, for...in and JSON.stringify.
⚠ Disadvantage: hidden._secret still READS the value (no get trap here), so this is not real security; use #private fields for that.

5. Arrays & functions

Example 6: negative array indexes
const neg = new Proxy([1, 2, 3], {
  get: (t, k, r) =>
    typeof k === "string" && /^-\d+$/.test(k) ? t[t.length + Number(k)] : Reflect.get(t, k, r)
});
console.log(neg[-1], neg.length);   // → 3 3
What happens: property keys arrive as strings ("-1"); the trap converts negative ones to length + index, everything else is forwarded.
✅ Shows the idea behind arr.at(-1) (ES2022), which you should use in real code.
Example 7: apply trap on a function
const fn = new Proxy(function (a, b) { return a + b; }, {
  apply(target, thisArg, args) {
    console.log("call", args);
    return target(...args) * 10;
  }
});
console.log(fn(1, 2));   // → call [1, 2], then 30
What happens: calling the proxy runs apply with the arguments array.
✅ Uses: logging, timing, caching (memoization) or argument checks around any function.

6. Reflect & revocable proxies

Example 8: Reflect methods return results instead of throwing
console.log(Reflect.has({ a: 1 }, "a"));                          // → true   (same as "a" in obj)
console.log(Reflect.ownKeys({ a: 1, [Symbol("s")]: 2 }));          // → ['a', Symbol(s)]   (includes symbols)
console.log(Reflect.defineProperty(Object.freeze({}), "x", { value: 1 }));   // → false (no exception)
What happens: Reflect offers the same operations as functions; failures return false instead of throwing (unlike Object.defineProperty).
✅ Advantage: inside traps, Reflect.method(...arguments) is the correct way to keep default behaviour (including getters' this via receiver).
Example 9: Proxy.revocable()
const { proxy, revoke } = Proxy.revocable({ a: 1 }, {});
console.log(proxy.a);   // → 1
revoke();
proxy.a;                // → TypeError: Cannot perform 'get' on a proxy that has been revoked
What happens: after revoke(), every operation on the proxy throws.
✅ Use: give temporary access to an object (e.g. to a plugin) and take it away later.
Proxy हा object भोवती पहारेकरी आहे: वाचणे, लिहिणे, in, function call अशा क्रिया traps मधून जातात. Validation, default values, logging आणि Vue सारखी reactivity यासाठी वापरतात. Reflect मूळ (default) काम करतो. Proxy थोडे slow असतात.

7. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. What is a Proxy and what is a trap?
  • A wrapper that intercepts operations on a target object; a trap is the handler function for one operation (get, set, has, deleteProperty, apply, construct…).
Q2. Why use Reflect inside traps?
  • It performs the default operation correctly (with receiver/this) and returns a boolean instead of throwing.
Q3. Real-world uses of Proxy?
  • Validation, default values, logging/debugging, reactivity (Vue 3), mocking in tests, negative indexes, access control.
Q4. Downsides?
  • Slower than plain objects, harder to debug, and some built-ins (Map, Date, #private fields) break when wrapped, because their internal slots live on the target.
Q5. Output-based questions
const p = new Proxy({}, { get: () => 42 }); console.log(p.anything, p.x + 1);   // → 42 43
const t = {}; const q = new Proxy(t, {}); q.a = 1; console.log(t.a, q === t);  // → 1 false   (empty handler forwards everything)
console.log(Reflect.has([10], 0), Reflect.ownKeys([10]));                     // → true ['0', 'length']
  • What happens: three output questions: a get trap answers every key; an empty handler forwards to the target (but the proxy is a different object); Reflect helpers.
  • Output: 42 43, 1 false, true ['0', 'length'].
TrapIntercepts
get / setobj.x / obj.x = v
has"x" in obj
deletePropertydelete obj.x
ownKeysObject.keys, for...in
apply / constructfn(), new Fn()
थोडक्यात: new Proxy(target, handler) — traps मध्ये आपले logic, आणि default कामासाठी Reflect. Validation आणि reactivity हे सर्वात जास्त विचारले जाणारे उपयोग आहेत.

Chapter 62: Synchronous vs Asynchronous JSBlocking vs non-blocking · single thread · Web APIs · execution order
CHAPTER 62 INDEX
  1. What are Synchronous and Asynchronous?
  2. Synchronous Code
  3. Asynchronous Code
  4. Notes: Single Thread & Web APIs
  5. Returning a Value from Async Code
  6. console.dir()
  7. Interview Questions & Revision

1. What are Synchronous and Asynchronous?

Your Notes (19_synchronousAsynchronous.js/sync_async.js):
  1. JS executes the synchronous code first and then executes the asynchronous code (callbacks).
  2. Synchronous code is executed line by line, blocking further execution until each line is completed.
  3. Asynchronous code allows other code to continue executing while it waits for an asynchronous operation to finish.
Definition: Synchronous = each statement runs to completion before the next one (blocking). Asynchronous = a slow task (timer, network, file) is handed to the environment (browser Web APIs / Node libuv); JS continues with the next lines, and the task's callback is queued and run later, when the call stack is empty.

2. Synchronous

Your Notes:
  1. Code is executed line by line.
  2. Synchronous is a blocking architecture (i.e. it blocks the execution of subsequent code until the current task is finished).
  3. Execution of each task depends on the completion of the previous task, because it works serially, i.e. each instruction waits for the previous instruction to complete execution.
  4. Due to its synchronous nature, sometimes an important instruction gets blocked by some previous instruction, which causes a delay in the user interface.
  5. Tasks are executed one after another in a sequential manner; each operation must be completed before the next.
// # here code is executed line by line, i.e. the next line is blocked until the previous one completes
console.log("start");
console.log("work in progress");
console.log("end");

const fun2 = () => console.log("function 2 is called..");
const fun1 = () => {
  console.log("function 1 is called");
  fun2();
  console.log("function 2 invoke here....");
};
fun1();
// → start → work in progress → end → function 1 is called → function 2 is called.. → function 2 invoke here....
  • What happens: synchronous code runs line by line; calling fun1 runs it completely (including fun2) before the next line.
  • Output: start, work in progress, end, function 1 is called, function 2 is called.., function 2 invoke here....
  • ✅ Predictable order.
  • ⚠ A slow line blocks everything after it.

3. Asynchronous

Your Notes:
  1. Code is executed "in parallel". ✔ JS itself never runs your code in parallel; it has ONE thread. Only the WAITING (timer, network, file I/O) happens in the background (Web APIs / Node); the callback then runs on the same single thread later. This is concurrency, not parallelism.JavaScript चा code कधीच एकाच वेळी दोन ठिकाणी (parallel) चालत नाही, कारण thread एकच आहे. फक्त वाट पाहण्याचे काम (timer, API) browser/Node background मध्ये करतो, आणि नंतर callback त्याच thread वर चालतो. याला concurrency म्हणतात, parallelism नाही.
  2. Asynchronous is a non-blocking architecture (it does not block the execution of the subsequent code; instead it uses mechanisms like callbacks, promises or async/await to handle asynchronous operations).
  3. Execution of one task does not depend on another task.
  4. Tasks can be in progress simultaneously.
  5. JS starts a long-running task and continues running other tasks while it is in progress.
  6. Asynchronous code execution allows the next instruction to execute immediately and does not block the flow because of a previous instruction.
function fun3() {
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log("function is called...");
  }, 2000);
}
function fun4() {
  console.log("function 4 is called ");
  fun3();
  console.log("function 3 again called.");
}
fun4();
// → function 4 is called
// → function 3 again called.
// → function is called...   (after 2 s, after ALL the synchronous code of the file)
  • What happens: setTimeout hands the callback to the timer and returns immediately; the callback runs after 2 s, when the stack is empty.
  • Output: function 4 is called, function 3 again called., then function is called... after 2 s.
  • ✅ Long waits don't block the page.

4. Notes: Single Thread, Call Stack & Web APIs

Your Notes:
  1. JavaScript is a single-threaded language, and it cannot execute this setTimeout callback in parallel while our code is being executed.
  2. So JS first executes all the synchronous code and then executes the asynchronous code; setTimeout is part of the Web API (provided by the browser/Node, not by the JS engine).
  3. So we use setTimeout to simulate an asynchronous process.
  4. I.e. in JS the synchronous code is executed first, then the asynchronous code (callbacks) starts executing.
Important info:
  1. JS is a single-threaded programming language.
  2. This means that the JS engine has only one call stack; therefore it can do only one thing at a time. ✔ "only on call stack" → only ONE call stack."on" नाही, "one": JS engine कडे एकच call stack असतो.
  3. When executing a script, the JS engine executes code from top to bottom, line by line, in order, in a synchronous manner.
  4. Asynchronous means the JS engine can execute other tasks while waiting for another task to complete (it can handle multiple operations concurrently). For example: ✔ "currently" → concurrently."currently" नाही, "concurrently" (एकाच कालावधीत अनेक कामे हाताळणे).
    1. JS requests data from the server,
    2. and meanwhile displays a spinner.
Figure 124: How async works on one thread: the call stack hands the timer to Web APIs, the callback waits in the queue, and the event loop runs it when the stack is empty.
JS ला एकच thread आणि एकच call stack आहे, म्हणून तो एका वेळी एकच काम करतो. setTimeout, fetch सारखी कामे browser च्या Web APIs कडे जातात. ती पूर्ण झाली की callback queue मध्ये थांबतो, आणि call stack रिकामा झाल्यावर event loop तो चालवतो. म्हणून आधी सगळा synchronous code, मग asynchronous callbacks.

5. Returning a Value from Async Code

Your Notes:
Example 1
console.log("start.....");
function importantAction(username) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    return `subscribed to the ${username}`;   // returns to the timer, not to importantAction's caller
  }, 1000);
}
const call = importantAction("vishal");
console.log(call);   // it returns undefined
// also this is an asynchronous function
console.log("stop");
  • What happens: return inside the timer callback returns to the timer, not to importantAction; importantAction itself returns undefined right away.
  • Output: start....., undefined, stop.
  • ⚠ You can't return a value from async code directly.
to solve this issue, we use a callback function here
// # to solve this issue, we use a callback function here
function interactiveAction1(user_name, cb) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    cb(user_name);
  }, 1000);
}
let res = interactiveAction1("akshu", (message) => {
  console.log(message);   // → akshu   (after 1 s)
});
// (res itself is undefined; the result arrives only inside the callback, or use a Promise, Chapter 64+)
  • What happens: pass a callback; it is called with the result when the timer finishes.
  • Output: akshu after 1 s.
  • ✅ The first way to get async results; promises are the modern way.

Your Notes: the method console.dir() displays an interactive list of the properties of the specified JavaScript object. 
const person = {

};
console.dir(person);   // → { name: 'John', age: 30, greet: [Function: greet] }
console.log(person);   // → same for a plain object
// The difference shows with DOM elements: console.log(document.body) prints the HTML tree,
// console.dir(document.body) prints it as a JS object with all its properties.
  • What happens: console.dir shows an object's properties; for plain objects it looks the same as console.log.
  • Output: the object twice.

→ function 4 is called → function 3 again called. → start..... → undefined → stop → {person} → {person}

7. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. Is JavaScript synchronous or asynchronous?
  • The language is synchronous and single-threaded; async behaviour comes from the environment (Web APIs / Node) plus the event loop, callbacks, promises and async/await.
Q2. If JS is single-threaded, how does setTimeout not block?
  • setTimeout only registers the timer with the browser and returns immediately. The browser counts the time; when it is done, the callback is queued, and the event loop runs it once the call stack is empty.
Q3. Does setTimeout(fn, 0) run immediately?
  • No. It runs after all the current synchronous code and after pending microtasks (promise callbacks); 0 is only a minimum delay.
Q4. Concurrency vs parallelism?
  • Concurrency = several tasks in progress at once by switching (JS's event loop). Parallelism = truly running at the same moment on several threads/cores (Web Workers, worker_threads).
Q5. Output-based questions
console.log(1);
setTimeout(() => console.log(2), 0);
for (let i = 0; i < 1e9; i++) {}      // a long blocking loop
console.log(3);                       // → 1 3 2 (2 waits for the loop, even with 0 ms)
setTimeout(() => console.log("a"), 100);
setTimeout(() => console.log("b"), 50);   // → b a
  • What happens: the 0 ms timer still waits for the long loop to finish (sync code first); shorter timers fire first.
  • Output: 1 3 2, then b a.
  • ⚠ "0 ms" means "as soon as possible after the current code", not immediately.
SynchronousAsynchronous
Line by line, blockingNon-blocking; the result comes later
The next line waitsThe next line runs immediately
e.g. console.log, loops, mathe.g. setTimeout, fetch, events, file I/O
Return value available directlyUse a callback, promise or await
थोडक्यात: synchronous = ओळीने, blocking. asynchronous = वेळखाऊ काम background मध्ये, बाकी code पुढे चालू. JS single-threaded आहे; Web APIs आणि event loop मुळे async शक्य होते. async function मधून थेट return मिळत नाही, callback किंवा promise वापरा.

1. Callback: Why Promises Came into the Picture

Your Notes (18_promise/promise.js): Why are callbacks essential in JS?
  1. Callbacks are essential in JS because they allow you to handle asynchronous operations efficiently without blocking the main execution flow of your code or program; that's why callbacks are needed.
  2. JavaScript is single-threaded, which means it can only execute one task at a time. Many tasks (like reading files, making API requests, or waiting for user input) take time to complete.
  3. Instead of blocking the entire program while waiting for these tasks to finish, you use callbacks to specify what should happen once the operation is complete. (It can't block while waiting for long-running tasks like API calls or file reading.)
  4. So it uses asynchronous callbacks to schedule what should happen after the task finishes, without blocking the rest of the program.
Definition: A callback is a function passed as an argument to another function, to be called later, for example when an async task (timer, network, file) finishes. The browser/Node runs the slow work in the background; the event loop calls the callback when the call stack is free.
JavaScript एका वेळी एकच काम करतो (single-threaded). API call सारखे वेळखाऊ काम पूर्ण होईपर्यंत program थांबू नये म्हणून आपण callback देतो: "काम झाल्यावर हा function चालव". तोपर्यंत बाकीचा code पुढे चालत राहतो.

2. Example without a Callback (Synchronous Code)

Your Notes:
  1. The program would halt and wait for the API request to return.
  2. When you write synchronous code, the program executes each statement one after the other in a linear fashion.

If there's a time-consuming task, like an API call, the program will pause at that line and wait until it gets the result. Once the result is returned, it moves on to the next line of code. Explanation: this simulates synchronous behavior. The code waits for fetchUser() to finish before moving to the next line. It's blocking: fine for quick tasks, but not suitable for real API calls, which take time. 
// # without callback
function fetchUser() {
  const user = { name: "vishal", age: 29 };
  console.log(user);
  return user;
}
console.log("startFetching..");
const data = fetchUser();
console.log("data", data);
console.log("end program");
// → startFetching.. → { name: 'vishal', age: 29 } → data { … } → end program   (strictly in order)
// This simulates synchronous behavior.
// The code waits for fetchUser() to finish before moving to the next line.
// ✔ the comments said fetchUserData(); the function here is fetchUser()
  • What happens: a normal function returns its result immediately, so everything runs in order.
  • Output: startFetching.., the user, data {...}, end program.

3. Adding Asynchronous Nature with a Callback

Your Notes: with a callback, the program continues executing other code while the API request is being processed. Once the request finishes, the callback is executed with the result. 
function fetchUserData(cb) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    const user = { name: "vishal", age: 29 };
    cb(user);
  }, 4000);
}
console.log("start execution..");
fetchUserData(function (user) {
  console.log("user_data :", user);
});
console.log("end of the program");
// → start execution..
// → end of the program
// → user_data : { name: 'vishal', age: 29 }   (after 4 s)
  • What happens: the data is ready only after 4 s, so it is passed to a callback; the rest of the program continues meanwhile.
  • Output: start execution.., end of the program, then user_data after 4 s.

4. Interview: Returning a Value from setTimeout

Your Notes (interviewquestion.js):
Example 1
function fun1(name) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    return name;   // returns to the TIMER, not to the caller of fun1
  }, 0);
}
let call = fun1("vishal");
console.log(call);   // here it returns undefined (fun1 itself returns nothing)
  • What happens: return inside setTimeout doesn't return from fun1.
  • Output: undefined.
to fix this issue we have to use a callback
// # to fix this issue we have to use a callback
function fun2(userName, cb) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    cb(userName);
  }, 0);
}
function fun3(lName, cb) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    cb(lName);
  }, 0);
}
function fun4(age, cb) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    cb(age);
  }, 1000);
}
  • What happens: each function delivers its result through a callback.
  • Output: (definitions only).
if you have functions that need to be called one after another
// # if you have functions that need to be called one after another
const res = fun2("vishal", function (user) {
  console.log(user);              // → vishal
  fun3("shinde", function (lName) {
    console.log(lName);           // → shinde
    fun4(56, function (age) {
      console.log(age);           // → 56   (after 1 s)
    });
  });
});
res;   // undefined (fun2 returns nothing); this line does nothing
  • What happens: to run them in order, each next call goes inside the previous callback: the nesting grows to the right.
  • Output: vishal, shinde, 56 (after 1 s).
  • ⚠ This growing pyramid is callback hell.
If you notice, there is nesting of callback functions, which makes your code a little messy. If you have more callback functions nested inside each other, it forms a weird-looking pyramid-like structure, sometimes called the pyramid of doom, and this concept is known as callback hell. It's called callback hell because it has so many nested callbacks, one inside another, that it is very hard to read and understand the code. What is the solution for this problem? (→ Promises, Chapter 64.)
setTimeout मधला return फक्त timer ला value देतो, fun1 ला नाही. म्हणून call = undefined. बाहेर value हवी असेल तर callback (किंवा promise) वापरावा लागतो.

5. Callback Hell

Your Notes (promise.js):
  1. So here callbacks are used to handle the asynchronous operations in your code.
  2. But when multiple asynchronous operations depend on each other, i.e. if you have several asynchronous operations that need to run in sequence and each one depends on the result of the previous operation, you end up nesting callbacks within each other, which makes the code difficult to follow.
  3. So callback hell occurs when you have multiple nested callbacks, especially in asynchronous code, and the code becomes hard to read, maintain and debug.
Why callbacks? Callbacks are needed to:
  1. handle asynchronous operations (API calls, file reads, etc.);
  2. avoid blocking the main execution thread in JavaScript (which is single-threaded);
  3. define what to do after an async operation completes.

Problem: when multiple asynchronous operations depend on each other, you need to nest callbacks, which leads to callback hell. Example: 
console.log("start");
function importantAction(user_name, cb) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log(user_name);
    cb(user_name);
  }, 2000);
}
function likeVideo(user_name, video, cb) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log(user_name + " " + video + " ");
    cb(user_name, video);
  }, 500);
}
function sharedVideo(user_name, video, like, cb) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log(user_name + " " + video + " " + like);
    cb(user_name, video, like);
  }, 1000);
}
importantAction("vishal", (user_name) => {
  return likeVideo(user_name, "js", (user_name, video) => {
    return sharedVideo(user_name, video, "youtube", (user_name, video, like) => {
      console.log(user_name + " " + video + " " + like);
    });
  });
});
// intended output: start → vishal → vishal js → vishal js youtube → vishal js youtube
  • What happens: three dependent steps nested inside each other's callbacks (2 s, then 0.5 s, then 1 s).
  • Output: start, vishal, vishal js, vishal js youtube ×2.
  • ⚠ Hard to read, hard to handle errors at every level.
✔ (verified in Node) in promise.js, importantAction / likeVideo / sharedVideo are declared with the SAME names 3 times (promise version, callback version, promise version). Function declarations are hoisted and the LAST one wins for the whole file, so likeVideo("js").then(…) at line 106 calls the callback version, which returns undefined → TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'then'), and the file stops there. Give each version its own name (e.g. likeVideoCb) or put them in separate files. एकाच नावाचे function declarations file मध्ये 3 वेळा लिहिले आहेत. hoisting मुळे शेवटचे declaration संपूर्ण file साठी वापरले जाते. त्यामुळे likeVideo("js") callback version ला call करतो, तो undefined परत करतो, आणि .then वर TypeError येऊन file तिथेच थांबते. प्रत्येक version ला वेगळे नाव द्या.

6. Why It's a Problem

Your Notes:
  1. Code becomes deeply nested.
  2. Hard to read and debug.
  3. Difficult to handle errors in each step.
  4. Difficult to scale or modify.
Callback hell refers to a situation in programming where callbacks are nested within each other, creating a deep, pyramidal structure. This makes the code harder to read, understand, maintain and debug. It is especially common in JavaScript, where asynchronous operations (like network requests, timers or file I/O) require callbacks to handle the results.
So callbacks face the issue of callback hell. Issues with callback hell:
  1. Indentation and readability (it creates a nested structure): as the level of nesting increases, the code becomes more difficult to read and maintain.
  2. Error handling: managing errors at every level of nesting becomes complicated.
  3. Reusability: the functions are tightly coupled, making them difficult to reuse in different contexts.
  4. Readability: the code is difficult to read because of the deep nesting.
  5. Maintainability: as more features are added, maintaining the code becomes complicated due to the complex structure.
  6. Reusability: it's harder to reuse functions, as the logic is tied up in deeply nested callbacks.
Problems with callbacks (from your combinator notes):
  1. callback hell (the nested structure becomes unreadable);
  2. inversion of control: you hand control of your function to another function, and hope it calls your callback correctly (once, not twice, not never, with the right arguments).
Figure 125: Callback hell: each dependent step nests one level deeper (pyramid of doom).
Callback hell म्हणजे एकमेकांवर अवलंबून असलेल्या async कामांसाठी callback च्या आत callback लिहित जाणे. त्यामुळे code पिरॅमिडसारखा तिरका होतो (pyramid of doom). तो वाचायला, debug करायला आणि errors हाताळायला कठीण होतो. Inversion of control म्हणजे आपला callback दुसऱ्याच्या हातात देणे आणि तो योग्य वेळी, फक्त एकदाच call करेल अशी आशा ठेवणे.

7. Callback Hell in Depth (23_callback/callBackHell.js)

Your Notes: callback hell
  1. Callback hell, also known as the "pyramid of doom", refers to a situation in asynchronous JavaScript programming where multiple nested callback functions are used to handle asynchronous operations.
  2. This happens when multiple asynchronous operations depend on each other, and each operation requires a callback to execute the next step.
  3. This often results in code that is difficult to read, understand and maintain because of its deeply nested structure.
  4. Callback hell refers to a situation in asynchronous programming where callbacks are nested within callbacks, leading to code that is difficult to read, debug and maintain.
  5. Callback hell occurs when multiple callbacks are nested inside each other.
  6. Callback hell leads to complex, hard-to-maintain code. ✔ "create a complete … code" → COMPLEX code."complete" नाही, "complex" (गुंतागुंतीचा) code.
  7. Callback hell is a phenomenon that happens when multiple callbacks are nested on top of each other.
When does callback hell occur?
  1. When you are dealing with a series of asynchronous operations (like reading a file, making an API request or handling events) that depend on each other, and you need to wait for a response before executing the next part of the code, so you handle them using callback functions.
  2. Multiple dependent asynchronous operations: each step in an asynchronous process depends on the result of the previous step, requiring nested callbacks. Imagine you need to do three asynchronous tasks sequentially:
Example 1
task1(function (result1) {
  task2(result1, function (result2) {
    task3(result2, function (result3) {
      // Final result processing
      console.log("All tasks completed with result:", result3);
    });
  });
});
// ⚠ this is a SHAPE example: task1/task2/task3 are not defined, so running the file stops here with
//   ReferenceError: task1 is not defined (verified in Node). Keep it commented out, or define the tasks.
  • What happens: the typical callback-hell shape (task1 → task2 → task3); the tasks aren't defined, so running it throws.
  • Output: ReferenceError as written.
1. Task 1 starts with a callback for task1.
// 1. Task 1 starts with a callback for task1.
// 2. Once task1 is complete, Task 2 starts with its callback, and Task 3 is nested inside Task 2.
// 3. This results in deep nesting, as each function needs to wait for the previous one to finish before executing.

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("work 1 is done");
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log("work 2 is done");
    setTimeout(() => {
      console.log("work 3 is done");
    });
  });
});
// → work 1 is done → work 2 is done → work 3 is done
  • What happens: nested timers run one after another.
  • Output: work 1 is done, work 2 is done, work 3 is done.
task1, task2, task3 कुठेही define केलेले नाहीत, म्हणून file पहिल्याच ओळीवर ReferenceError देऊन थांबते. हे फक्त आकार (shape) दाखवण्याचे उदाहरण आहे; ते comment करा किंवा functions define करा. Example of callback hell: 
console.log("start");
function importantAction(username, callback) {
  setTimeout(() => { callback(`welcome ${username}`); }, 1000);
}
function likeTheVideo(video, callback) {
  setTimeout(() => { callback(`please like the video ${video}`); }, 500);
}
function shareVideo(videotaped, callBack) {
  setTimeout(() => { callBack(`please share the video ${videotaped}`); }, 300);
}
// functions executing without callback chaining
importantAction("akshu", function (username) { console.log(username); });
likeTheVideo("java", function (message) { console.log(message); });
shareVideo("testing", function (message) { console.log(message); });
// → please share the video testing (300 ms) → please like the video java (500 ms) → welcome akshu (1 s)
  • What happens: three independent timers run in parallel; they finish in order of their delays, not in code order.
  • Output: share (300 ms), like (500 ms), welcome (1 s).
  • ⚠ Without chaining, async steps don't wait for each other.
What happens in the above code, where each function is executed separately?
  1. These functions are executed independently of each other.
  2. importantAction is called first, but likeTheVideo and shareVideo are called immediately after it (without waiting for the previous ones to finish).
  3. Each of the functions (importantAction, likeTheVideo and shareVideo) runs concurrently, without any sequence dependency between them, so the shortest timer prints first. ✔ "run in parallel" → their TIMERS run concurrently; the callbacks still run one at a time on the single JS thread (Chapter 62)."parallel" नाही: फक्त timers एकाच वेळी चालतात, पण callbacks JS च्या एकाच thread वर एकामागून एक चालतात. म्हणून सर्वात लहान timer चा output आधी येतो.
Advantages: the code is more straightforward and doesn't require deep nesting; functions are executed as soon as possible, so there is no waiting for each one to complete before the next starts.
Disadvantages: if you need to ensure a specific order of execution, this approach doesn't provide that sequence by default. You would have to add logic (e.g. chaining callbacks or using Promises) to ensure the correct order. 
// callback chaining
importantAction("vishal", function (username) {
  console.log(username);
  likeTheVideo("javascript", function (message) {
    console.log(message);
    shareVideo("node js", function (message) {
      console.log(message);
    });
  });
});
// → welcome vishal (1 s) → please like the video javascript (+0.5 s) → please share the video node js (+0.3 s)
  • What happens: chaining by nesting forces the order: each step starts only after the previous callback.
  • Output: welcome vishal, like…, share… (one after another).
What happens in callback chaining? This is a typical callback chain, where the functions are executed in sequence. importantAction starts first. After 1 second, it logs the welcome message and then calls likeTheVideo. After another 500 ms, it logs the message to like the video and calls shareVideo. Finally, after 300 ms, it logs the message to share the video.
Advantages: ensures that each step happens one after the other in a predictable sequence.
Disadvantages: can lead to "callback hell" or the "pyramid of doom", where functions are nested too deeply, making the code harder to read and maintain.
Note: notice the nesting of callbacks: your code becomes messier, a weird-looking pyramid-like structure, sometimes called the pyramid of doom. With more nested functions, this concept is called callback hell (so many callback functions nested inside each other that it is very hard to read and understand). So what is the solution for this code? Promises.

How is callback hell problematic? (What are the issues with callbacks?)

  1. In callback hell, your code starts to grow horizontally instead of vertically.
  2. Nested callbacks: when you have multiple asynchronous operations that depend on each other, you might end up nesting callbacks within each other; the indentation deepens, creating a pyramid-like structure.
  3. Readability: callback hell makes your code less readable and harder to understand, because it introduces a lot of indentation and visual noise.
  4. Error handling: handling errors in a nested callback structure can be complex: you need to make sure you handle each error at the appropriate level and propagate it correctly. This can lead to error-prone code, especially when dealing with different error scenarios in different layers of nesting. Handling errors in multiple nested callbacks is cumbersome: each callback needs its own error handling, which leads to repetitive and inconsistent error-handling code. If an error occurs in one of the callbacks, the entire chain may fail, and debugging that error could require tracking multiple callback chains. ✔ "error-porn code" → error-PRONE code."error-porn" नाही, "error-prone" (चुका होण्याची शक्यता जास्त असलेला) code.
  5. Maintainability: with deeply nested callbacks, managing changes in the logic becomes difficult. If a bug occurs, debugging it becomes challenging, as you need to trace through multiple levels of nesting. Adding new features or modifying the flow often requires significant refactoring, which risks introducing more bugs.
  6. Debugging: debugging code with deeply nested callbacks can be frustrating; identifying the source of an issue, setting breakpoints and inspecting variables is more challenging because of the complex structure of the code.
  7. Testing: unit testing is harder due to the nested structure. Since the functions are tightly coupled and depend on one another, isolating them for testing can be complex and inefficient.
  8. Scalability: adding more functionality to an application that uses callback hell can lead to even deeper nesting, making the code less scalable. The complexity grows quickly as new requirements are added, leading to a less robust and extensible codebase.

To address the issues associated with callback hell, JavaScript introduced several techniques and patterns:

  • Promises: promises are a more structured way to handle asynchronous operations, making code more readable and maintainable. Promises let us chain operations and handle errors more gracefully. Promises also enable the async/await syntax, which makes asynchronous code look more like synchronous code. ✔ "make synchronous code more look like synchronous code" → makes ASYNCHRONOUS code look like synchronous code.async/await मुळे asynchronous code synchronous सारखा दिसतो.
  • async/await: the async/await syntax is built on top of promises and provides a more natural way to write asynchronous code that resembles synchronous code. It reduces nested callbacks.
  • Modularization: breaking your code into smaller, modular functions can help reduce the depth of callback nesting. This makes the code more organized and easier to manage.
  • Named functions: using named functions instead of anonymous functions as callbacks makes your code more readable and reduces the indentation level.
NOTE: using the promise and async/await approach lets us write asynchronous code in a more linear and structured fashion, reducing the nesting and making complex asynchronous flows easier to manage. Promises let you chain .then() calls, enabling a clear and linear flow of logic. 
// the same chain with named functions (no promises yet): flat instead of a pyramid
function onWelcome(msg) { console.log(msg); likeTheVideo("javascript", onLike); }
function onLike(msg)    { console.log(msg); shareVideo("node js", onShare); }
function onShare(msg)   { console.log(msg); }
importantAction("vishal", onWelcome);
  • What happens: named functions instead of inline callbacks keep the code flat.
  • Output: same order as above.
  • ✅ A simple way to reduce callback hell without promises.
callBackHell.js सारांश: एकमेकांवर अवलंबून async कामे callback च्या आत callback लिहून केल्यास pyramid of doom तयार होतो. स्वतंत्र calls लगेच सुरू होतात आणि ज्याचा timer लहान तो आधी संपतो. क्रम हवा असल्यास chaining करावे लागते, पण त्यामुळे nesting वाढते. उपाय: promises, async/await, named functions आणि लहान modular functions.

8. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. What is a callback function? Is every callback asynchronous?
  • A function passed to another function to be called later. No: arr.map(cb) calls its callback synchronously; setTimeout(cb) calls it asynchronously.
Q2. What is callback hell and how do you avoid it?
  • Deeply nested dependent callbacks. Avoid it with named functions, Promises (flat .then chains), async/await, and one central error handler.
Q3. What is inversion of control?
  • Giving your continuation (callback) to third-party code: it may call it twice, never, too early or with wrong args. Promises fix this: they settle once, and YOU attach handlers.
Q4. Why can't you return a value from inside setTimeout?
  • The outer function has already returned (undefined) before the timer fires. Pass a callback, or return a Promise and resolve it inside the timer.
Q5. Output-based questions
console.log("A");
setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 0);
console.log("C");                     // → A C B
function f(cb) { cb(); console.log("D"); }
f(() => console.log("E"));            // → E D (synchronous callback)
function g() { setTimeout(() => { return 5; }); }
console.log(g());                     // → undefined
  • What happens: async callback runs after sync code (A C B); a sync callback runs immediately (E D); returning from a timer gives nothing to the caller.
  • Output: A C B, E D, undefined.
ConceptRemember
CallbackA function passed to run later
Async callbackRuns after the current code finishes (timer / IO)
Callback hellNested dependent callbacks → pyramid
Inversion of controlTrusting other code to call you correctly
FixPromises, chaining, async/await
थोडक्यात: callback = नंतर चालवायला दिलेला function. एकमेकांवर अवलंबून callbacks nest केल्यास callback hell होतो. setTimeout मधून return करता येत नाही. उपाय: Promise आणि async/await.
