Chapter 64: Promises: BasicsStates · executor · resolve / reject · then / catch / finally · async/await intro
CHAPTER 64 INDEX
  1. What is a Promise?
  2. Promise States
  3. How .then() Works
  4. Creating a Promise (executor, resolve, reject)
  5. Promise.resolve() & Promise.reject()
  6. Functions that Return a Promise
  7. State Rules
  8. Consuming a Promise: then / catch / finally
  9. Consuming with async/await
  10. Separate onFulfilled / onRejected Handlers
  11. Summary & Advantages
  12. Running Promises "Recursively"
  13. Interview Questions & Revision

1. Promise

Your Notes (promise.js):
  1. A promise is a good way to handle asynchronous operations (or a placeholder for the result of an asynchronous operation).
  2. A promise in JavaScript is an object that represents the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation, with its resulting value.
  3. A promise basically represents the upcoming completion or failure of an asynchronous operation or event, with its resulting value.
  4. They are a cleaner and more structured way that helps avoid "callback hell".
  5. In JavaScript, a promise is an object that encapsulates the result of an asynchronous operation. ✔ "result of an Synchronous operation" → ASYNCHRONOUS operation (same fix in the Summary below).Promise हा asynchronous (नंतर पूर्ण होणाऱ्या) कामाचा result ठेवतो, synchronous नाही.
  6. Promises provide a structured way to handle asynchronous tasks and offer significant advantages over traditional callbacks.
Definition: A Promise is an object with a state (pending → fulfilled or rejected) and a result (value or reason). It settles only ONCE. You react to it with .then / .catch / .finally or await; those callbacks always run asynchronously (as microtasks).

2. Promise States

Your Notes:
  1. A promise has 3 conditions or states:
    1. pending
    2. fulfilled, with a result value
    3. rejected, with a reason
  2. A promise has built-in methods like then and catch to handle the result of an asynchronous operation when it completes or encounters an error.
  3. You need to use the .then() method (or await) to handle the promise. ✔ "you must need to use .then()": .then() OR await (async/await, section 9).promise हाताळायला .then() किंवा await दोन्ही चालतात.
  4. promise.then(onFulfilled, onRejected): the .then() method takes 2 arguments, one for success and another for failure. The 2nd argument is optional.
Note:
  1. At the beginning the state of a promise is pending (indicating the asynchronous operation is in progress), so while the promise object is pending, the result is undefined. ✔ "synchronous operation in process" → ASYNCHRONOUS operation.pending म्हणजे asynchronous काम अजून चालू आहे.
  2. Depending on the result of the asynchronous operation, the state changes to either fulfilled or rejected.
  3. So the fulfilled state indicates that the asynchronous operation completed successfully (when the promise object is fulfilled → the result is the value).
  4. So the rejected state indicates that the asynchronous operation failed (when the promise object is rejected → the result is an error object).
Figure 126: Promise states: pending settles once, to fulfilled or rejected.
Promise च्या 3 अवस्था: pending (काम चालू), fulfilled (यश, value मिळते), rejected (अपयश, error मिळते). एकदा fulfilled किंवा rejected झाल्यावर (settled) state कधीच बदलत नाही.

3. How the .then() Method Works

Your Notes: promise.then(onFulfilled, onRejected)
  1. onFulfilled is a function used to handle the success (the resolved value).
  2. onRejected is a function used to handle the failure (the rejection reason); it is optional.
promise.then((res) => {
  resolved(res);   // ⚠ resolved isn't defined here; normally you would just use res, e.g. console.log(res)
}).catch((error) => console.log(error));
  • What happens: then receives the resolved value; catch receives the error.
  • Output: (depends on the promise).
If you want to handle failures separately, you can also use .catch().

4. Create a Promise

Your Notes:
  1. Create a promise using the Promise() constructor.
  2. Calling this constructor creates a new instance of the Promise class; it takes a function, often referred to as the executor function.
  3. So the Promise constructor accepts a callback function with 2 arguments, resolve and reject, that typically performs an asynchronous operation (so this callback is referred to as the executor function). The executor runs immediately (synchronously).
  4. In a Promise object, resolve and reject are functions used to determine the final state of the promise:
    1. resolve(value): marks the promise as fulfilled and passes the provided value to the .then() method.
    2. reject(error): marks the promise as rejected and passes the error to the .catch() method for handling.
let newPromise = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  setTimeout(() => {
    const result = false;
    if (result) resolve("fetch data");
    else reject(new Error("not fetch"));
  }, 2000);
});
// 1. to run or execute the promise, use .then()
// 2. then() runs when the promise is fulfilled
// 3. if it fails, the promise is not fulfilled, and we get the result in catch
newPromise
  .then((res) => {
    console.log(res);
  })
  .catch((e) => {
    console.log(e);   // → Error: not fetch   (after 2 s)
  });
// 1. then() is used to get the result when the promise is fulfilled
// 2. catch() is used to get the error when the promise fails
  • What happens: the executor runs a 2-second task; because result is false it calls reject, so .catch runs instead of .then.
  • Output: Error: not fetch (after 2 s).
  • ✅ Promises separate the success and error paths cleanly.
  • ⚠ Always reject with an Error object to keep the stack trace.
✔ ".then() is used to run or execute the promise". The promise is already running from the moment new Promise(…) is called; .then() only SUBSCRIBES to its result.new Promise(...) लिहिल्याबरोबर executor लगेच चालतो. .then() promise चालवत नाही, फक्त result आल्यावर काय करायचे ते सांगतो.

5. How to Define a Promise that is Directly Resolved or Rejected

Your Notes:
1. a directly resolved promise
// 1. a directly resolved promise
let promise = Promise.resolve("fetch successFully...");
console.log(promise);   // → Promise { 'fetch successFully...' }
promise
  .then((result) => console.log(result))   // → fetch successFully...
  .catch((error) => console.log(error));
  • What happens: Promise.resolve creates an already-fulfilled promise; then still runs asynchronously.
  • Output: Promise { 'fetch successFully...' }, then fetch successFully...
  • ✅ Wrap a plain value as a promise.
2. a directly rejected promise
// 2. a directly rejected promise
let promise1 = Promise.reject("failed to fetch....");
console.log(promise1);  // → Promise { <rejected> 'failed to fetch....' }
promise1.then((res) => console.log(res)).catch((error) => console.log(error));   // → failed to fetch....
  • What happens: Promise.reject creates an already-rejected promise; catch handles it.
  • Output: Promise { … }, failed to fetch....

6. Creating a Promise by Defining a Function that Returns One

Your Notes: you can create a promise by defining a function that returns a promise. This function usually encapsulates some asynchronous operation; inside it you manually create a promise and resolve or reject it based on the result of the asynchronous operation (here each promise is handled separately). 
function importantAction(user_name) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => {
      resolve(user_name);
    }, 2000);
  });
}
function likeVideo(video) {
  return new Promise((resolved, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => {
      resolved(video);
    }, 3000);
  });
}
function sharedVideo(shared) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => {
      resolve(shared);
    }, 1000);
  });
}
importantAction("vishal").then((result) => console.log(result))
  .catch((error) => console.log(error));
likeVideo("js")
  .then((res) => console.log(res))
  .catch((error) => console.log(error));
sharedVideo("on youtube")
  .then((result) => console.log(result))
  .catch((error) => console.log(error));
// intended output (all start together): on youtube (1 s) → vishal (2 s) → js (3 s)
// ⚠ in your file this crashes at likeVideo("js") because of the duplicate declarations (see Chapter 63 §5)
  • What happens: three promises start at the same time, so their results arrive in order of their delays.
  • Output: on youtube (1 s), vishal (2 s), js (3 s).
  • ⚠ Starting them together doesn't make them run in sequence; chain them if order matters.

7. Note: State Rules

Your Notes:
  1. Promises cannot go from the fulfilled state to the rejected state or vice versa, and they cannot go back from the fulfilled or rejected state to the pending state.
  2. Once a new promise object is created, its state is pending.
  3. If a promise reaches the fulfilled or rejected state, it is settled. ✔ "state if resolved". The correct term for "fulfilled or rejected" is SETTLED. ("Resolved" means the promise is locked to an outcome, which may be another promise.)fulfilled किंवा rejected झालेल्या promise ला "settled" म्हणतात. "resolved" याचा अर्थ थोडा वेगळा आहे.
new Promise((res, rej) => { res(1); rej("x"); res(2); }).then(console.log);   // → 1 (only the FIRST call counts)
  • What happens: a promise settles only once: the first resolve wins and later calls are ignored.
  • Output: 1.
  • ✅ Fixes the "callback called twice" problem.

8. How to Consume a Promise

Your Notes: to consume a promise in JS:
  1. use the then(), catch() and finally() blocks
  2. or use async/await
Example 1
// ex
const fetchData = () => {
  return new Promise((resolved, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => {
      //   resolved("fetch data successfully....");
      reject("failed to load...");
    }, 1000);
  });
};
  • What happens: a function that returns a promise which rejects after 1 s.
  • Output: (definition).
1. consume the promise using then(), catch() and finally()
// 1. consume the promise using then(), catch() and finally()
fetchData()
  .then((result) => {
    console.log("result123", result);
    console.log(result);
  })
  .catch((error) => {
    console.log(error);   // → failed to load...
  })
  .finally(() => {
    console.log("clean up function always run if the promise is resolved or not..");
  });
  • What happens: then for success, catch for failure, finally always runs at the end.
  • Output: failed to load..., then the cleanup message.
  • ✅ finally is ideal for hiding loaders.

1. then() method

  1. The then() method is used to handle the result of a Promise once it has been fulfilled (resolved) or rejected.
  2. Syntax: promise.then(onFulfilled, onRejected)
  3. then() accepts two callback functions:
  4. onFulfilled: this function is called when the promise is fulfilled (resolved).
  5. onRejected: this function is called when the promise is rejected.
  6. Both callbacks are optional, meaning you can provide either or both of them.

2. catch() method

  1. The catch() method is used to handle errors when a promise is rejected.
  2. Syntax: promise.catch(onRejected)
  3. catch() is essentially shorthand for then(undefined, onRejected).
  4. It is used when you are only interested in handling the rejection and not the fulfillment of the promise.

3. finally() method

  1. The finally() method is used to execute a block of code after the promise has settled, regardless of whether it was fulfilled or rejected.
  2. Syntax: promise.finally(onSettled)
  3. The code inside finally() runs after the promise settles, whether the promise was fulfilled or rejected. (It receives no argument and passes the original result through.)

9. Consuming a Promise with async/await

Your Notes: we can also consume a promise using async/await: 
const ConsumePromise = async () => {
  try {
    const data = await fetchData();
    console.log("data", data);
  } catch (error) {
    console.log(error);        // → failed to load...
  } finally {
    console.log("finish...");  // → finish...
  }
};
console.log(fetchData);        // → [Function: fetchData]
let res = ConsumePromise();
console.log("res..", res);     // → res.. Promise { <pending> }
// ✔ comment said "here return promise as reject". The error is CAUGHT inside, so this promise
//    FULFILLS with undefined; it is pending at the moment it is logged
  • What happens: the same promise consumed with async/await + try/catch/finally; an async function always returns a promise (pending when logged).
  • Output: [Function: fetchData], res.. Promise { }, failed to load..., finish...
  • ✅ Reads like synchronous code.
ConsumePromise मधला error try/catch ने पकडला गेला, म्हणून तो promise reject होत नाही, undefined value ने fulfil होतो. log केला तेव्हा तो अजून pending होता. async/await: a cleaner way to handle promises
  • async makes a function return a promise.
  • await waits for the promise to resolve or reject.
  • If resolved → it continues in the try block.
  • If rejected → it goes to the catch block.

10. Example 2: Separate Handler Functions

Your Notes:
Example 1
let success = true;
function getUser() {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    if (success) {
      setTimeout(() => {
        resolve([
          { username: "vishal", email: "shindev05@gmail.com" },
          { username: "shinde", email: "test@gamil.com" },
        ]);
      }, 2000);
    } else {
      reject("failed to load user data...");
    }
  });
}
  • What happens: getUser resolves with an array after 2 s, or rejects at once if success is false.
  • Output: (definition).
if you don't want to use catch, you can handle everything with then only; define handler f
// # if you don't want to use catch, you can handle everything with then only; define handler functions this way:
function onFulfilled(user) {
  console.log("user345", user);
  // # What it does:
  // It is a callback function that is used when a Promise is resolved (fulfilled).
  // The user parameter receives the resolved value from the Promise.
  // It logs the message "user345" followed by the data it received.
}
function onRejected(error) {
  console.log(error);
}
  • What happens: separate named handler functions for success and failure.
  • Output: (definitions).
What it does:
// # What it does:
// This is a callback function that runs when a Promise is rejected (failed).
// The error parameter receives the rejected error message.
// It logs the error to the console.
getUser()
  .then(onFulfilled, onRejected)
  .finally(() => {
    console.log(' "Promise settled (fulfilled or rejected). Cleanup actions can be performed here "');
  });
// → user345 [ {…}, {…} ]  → "Promise settled …"   (after 2 s)
  • What happens: then(onFulfilled, onRejected) passes both handlers in one call; finally runs after either.
  • Output: user345 […], then the settled message.
  • ⚠ then(ok, err) doesn't catch errors thrown inside ok; a trailing .catch does.
Note: then(onFulfilled, onRejected) is NOT the same as .then(onFulfilled).catch(onRejected): with the 2-argument form, an error thrown inside onFulfilled is not caught by onRejected.

11. Summary & Advantages

Your Notes (Summary):
  1. A Promise is an object that encapsulates the result of an asynchronous operation (✔ "synchronous").
  2. A promise gives trust and a guarantee for your whole transaction. ✔ "garrulity" → guarantee."garrulity" नाही, "guarantee" (हमी).
  3. Promise objects are immutable (yes: once a Promise is settled (resolved or rejected), its state cannot change). Also, the .then(), .catch() and .finally() methods let you handle the result, but they don't change the original Promise (each returns a NEW promise).
  4. A promise starts in the pending state and ends in either the fulfilled state or the rejected state. The then() method schedules or handles a promise by giving it a callback to execute when the promise is fulfilled, and the catch method schedules a callback to invoke when the promise is rejected.
  5. Place the code you want to execute whether the promise is fulfilled or rejected in the finally() method.
What are the advantages of promises? Promises in JavaScript provide asynchronous execution, improved readability, better error handling, chaining for sequential operations, and avoidance of callback hell. Here are the advantages, each explained separately:
  1. Asynchronous execution: promises allow non-blocking code execution, so the program continues running while waiting for an operation to complete.
  2. Improved readability: promises make asynchronous code more readable and structured compared to nested callbacks.
  3. Better error handling: errors can be caught using .catch(), making debugging and handling failures easier.
  4. Chaining for sequential operations: multiple asynchronous tasks can be executed in sequence using .then(), avoiding deeply nested callbacks.
  5. Avoidance of callback hell: promises prevent excessive nesting of callbacks, making the code cleaner and more maintainable.
  6. It solves the issue of inversion of control.
Promises solve these issues:
  1. promises flatten the nesting and improve readability (by promise chaining);
  2. they give control back to the caller;
  3. better error handling using .catch().

12. How to Run Promises "Recursively"

Your Notes:
  1. Recursion is the process in which a function repeatedly calls itself until a condition is met that makes it stop.
  2. Recursion is the technique of making a function call itself. (A recursive function is a function that calls itself during its execution.)
function importantAction(user_name) {
  return new Promise((resolved, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => { resolved(`subscribed to the ${user_name}`); }, 500);
  });
}
function likeVideo(video) {
  return new Promise((resolved, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => { resolved(`like the video ${video}`); }, 100);
  });
}
function sharedVideo(shared) {
  return new Promise((resolved, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => { resolved(`share the video ${shared}`); }, 2000);
  });
}
promiseRecursively([
  importantAction("vishal"),
  likeVideo("js"),
  sharedVideo("social media"),
]);
function promiseRecursively(functionPromise) {
  if (functionPromise.length === 0) return;
  let currentPromise = functionPromise.shift();
  currentPromise
    .then((res) => console.log(res))
    .catch((err) => console.log(err));
  promiseRecursively(functionPromise);
}
// → like the video js (100 ms) → subscribed to the vishal (500 ms) → share the video social media (2 s)
  • What happens: the recursive function attaches handlers to promises that are ALREADY running, so it doesn't wait; results arrive by delay.
  • Output: like (100 ms), subscribed (500 ms), share (2 s).
  • ⚠ Passing promises means the work has already started.
✔ this is NOT sequential. All 3 promises START when the array is built (the functions are already called), and the recursion only attaches handlers without waiting, so the results print in timer order. For true one-by-one execution, pass FUNCTIONS and recurse inside .then: 
function runSequentially(tasks) {
  if (tasks.length === 0) return Promise.resolve();
  const [first, ...rest] = tasks;
  return first().then((res) => {
    console.log(res);
    return runSequentially(rest);   // the next task starts only after this one finishes
  });
}
runSequentially([() => importantAction("vishal"), () => likeVideo("js"), () => sharedVideo("social media")]);
// → subscribed to the vishal → like the video js → share the video social media
  • What happens: pass FUNCTIONS that create promises and start the next one inside then: true sequential execution.
  • Output: subscribed, like, share (in order).
  • ✅ The pattern behind sequential async loops.
array बनवतानाच तिन्ही functions call होतात, म्हणून तिन्ही promises एकाच वेळी सुरू होतात. recursion फक्त .then जोडते, थांबत नाही, त्यामुळे output timer च्या क्रमाने येतो. क्रमाने चालवायचे असल्यास functions पाठवा आणि पुढचा call .then च्या आत करा.

13. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. What is a Promise? What are its states?
  • An object representing the future result of an async operation: pending → fulfilled (value) or rejected (reason). It settles once and is immutable after that.
Q2. Does the executor run synchronously?
  • Yes. new Promise(fn) calls fn immediately. Only the .then/.catch/.finally callbacks run later (as microtasks), even if the promise is already resolved.
Q3. then(a, b) vs then(a).catch(b)?
  • In then(a, b), b does not catch errors thrown inside a; in then(a).catch(b) it does. Prefer one .catch at the end.
Q4. What does finally receive and return?
  • No arguments. It passes the original value/reason through (unless it throws or returns a rejected promise). Use it for cleanup like hiding loaders.
Q5. How do you convert a callback API into a Promise (promisify)?
  • const wait = ms => new Promise(res => setTimeout(res, ms));. Wrap the call, then resolve in the success callback and reject in the error callback (Node: util.promisify).
Q6. Output-based questions
console.log(1);
new Promise((r) => { console.log(2); r(3); }).then(console.log);
console.log(4);                                   // → 1 2 4 3
Promise.resolve(1).finally(() => 9).then(console.log);   // → 1
new Promise((r, j) => { r("a"); j("b"); }).then(console.log, console.log);   // → a
Promise.reject("x").catch((e) => e + "!").then(console.log);   // → x!
  • What happens: the executor runs synchronously (2 before 4); then callbacks run later. finally passes the value through; only the first settle counts; catch can recover with a new value.
  • Output: 1 2 4 3, 1, a, x!.
  • ✅ Top interview output questions.
APIMeaning
new Promise((resolve, reject) => …)Create; the executor runs immediately
.then(onF, onR)Handle success (and optionally failure)
.catch(onR)= then(undefined, onR)
.finally(fn)Always runs; passes the result through
Promise.resolve / rejectAn already-settled promise
async / awaitPromise code written like sync code (try/catch)
थोडक्यात: Promise = भविष्यातील result. pending → fulfilled/rejected, फक्त एकदाच. executor लगेच चालतो, .then नंतर (microtask) चालतो. .catch errors पकडतो, .finally नेहमी चालतो. async/await हीच गोष्ट सोप्या पद्धतीने लिहितो.

1. To Solve Callback Hell, Promises Came into the Picture

Your Notes (promise.js): remove the callback, define a promise, and resolve the promise inside the setTimeout. 
console.log("start");
function importantAction(userName) {
  return new Promise((resolved, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => { resolved(`subscript to the ${userName}`); }, 0);
  });
}
function likeTheVideo(video) {
  return new Promise((resolved, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => { resolved(`like the Given ${video} video`); }, 0);
  });
}
function shareVideo(video) {
  return new Promise((resolved, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => { resolved(`share the give ${video}`); }, 0);
  });
}
console.log("stop");
  • What happens: three functions that each return a promise resolving after 0 ms; start/stop print first because they're synchronous.
  • Output: start, stop.

2. Handling the Promises Separately

Your Notes: 
importantAction("vishal")
  .then((res) => { console.log(res); })
  .catch((err) => { console.log(err); });
likeTheVideo("vishal")
  .then((res) => { console.log(res); })
  .catch((err) => { console.log(err); });
shareVideo("vishal")
  .then((res) => { console.log(res); })
  .catch((err) => { console.log(err); });
// → start → stop → subscript to the vishal → like the Given vishal video → share the give vishal
  • What happens: three independent promises, each handled separately: no guaranteed order between them (here they resolve in start order).
  • Output: subscript…, like…, share….
  • ⚠ Independent calls don't wait for each other.
  1. This approach works fine for independent promises,
  2. handling the promises separately as in the current code.
  3. Each function (importantAction, likeTheVideo and shareVideo) returns a promise, and you use .then() and .catch() to handle the resolved or rejected values independently for each one.
But I want to run these promises sequentially, meaning I want to wait for one promise to complete before starting the next one. You can chain the promises like this: the approach below runs the promises sequentially by chaining .then() calls, so each promise waits for the previous one to complete before starting the next one.

3. Approach 2: Nested .then() (Promise Hell)

Your Notes: 
importantAction("vishal")
  .then((res) => {
    console.log(res);
    likeTheVideo("javascript")
      .then((res) => {
        console.log(res);
        shareVideo("node js")
          .then((res) => { console.log(res); })
          .catch((err) => { console.log(err); });
      })
      .catch((err) => { console.log(err); });
  })
  .catch((err) => { console.log(err); });
  • What happens: nesting .then inside .then forces the order, but rebuilds the pyramid.
  • Output: the three messages in order.
  • ⚠ Nested then = callback hell again; each level also needs its own catch.
So now it looks like a much cleaner approach: we don't pass a callback as an argument; we can just do .then(), pass the next action, and we also have error handling.
But if you notice, there is nesting of callback functions, which makes your code a little messy. With more callbacks nested inside each other it forms a weird-looking pyramid-like structure, sometimes called the pyramid of doom, and this concept is known as promise hell. It's called promise hell because there are so many nested callbacks, one inside another, that the code is very hard to read and understand. What is the solution for this problem? Promise chaining.
  • Your code works functionally, but the structure is not recommended due to nested .then() blocks and repeated .catch() calls, which make the code hard to read, error-prone and difficult to maintain.
  1. This approach can become difficult to maintain and read as the number of chained promises grows, which is often referred to as "callback hell" or "promise hell",
  2. which happens when you nest multiple .then() and .catch() calls within each other.
  3. This makes the code harder to maintain and debug; it creates a pyramid-like structure.
  4. So you can also write the above code in the following way. Both are the same, but instead of every function having its own catch block, there is one common catch block for all the promises/functions.
  5. This is a much cleaner and more structured approach: we don't pass a (callback) function as an argument, we just do .then() and pass the next action, and at the end we have error handling.
// # solution 3
importantAction("vishal")
  .then((res) => {
    console.log(res);
    likeTheVideo("like javascript interview").then((res) => {
      console.log(res);
      shareVideo("javascript interview video").then((res) => {
        console.log(res);
      });
    });
  })
  .catch((err) => { console.log(err); });
// # You're nesting .then() inside .then(), which brings back the problem of callback hell
  • What happens: same nesting with one outer catch; errors from the inner promises aren't caught by it (they aren't returned).
  • Output: the three messages in order.
  • ⚠ Unreturned inner promises escape the outer catch.
Problems with this approach:
  1. Nested structure: it gets more complex as you add more async steps.
  2. Poor error handling: the inner promises (likeTheVideo, shareVideo) are not part of the main chain (they aren't returned), so if an error occurs in them, the outer .catch() won't catch it.
  3. Harder to read: indentation grows rapidly and readability suffers.
  1. importantAction('vishal') resolves, and its result is logged.
  2. Once importantAction resolves, you call likeTheVideo('like javascript interview') in the next .then(),
  3. and once that resolves, you call shareVideo('javascript interview video').
  4. Each .then() returns a promise and, upon resolution, logs the result.
  5. But it still uses nested .then() blocks, which can quickly become harder to manage and read as more asynchronous tasks are added.
  6. So the above code shows a pyramid-like structure. Then why use promises if we face a pyramid-like structure (promise hell) again? Here the nested promises make the code harder to understand.
  7. This works fine for small tasks, but as the complexity increases (more tasks or nested functions), the nesting could get deep, which might lead to harder-to-read and harder-to-maintain code.
  8. Don't worry, promises give us more than one approach for this: promise chaining.
  9. First we call the first promise; it returns a new promise (the next promise). Once we return the new promise, we chain another .then() to handle it.

4. Cleaner Approach: the Flat Promise Chain

Your Notes: cleaner approach (avoiding deep nesting): you can flatten the promise chain to avoid nesting. 
importantAction("vishal")
  .then((res) => {
    console.log(res);
    // here it returns a new promise
    return likeTheVideo("javascript interview question");
    // then we chain another then() to handle that promise
  })
  .then((res) => {
    console.log(res);
    // this returns another new promise
    return shareVideo("javascript interview question");
    // then we chain another then() to handle that promise
  })
  .then((res) => {
    console.log(res);
    // and at the end we handle errors using catch
  })
  .catch((err) => {
    console.log("catch blocked called");
    console.log(err);
  });
// Each .then() returns a Promise, which allows the next .then() to wait for its resolution; hence it forms a chain.
  • What happens: return the next promise from each then; the next then waits for it. One catch at the end handles errors from any step.
  • Output: the three messages in order.
  • ✅ Flat, readable chain with one error handler.
Important explanation about the promise chain: the code above is much clearer than the previous approach; this is called promise chaining. We call it promise chaining because we chain these promises: we return a promise and then chain another one after it, passing the value of the previous promise along.
This approach is called promise chaining because we are chaining multiple .then() calls together. In each .then() block we either return a value or another Promise. If we return a Promise, the next .then() waits for it to resolve before running. This creates a chain of asynchronous operations, where each step waits for the previous one to complete.
Why it's better than the previous (nested) approach:
  • cleaner and more readable
  • avoids "callback hell" or a deeply nested structure
  • easier to maintain and debug
  • handles errors in one centralized .catch().

5. Execution Flow of the Above Code

Your Notes: Initial importantAction promise: importantAction('vishal') returns a Promise. This promise is asynchronous and takes some time to resolve or reject. The then() method attaches a callback to be executed when the promise is resolved (i.e., when importantAction completes its task).
  1. First .then() call: after the importantAction promise resolves, the result (res) is passed to this .then() callback. console.log(res) prints the result of importantAction('vishal') (e.g. "subscript to the vishal"). Once console.log executes, it proceeds to the next asynchronous task: likeTheVideo(…).
  2. Second likeTheVideo promise: after importantAction completes, likeTheVideo is called, which also returns a Promise. Since likeTheVideo is asynchronous, it runs in the background and the code continues until it resolves. Once likeTheVideo resolves, the result is passed to the next .then() block.
  3. Second .then() call: when the likeTheVideo promise resolves, its result (res) is passed to this .then() callback and logged (e.g. "like the Given javascript interview question video"). Then it proceeds to the next asynchronous task: shareVideo(…).
  4. Third shareVideo promise: shareVideo is called, which also returns a Promise. This promise resolves once the asynchronous operation inside shareVideo completes.
  5. Third .then() call: after shareVideo resolves, its result (res) is passed to this .then() callback and logged (e.g. "share the give javascript interview question").
Catching errors with .catch():
  1. If any of the promises (importantAction, likeTheVideo or shareVideo) is rejected (i.e. it throws an error), the error is passed to the .catch() block.
  2. catch() logs the error using console.log(err).

This ensures that if there's an issue with any of the promises (e.g. a network error or invalid data), you can handle it gracefully and prevent unhandled promise rejection errors. Why use .then() chaining?
  1. Sequential execution: each task (e.g. likeTheVideo, shareVideo) starts only after the previous task has completed. This ensures tasks are executed in the desired order.
  2. Asynchronous nature: even though tasks are executed one after another, the asynchronous operations (e.g. network requests, timeouts) don't block the main thread, allowing the application to remain responsive.
  3. Error handling: using .catch() at the end of the chain lets you handle errors from any of the promises in a single place, which removes the need for multiple .catch() blocks nested inside each .then().
Chaining: you chain .then() calls to execute asynchronous tasks one after another:
  1. First, importantAction('vishal') is called, then the .then() callback executes.
  2. Then likeTheVideo is called in the first .then(), and its result is passed to the next .then().
  3. Finally, shareVideo is called, and the result is logged in the final .then().
So the above concept is called promise chaining:
  1. Cleaner structure: the promise chain is flatter, making it easier to read.
  2. Simplified flow: each .then() simply returns the next promise, which keeps things organized; so a flattened promise chain improves readability and maintainability.
  3. Single error handler: with a flat structure, you only need one .catch() to handle any errors from the entire chain.

6. Why Do We Use Promise Chaining?

Your Notes: we use promise chaining to handle multiple asynchronous operations in a sequential manner while maintaining readability and avoiding deeply nested callbacks (callback hell).
  1. Sequential execution: ensures that one asynchronous operation completes before the next one starts. Example: fetch user details → get user orders → process order payments.
  2. Avoid callback hell: without chaining, nested callbacks can become hard to read and maintain. Promise chaining keeps code flat and structured.
  3. Error handling simplification: a single .catch() at the end of the chain can handle errors for all previous promises.
  4. Improved readability: code flows top to bottom, making it easier to understand.
  1. So when chaining these promises, we return a new promise and chain another promise after it, one after another; we pass the result of the previous promise to the next one, so each promise depends on the previous one.
  2. Promise chaining refers to the way promises can be linked together, one after another.
  3. Each .then() or .catch() method attached to a promise returns a new promise,
  4. and that returned promise can be chained with the next .then() call to continue the sequence of asynchronous operations.
  5. Also, if you think about your code, this is a pretty lengthy way of doing it, so there is one more approach, called the promise combinator, which makes our work super easy.
  6. With many different promises, the code can become lengthy and harder to maintain. The code becomes more verbose, especially when you have several asynchronous operations that depend on each other. This is where combinators (such as Promise.all(), Promise.allSettled(), Promise.race(), Promise.any()) or async/await can help, making the code shorter, cleaner and more readable.

7. What is Promise Chaining? (promiseChain.js)

Your Notes (18_promise/promiseChain.js):
  1. Promise chaining is a technique in JS where multiple asynchronous operations are performed in sequence, with each subsequent operation starting after the previous one has completed.
  2. This is achieved by returning a new promise from the .then() handler of the previous promise.
  3. Promise chaining is a technique where multiple .then() handlers are used to handle asynchronous operations in a structured way: each then() returns a new promise, which allows chaining multiple asynchronous operations in a linear fashion.
  4. Instead of nesting multiple callbacks (as in callback hell), promise chaining ensures:
    1. cleaner and more reusable code;
    2. sequential execution of asynchronous operations;
    3. error handling using catch().
Promise chaining means using multiple .then() methods one after another, so that the output of one promise is passed as input to the next; it helps to run asynchronous operations in sequence.
Why "chaining"? Because each .then() returns a new promise, you can attach another .then() to it. This creates a chain of promises.
Benefits:
  • avoids callback hell (deeply nested functions)
  • makes async tasks run sequentially, in order
  • each .then() receives the result of the previous promise
  • errors can be handled in one .catch() at the end.

In short: promise chaining is a way of executing asynchronous tasks step by step, where the result of one .then() is passed down to the next .then().
Promise chaining:
  1. a JS pattern that chains promises to execute asynchronous operations in sequence.
  2. Def: sometimes you want to execute two or more related asynchronous operations, where the next operation starts with the result from the previous step.

8. Example 1: Resolving with Another Promise

Your Notes: 
const firstPromise = new Promise((res, rej) => {
  res("first");
});
const secondPromise = new Promise((res, rej) => {
  res(firstPromise);   // resolving with a promise → secondPromise ADOPTS its state
});
secondPromise
  .then((result) => { console.log(result); })   // → first   (not a Promise object)
  .catch((error) => { console.log(error); });
  • What happens: resolving with a promise makes the outer promise adopt its result.
  • Output: first.
  • ✅ Promises never resolve to a promise; they unwrap.

9. Example 2: Separate vs Nested vs Flat

Your Notes: 
function importantAction(user_name) {
  return new Promise((resolved, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => { resolved(`${user_name}`); }, 0);
  });
}
function likeVideo(video) {
  return new Promise((resolved, rejected) => {
    setTimeout(() => { resolved(`${video}`); }, 1000);
  });
}
function sharedVideo(shared) {
  return new Promise((resolved, rejected) => {
    setTimeout(() => { resolved(`${shared}`); }, 2000);
  });
}
importantAction("vishal").then((res) => { console.log("res1", res); });   // → res1 vishal
likeVideo("javascript").then((res) => { console.log("res2", res); });     // → res2 javascript (1 s)
sharedVideo("subscribed")
  .then((res) => { console.log("res3", res); })                           // → res3 subscribed (2 s)
  .catch((err) => { console.log("error", err); });
  • What happens: three independent promises with different delays.
  • Output: res1 vishal, res2 javascript (1 s), res3 subscribed (2 s).
In the above example, you can also see that we execute each promise individually. But in some cases I want to run the promises sequentially, where one promise depends on another. There is more than one approach to do that: 
// 1. promise chaining (nested version)
importantAction("shinde")
  .then((res) => {
    console.log("new res", res);
    return likeVideo("Node").then((res) => {
      console.log("new res1", res);
      return sharedVideo("sub").then((res) => {
        console.log("new res 2", res);
      });
    });
  })
  .catch((err) => { console.log("new error", err); });
// after one promise resolves, we define the next promise
// #  This works, but it's not ideal because you're nesting promises, which makes it look like callback hell again.
// # This defeats the purpose of promises: promises were introduced to avoid such nesting.
  • What happens: nested but RETURNED promises: it works and errors reach the catch, but it still looks like a pyramid.
  • Output: new res shinde, new res1 Node, new res 2 sub.
Nested StyleChained Style
Harder to read and maintainEasier to read and extend
Looks like "callback hell" againClean, linear flow
Each .then() contains another .then()Each .then() handles one step only
Mixing logic in nested functionsLogic stays flat and clear
// #  Better: flattened promise chaining
// If each promise depends on the previous one, use flat chaining
importantAction("shinde")
  .then((res) => {
    console.log("new res", res);       // → new res shinde
    return likeVideo("Node");
  })
  .then((res) => {
    console.log("new res1", res);      // → new res1 Node   (+1 s)
    return sharedVideo("sub");
  })
  .then((res) => {
    console.log("new res 2", res);     // → new res 2 sub   (+2 s)
  })
  .catch((err) => { console.log("new error", err); });
  • What happens: the flat version of the same chain.
  • Output: new res shinde, new res1 Node (+1 s), new res 2 sub (+2 s).
  • ✅ Preferred style.
Key points of promise chaining:
  1. Sequential execution: each operation in the chain depends on the result of the previous operation.
  2. Error handling: if any promise in the chain is rejected, the chain skips the subsequent .then() handlers and executes the nearest .catch() block.
  3. Cleaner syntax: promises make the code more readable and manageable, avoiding deeply nested callbacks (commonly known as "callback hell").
Means: structured asynchronous flow (clearly defines the sequence of operations); error handling (centralized error handling through .catch()); readability (easier to understand and maintain than nested callbacks).
Why do we call it promise chaining?
  1. We call it promise chaining because it involves executing a series of asynchronous tasks in sequence,
  2. where each task depends on the result of the previous one.

By "chaining" .then() methods, each promise is linked or "chained" to the one before it, ensuring that the tasks execute in order.
Key reasons for promise chaining:
  1. Sequential execution: in promise chaining, each asynchronous operation runs only after the previous one completes.
  2. This creates a clear sequence of dependent operations, unlike parallel execution, where tasks can run independently.
  3. The setTimeout() function simulates an asynchronous operation.

10. Returning Values in a Chain

Your Notes: 
let p = new Promise((resolved, reject) => {
  setTimeout(() => { resolved(10); }, 3 * 100);
});
p.then((res) => {
  console.log("res", res);   // → res 10
  return res * 2;
})
  .then((res) => {
    console.log("res", res); // → res 20
    return res * 3;
  })
  .then((res) => {
    console.log(res);        // → 60
    return res * 4;
  });
//  # this is an example of promise chaining
  • What happens: each then receives the previous then's return value.
  • Output: res 10, res 20, 60.
  • ✅ Transform a value step by step.
  1. Handling dependent results: in many cases, the result of one operation is required for the next operation. For example, you might need to fetch user data from an API and then use that data to fetch additional information from another API. Promise chaining lets you pass the result of one promise to the next in the chain.
  2. Error handling: in a promise chain, you can catch errors in one place rather than handling them individually for each asynchronous operation. The catch block at the end of the chain handles any errors that occur in any of the previous promises in the chain.
How promise chaining works: when a .then() block is attached to a promise, it returns a new promise. If the handler function in .then() returns a value, that value becomes the resolution value of the new promise. If it returns another promise, the chain waits for that promise to resolve before continuing.
NOTE: by using promise chains our code becomes pretty lengthy, so there is one more approach in promises, called the promise combinator.

11. Calling then() Multiple Times Is Not Promise Chaining

Your Notes: when you call the then() method multiple times on the same promise, it is not promise chaining. 
let p1 = new Promise((res, rej) => {
  setTimeout(() => { res(10); }, 3 * 100);
});
p1.then((res) => { console.log(res); return res * 2; });   // → 10
p1.then((res) => { console.log(res); return res * 3; });   // → 10
p1.then((res) => { console.log(res); return res * 4; });   // → 10
  • What happens: three separate then calls on the SAME promise: each gets the original value, they don't chain.
  • Output: 10, 10, 10.
  • ⚠ Chaining = calling then on the RESULT of then.
In this example we have multiple handlers for one promise. These handlers have no relationship; they execute independently and don't pass the result from one to another like the promise chain above.

12. Returning a Promise

Your Notes: when you return a value in the then() method, the then method returns a new Promise that immediately resolves to the return value. You can also return a new promise in the then method: 
let p3 = new Promise((resolved, reject) => {
  setTimeout(() => { resolved(10); }, 3 * 100);
});
p3.then((result) => {
  console.log("1", result);           // → 1 10
  return new Promise((resolved, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => { resolved(result * 2); }, 3 * 100);
  });
})
  .then((result) => {
    console.log("2", result);         // → 2 20
    return new Promise((resolved, rejected) => {
      setTimeout(() => { resolved(result * 3); }, 3 * 100);
    });
  })
  .then((result) => {
    console.log("3", result);         // → 3 60
    return new Promise((resolved, rejected) => {
      setTimeout(() => { resolved(result * 3); }, 3 * 100);
    });
  })
  .then((result) => {
    console.log("4", "result", result);   // → 4 result 180
  })
  .catch((error) => { console.log("error", error); });
// use the above approach when you need to pass the result from the previous (async) task to the next one.
  • What happens: returning a new promise inside then makes the next step wait for it (300 ms each).
  • Output: 1 10, 2 20, 3 60, 4 result 180.
  • ✅ Pass a result from one async task to the next.

13. Real Example: User → Services → Cost

Your Notes: the following functions illustrate three asynchronous operations. Suppose you want to perform the following asynchronous operations sequentially: get the user from the database; get the services of the selected user; calculate the service cost of the user. ✔ "three synchronous operations" → ASYNCHRONOUS. Also "teh" → the, and "getServicesConst" means getServicesCost (the name is kept as in your code).ही तिन्ही कामे asynchronous आहेत. "Const" म्हणजे इथे "Cost" (किंमत) असा अर्थ आहे. 
function getUser(userId) {
  return new Promise((resolved, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => {
      resolved({ userId: userId, username: "admin" });
    }, 3 * 100);
  });
}
function getServices(user) {
  return new Promise((resolved, reject) => {
    console.log(`get teh services of the user ${user.username} from the api`);
    setTimeout(() => { resolved(["email", "vpn", "cdn"]); }, 3 * 100);
  });
}
function getServicesConst(services) {
  return new Promise((resolved, reject) => {
    console.log(`calculate the services const of the ${services}`);
    setTimeout(() => { resolved(services.length * 1000); }, 3 * 100);
  });
}
getUser(100)
  .then((result) => {
    console.log(result);               // → { userId: 100, username: 'admin' }
    return getServices(result);
  })
  .then((result) => {
    console.log(result);               // → [ 'email', 'vpn', 'cdn' ]
    return getServicesConst(result);
  })
  .then((result) => {
    console.log("1234", result);       // → 1234 3000
  })
  .catch((error) => { console.log(error); });

// you can also use the following approach (pass the functions directly)
getUser(100)
  .then(getServices)
  .then(getServicesConst)
  .then((result) => {
    console.log("result1234", result); // → result1234 3000
  });
  • What happens: real-world chain: get user → get their services → calculate cost; functions can be passed directly to then.
  • Output: user object, ['email', 'vpn', 'cdn'], 1234 3000, result1234 3000.
  • ✅ then(getServices) works because getServices takes one argument.
The same chain with async/await: 
async function run() {
  const user = await getUser(100);
  const services = await getServices(user);
  const cost = await getServicesConst(services);
  console.log(cost);   // → 3000
}
  • What happens: the same chain with async/await.
  • Output: 3000.
  • ✅ Even easier to read.

14. Why Promise Combinators Came into the Picture

Your Notes (promise.js): what is a promise combinator / the promise API?
  1. The Promise API in JavaScript provides methods to work with multiple Promises efficiently.
  2. A promise combinator is a function or method in JavaScript that lets you work with multiple promises simultaneously, combining their results or handling their outcomes collectively. (They help in running multiple asynchronous tasks in parallel or managing their results efficiently.)
  3. These combinators make it easier to manage multiple asynchronous operations and control how you handle their results or failures.
  4. Promise combinators are especially useful when you need to work with multiple asynchronous operations and want to control how they resolve or reject.
  5. While promise chaining is great for sequential operations (where one task depends on the result of the previous one), it doesn't handle multiple independent promises well.
1. We used callbacks in JavaScript: JavaScript is single-threaded, so to handle asynchronous operations (like API calls, file reading, timers, etc.), we use callbacks.
Problems with callbacks:
  1. callback hell (the nested structure becomes unreadable);
  2. inversion of control: you hand control of your function to another function and hope it calls your callback correctly.

3. Promises solve these issues:
  1. promises flatten the nesting and improve readability by promise chaining;
  2. they give control back to the caller;
  3. better error handling using .catch().

Problem with promises:
  1. When you have to run multiple asynchronous operations in parallel or coordinate multiple promises, chaining is not enough or becomes hard to manage.
  2. While promise chaining is great for sequential operations (where one task depends on the result of the previous one), it doesn't handle multiple independent promises well.
  3. While basic promises solved many issues, handling multiple promises efficiently still needed improvement, so the promise API (combinators) was introduced.
Example: if you want to:
  1. wait for multiple promises to finish (also handle multiple promises at once);
  2. take the first successful result;
  3. run promises in a race;
  4. handle both success and failure cases.

Chaining doesn't help. That's where promise combinators were introduced.
Then the solution for that: Promise Combinators
CombinatorPurpose
Promise.all()Wait for all promises to fulfill; reject as soon as ANY one rejects
Promise.race()Return the first settled promise (success or fail)
Promise.allSettled()Wait for all promises to settle (resolve or reject)
Promise.any()Return the first fulfilled promise (ignore rejects)
✔ Promise.all row said "Wait for all promises to finish (success or fail)". That describes allSettled; Promise.all rejects immediately on the first failure (verified: "reject in p3")."success किंवा fail, सगळ्यांची वाट पाहणे" हे allSettled चे काम आहे. Promise.all पहिल्याच reject वर लगेच reject होतो.

15. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. What does .then() return?
  • Always a NEW promise. It resolves with the handler's return value; if the handler returns a promise, it adopts that promise; if the handler throws, it rejects.
Q2. Why must you "return" inside .then()?
  • Without return, the next .then() doesn't wait (it receives undefined) and the inner promise's errors escape the outer .catch: the "floating promise" bug.
Q3. Chaining vs calling .then() several times on the same promise?
  • Chaining passes the result step by step (10 → 20 → 60). Multiple .then() calls on one promise are independent listeners that all receive the same value (10, 10, 10).
Q4. Where should .catch() go, and what happens after it?
  • Usually at the end. A .catch that returns a value RECOVERS the chain, so later .then()s run with that value; rethrow to keep it rejected.
Q5. Output-based questions
Promise.resolve(1)
  .then((x) => x + 1)
  .then((x) => { throw x * 10; })
  .then(() => console.log("skip"))
  .catch((e) => e + 1)
  .then(console.log);                 // → 21
Promise.resolve(2).then((x) => { Promise.resolve(x * 2); }).then(console.log);   // → undefined (no return)
const p = Promise.resolve(5); p.then((x) => x * 2); p.then(console.log);         // → 5
  • What happens: a thrown value skips the next then and lands in catch; catch returns a value that continues the chain; forgetting return gives undefined; then on the same promise doesn't change it.
  • Output: 21, undefined, 5.
RuleEffect
return valueThe next .then gets it
return promiseThe next .then waits for it
throw / rejected promiseJump to the nearest .catch
.catch returns a valueThe chain recovers
No returnThe next step gets undefined; errors escape
थोडक्यात: nested .then पुन्हा pyramid बनवतो. प्रत्येक .then मधून return करून chain flat ठेवा आणि शेवटी एकच .catch लावा. एकाच promise वर अनेक .then म्हणजे chaining नाही. स्वतंत्र (parallel) कामांसाठी combinators वापरा.

Chapter 66: Promise CombinatorsPromise.all · allSettled · race · any · resolve/reject vs combinators
CHAPTER 66 INDEX
  1. What is a Promise Combinator?
  2. Promise.resolve() & Promise.reject()
  3. Promise.all()
  4. Promise.allSettled()
  5. Promise.race()
  6. Promise.any()
  7. Differences between the Combinators
  8. Interview Questions & Revision

1. What is a Promise Combinator?

Your Notes (18_promise/combinator.js): a Promise Combinator is a built-in JavaScript method that helps you manage multiple promises at once.
  1. Instead of waiting for or chaining promises one by one, combinators let you work with them together: in parallel, in a race, or handling all results regardless of success/failure.
Why do we need promise combinators? Suppose you want to:
  1. Wait for multiple API calls to complete before proceeding (i.e. promises run in parallel).
  2. Get the first successful result among many.
  3. Know the result of each promise, even if one fails. It is also faster and more efficient, and you get all the results together.
  4. Chaining .then() doesn't handle that well.
  5. Promise chaining is good when each step depends on the previous result,
  6. but not good for parallel/independent promises.
What are the types of promise combinator? Promise combinators help us execute multiple promises at one time and return the result accordingly. There are 4 promise combinators available in JavaScript:
  1. Promise.all
  2. Promise.allSettled
  3. Promise.race
  4. Promise.any
✔ Note: combinators don't "execute" promises; the promises are already running when created. Combinators WAIT for them together and combine their results.combinator promises चालवत नाहीत. promises तयार होताच चालू होतात; combinator फक्त त्यांच्या results ची एकत्र वाट पाहतो आणि ते एकत्र करतो.

2. What are resolve and reject in Promises?

Your Notes:

1. Promise.resolve()

  1. Promise.resolve() is a method that returns a resolved promise.
  2. When a Promise is resolved, it means the operation was successful, and the result is passed to .then().
  3. If you pass a non-promise value to Promise.resolve(), it returns a promise that resolves to that value.
  4. If you pass a (native) promise, it just returns that same promise, whatever its state. ✔ "If you pass an already resolved promise, it just returns that promise". This is true for ANY native promise (pending or rejected too): Promise.resolve(p) === p. So Promise.resolve(Promise.reject(x)) is still rejected.Promise.resolve ला कोणताही native promise दिला (pending किंवा rejected सुद्धा) तरी तोच promise परत मिळतो. म्हणजे rejected promise दिल्यास तो rejected च राहतो.

2. Promise.reject()

  1. Promise.reject() is a method that returns a rejected promise.
  2. It is used when you want to immediately return a promise that is rejected with a specific reason.
  3. When a Promise is rejected, it means the operation failed, and the error is passed to .catch().
  4. The provided reason becomes the rejection reason of the returned promise.
Why they're not considered combinators (resolve and reject):
  1. Promise combinators like Promise.all(), Promise.race(), Promise.any() and Promise.allSettled() are used to combine multiple promises and manage their resolutions or rejections in different ways.
  2. Promise.resolve() and Promise.reject() simply create single promises that are already resolved or rejected.
  3. They don't combine multiple promises or manage multiple async operations in one go. So, while Promise.resolve() and Promise.reject() are important for handling promises, they are not classified as "combinators", because they don't combine multiple promises into one.

3. Promise.all()

Your Notes (promiseAll.js):
  1. Promise.all is used to run all promises (multiple asynchronous tasks) in parallel and wait until all of them complete successfully; at the end it returns an array with the values of all the fulfilled promises.
  2. If any one of the promises fails, the whole Promise.all fails.
  3. Promise.all waits for all the input promises to be resolved and returns a new promise that resolves to an array containing the results of the input promises (it waits for all of them to finish), in the SAME order as the input, not in completion order.
  4. It takes an array (or iterable) of promises as input and returns a single promise that resolves when all the input promises have resolved, or rejects as soon as any one of the input promises rejects.
  5. If one of the promises is rejected, Promise.all() immediately (as soon as possible) returns a new promise that rejects with the error of the first rejected promise; Promise.all doesn't care whether the other input promises resolved or rejected. (They keep running; their results are just ignored.)
  6. Promise.all() is a fail-fast process.
const p1 = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  setTimeout(() => {
    const shouldReject = false;   // Set to true to trigger rejection
    if (shouldReject) { reject("Error in promise"); } else { resolve(10); }
  }, 2000);
});
const p2 = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  setTimeout(() => {
    const shouldReject = false;
    if (shouldReject) { reject("error in p2"); } else { resolve(20); }
  }, 1500);
});
const p3 = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  setTimeout(() => {
    const shouldReject = true;
    if (shouldReject) { reject("reject in p3"); } else { resolve(99); }
  }, 1000);
});
// Promise.all takes an array of all the promises
// it returns the fulfilled values of all the promises inside an array
let result = Promise.all([p1, p2, p3])
  .then((result) => { console.log(result); })
  .catch((error) => { console.log(error); });
// → reject in p3   (after 1 s: p3 rejects first, so Promise.all fails fast; verified in Node)
// with p3 resolving instead → [10, 20, 99]  (input order, even though p3 finished first)
// It accepts a list of promises and returns a new promise that resolves to an array of the results of the input
// promises if all the input promises are resolved, or rejects with the error of the first rejected promise.
  • What happens: Promise.all waits for ALL promises and gives their values in input order; if any rejects, it rejects immediately with that reason (fail-fast).
  • Output: reject in p3 (after 1 s); [10, 20, 99] if all succeed.
  • ✅ Run independent requests in parallel and wait for all.
  • ⚠ One failure loses all results; use allSettled if partial results are fine.

4. Promise.allSettled()

Your Notes (promiseAllSettled.js):
  1. It waits for all promises to settle, whether they are resolved or rejected.
  2. It has the same syntax as Promise.all and Promise.race, but the functionality is a bit different.
  3. It works exactly like Promise.all, but even if one of the promises fails, it still returns the results of all the promises, including the fulfilled ones.
  4. In Promise.all, if any one of the promises fails, the whole Promise.all() fails.
  5. With Promise.allSettled(), if any one promise fails, it still returns all the array items, each marked fulfilled or rejected; i.e. Promise.allSettled doesn't care whether any one rejects or resolves: it goes through all the promises and returns the results as an array. ✔ "i.e promise.all does not matter…" → this sentence describes Promise.ALLSETTLED.हे वाक्य Promise.all बद्दल नाही, Promise.allSettled बद्दल आहे.
// p1 → 10 (2 s), p2 → rejects "error in p2" (1.5 s), p3 → 99 (1 s)
let result = Promise.allSettled([p1, p2, p3])
  .then((result) => { console.log(result); })
  .catch((error) => { console.log(error); });   // allSettled never rejects
// → [
//     { status: 'fulfilled', value: 10 },
//     { status: 'rejected',  reason: 'error in p2' },
//     { status: 'fulfilled', value: 99 }
//   ]   (verified in Node)
  • What happens: allSettled waits for every promise and reports each outcome (fulfilled/value or rejected/reason); it never rejects.
  • Output: the three status objects.
  • ✅ Dashboards where some widgets may fail.
  1. Use case: useful when you need to handle a collection of promises and want the results of all of them, regardless of success or failure.
  2. Purpose: Promise.allSettled() is used to wait for multiple promises to settle (resolve or reject) and get the result of each promise.
  3. Output: it returns an array of objects, each containing the status ("fulfilled" or "rejected") and either a value (for resolved promises) or a reason (for rejected promises).

5. Promise.race()

Your Notes (promiseRace.js):
  1. Promise.race() is a method in JavaScript that returns a promise which resolves or rejects as soon as any one of the promises in the iterable (array or collection) resolves or rejects.
  2. It gives the value of the first settled promise; it may be resolved or rejected.
  3. It "races" the promises against each other, and the one that settles (resolves or rejects) first is the result.
  4. If the first promise to settle is resolved, Promise.race() resolves with that value.
  5. If the first promise to settle rejects, Promise.race() rejects with that reason.
  6. The remaining promises are ignored once the first one settles (resolves or rejects).
console.log("start");
function importantAction(user_name) {
  return new Promise((resolved, rejected) => {
    setTimeout(() => { resolved(`${user_name}`); }, 2000);
  });
}
function likeVideo(video) {
  return new Promise((resolved, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => { resolved(`${video}`); }, 1000);
  });
}
function sharedVideo(shared) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => { reject(`${shared}`); }, 500);
  });
}
Promise.race([importantAction("vishal"), likeVideo("node js"), sharedVideo("javascript")])
  .then((result) => { console.log(result); })
  .catch((error) => { console.log("error :", error); });
// → start → error : javascript   (sharedVideo settles first at 500 ms, and it rejects; verified in Node)
  • What happens: race settles as soon as the FIRST promise settles, whether it succeeds or fails.
  • Output: start, error : javascript.
  • ✅ Timeouts: race a request against a timer that rejects.
  1. No matter whether a promise is fulfilled or rejected: whichever promise settles first, that result is returned (here the first one to settle is a rejection, so race rejects).
  2. Purpose: Promise.race() returns the first settled promise, whether resolved or rejected.
  3. Behavior: if one promise resolves or rejects, Promise.race() settles with that result immediately and ignores the remaining promises.
  4. Promise.race() takes an array of promises and returns a new promise that resolves or rejects as soon as any one of the promises resolves or rejects. It doesn't wait for all promises to settle.
  5. If the first promise resolves, the resulting promise resolves with that value.
Real use, a timeout: Promise.race([fetch(url), new Promise((_, rej) => setTimeout(() => rej("timeout"), 5000))])

6. Promise.any()

Your Notes (promiseAny.js):
  1. It is like Promise.race, but what it does is different:
  2. it only returns the first fulfilled promise and ignores all the rejected promises.
  3. It waits for the first successful promise.
  4. If all the promises are rejected, it gives an AggregateError with an array of all the promise errors.
// p1, p2, p3: all three reject ("Error in promise", "error in p2", "reject in p3")
Promise.any([p1, p2, p3])
  .then((result) => { console.log(result); })
  .catch((error) => { console.log(error); });
// → [AggregateError: All promises were rejected] {
//     [errors]: [ 'Error in promise', 'error in p2', 'reject in p3' ]
//   }   (verified in Node; error.errors holds the reasons, in input order)
  • What happens: any resolves with the first SUCCESS; only if all reject does it reject with an AggregateError listing every reason.
  • Output: AggregateError with the three errors.
  • ✅ Use the fastest of several mirrors/servers.
If all promises are rejected, it throws an AggregateError, which contains all the rejection reasons: AggregateError: All promises were rejected. Promise.any() takes an array of promises and returns a new promise that resolves as soon as any one of the promises resolves. If all promises reject, the resulting promise rejects with an AggregateError that contains all the reasons for rejection.
Figure 128: The four promise combinators applied to the same three promises.
all = सगळे यशस्वी हवे, एक जरी fail झाला तर लगेच reject. allSettled = सगळ्यांची वाट पाहतो आणि प्रत्येकाचा status देतो, कधीच reject होत नाही. race = जो आधी settle होईल (यश किंवा अपयश) तो जिंकतो. any = पहिला यशस्वी promise जिंकतो; सगळे fail झाल्यास AggregateError.

7. What are the Differences between the Promise Combinators?

Your Notes (combinator.js):

Promise.all()

  1. Resolves only if all promises resolve. It rejects if any promise in the array fails.
  2. Stops waiting as soon as one promise rejects and returns that rejection (the other promises keep running in the background; Promise.all just ignores them).
  3. Returns an array of resolved values, or a single rejection.
  4. Used when you need all promises to succeed and you want the operation to halt on any failure.

Promise.allSettled()

  1. Resolves after all promises settle (resolved or rejected).
  2. Waits for all promises to settle and gives individual results.
  3. Returns an array of objects describing the outcome of each promise (fulfilled/rejected).
  4. Used when you want to know the result of every promise, regardless of whether some fail or succeed.

What is the difference between Promise.race() and Promise.any()?

Promise.race()
  1. Promise.race() returns the first settled promise; it may be fulfilled or rejected.
✔ your heading here said "# promise.any()" but the text describes Promise.RACE().इथे heading promise.any() लिहिले होते, पण मजकूर Promise.race() बद्दल आहे. Promise.any()
  1. Promise.any returns the first fulfilled promise.
  2. If all the promises are rejected, it returns an AggregateError with an array of all the promises' rejection errors.
CombinatorResolves whenRejects whenResultES
allAll fulfillThe first rejection[values]2015
allSettledAll settleNever[{status, value/reason}]2020
raceThe first to settle fulfillsThe first to settle rejectsOne value/reason2015
anyThe first fulfillsAll rejectOne value / AggregateError2021

8. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. Promise.all vs Promise.allSettled?
  • all is fail-fast and gives an array of values; allSettled always waits for all and gives status objects. Use all when everything is required; use allSettled for "show what succeeded" dashboards.
Q2. Promise.race vs Promise.any?
  • race takes the first SETTLED (a fast failure wins); any takes the first FULFILLED and rejects only if all fail (AggregateError).
Q3. What does Promise.all([]) return? What about non-promise values?
  • [] resolves immediately with []. Non-promise values are treated as already resolved: Promise.all([1, Promise.resolve(2)]) → [1, 2]. Note: Promise.race([]) stays pending forever; Promise.any([]) rejects with an AggregateError.
Q4. Does Promise.all cancel the other promises when one fails?
  • No. Promises can't be cancelled; the others keep running. Use AbortController to really cancel fetches.
Q5. Implement Promise.all (polyfill).
function myAll(promises) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const results = []; let done = 0;
    if (promises.length === 0) return resolve(results);
    promises.forEach((p, i) => {
      Promise.resolve(p).then((v) => {
        results[i] = v;                         // keep the INPUT order
        if (++done === promises.length) resolve(results);
      }, reject);                               // first rejection rejects all
    });
  });
}
  • What happens: a Promise.all polyfill: count completions, store each value at its index, reject on the first error, resolve [] for empty input.
  • Output: (function).
  • ✅ Common interview task.
Q6. Output-based questions
const ok = (v, t) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(() => r(v), t));
const bad = (v, t) => new Promise((_, j) => setTimeout(() => j(v), t));
Promise.all([ok(1, 300), ok(2, 100)]).then(console.log);        // → [1, 2]
Promise.race([ok("a", 200), bad("b", 100)]).catch(console.log); // → b
Promise.any([bad("x", 50), ok("y", 200)]).then(console.log);    // → y
Promise.allSettled([bad("e", 10)]).then((r) => console.log(r[0].status));   // → rejected
  • What happens: four quick checks: all keeps input order, race takes the first settled, any skips failures, allSettled reports status.
  • Output: [1, 2], b, y, rejected.
थोडक्यात: combinators अनेक स्वतंत्र promises एकत्र हाताळतात. all = सगळे हवे (fail-fast), allSettled = सगळ्यांचा हिशोब, race = पहिला settle, any = पहिला success. Promise.resolve/reject हे combinators नाहीत, ते फक्त एक promise बनवतात.
