CHAPTER 67 INDEX
  1. Output Q1: Rejection Skips the .then()s
  2. Output Q2: catch Returns a Value
  3. Output Q3: The Long Chain
  4. Interview: job(state) with Bugs
  5. Interview: the Executor Runs Synchronously
  6. Interview: throw vs return new Error
  7. Interview Questions & Revision

1. Output-Based Question 1

Your Notes (promiseChain.js): 
function job() {
  return new Promise((res, rej) => {
    rej();
  });
}
let promise = job();
promise
  .then(() => { console.log("success!"); })
  .then((result) => { console.log("success2"); })
  .then((res) => { console.log("success3"); })
  .catch((error) => { console.log("error", error); })
  .then(function () { console.log("success4"); });
// intended output: error undefined → success4
//   the rejection skips all 3 .then()s, the catch handles it (and RECOVERS the chain), so the last .then runs
// ⚠ actual output in your file: "error error". job() is declared 3 times in promiseChain.js; the LAST
//   declaration, job(state), wins (hoisting), so job() → state undefined → reject("error")
  • What happens: a rejection skips every then until a catch; catch handles it and the chain continues as fulfilled, so the final then runs.
  • Output: error undefined, success4 (in your file: error error because job is redeclared).
  • ⚠ Duplicate function declarations: the last one wins everywhere.
✔ (verified in Node) the 3 function job(...) declarations in one file override each other: the last one is used everywhere. Use different names (job1, job2, job3).एकाच file मध्ये job 3 वेळा declare केल्यामुळे hoisting ने शेवटचे job(state) सगळीकडे वापरले जाते. म्हणून error undefined ऐवजी "error error" येते. वेगवेगळी नावे द्या.

2. Output-Based Question 2

Your Notes: 
function job(state) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    if (state) { resolve("success"); } else { reject("error"); }
  });
}
let promise1 = job(true);
promise1
  .then((data) => {
    console.log(data);         // → success
    return job(false);
  })
  .catch((error) => {
    console.log("failed", error);   // → failed error
    return "error caught";     // this is not a failed promise, it is a string, so it is a resolved promise and it goes to the then() block
  })
  .then(function (data) {
    console.log(data);         // → error caught
    return job(true);          // this resolves the promise, but there is no further then block, so execution stops
  })
  .catch(function (error) {
    console.log(error);        // (not called)
  });
  • What happens: job(false) rejects → catch logs and returns a string, which fulfils the chain → the next then gets "error caught".
  • Output: success, failed error, error caught.
  • ✅ catch can recover by returning a value.

3. Output-Based Question 3: the Long Chain

Your Notes: 
let promise3 = job(true);
promise3
  .then((data) => {
    console.log(data);              // → success   (returns nothing → next gets undefined)
  })
  .then(function (data) {
    if (data !== "victory") {
      throw "defect";               // data is undefined ≠ "victory" → the promise REJECTS with "defect"
    }
    return job(true);
  })
  .then(function (data) {
    console.log(data);              // skipped
  })
  .catch((error) => {
    console.log("failed", error);   // → failed defect
    return job(false);
  })
  .then(function (data) {
    console.log(data);              // skipped (job(false) rejected)
    return job(true);
  })
  .catch(function (error) {
    console.log("error", error);    // → error error
    return "return caught";
  })
  .then((data) => {
    console.log(data);              // → return caught
    return new Error("test");
  })
  .then(function (data) {
    console.log("success: ", data.message);   // → success:  test
  })
  .catch(function (data) {
    console.log("error:", data.message);
  });
// ✔ was "new error('test')" (small e) → ReferenceError: error is not defined, so the output ended with
//    "error: error is not defined" (verified in Node). With new Error the last line is "success:  test".
// ✔ the comment "throw 'defect' // this promise resolved" → throw makes the promise REJECT
  • What happens: the first then returns nothing (undefined), so the next one throws "defect" → catch → job(false) rejects → next then skipped → catch returns a string → then returns an Error OBJECT (not thrown) → next then gets it as data.
  • Output: success, failed defect, error error, return caught, success: test.
  • ⚠ Returning an Error doesn't reject; you must throw it.
"new error" मध्ये लहान e असल्यामुळे ReferenceError आला. Error constructor चे नाव मोठ्या E ने (Error) लिहितात. throw केल्यावर promise reject होतो, resolve नाही.

4. Interview: job(state) (interviewquestion.js)

Your Notes: 
function job(state) {
  return new Promise(function (resolve, reject) {
    if (true) {            // ⚠ should be: if (state)
      resolve("success");
    } else {
      reject("error");
    }
  });
}
let promise6 = job(true);
promise6.then(function (data) {
  console.log(data);       // → success
  return job(false);
}).catch(function (error) {
  console.log(error);
  return "error caught";   // so here it returns a non-empty string, which is not a rejection; the chain resolves and goes to the next then block
}).then(function () {
  console.log(data);       // ⚠ data is not a parameter here
  return job(true);
}).catch(function (error) {
  console.log(error);
});
// actual output (verified in Node): success → success(skipped catch) … → ReferenceError: data is not defined
//   1. if (true) ignores state, so job(false) RESOLVES with "success" and the first catch never runs
//   2. .then(function () { console.log(data) }) has no data parameter → ReferenceError → caught by the last catch
// ✔ fixed version: if (state) and .then(function (data) {…}) → success → error → error caught
  • What happens: if (true) ignores state, so job(false) resolves; the then without a data parameter throws ReferenceError, which the last catch prints.
  • Output: success, success, ReferenceError: data is not defined.
  • ⚠ Wrong conditions and missing parameters create confusing output.
✔ if (true) → if (state); add the missing data parameter. Note the reason: returning a string from catch "is not a false value" is not why the chain continues. ANY returned value (even false or undefined) fulfils the next promise; only throw or a rejected promise rejects it. if (true) मुळे job(false) सुद्धा resolve होतो. आणि .then(function(){…}) मध्ये data parameter नाही, म्हणून ReferenceError येतो. catch मधून कोणतीही value (false सुद्धा) return केली तरी chain पुढे fulfilled होते; फक्त throw किंवा rejected promise ने reject होते.

5. Interview: Is the Promise Executor Synchronous?

Your Notes: 
console.log("start");
const promise12 = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  console.log(1);
  console.log(2);
});
promise12.then((result) => {
  console.log(result);
}).catch((error) => {
  console.log(error);
});
console.log("end");
// output: start, 1, 2, end
  • What happens: the executor runs synchronously, but it never calls resolve/reject, so the promise stays pending and then/catch never run.
  • Output: start, 1, 2, end.
  • ⚠ A promise that never settles silently hangs your code.
JavaScript first executes the synchronous code, then the asynchronous code. When you define a promise, the executor is synchronous code; once the promise is resolved or rejected, the asynchronous part (the .then/.catch callbacks) starts. I.e. once the promise is initialized and all the synchronous code has executed, the asynchronous code executes (the above example is based on that: only when the promise is resolved or rejected do the asynchronous callbacks apply). ✔ Note: here resolve/reject is NEVER called, so the promise stays pending forever and neither .then nor .catch ever runs. If resolve(3) were added, the output would be start 1 2 end 3.executor मधील code लगेच (synchronously) चालतो, म्हणून 1, 2 हे "end" च्या आधी येतात. या उदाहरणात resolve/reject कधीच call होत नाही, म्हणून promise कायम pending राहतो आणि .then/.catch चालतच नाहीत.

6. Interview: throw vs return new Error

Your Notes: 
function job1(state) {
  return new Promise(function (resolved, reject) {
    if (state) { resolved("success"); } else { reject("error"); }
  });
}
let promise = job1(true);
promise.then(function (data) {
  console.log(data);        // success
  return job1(true);
}).then(function (data) {
  if (data !== "victory") {
    throw "defect";
    // here we check whether data is victory; data is "success", not "victory", so it throws an error;
    // the return job1(true) is never reached, and it goes to the next catch block
  }
  return job1(true);
}).then(function (data) {
  console.log(data);        // skipped
}).catch(function (error) {
  console.log(error);       // defect
  return job1(false);
}).then(function (data) {
  console.log(data);        // skipped
  return job1(true);
}).catch(function (error) {
  console.log(error);       // error
  return "error caught";
}).then(function (data) {
  console.log(data);        // error caught
  // By itself, this is not a rejected Promise.
  // It is simply returning an Error object, not throwing it or rejecting a promise
  return new Error("text");
  // again this is not a rejected promise; it is again a resolved promise
}).then(function (data) {
  console.log("data....", data);          // → data.... Error: text  (with stack trace)
  console.log("success", data.message);   // success text
}).catch(function (data) {
  console.log("data");
  console.log("error", data.message);
});
// verified output: success → defect → error → error caught → data.... Error: text → success text
  • What happens: the full chain step by step: success → throw "defect" → catch returns job1(false) → reject "error" → catch returns a string → then returns an Error object (fulfilled) → next then logs its message.
  • Output: success, defect, error, error caught, data.... Error: text, success text.
  • ✅ Practise reading chains: rejection jumps to the next catch, a return value continues the chain.
Figure 129: What decides the next step of a chain: return (fulfil) vs throw (reject).
.then/.catch मधून काहीही return केले (Error object सुद्धा) तरी पुढचा promise fulfilled होतो आणि पुढचा .then चालतो. throw केल्यास किंवा rejected promise return केल्यास पुढचे .then वगळून .catch चालतो. .catch ने value return केली की chain पुन्हा सुरळीत होते.

7. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. What is the difference between throw new Error() and return new Error() inside .then?
  • throw rejects the next promise (goes to .catch). return just passes the Error object as a normal value (goes to .then).
Q2. What happens after a .catch() in the middle of a chain?
  • If it returns a value (or nothing), the chain continues as fulfilled. If it throws or returns a rejected promise, the next .catch handles it.
Q3. Why do function declarations with the same name break promise demo files?
  • Declarations are hoisted and the last one wins for the whole scope, so earlier calls use the wrong version. Use unique names, const function expressions (which give a SyntaxError on redeclare), or modules.
Q4. Order: sync code, microtasks (promises), macrotasks (setTimeout)?
  • Sync first, then ALL microtasks (.then callbacks, queueMicrotask), then one macrotask (a timer), and repeat. So a resolved promise's .then runs before setTimeout(…, 0).
Q5. Output-based questions
console.log("A");
setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("C"));
new Promise((r) => { console.log("D"); r(); }).then(() => console.log("E"));
console.log("F");                    // → A D F C E B
Promise.reject("x").then(() => 1).catch((e) => console.log(e)).then((v) => console.log(v));   // → x, undefined
Promise.resolve().then(() => { throw new Error("boom"); }).catch((e) => console.log(e.message));   // → boom
  • What happens: sync logs first (A D F), then microtasks (promise thens: C E), then the timer (B). catch returns undefined to the next then; a throw inside then goes to catch.
  • Output: A D F C E B, x, undefined, boom.
  • ✅ The most common async output question.
Inside a handlerThe next step
return value / Error object.then (fulfilled)
return nothing.then receives undefined
throw / rejected promise.catch
catch returnsThe chain recovers → .then
Executor without resolve/rejectPending forever
थोडक्यात: throw = reject, return = fulfil (Error object return केला तरी). catch नंतर chain पुन्हा चालू होते. executor synchronous असतो. sync code → microtasks (promise) → macrotasks (setTimeout) असा क्रम असतो. एकाच नावाची functions पुन्हा declare करू नका.

शेवटची comment /* बंद केलेली नाही, म्हणून संपूर्ण file SyntaxError देते आणि एकही ओळ चालत नाही. तसेच एकाच नावाची functions अनेकदा declare केल्यामुळे शेवटचीच वापरली जाते, आणि resold/resolve या typo मुळे ReferenceError येतो.

1. async/await

Your Notes (20_async_await/async_awati.js):
  1. async/await is a modern way to handle asynchronous operations; it makes code more readable compared to callbacks and promises.
  2. async defines an asynchronous function, which always returns a promise.
  3. Inside the async function we use the await keyword to pause execution until the promise is resolved, making async code look like synchronous code.
  4. If an async function returns a value, JS automatically wraps it in a resolved promise.
  5. If an error is thrown, it returns a rejected promise.
  6. This approach simplifies code structure and improves readability.
  7. async and await are used to handle Promises (the await keyword can only be used inside an async function, or at the top level of an ES module).
Definition: async function f() always returns a Promise (its return value fulfils it, a throw rejects it). await p pauses only THAT function until p settles: fulfilled → the value; rejected → it throws (catch with try/catch). The rest of the program keeps running; the function resumes later as a microtask.

2. Why Use async/await? How It Works

Your Notes:
  1. Cleaner syntax: avoids deep .then() chaining (callback hell).
  2. Easier to read and maintain.
  3. Better error handling using try...catch.
async function:
  1. A function declared with async automatically returns a Promise.
  2. Inside an async function, you can use await to pause execution until a Promise resolves.

await keyword:
  1. Used inside async functions to wait for a Promise to resolve.
  2. It makes asynchronous code look more like synchronous code.

3. Advantages of async/await

Your Notes:
  1. Improved readability: using async/await makes asynchronous code look like synchronous code, easier to read and maintain compared to the traditional callback and promise-based approaches.
  2. Sequential flow: helps you write asynchronous code in a way that resembles synchronous code.
  3. Error handling: async/await works seamlessly with try/catch blocks for error handling, providing a more intuitive way to manage errors, as in synchronous code; this is much cleaner than chaining .catch() in a promise chain.
  4. Sequential execution: with async/await, asynchronous operations can be written sequentially, avoiding deeply nested callbacks; each await waits for the previous one to resolve before moving on.
  5. You can still run asynchronous operations in parallel by using Promise.all with async/await, improving performance when tasks are independent.

4. Why Do We Still Need Promises if We Use async/await?

Your Notes:
  1. Because async/await is built on top of Promises. It does not replace Promises; it provides a cleaner, more readable syntax for working with them.
Think of it like this:
  • Promise = the core engine (how asynchronous work happens)
  • async/await = new driving controls (how we write the code). You still need Promises
  • async/await just gives you a better way to consume them. Internally, it still uses Promises under the hood.
async/await हे promise ला पर्याय नाही, तर promise वापरण्याची सोपी पद्धत आहे (syntactic sugar). async function नेहमी promise परत करतो, आणि await त्या function ला promise settle होईपर्यंत थांबवतो. बाकीचा program मात्र चालूच राहतो.

5. What is the Difference between a Promise and async/await?

Your Notes: both are used to handle asynchronous operations in JS.

1. Promise

  1. A promise is an object that represents the upcoming completion or failure of an asynchronous operation or event, with its resulting value.
  2. Promises were introduced in ES6 (ES2015). ✔ "ES1 6" → ES6 (2015).Promise ES6 (2015) मध्ये आले.
  3. A promise is used to handle an asynchronous operation.
  4. Promises use .then() and .catch() to handle the result (i.e. basically, promises use the chaining syntax with .then() and .catch() to handle the asynchronous operation).
  5. Readability: promises can get nested and messy.
  6. For error handling, .catch() is used (i.e. errors in promises are typically handled with the .catch() method or by passing a second callback to .then()). ✔ "changing the second .then() callback" → PASSING a second callback to .then(onFulfilled, onRejected)."changing" नाही, .then ला दुसरा callback (onRejected) "pass" करणे.
  7. Works everywhere.
  8. You define a function that returns a promise, then chain a .then() callback to handle the successful result and .catch() to handle the error when the promise is rejected.
  9. So this can lead to callback (promise) hell if you have multiple asynchronous operations.

2. async-await

  1. async-await is syntactic sugar over promises, built on top of Promises for better readability (i.e. a more synchronous-looking syntax for handling promises).
  2. Introduced in ES8 (2017).
  3. async/await is used to handle promises more cleanly (i.e. it can significantly improve code readability and maintainability, especially when dealing with more complex asynchronous code).
  4. It uses the async and await keywords to handle the promise.
  5. Using async/await is cleaner and easier to read.
  6. For error handling, the try/catch block is used (i.e. in async/await you handle errors the traditional way, with a try/catch block).
  7. await only works inside an async function (or at the top level of an ES module).
  8. In async/await, errors are automatically propagated up the call stack, making them easier to track and handle.
Note: async/await is basically a replacement for .then() and .catch() that makes code cleaner and easier to read.
FeaturePromise (.then)async/await
IntroducedES6 (2015)ES8 (2017)
StyleChaining callbacksLooks synchronous
Errors.catch()try/catch
Parallel workPromise.all directlyawait Promise.all([...])
DebuggingHarder (callbacks)Easier (line by line)

6. First Example: Sequential awaits

Your Notes:
Example 1
console.log("start");
function importantAction(user_name) {
  return new Promise((resolved, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => { resolved(`subscribed to the ${user_name}`); }, 500);
  });
}
function likeVideo(video) {
  return new Promise((resolved, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => { resolved(`like the video ${video}`); }, 100);
  });
}
function sharedVideo(shared) {
  return new Promise((resolved, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => { resolved(`share the video ${shared}`); }, 2000);
  });
}
console.log("end");
  • What happens: three promise-returning functions with different delays (definitions + sync logs).
  • Output: start, end.
1. an asynchronous function is created by adding the async keyword before the function
// 1. an asynchronous function is created by adding the async keyword before the function
// 2. here we create a function and call the promise-returning functions inside it, like importantAction
// 3. here we don't use .then(); with .then() we would get the promise object, but we want the result
const result = async () => {
  const m1 = await importantAction("vishal");   // waits 500 ms
  const m2 = await likeVideo("js");             // then 100 ms
  const m3 = await sharedVideo("on youtube");   // then 2000 ms  → total ≈ 2.6 s (sequential)
  //   console.log(m1 + " " + m2 + " " + m3 + " ");
  return m1, m2, m3;
};
console.log(result());   // → Promise { <pending> }   (an async function ALWAYS returns a promise)
// ✔ "return m1, m2, m3" uses the COMMA operator → returns only m3 ("share the video on youtube").
//    To return all three: return [m1, m2, m3]  (or an object), and read it with await result() / result().then(...)
  • What happens: await pauses the async function until each promise settles, one after another (~2.6 s total); the async function itself returns a pending promise immediately.
  • Output: Promise { }.
  • ✅ Async code that reads top-to-bottom.
  • ⚠ return m1, m2, m3 returns only m3 (comma operator); return an array instead.
return m1, m2, m3 मध्ये comma operator मुळे फक्त शेवटची value (m3) परत येते. तिन्ही हव्या असतील तर array [m1, m2, m3] return करा. async function नेहमी promise देतो, म्हणून console.log(result()) मध्ये Promise { <pending> } दिसते.

7. How to Handle Errors in async/await

Your Notes: to handle errors in async/await, use the traditional try, catch and finally blocks. 
const res1 = async () => {
  try {
    let p1 = await importantAction("vishal shinde");
    let p2 = await likeVideo("js");
    let p3 = await sharedVideo("youtube");
    let result = p1 + " " + p2 + " " + p3;
    console.log(result);   // → subscribed to the vishal shinde like the video js share the video youtube
    return result;
  } catch (e) {
    console.log("error", e);
  }
};
console.log(res1());   // → Promise { <pending> }
res1();
console.log(res1());   // → Promise { <pending> }
// res1 is called 3 times, so the result line is printed 3 times (≈ 2.6 s later)
  • What happens: try/catch around awaits handles any rejection; calling res1 three times runs it three times.
  • Output: Promise { } twice, then the result line three times (~2.6 s later).

8. Output-Based Questions

Your Notes:
1. The executor runs synchronously
// 1.
const promise = new Promise((resolved, reject) => {
  console.log(1);
  resolved(2);
});
console.log(promise);   // → Promise { 2 }   (already fulfilled: the executor ran synchronously)
// inside the promise, JavaScript runs any synchronous code first, then the asynchronous part (.then)
promise.then((result) => {
  console.log("result", result);   // → result 2   (later, as a microtask)
  return result;
}).catch((error) => {
  console.log(error);
});
console.log(promise);   // → Promise { 2 }
  • What happens: the code inside new Promise runs immediately (1 is logged, the promise is already fulfilled); .then runs later as a microtask.
  • Output: 1, Promise { 2 }, Promise { 2 }, result 2.
2. resolve() doesn't stop the executor
// 2
console.log("hi");
const p1 = new Promise((resolved, reject) => {
  console.log(1);
  resolved(2);
  console.log(3);   // resolve() does NOT stop the executor → 3 is still printed
});
p1.then((r) => console.log(r)).catch((error) => console.log(e));
// → hi 1 3 … 2
// ⚠ the catch logs "e" but the parameter is "error"; it would throw ReferenceError if p1 ever rejected
  • What happens: code after resolve still runs.
  • Output: hi 1 3 … 2.
  • ⚠ Use return resolve(x) if nothing should run after it.
3. Sync logs before the then callback
// 3
console.log("hi1");
const fn = () => {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    console.log(1);
    resolve("success");
  });
};
console.log("middle");
fn().then((r) => console.log(r)).catch((e) => console.log(e));
console.log("end");
// → hi1 middle 1 end … success
  • What happens: fn() runs its executor immediately (1); then waits for the stack to clear.
  • Output: hi1 middle 1 end … success.
Combined order in your file (verified): 1 → Promise {2} → Promise {2} → hi → 1 → 3 → hi1 → middle → 1 → end → (microtasks) result 2 → 2 → success. All the synchronous logs come first, then the .then callbacks in the order they were registered.
Figure 130: await pauses only the async function; the rest of the program keeps running, and the function resumes when the promise settles.

9. Which One to Use? & Summary

Your Notes:
  1. Use async/await when you need cleaner, readable and sequential async operations.
  2. Use Promise (combinators) when dealing with multiple independent async operations that can run in parallel (they can be combined: await Promise.all([...])).
Why we use async/await instead of promises:
  1. async/await can greatly improve the readability of asynchronous code compared to callbacks and .then() chaining when dealing with promises.
  2. Problems with promises: 1. chaining can get messy. When we have many promise calls, it's easy for the code to become deeply nested, and that makes it hard to read and understand; this is called callback hell.
  3. Error handling is tricky: in promises we need to handle errors in a catch at the end of each chain; this can get confusing when there are many steps in your code.
  4. async/await fixes the messiness and confusion of promises, making your code simpler and more manageable: there's no need to chain .then() and .catch(), and error handling just uses a try/catch block, so it is much easier to read and understand, like regular code, without a bunch of nested callbacks.
Summary about async/await
  1. async/await makes promises easier to write and makes complex code simple.
  2. async makes a function return a promise.
  3. await makes a function wait until a promise is settled (resolved or rejected).
  4. fetch() always returns a promise, so you can consume it with await (or .then()). ✔ "If you used fetch method it always async await return promise" → fetch returns a promise; await (or .then) consumes it.fetch नेहमी promise परत करतो; तो await किंवा .then ने वापरता येतो.
  5. An async function usually contains await, but it doesn't have to. ✔ "If you define an async function it always contains await". await is optional; an async function without await still returns a promise.async function मध्ये await असलाच पाहिजे असे नाही. await नसला तरी तो promise परत करतो.
  6. async/await does NOT give error handling by default; you add it with try/catch (or .catch() on the returned promise). ✔ "If you used async and await by default provided error handling". An uncaught rejection inside still rejects the returned promise (an unhandled rejection).async/await मध्ये error handling आपोआप मिळत नाही; try/catch लिहावा लागतो, नाहीतर unhandled rejection येतो.
  7. So the awaited code should be written inside a try/catch block (or handled by the caller).

10. Error Handling in async/await

Your Notes: if a promise resolves, await returns the result; if a promise is rejected, await throws the error, just as if there were a throw statement.
Rejected await = throw
async function getUser(userId) {
  await Promise.reject(new Error("invalid user Id"));
}
// is the same as:
async function getUser(userId) {
  throw new Error("invalid user id");
}
// (both return a promise rejected with the Error)

async function getUser(userId) {
  try {
    const user = await Promise.reject(new Error("invalid user id "));
  } catch (error) {
    console.log(error);   // → Error: invalid user id
  }
}
  • What happens: awaiting a rejected promise throws inside the async function; it's the same as throwing directly; try/catch catches it.
  • Output: Error: invalid user id.
One try/catch for several awaits
// - it is possible to catch errors caused by one or more awaited promises

async function showServices() {
  try {
    let user = await getUser(100);
    let services = await getServices(user);
    let cost = await getServiceCost(services);
    console.log(`the services cost is ${cost}`);
  } catch (error) {
    console.log(error);   // ONE catch for all three awaits
  }
}
// ✔ was 'the services cost is ${cost}' with single quotes → ${} is NOT interpolated; use backticks
// ⚠ getServiceCost is not defined anywhere (the functions are named getServicesCost); showServices() is never called
  • What happens: any of the awaited steps failing jumps to the single catch.
  • Output: (not called in your file).
  • ✅ Much simpler than a catch per step.
  • ⚠ Use backticks for ${} interpolation.
'...${cost}' हे single quotes मध्ये लिहिल्यामुळे ${cost} जसेच्या तसे छापले जाते. template literal साठी backticks (`) लागतात. getServiceCost हे नाव कुठेही define केलेले नाही.

11. The await & async Keywords

Your Notes: the await keyword
  1. Use the await keyword to wait for a promise to settle, in either the resolved or the rejected state. ✔ "stalled" → SETTLED."stalled" नाही, "settled" (पूर्ण झालेला).
  2. You can use the await keyword only inside an async function.
  3. It is used before a promise, and it pauses the function's execution until the promise is settled (fulfilled or rejected).
  4. If the promise is fulfilled, the result is returned; if the promise is rejected, an exception is thrown, which you can catch using a try/catch block.
async function example() {
  try {
    const result = await someAsyncfunction();
    console.log(result);
  } catch (error) {
    console.log(error);
  }
}
// In the above example, the await keyword instructs the JavaScript engine to wait for someAsyncfunction() to
// complete before displaying the message.
// ✔ the comment said "wait for the sayHi() function"; this example awaits someAsyncfunction()
// If you use the await operator outside an async function, you get an error
// (SyntaxError in classic scripts; top-level await is allowed only in ES modules).
  • What happens: await waits for the promise before the next line; outside an async function (classic script) it's a SyntaxError.
  • Output: (depends on someAsyncfunction).
  • ⚠ Top-level await works only in ES modules.
The async keyword:
  1. The async keyword lets you define a function that handles asynchronous operations.
  2. To define an async function, place the async keyword in front of the function keyword, as follows.
  3. When you declare a function as async, the function always returns a promise, either explicitly or implicitly.
  4. Inside the async function you use the await keyword to pause the execution of the function until the promise is resolved; this lets you write asynchronous code in a more sequential and readable manner.
Example 1
async function fetchData() {
  const response = await fetch("https://api.google.com");
  const data = await response.json();
  return data;
}
  • What happens: a typical fetch: await the response, then await response.json().
  • Output: (the parsed data).
  • ⚠ fetch only rejects on network errors; check response.ok for 404/500.
New example explanation
// # New example explanation
async function sayHi() {
  return Promise.resolve("hi");
}
// here the sayHi function returns a promise that you can consume
sayHi().then(console.log);   // → hi
// Asynchronous functions execute asynchronously via the event loop.
// It always returns a promise.

// // Example:
// sayHi()  // the function returns a promise; you can consume it.
// async function sayHi() {
//   return Promise.resolve('hi');
// }
// // Besides regular functions, you can use the async keyword in a function expression
// let sayHi = async function () {
//   return 'hi'
// }
// // arrow function
// let sayHi = async () => 'Hi'
  • What happens: an async function's return value is wrapped in a promise (returning a promise just adopts it).
  • Output: hi.

12. Why Was async/await Introduced Instead of Just Promises?

Your Notes:
  1. Promise chaining is the technique for handling asynchronous operations sequentially using promises.
  2. While it's a powerful and versatile approach, there are some common problems and challenges associated with it:
  3. Callback hell (pyramid of doom): if you have multiple asynchronous operations to perform sequentially, chaining promises can lead to a deeply nested code structure, which can be hard to read; this is often referred to as callback hell or the pyramid of doom. 
    // asyncFunction().then((result1) => {
//   return asyncFunction2(result1);
// }).then((result2) => {
//   return asyncFunction3((result2) => {
//   }).then((result3) => {
//     return asyncFunction4(result3)
//   })
// })
    • What happens: (commented) a then-chain that gets nested and messy; async/await fixes this.
    • Output: (no output).
  4. Error handling: proper error handling in a promise chain can be challenging; errors that occur at any stage in the chain are caught in the .catch() block at the end, making it difficult to pinpoint exactly where the error occurred.
  5. Readability and maintainability:
    1. promise chains can be difficult to read and maintain as they grow in length;
    2. it's easy to lose track of the flow of the code, especially with multiple .then() blocks.
  6. Inflexibility: changing the order of, or adding new steps to, a sequence of asynchronous operations can require significant modification of the existing promise chain, potentially introducing bugs.
  7. Limited parallelism: promise chaining is inherently sequential, which means the operations in the chain are executed one after another. If you have independent asynchronous tasks that could run in parallel, promise chaining may not be the most efficient approach. ✔ "independent synchronous task" → independent ASYNCHRONOUS tasks. (Note: async/await with sequential awaits has the same limitation; for parallel work use await Promise.all.)इथे "asynchronous" कामे असा अर्थ आहे. sequential await सुद्धा एकामागून एकच चालतात; parallel साठी await Promise.all वापरा.
So, in conclusion, to address these challenges and make code more readable and maintainable, modern JavaScript introduced async/await. async/await provides better error handling, improved readability and greater flexibility in managing asynchronous operations.

13. Callback → Promise → async/await: the getUser Example

Your Notes: version 1, nested callbacks 
function getUser(userId, callback) {
  console.log("Get user from the database");
  setTimeout(() => {
    callback({ userId: userId, username: "vishal" });
  }, 1000);
}

  console.log(`get services of ${user.username} from the api`);
  setTimeout(() => { callback(["Email", "Vpn", "Cdn"]); }, 2 * 1000);
}

// - here are the nested callback functions
getUser(100, (user) => {

      console.log(`the services const is ${cost}`);
    });

});
// output (when run on its own)

// get services of vishal from the api
// calculate services cost of Email,Vpn,Cdn
// the services const is 300
// ⚠ in your single file, the LATER promise versions of getUser/getServices override these (hoisting),
//   so this nested-callback call never reaches its callbacks

  • ⚠ In one file, later declarations with the same names replace these.
Version 2, promises: to avoid this callback hell issue, ES6 introduced the promise, which lets you write asynchronous code in a more manageable way. First we need to return a promise from each function: 
function getUser(userId) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    console.log(`get user form the database`);
    setTimeout(() => {
      resolve({ userId: userId, username: "vishal" });

}
function getServices(user) {

    setTimeout(() => { resolve(["Email", "vpn", "Cdn"]); }, 2 * 1000);
  });
}
function getServicesCost(services) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    console.log(`calculate services cost of ${services}`);
    setTimeout(() => {

    }, 3 * 1000);   // ✔ your code had "}) }, 3 * 1000)". The 3000 was passed to new Promise(...)

// here we chain the promises

  • What happens: the promise version, chained by passing the functions to then.
  • Output: the three logs, then 300.
  1. ES2017 introduced the async/await keywords, built on top of promises, letting you write asynchronous code that looks like synchronous code and is more readable. ✔ "looks like asynchronous code" → looks like SYNCHRONOUS code.async/await मुळे asynchronous code "synchronous" सारखा दिसतो.
  2. Technically speaking, async/await is syntactic sugar for promises.
  3. If a function returns a promise, you can place the await keyword in front of the function call, like let result = await f();
  4. await will wait for the promise returned from f() to settle.
  5. The await keyword can be used only inside an async function.
Version 3, async/await (your file repeats the promise functions once more here; that copy has (resold, reject) but calls resolve(...) → ReferenceError: resolve is not defined. Fixed below):
Example 1
function getServices(user) {

    console.log(`get The services of ${user.username} from the api`);

getUser(100).then(getServices).then(getServicesCost).then(console.log);

Instead of that, define an async function that calls the three asynchronous operations in

  let services = await getServices(user);

एकच काम तीन पद्धतींनी: (1) callbacks, म्हणजे आत आत nesting; (2) promises, म्हणजे .then().then() chain; (3) async/await, म्हणजे वरून खाली साध्या code सारखे. तिन्हीचा result एकच (300) आहे, पण async/await वाचायला सर्वात सोपे आहे.

14. Which One Do You Prefer: async/await or Promises?

Your Notes: Use async/await when:
  1. You want cleaner, more readable and easier-to-understand code.
  2. You need to write code that looks synchronous (top-to-bottom flow) but still handles asynchronous operations.
  3. You are working with try/catch blocks for error handling.
I generally prefer async/await because it makes the code more readable and easier to debug, especially when handling sequential asynchronous operations. It avoids the "promise chaining" mess and allows using try/catch for cleaner error handling.
Use .then() / Promises when:
  1. You need to handle multiple promises in parallel (e.g. Promise.all).
  2. You're doing simple chaining and don't want to mark the whole function as async.
  3. You're writing library or framework code where you want to return raw Promises.
  4. I need to run multiple async tasks in parallel (Promise.all() is great for that).
  5. I'm working with stream-based or event-driven async operations where .then() chaining makes sense.
Which is better, promises or async/await?
✅ Use async/await whenever possible → cleaner, more readable, easier to maintain.
✅ Use Promises directly only when: you need to run multiple tasks in parallel (Promise.all, Promise.race), or you're writing a quick one-liner without needing a whole function.
Extra Details: sequential vs parallel awaits 
// sequential: ≈ 500 + 100 + 2000 = 2.6 s
const a = await importantAction("v"); const b = await likeVideo("js");
// parallel: ≈ 2 s (the slowest one)
const [x, y, z] = await Promise.all([importantAction("v"), likeVideo("js"), sharedVideo("yt")]);
// ⚠ await inside forEach does NOT wait: arr.forEach(async x => await f(x))
//    use for...of (sequential) or await Promise.all(arr.map(f)) (parallel)
  • What happens: separate awaits run one after another (sum of delays); Promise.all runs them together (the slowest delay). await inside forEach doesn't wait.
  • Output: (notes).
  • ✅ Use Promise.all for independent requests.

15. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. What does an async function return?
  • Always a Promise: its return value fulfils it, a thrown error rejects it, and a returned promise is adopted. async () => 5 gives Promise {5}.
Q2. Does await block the whole program?
  • No. It pauses only the current async function; the call stack is free for other code. The function resumes as a microtask when the promise settles.
Q3. How do you handle errors with async/await?
  • Wrap the awaits in try/catch(/finally), or call f().catch(...). A rejected awaited promise throws at the await line.
Q4. How do you run awaits in parallel?
  • Start all the promises first, then await Promise.all([...]) (or allSettled). Consecutive awaits are sequential and slower.
Q5. Can you use await in forEach / at the top level?
  • forEach ignores the returned promises, so it doesn't wait: use for...of or Promise.all with map. Top-level await works only in ES modules (type="module", .mjs).
Q6. Output-based questions
async function f() { console.log(2); await null; console.log(4); }
console.log(1); f(); console.log(3);                 // → 1 2 3 4
const g = async () => { throw new Error("x"); };
g().catch((e) => console.log(e.message));            // → x
console.log(typeof (async () => 1)().then);          // → function
async function h() { return 1, 2, 3; }  h().then(console.log);   // → 3 (comma operator)
  • What happens: an async function runs synchronously until its first await; throwing rejects its promise; it always returns a promise; return 1, 2, 3 returns 3.
  • Output: 1 2 3 4, x, function, 3.
PointRemember
asyncAlways returns a Promise
awaitPauses only this function until the promise settles
Errorstry/catch; a rejection = a throw at the await line
Parallelawait Promise.all([...])
Built onPromises (syntactic sugar), ES2017
थोडक्यात: async function नेहमी promise देतो. await फक्त त्या function ला थांबवतो, पूर्ण program ला नाही. errors साठी try/catch लागतो. स्वतंत्र कामे parallel करण्यासाठी await Promise.all वापरा. forEach मध्ये await थांबत नाही.

1. The Event Loop: the Setting

Your Notes (41_eventLoop/eventLoop.js): JS is a synchronous, single-threaded language: it has one call stack, so it does only one thing at a time. The call stack is present in the JS engine, and the whole JS code runs inside the call stack. 
// ex.
function a() {
  console.log('x')
  a();
  console.log('end)
}
// ✔ missing closing quote ('end'), and a() calls ITSELF with no exit condition → infinite recursion →
//    RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded (stack overflow, §5). As an event-loop example, call a() once from outside.
  • What happens: a function that calls itself with no stop condition fills the call stack.
  • Output: RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded (plus the missing quote is a SyntaxError).
  • ⚠ Recursion always needs a base case.
When you execute the above piece of code, or any JavaScript code, JS creates a global execution context, and this global execution context is pushed onto the call stack; the whole JS code runs line by line in the global execution context.
The browser has a JavaScript engine, local storage and timers, so the browser has superpowers to communicate with the external world. So while running JavaScript code, we need the browser's superpowers; the JS engine needs some kind of connection, some way to access those superpowers. So the browser provides Web APIs: to access these superpowers we need the Web APIs.
List of Web APIs: Timers: setTimeout, setInterval · Network: fetch, XMLHttpRequest · DOM: document.querySelector, addEventListener · Storage: localStorage, sessionStorage · Geolocation, File API, Console API, etc.
Note: 1. the browser has window as its global object, and through the window object the browser gives these superpowers to the JS engine.
Definition: The event loop is the runtime's scheduler: forever, it (1) runs the current task to completion on the call stack, (2) then drains the whole microtask queue (promise reactions, await continuations, queueMicrotask), (3) lets the browser render if needed, and (4) takes the next macrotask (timer, I/O, UI event, message) and repeats. This gives a single thread non-blocking concurrency.
Event loop म्हणजे runtime चा "वेळापत्रक बनवणारा": call stack रिकामा झाला की आधी सगळे microtasks (promise.then, await नंतरचा भाग) चालवतो, मग गरज असल्यास page render होतो, आणि मग एक macrotask (setTimeout, click, I/O) घेतो. हे चक्र सतत चालू असते, म्हणून single thread असूनही JS अडकत नाही.

2. Definition of the Event Loop

The event loop is a fundamental concept in JavaScript that handles asynchronous operations like: setTimeout(), Promises, AJAX calls, user interactions, event listeners.

  1. The event loop is a tiny component within the JavaScript runtime.
  2. The event loop is the mechanism in JavaScript that handles asynchronous operations, ensuring that non-blocking tasks are executed efficiently.
  3. The event loop is a constantly (continuously) running process that coordinates tasks between the call stack and the callback queue to achieve concurrency, so the event loop continuously checks the call stack and the callback queue (i.e. it monitors both the call stack and the callback queue).
  4. If there is a callback function waiting in the callback queue, the event loop checks whether the call stack is empty; as soon as the stack is empty, it takes that callback function from the callback queue and pushes it onto the call stack to be executed. This continuous process is called the event loop.
  5. The event loop especially explains how asynchronous code execution works,

i.e. it is the heart of JS's concurrency model and plays a significant role in event handling, callbacks and non-blocking operations; JS is a single-threaded language, which means JS can do one thing at a single point in time. ✔ "js currency model" → CONCURRENCY model."currency" (पैसा) नाही, "concurrency" (एकाच वेळी अनेक कामे हाताळणे).

The event loop and the callback queue are part of:
  1. the JavaScript runtime environment.
  2. They are not part of the JavaScript language (or the engine) itself, but are provided by the runtime / host, like browsers (Chrome: the V8 engine + Blink's event loop) and Node.js (built on V8, adding libuv's event loop and APIs like the file system, HTTP, etc.).
✔ "Browser engines (e.g. Chrome's V8)": V8 is the JavaScript ENGINE (call stack + heap); the event loop and the task queues belong to the HOST: the browser (or libuv in Node).V8 हा फक्त JS engine आहे (call stack + heap). event loop आणि queues browser (किंवा Node मध्ये libuv) देतो.

Web APIs / Node APIsHandle async operations (e.g. setTimeout, HTTP requests)
Callback Queue (Macrotask / Task Queue)Stores callbacks from Web APIs (e.g. setTimeout)
Microtask QueueStores microtasks (e.g. Promise.then)
Event LoopCoordinates the execution of the stack, the microtasks and the callback queue
✔ the table labelled the callback queue "(Microtask Queue)"; the callback queue is the MACROTASK (task) queue; the microtask queue is the separate row below it.callback queue म्हणजे macrotask queue. microtask queue वेगळी आहे. How it all works together:
  1. Synchronous code runs on the call stack.
  2. Async operations (like timers, fetch) go to the Web APIs.
  3. When the async operations complete, their callbacks are sent to:
    1. the microtask queue (if it's a promise, etc.);
    2. the macrotask queue (if it's a timer, event listener, etc.).
  4. The event loop: waits until the call stack is empty; once the call stack is empty,
    1. it runs ALL the microtasks;
    2. then it picks ONE macrotask from the callback queue and puts it on the call stack (then microtasks again, and so on).

                   ▼

         └──────────────────────┘
         ┌──────────────────────┐
         │ Microtask Queue      │ (Promise.then, queueMicrotask)
         └──────────────────────┘

So, to summarize:
  1. the event loop and the callback queue are part of the JavaScript runtime environment (like browsers or Node.js), not the core JS language.
  2. They help manage and schedule asynchronous code execution.
