4. Call Stack, Stack Overflow & Execution Context (recap of Chapter 14)

What is the call stack?
  1. The call stack is a special data structure that keeps track of function calls in the order they are executed.
  2. The call stack is a fundamental mechanism that keeps track of function calls and ensures that functions are executed in the correct order, following the "Last In, First Out" (LIFO) principle.
  3. The call stack works in a LIFO manner (the last function called is the first one to be resolved).
  4. JavaScript uses a single thread to execute code, meaning only one function can be executing at a time; the call stack keeps track of which function is currently running.
How the call stack works:
  1. Function invocation: when a function is called, a new execution context is created; this context contains information about the function's execution, such as the values of its parameters and variables.
  2. Push onto the stack: the execution context of the called function is added ("pushed") onto the top of the call stack.
  3. Function execution: the JavaScript engine executes the code within the function's execution context.
  4. Return: once a function finishes executing, its execution context is removed ("popped") from the top of the call stack, and control returns to the calling function.

Call stack (summary): a stack that keeps track of function calls. LIFO: the last function pushed is the first to pop. When a function is called, its execution context is created and pushed onto the stack; when a function returns, its execution context is popped from the stack.
What is a stack overflow? When too many execution contexts are added to the call stack (e.g. infinite recursion), it exceeds the memory limit and crashes.
  1. The call stack has a fixed size, depending on the implementation of the host environment, either the web browser or Node.js.
  2. So if the number of execution contexts exceeds the size of the stack, a stack overflow error occurs.
  3. This usually happens due to excessive or infinite recursion, where a function keeps calling itself without an exit condition.

What is the global execution context?
  1. Definition: the default context where JavaScript code starts executing.
  2. The global execution context is the default context in which any JavaScript code runs outside of functions.
  3. It is the first context created when a JavaScript program is executed, and it serves as the environment for all global code, variables and functions.

The two phases of the global execution context:
  1. Creation phase: when the JavaScript engine starts executing code, it creates a global execution context. During this phase the engine:
    1. creates a global object (e.g. window in browsers, global in Node.js);
    2. sets up the this keyword to refer to the global object;
    3. initializes all the declared variables (without assigning their values yet) and functions (i.e. memory allocation: the JavaScript engine allocates memory for the variables and functions declared in the global scope).
  2. Execution phase:
    1. the JavaScript code is executed line by line;
    2. variables and functions are assigned their respective values;
    3. the this keyword continues to refer to the global object;
    4. the global execution context is the first context created when a JavaScript program starts;
    5. after the global context is created, other execution contexts are created for any functions called, and they are pushed onto the call stack;
    6. the global execution context stays at the bottom of the call stack throughout the program's execution.
Global Execution Context (GEC), short version: Definition: the default context where JavaScript code starts executing. Phases:
  1. creation phase: creates the global object (window in browsers, global in Node.js), sets this to the global object, allocates memory (variables: undefined, functions: a reference);
  2. execution phase: executes the code line by line, assigns values and invokes functions.

What is an execution context?
  1. An execution context is an abstract concept of an environment where JavaScript code is evaluated and executed (or: the environment in which a piece of code is evaluated and executed).
  2. It is a container for all the information that the JavaScript engine needs to execute a function or evaluate a block of code. If you call any function, it creates an execution context for that function. There are three types of execution contexts in JavaScript: 1. the global execution context; 2. the function execution context;
  3. the eval execution context (rarely used in modern JavaScript).

Execution context (summary): the environment in which code is executed. Types:
  1. global,
  2. function,
  3. eval (rarely used).
  • Components of an execution context: 1. the variable environment (memory)
  • 2. the scope chain
  • 3. the value of this.

5. Explain the Execution Stack (Call Stack), Web APIs & the Message Queue

  1. The execution stack, also known as the call stack, is a data structure used by JavaScript to manage the execution of function calls; it keeps track of the functions called during the execution of a program, and it follows a Last In, First Out (LIFO) order.
  2. When a function is called, a new function execution context is created and pushed onto the call stack.
  3. When the function finishes execution, its context is popped off the stack.
  4. The call stack ensures that JavaScript executes functions in the correct order and maintains the proper scope and execution context.
Key concepts:
  1. Global Execution Context (GEC): the default execution context where the global code runs. When the program starts, the global execution context is pushed onto the call stack; it remains there until the script finishes execution.
  2. Web APIs: Web APIs refer to the browser APIs (or environments like Node.js) that allow JavaScript to interact with the web, perform AJAX calls, or handle asynchronous tasks like setTimeout(), DOM manipulation or HTTP requests. These tasks are non-blocking and run asynchronously; they don't execute directly on the call stack, and are instead handled by the web browser or the Node.js environment.
  3. Message queue (task queue): the message queue is where the callbacks of asynchronous tasks are placed after the Web APIs finish their work. The queued callbacks are categorized into:
    1. Microtasks:
      1. these include promise reactions and MutationObserver callbacks;
      2. microtasks have higher priority than macrotasks and are executed right after the current script/task completes, before the next macrotask.
    2. Macrotasks:
      1. these include setTimeout(), setInterval(), I/O tasks and network/AJAX completion events;
      2. their callbacks run only when the execution stack is empty and the microtask queue has been drained.
    ✔ Clarified: technically the microtask queue is a SEPARATE queue from the (macro)task queue, not a part of the message queue.microtask queue ही message (task) queue चा भाग नाही, ती वेगळी queue आहे.
  4. Event loop: the event loop is responsible for managing the execution of tasks. It checks whether the call stack is empty; if the stack is empty, it pushes the tasks from the queues (starting with the microtasks) onto the call stack for execution.

6. Trace 1: Start / Promise / setTimeout

console.log("Start");
setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("Inside setTimeout");
}, 2000);
Promise.resolve().then(() => {
  console.log("Inside Promise");
});
console.log("End");
// → Start → End → Inside Promise → (2 s) Inside setTimeout
  • What happens: sync code first; then the promise callback (microtask); then the timer (macrotask) after 2 s.
  • Output: Start, End, Inside Promise, Inside setTimeout.
Step-by-step execution:
  1. Global execution context: the program begins executing and enters the global execution context. The first statement, console.log("Start"), is executed and "Start" is logged.
  2. setTimeout(): the setTimeout() function is called; this is a Web API call. The JavaScript engine hands the setTimeout callback to the Web API (browser or Node.js), which will queue it after 2000 ms (2 seconds). The callback is not executed immediately; instead, it is placed in the (macrotask) queue after the delay. ✔ heading "etTimeout()" → setTimeout()."etTimeout" नाही, setTimeout.
  3. Promise: Promise.resolve().then() is called. This creates a microtask, which is added to the microtask queue, which has a higher priority than the macrotask queue (like setTimeout).
  4. console.log("End"): the next statement, console.log("End"), is executed, logging "End" to the console.
  5. The call stack is empty: at this point, all the synchronous code has executed, and the call stack is empty.
  6. Event loop: the event loop checks the call stack. Since the stack is empty, the event loop moves to the queues. First, the event loop checks the microtask queue: the promise callback is executed and "Inside Promise" is logged. Then, the event loop moves to the macrotask queue: the setTimeout callback is executed, and "Inside setTimeout" is logged after the specified delay.
✔ Note (verified in Node): in your FILE, fun1() (Trace 2) is also synchronous code at the top level, so the real full output is: Start → End → function 1 is starting → function 1 end the execution → Inside Promise → Inside setTimeout (2 s) → function 2 is running... (3 s).file मध्ये fun1() सुद्धा synchronous आहे, म्हणून त्याचे दोन्ही logs "Inside Promise" च्या आधी येतात.

7. Trace 2: fun1 → fun2 → setTimeout

const fun2 = () => {
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log("function 2 is running...");
  }, 3000);
};
const fun1 = () => {
  console.log("function 1 is starting");
  fun2();
  console.log("function 1 end the execution");
};
fun1();
// → function 1 is starting → function 1 end the execution → (3 s) function 2 is running...
  • What happens: fun2 only schedules a timer and returns; fun1 finishes; 3 s later the callback runs.
  • Output: function 1 is starting, function 1 end the execution, function 2 is running....
Example explanation:
  1. If you call any function, it creates an execution context. An execution context has two phases:
    1. the creation phase;
    2. the execution phase.
  2. CREATION PHASE: when the JavaScript engine executes the script for the first time, it creates the global execution context; during this phase the JavaScript engine performs the following tasks:
    1. creates the global object: window in the browser;
    2. creates this and binds it to the global object;
    3. sets up memory for storing variables and function references;
    4. stores the function declarations in memory and the variables within the global execution context with the initial value undefined.
  3. EXECUTION PHASE:
    1. after creating the global execution context, it moves to the execution phase;
    2. during the execution phase, the JavaScript engine executes the code line by line, assigns values to the variables and executes the function calls;
    3. each function call creates a new function execution context (including an arguments object that references all the parameters of the function).
In the above example:
  1. You call fun1(), so a fun1() execution context is created.
  2. Then the console.log is executed and prints whatever is written, and its execution context is removed from the execution stack.
  3. Then the next line executes: it has the function call fun2(). Any function you call gets its own execution context, like the fun2() execution context.
  4. In fun2, the first line has the setTimeout() function, which also gets its own execution context (setTimeout is a function call too).
  5. setTimeout() comes under the Web API part. Inside the setTimeout is console.log('function 2 is running...'), but it waits for 3 SECONDS, so that console.log doesn't create its execution context yet: it's a time-based event, set for 3000 ms, and its callback waits 3 seconds. ✔ 3000 ms = 3 SECONDS, not "3 millisecond" (the same fix in steps 6 and 11).3000 ms म्हणजे 3 सेकंद, 3 millisecond नाही.
  6. We pass this callback function to the Web API for 3 seconds; once it is handed to the Web API, the setTimeout() execution context vanishes (is removed) from the execution stack.
  7. Now the execution stack has the fun2 context; fun2 checks whether it has anything more to execute; if not, fun2 also vanishes (removes its execution context) from the execution stack.
  8. The execution stack now has the fun1() context; it checks whether it has anything left to execute; it has the console.log, which gets its execution context, executes, and is removed from the execution stack.
  9. The fun1() execution context in the execution stack checks whether it has anything left to execute; if not, it vanishes (removes the fun1() execution context) from the execution stack.
  10. Now the execution stack is empty (except for the global context).
  11. The Web API holds the callback function and waits 3 seconds; once the 3 s complete, the Web API passes this callback function to the message queue.
  12. When the callback function is in the message queue, the event loop checks whether the execution stack is empty; if it is, the callback moves from the message queue to the execution stack and runs.
NOTE: whatever is in the Web API is passed to the message queue, and the event loop moves whatever the Web API passed to the message queue onto the execution stack when the execution stack is empty; there it gets its position in the execution stack, gets its execution context, executes, prints, and then its execution context is removed.

8. Event Loop: Definitions & Benefits

The Event Loop is a core part of JavaScript's concurrency model that handles asynchronous operations. It ensures non-blocking behaviour by coordinating tasks, callbacks and promises. "The event loop is what allows JavaScript to handle asynchronous operations in a non-blocking way, by processing the call stack and handling tasks from the task/microtask queues."

Definition of the event loop:
  1. The event loop is a process that waits for the call stack to be clear before pushing callbacks from the MESSAGE queue to the call stack (execution stack).

Once the call stack is clear, the event loop triggers and checks the MESSAGE queue for available callbacks. Def: JavaScript has a runtime model based on an event loop, which is responsible for executing the code, collecting and processing events, and executing queued sub-tasks. If the call stack is empty and there is a callback function in the task queue, it is dequeued from the task queue and run by pushing it onto the call stack. The JavaScript event loop is a constantly running process that coordinates tasks between the call stack and the callback queue to achieve concurrency.
What are the benefits of the event loop? We use a single-threaded event loop, which makes it very easy to access and modify mutable state between requests (no locks needed). Also, the event loop is a constantly running process that monitors both the call stack and the callback queue: if the call stack is not empty, the event loop waits until it is empty and then places the next function from the callback queue onto the call stack. If the callback queue is empty, nothing happens.
  1. Non-blocking I/O: JavaScript can perform long-running operations like network requests, file access or timers without blocking the main thread. It allows the rest of the code (e.g. UI rendering, animations) to continue running smoothly.
  2. Improved performance: the event loop processes tasks asynchronously, letting JavaScript handle multiple events efficiently without creating new threads. Instead of waiting for each task to complete, it adds them to a task queue and handles them when the call stack is empty.
  3. Simplified concurrency:
    1. JavaScript avoids the complexity of multithreading (like race conditions or deadlocks).
    2. It runs on a single thread, and the event loop ensures operations are executed in a predictable order.
  4. Responsive user interfaces: while waiting for events (e.g. click, input, timers), the event loop lets the browser continue rendering the UI. This keeps the app responsive and avoids "freezing" the screen (as long as no single task runs too long).
  5. Efficient resource usage: instead of spawning multiple threads (which consume memory/CPU), JavaScript uses callbacks, promises, microtasks/macrotasks and the event loop to schedule work. This results in lightweight and scalable applications.
  6. Foundation for async features (Promises, async/await): 1. Promises, async/await, setTimeout and fetch() all rely on the event loop. These features make asynchronous code more readable and manageable.
  7. Handles external events:
    1. the event loop listens for external events like:
    2. mouse clicks,
    3. keyboard input,
    4. server responses,
    5. timer completions.

    These are all queued and handled without blocking the main execution.
Call stack, Web APIs and message queue, summary: the call stack executes synchronous code. Web APIs handle asynchronous tasks and move their callbacks to the queues. The message queue holds tasks that are ready to run (macrotasks; microtasks have their own queue). The event loop manages the order in which tasks are processed, executing microtasks first and then macrotasks.

9. What are Web APIs and the Browser Environment?

  1. A Web API (API = Application Programming Interface) refers to a set of functions or protocols provided by the browser environment or the platform (like Node.js in server-side JavaScript) that lets JavaScript interact with the browser and perform various tasks.
  2. These tasks include interacting with the DOM, handling events, making network requests, accessing storage, managing timers, and much more. In JavaScript, Web APIs are provided by the browser to handle asynchronous tasks, offloading them from the call stack to the task queue. These APIs handle long-running tasks asynchronously, allowing the main thread (JavaScript's call stack) to stay non-blocking while waiting for responses or performing tasks.
  1. Fetch API: used for making network requests asynchronously; it lets you fetch resources from a server, such as making AJAX calls or fetching data from APIs. It returns a Promise, which resolves once the network request completes (its .then callbacks then run as MICROtasks).
  2. Timers API (setTimeout, setInterval): setTimeout() lets you execute a function after a specified delay; setInterval() repeatedly executes a function at specified intervals.
  3. Console API: provides methods for logging information to the browser's console; common methods include console.log(), console.error() and console.warn().
  4. Geolocation API: lets you get the geographical location of a device, such as the user's latitude and longitude; useful for location-based features like maps or nearby places.
  5. Web Storage API (localStorage, sessionStorage): provides two types of storage in the browser. localStorage stores data persistently across sessions (until manually deleted); sessionStorage stores data for the duration of a session (until the browser tab is closed).
Also: the URL API, the HTML DOM API, the Performance API, the File API.
Web APIs & the browser environment: APIs provided by the browser, or a runtime like Node.js, for asynchronous and system-level operations. Examples:
  1. timers: setTimeout, setInterval;
  2. network: fetch, XMLHttpRequest;
  3. DOM: document.querySelector, addEventListener;
  4. storage: localStorage, sessionStorage;
  5. Geolocation, the File API, the Console API, etc.

Task queues: 1. the microtask queue (high priority): Promise.then, MutationObserver; executed before the next macrotask. Macrotask queue: setTimeout, setInterval, DOM events.
Benefits of the event loop:
  1. enables non-blocking async execution;
  2. allows JavaScript (single-threaded) to manage I/O operations, user input and network requests efficiently;
  3. simplifies working with mutable state.

What is the message queue, or callback queue (macrotask queue)? 1. The callback queue (also called the macrotask queue) is where JavaScript stores asynchronous callbacks once their associated tasks (like timers or events) are ready to be executed.
Role in the event loop:
  1. the event loop checks the call stack;
  2. if the call stack is empty, the event loop:
  3. first executes all the microtasks (like Promise.then);
  4. then picks the next task from the callback queue (macrotask queue) and pushes it onto the call stack.

10. Microtasks & Macrotasks (macro&microTask.js)

JavaScript event loop overview:
  1. The event loop in JavaScript manages the execution of synchronous and asynchronous code.
  2. It runs continuously and does the following:
    1. executes the synchronous (call stack) code first;
    2. then processes the microtask queue;
    3. then picks and executes one task from the macrotask queue.

    Repeats the loop.
  1. JavaScript starts by running all the synchronous code on the call stack.
Macrotasks: when a macrotask (like setTimeout) is scheduled, it is added to the task queue. Microtasks: when a microtask (like a promise reaction) is scheduled, it is added to the microtask queue.
Microtask queue processing: after the synchronous code finishes executing (the call stack is empty), the event loop first checks the microtask queue and processes all the microtasks before moving on to the task queue.
Macrotask queue processing: once all the microtasks have been processed, the event loop picks the next macrotask from the task queue and executes it.
What are tasks? There are two types of asynchronous tasks:
TypeQueuePriority
MacrotaskTask queueLower
MicrotaskMicrotask queueHigher

Macrotask: also known as the callback queue or message queue

  1. Also called: the task queue, the callback queue.
  2. Scheduled to run after the current script and after all the microtasks are done (i.e. a macrotask, also called a task, is any task scheduled to run in the task queue).
  3. The macrotask queue holds tasks that need to be executed after the currently executing code has completed.
  4. One macrotask runs per event-loop iteration.
  5. Examples of macrotasks:
    1. setTimeout();
    2. setInterval();
    3. setImmediate() (Node.js);
    4. the network-completion events behind fetch() (its .then is a microtask);
    5. UI events (click, scroll);
    6. I/O tasks.
    ✔ "fetch() callbacks" as a macrotask is misleading: fetch returns a promise, and .then(callback) on it runs as a MICROTASK (verified in Node: after queueMicrotask/await, but before setTimeout 0).fetch().then(...) चा callback microtask म्हणून चालतो; network पूर्ण होण्याचा event हा task असतो.
  6. The JavaScript engine processes one macrotask from the task queue at a time, after the current stack of synchronous code has finished.
  7. After a macrotask is processed, the JavaScript engine processes all the pending microtasks before picking the next macrotask.
Characteristics:
  1. lower priority than microtasks;
  2. runs after the microtasks;
  3. executed in FIFO order (first in, first out);
  4. can be delayed if the microtask queue grows large.

Microtasks

  1. A microtask is a smaller, more immediate task that is placed in the microtask queue (separate from the macrotask queue).
  2. Executed immediately after the current synchronous code, before any macrotask.
  3. All the microtasks run before the next macrotask.
  4. Examples of microtasks:
    1. Promise.then(), Promise.catch(), Promise.finally();
    2. queueMicrotask() (explicitly queues a microtask);
    3. MutationObserver callbacks (a DOM-change observation mechanism);
    4. the continuation after await.
  5. Microtasks are executed immediately after the current task (whether it's synchronous code or a macrotask) finishes, but before any new macrotasks.
  6. The JavaScript engine processes all the microtasks in the queue before moving on to the next macrotask.
Characteristics:
  1. higher priority than macrotasks;
  2. executed before rendering and before the next macrotask;
  3. can block rendering if too many are queued.
Microtask before macrotask
console.log("start");
setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("macro task: setTimeout");
}, 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => {
  console.log("micro task: promise");
});
console.log("end");
// start
// end
// micro task: promise
// macro task: setTimeout
// Synchronous code: 'start', 'end' → immediately
// Promise.then() → microtask → executes after sync
// setTimeout() → macrotask → executes after microtasks
  • What happens: sync logs first, then ALL microtasks (promise), then one macrotask (timer).
  • Output: start, end, micro task: promise, macro task: setTimeout.
  • ✅ Rule: after each macrotask, the microtask queue is emptied completely.
Microtask inside a macrotask
console.log("1");
setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("2");   // macro
  Promise.resolve().then(() => {
    console.log("3");   // micro inside macro
  });
}, 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => {
  console.log("4");   // micro
});
console.log("5");
// output
// 1
// 5
// 4
// 2
// 3
// Flow:
// Synchronous: 1, 5
// Microtask queue: 4
// Macrotask queue: 2, then its microtask 3

// ✔ note (verified in Node): when BOTH snippets run in the same file, all sync logs come first:
//   start, end, 1, 5, micro task: promise, 4, macro task: setTimeout, 2, 3
  • What happens: 1 and 5 are sync; 4 is a microtask; then the timer prints 2 and queues 3, which runs before the next macrotask.
  • Output: 1, 5, 4, 2, 3 (in one file: start, end, 1, 5, micro…, 4, macro…, 2, 3).
Summary table
FeatureMicrotaskMacrotask
QueueMicrotask queueMacrotask queue
PriorityHigherLower
Exec TimingAfter the current script, before renderingAfter microtasks (and possibly rendering)
Triggered byPromises, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver, awaitsetTimeout, setInterval, events, I/O / network completion
Blocking RenderingYes, if overloaded (the loop can't move on)Yes, if a single task runs long (render waits for it to finish)
Execution FrequencyAll microtasks run before the next macrotaskOne macrotask per event-loop round
✔ "Blocking Rendering: macrotask: No". A long-running macrotask also blocks rendering (the page can only paint between tasks); the difference is that a FLOOD of microtasks never lets the loop reach the render step.एखादा मोठा macrotask सुद्धा rendering थांबवतो (page फक्त tasks च्या मध्ये paint होते). फरक इतकाच की microtasks ची न संपणारी साखळी loop ला पुढे जाऊच देत नाही. Important notes:
  1. Microtasks run first, even if both macro- and microtasks are scheduled at the same time.
  2. If microtasks keep adding more microtasks, they can starve the event loop (blocking macrotasks).
  3. The event loop won't proceed to the next macrotask until all the microtasks are cleared.

Whatever callback functions are present in the Web API/host, their tasks may be:
  1. macrotasks;
  2. microtasks.

MACROTASK

setTimeout(); setInterval(); the fetch API's network events; user interactions like click events.
  1. Granularity: a macrotask is a discrete unit of work (a whole script, a timer callback, an event handler).
  2. Execution order: macrotasks are executed in the order they are scheduled, one after the other.
  3. Use case: used for operations like I/O tasks (file reading, network requests) or handling user interactions.
  4. Event loop: macrotasks are processed on the main thread, one per loop turn, so the browser can render in between and stay responsive.
  5. Examples: loading large datasets, complex data processing in a timer callback, a click handler.
Macrotasks represent larger, independent units of work. Macrotasks: larger, time-consuming tasks (e.g. I/O operations, events) that run sequentially in the event loop. ✔ "rendering graphics / rendering a complex UI" isn't a macrotask; rendering is a separate step of the loop (requestAnimationFrame callbacks run just before it). And "large/time-consuming" isn't the definition: a task is defined by WHERE it is queued, not by its size.rendering हा macrotask नाही, तो loop चा वेगळा टप्पा आहे. task मोठा की लहान यावरून तो macro/micro ठरत नाही, तर तो कोणत्या queue मध्ये जातो यावरून ठरतो.

Microtask

promise callbacks (then/catch/finally); async/await continuations. So these microtasks and macrotasks ultimately need to be executed by the JavaScript runtime, and microtasks take precedence (higher priority): the event loop first picks the microtasks and places them on the stack before any macrotask is picked up.
  1. Granularity: a microtask is a small follow-up job that must run as soon as the current task ends.
  2. Execution order: microtasks are executed immediately after the current macrotask finishes, but before the next macrotask starts. Microtasks have higher priority than macrotasks.
  3. Use case: used for lightweight follow-up work like handling promise results or scheduling simple asynchronous operations.
  4. Event loop: microtasks also belong to the event loop but are processed before the next macrotask in the queue.
  5. Examples: resolving a promise (its then callbacks), the code after await, queueMicrotask callbacks.
Microtasks represent small, quick tasks that have higher priority. Micro tasks: smaller, lightweight jobs (e.g. promise callbacks) that run immediately after the current macrotask and before the next one. ✔ "event listeners", "executing a callback function", "updating the UI in response to user actions" are NOT microtasks: event listeners run as macrotasks (UI events), and a plain callback is microtask/macrotask only depending on who queues it.event listeners हे macrotasks आहेत. कोणताही साधा callback आपोआप microtask नसतो; तो कोणत्या queue मध्ये जातो यावर ठरते.
Note: so macro- and microtasks have separate queues, and the microtask queue has higher priority and is completed first. JavaScript executes the program through the event loop, and the complete execution of a program takes several rounds of the loop: in each round, the event loop starts with the current (synchronous/task) code in the current scope and ends by clearing the microtask queue.

11. What is the Difference between a Microtask and a Macrotask?

Aspect🟩 Microtask🟦 Macrotask
Execution TimingAfter the current synchronous code, before the next macrotaskAfter the current script and after all microtasks
PriorityHigher priorityLower priority
Queue TypeMicrotask queueTask (macrotask) queue
Processed WhenImmediately after the current script execution endsAfter microtasks and possibly after rendering
Event Loop BehaviorAll microtasks run before the next macrotaskOnly one macrotask runs per event-loop cycle
ExamplesPromise.then() / .catch() / .finally(); queueMicrotask(); MutationObserver; awaitsetTimeout(); setInterval(); setImmediate() (Node.js); DOM events (click, scroll); network/I/O completion
Use CaseFor small, urgent tasks that need to run right after the current executionFor larger tasks like timers, UI events or I/O operations
Rendering ImpactExecuted before the browser re-rendersThe browser may render between macrotasks
Blocking RiskYes: a long microtask queue can block the event loopLower: only one macrotask runs per loop, then microtasks follow (but one LONG task still blocks)
Re-entrancy RiskHigher: recursive microtasks can block the loopLower: only processed once per loop cycle
Extra: Node.js order (process.nextTick & setImmediate) 
// Node: sync → process.nextTick queue → promise microtasks → timers (setTimeout 0) / setImmediate (check phase)
setTimeout(() => console.log("timeout"));
setImmediate(() => console.log("immediate"));
process.nextTick(() => console.log("nextTick"));
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("promise"));
// → nextTick, promise, then timeout/immediate (their order is not guaranteed in the main module)
  • What happens: Node's order: sync → process.nextTick → promise microtasks → timers / setImmediate.
  • Output: nextTick, promise, then timeout and immediate (order not guaranteed).
  • ⚠ Too many nextTicks can starve the event loop.

12. Output Puzzles (verified in Node)

setTimeout(() => console.log("T"), 0);
fetch("data:,x").then(() => console.log("fetch then"));
queueMicrotask(() => console.log("qm"));
(async () => { console.log("A1"); await null; console.log("A2"); })();
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("P"));
console.log("sync");
// → A1, sync, qm, A2, P, fetch then, T
// (A1 is synchronous: an async function runs synchronously until its first await)
  • What happens: A1 runs synchronously (an async function starts immediately), then sync; microtasks run in queue order (qm, A2, P), then the fetch result, then the timer.
  • Output: A1, sync, qm, A2, P, fetch then, T.

13. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. What is the event loop?
  • The host's loop that, whenever the call stack is empty, drains all microtasks, lets the browser render, then runs the next macrotask, forever. It is what makes single-threaded JS non-blocking.
Q2. Microtask vs macrotask, with examples?
  • Microtasks: promise reactions, await continuations, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver; all of them run after the current task. Macrotasks: timers, UI events, I/O, message events; one per loop turn.
Q3. Why does setTimeout(fn, 0) run after Promise.resolve().then(fn)?
  • The timer callback is a macrotask; the promise callback is a microtask, and all microtasks run before the next macrotask.
Q4. Can promises freeze the page?
  • Yes: a microtask that keeps queueing microtasks (or a long synchronous loop) never lets the loop reach rendering or other tasks. Break heavy work into chunks with setTimeout or use a Web Worker.
Q5. Output-based questions
console.log(1);
setTimeout(() => console.log(2));
Promise.resolve().then(() => { console.log(3); setTimeout(() => console.log(4)); });
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(5));
console.log(6);
// → 1, 6, 3, 5, 2, 4
  • What happens: sync (1, 6) → microtasks (3, 5; 3 schedules timer 4) → macrotasks in order (2, then 4).
  • Output: 1, 6, 3, 5, 2, 4.
  • ✅ Classic interview question.
PieceRemember
Call stackSync code, LIFO, one at a time
Web APIsTimers, fetch, DOM events: run outside the stack
Microtask queuethen/catch/finally, await, queueMicrotask: ALL, first
Macrotask queuesetTimeout/Interval, events, I/O: ONE per turn
Event loopStack empty → microtasks → render → one macrotask → repeat
थोडक्यात: sync code आधी. मग सगळे microtasks (promise, await). मग page render. मग एक macrotask (setTimeout, click). पुन्हा हेच चक्र. fetch().then हा microtask आहे, event listener macrotask. microtasks च्या अंतहीन साखळीने page अडकू शकतो.

1. The window Object

Your Notes (29_bomObject/windowObject.js): what it is
  1. The global object in the browser.
  2. It represents the entire browser window/tab.
  3. Everything in the browser is inside window, including: document; the BOM (e.g. location, navigator); global functions (alert(), setTimeout()). I.e. window is the global object, and the BOM is a part of it, a subset.
window = the entire browser-tab object. BOM = features provided by the browser outside the page content, like:
  1. window.location
  2. window.history
  3. window.navigator
  4. window.screen
  5. window.alert(), window.confirm()
ConceptBelongs ToDescription
windowGlobal objectTop-level object for everything in browser JavaScript
BOMPart of windowHandles browser features (like tabs, URL, alerts, history, etc.)
DOMPart of windowHandles HTML document content and structure
Definition: In the browser, window is the global object (globalThis === window): global var variables and function declarations become its properties, and you can omit "window." (alert() = window.alert()). It holds the DOM (window.document, the page) and the BOM (location, history, navigator, screen, storage, timers, dialogs: the browser around the page).
Browser मध्ये window हा सर्वात वरचा (global) object आहे: एक tab म्हणजे एक window. त्यात document (DOM, म्हणजे page चा content) आणि BOM (location, history, navigator, screen, alert इत्यादी browser ची वैशिष्ट्ये) दोन्ही असतात. window. न लिहिताही ते वापरता येतात.

2. BOM in JavaScript: Browser Object Model

Your Notes: the BOM (Browser Object Model) allows JavaScript to interact with the browser itself, outside of the HTML content. It provides objects and methods to control the browser window and interact with the environment.
  1. The main container (i.e. the global object).
  2. Any operation related to the entire browser window can be part of the window object. ✔ "any operator related to" → any OPERATION related to the browser window."operator" नाही, "operation" (browser window शी संबंधित कोणतीही क्रिया).
  3. The global object in browsers. It represents the browser window/tab.
Figure 132: window contains both the DOM (document, the page) and the BOM (browser features).

3. window & document in Code

window object
// # window object
console.log(window);                 // returns the window object
console.log(window.localStorage);    // access to this site's persistent storage (per origin)
// ✔ note: "global storage" → it is storage per ORIGIN (protocol + domain + port), not shared by all sites

// get the width and height (of the viewport)
console.log(window.innerWidth);
console.log(window.innerHeight);
  • What happens: window is the browser's global object; it holds localStorage, viewport sizes and everything else.
  • Output: the window object, its storage, the viewport width/height.
  • ⚠ window exists only in browsers (globalThis works everywhere).
Document Object
// # Document Object
// Represents the DOM (HTML) loaded in the window.
// It's part of the window object.
// the document is an object of the window
console.log(window.document);         // returns the whole document object
console.log(window.document.title);   // → "JavaScript BOM & DOM Example"
// we can access the document object directly
console.log(document.body);
  • What happens: document (the DOM) is a property of window, so window.document and document are the same.
  • Output: the document, its title, the body element.

🔍 What it ModelsThe browser environment
📦 Core Objectswindow, navigator, screen, location, history, alert(), setTimeout()
📚 UsageAllows interaction with browser-specific features
📌 Examplewindow.alert("Hello") or navigator.userAgent
🌐 StandardHistorically not standardized; today most of it IS (HTML Living Standard: window, location, history, navigator, timers, storage)
⚙️ ManipulationControls browser settings, popup boxes, redirects, etc.
✔ "BOM: Not officially standardized by W3C (varies across browsers)". That was true years ago; the HTML Living Standard (WHATWG) now defines window, location, history, navigator, setTimeout and storage, so they behave the same across modern browsers. "BOM" is just an informal name for this group.पूर्वी BOM standard नव्हता, पण आज HTML Living Standard मध्ये window, location, history, navigator इत्यादी ठरवलेले आहेत, म्हणून आधुनिक browsers मध्ये ते सारखेच चालतात. Key differences
DOMBOM
Models the web document structureModels the browser and its components
Part of the W3C/WHATWG DOM standardMostly in the HTML standard now (historically browser-specific)
Accessed via the document objectAccessed via the window object
Used to manipulate page contentUsed to interact with browser features
window vs document
windowdocument
DefinitionThe browser's window/tabThe HTML page loaded inside the window
ScopeGlobal (top-level) objectChild of window
Examplewindow.innerWidthdocument.getElementById("id")
✔ in your table the last three rows (Definition / Scope / Example) were placed under the DOM | BOM headers, so "Browser's window/tab" appeared under DOM. Those rows compare WINDOW vs DOCUMENT; they are moved into their own table above.शेवटच्या तीन ओळी (Definition/Scope/Example) DOM|BOM खाली लिहिल्यामुळे उलट्या वाटत होत्या. त्या window vs document ची तुलना आहेत, म्हणून वेगळ्या table मध्ये ठेवल्या. Quick analogy: think of a web page as a book. The DOM is the content (chapters, headings, paragraphs). The BOM is the frame around the book (bookmark, page size, reader settings).

5. BOM Objects in Code (windowObject.js)

BOM
// # BOM
console.log(window.console)   // represents the console object
  • What happens: console is also part of window (BOM).
  • Output: the console object.
window.open()
// # window.open()
// Opens a new tab
window.open("https://www.google.com", "_blank");
// ⚠ called on page load (not from a click), most browsers BLOCK it as a popup; call it from a user action
  • What happens: window.open opens a new tab/window.
  • Output: a new tab (if allowed).
  • ⚠ Browsers block popups not triggered by a click.
window.location
// # window.location
// Gives access to the current URL and allows redirection
console.log(window.location.href);       // full URL
console.log(window.location.hostname);   // domain name
console.log(window.location.pathname);   // path after the domain
console.log(window.location.search);     // query string ("?q=js")
// redirect example
// if (confirm("Go to YouTube?")) window.location.href = "https://youtube.com";
  • What happens: location shows the parts of the current URL; assigning href redirects.
  • Output: full URL, hostname, path, query string.
window.history
// # window.history
// Allows navigation through the browser history.
window.history.back();      // Go back
window.history.forward();   // Go forward
// ⚠ running these at load time navigates away immediately (if there is history), so the rest of the page is lost
  • What happens: history.back/forward move through the tab's history like the browser buttons.
  • Output: navigation (if there is history).
  • ⚠ Running them on load immediately leaves the page.
window.screen
// # window.screen
// Gives info about the user's physical screen.
console.log(window.screen.width);         // Full screen width
console.log(window.screen.availWidth);    // Available width (excludes the taskbar)
console.log(window.screen.colorDepth);    // Bits per pixel (color depth), e.g. 24
console.log(window.screen.orientation);   // Orientation info (an object; .type → "landscape-primary")
  • What happens: screen describes the physical display.
  • Output: screen width, available width, color depth, orientation.
window.navigator
// # window.navigator
// Provides info about the browser and OS.
console.log(navigator.userAgent);       // Browser details
console.log(navigator.language);        // e.g. "en-US"
console.log(navigator.cookieEnabled);   // true if cookies are enabled
console.log(navigator.platform);        // OS info (e.g. "Win32"), deprecated; may be empty in future
console.log(navigator.onLine);          // true if the browser is online
  • What happens: navigator gives browser/OS info and online status.
  • Output: user agent, language, true, platform, online status.
  • ⚠ Don't detect browsers by userAgent; test for features instead.
localStorage (persistent key-value storage)
// # localStorage (persistent key-value storage)
localStorage.setItem("name", "Vishal");
console.log(localStorage.getItem("name"));   // "Vishal"
localStorage.removeItem("name");             // delete the key
  • What happens: localStorage keeps key/value strings per site, even after closing the browser.
  • Output: Vishal.
Pop-up dialogs (BOM)
// # Pop-up dialogs (BOM)
alert("This is a message");                   // Just a message
let confirmResult = confirm("Are you sure?"); // true/false
let name = prompt("What is your name?");      // returns the input string, or null on Cancel
// ⚠ these dialogs BLOCK the page (and JS) until the user responds
  • What happens: alert shows a message, confirm returns true/false, prompt returns the text or null; all three block the page.
  • Output: (dialogs).
  • ⚠ Blocking dialogs are bad UX; use custom modals in real apps.
✔ Note: in index.html the <script src="windowObject.js"> tag is commented out, so this file never runs on that page; the page uses its own inline functions instead (§6).index.html मध्ये windowObject.js चा script tag comment केलेला आहे, म्हणून ही file त्या page वर चालत नाही. page मध्ये स्वतःचे functions आहेत.
Extra Details: location, history & storage 
location.assign(url);    // go to url (adds a history entry)
location.replace(url);   // go to url WITHOUT adding a history entry (the Back button won't return)
location.reload();
history.go(-2);          // two pages back
history.pushState({ page: 2 }, "", "/page2");   // change the URL without reloading (SPAs / routers)
new URLSearchParams(location.search).get("q");  // read ?q=…

// localStorage vs sessionStorage vs cookies
// localStorage   → ~5 MB, survives browser restarts, per origin, strings only (use JSON.stringify)
// sessionStorage → per TAB, cleared when the tab closes
// cookies        → ~4 KB, sent to the server with every request, can have an expiry / HttpOnly
  • What happens: location.assign/replace/reload, history.go/pushState (change the URL without reloading, used by SPA routers), URLSearchParams for query values; storage comparison.
  • Output: (notes).
  • ✅ pushState is how React/Vue routers work.

<script>
  // WINDOW OBJECT METHODS
  function showWindowDetails() {
    console.log("=== WINDOW OBJECT ===");
    console.log("Window inner width:", window.innerWidth);
    console.log("Window inner height:", window.innerHeight);
    console.log("Is this window the top window?", window.top === window);   // false inside an iframe
    window.open("https://www.google.com", "_blank");   // Open a new tab (allowed: it's a click)
  }
  // DOCUMENT OBJECT METHODS

    console.log("=== DOCUMENT OBJECT ===");

    console.log("Body element:", document.body);
    console.log("All links:", document.links);

  // NAVIGATOR OBJECT

    console.log("=== NAVIGATOR OBJECT ===");
    console.log("User agent:", navigator.userAgent);
    console.log("Platform:", navigator.platform);
    console.log("Language:", navigator.language);
    console.log("Cookies enabled:", navigator.cookieEnabled);
    console.log("Online status:", navigator.onLine ? "Online" : "Offline");
  }
  // LOCATION OBJECT
  function showLocationDetails() {
    console.log("=== LOCATION OBJECT ===");
    console.log("Current URL:", location.href);
    console.log("Protocol:", location.protocol);   // "https:" / "file:"
    console.log("Host:", location.host);           // hostname + port
    console.log("Pathname:", location.pathname);
    console.log("Search params:", location.search);
    // Uncomment below to redirect:
    // location.href = "https://youtube.com";
  }
  // HISTORY OBJECT
  function goBack() {
    history.back();      // Go back to the previous page
  }
  function goForward() {
    history.forward();   // Go forward to the next page
  }
  // SCREEN OBJECT
  function showScreenDetails() {
    console.log("=== SCREEN OBJECT ===");
    console.log("Full width:", screen.width);
    console.log("Full height:", screen.height);
    console.log("Available width:", screen.availWidth);
    console.log("Color depth:", screen.colorDepth);
    console.log("Orientation:", screen.orientation.type);
  }
  // localStorage / sessionStorage example
  function storageExample() {
    console.log("=== STORAGE OBJECT ===");
    localStorage.setItem("user", "Vishal");
    const user = localStorage.getItem("user");
    console.log("Stored user:", user);   // → Stored user: Vishal
    localStorage.removeItem("user");
    console.log("Removed user from localStorage.");
    sessionStorage.setItem("sessionId", "abc123");
    console.log("Session ID:", sessionStorage.getItem("sessionId"));   // → abc123
  }
  // Dialog boxes
  function showDialogs() {
    alert("This is a simple alert box.");
    const confirmResult = confirm("Do you like JavaScript?");

</script>
  • What happens: an HTML page whose buttons call functions that read window, document, navigator, location, history, screen, storage and dialogs.
  • Output: logs for each button click.
  • ✅ Run it in a browser to explore the BOM interactively.

7. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. What is the window object?
  • The browser's global object (one per tab/iframe). It exposes the DOM (document), the BOM APIs (location, history, navigator, screen, storage, timers, dialogs) and global var/function declarations; in Node the global object is global, and globalThis works everywhere.
Q2. BOM vs DOM?
  • DOM = the page's content tree (document, elements), which you manipulate. BOM = the browser around the page (URL, history, device info, dialogs, storage). window holds both.
Q3. localStorage vs sessionStorage vs cookies?
  • localStorage: persistent, per origin, ~5 MB. sessionStorage: per tab, cleared on close. Cookies: small, sent with every HTTP request, can be HttpOnly/secure (good for auth sessions).
Q4. location.href vs location.replace()?
  • Setting href (or assign) adds a history entry, so Back returns; replace() swaps the current entry, so Back skips it (good for redirects after login).
Q5. Output-based questions
var a = 1; let b = 2;
console.log(window.a, window.b);           // → 1 undefined (let/const are not window properties)
console.log(window === globalThis);        // → true (browser)
console.log(typeof window.document);       // → object
localStorage.setItem("n", 5);
console.log(typeof localStorage.getItem("n"));   // → string (storage keeps strings)
console.log(prompt("x") === null);         // → true if the user clicks Cancel
  • What happens: var becomes a window property, let doesn't; window === globalThis in browsers; storage converts values to strings; prompt Cancel gives null.
  • Output: 1 undefined, true, object, string, true.
ObjectUse
windowGlobal object; innerWidth/Height, open, top
documentDOM: the page content
locationURL parts, redirect (href, assign, replace, reload)
historyback, forward, go, pushState
navigatoruserAgent, language, onLine, cookieEnabled
screenwidth, availWidth, colorDepth, orientation
localStorage / sessionStoragesetItem, getItem, removeItem, clear
alert / confirm / promptBlocking dialogs: undefined / boolean / string|null
थोडक्यात: window = global object (एक tab). त्यात DOM (document, page चा content) आणि BOM (location, history, navigator, screen, storage, dialogs) असतात. window.open फक्त click मधून चालवा. storage मध्ये strings साठवल्या जातात. var global ला window property बनतो, let/const नाही.

1. Local Storage

Your Notes (42_localStroage/localstroage.js):
  1. localStorage stores data in the browser
  2. with no expiration time,
  3. even after the browser is closed.

Use cases:
  1. persisting user preferences (e.g. dark mode);
  2. saving shopping-cart data;
  3. caching user data offline.

Key properties:
PropertyValue
Max Size~5–10 MB
ExpiryNever (unless cleared manually or programmatically)
ScopePer origin (shared between tabs of the same origin)
Sent withNot sent with HTTP requests
Accessible from JSYes
FeatureDescription
Storage SizeCan store up to 5–10 MB (much larger than cookies).
PersistentData is saved even after the browser is closed and reopened.
Origin SpecificAccessible only from the same origin (protocol + domain + port).
Client-Side OnlyNot sent to the server with each HTTP request (unlike cookies).
Key-Value StoreStores data as strings in key-value pairs.
✔ "same origin (domain + port)" → an origin is PROTOCOL + domain + port: http://site.com and https://site.com have separate storage.origin म्हणजे protocol + domain + port. http आणि https साठी storage वेगवेगळे असते.
1. store data in local storage
// ex
// 1. store data in local storage
localStorage.setItem('name', 'vishal');
  • What happens: setItem stores a string under a key for this site permanently.
  • Output: (no output).
2. get data from local storage
// 2. get data from local storage
console.log('stored data:', localStorage.getItem('name'));   // → stored data: vishal
  • What happens: getItem reads it back (null if missing).
  • Output: stored data: vishal.
3. remove the data from local storage
// 3. remove the data from local storage
console.log(localStorage.removeItem('name'))                  // → undefined (removeItem returns nothing)
  • What happens: removeItem deletes one key and returns undefined.
  • Output: undefined.
4. clear all local storage data
// 4. clear all local storage data
console.log('clear local storage :', localStorage.clear())    // → clear local storage : undefined
// ✔ "remote the data" → REMOVE the data; and getItem of a missing key → null
  • What happens: clear deletes every key of this site.
  • Output: clear local storage : undefined.
Definition: Web Storage (localStorage / sessionStorage) is a synchronous, per-origin key → value store in the browser. Keys and values are always STRINGS; the API is setItem, getItem (null if missing), removeItem, clear, key(i), length. localStorage survives restarts; sessionStorage lives as long as the tab. Neither is sent to the server.
localStorage मध्ये browser मध्ये string स्वरूपात data कायमचा साठतो (browser बंद केला तरी राहतो), आणि तो server ला पाठवला जात नाही. sessionStorage तसाच आहे, पण फक्त त्या tab पुरता असतो आणि tab बंद केल्यावर पुसला जातो.

2. Session Storage

Your Notes (sessionStorage.js):
  1. sessionStorage is a Web API
  2. that stores data only for the current browser tab/session.
  3. In JavaScript, sessionStorage is a built-in Web API that lets you store key–value data in a web browser for the duration of the page session. The data persists only while the browser tab (or window) is open; once the tab or window is closed, the data is automatically deleted. It is specific to the tab: another tab with the same site won't see the same sessionStorage data. (It does survive page reloads, and "Duplicate tab" copies it.)
Use cases:
  1. temporary storage, like form data while navigating within a tab;
  2. it doesn't persist after the tab/window is closed;
  3. storing form data temporarily;
  4. a temporary authentication token for the current session;
  5. shopping-cart data for a single visit;
  6. user-interface state (like the active tab or filter selections) while browsing a site.

Preventing form resubmission on reload (e.g. remembering that the form was already submitted).
Key points:
PropertyValue
Max Size~5–10 MB
ExpiryWhen the tab/window is closed
ScopePer tab (different for each open tab)
Sent withNot sent with HTTP requests
Accessible from JSYes
FeatureDetails
ScopeTab-specific (not shared across tabs, even for the same domain)
PersistenceUntil the tab/window is closed
Storage LimitAround 5–10 MB (varies by browser)
Data FormatStores only strings (you can store objects by converting them to JSON)
AccessAvailable via window.sessionStorage
sessionStorage ensures the data is gone automatically when the session ends (the tab is closed).
example
// example
// 1. add data into session storage.
sessionStorage.setItem('name', 'vishal shinde');
  • What happens: sessionStorage has the same API but is per tab.
  • Output: (no output).
2. get data from session storage
// 2. get data from session storage
console.log(sessionStorage.getItem('name'));      // → vishal shinde
  • What happens: read from sessionStorage.
  • Output: vishal shinde.
3. remove data from session storage
// 3. remove data from session storage
console.log(sessionStorage.removeItem('name'))    // → undefined
// clear the whole session storage
console.log(sessionStorage.clear());              // → undefined

let cart = { item: "Book", quantity: 2 };
sessionStorage.setItem("cart", JSON.stringify(cart));
let cartData = JSON.parse(sessionStorage.getItem("cart"));
console.log(cartData.item);   // Book
  • What happens: remove/clear; objects must be stored as JSON and parsed back.
  • Output: undefined, undefined, Book.
  • ✅ Keep a shopping cart only for this tab.

3. Storing Objects: Serialization

To store data in cookies, localStorage and sessionStorage, we need serialization and deserialization, but only when storing non-string data like objects or arrays.

Storage TypeStores Strings Only?Need Serialization for Objects/Arrays?
Cookies✅ Yes✅ Yes (+ encodeURIComponent for special characters)
localStorage✅ Yes✅ Yes
sessionStorage✅ Yes✅ Yes
  1. They are always stored as strings.

If you store an object or array, you need to: serialize with JSON.stringify(), and deserialize with JSON.parse(). 
localStorage.setItem("user", { name: "v" });
localStorage.getItem("user");          // → "[object Object]"   (the object was converted with toString!)
localStorage.setItem("n", 5);
typeof localStorage.getItem("n");      // → "string"
// safe helpers
const save = (k, v) => localStorage.setItem(k, JSON.stringify(v));
const load = (k, fallback = null) => { try { return JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(k)) ?? fallback; } catch { return fallback; } };
  • What happens: storing an object without JSON saves "[object Object]"; numbers come back as strings. Helper functions handle JSON and bad data safely.
  • Output: "[object Object]", "string".
  • ✅ Always JSON.stringify/parse.
When do we use cookies? Use cookies when data (like session/auth tokens) needs to be sent to the server with every HTTP request.
When do we use sessionStorage? 🕒 Use sessionStorage for temporary data that should be cleared when the browser tab is closed.
When do we use localStorage? 🗄️ Use localStorage to store persistent data on the client side that should remain even after the browser is closed.

4. Cookies

Your Notes (cookies.js):
  1. Cookies are small pieces of data (usually < 4 KB) stored on the user's computer by the browser,
  2. sent to the server with every (matching) HTTP request.

Use cases:
  1. storing login sessions (e.g. authentication tokens);
  2. tracking user behaviour (analytics, ad personalization);
  3. remembering user preferences (e.g. language selection).
#Use CaseDescriptionReal-World Example
1Session ManagementTo track user sessions (logged-in status)Staying logged into Gmail or Facebook
2User AuthenticationStore tokens/session IDs to validate identityA JWT or session ID stored in a cookie after login
3User PreferencesSave settings like theme, language, font sizeLight/dark mode saved in a cookie
4Shopping CartsRetain cart items across sessions/pagesAmazon remembers cart items even after refresh
5Tracking and AnalyticsTrack user behaviour, page visits, conversionsGoogle Analytics uses cookies to identify repeat visits
6Advertisement TargetingDeliver personalized ads based on user behaviourFacebook or YouTube showing ads based on your history
7Security MeasuresPrevent CSRF attacks (SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens)A CSRF token stored in a cookie for form validation
8A/B TestingIdentify which version of a page a user should seeShow different layouts to users and store the variant in a cookie
9Multi-language SitesRemember the selected languagelang=en stored in a cookie when the user selects English
10Geolocation PreferencesStore the user's location for regional contentShow local news based on a previously selected city
Key points:
PropertyValue
Max Size~4 KB
ExpirySet manually using expires or max-age (else a session cookie)
ScopeDomain + Path
Sent withEvery HTTP request to the matching domain
Accessible from JSIf not HttpOnly
🔑 Point📌 Description
1. Stored in BrowserCookies are small text entries stored in the user's browser (on their computer/mobile).
2. Key-Value PairCookies store data as key=value pairs, e.g. username=Vishal.
3. Auto-sent to ServerCookies are automatically sent to the server with every request to the same domain.
4. Limited SizeMax size per cookie: ~4 KB. Browsers allow dozens of cookies per domain (commonly ~50–180).
5. Expiry ControlCookies can be session-based (deleted on close) or persistent (with expires/max-age).
6. Domain & Path SpecificCookies can be set for specific domains/subdomains and paths.
7. Security OptionsUse HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite flags to protect against attacks like XSS or CSRF.
8. Accessible in JSCan be read/written via document.cookie, unless marked HttpOnly.
9. Used for SessionsCommonly used to manage login sessions and user authentication.
10. Used for TrackingAlso used in analytics, A/B testing and ad targeting to track user behaviour.
// Setting a cookie
document.cookie = "username=Vishal; expires=Tue, 10 Sep 2025 12:00:00 UTC; path=/";
// Reading cookies
console.log(document.cookie);   // "username=Vishal"
// ✔ that expiry date is in the PAST (today is after 10 Sep 2025), so the browser deletes the cookie
//    immediately and document.cookie is "" — setting a past date is actually how you DELETE a cookie.
//    Use a future date or max-age:  document.cookie = "username=Vishal; max-age=86400; path=/";   (1 day)

// Security tips
// Use HttpOnly to prevent JavaScript access (helps prevent XSS token theft) — only the SERVER can set it (Set-Cookie header);
//   document.cookie cannot create or read HttpOnly cookies.
// Use Secure to send cookies only over HTTPS.
// Use SameSite=Lax/Strict to stop the cookie being sent on cross-site requests (CSRF protection).
  • What happens: document.cookie = "name=value; expires=…; path=/" adds/updates one cookie; reading it returns all cookies as one string.
  • Output: "" here, because the expiry date is in the past (that deletes the cookie).
  • ✅ Cookies are sent to the server automatically (sessions/auth).
  • ⚠ Use max-age or a future date; HttpOnly can only be set by the server.
दिलेली expiry तारीख (10 Sep 2025) भूतकाळातील आहे, म्हणून cookie लगेच delete होते. भविष्यातील तारीख किंवा max-age द्या. HttpOnly फक्त server Set-Cookie header ने लावू शकतो; JS ने नाही. 
// read one cookie by name
const getCookie = (name) => document.cookie.split("; ").find((c) => c.startsWith(name + "="))?.split("=")[1];
// delete: same name + path, with a past date (or max-age=0)
document.cookie = "username=; max-age=0; path=/";
// server-side (HTTP response header):
// Set-Cookie: sid=abc123; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/; Max-Age=3600
  • What happens: read one cookie by splitting the string; delete with max-age=0; servers set secure cookies with Set-Cookie.
  • Output: (helpers).
  • ✅ HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite for auth cookies.
Figure 133: Cookies vs sessionStorage vs localStorage at a glance.

5. Differences between Cookies, sessionStorage and localStorage

FeatureCookieSession StorageLocal Storage
Max Size~4 KB~5–10 MB~5–10 MB
ExpirationSet manually (else at browser close)On tab/window closeNever (until cleared)
Accessible in JSYes (unless HttpOnly)YesYes
Sent to serverYes (automatically)NoNo
ScopeDomain + PathPer tab/per window (+ origin)Origin-wide
Use CaseAuth, trackingTemp form/session dataPreferences, caching
When to use what?
  1. Cookies: when you need data to be sent to the server (e.g. auth tokens).
  2. Session storage: for temporary data in a single session/tab (e.g. a multi-step form).
  3. Local storage: for long-term storage (e.g. theme settings, cached data).

6. The Demo Page & Security

<h3>Local storage</h3>
<!-- <script src="localstroage.js"></script> -->

<script src="cookies.js"></script>
<!-- only cookies.js runs; un-comment one file at a time to test the others -->
  • What happens: the test page loads only cookies.js.
  • Output: (no output).
Security & practical notes
  1. Anything in localStorage/sessionStorage can be read by ANY script on the page, so one XSS bug can steal it. Don't keep long-lived auth tokens there; prefer HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookies.
  2. Never store passwords or sensitive personal data in client storage.
  3. Web Storage is synchronous: storing large blobs blocks the main thread; use IndexedDB for big/structured data.
  4. The storage event fires in OTHER tabs of the same origin when localStorage changes: window.addEventListener("storage", e => console.log(e.key, e.newValue)) (sync logout across tabs).
  5. Quota exceeded → setItem throws (QuotaExceededError): wrap it in try/catch. Private mode may limit or clear storage.

7. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. localStorage vs sessionStorage vs cookies?
  • Size: 5–10 MB / 5–10 MB / 4 KB. Lifetime: forever / tab / expiry. Sent to the server: no / no / yes. Scope: origin / tab + origin / domain + path. JS access: yes / yes / unless HttpOnly.
Q2. How do you store an object in localStorage?
  • JSON.stringify when saving and JSON.parse when reading (handle null and parse errors). Storing it directly saves "[object Object]".
Q3. Where should you store a JWT / auth token?
  • Preferably in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie set by the server (JS can't read it, so XSS can't steal it), plus CSRF protection. localStorage is readable by any injected script.
Q4. How do you delete a cookie, and why can't JS read some cookies?
  • Set the same name/path with max-age=0 (or a past expires date). HttpOnly cookies are hidden from document.cookie by design.
Q5. Output-based questions
localStorage.setItem("a", 1);
console.log(typeof localStorage.getItem("a"));   // → string
console.log(localStorage.getItem("missing"));    // → null
localStorage.setItem("o", { x: 1 });
console.log(localStorage.getItem("o"));          // → [object Object]
console.log(JSON.parse(JSON.stringify([1, 2])).length);   // → 2
  • What happens: four output questions: storage stores strings, missing key is null, objects become [object Object], JSON round-trip works.
  • Output: string, null, [object Object], 2.
NeedUse
Persist preferenceslocalStorage
Per-tab temporary statesessionStorage
Data the server must receiveCookie (HttpOnly for auth)
Big/structured offline dataIndexedDB
थोडक्यात: localStorage = कायमचा, सगळ्या tabs साठी; sessionStorage = फक्त त्या tab पुरता; cookie = छोटा (4 KB) आणि प्रत्येक request सोबत server ला जातो. सगळे strings साठवतात, म्हणून objects साठी JSON.stringify/parse. auth token साठी HttpOnly cookie सुरक्षित, localStorage नाही.
