Chapter 72: Same-Origin Policy & CORSOrigin · what SOP blocks/allows · CORS headers · simple vs preflight · credentials · fixes
CHAPTER 72 INDEX
  1. What is the Same-Origin Policy?
  2. What is an Origin?
  3. What SOP Blocks & Allows
  4. What is CORS?
  5. CORS Errors & Fixes
  6. How CORS Works
  7. Simple Requests
  8. Preflighted Requests
  9. Credentials & Common Mistakes
  10. Interview Questions & Revision

1. What is the Same-Origin Policy (SOP)?

Your Notes (43_cors/sameOriginPolicy&cors.js):
  1. The Same-Origin Policy (SOP) is a security feature implemented by web browsers
  2. to restrict how documents or scripts from one origin can interact with resources from another origin.
Purpose of the Same-Origin Policy: 1. To protect users from malicious websites accessing sensitive data from other websites via:
  1. cookies;
  2. DOM access;
  3. AJAX requests (reading the responses);
  4. localStorage, sessionStorage.

Why SOP is important:
  1. without the Same-Origin Policy, any website you visit could:
  2. steal your session cookies;
  3. read your emails or banking info;
  4. trick you into performing unintended actions (CSRF; note that SOP alone does NOT fully stop CSRF, because requests can still be sent: SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens do).
Definition: SOP is the browser rule that a page's JavaScript may freely READ only resources from its own origin. Cross-origin requests may still be SENT (links, forms, images, fetch), but JS can't read the cross-origin response, DOM or storage unless the other origin opts in via CORS headers. CORS is a controlled relaxation of SOP, decided by the SERVER and enforced by the BROWSER.
Same-Origin Policy म्हणजे browser चा नियम: एका site चा JS दुसऱ्या site चा data (response, DOM, storage) वाचू शकत नाही. request पाठवता येते, पण उत्तर वाचता येत नाही. दुसऱ्या server ने CORS headers देऊन परवानगी दिली तरच browser ते उत्तर वाचू देतो.

2. Definition of "Origin"

  1. An origin is defined by the combination of: the scheme (protocol: http or https), the host (like example.com, example.in) and the port.
PartExample
Schemehttp, https
Hostexample.com
Port80, 443, etc.
Two URLs have the same origin only if all three match exactly.
URL 1URL 2Same Origin?
https://example.com/page1https://example.com/page2✅ Yes (the path doesn't matter)
http://example.comhttps://example.com❌ No (scheme)
https://example.comhttps://sub.example.com❌ No (host)
https://example.com:443https://example.com:8443❌ No (port)
new URL("https://example.com:443/a?x=1").origin;   // "https://example.com" (default port omitted)
location.origin;                                    // the current page's origin
  • What happens: an origin = scheme + host + port; default ports are left out.
  • Output: "https://example.com", the page's origin.
  • ✅ Same-origin policy compares exactly these three parts.
Figure 134: The parts of a URL that make up its origin.

3. What the Same-Origin Policy Blocks & Allows

What SOP blocks
Attempted ActionAllowed?
One site's JS reading the DOM of another site (e.g. an iframe)❌ No
One site's JS accessing the cookies of another site❌ No
AJAX (XHR or fetch) to a different origin: reading the response❌ No (unless CORS is enabled)
✔ Clarified: for fetch/XHR, the browser usually DOES send the cross-origin request (and the server processes it); SOP blocks your JS from READING the response. That's why a "simple" POST can still change data on a server: SOP/CORS protect the reader, not the server.cross-origin request सहसा server पर्यंत जाते आणि server ती process करतो; browser फक्त तुमच्या JS ला उत्तर वाचू देत नाही. म्हणून CORS server चे संरक्षण करत नाही. What SOP allows
ActionAllowed?
Navigating to another origin (e.g. an <a> tag)✅ Yes
Submitting a form to another origin✅ Yes
Embedding an image from another origin✅ Yes
Loading a script or style from another origin✅ Yes (but with limited access)
How to bypass (relax) the Same-Origin Policy: 1. CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing): 1. the server must explicitly allow other origins using HTTP headers: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://your-app.com
Summary table
ConceptDescription
SOPRestricts access between different origins
OriginDefined by scheme, host and port
BlockedCross-origin JS DOM access, cookies, reading AJAX responses without CORS
AllowedNavigation, form submission, media embedding
Bypass MethodsCORS, postMessage, (legacy) JSONP

4. What is CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)?

  1. CORS is a security feature implemented by browsers
  2. to control how web pages can make requests to a different origin (domain) than the one that served the web page.
  3. It's essentially a relaxation of the Same-Origin Policy, but only if the server explicitly allows it.
  4. A way to allow cross-origin requests.
  5. CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser security mechanism that allows or blocks web applications running at one origin (domain) from accessing resources from a different origin.
  6. The underlying security rule is called the Same-Origin Policy, and CORS is the tool that controls which cross-origin requests are allowed.
Why does CORS exist?
  1. Browsers block reading responses from one origin to another unless the destination server gives permission.
  2. This prevents malicious websites from reading sensitive data from another origin.

What CORS (with SOP) protects against: 1. it prevents malicious websites from reading your private data from another domain. Example: attacker.com shouldn't be able to read content from yourbank.com.

5. CORS Errors & How to Fix Them

When do you see a CORS error?
  1. You're calling a different origin (a different domain, protocol or port).
  2. The server doesn't include CORS headers allowing your origin.
  3. You're making a non-simple request (e.g. using PUT, DELETE, custom headers or Content-Type: application/json), which triggers a preflight request that the server doesn't answer correctly.

How to avoid / fix CORS errors:
  1. Enable CORS on the server. The server must include headers like: 
    Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://your-client.com
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization
    • What happens: response headers the SERVER sends to allow a specific origin, methods and request headers.
    • Output: (headers).
    • ⚠ CORS is enforced by the browser but configured on the server.
  2. Use a proxy server. 1. You can avoid CORS on the client by setting up a backend proxy that talks to the external API (server-to-server calls have no CORS; dev servers like Vite/webpack offer a proxy option).
  3. Browser plugin (dev only). 1. You can install a plugin like "Allow CORS: Access-Control-Allow-Origin" in Chrome for development purposes. NEVER use this in production: it breaks the security model.
Summary table
TopicDescription
CORSA mechanism to allow restricted resources on a web page to be requested from another origin
Triggered WhenMaking a request from one origin to another
Error CauseThe server didn't respond with the appropriate Access-Control-Allow-* headers
Fix (Preferred)Add proper CORS headers on the server
Workaround (Dev)Use a proxy or a CORS browser extension
Note: a CORS error can only be fixed on the SERVER (or by routing through your own server); adding Access-Control-* headers to the browser's REQUEST does nothing, and mode: "no-cors" just gives you an empty "opaque" response.

6. How CORS Works

  1. The browser sends the request to the server (adding an Origin: https://your-app.com header).
  2. The server must respond with special HTTP headers:
  3. Access-Control-Allow-Origin (optionally Access-Control-Allow-Methods, Access-Control-Allow-Headers).
  4. If the headers are present and correct, the browser lets your JS read the response.
  5. If not, the browser blocks it automatically (a CORS error in the console).
Figure 135: A preflighted CORS request: OPTIONS check first, then the real request; the browser checks the Allow-* headers.

7. What is a Simple Request in CORS?

  1. A simple request is a "safe" request that:
  2. uses one of these HTTP methods:
    1. GET
    2. POST
    3. HEAD
  3. uses only simple (CORS-safelisted) headers:
    1. Accept
    2. Accept-Language (also Content-Language)
    3. Content-Type, which must be text/plain, application/x-www-form-urlencoded or multipart/form-data (the ones HTML forms use).
No authentication headers (like Authorization) or custom headers. 
// ex.
fetch("http://localhost:5000/data");
  • What happens: a simple GET from another origin: allowed only if the response carries Access-Control-Allow-Origin.
  • Output: (CORS error in the console if the server doesn't allow it).
Behind the scenes: the browser makes this request directly, without any pre-check; the server answers with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:3000, and the browser accepts the response.

8. What is a Preflighted CORS Request?

  1. When the request is more "risky", the browser double-checks with the server before sending the real request. This is called a preflight request; it uses the OPTIONS method.
  2. A preflighted request is one that doesn't meet the conditions for a simple request. The browser sends a preflight OPTIONS request to ask the server whether the actual request is safe to send.
What triggers a preflight?
  1. You use methods like PUT, DELETE, PATCH.
  2. You use headers like Authorization, X-Custom-Header.
  3. You use Content-Type: application/json.
// ex.
fetch("http://localhost:5000/user", {
  method: "PUT",
  headers: {
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "Authorization": "Bearer myToken"
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({ name: "Vishal" })
});
  • What happens: PUT with JSON and an Authorization header is not a "simple" request, so the browser sends a preflight OPTIONS first.
  • Output: (preflight, then the real request).
Behind the scenes: the browser first sends: 
OPTIONS /user HTTP/1.1
Origin: http://localhost:3000
Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT
Access-Control-Request-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization
  • What happens: the preflight request: the browser asks permission for the method and headers.
  • Output: (request headers).
The server must respond with: 
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:3000
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: PUT
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization
(optional) Access-Control-Max-Age: 600     ← cache the preflight for 10 minutes
  • What happens: the server's preflight answer; Max-Age caches it.
  • Output: (response headers).
If the response is valid, the browser sends the actual PUT request.

9. Credentials & Common Mistakes

Example 1
// sending cookies cross-origin needs BOTH sides:
fetch("https://api.site.com/me", { credentials: "include" });
// server:
// Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.site.com   ← must be the exact origin, NOT "*"
// Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
// (and the cookie must be SameSite=None; Secure for cross-site use)
  • What happens: cookies cross-origin need credentials: 'include' on the client AND Allow-Credentials + an exact origin (not *) on the server.
  • Output: (no output).
  • ⚠ SameSite=None; Secure is also needed for cross-site cookies.
Express example
// Express example
app.use(require("cors")({ origin: "https://app.site.com", credentials: true }));
  • What happens: the Express cors middleware sets these headers for you.
  • Output: (server code).
  1. "*" can't be combined with credentials.
  2. The server must answer the OPTIONS preflight too (many frameworks forget the route or auth-protect it).
  3. JS can only read "safelisted" response headers unless the server sends Access-Control-Expose-Headers.
  4. Postman/curl never show CORS errors: CORS is enforced only by browsers.
cookies सोबत cross-origin request साठी fetch मध्ये credentials: "include" आणि server कडून नेमका origin (* नाही) + Allow-Credentials: true लागतो. CORS फक्त browser लागू करतो; Postman मध्ये CORS error येत नाही. CORS error नेहमी server बाजूने सोडवा.

10. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. What is an origin and the Same-Origin Policy?
  • Origin = scheme + host + port. SOP: scripts may read only same-origin responses, DOM and storage; cross-origin embedding/navigation is allowed, but reading is not.
Q2. What is CORS and who enforces it?
  • A header-based opt-in by the SERVER (Access-Control-Allow-*), enforced by the BROWSER, letting a page read cross-origin responses. It is not a server-side security feature.
Q3. Simple vs preflighted request?
  • Simple: GET/POST/HEAD with safelisted headers and form content types → sent directly. Otherwise (PUT/DELETE, JSON, Authorization, custom headers) the browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight.
Q4. How do you fix "No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header" in development and in production?
  • Production: configure the API's CORS headers (exact origins, methods, headers, credentials). Development: a dev-server proxy, or your own backend proxy. Never rely on browser extensions or no-cors.
Q5. Output/behaviour questions
// page at http://localhost:3000
fetch("http://localhost:3000/api")     // same origin → no CORS check
fetch("http://localhost:5000/api")     // different PORT → cross-origin → needs CORS
fetch("https://localhost:3000/api")    // different SCHEME → cross-origin
fetch(url, { mode: "no-cors" })        // succeeds but the response is opaque: status 0, empty body
  • What happens: same scheme + host + port = no CORS; a different port or scheme is cross-origin; no-cors gives an unreadable (opaque) response.
  • Output: (notes).
  • ⚠ no-cors doesn't "fix" CORS; you just can't read the data.
HeaderPurpose
Origin (request)Who is asking
Access-Control-Allow-OriginWhich origin may read the response
Access-Control-Allow-Methods / -HeadersWhat the preflight allows
Access-Control-Allow-CredentialsAllow cookies/auth (not with *)
Access-Control-Max-AgeCache the preflight
थोडक्यात: origin = scheme + host + port. SOP दुसऱ्या origin चे उत्तर वाचू देत नाही. CORS headers देऊन server परवानगी देतो, आणि browser ते तपासतो. PUT/DELETE/JSON/Authorization असल्यास आधी OPTIONS preflight जातो. CORS error ची दुरुस्ती नेहमी server वर (किंवा proxy ने) होते.

index.html रिकामी आहे, म्हणून document.js कुठेच load होत नाही. शिवाय JS file मध्ये थेट HTML लिहिल्यामुळे आणि button दोनदा declare केल्यामुळे SyntaxError येतात, आणि संपूर्ण file चालत नाही.

2. Document Object Model

Your Notes (30_domObject/document.js):
  1. The document is a child (part) of the window object. (Whatever is present inside the document is always present inside the window, because the document is a child of the window object.) I.e. if you have any work regarding the HTML, you use the document object.
  2. The window object represents the global window in a browser; both the Browser Object Model and the Document Object Model are part of the window object. So the window object contains:
    1. the BOM (browser object model);
    2. the DOM (document object model).
What is the document object?
  1. The document object is part of the Window object.
  2. It represents the web page loaded in the browser; it is a tree-like structure.
  3. It is the entry point to the DOM (Document Object Model).
  4. It allows JavaScript to read, modify, add or remove elements in an HTML document.
Definition: The DOM is the browser's live, in-memory object tree built by parsing the HTML. Every tag, text run and comment becomes a node object with properties and methods; document is the root and the entry point. Changing a node changes the rendered page immediately (but not the .html file on disk).
DOM म्हणजे browser HTML वाचून memory मध्ये तयार करतो ते झाडासारखे (tree) object structure. प्रत्येक tag, text आणि comment एक node असतो. document हा सगळ्यात वरचा entry point आहे. JS ने node बदलला की page लगेच बदलतो, पण मूळ HTML file बदलत नाही.

3. Relationship: window > document > HTML

✔️ Window:
  1. The global object in the browser.
  2. Represents the browser window.
  3. Encompasses both the DOM and the BOM.

✔️ Document:
  1. Child of window.
  2. Entry point to the DOM.
  3. Deals with HTML content only.

4. DOM & BOM Feature Tables

Document Object Model (DOM):
FeatureDescription
StructureTree-like structure of HTML elements
FocusWeb page content (HTML elements, attributes, text)
UseJavaScript uses the DOM to interact with and manipulate content
Root Nodedocument.documentElement (returns <html>)
Main Objectdocument
Exampledocument.getElementById('heading')
I.e.
  1. The DOM is primarily concerned with the content of the web page: it is a tree-like structure that allows JavaScript to interact with and manipulate the HTML elements.
  2. The DOM is focused on the content of the page.

DOCUMENT (deals with the document, the HTML elements themselves).
Browser Object Model (BOM):
FeatureDescription
StructureRepresents browser-specific APIs
FocusInteracting with the browser, not web page content
UseManage the browser window, history, location, screen, etc.
Main Objectwindow
Examplealert(), navigator, location.href, setTimeout()
I.e.
  1. The BOM represents the browser as an object and provides methods and properties for interacting with the browser itself (not related to the content of the web page).
  2. The BOM is focused on the browser environment.
  1. Objects like:
    1. navigator
    2. screen
    3. location
    4. frames
    5. history
    6. XMLHttpRequest
  2. Methods like:
    1. setInterval()
    2. setTimeout()
  3. Properties like:
    1. innerHeight
    2. innerWidth (these properties give the width and height of the browser's viewport).
    ✔ "innerHight" → innerHeight."innerHight" नाही, innerHeight.
  4. Functions:
    1. alert
    2. confirm
    3. prompt are also part of the BOM (they are not directly related to the document, but are pure browser methods of communicating with the user).
JavaScript:
  1. JavaScript is used to interact with and manipulate the HTML elements.
  2. OBJECT
  3. ARRAY
  4. FUNCTION (the language's own building blocks, independent of the browser).

5. DOM Node Types & the DOM Tree

DOM node types:
  1. Element node: HTML tags (nodeType 1)
  2. Text node: text content (3)
  3. Attribute node: element attributes (2); legacy: attributes are NOT children in the tree; read them with getAttribute
  4. Comment node: HTML comments (8)
  5. Document node: the root of the document (9)
  6. DocumentType node: the DOCTYPE declaration (10)
DOM:
  1. The first element inside the document is html. (The very first CHILD NODE is the <!DOCTYPE html> node; the first ELEMENT is <html>.)
  2. html (html is the root element of the document).
  3. body: after head comes the body tag (which contains other tags like the anchor tag, paragraph tag and so on).
  4. head: the head tag (contains the title, metadata and links).
This entire DOM tree is accessible to JavaScript as an object.
DOM info:
  1. When a web browser loads an HTML document, it parses the HTML source code and creates a tree-like structure known as the document object.
  2. This DOM tree represents the structure of the HTML document, with each HTML element being a node in the tree.
  3. This entire DOM tree is then accessible to JavaScript as an object: JavaScript can interact with the object to manipulate the content, structure and style of the document dynamically.
  4. The DOM essentially serves as an interface between the HTML document and JavaScript, providing a way to access and modify the document's structure and content.
  5. The Document Object Model (DOM) is an application programming interface (API). The DOM tree is the structure of your HTML document as represented by the DOM API. This API then gives us many methods and properties that we can use to manipulate the tree, and therefore, by extension, the document. ✔ "(apo)" → API."apo" नाही, API (Application Programming Interface).
Figure 136: The DOM tree: document → doctype + html → head/body → elements and text nodes.

6. How Does the DOM Work?

  1. The DOM is a tree-like structure of the HTML document.
  2. The DOM provides a way to interact with the HTML document using JavaScript.
  3. The DOM is used, with the help of JavaScript, to change or manipulate the content of the HTML.
  4. The DOM is a bridge between HTML and JavaScript.
  5. The DOM provides properties and methods; with the help of these methods and properties we dynamically change the content of the HTML document using JavaScript.

7. What is the Difference between the DOM and the BOM?

DOM: a child object (part) of the global object, window. The DOM is a programming interface: it interacts with the HTML document and controls the web content. The DOM represents the HTML document as a tree-like structure where each node is an object corresponding to a part of the document (like an element, attribute or text). The DOM is primarily concerned with the content of the web page and allows JavaScript to interact with and manipulate the HTML elements. The DOM is focused on the content of the page: manipulating elements, attributes and text. The main object is document. The DOM is a live representation of our HTML document.
BOM: the BOM is also part of the global object, window. The BOM is also a programming interface, provided by the browser to interact with the browser itself. The BOM provides methods and properties to control the browser window, manage navigation and handle cookies. The BOM represents the browser as an object and provides methods and properties for interacting with the browser itself (not related to the content of the web page). The BOM is focused on the browser environment: manipulating or maintaining the history, location and navigator objects. The main object is window.
FeatureDOMBOM
PurposeWork with web page contentWork with browser features
Main Objectdocumentwindow
FocusHTML structure, contentBrowser APIs, environment
Access ElementsgetElementById, etc.alert, location, navigator, screen, etc.
StructureTree of nodesNo structured tree
ScopeInside the web pageOutside (browser environment)
(See Chapter 70 for the BOM objects in detail.) 
console.log(document);   // returns the entire document object
// $0 is used to get the currently selected element (only in the browser DevTools console, not in your code)
  • What happens: document is the whole page as a tree of objects.
  • Output: the document.

querySelectorAll(selector)NodeList of all matches (STATIC)
Difference: innerHTML, innerText, textContent
PropertyDescription
innerHTMLIncludes HTML tags
innerTextOnly visible text (respects styles)
textContentAll text (including hidden, no formatting)

9. NodeList vs HTMLCollection, Iteration & "Very Important"

NOTE: when you work with the DOM, most of the time each part of the DOM has 2 such properties, like childNodes and children:
  1. childNodes basically returns a NodeList (childNodes represents the node tree structure: ALL node types). NodeList means a representation of the DOM tree-structure data. It returns something like: NodeList(10) [text, h1, text, h3, text, div, text, comment, text, script]
  2. children returns an HTMLCollection (the actual collection of HTML elements). HTMLCollection means a representation of the HTML (element) data. It returns something like: HTMLCollection(4) [h1, h3, div, script]
✔ Clarified: the real difference is WHAT they contain (all nodes vs elements only) and their type: NodeList has forEach; HTMLCollection doesn't (use for…of or Array.from). HTMLCollections are LIVE (they update when the DOM changes); querySelectorAll's NodeList is STATIC (a snapshot), while childNodes' NodeList is live.childNodes = सगळे nodes (text, comment सकट), NodeList मध्ये. children = फक्त elements, HTMLCollection मध्ये. NodeList वर forEach चालतो, HTMLCollection वर नाही. HTMLCollection live असते (DOM बदलला की आपोआप बदलते); querySelectorAll ची NodeList static असते. DOM iteration: use forEach (or Array.from) to iterate through a NodeList, or convert it to an array for more flexible operations; you can also use a for…of loop or a for loop.
Very important:
  1. When you use the browser's developer-tools console to select an element and change its text content using JavaScript, you are directly manipulating the DOM object in memory.
  2. Since the DOM is a live representation of the document, any changes you make to DOM objects are immediately reflected in the rendered web page. However, these changes are temporary and exist only in the current session: when you refresh the page or navigate away, the browser reloads the original HTML document from the server, and the DOM is reconstructed during the parsing process. Any modifications made to the DOM objects during the previous session are lost, and the page returns to its original state.

12. firstChild vs firstElementChild (and lastChild)

firstChild
  • Definition: returns the first child node of an element, including text nodes, comment nodes or element nodes.
  • Characteristics: includes all node types (e.g. elements, text nodes, comments); may return a text node if whitespace (like line breaks or spaces) exists before the first element node; useful when you need to work with all types of child nodes, not just elements.
firstElementChild
  • Definition: returns the first element child of an element, ignoring text nodes and comments.
  • Characteristics: only considers element nodes; ignores text nodes, comments and whitespace; useful when you are only interested in elements, not other node types.
Example 1

  • Output: #text.
text

console.log("first-Child-element of body", firstChildElement);
// returns h1 (actual HTML data)

// How to navigate to the last child node or element:
// lastChild / lastElementChild
const lastChildNode = document.body.lastChild;
console.log("last-Child-Node of body", firstChildNode);
  • What happens: firstElementChild gives h1; lastChild is read but the log prints firstChildNode (copy-paste).
  • Output: h1, #text.
text
// #text
// ✔ it logs firstChildNode instead of lastChildNode (copy-paste); the comments above it also said firstChild

// the last child element with the 2nd property: lastElementChild
const lastChildElement = document.body.lastElementChild;
console.log("last-Child-element of body", lastChildElement);
// returns the script as the last child element
  • What happens: lastElementChild gives the last element.
  • Output: the script tag.

15. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. What is the DOM?
  • A live tree of objects (nodes) that the browser builds from HTML, plus an API to read and change it. document is the root; changes re-render the page but don't modify the source file.
Q2. childNodes vs children?
  • childNodes: a NodeList of ALL child nodes (elements, text incl. whitespace, comments). children: an HTMLCollection of child ELEMENTS only. Same for firstChild/firstElementChild, nextSibling/nextElementSibling.
Q3. NodeList vs HTMLCollection?
  • HTMLCollection: elements only, always live, accessible by index/name, no forEach. NodeList: any nodes, has forEach; live from childNodes, static from querySelectorAll. Convert either with Array.from or [...x].
Q4. parentNode vs parentElement?
  • Same for normal elements; for <html>, parentNode is the document while parentElement is null (the document isn't an element).
Q5. Output-based questions
// <body>\n  <h1>Hi</h1>\n</body>
console.log(document.body.firstChild.nodeName);          // → #text (whitespace)
console.log(document.body.firstElementChild.nodeName);   // → H1
console.log(document.childNodes.length);                 // → 2 (doctype + html)
console.log(document.documentElement.parentElement);     // → null
console.log(typeof document.body.children.forEach);      // → undefined (HTMLCollection)
  • What happens: five output questions: whitespace text nodes, element names, document's children, html has no parent element, HTMLCollection has no forEach.
  • Output: #text, H1, 2, null, undefined.

Root / body / headdocumentElement, body, head

First/lastfirstElementChild / lastElementChild

थोडक्यात: DOM = HTML चे live object tree. "Element" असलेले properties (children, firstElementChild, nextElementSibling) फक्त tags देतात; बाकीचे text/whitespace सुद्धा देतात. HTMLCollection live असते आणि त्यावर forEach नाही. HTML JS file मध्ये लिहू नका आणि एकाच नावाचे let/const दोनदा declare करू नका.

1. DOM Search: getElementById

let finElementById = document.getElementById("heading");
console.log("findElementById", finElementById);
// it returns the element which has the id "heading"; then we get the data of this element
console.log("element data using innerHTML :", finElementById.innerHTML);
console.log("element data using innerText:", finElementById.innerText);
console.log("element data using textContent:", finElementById.textContent);
// ⚠ if no element has id="heading" (your index.html is empty), getElementById returns null → TypeError on .innerHTML
  • What happens: getElementById returns one element (or null); innerHTML includes tags, innerText only visible text, textContent all text.
  • Output: the element and its three text views.
  • ⚠ Check for null before using the element.

2. getElementsByClassName

let finElementByClass = document.getElementsByClassName("list-of-nodes");
// console.log('finElementByClass', finElementByClass)
// it returns the elements which have the class "list-of-nodes"; then we get the data of these elements.
// So basically this method returns an HTMLCollection. This collection is iterable, so we can get the data of
// this iterable object using the spread operator, like:
console.log("finElementByClass", ...finElementByClass);

// you can also use a for…of loop and get the data from each element
for (let data of finElementByClass) {
  // console.log("data", data);
  console.log("data", data.innerHTML);
  console.log("data", data.innerText);
  console.log(data.textContent);
}
  • What happens: getElementsByClassName returns a live HTMLCollection; spread or for…of to loop.
  • Output: each element's HTML/text.

3. What is the Difference between innerHTML, innerText and textContent?

  1. innerHTML (displays the inner HTML inside the given element). Definition: retrieves or sets the HTML content inside an element, including any tags and their attributes. Usage: used to get or modify the entire HTML structure inside an element. The innerHTML property returns the complete content, including all HTML tags inside the element and their text content.
  2. innerText (hidden content is not displayed). Definition: retrieves or sets the visible text content of an element, as rendered by the browser. Usage: used to get or modify the text that a user can see, excluding hidden elements. innerText gives the text as it appears on screen, considering styling and excluding hidden elements.
  3. textContent. Definition: retrieves or sets the text content of an element, including hidden elements, without formatting or HTML tags. Usage: used to get or set all the text content within an element, regardless of visibility. textContent gives the text as it is in the markup, including hidden text and without considering styling.
Best use cases: innerHTML: when you want to inject or extract HTML, including tags. innerText: when you want to get the visible text only, as seen by users. textContent: when you want to get the raw text, including hidden elements, fast and safely. 
// ex.
// (this markup must be in the .html file; written raw in a .js file it is a SyntaxError)
// <div id="example">
//   <p>
//     Hello <span style="display: none;">Invisible</span> <b>World</b>
//   </p>
// </div>
const el = document.getElementById("example");
console.log("innerHTML:", el.innerHTML);
console.log("innerText:", el.innerText);
console.log("textContent:", el.textContent);
// output explanation
  • What happens: same text read three ways: innerHTML keeps markup, innerText respects CSS (hidden text left out), textContent includes hidden text.
  • Output: (the three outputs).
  • ✅ textContent is fastest and safest.
PropertyOutputDescription
innerHTML<p>Hello <span style="display: none;">Invisible</span> <b>World</b></p>Returns the HTML markup inside the element
innerTextHello WorldReturns only visible text (ignores display: none)
textContentHello Invisible WorldReturns all text, even hidden, without HTML
✔ Note: setting innerHTML with user input (e.g. a todo text) is an XSS risk: <img src=x onerror=alert(1)> would run. Use textContent for plain text.user चा input innerHTML ने टाकल्यास त्यातील script चालू शकते (XSS हल्ला). साध्या text साठी textContent वापरा.
Figure 137: innerHTML vs innerText vs textContent on the same element.
innerHTML = tags सकट HTML. innerText = स्क्रीनवर दिसणारा text (लपलेला नाही). textContent = सगळा text, लपलेला सुद्धा, tags शिवाय (सर्वात जलद आणि सुरक्षित).

getElementsByTagName

console.log("get-element-by-tagname :", getElementByTagName);
// it returns an HTML collection; we need to iterate using the spread operator or a for loop
// console.log('get-element-by-tagname :', ...getElementByTagName);
for (let tag of getElementByTagName) {
  console.log("tag", tag);

  • What happens: all elements with a tag name, as a live HTMLCollection.
  • Output: the
  • elements.

console.log(elements);   // → "hi welcome to the javascript" (just the assigned string)
// ✔ this sets an "innerHTML" property on the NodeList ITSELF, which changes nothing on the page
//    (your own summary note below says so). Loop over it:
//    document.getElementsByName("vishal").forEach(el => el.innerHTML = "hi welcome to the javascript");
  • What happens: returns a NodeList; assigning .innerHTML to the list changes nothing on the page.

5. querySelector & querySelectorAll

// query selector
const findByElementQuerySelector = document.querySelector("#heading");
// here we change the HTML content dynamically with the help of JavaScript
// the DOM is the way for JavaScript to communicate with, navigate and manipulate HTML
console.log(
  "findByElementQuerySelector",
  (findByElementQuerySelector.innerHTML = "welcome to javascript document object model")
);
console.log("findByElementQuerySelector", findByElementQuerySelector.innerText);
console.log("findByElementQuerySelector", findByElementQuerySelector.textContent);

const findElementByQuerySelectAll = document.querySelectorAll("li");
console.log("findElementByQuerySelectAll", findElementByQuerySelectAll);
// loop over the result
findElementByQuerySelectAll.forEach((ele) => {
  console.log("ele", ele);
});
  • What happens: querySelector returns the FIRST match for any CSS selector; querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList (has forEach).
  • Output: the updated heading text, the
  • NodeList.
  • ✅ One API for ids, classes, attributes, nested selectors.

6. What is the Difference between getElementById and querySelector?

getElementById
Syntax: document.getElementById('id'); Returns a reference to the element by its id. If the element with the specified id is not in the document, it returns null.
getElementsByClassName
Syntax: document.getElementsByClassName('className'); Returns the elements with that class name, as an HTMLCollection. ✔ "document.getElementByClass('id')" doesn't exist; the method is getElementsByClassName (plural "Elements"), its argument is a class name, and when nothing matches it returns an EMPTY HTMLCollection (length 0), never null.getElementByClass असा method नाही; getElementsByClassName आहे. काही न सापडल्यास तो null नाही, तर रिकामी (length 0) HTMLCollection देतो.
What is querySelector?
Syntax: document.querySelector(selectors); Returns the first element within the document that matches the specified group of selectors. It returns null if no match is found. ✔ spelling "quaySelector / quarry selector" → querySelector."quarry/quay" नाही, querySelector.
getElementByIdquerySelector
ArgumentAn id, without #Any CSS selector ("#id", ".cls", "ul > li:first-child")
ReturnsThe element or nullThe first match or null
SpeedFastestSlightly slower (selector parsing)
Available ondocument onlydocument AND any element (search inside it)

7. Summary: Searching in DOM Objects

1. How to search for an element and its reference:
document.getElementById('id').innerHTML = 'rendering or replacing content';
  • Use an id in an HTML tag only for unique elements.
  • When you write an id selector, use #.
  • When you write a class selector, use . (in querySelector; getElementById/getElementsByClassName take the plain name).
innerHTML: it is a property (part of the Document Object Model) that allows JavaScript code to manipulate the website being displayed. It allows rendering and replacing everything within the given DOM element. innerHTML is used to add dynamic HTML to HTML documents.
You can use the following methods: 
// 1. const data = document.getElementsByClassName('child1').innerHtml = document.body.style.color = 'green';
// 2. const data = document.getElementById('12').innerHtml = document.body.style.color = 'red';
// 3. const data = document.getElementsByTagName('div').innerHtml = document.body.style.color = 'red'
// 4. const data = document.getElementsByName('vishal').innerHtml = document.body.style.color = 'red';
// # document.getElementsByName('vishal') returns a NodeList of all elements with the name attribute set to 'vishal'.
//   You cannot directly set innerHtml on a NodeList; instead, you need to access the individual elements within
//   the list. We need to iterate.
// 5. querySelector
// querySelector takes a class name or an id name (any CSS selector).
// const child = document.querySelector('.main');
// returns the first matching element
// const data = document.querySelector('.child1').innerHtml = document.body.style.color = 'green';
// 6. querySelectorAll returns all the matching elements.
// const data = document.querySelectorAll('.child1').innerHtml = document.body.style.color = 'green';
  • What happens: notes: methods that return collections need a loop; querySelector takes any CSS selector.
  • Output: (notes).
✔ these one-liners don't do what they look like. (1) The property is innerHTML (capital HTML); "innerHtml" just creates a useless new property. (2) a = b = c assigns from RIGHT to LEFT: it colours the WHOLE body, then stores 'green' in innerHtml; the content isn't changed. (3) Collections (1, 3, 4, 6) need a loop. Correct: document.querySelectorAll('.child1').forEach(el => el.style.color = 'green'); innerHtml नाही, innerHTML (मोठे HTML). a = b = c उजवीकडून डावीकडे चालते, म्हणून body चा रंग बदलतो आणि content बदलत नाही. collections वर loop करावा लागतो.

8. What is the Use of createElement()?

Your Notes: the createElement() method in JavaScript is used to create a new DOM element dynamically. It is commonly used to add elements to the DOM programmatically. It creates HTML element nodes with the specified name via JavaScript. The method takes the name of the element as its parameter and creates a new element node: document.createElement(tagName);
Example 1
// Step 1: create a new <p> element
const newElement = document.createElement("p");
// Step 2: add text content to the element
newElement.textContent = "Hello, this is a dynamically created paragraph!";
// Step 3: append the element to the body
document.body.appendChild(newElement);
  • What happens: create an element, set its text, attach it to the page.
  • Output: a new paragraph on the page.
  • ✅ textContent avoids HTML injection.
example 2
// example 2
// Create a new button element
const button = document.createElement("button");
// Set the text content
button.textContent = "Click Me";
// Add a click event listener
button.addEventListener("click", () => {
  alert("Button clicked!");
});
// Append the button to the body
document.body.appendChild(button);
// ⚠ "button" is declared AGAIN later (let button = …) → SyntaxError for the whole file; rename one (e.g. newButton)
  • What happens: create a button, add a click listener, append it.
  • Output: a working button (alert on click).
  • ⚠ Duplicate const/let names in one file stop the whole file.

If you want the actual elements inside the body, use:
// # If you want the actual elements inside the body, use:
document.body.children;
HTMLCollection[div.main];   // Returns the actual (parent) child elements in the body.
// ✔ "HTMLCollection[div.main]" is how the CONSOLE displays the result, not code; as code it throws
//    ReferenceError: div is not defined. Keep it as a comment: // → HTMLCollection [div.main]
  • What happens: children gives elements only; the next line is console output, not code.
  • Output: (ReferenceError as written).
Does an element have child nodes or not?
// # Does an element have child nodes or not?
document.body.hasChildNodes();   // true
  • What happens: hasChildNodes checks for any child node.
  • Output: true.

11. Common DOM Methods

  • createElement(tagName): creates a new HTML element.
  • appendChild(node): appends a node as the last child of a parent node.
  • removeChild(node): removes a child node from its parent (modern: node.remove()).
  • addEventListener(event, callback_function): creates a new event listener to handle an event.
  • removeEventListener(event, function): removes an event listener.
  • setAttribute(name, value): sets the value of an attribute on an element.
  • getAttribute(name): gets the value of a specific attribute on an element.
✔ "appendChild(nde)" → node; "even listener" → event listener."nde" नाही "node", आणि "even" नाही "event" listener. 
// more you'll use daily
el.classList.add("active"); el.classList.toggle("hide"); el.classList.contains("x");
el.style.color = "red";        el.dataset.id;   // reads data-id="…"
parent.insertBefore(newNode, refNode); el.replaceWith(other); el.cloneNode(true);
el.insertAdjacentHTML("beforeend", "<li>x</li>");
  • What happens: everyday DOM helpers: classList, style, dataset, insertBefore, replaceWith, cloneNode, insertAdjacentHTML.
  • Output: (notes).

12. What is the Difference between the append() and appendChild() Methods in the DOM?

append()
  • Definition: adds one or more elements, text strings or DOM nodes to the end of a parent element.
  • Accepts multiple arguments (you can add multiple things at the same time).
  • Can add both Node objects (elements) and plain text strings.
  • Does not return the appended node (returns undefined).
  • If appending a text string, it automatically creates a text node.
  • You can add text or elements to a parent element.
const parent11 = document.getElementById("parent");
// Append a new paragraph and text
parent11.append("Hello World", document.createElement("p"));
  • What happens: append accepts several nodes AND strings.
  • Output: "Hello World" + an empty

    .

appendChild()
  • Definition: adds a single Node object to the end of a parent element.
  • Key features: only accepts a Node object (e.g. an element or text node); you can only add one element (or node) at a time.
  • Throws an error if you pass a plain string (TypeError: parameter 1 is not of type 'Node').
  • Returns the appended node.
  • Cannot add plain text (it must be inside a node).
const parent1 = document.getElementById("parent");
// Create a new paragraph element
const paragraph = document.createElement("p");
paragraph.textContent = "Hello World";
// Append the paragraph to the parent
parent1.appendChild(paragraph);
  • What happens: appendChild accepts one node only.
  • Output:

    Hello World

    added.
  • ⚠ appendChild can't take a string; use append for text.
  • append(): for adding text + elements together, or multiple things at once.
  • appendChild(): for adding only one node (not plain text).
Note: appending a node that is already in the DOM MOVES it (a node can have only one parent).

13. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. innerHTML vs innerText vs textContent?
  • innerHTML: markup with tags (parses HTML when set, so beware of XSS). innerText: visible, CSS-aware text (triggers layout, slower). textContent: all text, including hidden, raw and fast; the safe choice for setting plain text.
Q2. querySelectorAll vs getElementsByClassName?
  • qSA takes any CSS selector and returns a STATIC NodeList with forEach. gEBCN takes a class name (no dot) and returns a LIVE HTMLCollection without forEach.
Q3. append vs appendChild?
  • append: many nodes/strings, returns undefined. appendChild: exactly one Node, returns it, and a string throws a TypeError.
Q4. How do you remove an element? Add many elements efficiently?
  • el.remove() (or parent.removeChild(el)). For many elements, build them in a DocumentFragment (or one string with insertAdjacentHTML), then insert once to avoid repeated reflows.
Q5. Output-based questions
// <ul><li class="a">1</li><li class="a">2</li></ul>
const live = document.getElementsByClassName("a");
const snap = document.querySelectorAll(".a");
document.querySelector("ul").append(Object.assign(document.createElement("li"), { className: "a" }));
console.log(live.length, snap.length);              // → 3 2 (live vs static)
console.log(document.getElementById("nope"));       // → null
console.log(document.getElementsByClassName("nope").length);   // → 0 (not null)
console.log(document.createElement("p").appendChild(document.createTextNode("x")).nodeName);   // → #text
  • What happens: getElementsByClassName is LIVE (updates automatically), querySelectorAll is a snapshot; missing id → null, missing class → empty collection; appendChild returns the appended node.
  • Output: 3 2, null, 0, #text.

One by id / selectorgetElementById / querySelector
ManyquerySelectorAll (static) / getElementsBy* (live)
Read/set texttextContent (safe) / innerText (visible)
Set HTMLinnerHTML / insertAdjacentHTML (trusted content only)
Create & insertcreateElement + append / appendChild
Removeel.remove()
थोडक्यात: element शोधण्यासाठी getElementById / querySelector(All). collections वर loop करा. text साठी textContent (सुरक्षित), HTML साठी innerHTML (फक्त विश्वासाचा content). createElement + append ने नवीन element जोडा, remove() ने काढा. append अनेक गोष्टी आणि text घेतो; appendChild एकच node घेतो.

1. Events in JavaScript

Your Notes (25_event/Event.js): An event is a signal that something has happened (like a click or a key press), and you can write code to respond to it.
An event in JavaScript is an action or occurrence that happens in the browser, which can be detected and responded to using JavaScript code.
Common examples of events:
Event TypeDescription
clickWhen a user clicks an element
submitWhen a form is submitted
keydownWhen a key is pressed
loadWhen a page finishes loading
mouseoverWhen the mouse hovers over an element
inputWhen an input value changes
Definition: An event is a notification from the browser that something happened (a user action, a page load, a timer, a network response). You register a listener (handler), a function the browser calls with an event object when that event fires on an element. Events travel through the DOM in 3 phases: capturing (down) → target → bubbling (up).
Event म्हणजे browser मध्ये घडलेली एखादी गोष्ट: click, key दाबणे, page load होणे. आपण त्या event साठी handler (function) लावतो; event घडल्यावर browser तो function event object सह चालवतो.

2. Topics of This Folder & What is an Event Object?

Your Notes: topics (how to write events in JavaScript):
  1. What is the Event object
  2. Mouse events in JavaScript
  3. Keyboard events in JavaScript
  4. InputEvent in JavaScript
✔ the heading says "3 ways of writing events" but lists 4 TOPICS. The 3 ways (inline, DOM property, addEventListener) are in §7.heading मध्ये "3 ways" लिहिले आहे पण खाली 4 topics आहेत. events लिहिण्याच्या 3 पद्धती §7 मध्ये दिल्या आहेत. What is an Event Object?
  1. The event object in JavaScript represents the event that occurs when interacting with an HTML element.
  2. It is automatically passed to the event handler (the function used in addEventListener, or an inline handler).
  3. It provides information about the event, such as its type, the target element, the current element, and additional details specific to the event type (e.g. the mouse position for a click event).
  4. You access the event object as a parameter in your event handler.

3. HTML Events are "Things" that Happen to HTML Elements

Your Notes:
  1. When JavaScript is used in an HTML page, JavaScript reacts to these events.
  2. An HTML event can be something the browser does or something a user does:
  3. an HTML page has finished loading,
  4. an HTML input field changed,
  5. an HTML button was clicked.
  6. Often when events happen, you may want to do something.

4. What is the Use of event.preventDefault()?

Your Notes: in JavaScript, e.preventDefault() (or event.preventDefault()) is used to prevent the browser's default behavior for a particular event.
EventDefault BehaviorWhy Use preventDefault()
form submitPage reloads or navigates to the action URLStop the reload; handle the submission via JavaScript
anchor clickNavigates to the href linkPrevent navigation (e.g. a single-page app)
drag/dropThe file gets opened in the browserHandle the file manually
form.addEventListener("submit", (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();               // no page reload
  const data = new FormData(form);  // handle it with JS (fetch…)
});
  • What happens: preventDefault stops the form from reloading the page; FormData reads all its fields.
  • Output: (no reload).
  • ✅ Submit forms with fetch and show results without leaving the page.

5. The Event Object (Event.js)

Your Notes: 
const element = document.getElementById("eve");
console.log(element);   // → <button id="eve">click me</button>
element.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  console.log("event-object:", event);   // Logs the event object (a PointerEvent / MouseEvent)
  //* Logs the event object

  // # type: of the event (returns the type of event)
  console.log("type-of-event: ", event.type);          // → click

  // # target: (returns the element that triggered the event)
  console.log("target-element: ", event.target);       // → <button id="eve">

  // # currentTarget: the element to which the event handler is attached.
  console.log("current-Target", event.currentTarget);  // → <button id="eve"> (same here)

  // # preventDefault(): prevents the browser's default action for the event (i.e. stopping a form submission or a navigation)
  event.preventDefault();   // stop the navigation (⚠ a plain button has no default action, so this does nothing here)

  // # stopPropagation(): used to stop the event from bubbling up to the parent elements (or capturing down)
  event.stopImmediatePropagation();
  // ✔ the comment says stopPropagation but the code calls stopImmediatePropagation. Difference:
  //    stopPropagation() → stops travel to parent elements; stopImmediatePropagation() → ALSO stops the other
  //    listeners on the SAME element from running

  // # clientX / clientY (for mouse events)
  // The X and Y coordinates of the mouse pointer relative to the viewport
  console.log(event.clientX + " and " + event.clientY);   // e.g. 52 and 310

  // # for keyboard events: key / code
  // Provides information about the key pressed during a keydown or keyup event.
  element.addEventListener("keydown", (event) => {
    console.log("key-pass", event.key);    // e.g. "a"
    console.log("key-code", event.code);   // e.g. "KeyA"
  });
  // ⚠ this adds a NEW keydown listener on EVERY click (after 3 clicks, each key logs 3 times); register it once,
  //   outside the click handler. A button only gets keydown while it has focus.
});
  • What happens: the event object describes what happened: type, target (where it started), currentTarget (where the listener is), mouse coordinates, key info; preventDefault/stopPropagation control behaviour.
  • Output: click, the button twice, coordinates.
  • ⚠ Adding a listener inside another listener adds a new one every click.
click handler च्या आत keydown listener लावल्याने प्रत्येक click ला नवीन listener जोडला जातो, आणि एक key दाबल्यावर अनेक वेळा log होते. तो बाहेर एकदाच लावा. stopPropagation आणि stopImmediatePropagation वेगळे आहेत: दुसरा त्याच element वरचे इतर listeners सुद्धा थांबवतो.
Figure 138: Event flow: capturing down to the target, then bubbling up; target vs currentTarget.
Event प्रथम document कडून खाली target पर्यंत येतो (capturing), मग target वर चालतो, आणि मग वर parents कडे जातो (bubbling). event.target म्हणजे जिथे event घडला, आणि event.currentTarget म्हणजे ज्या element चा listener आत्ता चालू आहे. parent वर listener लावल्यास दोन्ही वेगळे असू शकतात.

6. Inline Event Object

Your Notes: in inline event handlers, the event object is not explicitly passed, but it can still be accessed as event: 
{
  /* <button onclick="console.log(event)">Click me</button> */
}
// Here, event refers to the event object, which works in inline handlers but is not recommended in modern JavaScript.
  • What happens: inline handlers get an implicit event variable.
  • Output: (markup).
  • ⚠ Inline handlers mix HTML and JS; avoid them.
✔ "event refers to the global event object". Inside an inline attribute, the browser wraps your code in function (event) { … }, so event is that handler's PARAMETER. (window.event is a separate, deprecated global.)inline handler मध्ये browser तुमचा code function(event){...} मध्ये गुंडाळतो, म्हणून event हा त्याचा parameter असतो, global नाही.

7. Ways to Write Events in JavaScript

Your Notes:
  1. inline events
  2. DOM event handler (on-property)
  3. addEventListener event handler

1. Inline events

1. onclick event: using alert() → using an inline event 
<a href="#" class="button_su_inner" onclick="alert('Hi welcome')">
  <span class="button_text"> Simple inline alert</span>
</a>

another example:
<h1>Inline Events</h1>
<button onclick="alert('welcome to event in javascript')" id="btn">
  Click on inline event
</button>
  • What happens: inline onclick attributes run the JS string on click.
  • Output: alerts on click.
# ondblclick event: 
<button ondblclick="alert('welcome to javascript event : ondblclick')">ondblclick event</button>
  • What happens: inline ondblclick.
  • Output: alert on double-click.
  1. In inline events, if you define the same event again and again, it overrides the event, and you see only one action. ✔ it depends HOW it is "defined again". The same attribute written twice in one tag (onclick="a()" onclick="b()") → the HTML parser keeps the FIRST and ignores the rest. Assigning el.onclick again in JS → the LAST assignment wins.एकाच tag मध्ये onclick दोनदा लिहिल्यास HTML parser पहिलाच ठेवतो. JS मध्ये el.onclick पुन्हा assign केल्यास शेवटचा जिंकतो.
  2. Inline event handlers do not allow you to stack multiple event listeners on the same event.
  3. If multiple inline handlers are set for the same event, only one survives, unless you explicitly call multiple functions inside the handler: onclick="a(); b()".
  4. If you call a function in an inline event attribute like onclick, you need to put parentheses after the function name: onclick="greet()". (In JS it's the opposite: el.onclick = greet, without ().)

2. DOM event handler

1. click event using a DOM event handler: 
const button = document.getElementById('btn').onclick = function () {
  alert('welcome to dom event handler : onclick')
}
console.log(button);    // → the function itself (the value of an assignment expression)

const button1 = document.getElementById('btn').onclick = () => {
  alert('welcome to dom event handler : onclick')
  console.log('inline event called.')
}
console.log(button1);   // → the arrow function
// the second assignment REPLACES the first handler (one onclick per element)
  • What happens: the element.onclick property holds ONE handler; assigning again replaces the first.
  • Output: the two functions.
  • ⚠ Only one handler per event with this method.

3. addEventListener event handler

const newButton = document.getElementById('btn1');
console.log(newButton);
newButton.addEventListener('click', () => {
  alert('welcome ot addEventListener event in javascript')
  console.log('event lister called first')
})
  • What happens: addEventListener attaches a handler; several can be added to the same event.
  • Output: the button, then alert + log on click.
  • ✅ The recommended way: multiple listeners, options, removable.
With addEventListener, if you register the same event multiple times, it does not override: every handler runs. addEventListener lets you stack multiple event listeners on the same event (multiple listeners for the same event, without overriding each other).
Events लिहिण्याच्या 3 पद्धती: (1) inline: HTML मध्ये onclick="..." (2) DOM property: el.onclick = fn, एकच handler, नवीन दिल्यास जुना जातो (3) addEventListener: अनेक handlers चालतात, removeEventListener ने काढता येतात, आणि options (once, capture) मिळतात. सर्वोत्तम: addEventListener.

  • What happens: the demo page showing all three ways (inline attribute, DOM property, addEventListener).
  • Output: (markup).
✔ Note: id="btn" is used TWICE (the inline onclick button and the "DOM event handler" button). IDs must be unique; getElementById('btn') returns only the FIRST one, so the DOM-handler demo would replace the inline button's handler and the second button would get nothing. Use id="btn0" for the second one.id="btn" दोन buttons ला दिला आहे. id unique असावा; getElementById फक्त पहिला element देतो. म्हणून दुसऱ्या button ला वेगळा id द्या. Note: mouseover/mousemove with alert() fire again and again (an alert on every mouse move), so the page becomes hard to use; use console.log or change a style instead for such demos.

9. Differences between Inline Events and addEventListener()

Your Notes:

1. Inline event handlers

  1. Events are defined directly within HTML attributes: <button onclick="alert('Clicked!')">Click Me</button>
  2. With inline/on-property handlers only one handler can be specified per event: if you assign a new onclick, it overwrites the existing one. I.e. inline event handlers (onclick) overwrite any previously set handler, so only one event handler can exist for a given event at a time. 
    const button3 = document.querySelector("#btn2").onclick = function () { alert('override the event in inline event handler') };
console.log(button3)
    • What happens: assigning onclick in JS overrides the inline handler on the same element.
    • Output: the function.
    (I.e. with inline events, if you define the same event again and again, it overrides the event and only one action shows.)
  3. Inline event handlers can't be removed with removeEventListener; you remove them by changing the HTML or with el.onclick = null / el.removeAttribute("onclick"). ✔ "Cannot be removed without modifying the HTML directly". Setting el.onclick = null from JS removes it too.inline handler सुद्धा JS मध्ये el.onclick = null करून काढता येतो.

2. addEventListener

  1. addEventListener() listeners are attached programmatically in JavaScript using the addEventListener() method. 
    const button = document.querySelector("#btn2");
button.addEventListener("click", () => alert("Clicked!"));
button.addEventListener('click', () => alert('click2'))   // both run, in order: Clicked! → click2
    • What happens: two addEventListener calls → both run in order.
    • Output: Clicked!, click2.
  2. addEventListener supports attaching multiple handlers to the same event without overwriting. I.e. addEventListener allows attaching multiple event listeners for the same event on the same element. All attached listeners are executed when the event occurs, unless you manually remove them with removeEventListener. I.e. with addEventListener, if you define the same event again and again, it does not override; it calls the handlers one by one.
  3. Handlers can be removed using removeEventListener if a named function (the same reference) is used.
FeatureInline / onclick propertyaddEventListener
WhereHTML attribute / el.onclickJS method
Multiple handlersNo (one per event)Yes (all run in order)
Removeel.onclick = nullremoveEventListener(type, sameFn)
OptionsNoneonce, capture, passive, signal
Separation of HTML/JSPoor (mixed)Good

10. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. event.target vs event.currentTarget?
  • target = the element where the event originated (e.g. the clicked child); currentTarget = the element whose listener is running now (where addEventListener was called). They differ when the event bubbles to a parent.
Q2. preventDefault vs stopPropagation vs stopImmediatePropagation?
  • preventDefault stops the browser's default ACTION (submit, link navigation) but the event still travels; stopPropagation stops the TRAVEL to other elements; stopImmediatePropagation also stops the remaining listeners on the same element.
Q3. What are event bubbling and capturing?
  • Capturing: window → … → target (listeners with {capture: true}). Bubbling: target → … → window (the default). Most events bubble; some don't (focus, mouseenter/mouseleave).
Q4. Why is addEventListener preferred over onclick?
  • Multiple listeners, easy removal, options (once/capture/passive), and it keeps HTML and JS separate (works with CSP, which blocks inline handlers).
Q5. Output-based questions
btn.onclick = () => console.log("A");
btn.onclick = () => console.log("B");
btn.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("C"));
btn.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("D"));
// click → B C D   (onclick kept only the last one; listeners stack)
const h = () => console.log("E");
btn.addEventListener("click", h); btn.addEventListener("click", h);   // the same reference twice → added ONCE
btn.removeEventListener("click", () => console.log("C"));              // does nothing (a different function)
  • What happens: onclick keeps only the last one (B); listeners stack (C, D); the same function reference is added once; removeEventListener needs the SAME function reference.
  • Output: B C D.
  • ⚠ Anonymous functions can't be removed later.
ItemRemember
Event objecttype, target, currentTarget, clientX/Y, key/code
preventDefault()Cancels the default browser action
stopPropagation()Stops bubbling/capturing
3 waysInline attribute, el.onX property, addEventListener
Best practiceaddEventListener with named functions

1. Mouse Events in JavaScript

Your Notes (MouseEvent.js): the mouse event object. Events that occur when the mouse interacts with the HTML document belong to the MouseEvent object.
  1. onclick: the user clicks on an element.
  2. oncontextmenu: the user RIGHT-clicks on an element (to open the context menu). ✔ the note said "the user click on an element" (same as onclick). contextmenu = the right click / context-menu key.oncontextmenu म्हणजे right-click (context menu उघडणे), साधा click नाही.
  3. ondblclick: the user double-clicks on an element.
  4. onmousedown: the mouse button is pressed over an element (a pointing-device button is pressed on an element).
  5. onmouseenter: the pointer is moved onto an element (when the mouse enters an element). Does NOT bubble and doesn't fire again when moving between children.
  6. onmouseleave: the pointer is moved out of an element (when the mouse leaves an element). Does not bubble.
  7. onmousemove: the pointer is moving over an element (fires many times per second).
  8. onmouseout: the mouse pointer moves out of an element (bubbles; ALSO fires when moving onto a child element).
  9. onmouseover: the mouse pointer moved over an element (bubbles; also fires when moving between children).
  10. onmouseup: the mouse button is released over an element.
Order for one click: mousedown → mouseup → click; for a double click: … click → dblclick.
Mouse events: click, contextmenu (right click), dblclick, mousedown (बटण दाबणे), mouseup (सोडणे), mouseenter/mouseleave (आत/बाहेर, bubble होत नाहीत), mouseover/mouseout (children वर जातानाही fire होतात, bubble होतात), mousemove (हलवताना सतत fire होतो).

Your Notes (KeybordEvent.js): events that occur when a user presses a key on the keyboard. They belong to the KeyboardEvent object:

5. Input Events (InputEvent.js)

Your Notes: 1. input events in JavaScript (the 'change' event is used like onclick)
  1. The input event in JavaScript is used to get the value of an element every time it changes (on every keystroke).
  2. The change event in JavaScript is used to get the value of an input after it has changed and the user presses Enter or leaves the field (loses focus).
You can define the change handling in two ways:
  1. using addEventListener (below),
  2. using the onchange attribute (onChnage.html).
const handleInput = (e) => {
  document.querySelector('.inputValue').textContent = e.target.value
  document.querySelector('.inputName').textContent = e.target.name
  document.querySelector('.inputType').textContent = e.inputType
  document.querySelector('.eventType').textContent = e.type
}
const input = document.getElementById('myInput');
console.log(input);
// input.addEventListener('input', handleInput)
input.addEventListener('change', handleInput)
// ⚠ e.inputType ("insertText", "deleteContentBackward") exists only on 'input' events (InputEvent);
//   with 'change' it is undefined, so .inputType shows "undefined"
  • What happens: change fires when the field loses focus after its value changed; input fires on every keystroke. inputType exists only on input events.
  • Output: the value, name, "undefined", change.
  • ✅ Use input for live search, change for final values.

Your Notes (todo):
  1. The onchange event occurs when the value of an element has been changed.

  5. this method adds the onchange handler directly to the HTML element.

7. What is the Difference between the onclick Event and addEventListener()?

Your Notes:

onclick

  1. It's a property on DOM elements that you assign a function to, to handle the click event.
  2. When you assign a new function to onclick, it overwrites any previously assigned handler. You can only have one onclick handler at a time.
  3. To remove the event handler, you can set element.onclick = null;, which removes the click handler.
  4. It provides no options; it is limited to handling the event in a straightforward way.
  5. It always listens during the bubbling phase (and at the target), meaning a parent's onclick fires after the child elements have handled the event.

addEventListener

  1. It's a method used to register event listeners for specific events (not just click) on DOM elements.
  2. It allows you to attach multiple event listeners to the same event. Each listener is called when the event occurs, and they don't override each other.
  3. You need to call removeEventListener to remove a specific listener, and it requires a reference to the exact function that was added: element.removeEventListener("click", handleClick);
  4. It provides more flexibility with options like { once: true }, which makes the event listener execute only once and then automatically remove itself.
  5. It lets you choose whether to listen during the capturing phase (before child elements) or the bubbling phase (after child elements) by passing the { capture: true } option.
Listener options: once, capture, passive
function handleClick() { console.log("clicked"); }
btn.addEventListener("click", handleClick, { once: true });        // auto-removed after the first click
parent.addEventListener("click", () => {}, { capture: true });     // runs before the child's listeners
window.addEventListener("scroll", onScroll, { passive: true });     // promises no preventDefault → smoother scrolling
  • What happens: once removes the listener after one call; capture runs it on the way down; passive promises no preventDefault (smoother scrolling).
  • Output: (no output).
Event delegation
// event delegation: ONE listener on the parent handles all children (even ones added later)
list.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
  if (e.target.matches("li")) console.log("clicked", e.target.textContent);
});
  • What happens: one listener on the parent checks e.target.matches("li"); it works for items added later too.
  • Output: clicked + the item text.
  • ✅ Fewer listeners, dynamic lists.

8. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. input vs change event?
  • input fires on every modification (each keystroke, paste); change fires when the value is committed: on blur/Enter for text inputs, immediately for checkbox/radio/select.
Q2. mouseenter vs mouseover (and mouseleave vs mouseout)?
  • mouseover/mouseout bubble and also fire when moving onto/off child elements; mouseenter/mouseleave don't bubble and fire only for the element itself, which is usually what you want for hover effects.
Q3. keydown vs keypress vs keyup? e.key vs e.code?
  • keydown fires for all keys (and repeats); keypress is deprecated (character keys only); keyup fires on release. e.key is the produced value ("a"/"A"); e.code is the physical key ("KeyA"), independent of the layout.
Q4. What is event delegation and why use it?
  • Put one listener on a common parent and use e.target (with matches/closest) to handle the children. Fewer listeners, and it works for dynamically added elements. It relies on bubbling.
Q5. Output-based questions
// <div id="p"><button id="c">x</button></div>
p.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("parent"));
c.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("child"));
// click button → child → parent (bubbling)
p.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("cap"), { capture: true });
// click button → cap → child → parent
c.addEventListener("click", (e) => e.stopPropagation());
// click button → cap → child (parent's bubbling listener no longer runs)
  • What happens: bubbling: child then parent; a capture listener runs first; stopPropagation at the child stops the bubbling.
  • Output: child parent; cap child parent; cap child.
GroupEvents
Mouseclick, dblclick, contextmenu, mousedown/up, mouseenter/leave, mouseover/out, mousemove
Keyboardkeydown, keyup (keypress deprecated); e.key, e.code
Forminput (live), change (commit), submit, focus/blur
Listener optionsonce, capture, passive, signal
थोडक्यात: mouse events (click, dblclick, contextmenu, enter/leave...), keyboard events (keydown/keyup, e.key), form events (input = live, change = commit). addEventListener मध्ये once/capture options आहेत. delegation म्हणजे parent वर एक listener लावून e.target ने children हाताळणे.
