1. Event Propagation

Your Notes (39_eventPraPogationAndDelegation/eventPropagation/eventPrapogation.js):
  1. Event propagation refers to the process of how events are propagated (travel) through the DOM (Document Object Model) hierarchy. (I.e. event propagation in the DOM describes how events move through the HTML element hierarchy when an event is triggered.)
  2. Event propagation is a way to describe the sequence of event handlers that fire in a web browser. (I.e. the event propagation mode determines the order in which elements receive the event.)
  3. Event propagation is a mechanism in the DOM that defines how events travel (flow, propagate) through the HTML elements in response to an event (like a click or key press).
  4. It determines the order in which event handlers are triggered for nested elements.
  5. Event propagation is crucial for managing and handling events in complex web applications.
  6. The event propagation mode determines the order in which elements receive the event.
Definition: When an event happens on an element, the browser dispatches it along the path window → document → html → body → … → target. It travels DOWN (capturing), arrives at the target, then travels back UP (bubbling). Every listener on that path whose phase matches runs; stopPropagation() ends the journey.
Event propagation म्हणजे event DOM मध्ये कसा प्रवास करतो: आधी window पासून target पर्यंत खाली (capturing), मग target वर, आणि मग परत वर parents कडे (bubbling). त्या मार्गावर असलेले listeners या क्रमाने चालतात.

2. The 3 Phases of Event Propagation

  1. Capturing phase (trickles down)
  2. Target phase (hits the target element)
  3. Bubbling phase (bubbles up)
✔ the heading said "2 phases" but lists (correctly) THREE phases.heading मध्ये "2 phase" लिहिले आहे, पण phases 3 आहेत (capturing, target, bubbling).
PhaseDescriptionListener option
CapturingThe event moves top → targetaddEventListener(..., true) / { capture: true }
TargetThe event is at the actual target element(both kinds run)
BubblingThe event moves target → topaddEventListener(..., false) (default)
Event flow recap:
  1. When an event is triggered, it goes through three phases:
  2. capturing phase: document → down to the target;
  3. target phase: the event hits the target element;
  4. bubbling phase: target → up to the document (bubbles up).
Figure 140: The three phases of event propagation for a click on the button.

3. Capturing, Target & Bubbling Phases

What is the event capturing phase?
  1. The event starts from the top and goes to the bottom.
  2. The event starts from window → document → html → body → down to the target element.
  3. In this phase, the event travels from the outermost ancestor to the actual target element.
  4. The event starts from the root of the DOM and goes down to the target element; handlers registered for the capturing phase are executed.
  5. The event starts at the root of the DOM tree and propagates downward through the parent elements until it reaches the target element.
  6. With event capturing, the event is first captured by the outermost element and propagated to the inner elements.
  7. Capturing is also called trickling, which helps you remember the propagation order.
  8. Going from the window to the event target.
What is the target phase? 1. The event reaches the target element where the event was triggered, and the handlers registered on the target are executed (both capture and bubble listeners of the target itself).
What is the event bubbling phase?
  1. Event bubbling is one of the phases of the DOM event flow, where the event starts from the target element and propagates upward to its ancestors.
  2. Event bubbling makes the event execution process go from bottom to top. With event bubbling, the event is first handled by the innermost element and then propagated to the outer elements.
  3. The event starts from the target element and bubbles up to the root of the DOM; handlers registered for the bubbling phase are executed.
  4. After the event reaches the target element, it propagates back up (or "bubbles") through its ancestors until it reaches the root again, and any event handlers attached to these ancestor elements are triggered in this phase.
  5. The event flows from the child button back up to the parent div, and eventually to the document: from the event target's parent back to the window.
Note: not every event bubbles: focus, blur, mouseenter, mouseleave, load and scroll (on elements) don't. Use focusin/focusout for delegation.

4. Which Phase Is Used by Default? How Do You Stop Propagation?

  1. By default it is bottom to top (i.e. the target element up to the root element): by default, listeners run in the bubbling phase.

So event propagation defines the order in which elements receive the event.
  1. Capture phase: TOP → BOTTOM (root of the DOM ⇒ target element): window ⇒ document ⇒ html ⇒ body ⇒ button (TARGET PHASE)
  2. Bubble phase: BOTTOM → TOP (target element ⇒ root of the DOM): (TARGET PHASE) <button> ⇒ div ⇒ body ⇒ html ⇒ document ⇒ window
If listeners run in a certain order, can we change the sequence? This complete process of deciding when, and in which direction, an event is handled is called event propagation.
Is there any way to stop this bubbling?
  1. To stop bubbling (and capturing), use the event.stopPropagation() method inside the event handler (callback function).
  2. By default it is the bubbling process: when we click on the button, the event bubbles up; the way to prevent that is called stopping propagation. I.e. when we click on the button, only the button's event runs, and the propagation to the other elements is stopped.
Note: stopImmediatePropagation() additionally stops the OTHER listeners on the same element. Avoid stopping propagation casually: it breaks delegated handlers and analytics higher up.

5. How to Achieve the Capturing Phase in Event Propagation

  1. To achieve event capturing, use the third parameter of the addEventListener method, which specifies whether the event should be captured during the capturing phase.
  2. Setting it to true activates the capture phase (i.e. pass the third parameter of addEventListener as capture: true).
  3. To achieve event capturing, you pass the third parameter to addEventListener as { capture: true }, an object.
  4. By setting { capture: true } in the addEventListener() method, you switch the event listener to the capturing phase.
el.addEventListener("click", handler, true);              // old boolean form
el.addEventListener("click", handler, { capture: true }); // options-object form
el.removeEventListener("click", handler, { capture: true });   // must match the capture flag to remove it
  • What happens: the third argument (true or { capture: true }) puts the listener in the capturing phase; removeEventListener must match the same capture flag.
  • Output: (no output).
  • ⚠ Mismatched capture flags mean the listener is never removed.

6. What is the Difference between e.target, e.currentTarget and this?

All of these are very important to know if you want to tackle event propagation.

1. event.currentTarget
  1. event.currentTarget represents the element to which the event listener (that is currently running) is attached.
  2. It refers to the element the event listener is attached to; this is particularly useful with event delegation, where you attach an event listener to a common ancestor of multiple elements.
  3. This is the element that is currently handling the event, regardless of where the event originated.
  4. It always points to the element the running handler is attached to, regardless of where the event was actually triggered.
2. event.target
  1. event.target represents the actual DOM element on which the event originated.
  2. It refers to the element that triggered the event.
  3. It may be any descendant element within the element that has the listener, and it accurately identifies the element that triggered the event (this is the actual element where the event occurred), e.g. the element that was clicked or that the user interacted with.
  4. If you click a button within a div, event.target refers to the button, not the div.
  5. event.target always points to the button here, because that is where the bubbling originated.
✔ one line under event.target said "it is references to the element that the event listener is attached to"; that describes currentTarget, not target."listener ज्या element वर लावला तो" हे currentTarget चे वर्णन आहे, target चे नाही. target म्हणजे जिथे event प्रत्यक्ष घडला तो element. this.tagName
  1. this in the context of a (normal-function) event handler refers to the element the event listener is attached to (= e.currentTarget). In an arrow-function handler, this is NOT the element.
  2. You can access its tagName property to get the tag name of that element (e.g. "DIV", "BUTTON", "A"; uppercase in HTML documents).
  3. This tells you which LISTENER's element is running, not which element triggered the event; for that, use event.target. ✔ "This is often used to determine the type of element that triggered the event". this = currentTarget, the element with the listener, not the trigger.this म्हणजे listener असलेला element (currentTarget). event कोणी सुरू केला ते event.target सांगतो.
console.log('tagName', this.tagName)
// it prints BUTTON, FORM, DIV as the event bubbles through the handlers on those elements
  • What happens: in a normal function listener, this is the element the listener is on, so its tagName changes as the event bubbles.
  • Output: BUTTON, FORM, DIV.
Conclusion about e.target and e.currentTarget: e.target:
  1. refers to the element that triggered the event;
  2. this is the actual element where the event occurred.
  • e.currentTarget: 1. refers to the element the event listener is attached to
  • 2. this is the element that is currently handling the event, regardless of where the event originated.
Featureevent.targetevent.currentTarget
DefinitionThe actual element that triggered the eventThe element on which the event listener is attached
Use CaseWhen you want to know which child element was clicked inside a parentWhen you want to reference the listener's element
Can they differ?Yes: during bubbling/delegation, target = the child, currentTarget = the parent with the listener (equal only when the listener is on the clicked element)
Changes during bubbling?No: it stays the same (the origin of the event)Yes: it changes as the event bubbles through the parents

No" (it CAN differ from target; it always equals the element with the listener).bubbling दरम्यान target बदलत नाही (मूळ element तोच राहतो), पण currentTarget प्रत्येक parent वर बदलतो. delegation मध्ये दोन्ही वेगळे असतात. Summary:
  1. target → who started the event;
  2. currentTarget → who is handling the event;
  3. use target to detect what the user actually clicked;
  4. and currentTarget to refer back to the element your event listener is attached to.

7. Why Do We Use e.preventDefault() in Event Handling?

  1. When you're handling events in JavaScript (especially in forms or links), e.preventDefault() is used to stop the default action that the browser would normally perform.
  2. e.preventDefault() is a method used in JavaScript to prevent the default behaviour of an event. e is the event object, which is automatically passed to the event-listener function.
    1. Forms: by default, submitting a form reloads the page.
    2. Anchor tags (<a>): clicking an anchor tag navigates to a new page.
Why use it?
  1. To handle form data with JavaScript without refreshing the page.
  2. To build Single Page Applications (SPAs), where navigation is handled by React/Vue, etc.
  3. To add custom behaviour to elements (like drag & drop, buttons, etc.).

Note: preventDefault does NOT stop propagation, and stopPropagation does NOT prevent the default action; they are independent (the demo below uses both).

8. What is the Difference between the Bubbling Phase and the Capture Phase?

✔ "bugling phase" → BUBBLING phase."bugling" नाही, bubbling.
FeatureEvent BubblingEvent Capturing
OrderThe event starts from the target element → goes upward to parent, grandparent, document.The event starts from the top (document/root) → goes downward to the target element.
Default BehaviorBubbling is the default in JavaScript.Capturing needs to be explicitly enabled.
When Listener RunsRuns after: child → parent → grandparent.Runs before: parent → child → target.
UseThe most common (default) way to handle events.Rarely used; useful when you want the parent to handle the event before the child.
How to Enableelement.addEventListener("click", handler, false) (or just omit the third param).element.addEventListener("click", handler, true) (third param = true).

<h1>Event Propagation</h1>
<div id="outerDiv">
  <span>Div</span>

<script>

  let button = document.getElementById("myButton");

  div.addEventListener("click", function (e) {
    console.table([{ description: "i am outer div", target: e.target.tagName,
      CurrentTarget: e.currentTarget.tagName, thisName: this.name }]);
  });
  form.addEventListener("click", function (e) {
    console.table([{ description: "i am form", target: e.target.tagName,
      CurrentTarget: e.currentTarget.tagName, thisName: this.name }]);
  });
  button.addEventListener("click", function (e) {

    e.stopPropagation();   // the form and div handlers will NOT run

      CurrentTarget: e.currentTarget.tagName, thisName: this.name }]);
  });

  // click "Form"    → i am form | SPAN | FORM | ""   then   i am outer div | SPAN | DIV | undefined
  // click "Div"     → i am outer div | SPAN | DIV | undefined

  • What happens: one click travels up: button → form → div. stopPropagation on the button stops it there; target is where the click started, currentTarget is where the listener sits.
  • Output: see the per-click outputs.

}, { capture: true });   // in addEventListener, the third parameter is { capture: true } (an object)

10. Event Delegation (with the Bubbling Phase)

Your Notes (eventDelegation/eventDelegation.js):
  1. Event delegation is a JS pattern to handle events efficiently.
  2. Event delegation is a technique in JavaScript where you attach a single event listener to a parent element instead of adding event listeners to individual child elements (so the event is added to the parent element instead of to every element).
  3. The event listener on the parent element can handle events triggered by its child elements, thanks to event bubbling.
  4. Event delegation is a technique in JS where you attach a single event listener to a common ancestor of multiple elements, instead of attaching individual event listeners to each of those elements.
Important:
  1. Event bubbling:
    1. when an event is triggered on an element, it first runs the handlers on that element and then propagates (bubbles) to its parent element;
    2. i.e. if you click a child element, its parent and all other ancestors also receive the event, unless it is stopped.
  2. Single event listener: instead of attaching event listeners to multiple child elements, you can take advantage of event bubbling by placing a single listener on a common parent; when the event bubbles up to the parent, you can determine which child element triggered the event by using event.target.
Advantages of event delegation:
  1. Performance: you avoid attaching multiple event listeners to each child element, reducing memory usage, especially when many child elements are created dynamically.
  2. Dynamic content: it handles events on elements that are added to the DOM dynamically after the initial page load, without needing to reattach event listeners.
  3. This is particularly useful for optimizing performance and managing events on a large number of elements efficiently.
  4. When an event occurs, the listener checks the event.target property to determine which specific element triggered the event (i.e. event delegation means using event propagation (bubbling) to handle an event at a higher level in the DOM than the element on which the event originated).
Which phase handles event delegation?
  1. The bubble phase handles event delegation (usually; a capturing listener on the parent can also delegate).
  2. Event delegation is a concept in JS where, instead of attaching event listeners to individual elements, you attach a single event listener to a common ancestor of those elements.
  3. This is particularly useful when you have a large number of similar elements and want to reduce the number of event listeners.
Figure 141: Event delegation: one listener on the parent handles every (current and future) child through bubbling.
Event delegation म्हणजे प्रत्येक child वर listener न लावता parent वर एकच listener लावणे. child वरचा click bubble होऊन parent पर्यंत येतो, आणि event.target (किंवा closest) ने कोणता child click झाला ते ओळखतो. फायदा: कमी memory, आणि नंतर जोडलेल्या elements साठी सुद्धा आपोआप चालते.

Your explanation (comments after the HTML):
  • We have an unordered list (<ul>) containing list items (<li>).
  • Instead of attaching a separate click event listener to each list item, we attach a single event listener to the <ul> element with the id "item". ✔ the comment says id "myList", but the HTML uses id="item".comment मध्ये "myList" लिहिले आहे, पण HTML मध्ये id="item" आहे.

  • This approach is more efficient and scalable, because you only need one event listener, regardless of how many list items there are.

A more robust delegated handler (works even when the clicked target is a CHILD inside the li, e.g. <li><b>item</b></li>): 
list.addEventListener("click", (e) => {

  if (!li || !list.contains(li)) return;       // the click wasn't on an item of THIS list
  console.log(li.textContent, li.dataset.id);  // use data-* attributes to know what to do
});

  • What happens: closest("li") finds the item even when an inner element was clicked; contains() makes sure it belongs to this list; data-* attributes carry ids; new items work automatically.

12. Extra / Advanced (added for interviews)

1. event.eventPhase: which phase is this listener running in? 
// Event.CAPTURING_PHASE = 1, Event.AT_TARGET = 2, Event.BUBBLING_PHASE = 3 (0 = NONE, not being dispatched)
parent.addEventListener("click", (e) => console.log("capture", e.eventPhase), true);   // → capture 1
child.addEventListener("click",  (e) => console.log("target",  e.eventPhase));         // → target 2
parent.addEventListener("click", (e) => console.log("bubble",  e.eventPhase));         // → bubble 3
// (constants verified in Node: 1 2 3)
  • What happens: e.eventPhase tells the phase: 1 capturing, 2 at target, 3 bubbling.
  • Output: capture 1, target 2, bubble 3.
2. event.composedPath(): the full route of the event 
button.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
  console.log(e.composedPath());   // [button, span, div, form, div#outerDiv, body, html, document, Window]
});
// capturing walks this array from the END to the start; bubbling walks it from the start to the end.
// It is also the only way to see the real inner target inside a Shadow DOM.
  • What happens: composedPath() lists every element the event travels through, from target to window.
  • Output: [button, span, div, form, …, Window].
3. Custom events: create and dispatch your own events 
const evt = new CustomEvent("cart:add", {
  detail: { id: 7, qty: 2 },   // your data travels in e.detail
  bubbles: true,               // ⚠ default is FALSE: without it, ancestors (delegation) won't see it
  cancelable: true,            // allows e.preventDefault()
});
document.addEventListener("cart:add", (e) => console.log("added", e.detail.id));
productButton.dispatchEvent(evt);   // → added 7
// dispatchEvent returns false if any listener called preventDefault() (verified in Node: false)
  • What happens: CustomEvent carries data in detail; bubbles: true is needed for ancestors to hear it; dispatchEvent fires it.
  • Output: added 7.
  • ✅ Components can talk to each other without direct references.
  • ⚠ bubbles defaults to false.
4. event.defaultPrevented: did someone already cancel the default? 
link.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
  if (e.defaultPrevented) return;   // another handler (e.g. a router) already handled it
  // … normal behaviour
});
// verified in Node: after a listener calls preventDefault() on a cancelable event → defaultPrevented === true
  • What happens: defaultPrevented tells you another handler already cancelled the default.
  • Output: (no output).
5. Removing listeners the modern way: once and AbortController 
btn.addEventListener("click", pay, { once: true });   // runs once, then removes itself

const controller = new AbortController();
window.addEventListener("scroll", onScroll, { signal: controller.signal });
window.addEventListener("resize", onResize, { signal: controller.signal });
controller.abort();   // removes BOTH listeners at once (no need to keep function references)
// verified in Node: after abort(), the signal-based listeners no longer run; a once-listener runs only the first time
  • What happens: once removes the listener after the first call; an AbortController signal removes many listeners at once.
  • Output: (no output).
  • ✅ Clean up listeners easily (no stored function references).
6. passive listeners (scroll / touch performance) 
window.addEventListener("touchmove", onMove, { passive: true });
// you promise not to call preventDefault() → the browser can scroll immediately without waiting for your JS
// (calling preventDefault inside a passive listener is ignored, with a console warning)
  • What happens: passive listeners promise not to call preventDefault, so scrolling isn't delayed.
  • Output: (no output).
7. Practical delegation: a dynamic todo list with ONE listener 
<ul id="todos">
  <li data-id="1">Learn JS <button data-action="edit">✏️</button> <button data-action="delete">🗑️</button></li>
</ul>

const list = document.getElementById("todos");
list.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
  const btn = e.target.closest("button[data-action]");   // the clicked action (even if an icon inside it was clicked)
  if (!btn || !list.contains(btn)) return;
  const li = btn.closest("li");
  const id = li.dataset.id;
  if (btn.dataset.action === "delete") li.remove();
  if (btn.dataset.action === "edit") li.firstChild.textContent = prompt("New text", li.firstChild.textContent.trim()) + " ";
});
// new <li> items added later work automatically: no new listeners needed
  • What happens: one listener handles edit and delete buttons for all todos via data-action and closest().
  • Output: items removed/edited on click.
  • ✅ Real-world delegation.
8. Delegation pitfalls
  1. A child calling e.stopPropagation() silently breaks every delegated listener above it (and analytics). Prefer checking e.defaultPrevented or a flag over stopping propagation.
  2. Non-bubbling events can't be delegated in the bubble phase: use focusin/focusout instead of focus/blur, mouseover/mouseout instead of mouseenter/mouseleave (or listen with capture: true).
  3. Always use closest() + contains(): e.target may be a nested icon/span, or an element outside your list (in nested components).
  4. Very frequent events (mousemove, scroll) delegated at the document level run for EVERY move: throttle them (Chapter 80).
Figure 142: Custom events: create with detail, dispatch on an element, and catch them higher up only if bubbles: true.
जास्तीचे मुद्दे: eventPhase (1 = capture, 2 = target, 3 = bubble) सांगतो की listener कोणत्या phase मध्ये चालू आहे. composedPath() event चा पूर्ण मार्ग देतो. CustomEvent ने स्वतःचे events बनवता येतात (detail मध्ये data), पण bubbles: true दिल्याशिवाय parent ला ते दिसत नाहीत. once आणि AbortController ने listeners सहज काढता येतात. passive: true ने scroll वेगवान होतो. delegation मध्ये closest + data-action वापरा, आणि child मध्ये stopPropagation टाळा.

13. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. Explain event bubbling and capturing.
  • A click is dispatched window → … → target (capturing, listeners with capture: true), then at the target, then target → … → window (bubbling, the default). Listeners on the path run in that order.
Q2. e.target vs e.currentTarget?
  • target = where the event originated (it stays fixed); currentTarget = the element whose listener is running (it changes while bubbling). In a normal-function handler, this === currentTarget.
Q3. What is event delegation and its limitations?
  • One listener on an ancestor handles its children via bubbling (fewer listeners, works for dynamic items). Limitations: non-bubbling events (focus → use focusin; mouseenter → use mouseover), and stopPropagation in a child breaks it; use closest() for nested targets.
Q4. stopPropagation vs preventDefault vs return false?
  • stopPropagation stops the event's travel; preventDefault cancels the browser's default action; return false only works for on-property handlers (cancels the default), and does nothing in addEventListener.
Q4a. How do you create and listen to a custom event? Why might the parent not receive it?
  • el.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("name", { detail: data, bubbles: true })), and listen with addEventListener("name", e => e.detail). CustomEvent does NOT bubble by default; without bubbles: true only listeners on el itself run.
Q4b. How do you remove many listeners at once, or a listener after its first run?
  • Pass { signal: controller.signal } to each addEventListener and call controller.abort(); use { once: true } for a one-time listener. removeEventListener needs the exact same function reference and capture flag.
Q4c. How do you know which phase a listener is in, and the full path of the event?
  • e.eventPhase gives 1 (capturing), 2 (at target) or 3 (bubbling); e.composedPath() returns the array of elements from the target up to window.
Q5. Output-based questions
// <div id="a"><button id="b">x</button></div>
a.addEventListener("click", () => log("a-bubble"));
a.addEventListener("click", () => log("a-capture"), true);
b.addEventListener("click", () => log("b"));
// click b → a-capture, b, a-bubble
b.addEventListener("click", (e) => e.stopPropagation());
// click b → a-capture, b   (a-bubble is gone; capture already ran)
a.addEventListener("click", function (e) { log(e.target.id, e.currentTarget.id, this.id); });
// click b → b a a
  • What happens: capture runs before target and bubble; stopPropagation at the target removes later bubble listeners; target/currentTarget/this in a delegated listener.
  • Output: a-capture b a-bubble; a-capture b; b a a.
ConceptRemember
PhasesCapturing ↓ → target → bubbling ↑ (default)
Capture listeneraddEventListener(type, fn, { capture: true })
StopstopPropagation / stopImmediatePropagation
target / currentTarget / thisOrigin / listener element / listener element (normal fn)
DelegationParent listener + e.target.closest(selector)
Non-bubblingfocus/blur, mouseenter/leave → focusin/out, mouseover/out
थोडक्यात: event आधी वरून खाली (capturing), मग target, मग खालून वर (bubbling, default) जातो. target = मूळ element (बदलत नाही), currentTarget = listener असलेला element (bubbling मध्ये बदलतो). delegation = parent वर एक listener + closest(). HTML मध्ये नसलेले id वापरल्यास null.addEventListener चा TypeError येतो.
Chapter 78: Timing EventssetTimeout · clearTimeout · setInterval · clearInterval
CHAPTER 78 INDEX
  1. Timing-Based Events
  2. setTimeout()
  3. clearTimeout()
  4. setInterval()
  5. clearInterval()
  6. setTimeout vs setInterval
  7. Interview Questions & Revision

1. Timing-Based Events

Your Notes (TimeBasedEvent.js):
  1. setTimeout(): the setTimeout function is used to execute a function or block of code after a specified delay in milliseconds.
  2. setInterval(): the setInterval function is used to repeatedly execute a function or block of code at a specified interval in milliseconds.
  3. clearTimeout(): if you want to cancel a scheduled timeout before it occurs, you can use clearTimeout(). The global clearTimeout() method cancels a timeout previously established by calling setTimeout().
  4. clearInterval(): if you want to cancel a scheduled interval, you can use the clearInterval function. The global clearInterval() method cancels an interval previously established by calling setInterval(). ✔ "cancels a timeout previously established by calling setInterval()" → cancels an INTERVAL.clearInterval हा setInterval ने बनवलेला interval थांबवतो (timeout नाही).
The above four methods are connected to each other. The window object allows the execution of code at specified time intervals; these time intervals are called timing events. (They are provided by the browser / Node, not by the JS engine.)
setTimeout = ठराविक वेळेनंतर एकदा चालव. setInterval = ठराविक अंतराने पुन्हा पुन्हा चालव. clearTimeout / clearInterval = ते रद्द कर. हे चारही browser (window) देतो, आणि setTimeout/setInterval एक id परत करतात, जो clear करताना लागतो.

2. setTimeout(function, milliseconds)

Def: executes a function after waiting a specified number of milliseconds. 
function displayName(name) {
  console.log("start");
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log("myName", name);   // intended: → myName vishal shinde (after 3 s)
  }, 3000);
  console.log("end");
}
displayName("vishal shinde");
  • What happens: setTimeout schedules the callback once after 3 s; the function continues immediately.
  • Output: start, end, then myName vishal shinde after 3 s.
✔ (verified in Node) displayName is declared AGAIN below (the clearTimeout version). Function declarations are hoisted and the last one wins for the whole file, so BOTH calls run the clearTimeout version: "myName vishal shinde" is never printed. Name them displayName1 / displayName2. displayName हे नाव दोनदा declare केले आहे. hoisting मुळे दोन्ही calls दुसरे (clearTimeout वाले) version चालवतात, म्हणून "myName ..." कधीच छापले जात नाही. वेगळी नावे द्या.

3. clearTimeout()

Your Notes: it prevents the original setTimeout from running (clearTimeout cancels the timeout). clearTimeout() is a method in JavaScript used to cancel a timeout that was previously established by calling setTimeout(). When you schedule a function to execute after a certain delay using setTimeout(), clearTimeout() can prevent that function from being executed if it's called before the timer expires. 
function displayName(name) {
  console.log("start");
  // Set a timeout to display the name after 3 seconds
  const timeoutId = setTimeout(() => {
    console.log("My name is", name);
  }, 3000);
  console.log("end");
  // Simulate cancelling the timeout after 1 second
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log("Timeout cleared, name will not be displayed");
    clearTimeout(timeoutId);   // Cancels the original timeout
  }, 1000);   // Cancel the timeout before it can trigger
}
displayName("Vishal Shinde");
// → start → end → (1 s) Timeout cleared, name will not be displayed   ("My name is" never prints)
  • What happens: setTimeout returns an id; clearTimeout(id) cancels it before it runs (here after 1 s).
  • Output: start, end, Timeout cleared…
  • ✅ Cancel pending actions (e.g. hide a tooltip timer).

4. setInterval(function, milliseconds)

Your Notes: the same as setTimeout(), but it repeats the execution of the function continuously. setInterval() is a JavaScript function that repeatedly calls a specified function (or executes a code snippet) at a fixed time interval, measured in milliseconds. Unlike setTimeout(), which runs the function once after a delay, setInterval() continues to call the function at regular intervals until it's explicitly stopped using clearInterval(). 
// Function to be executed every 2 seconds
const intervalId = setInterval(() => {
  console.log("This will run every 2 seconds.");
}, 2000);
// Stop the interval after 6 seconds
setTimeout(() => {
  clearInterval(intervalId);   // Stops the repeated function calls
  console.log("Interval cleared.");
}, 6000);
// → prints at 2 s and 4 s, then "Interval cleared." at 6 s (verified: only 2 runs, the 6 s tick is cancelled)
  • What happens: setInterval repeats every 2 s until clearInterval stops it at 6 s.
  • Output: two messages, then Interval cleared.
  • ⚠ Always keep the id and clear intervals, or they run forever.

5. clearInterval()

Your Notes: a JavaScript method used to stop an interval that was previously established using the setInterval() method. When you repeatedly execute a function at a specified time interval with setInterval(), clearInterval() lets you cancel the ongoing execution. The clearInterval() function cancels further execution of the interval, stopping the repeated action. 
// Start an interval that logs a message every second
const intervalId1 = setInterval(() => {
  console.log("This message appears every second.");
}, 1000);
// After 5 seconds, stop the interval
setTimeout(() => {
  clearInterval(intervalId1);   // Cancels the interval
  console.log("Interval cleared.");
}, 5000);
// → 4 messages (1, 2, 3, 4 s) then "Interval cleared." (verified in Node)
  • What happens: every second for 5 s, then cleared.
  • Output: 4 messages, then Interval cleared.
Full verified output of the file: 
start → end → start → end
→ (1 s) Timeout cleared… ×2 (both calls use the 2nd displayName)
→ This message appears every second. (1 s) → This will run every 2 seconds. (2 s) → …every second (2 s, 3 s)
→ …every 2 seconds (4 s) → …every second (4 s) → Interval cleared. (5 s) → Interval cleared. (6 s)
  • What happens: combined output when all examples run in one file (the second displayName replaces the first).
  • Output: (timeline).
Figure 143: setTimeout runs once after the delay; setInterval repeats until clearInterval.

6. What is the Difference between setTimeout() and setInterval()?

setTimeout():
  1. Executes a function once after a specified delay (executes once after the delay).
  2. Usage: when you want to run code after a certain delay, but only once.
  3. The function provided will execute once after the delay specified in milliseconds.
  4. Clears automatically after execution.
  5. Returns a timeout ID.
  6. For the delayed execution of code, one time.
  7. The setTimeout method in JavaScript is used to call a function after a certain delay. ✔ "used to call a function for a certain period of time" → AFTER a certain delay (it runs once; it doesn't keep running "for" a period).setTimeout function ला ठराविक वेळ "चालवत" नाही, तर ठराविक वेळ "नंतर" एकदा चालवतो.
  8. setTimeout() is cancelled by the clearTimeout() method.
setInterval():
  1. Executes a function repeatedly at a specified interval (executes repeatedly at the interval).
  2. Usage: when you want to run code at regular intervals, such as updating the UI or making repeated network requests.
  3. The function will keep executing every 2 seconds (or the specified interval) until it is manually stopped using clearInterval().
  4. It needs to be manually cleared with clearInterval().
  5. Returns an interval ID.
  6. For the repeated execution of code at fixed intervals.
  7. The setInterval() method in JavaScript is used to call a function repeatedly at specified intervals of time.
  8. The setInterval() method is cancelled by the clearInterval() method.
  1. Use setTimeout() when you need to delay a task a single time.
  2. Use setInterval() when you need to repeatedly execute a task at regular intervals.
setTimeoutsetInterval
RunsOnce, after the delayEvery N ms, until cleared
CancelclearTimeout(id)clearInterval(id)
UseDelay, debounceClocks, polling
Delay guaranteeMinimum only: runs when the call stack is free (event loop)
Extra Details 
// recursive setTimeout = a safer interval (the next run is scheduled only after the previous one finishes)
function tick() { console.log("tick"); timer = setTimeout(tick, 1000); }
let timer = setTimeout(tick, 1000);
// passing arguments: setTimeout(fn, 1000, "a", "b") → fn("a", "b")
// delay 0 still waits for the current code + microtasks (Chapter 62)
// a debounce built with setTimeout/clearTimeout:
function debounce(fn, ms) { let id; return (...a) => { clearTimeout(id); id = setTimeout(() => fn(...a), ms); }; }
  • What happens: a recursive setTimeout schedules the next run after the current one finishes (no overlapping); extra setTimeout arguments go to the callback; debounce uses clearTimeout + setTimeout.
  • Output: tick every second.
  • ✅ Safer than setInterval for slow tasks.

7. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. setTimeout vs setInterval?
  • Once vs repeatedly. Both return an id; cancel with clearTimeout/clearInterval. The delay is a minimum, not exact.
Q2. Why might setInterval drift or pile up, and what is the alternative?
  • If the callback is slow or the tab is busy, ticks get delayed and intervals become irregular. A recursive setTimeout schedules the next run only after the current one finishes.
Q3. What does setTimeout(fn, 0) do?
  • It queues fn as a macrotask: it runs after the current synchronous code and all pending microtasks (promise callbacks).
Q4. Implement debounce with setTimeout.
  • Keep an id in a closure; on each call do clearTimeout(id) then id = setTimeout(fn, ms). Only the last call within ms runs (used for search boxes and resize).
Q5. Output-based questions
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);   // → 3 3 3
for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) setTimeout(() => console.log(j), 0);   // → 0 1 2
const id = setTimeout(() => console.log("x"), 0); clearTimeout(id);  // → (nothing)
setTimeout(() => console.log("T"), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("P"));   // → P T
  • What happens: var shares one i (3 3 3), let doesn't (0 1 2); a cleared timer never runs; promise microtasks run before timers.
  • Output: 3 3 3, 0 1 2, (nothing), P T.
FunctionRemember
setTimeout(fn, ms, ...args)Once, after ms; returns an id
clearTimeout(id)Cancel a pending timeout
setInterval(fn, ms)Repeat every ms; returns an id
clearInterval(id)Stop the repeating
थोडक्यात: setTimeout एकदा, setInterval वारंवार; दोन्ही id देतात आणि clear ने थांबतात. delay हा किमान वेळ आहे, अचूक नाही. var/let loop चा प्रश्न आणि debounce interview मध्ये नक्की विचारतात. एकाच नावाचे functions दोनदा declare करू नका.

1. Debouncing

Your Notes (27_debouncing/debounCing.js):
  1. Debouncing is a programming technique used to limit the frequency of function calls, particularly in situations where a function is being called repeatedly in a short period of time: the function only runs after the user stops doing something for X ms.
  2. Debouncing ensures that a function is only called after a certain amount of time has passed since the last call.
  3. If multiple calls are made within the specified time period, the function will be called once, after the time period has expired.
  4. Debouncing is useful when you want to delay the execution of a function until the user has stopped interacting with the application.
  5. So it is like a timeout mechanism that ensures a function is only called after a certain amount of time has passed since the last call (or prevents expensive function calls).
  6. Debouncing in JavaScript is a programming pattern used to limit the rate at which a function gets executed.
  7. It delays the execution of a function until after a certain period of inactivity.
  8. It ensures that a function is not called too frequently, especially in response to rapidly occurring events such as window resizing, scrolling or key presses.
  9. Debouncing is a way to optimize (the performance of) event handling in JavaScript.
  10. This way, the function only executes after the events have stopped firing for the specified delay period.
Definition: A debounced function postpones its execution until delay ms have passed WITHOUT another call. Every new call cancels the pending timer (clearTimeout) and starts a fresh one (setTimeout); only the LAST call of a burst runs. It is built from a closure (to keep timerId) plus setTimeout/clearTimeout (Chapter 78).
Debouncing म्हणजे: user थांबल्यानंतरच काम करा. प्रत्येक नवीन event जुना timer रद्द करून नवीन timer सुरू करतो. जोपर्यंत events येत आहेत तोपर्यंत function चालत नाही; शेवटच्या event नंतर ठराविक वेळ शांतता राहिली की function एकदाच चालतो.

2. Useful Scenarios & Benefits

Debouncing useful scenarios:
  1. Search input field: when a user types in a search field, you might want to delay the search query until they have stopped typing.
  2. Button click: debouncing can prevent multiple button clicks from triggering multiple function calls.
  3. Window resizing: debouncing can limit the frequency of resize event handlers.
By debouncing a function you can:
  1. Reduce the server load: reduce the number of unnecessary function calls or server requests, which can reduce the server load and improve scalability. ✔ "salability" → scalability."salability" नाही, "scalability" (जास्त users/load हाताळण्याची क्षमता).
  2. Improve performance: by minimizing the load on your system.
  3. Enhance the user experience: by preventing expensive and repetitive actions.
  4. Performance optimization: it reduces the number of function calls, which is especially useful for expensive operations like API requests or complex DOM manipulations.
  5. Prevent overloading: helps avoid overwhelming the system with too many rapid-fire function executions.

3. How Debouncing Works

  1. First event → the timer starts.
  2. If another event happens before the timer ends, the timer resets.
  3. The function executes only if no new event occurs during the delay.
Figure 144: Debouncing: every event resets the timer; the function fires once, after the burst stops.

4. Example: Search Input Field

Your Notes: suppose we have an input field that triggers a search query on every keystroke. Without debouncing, the search query would be triggered on every keystroke, leading to expensive server requests, slow performance and a poor user experience.
With debouncing, you can delay the search query until the user has stopped typing for a certain amount of time, e.g. 500 ms. This ensures that the search query is only triggered when the user has finished typing.
Use it when you care about the final action, not every step; when expensive operations (like API calls) should run only once.

5. There Are 2 Ways to Implement Debouncing in JS

  1. The lodash library: _.debounce(fn, 500) (with options like leading/trailing/maxWait).
  2. A custom ("polyfill") implementation: write your own debounce with a closure + setTimeout/clearTimeout (below).
✔ Note: strictly, a "polyfill" re-creates a STANDARD built-in that a browser is missing; debounce is not a built-in, so it's a custom utility implementation. Interviews still say "debounce polyfill".polyfill म्हणजे browser मध्ये नसलेल्या standard feature ची स्वतः लिहिलेली आवृत्ती. debounce हा built-in नाही, म्हणून त्याला custom implementation म्हणणे जास्त बरोबर; पण interview मध्ये "polyfill" असेच म्हणतात.

6. Demo 1: Search Input (index.html)

<h1>debouncing</h1>
<label for="input"> enter username </label>
<input type="text" id="input" placeholder="enter name" />
<script>
  let inputValue = document.getElementById("input");

  function getInputValue(event) {
    console.log("input:", event.target.value);
  }

  // Debouncing function: takes a callback function and a delay time in milliseconds
  function debouncingFunction(fun, delay) {
    // Declare a timer variable to track the ongoing timeout
    let timerId;

    // Return a new function that will be executed on every event trigger
    // The rest parameter captures any arguments passed to the original callback
    return function (...args) {
      // If a timer is already running, clear it (reset the clock)
      // This prevents the callback from running if events keep firing
      clearTimeout(timerId);

      // Set a new timeout to execute the callback after the specified delay
      // If no new events come in during the delay, the function will be executed
      timerId = setTimeout(() => {
        fun(...args);   // Call the original function with the latest arguments
      }, delay);
    };
  }

  const newFun = debouncingFunction(getInputValue, 1000);
  inputValue.addEventListener("input", newFun);
  // typing "vishal" quickly → ONE log: input: vishal (1 s after the last key)
</script>
  • What happens: every keystroke clears the previous timer and starts a new 1 s timer, so the function runs only once, 1 s after the user STOPS typing.
  • Output: input: vishal (once).
  • ✅ Search-as-you-type without sending a request per key.
  • ⚠ Adds a delay before the first result.
✔ the comment says "The spread operator captures any arguments"; in function (...args) the ... is the REST parameter (it collects). The spread is in fun(...args) (it expands). See Chapters 11–12.function (...args) मधला ... हा rest (गोळा करणारा) आहे; fun(...args) मधला ... हा spread (पसरवणारा) आहे. Improvement: keep this as well: timerId = setTimeout(() => fun.apply(this, args), delay). Otherwise a method that uses this loses it.

7. Demo 2: Button Click (btttonClickDebouncing.html)

<title>Debounce Polyfill Example</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: Arial, sans-serif; margin: 40px; }
  .counter { margin-top: 20px; }
  button { padding: 10px 20px; font-size: 16px; }
  .count-box { margin: 10px 0; font-size: 18px; }
</style>

<h2>Debounce Polyfill Example</h2>
<button class="increment_button">Click Me</button>
<div class="counter">
  <div class="count-box">Total Button Clicks: <span class="pressed_button">0</span></div>
  <div class="count-box">Debounced Trigger Count: <span class="increment_count">0</span></div>
</div>

<script>
  //! Polyfill of Debouncing
  const button = document.querySelector(".increment_button");
  const pressButton = document.querySelector(".pressed_button");
  const trigged = document.querySelector(".increment_count");

  let button_count = 0;
  let triggered_count = 0;

  // Debounce polyfill
  const my_debounce = (callback, timeDelay) => {
    let timer;
    return function (...args) {
      if (timer) clearTimeout(timer);
      timer = setTimeout(() => {
        callback(...args);
      }, timeDelay);
    };
  };

  const debounce = my_debounce(() => {
    trigged.innerHTML = ++triggered_count;
  }, 800);

  button.addEventListener("click", () => {
    pressButton.innerHTML = ++button_count;   // counts EVERY click
    debounce();                               // counts once per burst
  });
  // click 10 times fast → Total Button Clicks: 10, Debounced Trigger Count: 1
</script>
  • What happens: each click counts immediately, but the debounced counter increases only once per burst of fast clicks.
  • Output: Total 10, Debounced 1 (for 10 fast clicks).
  • ✅ Prevents double-submits / repeated saves.
(File name typo "btttonClickDebouncing" → buttonClickDebouncing. For numbers, textContent is safer than innerHTML.)

8. Demo 3: Window Resize (window_resize.html)

<title>Window Resize Without Throttling</title>
<h3>Window Resizing Without Throttling</h3>
<p id="windowResize">Window size will appear here.</p>
<script>
  const windowSize = document.getElementById("windowResize");

  function handleResize() {
    windowSize.textContent = `Width: ${window.innerWidth}, Height: ${window.innerHeight}`;
    console.log("Resized to:", window.innerWidth, window.innerHeight);
  }

  // Debouncing function: takes a callback function and a delay time in milliseconds
  function debouncingFunction(fun, delay) {
    // Declare a timer variable to track the ongoing timeout
    let timerId;
    // Return a new function that will be executed on every event trigger
    // The rest parameter captures any arguments passed to the original callback
    return function (...args) {
      // If a timer is already running, clear it (reset the clock)
      // This prevents the callback from running if events keep firing
      clearTimeout(timerId);
      // Set a new timeout to execute the callback after the specified delay
      // If no new events come in during the delay, the function will be executed
      timerId = setTimeout(() => {
        fun(...args);   // Call the original function with the latest arguments
      }, delay);
    };
  }

  let newFun = debouncingFunction(handleResize, 400);

  // ❗ Listening directly to resize events (no throttling)
  window.addEventListener("resize", newFun);
</script>
  • What happens: debounced resize handler: runs 400 ms after the user stops resizing.
  • Output: one log after resizing ends.
  • ✅ Expensive layout work only once.
✔ the title/heading/comment say "Without Throttling", but this page DOES use debouncing (newFun): the size updates once, 400 ms after you stop resizing. A better title: "Window Resize with Debouncing".title मध्ये "Without Throttling" लिहिले आहे, पण इथे debouncing वापरले आहे. resize थांबवल्यानंतर 400 ms ने size एकदाच दिसते.

9. Differences between Debouncing and Throttling in JS

Your Notes: throttling and debouncing are both techniques used to limit function calls, but they have different purposes.

1. Debouncing

  1. Ensures the function is called only after a certain amount of time has passed since the last call.
  2. When to use: when you want to delay a function call until a certain amount of time has passed since the last call; also when you want to prevent expensive function calls in situations like a search input field or a button click.
  3. You want to delay the function execution until the user has stopped interacting.
  4. Timing: debouncing waits for a certain amount of time to pass before calling the function.
  5. Frequency: debouncing limits the frequency of function calls by delaying execution.
  6. Useful for delaying a function call until the user has stopped interacting.
  7. It waits for a certain (quiet) time before invoking the function.
The purpose of debouncing is to delay the execution of a function until there is a pause in event occurrences for the specified period. It ensures that the function is only executed once after a series of rapid events.

2. Throttling

  1. Ensures a function is called at most once per fixed interval, regardless of how many times you call it.
  2. When to use: when you want to limit the frequency of function calls in a real application, to prevent overload (e.g. on the server), like scroll events and real-time updates.
  3. You want to ensure that a function is called at a fixed rate.
  4. Timing: throttling calls the function at a fixed rate.
  5. Frequency: throttling limits the frequency by spacing out the calls at a fixed interval of time.
  6. Useful for limiting the frequency of function calls in real-time applications.
  7. Throttling can be implemented by allowing the function to execute at a fixed interval or rate.
// verified simulation in Node: 20 calls, one every 20 ms (400 ms total)
debounce(fn, 100) → runs ONCE per burst, after it ends     (calls 1, 2, 3 within 100 ms → only 3 runs)
throttle(fn, 100) → runs at most every 100 ms              → runs for calls 0, 4, 8, 12, 16

function throttle(fn, delay) {
  let last = 0;
  return function (...args) {
    const now = Date.now();
    if (now - last >= delay) { last = now; fn.apply(this, args); }
  };
}
  • What happens: debounce waits for a pause and runs once; throttle runs at a steady maximum rate during the burst.
  • Output: debounce: only the last call; throttle: calls 0, 4, 8, 12, 16.
  • ✅ Debounce for "final value" (search); throttle for continuous updates (scroll).
FeatureDebouncingThrottling
RunsOnce, after the events stopRegularly, at most once per interval
TimerReset on every eventNot reset; a fixed window
Best forSearch box, validation, resize end, double-submitScroll, mousemove, game loops, progress, infinite scroll
During continuous eventsNever runs until they stopKeeps running at a steady rate
Debouncing: events थांबल्यानंतर एकदाच चालवा (search box). Throttling: events चालू असतानाही ठराविक अंतराने (उदा. दर 100 ms) एकदा चालवा (scroll). debounce मध्ये timer प्रत्येक event ला reset होतो, throttle मध्ये होत नाही.

10. Debouncing Summary Card

Definition: debouncing ensures that a function is called only once, after a specified delay has passed since the last event.
✔️ Use when: you want the function to run after the user stops performing an action; you care about the final state of a sequence of rapid events.
📌 Example scenarios: search input: trigger the API call after the user stops typing; form field validation: validate after typing stops; resize or scroll: adjust the layout after the action stops.
⏱️ Behavior: waits for a pause in event calls; delays execution until no new event occurs within the delay; cancels and resets the timer with every new event.
FeatureDebouncing
Execution FrequencyOnce, after the delay
Trigger ConditionAfter inactivity
Best ForInput fields, delayed validation
ExampleAutocomplete after typing ends
Immediate ExecutionNo (usually after the delay); a "leading" debounce can fire on the first event
In short:
  1. Use debouncing when you want to delay a function until the user stops performing an action (e.g. typing in a search box).
  2. Use throttling when you want to limit how often a function runs over time (e.g. handling scroll events every 100 ms).
Extra: a complete interview-ready debounce (this, leading option, cancel) 
function debounce(fn, delay, { leading = false } = {}) {
  let timerId;
  function debounced(...args) {
    const callNow = leading && !timerId;
    clearTimeout(timerId);
    timerId = setTimeout(() => {
      timerId = null;
      if (!leading) fn.apply(this, args);
    }, delay);
    if (callNow) fn.apply(this, args);   // leading edge: run immediately on the first event
  }
  debounced.cancel = () => { clearTimeout(timerId); timerId = null; };
  return debounced;
}
  • What happens: an advanced debounce: optional leading edge (run on the first event) and a cancel() method.
  • Output: (function).
  • ✅ Mirrors lodash's debounce options.

11. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. Implement debounce. Which JS concepts does it use?
  • A closure (timerId survives between calls), a higher-order function (takes fn, returns a new function), setTimeout/clearTimeout, rest/spread for the args, and apply to keep this.
Q2. Debounce vs throttle with a real example?
  • Debounce the search-suggestion API call (fire once after typing stops). Throttle the scroll handler for infinite scroll / a sticky header (fire every 200 ms while scrolling).
Q3. What is leading vs trailing debounce?
  • Trailing (the default) runs after the quiet period with the last args. Leading runs on the FIRST event and then ignores the rest until quiet: good for preventing a double form submit.
Q4. Why must the debounced function be created once, outside the handler?
  • The timer lives in its closure. Calling debounce(fn) inside the event handler creates a NEW closure each time, so nothing gets cancelled and every event still fires.
Q5. Output-based questions
const log = debounce((x) => console.log(x), 100);
log(1); log(2); log(3);                   // → 3 (once, 100 ms later)
setTimeout(() => log(4), 300);            // → 4 (a new burst)
// ❌ wrong usage:
input.addEventListener("input", (e) => debounce(search, 300)(e));   // fires for EVERY key (a new timer each time)
  • What happens: three quick calls → one call with the last value; a later call starts a new burst. Creating a new debounced function inside the listener breaks it.
  • Output: 3, then 4.
  • ⚠ Create the debounced function ONCE, outside the listener.
PointRemember
IdeaRun after X ms of silence
CoreclearTimeout(id); id = setTimeout(fn, delay)
UsesSearch, validation, resize, button spam
vs ThrottleDebounce = once at the end; throttle = steady rate
थोडक्यात: debounce = शांततेनंतर एकदाच चालवा. closure + clearTimeout + setTimeout ने बनतो. search box आणि button spam साठी वापरतात. throttle = ठराविक वेगाने चालवा (scroll). debounced function एकदाच बनवा, handler च्या आत नाही.

Chapter 80: ThrottlingWhat & why · how it works · scroll demo · 3 implementations · debounce vs throttle
CHAPTER 80 INDEX
  1. What is Throttling?
  2. How Throttle Works
  3. Benefits & Examples
  4. Debouncing vs Throttling (full table)
  5. Throttling Summary Card
  6. Scroll Demo (index.html)
  7. Implementation 2: Flag + setTimeout
  8. Implementation 3: myThrottle (walk-through)
  9. Interview Questions & Revision

1. Throttling in JS

Your Notes (28_throttling/throttling.js):
  1. Throttling is a technique in JS to limit the frequency of function calls, particularly in situations where a function is being called repeatedly in a short period of time.
  2. Throttling is a technique that ensures a function is called at most at a fixed rate, regardless of how many times it is called.
  3. It is like a rate limiter that prevents a function from being called too frequently.
  4. Throttling is useful when you want to limit the frequency of function calls but still want to allow the function to be called repeatedly.
  5. Throttling limits the frequency of a function but allows it to be called repeatedly at a specified interval.
  6. Throttling in JavaScript is an effective technique to limit the frequency at which a function is executed, to improve or maintain the performance of the application (or optimize the function's execution performance).
  7. By using throttling in JavaScript, the function is executed at most once per fixed interval of time (i.e. it limits the rate or frequency at which a function can be executed).
  8. Throttling blocks (drops) further calls for a certain time after a call. ✔ "Throttling delay the next() function call". A basic throttle doesn't DELAY or queue the extra calls; it IGNORES them until the interval is over (only lodash's trailing option runs one last call later).throttle मधले जास्तीचे calls उशिरा चालत नाहीत, ते सरळ दुर्लक्षित (drop) होतात. interval संपल्यानंतरचा पुढचा call च चालतो.
  9. Throttling is used to call a function at most once per particular fixed interval of time; only the first click executes immediately (in the leading/timestamp version). Throttling improves the user experience in situations where rapid changes may cause unwanted flickering and jittering.
  10. Throttling in JavaScript is a technique used to control how often a function is executed over time.
  11. Unlike debouncing, which delays the execution of a function until after a specific period of inactivity, throttling ensures that the function is called at regular intervals, regardless of how often the event is fired.
Definition: A throttled function runs at most once per delay ms. The first call runs (and opens a "closed window"); calls inside the window are ignored; after the window ends, the next call runs again. Unlike debounce, the timer is NOT reset by new events, so the function keeps running steadily during a continuous event.
Throttling म्हणजे function ला ठराविक वेगाने चालू देणे: उदा. दर 200 ms मध्ये जास्तीत जास्त एकदा. मधल्या वेळेतील calls दुर्लक्षित होतात. debounce events थांबण्याची वाट पाहतो, तर throttle events चालू असतानाही नियमितपणे चालतो (scroll साठी योग्य).

2. How Throttle Works

  1. Initial call: the function is called and the timer is started.
  2. Subsequent calls: if the function is called again before the timer expires, that call is ignored.
  3. Timer expires: when the timer expires, the function is allowed to be called again.
Figure 145: Throttling: the function runs at the start of each window; events inside a window are dropped.

3. Benefits & Examples of Throttling

Benefits of throttling:
  1. Improved performance: throttling can improve performance by reducing the number of function calls.
  2. Prevent overload: throttling can prevent overloading a server or API by limiting the frequency of requests.
  3. Enhanced user experience: throttling can enhance the user experience by preventing expensive or repetitive actions.
Examples of throttling:
  1. Scroll events: throttling can be used to limit the frequency of scroll event handlers.
  2. Real-time updates: throttling can be used to limit the frequency of updates in real-time applications, such as live updates or gaming.
Explanation: suppose you have a scroll event handler that makes an API call to fetch data. Without throttling, the API call would be made on every scroll event, leading to expensive API calls, slow performance, a poor user experience and increased server load. With throttling, you can limit the frequency of API calls to, say, every 200 ms; this ensures the API calls are only made at a fixed rate, even if the user scrolls frequently.

4. Debouncing vs Throttling

Feature / AspectDebouncingThrottling
DefinitionDelays execution until a period of inactivity has passedLimits execution to once every specified interval
Execution TimingExecutes after the user stops triggering the eventExecutes at regular intervals, even if the event continues
Execution FrequencyOnce after the final eventPeriodically, at most once per interval
Ideal Use CaseWhen you care about the final state after user inputWhen you care about intermediate updates during continuous activity
Typical ScenariosSearch box, form validation, window resize (after the resize ends)Scroll tracking, drag and drop, analytics logging
Delay Reset on Event✅ Yes: resets the timer on every event❌ No: runs at fixed intervals regardless
Immediate Execution❌ No: waits until inactivity (unless a "leading" debounce)✅ Optional: can execute immediately or wait for the interval
Function Call RateMinimized: only one call per pauseControlled: one call per interval
PreventsUnnecessary repeated execution during inputSystem overload by limiting function frequency
Timer UseWaits for no events during the delay to executeExecutes at most every X ms, ignoring events in between
FocusAccuracy after the user stops interactingSmooth performance during user interaction
Implementation ComplexitySlightly more involved (reset-timer logic)Simple: a timestamp check or a flag + setTimeout
✔ "Simpler to implement with a set interval". Throttle is NOT built with setInterval (that would run even with no events); it's built with a timestamp comparison or a flag reset by setTimeout (§6–8).throttle setInterval ने बनवत नाहीत (कारण तो events नसतानाही चालेल). timestamp ची तुलना किंवा flag + setTimeout वापरतात.

5. Throttling Summary Card

Definition: throttling ensures that a function is executed at most once every specified interval, regardless of how many times the event is triggered.
✔️ Use when: you want the function to run continuously, but at controlled intervals; you care about the intermediate states of a continuous event.
📌 Example scenarios: scroll handling: load content on scroll but limit the frequency; slider drag: update the position at intervals while dragging; analytics: track scroll or mouse movement at regular intervals.
⏱️ Behavior: allows execution once per fixed time interval; ignores additional calls within the interval.
FeatureThrottling
Execution FrequencyPeriodic (every X ms)
Trigger ConditionAt fixed intervals
Best ForContinuous actions (scroll, drag)
ExampleInfinite scroll, drag updates
Immediate ExecutionYes (can be configured)
In short:
  1. Use debouncing when you want to delay a function until the user stops performing an action (e.g. typing in a search box).
  2. Use throttling when you want to limit how often a function runs over time (e.g. handling scroll events every 100 ms).

6. Scroll Demo (index.html): Implementation 1, Timestamp

<style>
  section { /* make the page scrollable */ height: 3000px; background-color: aqua; padding: 20px; }
  .counter { position: fixed; top: 10px; right: 30px; }
</style>

<h2>Throttling in js</h2>
<h1>scroll Event throttling</h1>
<div class="counter">
  <p id="normalCount">Normal Count: 0</p>
  <p id="throttleCount">Throttle Count: 0</p>
</div>
<section>
  <p>scroll done see counter are increment</p>
  <script>
    let n_count = document.getElementById("normalCount");
    let T_count = document.getElementById("throttleCount");
    let normalCount = 0;
    let throttleCount = 0;

    function handleNormalCount() {
      normalCount++;
      n_count.textContent = `normal count ${normalCount}`;
    }
    function handleThrottleCount() {
      throttleCount++;
      T_count.textContent = throttleCount;   // (tip: `Throttle Count: ${throttleCount}` to keep the label)
    }

    // throttleFunction takes a function `fun` and a delay in milliseconds
    const throttleFunction = (fun, delay) => {
      // Initialize the timestamp of the last time the function was called
      let lastCall = 0;
      // Return a new function that will act as the throttled version
      return function (...args) {
        // Get the current time in milliseconds
        let now = new Date().getTime();
        // Check if the time elapsed since the last call is less than the specified delay
        // If true, exit the function early (do not execute the original function)
        if (now - lastCall < delay) return;
        // Update the lastCall timestamp to the current time
        lastCall = now;
        // Call the original function `fun` with all the provided arguments
        fun(...args);
      };
    };

    const throttledHandler = throttleFunction(handleThrottleCount, 200);
    window.addEventListener("scroll", handleNormalCount);   // runs on EVERY scroll event
    window.addEventListener("scroll", throttledHandler);    // at most once per 200 ms
    // scroll for ~2 s → normal count ≈ 100+, throttle count ≈ 10
  </script>
</section>
  • What happens: the normal handler runs on every scroll event; the throttled one runs at most once every 200 ms by comparing timestamps.
  • Output: normal ≈ 100+, throttle ≈ 10 after 2 s of scrolling.
  • ✅ Smooth scroll handlers (infinite scroll, sticky headers).
  • ⚠ This version can miss the very last event.

7. Implementation 2: Flag + setTimeout ("also use this approach")

// throttleFunction is a higher-order function that creates a throttled version of the given function
// const throttleFunction = (fun, delay) => {
//   // Flag to control whether the function can be called
//   // Initially true, so the function can run the first time
//   let canCall = true;
//   // Return a new function that will be used as the throttled version
//   return function (...args) {
//     // If canCall is false, we're still within the throttle delay period,
//     // so we simply return and skip the function call
//     if (!canCall) return;
//     // If allowed, execute the original function with all the arguments
//     fun(...args);
//     // Immediately set canCall to false to block further calls
//     canCall = false;
//     // After the specified delay, allow function calls again by resetting canCall to true
//     setTimeout(() => {
//       canCall = true;
//     }, delay);
//   };
// };
// verified in Node: 25 calls every 40 ms with delay 200 → both versions run calls 0, 5, 10, 15, 20
  • What happens: the flag version: run, then block calls for delay ms with a timer.
  • Output: same calls run as the timestamp version (0, 5, 10, 15, 20).

8. Implementation 3: myThrottle (with your walk-through)

// const myThrottle = (callback, delay) => {
//   let lastExecutionTime = 0;   // Store the last execution time
//   // Return a new function that will be triggered on events (like scroll, resize, etc.)
//   return (...args) => {
//     // Get the current time in milliseconds
//     const currentTime = Date.now();
//     // Check if enough time has passed since the last function execution
//     if (currentTime - lastExecutionTime >= delay) {
//       // If enough time has passed, update the last execution time to the current time
//       lastExecutionTime = currentTime;
//       // Execute the callback function with the provided arguments
//       callback(...args);
//     }
//   };
// };
  • What happens: another timestamp version written as an arrow.
  • Output: (commented code).
Your explanation:
  • initially lastExecutionTime is zero. The 2nd event happens at 200 ms
  • it checks 200 − 0 = 200, which is less than the delay, so it returns. The next event happens at 700 ms
  • 700 − 0 = 700 is still less than the delay, so it returns again. The next event happens at 900 ms
  • 900 − 0 is greater than the delay, so the current time is assigned to lastExecutionTime and the callback executes. Then the next event happens at 1200 ms
  • 1200 − 900 = 300 is again less than the delay, so it returns. I.e. if an event happens at least "delay" ms after the last execution, it executes the callback and stores the current time as the last execution time
  • this cycle continues (and makes the API call).
✔ (1) "900 − 1200 return 300" → 1200 − 900 = 300. (2) This walk-through assumes a delay of about 800 ms (200 and 700 are blocked, 900 runs). (3) With real Date.now() values (≈ 1.7 trillion ms), currentTime − 0 is huge, so the VERY FIRST event always runs immediately; the "time starts at 0" picture is only a simplification. 1200 − 900 = 300 असे वजाबाकी करायची. ही walk-through सुमारे 800 ms delay गृहीत धरते. आणि खऱ्या Date.now() मुळे पहिलाच event नेहमी लगेच चालतो, कारण lastExecutionTime = 0 आणि आताचा वेळ खूप मोठा असतो.
Extra: a throttle that keeps this and runs the last call (trailing) 
function throttle(fn, delay) {
  let last = 0, timer = null;
  return function (...args) {
    const now = Date.now(), remaining = delay - (now - last);
    if (remaining <= 0) {                    // leading: run now
      clearTimeout(timer); timer = null;
      last = now; fn.apply(this, args);
    } else if (!timer) {                     // trailing: make sure the LAST event is not lost
      timer = setTimeout(() => { last = Date.now(); timer = null; fn.apply(this, args); }, remaining);
    }
  };
}
// alternative for visual updates: requestAnimationFrame-based throttling (≈ once per frame)
  • What happens: leading + trailing throttle: runs immediately, and also schedules one final run so the LAST event isn't lost.
  • Output: (function).
  • ✅ Use requestAnimationFrame for visual updates (once per frame).

9. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. Implement throttle (two ways).
  • Timestamp: run if Date.now() − last ≥ delay, then update last. Flag: if canCall, run, set canCall = false, and setTimeout(() => canCall = true, delay). Both use a closure.
Q2. Throttle vs debounce: which for scroll, search and resize?
  • Scroll/mousemove/drag → throttle (steady updates). Search box/validation → debounce (after typing stops). Resize → debounce if you need only the final size, throttle for live layout.
Q3. What are leading and trailing calls in throttling?
  • Leading = run on the first event immediately; trailing = also run once at the end of the window with the latest args, so the final position isn't lost. lodash _.throttle does both by default.
Q4. Why not use setInterval for throttling?
  • setInterval runs whether or not events happen and needs manual cleanup. Throttling should react to events, only limiting their rate.
Q5. Output-based questions
const t = throttle((x) => console.log(x), 1000);   // timestamp version (no trailing)
t(1); t(2); t(3);                // → 1   (2 and 3 are inside the 1 s window → ignored)
setTimeout(() => t(4), 1100);    // → 4   (a new window)
// debounce with the same calls would print only 3, then 4
  • What happens: timestamp throttle: the first call runs, calls inside the 1 s window are ignored, a call after the window runs again.
  • Output: 1, then 4.
  • ✅ Compare: debounce would print 3, then 4.
PointRemember
IdeaAt most once per X ms
Coreif (now - last >= delay) { last = now; fn() }
UsesScroll, drag, mousemove, analytics, games
vs DebounceThrottle = steady during activity; debounce = once after it stops
थोडक्यात: throttle = ठराविक वेळेत जास्तीत जास्त एकदा. timestamp किंवा flag + setTimeout ने बनतो (setInterval ने नाही). scroll, drag साठी वापरतात. मधले calls drop होतात; शेवटचा call हवा असल्यास trailing version वापरा.

Chapter 81: Web Workers & requestAnimationFramemain thread blocking · Web Workers · postMessage · onmessage · terminate · what workers can't do · requestAnimationFrame vs setTimeout · cancelAnimationFrame
CHAPTER 81 INDEX
  1. The problem: blocking the main thread
  2. Web Workers
  3. requestAnimationFrame
  4. Interview Questions & Revision

1. The problem: blocking the main thread

Definition: In the browser, JavaScript, rendering (layout, paint) and user input all share the main thread. A long synchronous task (a big loop, heavy parsing) blocks it, so the page freezes: clicks don't respond and animations stutter. A Web Worker runs JavaScript on a separate background thread; requestAnimationFrame schedules visual updates in sync with the screen's refresh.
Example 1: a blocking loop
button.onclick = () => {
  let sum = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < 3e9; i++) sum += i;   // several seconds of CPU work
  result.textContent = sum;                  // page frozen until this line
};
What happens: the loop never yields to the event loop, so no rendering or other events can happen until it ends.
⚠ Async/await or promises DON'T fix this: the CPU work still runs on the same thread. Move it to a Worker (or split it into chunks).

2. Web Workers

Example 2: main.js: create a worker and talk to it
// main.js
const worker = new Worker("worker.js");
worker.postMessage(3e9);                       // send data to the worker
worker.onmessage = (e) => {                    // receive the result
  result.textContent = e.data;
  worker.terminate();                          // free the thread when done
};
worker.onerror = (e) => console.error("worker failed:", e.message);
What happens: new Worker starts worker.js on another thread. Communication happens only through messages: postMessage sends, onmessage receives (data is in e.data).
✅ Advantage: the UI stays smooth while heavy work runs in parallel.
Example 3: worker.js: do the heavy work
// worker.js
self.onmessage = (e) => {
  let sum = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < e.data; i++) sum += i;
  self.postMessage(sum);                        // send the answer back
};
What happens: inside the worker, self is the worker's global scope. It receives the number, computes, and posts the result back.
Data passing: messages are COPIED with the structured clone algorithm (same as structuredClone); big ArrayBuffers can be transferred instead (postMessage(buf, [buf])) for zero-copy.
⚠ Workers have NO access to the DOM, window or document (no direct UI changes); they do have fetch, setTimeout, IndexedDB and importScripts / module imports. Starting a worker has a cost, so use them for really heavy tasks.
Figure 146: The main thread and a worker communicate only by copying messages.

3. requestAnimationFrame

Example 4: a smooth animation loop
const box = document.querySelector(".box");
let start;
function step(time) {                         // time = high-resolution timestamp (ms)
  if (start === undefined) start = time;
  const elapsed = time - start;
  box.style.transform = `translateX(${Math.min(elapsed / 5, 300)}px)`;
  if (elapsed < 1500) requestAnimationFrame(step);   // ask for the next frame
}
requestAnimationFrame(step);
What happens: the browser calls step right before painting the next frame (usually 60 times per second, matching the screen). Movement is based on elapsed time, so speed is the same on 60 Hz and 120 Hz screens.
✅ Advantages over setTimeout(fn, 16): synced with repaint (no jank or skipped frames), automatically paused in background tabs (saves battery/CPU).
⚠ It runs once per call, so you must call requestAnimationFrame again for the next frame. For simple transitions, CSS animations are even better.
Example 5: cancelAnimationFrame
let id = requestAnimationFrame(step);
stopButton.onclick = () => cancelAnimationFrame(id);   // stop the scheduled frame
What happens: requestAnimationFrame returns an id; cancelAnimationFrame(id) removes that pending callback (like clearTimeout).
✅ Also used to throttle scroll/resize work to once per frame (see Chapter 80).
setTimeout(fn, 16)requestAnimationFrame(fn)
Timing"about" 16 ms, driftsRight before each repaint
Background tabThrottled (≥ 1 s)Paused
Best forDelays, non-visual workAnimations, visual updates
JS, rendering आणि clicks एकाच main thread वर चालतात; मोठे काम ते अडवते. Web Worker वेगळ्या thread वर heavy काम करतो आणि postMessage ने उत्तर पाठवतो, पण त्याला DOM दिसत नाही. requestAnimationFrame screen refresh सोबत animation चालवतो, म्हणून ते setTimeout पेक्षा smooth असते.

4. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. Is JavaScript multi-threaded with Web Workers?
  • Each worker has its own thread, event loop and memory; they share nothing (except SharedArrayBuffer) and talk via messages. The language itself stays single-threaded per agent.
Q2. Can a worker change the DOM?
  • No. It sends a message, and the main thread updates the DOM.
Q3. Why requestAnimationFrame instead of setInterval for animation?
  • It is synced with the display refresh, avoids dropped/double frames and pauses in hidden tabs.
Q4. Does async/await stop a heavy loop from freezing the page?
  • No. CPU-heavy synchronous code blocks the thread whatever the syntax; use a worker or split the work into chunks.
Q5. Output-based questions
console.log(1); requestAnimationFrame(() => console.log("raf")); setTimeout(() => console.log("timeout")); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("micro")); console.log(2);
// → 1 2 micro, then usually timeout, then raf (raf waits for the next frame; exact order of timeout/raf is not guaranteed)
// worker: self.postMessage({ a: 1 }) → main: e.data is a COPY; changing it doesn't affect the worker's object
  • What happens: sync logs first, then the promise microtask; then usually the timeout, and requestAnimationFrame waits for the next frame. Messages to/from a worker are copies.
  • Output: 1 2 micro, then timeout / raf.
ToolUse
new Worker(url)Background thread
postMessage / onmessageSend / receive (copied)
terminate()Stop the worker
requestAnimationFrameRun before the next paint
cancelAnimationFrameCancel it
थोडक्यात: heavy CPU काम → Web Worker; animation → requestAnimationFrame. Worker ला DOM नाही, आणि data copy होऊन जातो.
