1. Math Object

Your Notes (24_mathObject/math.js):
  1. The Math object in JavaScript is used to perform mathematical tasks on numbers. (Math is a namespace object that contains static properties and methods for mathematical constants and functions.)
  2. If you want to use any Math property, you use it directly on the Math object: Math.PI, Math.round(x). ✔ "you have to use Math class". Math is NOT a class or constructor: new Math() → TypeError: Math is not a constructor; typeof Math → "object". You just call Math.method() directly.Math हा class नाही, तो एक साधा built-in object (namespace) आहे. new Math() केल्यास TypeError येतो. थेट Math.round() असे वापरतात.
Definition: Math is a built-in, non-constructible object holding constants (PI, E, LN2…) and static functions (round, floor, ceil, trunc, abs, pow, sqrt, min, max, random, log…). It works on Numbers (not BigInt) and converts its arguments with Number(): Math.abs("-3") → 3, Math.abs("x") → NaN.

2. Math.PI (a constant value)

Your Notes: 
console.log(Math.PI);   // → 3.141592653589793
// ✔ your heading says "Math.pi". Property names are case-sensitive: Math.pi → undefined; the constant is Math.PI
  • What happens: Math.PI is the constant π (case-sensitive).
  • Output: 3.141592653589793.

3. Math.round()

Your Notes: returns the value of x rounded to its nearest integer. In the round method, if the value after the point is less than .5 it gives the lower integer; if the value is greater than or equal to .5 it gives the next (higher) integer. 
let num = 10.5;
let num1 = 11.4;
console.log(Math.round(num));    // 11
console.log(Math.round(num1));   // 11
console.log("round value", Math.round(-4.6));   // -5
console.log("round value", Math.round(-4.2));   // -4
  • What happens: Math.round rounds to the nearest integer; .5 rounds up toward +∞ (so -4.5 → -4).
  • Output: 11, 11, -5, -4.
  • ⚠ Math.round(-2.5) is -2, not -3.
✔ Note: an exact .5 always rounds UP toward +∞, which surprises people with negatives: Math.round(-4.5) → -4 (not -5), Math.round(2.5) → 3, Math.round(-0.4) → -0 (verified in Node)..5 असताना round नेहमी वरच्या दिशेने (+∞ कडे) जातो. म्हणून Math.round(-4.5) = -4 येतो, -5 नाही.

4. Math.pow()

Your Notes: returns the value of x to the power y. 
console.log(Math.pow(2, 3));   // → 8
// same as
console.log(2 ** 3);           // → 8 (exponent operator, ES2016)
  • What happens: Math.pow(a, b) = a ** b.
  • Output: 8, 8.

5. Math.sqrt()

Your Notes: returns the square root of the given value. 
console.log(Math.sqrt(81));   // → 9
console.log(Math.sqrt(-1));   // → NaN (no real square root)
console.log(Math.cbrt(27));   // → 3 (cube root)
  • What happens: square root, NaN for negatives, cube root.
  • Output: 9, NaN, 3.

6. Math.abs() (returns the absolute value of a number)

Your Notes: 
console.log(Math.abs(-55));
console.log(Math.abs(-90.89));
console.log(Math.abs(10));
// output
// Math.abs(-55) → 55
// Math.abs(-90.89) → 90.89
// Math.abs(10) → 10
  • What happens: Math.abs removes the sign.
  • Output: 55, 90.89, 10.
Math.abs() only changes a negative value to positive; the digits stay the same: if the value has 2 decimals, they are kept, and a negative value is converted into a positive one.
Example: if you perform a subtraction and the result is a negative value, you can use the Math.abs() method to return the absolute value in positive form: 
console.log(Math.abs(4 - 6));   // 2   (distance between 4 and 6)
  • What happens: abs of a difference = distance between two numbers.
  • Output: 2.

7. Math.ceil(): Rounds a Number Upwards to the Nearest Integer

Your Notes: Math.ceil(x) returns the value of x rounded UP to its nearest integer. If you use the Math.ceil() method and there is ANY fractional part after the decimal point, it goes up to the next integer. ✔ "only a single value after the decimal, it increased by one". Any non-zero fraction, however many digits (4.0001), goes up to the next integer; a whole number stays the same (Math.ceil(4.0) → 4).दशांशानंतर कितीही अंक असले (4.0001) तरी ceil पुढचा integer देतो. पूर्णांक (4.0) तसाच राहतो.
Example 1
console.log(Math.ceil(4.5));    // 5
console.log(Math.ceil(4.1));    // 5
  • What happens: ceil rounds UP to the next integer.
  • Output: 5, 5.
In the ceil method, with a negative number it returns the number before the decimal as it 
// # In the ceil method, with a negative number it returns the number before the decimal as it is
console.log(Math.ceil(-4.1));   // -4
console.log(Math.ceil(-4.9));   // -4
// (reason: "up" means toward +∞, and -4 is greater than -4.1)
  • What happens: for negatives, "up" means toward zero.
  • Output: -4, -4.

8. Math.floor()

Your Notes: the Math.floor() method returns the value of x rounded DOWNWARD to its nearest integer. Whatever you write after the decimal, it returns only the rounded-down integer value. 
console.log(Math.floor(4.5));   // 4
console.log(Math.floor(4.1));   // 4

// If you give a negative value, it returns the next lower integer (the number before the decimal, minus 1)
console.log(Math.floor(-4.1));  // -5
console.log(Math.floor(-4.9));  // -5
// (reason: "down" means toward −∞, and -5 is smaller than -4.1)
  • What happens: floor rounds DOWN (toward −∞): negatives go further away from zero.
  • Output: 4, 4, -5, -5.
Figure 147: floor, ceil, trunc and round on a number line, for positive and negative values.
floor नेहमी डावीकडे (लहान बाजूला, −∞), ceil नेहमी उजवीकडे (मोठ्या बाजूला, +∞), trunc दशांश फक्त कापून टाकतो (0 कडे), आणि round जवळच्या integer कडे नेतो. म्हणून negative संख्यांवर floor(-4.1) = -5 आणि ceil(-4.1) = -4 येतात.

9. Math.min() & Math.max()

Your Notes: Math.min() can be used to find the lowest value in a list of arguments; Math.max() can be used to find the highest value in a list of arguments. 
console.log(Math.min(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7));   // → 0
console.log(Math.max(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7));   // → 7
  • What happens: min/max take separate numbers.
  • Output: 0, 7.
Extra Details: edge cases (verified) 
Math.max([1, 2]);         // NaN   → the array is ONE argument; use spread: Math.max(...[3, 9, 1]) → 9
Math.min();               // Infinity    Math.max();  // -Infinity   (the identity values)
Math.max(1, "5", 3);      // 5  (strings are converted)
Math.min(1, NaN);         // NaN (any NaN → NaN)
  • What happens: an array is one argument (→ NaN); spread it. With no arguments min is Infinity and max -Infinity; strings are converted; any NaN gives NaN.
  • Output: NaN, Infinity / -Infinity, 5, NaN.

10. Math.random()

Your Notes: the Math.random() function in JavaScript generates a pseudorandom floating-point number between 0 (inclusive) and 1 (exclusive). This means the generated number will always be greater than or equal to 0 and less than 1. 
console.log(Math.random());     // e.g. 0.7341…  (different every run)
let data = Math.random() * 10;  // 0 ≤ data < 10
console.log(data);              // e.g. 7.341…
console.log(Math.floor(data));  // an integer 0…9
// console.log(Math.random()*10);
// console.log(Math.floor(Math.random()*10));
  • What happens: Math.random() gives 0 ≤ x < 1; × 10 and floor give an integer 0–9.
  • Output: random values.
Random integer in a range (interview favourite) 
// inclusive min..max
const randInt = (min, max) => Math.floor(Math.random() * (max - min + 1)) + min;
randInt(1, 6);          // a dice roll: 1…6
const pick = (arr) => arr[Math.floor(Math.random() * arr.length)];   // a random array element
// ⚠ Math.random is NOT cryptographically secure: for tokens/OTP use crypto.getRandomValues / crypto.randomUUID()
  • What happens: random integer in [min, max]; random array element.
  • Output: e.g. 1–6.
  • ⚠ Not secure; use crypto.getRandomValues / randomUUID for tokens and OTPs.
Math.random() 0 ते 1 मधली (1 नाही) random संख्या देतो. min ते max integer साठी: Math.floor(Math.random() * (max - min + 1)) + min. password/OTP साठी Math.random सुरक्षित नाही; crypto वापरा.

11. Math.trunc()

Your Notes: the trunc() method returns the integer part of a number by removing any fractional (decimal) part. If the number is positive it returns a positive number, and if the number is negative it returns a negative number. 
console.log(Math.trunc(4.9));    // Output: 4
console.log(Math.trunc(4.1));    // Output: 4
console.log(Math.trunc(-4.9));   // Output: -4
console.log(Math.trunc(-4.1));   // Output: -4
  • What happens: trunc just removes the decimal part (toward zero).
  • Output: 4, 4, -4, -4.
Comparison with other methods:
  • Math.floor() rounds down to the nearest integer
  • Math.ceil() rounds up to the nearest integer
  • Math.trunc() just drops the decimal part without rounding.

If the argument is a positive number, Math.trunc() is equivalent to Math.floor(); otherwise Math.trunc() is equivalent to Math.ceil(): 
console.log(Math.trunc(4.9));    // Output: 4
console.log(Math.floor(4.9));    // Output: 4   // in floor, a negative value goes one lower
console.log(Math.trunc(-4.9));   // Output: -4
console.log(Math.ceil(-4.0));    // Output: -4
// ✔ note: to show trunc(-4.9) === ceil(-4.9), the demo should use Math.ceil(-4.9) → -4; ceil(-4.0) is trivially -4
  • What happens: trunc vs floor differ only for negatives (trunc(-4.9) = -4, floor = -5).
  • Output: 4, 4, -4, -4.
  • # floor madhe (in floor) a negative value goes one lower (−4.1 → −5).
  • # ceil madhe (in ceil) a negative value returns the same integer part (−4.9 → −4).
xroundfloorceiltrunc
4.55454
4.14454
-4.1-4-5-4-4
-4.5-4-5-4-4
-4.9-5-5-4-4

12. Math.log(x) & More Methods

Your Notes: Math.log(x) returns the natural logarithm (base e) of x. 
let lgoResult = Math.log(1);
let lgoresu = Math.log(2);
console.log(lgoResult, lgoresu);   // → 0 0.6931471805599453
// ✔ note: your file computes these but never prints them; console.log added to see the values
  • What happens: Math.log is the natural log (base e); log(1) = 0.
  • Output: 0 0.6931471805599453.
Extra Details: other useful Math members (verified) 
Math.E;            // 2.718281828459045     Math.LN2;   // 0.6931471805599453
Math.log10(1000);  // 3                     Math.log2(8); // 3
Math.sign(-3);     // -1 (1, -1, 0 or -0)   Math.hypot(3, 4); // 5
Math.cbrt(27);     // 3

// rounding to 2 decimals: the floating-point trap
Math.round(1.005 * 100) / 100;   // 1   (expected 1.01; 1.005 is really 1.00499999…)
(1.005).toFixed(2);              // "1.00" (a STRING) → for money, work in paise/cents (integers)
0.1 + 0.2;                       // 0.30000000000000004 → compare with Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON
  • What happens: more constants and functions; rounding 1.005 fails because it is stored as 1.00499…; toFixed returns a string.
  • Output: see comments.
  • ⚠ For money use integer paise/cents.

13. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. floor vs ceil vs trunc vs round?
  • floor → toward −∞, ceil → toward +∞, trunc → toward 0 (drops the fraction), round → nearest (.5 goes toward +∞). They differ only for negative numbers or .5 cases.
Q2. How do you generate a random integer between min and max?
  • Math.floor(Math.random() * (max - min + 1)) + min (inclusive). Without the +1, max is never produced.
Q3. How do you find the max of an array?
  • Math.max(...arr) or arr.reduce((a, b) => Math.max(a, b)) (for very large arrays, where spread can exceed the argument limit). Math.max(arr) → NaN.
Q4. Is Math a constructor? Why can't you do new Math()?
  • No. Math is a plain built-in object (namespace) with static members, so new Math() throws a TypeError. Compare: Date IS a constructor (new Date()).
Q5. Output-based questions
console.log(Math.round(-2.5));          // → -2
console.log(Math.floor(-0.5));          // → -1
console.log(Math.trunc("7.9"));         // → 7
console.log(Math.max());                // → -Infinity
console.log(Math.abs(null), Math.abs([]));   // → 0 0
console.log(Math.round(1.005 * 100) / 100);  // → 1
  • What happens: six output questions: round of -2.5, floor of -0.5, trunc converts strings, max(), abs of null/[], the 1.005 trap.
  • Output: -2, -1, 7, -Infinity, 0 0, 1.
MethodDoesExample
Math.PI / Math.EConstants3.14159…, 2.71828…
round / floor / ceil / truncTo an integer4.5 → 5 / 4 / 5 / 4
absAbsolute value-55 → 55
pow / **, sqrt, cbrtPowers & roots2**3 = 8, √81 = 9
min / maxSmallest / largest argumentMath.max(...arr)
random[0, 1) floatfloor(random*(max-min+1))+min
log / log10 / log2Logarithmslog(1) = 0
थोडक्यात: Math हा class नसलेला built-in object आहे (new Math() नाही). floor खाली, ceil वर, trunc दशांश काढतो, round जवळचा integer. negative संख्यांवर फरक दिसतो. random range साठीचे सूत्र लक्षात ठेवा. array साठी Math.max(...arr) वापरा.

1. Date Object

Your Notes (40_Date/date.js):
  1. A Date object contains a number that represents the milliseconds since 1 January 1970 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time).
  2. The Date() constructor creates a Date object; when called as a function (without new), it returns a string representation of the current time.
typeof Date();       // "string"   (verified)
typeof new Date();   // "object"
  • What happens: Date() called without new returns a STRING; new Date() returns a Date object.
  • Output: "string", "object".
  • ⚠ Always use new Date().
Definition: A Date is just ONE number: the milliseconds since the Unix epoch (1970-01-01T00:00:00Z), the "timestamp". Everything else (year, month, hours…) is computed from it, either in your LOCAL time zone (getHours, toString) or in UTC (getUTCHours, toISOString). Months are 0-based (0 = January); getDay is 0 = Sunday.
Date object मध्ये फक्त एक संख्या असते: 1 जानेवारी 1970 (UTC) पासूनचे milliseconds. वर्ष, महिना, तास हे सगळे त्या संख्येवरून local time zone किंवा UTC प्रमाणे काढले जातात. महिना 0 पासून मोजतात (0 = जानेवारी, 11 = डिसेंबर).

2. Ways to Create a Date

  1. new Date();
  2. new Date(date_string)
  3. new Date(year, month)
  4. new Date(year, month, day)
  5. new Date(year, month, day, hours)
  6. new Date(year, month, day, hours, minutes)
  7. new Date(year, month, day, hours, minutes, seconds)
  8. new Date(year, month, day, hours, minutes, seconds, milliseconds)
  9. new Date(milliseconds)

3. new Date() & new Date(dateString)

1. how to create a Date
// 1. how to create a Date
let date = new Date();
console.log(date);   // Sat Aug 02 2025 22:27:31 GMT+0530 (India Standard Time)   ← browser console
//                      2026-10-01T11:27:47.581Z                                   ← Node console (verified)
// The ISO 8601 format returns a string representation of the date and time, with the separators T and Z.
// Node.js (and some consoles) automatically show toISOString()-like output, which is in ISO 8601 and represents the date and time in UTC.
  • What happens: new Date() is the current date and time; consoles show it either as local text or as an ISO UTC string.
  • Output: the current date.
2. new Date(date_string): creates a date based on the provided string
// # 2. new Date(date_string): creates a date based on the provided string
// creates a Date object with the specified date and time:
// # note: give the date in "year-month-day" (ISO) format, and the time as "hours:minutes:seconds"
const data = "2024-09-21T02:39:03.238Z";
let curTime1 = new Date(data);
console.log(curTime1);   // → 2024-09-21T02:39:03.238Z   (Z = UTC)
  • What happens: an ISO string with Z is parsed as UTC.
  • Output: 2024-09-21T02:39:03.238Z.
ex 1
// ex 1
const onlyDate = "2024-12-11";   // date only
const dateObj2 = new Date(onlyDate);
console.log(dateObj2);   // → 2024-12-11T00:00:00.000Z  = Wed Dec 11 2024 05:30:00 GMT+0530 in India (verified)
// ✔ the comment said "Time is set to 00:00:00 in your local timezone". A DATE-ONLY ISO string is parsed
//    as UTC midnight, which is 05:30 IST (and the PREVIOUS day in the Americas!). A date-time string without Z
//    ("2024-12-11T00:00") is parsed as LOCAL time → 00:00 IST.
  • What happens: a date-only ISO string is parsed as UTC midnight, i.e. 05:30 in India and the previous day in America.
  • Output: 2024-12-11T00:00:00.000Z.
  • ⚠ Classic timezone bug.
ex 2
// ex 2
const specificDateTime = "2024/12/11 15:45:30";   // another format
const dateObj3 = new Date(specificDateTime);
console.log(dateObj3);   // → 2024-12-11T10:15:30.000Z (= 15:45:30 local IST)
// ⚠ "2024/12/11 …" is NOT a standard format; it works in browsers/Node but isn't guaranteed. Prefer ISO: "2024-12-11T15:45:30"
  • What happens: non-ISO formats usually work but aren't guaranteed.
  • Output: 2024-12-11T10:15:30.000Z (15:45:30 IST).
  • ✅ Prefer ISO strings.
ex 3: Unix timestamp (milliseconds)
// ex 3: Unix timestamp (milliseconds)
const unixTimestamp = 1700000000000;   // a Unix timestamp in milliseconds
const dateObj5 = new Date(unixTimestamp);
console.log(dateObj5);   // → 2023-11-14T22:13:20.000Z   (converts the timestamp to a Date object)
  • What happens: a number = milliseconds since 1 Jan 1970 UTC.
  • Output: 2023-11-14T22:13:20.000Z.
फक्त तारीख ("2024-12-11") दिल्यास ती UTC मध्यरात्र समजली जाते, म्हणून भारतात 05:30 वाजता दिसते. वेळेसह, Z शिवाय दिलेली string ("2024-12-11T00:00") local time म्हणून घेतली जाते. "2024/12/11" हा standard format नाही; ISO format वापरा.

4. new Date(year, month, …) & new Date(milliseconds)

4. new Date(year, month): creates a Date object with the specified year and month
// 4. new Date(year, month): creates a Date object with the specified year and month
let newDate = new Date(2020, 2);
console.log("newDate", newDate);       // → 1 MARCH 2020 00:00 local (2020-02-29T18:30:00.000Z in UTC): month 2 = March
  • What happens: with numbers, the MONTH is 0-based: 2 = March; time is local.
  • Output: 1 March 2020.
5. new Date(year, month, day): creates a Date object with the specified year, month and da
// 5. new Date(year, month, day): creates a Date object with the specified year, month and day
let newDate1 = new Date(2020, 1, 19);
console.log("newDate.....", newDate1); // → 19 Feb 2020 (month 1 = February)
// ✔ the comment said "new Date(year, day)" → (year, month, day)
  • What happens: (year, month, day) → 19 Feb 2020.
  • Output: 19 Feb 2020.
6. new Date(year, month, day, hours): creates a Date object with the specified year, month
// 6. new Date(year, month, day, hours): creates a Date object with the specified year, month, day and hours
let newDate2 = new Date(2020, 2, 1, 10);
console.log("newDate.....", newDate2); // → 1 Mar 2020 10:00 local
  • What happens: adds hours.
  • Output: 1 Mar 2020 10:00.
7. new Date(year, month, day, hours, min)
// 7. new Date(year, month, day, hours, min)
let newDate3 = new Date(2020, 2, 1, 10, 44);
console.log("newDate.....", newDate3); // → 1 Mar 2020 10:44
  • What happens: adds minutes.
  • Output: 1 Mar 2020 10:44.
8. new Date(year, month, day, hours, min, sec)
// 8. new Date(year, month, day, hours, min, sec)
let newDate4 = new Date(2020, 2, 1, 10, 44, 5);
console.log("newDate.....", newDate4); // → 1 Mar 2020 10:44:05
  • What happens: adds seconds.
  • Output: 1 Mar 2020 10:44:05.
9. new Date(year, month, day, hours, min, sec, ms): with milliseconds too
// 9. new Date(year, month, day, hours, min, sec, ms): with milliseconds too
let newDate5 = new Date(2020, 2, 1, 10, 44, 5);
console.log("newDate.....", newDate5);
// ✔ the ms argument is missing (same as #8). With ms: new Date(2020, 2, 1, 10, 44, 5, 250)
  • What happens: the milliseconds argument is missing in this example.
  • Output: same as above.
10. new Date(milliseconds): creates a Date object representing the number of milliseconds 
// 10. new Date(milliseconds): creates a Date object representing the number of milliseconds since the Unix epoch (January 1, 1970)
const ms1 = new Date().getTime();   // returns the date in milliseconds since 01 Jan 1970
console.log("ms1", ms1);
// ✔ note: this line shows getTime() (Date → ms); the constructor form is the reverse: new Date(ms1) (ms → Date)
  • What happens: getTime() gives milliseconds since the epoch; new Date(ms) goes the other way.
  • Output: a big number.
✔ Remember: in the numeric constructor, MONTH is 0-based (0 = Jan … 11 = Dec), but DAY is 1-based. Values overflow: new Date(2024, 0, 32) → 1 Feb 2024; new Date(2024, 2, 0) → 29 Feb 2024 (day 0 = the last day of the previous month, a handy trick for "days in a month").numeric constructor मध्ये महिना 0 पासून (0 = जानेवारी) पण दिवस 1 पासून असतो. जास्त value दिल्यास पुढच्या महिन्यात जाते; day 0 म्हणजे मागच्या महिन्याचा शेवटचा दिवस.

5. What is the Difference between toString() and toLocaleString()?

The Date().toLocaleString() and Date().toString() methods both return a string representation of a Date object in JavaScript, but they differ in formatting, localization, and how the date and time are represented.

1. new Date().toLocaleString() 
dateObj.toLocaleString([locales[, options]])
// Parameters:
// locales (optional) → a BCP 47 language tag, e.g. "en-US", "hi-IN", "fr-FR".
// options (optional) → an object to customize the output (like date style, time style, time zone).
  • What happens: toLocaleString(locales, options) formats for a language/region.
  • Output: (syntax).
  1. toLocaleString converts the date and time into a string using the current locale or a specified locale. ✔ "toLocalString" → toLocaleString (LocaLE)."toLocalString" नाही, toLocaleString.
  2. This method formats the date and time according to the conventions of a specific locale or language.
  3. By default, it uses the system's locale settings, but you can specify different locales and options.
  4. (You can provide options to format the output, e.g. adjusting the format of the date, time and time zone.)
Example 1
// 2024-09-21T02:44:57.320Z
let date1 = new Date().toLocaleString();
console.log(date1);   // 21/9/2024, 8:13:01 am   (en-IN style)
  • What happens: default locale formatting.
  • Output: e.g. 21/9/2024, 8:13:01 am.
customizable
// # customizable
let date2 = new Date().toLocaleString("de-DE");
console.log(date2);   // 21.9.2024, 08:23:45

console.log(date.toLocaleString("hi-IN"));
// "15/8/2025, 10:25:00 pm" (Hindi, India format)

console.log(date.toLocaleString("en-GB", { dateStyle: "full", timeStyle: "short" }));
// "Friday, 15 August 2025 at 22:25"

// You can control the format using an options object.
const date3 = new Date();
console.log(date3.toLocaleString('en-US', { weekday: 'long', year: 'numeric', month: 'long', day: 'numeric' }))
// → e.g. "Thursday, October 1, 2026"
// time zones too: date3.toLocaleString("en-US", { timeZone: "America/New_York" })
  • What happens: different locales and options (dateStyle, weekday, timeZone).
  • Output: German, Hindi, British and US formats.
  • ✅ Show dates in the user's format without libraries.
2. new Date().toString()
  1. Returns a string representation of the Date in a fixed (standard) format.
  2. This method returns a standard format for the date and time that is not affected by locale settings.
  3. The format typically includes the day of the week, month, day, year, time and time zone, in a fixed format: Sat Sep 21 2024 08:14:57 GMT+0530 (India Standard Time)
  4. It always returns a full, fixed-format string (the output is fixed and cannot be altered: you always get the same detailed format).
let curData = new Date().toString();
console.log("curData", curData);
  • What happens: toString gives the full local date text.
  • Output: the date string.
AspecttoLocaleString()toString()
PurposeFormats the date according to locale-specific conventionsReturns a fixed, human-readable string in English
Locale Sensitivity✅ Yes: follows the user/system locale or a specified locale❌ No: always a standard format, unaffected by locale
Customizability✅ Highly customizable using the options object❌ Not customizable
Time Zone Formatting✅ Can be customized using options (timeZone, etc.)✔️ Includes the system time zone, but not customizable
Typical Output Formate.g. "9/21/2024, 8:14:57 AM" (U.S. format)e.g. "Sat Sep 21 2024 08:14:57 GMT+0530 (India Standard Time)"
Use CasesDisplaying dates in user interfaces; showing localized formatsDebugging; logs; a consistent display format
ReturnsA string based on locale rules and optional settingsA fixed full string with date, time and time zone
Also: toISOString() → "2024-09-21T02:44:57.320Z" (always UTC; best for APIs/storage/JSON), toUTCString(), toDateString().

6. Date.now() & More Constructor Rules

Date.now():
// # Date.now():
// Returns the number of milliseconds elapsed since midnight, January 1 1970 (UTC, Coordinated Universal Time)
let sec = Date.now();
console.log(sec);   // 1726887911775   (milliseconds, despite the variable name "sec")
  • What happens: Date.now() gives the current timestamp in ms (static, no object needed).
  • Output: a big number.
  • ✅ Measure durations: end - start.
1. new Date(year, month, day, hours, minutes, seconds, milliseconds):
// 1. new Date(year, month, day, hours, minutes, seconds, milliseconds):
// in JavaScript, months count from 0 to 11 (January is 0 and December is 11)
var d = new Date(2018, 11, 24, 10, 33, 30, 0);
console.log("d", d.toLocaleString());   // → d 24/12/2018, 10:33:30 am   (verified, en-IN)
console.log("d", d.toString());         // → d Mon Dec 24 2018 10:33:30 GMT+0530 (India Standard Time)
  • What happens: months 0–11: 11 = December.
  • Output: 24/12/2018, 10:33:30 am.
2. if you pass more than one number to new Date(), you need to pass the month as well; wit
// 2. if you pass more than one number to new Date(), you need to pass the month as well; with only ONE number,
//    it is treated as MILLISECONDS, so you get a time near 1/1/1970
var a = new Date(2023, 3, 6);
console.log(a.toLocaleString());        // → 6/4/2023, 12:00:00 am   (6 April: month 3 = April)
// new Date(2023) → 1970-01-01T00:00:02.023Z (2023 ms after the epoch, verified)
  • What happens: with two or more numbers they mean year, month…; a single number means milliseconds.
  • Output: 6/4/2023 (6 April).
3. new Date(millisecond);
// 3. new Date(millisecond);
var v = new Date(0);
console.log(v.toLocaleString());        // → 1/1/1970, 5:30:00 am   (epoch 00:00 UTC = 05:30 IST)
// new Date(millisecond) creates a new Date object as zero time (the epoch) plus the given milliseconds

var s = new Date();
console.log(s);
console.log(s.toString());
  • What happens: new Date(0) is the epoch (05:30 IST).
  • Output: 1/1/1970, 5:30:00 am.

7. Methods in Date (Get)

  1. const curDate = new Date();
  2. toLocaleString → converts the date and time to the local format
  3. getFullYear → returns the current year
  4. getMonth → gets the current month (0–11!)
  5. getDate() → gets the current day of the month (1–31)
  6. getDay() → returns the current day of the week (0 = Sunday … 6 = Saturday)
  7. getTime() → returns the date in milliseconds
const c_date = new Date();
console.log(c_date);
console.log("covert date and time to local", c_date.toLocaleString());   // → 1/10/2026, 4:57:47 pm
console.log("getFull Year", c_date.getFullYear());   // → 2026
console.log("get month", c_date.getMonth());         // → 9   (October! add 1 for display)
console.log("get date", c_date.getDate());           // → 1
console.log("GetDay", c_date.getDay());              // → 4   (Thursday)
  • What happens: getters: year, month (0-based!), day of month, weekday (0 = Sunday).
  • Output: 2026, 9, 1, 4.
  • ⚠ Add 1 to getMonth() for display.
getMonth 0 पासून देतो (ऑक्टोबर = 9), म्हणून दाखवताना +1 करा. getDate म्हणजे महिन्याची तारीख, आणि getDay म्हणजे आठवड्याचा दिवस (0 = रविवार).

8. How to Set Individual Dates

When you set an individual date part, the method returns the new timestamp (milliseconds since 1 Jan 1970), and it CHANGES (mutates) the Date object itself. 
const cur_Date = new Date();
console.log(cur_Date.setFullYear(2022));          // → e.g. 1664623667654 (ms)
console.log(cur_Date.setFullYear(2022, 10, 5));   // year, month, day at once → 5 Nov 2022
console.log(cur_Date.setMonth(5));                // → June 2022
// ⚠ overflow trap (verified): new Date(2024, 0, 31).setMonth(1) → Sat Mar 02 2024 (31 Feb doesn't exist → rolls over)
  • What happens: setters change the date and return the new timestamp; overflowing dates roll over.
  • Output: timestamps.
  • ⚠ 31 Jan + setMonth(1) → 2 March.

9. Time Methods

  • getTime() → returns the number of milliseconds since 1 Jan 1970
  • getHours() → returns the hours of a date as a number (0–23)
  • getMinutes() → returns the current minutes
  • getSeconds() → returns the current seconds
  • getMilliseconds() → returns the current milliseconds
✔ "getSecond / getMillisecond" → getSecondS / getMillisecondS (plural), and likewise setSeconds / setMilliseconds below.getSecond नाही, getSeconds; getMillisecond नाही, getMilliseconds (अनेकवचन). 
const curTime = new Date();
// returns the number of milliseconds since 1 Jan 1970
console.log("time", curTime.getTime());
// returns the hours of a date as a number (0-23)
console.log(curTime.getHours());          // → 16
// returns the current minutes
console.log(curTime.getMinutes());        // → 57
// returns the current seconds
console.log(curTime.getSeconds());        // → 47
console.log(curTime.getMilliseconds());   // → 654
  • What happens: time getters.
  • Output: timestamp, hours, minutes, seconds, ms.
Set individual time: when we set an individual time part, the method always returns the time in milliseconds; all these methods return the number of milliseconds since 1 Jan 1970: setHours(), setMinutes(), setSeconds(), setMilliseconds(). 
const curTime12 = new Date();
console.log("return time in hours", curTime12.setHours(10));               // → a timestamp (not "10")
console.log("return time in millisecond", curTime12.setMilliseconds(10));
console.log("return time in setMinutes", curTime12.setMinutes(10));
  • What happens: time setters return the timestamp, not the value you set.
  • Output: timestamps.

10. Other Methods: toLocaleDateString / toLocaleTimeString & Date.parse()

// it returns only the current date
console.log(new Date().toLocaleDateString());   // → 1/10/2026
// it returns only the current time
console.log(new Date().toLocaleTimeString());   // → 4:57:47 pm
// it returns date and time
console.log(new Date().toLocaleString());       // → 1/10/2026, 4:57:47 pm

// parse():
// parses a string representation of a date and returns the number of milliseconds since January 1 1970
const time = new Date();
console.log("time", time);
const numTime = Date.parse(time);
console.log(numTime);   // returns the output in milliseconds → …067000
// ✔ (verified) passing a Date OBJECT makes it a string first ("Thu Oct 01 2026 16:57:47 GMT+0530"),
//    which has no milliseconds → .654 s becomes .000. Use time.getTime() for a Date; Date.parse is for STRINGS:
//    Date.parse("2024-09-21T02:39:03.238Z") → 1726886343238. Invalid strings → NaN.

// # Date.now(): a static method of the Date object
// # Date.now(): the method to get the timestamp right this second
// # new Date().getTime(): if you have an existing Date object from elsewhere and want its timestamp, use this.
  • What happens: date-only / time-only / both as text; Date.parse turns a STRING into ms (passing a Date object loses the milliseconds).
  • Output: the strings, a timestamp.
  • ✅ Use getTime() for Date objects.
Figure 148: A Date is one timestamp; you read it in local time or UTC, and watch out for the common traps.

11. Programs

1. Write a function to add a specified number of days to a given date
const addToDate = (date1, extraDay) => {
  console.log("date1", date1);   // → 2024-02-29T00:00:00.000Z
  console.log(extraDay);         // → 7
  const extraDayDate = date1.setDate(date1.getDate() + extraDay);   // setDate handles month overflow
  console.log(extraDayDate);     // → 1709769600000
  return new Date(extraDayDate);
};
const date11 = new Date("2024-02-29");   // ⚠ a date-only string = UTC midnight (05:30 in IST), not "Indian standard format"
console.log(date11);
const new_date = addToDate(date11, 7);
console.log(new_date);   // → 2024-03-07T00:00:00.000Z (29 Feb 2024 + 7 days, leap year handled; verified)
// ✔ setDate MUTATES date11 itself (verified): after the call date11 is also 7 March.
//    Pure version: const copy = new Date(date1); copy.setDate(copy.getDate() + extraDay); return copy;
  • What happens: setDate(getDate() + n) adds days and handles month/leap-year overflow; it mutates the original date.
  • Output: 2024-03-07T00:00:00.000Z.
  • ⚠ Copy the date first for a pure function.
2. Write a function to calculate the difference between two given days
const differencesOfDate = (day1, day2) => {
  let diff = day2 - day1;   // subtracting Dates converts them to ms → difference in milliseconds
  // calculate the days by dividing the result by the milliseconds per day
  const perDay = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;
  // 24 hours in a day.
  // 60 minutes in an hour.
  // 60 seconds in a minute.
  // 1000 milliseconds in a second.
  return Math.round(diff / perDay);   // round protects against DST hours (23/25-hour days)
};
const day1 = new Date("2024-02-19");
const day2 = new Date("2024-03-01");
console.log(differencesOfDate(day1, day2));   // → 11   (2024 is a leap year: Feb has 29 days; verified)
  • What happens: subtracting Dates gives milliseconds; divide by ms per day and round.
  • Output: 11.
  • ✅ Rounding protects against daylight-saving hours.
3. Show the live current time
const liveWatch = () => {
  return new Date().toLocaleTimeString();
};
const stop = setInterval(() => {
  console.log(liveWatch());   // → 4:57:48 pm, 4:57:49 pm
}, 1000);
setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("execution stop");
  clearInterval(stop);
}, 3000);
// verified: it prints only 2 times, not 3: the 3000 ms timeout is scheduled after the interval and clears it
// before (or at the same moment as) the 3rd tick. Use 3100 ms (or count the ticks) to get exactly 3.
  • What happens: setInterval updates every second; the timeout clears it after 3 s.
  • Output: 2 time strings, then execution stop.
Extra: handy date helpers 
const daysInMonth = (y, m) => new Date(y, m + 1, 0).getDate();   // daysInMonth(2024, 1) → 29
const isValid = (d) => d instanceof Date && !isNaN(d);             // new Date("abc") → Invalid Date (getTime() NaN)
const pad = (n) => String(n).padStart(2, "0");
const ddmmyyyy = (d) => `${pad(d.getDate())}-${pad(d.getMonth() + 1)}-${d.getFullYear()}`;
const age = (dob) => { const t = new Date(); let a = t.getFullYear() - dob.getFullYear();
  if (t < new Date(t.getFullYear(), dob.getMonth(), dob.getDate())) a--; return a; };
new Intl.RelativeTimeFormat("en", { numeric: "auto" }).format(-1, "day");   // "yesterday"
  • What happens: useful helpers: days in a month (day 0 of next month), validity check, dd-mm-yyyy, age, relative time.
  • Output: (helpers).

12. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. Why is new Date(2024, 1, 1) February, and why does getMonth() return 9 in October?
  • Months are 0-based in JavaScript's Date (0 = January … 11 = December); days are 1-based. Add 1 for display.
Q2. Why does new Date("2024-12-11") show 05:30 in India (or the previous day in the US)?
  • A date-only ISO string is parsed as UTC midnight; displaying it in local time shifts it. Use new Date(2024, 11, 11) or "2024-12-11T00:00" for local midnight, and toISOString for UTC.
Q3. Date.now() vs new Date().getTime() vs Date.parse()?
  • Date.now(): the current timestamp without creating an object. getTime(): the timestamp of an existing Date. Date.parse(string): string → timestamp (NaN if invalid; passing a Date drops its milliseconds).
Q4. How do you find the difference between two dates in days, and add days safely?
  • (d2 - d1) / 86 400 000, rounded (for DST). Add days with setDate(getDate() + n) on a COPY (set* mutates); overflow into the next month/year is handled automatically.
Q5. Output-based questions
console.log(new Date(2024, 0, 32).getDate());            // → 1   (rolls into February)
console.log(new Date(2024, 2, 0).getDate());             // → 29  (last day of Feb 2024)
console.log(new Date("abc").getTime());                  // → NaN
console.log(typeof Date(), typeof new Date());           // → string object
console.log(new Date(0).toISOString());                  // → 1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z
console.log(new Date(2024, 0, 31).setMonth(1) === new Date(2024, 2, 2).getTime());   // → true (overflow)
  • What happens: six output questions: day overflow, day 0 trick, invalid date, Date() vs new Date(), epoch ISO, setMonth overflow.
  • Output: 1, 29, NaN, string object, 1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z, true.
TaskMethod
Now (ms)Date.now()
Create localnew Date(y, m0, d, h, min, s, ms)
Create from ISO / msnew Date("2024-09-21T02:39:03Z") / new Date(ms)
ReadgetFullYear, getMonth (0-11), getDate, getDay (0 = Sun), getHours…
Change (mutates)setFullYear, setMonth, setDate, setHours… → return ms
FormattoLocaleString(locale, options), toISOString, toString
Difference(d2 - d1) / 86400000
थोडक्यात: Date म्हणजे 1970 पासूनचे milliseconds. महिना 0 पासून, getDay 0 = रविवार. "YYYY-MM-DD" UTC मध्ये parse होते. set* methods object बदलतात (mutate) आणि ms परत करतात. दाखवण्यासाठी toLocaleString, API साठी toISOString. Date.parse ला Date object देऊ नका, त्याने milliseconds जातात.

Chapter 84: ES6+ Features by Version (ES2015 → ES2023)What came in which year · examples · version-label corrections
CHAPTER 84 INDEX
  1. ES6 / ES2015
  2. ES2016 (ES7) & ES2017 (ES8)
  3. ES2018 (ES9) & ES2019 (ES10)
  4. ES2020 (ES11): BigInt, ??, ?., allSettled
  5. ES2021 (ES12): replaceAll, Logical Assignment, Numeric Separators
  6. ES2022–ES2023: findLast, toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced, with
  7. Version Cheat Sheet
  8. Interview Questions & Revision
Naming: since 2015 the ECMAScript spec is released every June and named by YEAR: ES6 = ES2015, ES7 = ES2016, ES8 = ES2017 … ES14 = ES2023. "ES6" is NOT a synonym for all modern JS; each later feature has its own year. ✔ your file labels later versions "ES6-2021" and "Es6-2022"; those are ES2021 (ES12) and ES2022/ES2023 (ES13/ES14). Also findLast and the toSorted/toReversed/toSpliced/with family are ES2023, not ES2022.2015 नंतर प्रत्येक वर्षी नवीन version येते: ES6 = 2015, ES7 = 2016 … ES14 = 2023. "ES6-2021" असे लिहिणे चुकीचे आहे; ते ES2021 (ES12) आहे.
ECMAScript म्हणजे JavaScript चा standard. 2015 (ES6) मध्ये खूप मोठे बदल आले, आणि त्यानंतर दर वर्षी काही नवीन features येतात. interview मध्ये "हे feature कोणत्या version मध्ये आले?" असे विचारतात, म्हणून हा chapter cheat sheet सारखा आहे.

1. ES6 – 2015

Your Notes (35_Es6Featues.js):
  1. let and const
  2. template literals
  3. object properties (shorthand properties & methods, computed keys: Chapter 21)
  4. array destructuring
  5. object destructuring
  6. spread operator (...): expands (spreads) the elements of an iterable
  7. rest parameter (...): lets you access an indefinite number of arguments as an array, written as ... followed by a variable name
  8. exponentiation operator ** (✔ this came in ES2016, not ES2015)
** (घात operator) ES6 मध्ये नाही, ES2016 मध्ये आला. तुमच्या list मधील इतर सगळे ES6 चेच आहेत. Also ES6: arrow functions, classes, modules (import/export), Promises, default parameters, Map/Set/WeakMap, Symbol, for…of, iterators & generators, Array.from/of/find/findIndex, Object.assign.

2. ES2016 (ES7) & ES2017 (ES8)

ES2016: Array.prototype.includes, and the exponentiation operator 2 ** 3.
ES8 – 2017 (your notes):
  1. string padding (padStart(), padEnd())
  2. Object.values()
  3. Object.entries()
  4. trailing commas in function parameter lists and calls (this feature allows trailing commas in function declarations and function calls; trailing commas in array and object literals were already allowed earlier)
Also ES2017: async/await, Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptors. 
"ab".padStart(5, "*");   // "***ab"   (verified)
"5".padStart(2, "0");    // "05"  → clocks, invoice numbers
  • What happens: padStart (ES2017) pads at the start to a target length.
  • Output: "***ab", "05".

3. ES2018 (ES9) & ES2019 (ES10)

ES9 – 2018:
  1. rest/spread for OBJECTS ({ ...obj }, const { a, ...rest } = obj; arrays had it since ES6)
  2. Promise.prototype.finally()
(also: async iteration for await…of, RegExp named groups / lookbehind / s-flag)
ES10 – 2019:
  1. Array.prototype.flat()
  2. Array.prototype.flatMap()
  3. Object.fromEntries()
  4. Symbol.prototype.description
  5. Optional catch binding: try { … } catch { … } (no (e) needed)
  6. String.prototype.trimStart()
  7. String.prototype.trimEnd()
Symbol("d").description;              // "d"
try { JSON.parse("{"); } catch { console.log("optional catch binding"); }   // verified
  • What happens: Symbol.description (ES2019) and optional catch binding (catch without (e)).
  • Output: "d", optional catch binding.

4. ES11 – 2020

1. BigInt: BigInt in JavaScript is a data type used to represent and perform operations on large integers that exceed the limits of regular numbers. Create a BigInt with the 'n' suffix, or with the BigInt() constructor. 
const anotherLargeNumber = BigInt(228282928292282992828229020202002929n)
console.log(anotherLargeNumber);   // → 228282928292282992828229020202002929n
const maxNumber = Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER;
// here we see the max safe number; if you want to work beyond this max number, you have to use BigInt
// if you add the suffix n at the end, then it is a BigInt number.
console.log(maxNumber)             // → 9007199254740991
// (BigInt(…n) is redundant: the literal 228…929n is already a BigInt. BigInt("228…") from a string is the useful form.)
// 2n ** 64n → 18446744073709551616n; typeof 10n → "bigint"; 1n + 1 → TypeError (no mixing)
  • What happens: BigInt (ES2020) handles integers beyond MAX_SAFE_INTEGER; write it with the n suffix.
  • Output: the big number, 9007199254740991.
  • ⚠ You can't mix BigInt and Number (1n + 1 → TypeError).
Nullish coalescing operator ??: in JavaScript the nullish coalescing operator (??) is a logical operator that provides a concise way to handle nullish (null or undefined) values: it returns its right-hand operand when its left-hand operand is null or undefined, and otherwise returns the left-hand operand. JavaScript has a few falsy values that || treats as false; with the nullish coalescing operator ??, only null and undefined are treated as "missing", and any other value (0, "", false) is kept. (Chapter 17)
Optional chaining operator: it provides a concise way to access the properties of an object without worrying about the existence of intermediate properties; it is particularly useful when working with nested objects, or accessing properties of objects that may be null or undefined. (Chapter 18) 
const person = {
  name: 'vishal',
  address: { city: "new York", zipCode: 12345 }
}
// accessing a nested property without optional chaining
// const city = person.address;
const city = person.address ? person.address.city : 'city is not available'
console.log(city)    // → new York
// using ?. (optional chaining), also with the nullish coalescing operator
const city1 = person.address?.city ?? 'city not available'
console.log(city1)   // → new York   (your file computes city1 but never prints it)
  • What happens: optional chaining + nullish coalescing (ES2020) replace long existence checks.
  • Output: new York, new York.
Promise.allSettled (ES2020): waits for all promises and reports each one's status (Chapter 66). (Your heading has no notes under it.)
Also ES2020: globalThis, dynamic import(), String.prototype.matchAll.

5. ES2021 (ES12)

1. replaceAll(searchValue, replacement): replaceAll in JavaScript is a function that replaces all occurrences of a specified value with another value in a given string. 
// ex: replacing multiple spaces with a single space
const text = 'vishal    shinde,      hi,'
const newText = text.replaceAll(/\s+/g, " ");
console.log(newText)   // → "vishal shinde, hi,"   (verified)
// with a regex, replaceAll REQUIRES the g flag (else TypeError); with a plain string, no regex is needed:
"a-b-c".replaceAll("-", "+");   // "a+b+c"
  • What happens: replaceAll (ES2021) with a global regex collapses multiple spaces.
  • Output: "vishal shinde, hi,", "a+b+c".
Logical assignment operators (||=, &&=, ??=)
  1. Logical OR assignment ||=: assigns the right-hand value to the left-hand operand if the left-hand operand is FALSY (false, null, undefined, 0, "", NaN); otherwise it leaves the left-hand side unchanged.
  2. Logical AND assignment &&=: assigns the right-hand value to the left-hand operand if the left-hand operand is TRUTHY; otherwise it leaves it unchanged.
  3. Nullish assignment ??=: assigns only if the left-hand operand is null or undefined.
✔ the operators are written ||= and &&= (one =), not "||==" / "&&==". And &&= assigns when the left side is TRUTHY (your note listed the falsy values for it, copied from ||=). ??= was missing.||= (एकच =) डावी बाजू falsy असेल तर assign करतो. &&= डावी बाजू truthy असेल तर assign करतो. ??= फक्त null/undefined असेल तर assign करतो. 
let a = 0;    a ||= 5;   // 5   (0 is falsy)
let b = 1;    b &&= 7;   // 7   (1 is truthy)
let c = null; c ??= 9;   // 9   (verified: 5 7 9)
  • What happens: logical assignment operators (ES2021).
  • Output: 5, 7, 9.
Numeric separator (_): the underscore is used as a numeric separator for readability: 1_000_000 === 1000000 (verified).
Also ES2021: Promise.any, AggregateError, WeakRef.

6. ES2022 – ES2023

Your notes (labelled "Es6 - 2022"):
  • Array.findLast(): lets you find an element from the last to the first element of the array, based on a condition. (ES2023)
  • Array.findLastIndex() (ES2023)
  • Array.prototype.toReversed() (ES2023)
  • Array.prototype.toSorted(compareFn) (ES2023)
  • Array.prototype.toSpliced(start, deleteCount, ...items) (ES2023)
  • Array.prototype.with(index, value): the with method in JavaScript is used to change the value of an element at a specific index in an array. It takes two arguments, the index of the element to change and the new value, and returns a new array with the changed element, leaving the original array unchanged. (ES2023)
const replaceWith = myLastName.endsWith(2, 'vishal');
console.log('original', myLastName);
console.log('new', replaceWith)
// ✔ this example should call .with(), not .endsWith() (a STRING method that checks the ending), and
//    myLastName must be an array: const myLastName = ["a", "b", "c"]; myLastName.with(2, "vishal") → ["a", "b", "vishal"]

[1, 2, 3].with(1, "x");        // [1, 'x', 3]
[3, 1, 2].toSorted();          // [1, 2, 3]   (original unchanged)
[1, 2, 3].toReversed();        // [3, 2, 1]
[1, 2, 3].toSpliced(1, 1);     // [1, 3]
[1, 2, 3, 4].findLast((x) => x % 2);   // 3   (all verified in Node)
  • What happens: ES2023 non-mutating array methods: with, toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced, plus findLast.
  • Output: [1,'x',3], [1,2,3], [3,2,1], [1,3], 3.
  • ⚠ The example in your notes used endsWith by mistake.
ES2022 itself: class fields, #private fields/methods, static blocks (Chapter 58), Array.prototype.at(), Object.hasOwn(), top-level await in modules, Error cause.
Figure 149: The ECMAScript timeline: the headline features of each yearly edition.

7. Version Cheat Sheet

EditionKey features
ES2015 (ES6)let/const, arrow, class, modules, template literals, destructuring, spread/rest (arrays), default params, Promise, Map/Set, Symbol, for…of
ES2016 (ES7)includes, **
ES2017 (ES8)async/await, Object.values/entries, padStart/padEnd, trailing commas in params
ES2018 (ES9)Object rest/spread, Promise.finally, for await…of
ES2019 (ES10)flat, flatMap, Object.fromEntries, trimStart/End, optional catch binding
ES2020 (ES11)BigInt, ??, ?., Promise.allSettled, globalThis, dynamic import()
ES2021 (ES12)replaceAll, ||= &&= ??=, numeric separators, Promise.any
ES2022 (ES13)Class fields, #private, static blocks, at(), Object.hasOwn, top-level await
ES2023 (ES14)findLast/findLastIndex, toSorted/toReversed/toSpliced/with
ES2024 (ES15)Object.groupBy / Map.groupBy, Promise.withResolvers

8. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. What are the major ES6 features?
  • let/const, arrow functions, classes, modules, template literals, destructuring, spread/rest, default parameters, Promises, Map/Set, Symbol, iterators/generators.
Q2. ?? vs ||, and ??= vs ||=?
  • || / ||= treat every falsy value (0, "", false) as missing; ?? / ??= only null and undefined. Use ?? for defaults when 0 or "" are valid values.
Q3. sort() vs toSorted()?
  • sort mutates the original array; toSorted (ES2023) returns a sorted COPY. Same pair: reverse/toReversed, splice/toSpliced; arr[i] = v vs arr.with(i, v).
Q4. When do you need BigInt?
  • For integers beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (2^53 − 1), e.g. IDs and crypto; you can't mix BigInt and Number in arithmetic, and Math methods don't accept BigInt.
Q5. Output-based questions
let x = 0;  x ||= 10;  let y = 0;  y ??= 10;
console.log(x, y);                                  // → 10 0
console.log(2 ** 3 ** 2);                           // → 512 (right-associative)
console.log(9007199254740993 === 9007199254740992); // → true (precision lost) → use BigInt
console.log([1, 2, 3].at(-1), "x".padEnd(3, "-"));  // → 3 x--
  • What happens: four output questions on ES6+ features.
  • Output: 10 0, 512, true, 3 x--.
थोडक्यात: ES6 = 2015, नंतर प्रत्येक वर्षी नवीन version. महत्त्वाचे: includes/** (2016), async/await (2017), object spread/finally (2018), flat/fromEntries (2019), ??/?./BigInt (2020), replaceAll/||=/??= (2021), #private/at (2022), toSorted/with/findLast (2023).

Chapter 85: ES6 Modules: export & importNamed & default exports · import forms · live bindings · type="module"
CHAPTER 85 INDEX
  1. What is a Module?
  2. Why Your Demo Doesn't Run
  3. Exporting (exportImport.js)
  4. Importing (app.js)
  5. Loading Modules in HTML (index.html)
  6. Named vs Default Exports
  7. Live Bindings & Module Features
  8. Interview Questions & Revision

1. What is a Module?

Definition: An ES module (ES6/ES2015) is a JS file with its own scope. Nothing in it is visible outside unless it is exported, and other files get it with import. Modules always run in strict mode, run only once (cached) no matter how many files import them, are deferred by default in the browser, and allow top-level await. ✔ the folder name says "Model". The term is MODULE (and in your notes "resume them into another model" → REUSE them in another MODULE)."Model" नाही, "Module". module म्हणजे स्वतंत्र scope असलेली JS file, जिच्यातील गोष्टी export करून दुसऱ्या file मध्ये import करता येतात.
Module म्हणजे स्वतःचा वेगळा scope असलेली file. त्यातील variables/functions बाहेर दिसत नाहीत, जोपर्यंत आपण export करत नाही. दुसऱ्या file मध्ये import करून ते वापरता येतात. यामुळे code लहान, वेगळ्या, reusable files मध्ये ठेवता येतो.
⚠ Why this folder's demo shows nothing in the browser (verified)
  1. class parson { constructor(){ super() } }: super() is only allowed in a class that extends another class → SyntaxError: 'super' keyword unexpected here (verified in Node). A SyntaxError in an imported module stops the WHOLE module graph, so app.js never runs.
  2. app.js imports './sort.js', which does not exist in the folder → a 404 network error, and again nothing runs.
  3. "./exportImport" has no extension: browsers don't guess extensions, so it must be "./exportImport.js".
  4. Opening index.html by double-clicking (file://) blocks module loading (CORS). Serve the folder (e.g. VS Code Live Server / npx serve).
हा demo browser मध्ये चालत नाही: (1) extends शिवाय super() मुळे SyntaxError, (2) sort.js file अस्तित्वातच नाही, (3) import path मध्ये .js नाही, (4) file:// वरून module load होत नाही, म्हणून Live Server वापरा.

2. Exporting (exportImport.js)

Your Notes:
Exporting variables and functions
// how to export variables, functions and classes from a module and reuse them in another module.
// ES6 module files are executed in strict mode only (which means that any variable or function declared in the
// module won't be added automatically to the global scope)

// You cannot export an anonymous function or class using this syntax (a named export needs a name;
// only "export default" can be anonymous).

// the export statement exposes the message variable to other modules.
export let message = "Hi, vishal";

// to export a variable, function or class, place the export keyword in front of it
export function getMessage() {
  return message
}

export function setMessage(message) {
  message = msg
}
// ✔ msg is not defined → ReferenceError when called; and the parameter "message" SHADOWS the
//    exported variable, so even message = "x" would only change the parameter. Fix:
//    export function setMessage(msg) { message = msg }
  • What happens: export in front of a declaration makes it importable; module code runs in strict mode. setMessage uses an undefined msg and its parameter shadows the exported message.
  • Output: (no output).
  • ⚠ Fix: export function setMessage(msg) { message = msg }.
Exporting a class (and a super() bug)
export class parson {
  constructor() {
    super()
  }
}
// ✔ SyntaxError: 'super' keyword unexpected here. super() needs "extends":
//    export class Person { constructor(name) { this.name = name } }
//    (and the class name should be Person; parson is a typo)
  • What happens: super() without extends is a SyntaxError.
  • Output: SyntaxError.
  • ⚠ Class names in PascalCase: Person.
Export later with export { }
// you can also define the function first and export it later
function foo() {
  return "Hello"
}
function bar() {
  return "buy"
}
export { foo };
// here we export the foo function to other modules, but not bar, because bar is not exported (so it is a private function)
  • What happens: define functions first, export only some; bar stays private to the module.
  • Output: (no output).
  • ✅ Clear list of the module's public API.
setMessage मध्ये msg कुठेही define नाही, आणि parameter चे नाव message असल्यामुळे बाहेरचा message झाकला जातो. setMessage(msg) { message = msg } असे लिहा. extends नसताना super() वापरल्यास SyntaxError येतो.

3. Importing (app.js)

Your Notes: 
// First specify what to import inside the curly braces; these are called bindings
import { message } from "./exportImport";   // this is called a NAMED import
// ✔ the comment said "nameSpace import". { message } is a NAMED import; a namespace import is
//    "import * as data" (below). Also add the extension: "./exportImport.js"

// if you want to import everything from the module (as a single object), use the * symbol
import * as data from "./exportImport"
console.log(data);   // → [Module] { foo, getMessage, message, parson, setMessage }   (the namespace object)

// To import both the default and the non-default bindings, specify a list of bindings after the import
// keyword with the following rules:
// The default binding must come first
// The non-default bindings must be surrounded by curly braces
import sort, { heapSort } from './sort.js'   // ⚠ sort.js does not exist in this folder → 404
sort([2, 1, 3]);
heapSort([3, 2, 1])

// To rename the default export, use the as keyword as follows:
// (your note has no example; here it is)
import { default as mySort } from './sort.js';   // rename the default
import { heapSort as hs } from './sort.js';       // rename a named import

const h1 = document.createElement('h1')
h1.textContent = message;   // → shows "Hi, vishal" on the page
document.body.appendChild(h1)
  • What happens: named imports use { }; * as data imports everything as one namespace object; default + named imports combine; as renames.
  • Output: the namespace object, then Hi, vishal on the page.
  • ⚠ Use file extensions (./x.js) in browsers; missing files → 404.

4. Loading Modules in HTML (index.html)

<body>
  <script type="module" src="app.js"></script>
</body>
  • What happens: type="module" lets the browser load ES modules.
  • Output: (markup).
  • ⚠ Modules don't work from file:// in most browsers; use a local server.
type="module" is required: without it, the import/export keywords give a SyntaxError ("Cannot use import statement outside a module"). Module scripts are deferred automatically (they run after the HTML is parsed), so the document.body code works even with the script in <head>.

5. Named vs Default Exports (complete, verified example)

// sort.js
export default function sort(a) { return [...a].sort((x, y) => x - y); }   // ONE default per module
export function heapSort(a) { return sort(a); }                             // any number of named exports

// app.js
import sort, { heapSort } from "./sort.js";   // default first, then {named}
import whateverName from "./sort.js";         // a default import can take ANY name
console.log(sort([2, 1, 3]), heapSort([3, 2, 1]));   // → [1, 2, 3] [1, 2, 3]

// other forms
export { foo as hello };                 // rename while exporting
export * from "./utils.js";              // re-export everything (barrel file)
const mod = await import("./sort.js");   // dynamic import → a Promise (lazy loading)
  • What happens: one default export per module (import with any name) + any number of named exports; renaming, re-exporting, dynamic import().
  • Output: [1, 2, 3] [1, 2, 3].
  • ✅ Dynamic import loads code lazily (code splitting).
Named exportDefault export
How manyMany per moduleAt most one
Syntaxexport const a / export { a }export default value
Importimport { a } (exact name, or { a as b })import anyName
Anonymous allowed?NoYes (export default function () {})
Figure 150: Modules: only exported names are visible to importers; imports are live, read-only bindings.

6. Live Bindings & Other Module Features (verified in Node)

import { message, setMessage } from "./fixed.js";
console.log(message);   // → Hi, vishal
setMessage("changed");
console.log(message);   // → changed   (imports are LIVE: they see the exporter's updates)
message = "x";          // ❌ TypeError: Assignment to constant variable (imports are read-only for the importer)
console.log(this);      // → undefined (module top level, strict mode)
  • What happens: imports are LIVE read-only bindings: they see the exporter's changes but can't be reassigned; top-level this is undefined in modules.
  • Output: Hi, vishal, changed, TypeError, undefined.
  • Each module is evaluated once; every importer shares the same instance (a natural singleton).
  • Imports are hoisted: they are resolved before any code in the file runs.
  • Module scope: top-level variables are not window properties.
  • CommonJS (Node's older system) uses require / module.exports: synchronous and value copies, vs ESM's import/export: static and live bindings.
import केलेली value "live" असते: export करणाऱ्या file ने ती बदलली तर import करणाऱ्याला नवीन value दिसते. पण import करणारा ती थेट बदलू शकत नाही (TypeError). module एकदाच चालतो आणि सगळे importers तेच instance वापरतात.

7. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. Named export vs default export?
  • Named: many per file, imported with the exact name in {} (can be renamed with as). Default: one per file, imported with any name and no braces. Named exports are better for tree-shaking and refactoring.
Q2. What is a namespace import?
  • import * as ns from "./m.js": ns is an object holding all the named exports (plus ns.default if one exists).
Q3. ES modules vs CommonJS?
  • ESM: import/export, static (analysed before running), live bindings, async loading, strict mode, top-level await. CJS: require/module.exports, dynamic, a copied value, synchronous; the default in older Node.
Q4. What is dynamic import() and when do you use it?
  • import("./x.js") returns a Promise of the module; it is used for lazy loading / code splitting (load a page's code only when needed).
Q5. Why does "Cannot use import statement outside a module" happen?
  • The file is loaded as a classic script. Use <script type="module"> in the browser, or "type": "module" / .mjs in Node.
Q6. Output-based questions
// counter.js
export let count = 0;
export const inc = () => count++;
// main.js
import { count, inc } from "./counter.js";
inc(); inc();
console.log(count);            // → 2 (live binding)
import * as c from "./counter.js";
console.log(typeof c.inc);     // → function
// export default const x = 1; → SyntaxError (default takes an expression: export default 1)
  • What happens: live binding with a counter; namespace import exposes the functions; export default can't take a declaration with const.
  • Output: 2, function.
SyntaxMeaning
export let a / export function fNamed export
export { a, b as c }Export a list / rename
export default xDefault export (one)
import { a } from "./m.js"Named import
import * as m from "./m.js"Namespace import
import d, { a } from "./m.js"Default + named
import("./m.js")Dynamic (Promise)
थोडक्यात: export ने बाहेर द्या, import ने घ्या. named अनेक असू शकतात आणि {} मध्ये import होतात; default एकच असतो आणि कोणत्याही नावाने import होतो. * as = सगळे एका object मध्ये. browser मध्ये type="module", path मध्ये .js, आणि server लागतो. imports live पण read-only असतात.

Chapter 86: Polyfills I: Array MethodsWhat a polyfill is · map · filter · forEach · reduce · NEW: some, every, find, findIndex, includes, flat, Array.from
CHAPTER 86 INDEX
  1. What is a Polyfill?
  2. map() Polyfill
  3. filter() Polyfill
  4. forEach() Polyfill
  5. reduce() Polyfill
  6. NEW: some() & every()
  7. NEW: find() & findIndex()
  8. NEW: includes()
  9. NEW: flat()
  10. NEW: Array.from()
  11. Interview Questions & Revision

1. What is a Polyfill?

Your Notes (33_polyfill/index.html): a polyfill is a piece of code (typically JavaScript) that provides modern functionality in older environments that do not natively support it. 
<p> polyfill is a piece of code (typically JavaScript) that provides modern functionality on older environments that do not natively support it</p>
<script src="fullExampleOfPolyfill.js"></script>
  • What happens: a polyfill adds a missing modern feature to old environments.
  • Output: (markup).
Definition: A polyfill re-implements a STANDARD built-in (Array.prototype.map, Promise, Function.prototype.bind…) in plain JS, usually guarded with if (!Array.prototype.flat) { … }, so old browsers get the same feature. In interviews, "write the polyfill of X" means: re-create X's exact behaviour (arguments, this, return value, edge cases such as sparse arrays and errors). Real projects use core-js / Babel instead of hand-written ones.
Polyfill म्हणजे जुन्या browser मध्ये नसलेले नवीन standard feature (map, bind, Promise) आपण स्वतः JS मध्ये लिहून देणे. interview मध्ये "polyfill लिहा" म्हणजे त्या method चे हुबेहूब वागणे (arguments, this, return value, sparse array, errors) पुन्हा तयार करणे.
Checklist for every array polyfill (what interviewers look for):
  1. Put it on Array.prototype with a function (not an arrow), because this = the array.
  2. Validate the callback: throw new TypeError(cb + " is not a function").
  3. Pass (element, index, array) to the callback, and support thisArg with cb.call(thisArg, …).
  4. Skip holes in sparse arrays with i in this (map must KEEP the hole positions).
  5. Return exactly what the native method returns (new array / undefined / single value / boolean / index).

2. map() Polyfill

Your Notes (mapPolyfill.js): 1. Array.map(callback(element, index, arr) => {})
Example 1
Array.prototype.myMap = function (callback) {
  // map returns a new array with transformed elements, so use an empty array to store the
  // resulting values after applying the callback function
  let temp = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < this.length; i++) {
    temp.push(callback(this[i], i, this));
  }
  return temp;
};
let num = [1, 2, 3, 4];
let newArr = num.myMap((ele, index, arr) => {
  return ele * 2;
});
console.log(newArr);   // → [2, 4, 6, 8]
  • What happens: myMap on Array.prototype: this is the array; the callback's results are pushed into a new array.
  • Output: [2, 4, 6, 8].
  • ✅ Shows how map works inside.
  • ⚠ push compacts holes; real map keeps them.
using the call method
// # using the call method
Array.prototype.myMap1 = function (callback, thisArg) {
  if (typeof callback !== "function") {
    throw new Error(callback + "is not function");
  }
  let temp = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < this.length; i++) {
    // Check if the index exists in the array (important for sparse arrays)
    if (i in this) {
      temp.push(callback.call(thisArg, this[i], i, this))
    }
  }
  return temp
};
let output = num.myMap1((ele, index, arr) => {
  return ele * 3
})
console.log(output)   // → [3, 6, 9, 12]
  • What happens: adds a function check, thisArg via call, and skips holes with `i in this`.
  • Output: [3, 6, 9, 12].
  • ⚠ push still shifts results after holes; write out[i] instead.
✔ (verified in Node) with a sparse array, push() SHIFTS the results: [1, , 3].myMap1(x => x*2) → [2, 6], but native map gives [2, <empty>, 6] (same length, hole kept). Fix: write by index, temp[i] = …, with temp = new Array(this.length). Also: throw a TypeError (not Error), with a space: callback + " is not a function".sparse array मध्ये push वापरल्याने results पुढे सरकतात आणि length कमी होते. native map hole जागेवरच ठेवतो, म्हणून temp[i] = ... असे index ने लिहा. 
// ✅ fixed map polyfill (verified: [1, , 3] → [2, <1 empty item>, 6])
Array.prototype.myMap = function (cb, thisArg) {
  if (typeof cb !== "function") throw new TypeError(cb + " is not a function");
  const out = new Array(this.length);
  for (let i = 0; i < this.length; i++) {
    if (i in this) out[i] = cb.call(thisArg, this[i], i, this);
  }
  return out;
};
  • What happens: the fixed version keeps holes in place (new Array(length) + out[i]) and throws TypeError like the real map.
  • Output: [2, <1 empty item>, 6] for [1, , 3].
  • ✅ Matches the built-in behaviour.
What is the use of thisArg in map(), filter() and forEach()?
  1. thisArg is an optional parameter.
  2. thisArg lets you specify a custom this value for the callback function (i.e. the value used as this inside the callback).
  3. If it is not provided, this defaults to undefined.
  4. thisArg sets the this context inside the callback function.
Note: thisArg has NO effect on arrow-function callbacks (arrows take this from outside), so test it with a normal function: [1].map(function () { return this.k; }, { k: 5 }) → [5].

3. filter() Polyfill

Your Notes (filterPolyfill.js): Array.filter((element, index, array) => {})
Example 1
// polyfill of the filter method
Array.prototype.myFilter = function (callback) {
  // the filter method returns a new array with the resulting elements.
  let temp = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < this.length; i++) {
    if (callback(this[i], i, this)) {
      temp.push(this[i]);
    }
  }
  return temp;
};
let arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
let output = arr.myFilter((element, index, arr) => {
  return element > 3;
});
console.log(output);   // → [4, 5]
  • What happens: myFilter pushes only the items whose callback returns truthy.
  • Output: [4, 5].
using the call method
// # using the call method
Array.prototype.myFilter1 = function (callback, thisArg) {
  if (typeof callback !== "function") {
    throw new Error(callback + "not a function ");
  }
  // Create a new array to store the filtered results
  let temp = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < this.length; i++) {
    // Check if the index exists in the array (important for sparse arrays)
    if (i in this) {
      if (callback.call(thisArg, this[i], i, this)) {
        temp.push(this[i]);
      }
    }
  }
  return temp;
};
let data = arr.myFilter1((ele, i, arr) => {
  return ele < 3;
})
console.log(data);   // → [1, 2]
// ✅ myFilter1 is correct (here push IS right: filter's result has no holes). Use TypeError + a space in the message.
  • What happens: with a type check, thisArg and hole skipping.
  • Output: [1, 2].
  • ✅ Correct: filter's result never has holes, so push is right here.

4. forEach() Polyfill

Your Notes (forEachPolyfill.js):
  1. arr.forEach(callback(element, index, arr) => {})
  2. Does not return a new array; the CALLBACK can modify the original array (forEach itself changes nothing). ✔ "modified original arr". forEach doesn't modify anything by itself; in your example the callback does it with arr[i] = ….forEach स्वतः array बदलत नाही; तुमच्या उदाहरणात callback मधील arr[i] = ... ने array बदलतो.
  3. Iterates over each element of the array by calling the given callback function.
  4. It always returns undefined.
  5. It is used for performing side effects, like logging, updating the UI or modifying objects.
polyfill of forEach
// # polyfill of forEach
Array.prototype.myForEach = function (callback) {
  for (let i = 0; i < this.length; i++) {
    callback(this[i], i, this);
  }
};
let num = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
let data = num.myForEach((ele, i, arr) => {
  return (arr[i] = ele * 2);
});
console.log(data);   // → undefined
console.log(num);    // → [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
  • What happens: myForEach calls the callback for each item and returns undefined; the callback mutates the array here.
  • Output: undefined, [2, 4, 6, 8, 10].
using the call method
// # using the call method
Array.prototype.myForEach1 = function (callback, thisArg) {
  if (typeof callback !== "function") {
    throw new Error(callback + "not a function");
  }
  for (let i = 0; i < this.length; i++) {
    // hasOwnProperty(): only checks whether the property exists as an own (direct) property of the object, not on its prototype.
    if (this.hasOwnProperty(i)) {
      callback.call(thisArg, this[i], i, this);
    }
  }
};
let modifiedArray = num.myForEach1((ele, i, arr) => {
  console.log(ele, i, arr);   // → 2 0 [2,4,6,8,10] … 10 4 [8,16,24,32,10]
  return (arr[i] = ele * 4);
});
console.log(modifiedArray);   // → undefined
// (note: arr is printed AFTER earlier items were changed, so you see the array mutating step by step)
  • What happens: with a type check, thisArg and own-index check (skips holes).
  • Output: the logs, undefined.

5. reduce() Polyfill

Your Notes (reducePolyfill.js): array.reduce(callback(accumulator, currentValue, index, array) => {})
  1. accumulator: accumulates the value of the previous computation (iteration).
The reduce method reduces an array to a single value by applying a callback function to each element, accumulating the result on each iteration, and returns a single value as output.
The reduce method has 2 parameters:
  1. the callback function;
  2. the initial value.
Array.prototype.myReduce = function (callback, initialValue) {
  let accumulator = initialValue !== undefined ? initialValue : this[0]
  let startIndex = initialValue !== undefined ? 0 : 1
  // here, if you don't give an initial value, the accumulator takes the first element's value by default,
  // and the current element starts from the 2nd element.
  // The callback is called with the current accumulator, the current element this[i], the index i, and the array itself (this).
  for (let i = startIndex; i < this.length; i++) {
    accumulator = callback(accumulator, this[i], i, this)
    // If no initialValue is provided, the first element of the array is used as the accumulator,
    // and no callback is invoked for the first element.
  }
  return accumulator;
}
let arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
let output = arr.myReduce((acc, ele, i, arr) => {
  return acc + ele
})
console.log(output)   // → 15
  • What happens: myReduce: start from the initial value, or from the first item and index 1.
  • Output: 15.
  • ⚠ Fails for an empty array without an initial value, and when the initial value is undefined on purpose.
✔ (verified in Node) (1) [].myReduce(fn) returns undefined, but native reduce throws TypeError: Reduce of empty array with no initial value. (2) Passing an initial value of undefined on purpose is treated as "no initial value"; check the ARGUMENT COUNT instead (arguments.length / rest). (3) Holes are not skipped.रिकाम्या array वर native reduce TypeError देतो, तर तुमचा polyfill undefined देतो. initial value आहे की नाही हे undefined तपासून नाही, तर arguments ची संख्या तपासून ठरवा. 
// ✅ fixed reduce polyfill (verified: [] → TypeError, [1,2,3] → 6, [[1],[2]] with [] → [1, 2])
Array.prototype.myReduce = function (cb, ...init) {
  if (typeof cb !== "function") throw new TypeError(cb + " is not a function");
  let i = 0, acc;
  if (init.length) acc = init[0];
  else {
    while (i < this.length && !(i in this)) i++;   // find the first real element
    if (i >= this.length) throw new TypeError("Reduce of empty array with no initial value");
    acc = this[i++];
  }
  for (; i < this.length; i++) if (i in this) acc = cb(acc, this[i], i, this);
  return acc;
};
  • What happens: fixed reduce: uses ...init to know whether an initial value was given, skips holes, throws TypeError for an empty array.
  • Output: TypeError for [], 6, [1, 2].
  • ✅ Exactly like the built-in.

6. NEW: some() & every()

Added (not in your folder), verified in Node: 
Array.prototype.mySome = function (cb, thisArg) {
  for (let i = 0; i < this.length; i++)
    if (i in this && cb.call(thisArg, this[i], i, this)) return true;   // stop at the first true
  return false;
};
Array.prototype.myEvery = function (cb, thisArg) {
  for (let i = 0; i < this.length; i++)
    if (i in this && !cb.call(thisArg, this[i], i, this)) return false; // stop at the first false
  return true;
};
[1, 2, 3].mySome((x) => x > 2);    // true
[1, 2, 3].myEvery((x) => x > 0);   // true
[].myEvery(() => false);           // true  (vacuous truth: no element fails)
  • What happens: some returns true at the first passing item; every returns false at the first failing one; empty arrays: every → true.
  • Output: true, true, true.

7. NEW: find() & findIndex()

Array.prototype.myFind = function (cb, thisArg) {
  for (let i = 0; i < this.length; i++)   // NOTE: find visits holes too (as undefined); no "i in this"
    if (cb.call(thisArg, this[i], i, this)) return this[i];
  return undefined;
};
Array.prototype.myFindIndex = function (cb, thisArg) {
  for (let i = 0; i < this.length; i++)
    if (cb.call(thisArg, this[i], i, this)) return i;
  return -1;
};
[5, 12, 8].myFind((x) => x > 10);         // 12
[5, 12, 8].myFindIndex((x) => x > 100);   // -1
  • What happens: find returns the first matching item (it visits holes); findIndex returns its index or -1.
  • Output: 12, -1.

8. NEW: includes()

Array.prototype.myIncludes = function (search, fromIndex = 0) {
  let i = fromIndex < 0 ? Math.max(this.length + fromIndex, 0) : fromIndex;
  for (; i < this.length; i++) {
    // SameValueZero: like === but NaN equals NaN
    if (this[i] === search || (search !== search && this[i] !== this[i])) return true;
  }
  return false;
};
[1, NaN].myIncludes(NaN);   // true   (indexOf(NaN) would give -1)
[1, 2].myIncludes("1");     // false  (no type conversion)
  • What happens: includes uses SameValueZero: like === but NaN equals NaN; a negative fromIndex counts from the end.
  • Output: true, false.
  • ✅ Interview: why includes finds NaN but indexOf doesn't.

9. NEW: flat() (an interview favourite)

Array.prototype.myFlat = function (depth = 1) {
  const out = [];
  const go = (arr, d) => {
    for (let i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
      if (!(i in arr)) continue;                        // flat removes holes
      Array.isArray(arr[i]) && d > 0 ? go(arr[i], d - 1) : out.push(arr[i]);
    }
  };
  go(this, depth);
  return out;
};
[1, [2, [3, [4]]]].myFlat();           // [1, 2, [3, [4]]]
[1, [2, [3, [4]]]].myFlat(Infinity);   // [1, 2, 3, 4]
  • What happens: recursive flat with a depth; holes are dropped.
  • Output: [1, 2, [3, [4]]], [1, 2, 3, 4].

10. NEW: Array.from()

Array.myFrom = function (source, mapFn) {
  const out = [];
  let i = 0;
  const iterable = source[Symbol.iterator] ? source : Array.prototype.slice.call(source);   // array-likes {length: n}
  for (const v of iterable) out.push(mapFn ? mapFn(v, i++) : v);
  return out;
};
Array.myFrom("abc");                            // ['a', 'b', 'c']
Array.myFrom({ length: 3 }, (_, i) => i * 2);   // [0, 2, 4]
Array.myFrom(new Set([1, 1, 2]));               // [1, 2]
  • What happens: Array.from polyfill: iterate an iterable (or slice an array-like), optionally mapping.
  • Output: ['a','b','c'], [0, 2, 4], [1, 2].
Figure 151: The common template behind every array-method polyfill.

11. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. Why use a function (not an arrow) for prototype polyfills?
  • Inside a prototype method, this must be the array the method was called on; an arrow would capture the outer this (window/undefined).
Q2. What edge cases make a map polyfill "correct"?
  • Callback type check (TypeError), thisArg via call, passing (el, i, arr), preserving holes in sparse arrays (out[i] = …, same length), and not visiting elements appended during iteration (cache the length).
Q3. How does reduce behave without an initial value?
  • It uses the first (existing) element as the accumulator and starts at the next index; on an empty array it throws a TypeError.
Q4. Why is modifying Array.prototype risky?
  • Assignment makes the method enumerable (it appears in for…in), and it may clash with future standard names or other libraries. Real polyfills use Object.defineProperty(…, {enumerable: false}) and only add a method if it is missing.
Q5. Output-based questions
console.log([1, , 3].map((x) => x * 2));            // → [2, <1 empty item>, 6]
console.log([].every(() => false), [].some(() => true));   // → true false
console.log([NaN].indexOf(NaN), [NaN].includes(NaN));      // → -1 true
console.log([1, [2, [3]]].flat());                        // → [1, 2, [3]]
console.log([1, 2, 3].reduce((a, b) => a + b, ""));       // → "123"
  • What happens: five output questions on map holes, empty every/some, NaN search, flat depth, string reduce.
  • Output: [2, <1 empty item>, 6], true false, -1 true, [1, 2, [3]], "123".
PolyfillReturnsKey detail
mapNew array, same lengthKeep holes (out[i] =)
filterNew array of matchespush only truthy
forEachundefinedSide effects only
reduceA single valueNo init → first element; empty → TypeError
some / everyBooleanShort-circuit; [].every → true
find / findIndexElement / indexundefined / -1
includesBooleanNaN-aware
flatNew arrayDepth (default 1), recursion
थोडक्यात: array polyfill = Array.prototype वर function, callback check, cb.call(thisArg, el, i, arr), holes skip करा, आणि native सारखाच return करा. map ने holes जपावे, reduce ने रिकाम्या array वर TypeError द्यावा. some/every/find/includes/flat हे नवीन polyfills interview साठी जोडले आहेत.
