Chapter 87: Polyfills II: call, apply, bind, once & Object Helperscall · apply · bind · once · NEW: Object.assign · Object.create · deepClone
CHAPTER 87 INDEX
  1. The Trick Behind call/apply/bind
  2. call() Polyfill
  3. apply() Polyfill
  4. bind() Polyfill
  5. Fixed call/apply/bind (verified)
  6. once() Polyfill
  7. NEW: Object.assign()
  8. NEW: Object.create()
  9. NEW: deepClone (structuredClone-like)
  10. Interview Questions & Revision

1. The Trick Behind call / apply / bind

Idea: this inside a function is the object before the dot (implicit binding, Chapter 37). So to run fn with this = ctx, temporarily put fn ON ctx (ctx.temp = fn), call ctx.temp(...args), then delete the property. call takes the arguments one by one, apply takes an array, and bind returns a NEW function that does this later.
Figure 152: How a call/apply polyfill sets this: attach the function to the context, call it, delete it.
call/apply/bind चा polyfill: function ला थोड्या वेळासाठी context object वर property म्हणून ठेवा, मग ctx.fn() असा call करा (त्यामुळे this = ctx होतो), आणि नंतर ती property काढून टाका. call ला arguments वेगवेगळे, apply ला array मध्ये, आणि bind नवीन function परत करतो.

2. Polyfill of the call() Method

Your Notes (callPolyfill.js): 1. It belongs to the prototype of Function. 
Function.prototype.myCall = function (context = {}, ...args) {
  // Default context: if no context is provided, a default empty object {} is used to avoid errors.
  // Check if 'this' is a function, as myCall can only be called on functions
  if (typeof this !== "function") {
    throw new Error(this + " is not callable");   // Throw an error if 'this' is not a function
  }
  // Assign the function (which 'this' refers to) to a property on the context object
  // so here we insert the function into the context and try to call it from there.
  // This allows us to call the function with the provided context
  context.fun = this;
  // then we need to use the arguments:
  // call the function using the context object and the provided arguments;
  // the function executes with 'context' as 'this' and 'args' as the parameters
  const result = context.fun(...args);
  // Remove the temporary 'fun' property from the context object
  // This cleanup is important to avoid polluting the context object
  delete context.fun;
  // Return the result of the function call
  return result;
};

let car = {
  color: "red",
  company: "Ferrari",
};
function purChanCar(currency, price) {
  console.log(`i have punchedCar ${this.company} car with color ${this.color} and price are ${currency} ${price}`);
}
purChanCar.myCall(car, "$", 90);
// → i have punchedCar Ferrari car with color red and price are $ 90
  • What happens: myCall temporarily puts the function on the context object (context.fun = this) and calls it as context.fun(...args), so this becomes the context; then it deletes the helper property.
  • Output: i have punchedCar Ferrari … $ 90.
  • ✅ Explains how call() sets this.
  • ⚠ context.fun could overwrite a real "fun" property; a Symbol key is safer.
✔ (verified in Node) (1) A default of {} differs from native call: fn.call() / fn.call(null) uses globalThis (non-strict) / undefined (strict). (2) A primitive context fails: purChanCar.myCall("str") → TypeError: context.fun is not a function (you can't add a property to a string); wrap it with Object(context). (3) The name "fun" would OVERWRITE a real property called fun on the object; use a unique Symbol key.default {} native सारखा नाही; primitive context ("str") वर property जोडता येत नाही म्हणून TypeError येतो; आणि "fun" नावामुळे object वरची खरी fun property overwrite होऊ शकते. उपाय: Object(ctx) आणि Symbol key.

3. Polyfill of the apply() Method

Your Notes (applyPolyfill.js):
  1. It belongs to the prototype of Function.
  2. The context is an object.
Function.prototype.myApply = function (context = {}, args = []) {
  // Check if 'this' is a function, as myApply can only be called on functions
  if (typeof this !== "function") {
    throw new Error(this + " is not callable");   // Throw an error if 'this' is not a function
  }
  // Check if args is an array
  if (!Array.isArray(args)) {
    throw new Error("Please provide the arguments as an array");   // Throw an error if args is not an array
  }
  // Assign the function (which 'this' refers to) to a property on the context object,
  // i.e. the object borrows the method (put the function inside the context to call it with the provided this value)
  context.fun = this;
  // Call the function using the context object and the arguments array
  const result = context.fun(...args);
  // Remove the temporary 'fun' property from the context object (avoid polluting it)
  delete context.fun;
  // Return the result of the function call
  return result;
};
let car = { color: "red", company: "Ferrari" };
function purChanCar(currency, price) {
  console.log(`i have punchedCar ${this.company} car with color ${this.color} and price are ${currency} ${price}`);
}
purChanCar.myApply(car, ["$", 90]);
// → i have punchedCar Ferrari car with color red and price are $ 90
  • What happens: myApply is the same, but the arguments come as an array (checked with Array.isArray).
  • Output: same sentence.
  • ⚠ apply(ctx) with no array should work; default args = [] handles it.
Note: native apply also accepts array-LIKE objects (e.g. arguments) and null/undefined for args, so Array.isArray is stricter than the real thing.

4. Polyfill of the bind() Method

Your Notes (bindPolyfill.js): 1. It also belongs to Function.prototype. 
Function.prototype.myBind = function (context = {}, ...args) {
  // First, check whether 'this' is a function:
  // bind can only be called on functions, so this ensures it's callable
  if (typeof this !== "function") {
    throw new Error(this + " are not callable");   // Throw an error if 'this' is not a function
  }
  // this assigns the function to a property of the context object.
  // Store a reference to the function in a temporary property on the context object;
  // this allows us to call the function with the specified context
  // (so we bind this function explicitly to the given object)
  context.fun = this;
  // The bind method returns a new function with the specified 'this' context.
  // This new function can be called later with additional arguments
  return function (...next) {
    // Call the original function using the context and both sets of arguments
    context.fun(...args, ...next);
  };
};
let car = { color: "red", company: "Ferrari" };
function purChanCar(currency, price) {
  console.log(`i have punchedCar ${this.company} car with color ${this.color} and price are ${currency} ${price}`);
}
// const newFunction = purChanCar.bind(car, "$", 90)
// newFunction();
const newFunction = purChanCar.myBind(car);
newFunction("$", 90);
// → i have punchedCar Ferrari car with color red and price are $ 90
  • What happens: myBind returns a new function that later calls the original with the saved context and both argument lists (partial application).
  • Output: same sentence.
  • ⚠ This version doesn't return the result and breaks with new.
✔ (verified in Node) (1) The returned function has no return, so a bound function that returns a value gives undefined (getN.myBind(car)() → undefined instead of the value). (2) car.fun is never deleted: the object is permanently polluted (typeof car.fun → "function"). (3) Native bind also works with new (the bound this is ignored and a new instance is created).bind polyfill मध्ये return राहिला आहे, म्हणून value परत मिळत नाही. car.fun कधीच delete होत नाही. आणि native bind new सोबतही चालतो.

5. Fixed call / apply / bind (verified in Node)

Function.prototype.myCall = function (ctx, ...args) {
  if (typeof this !== "function") throw new TypeError(this + " is not a function");
  ctx = ctx == null ? globalThis : Object(ctx);   // null/undefined → global; primitives → wrapper objects
  const key = Symbol("fn");                         // unique: never overwrites a real property
  ctx[key] = this;
  const result = ctx[key](...args);
  delete ctx[key];
  return result;
};
Function.prototype.myApply = function (ctx, args) {
  return this.myCall(ctx, ...(args ?? []));
};
Function.prototype.myBind = function (ctx, ...preset) {
  const fn = this;
  function bound(...rest) {
    return new.target
      ? new fn(...preset, ...rest)                  // called with new → ignore ctx
      : fn.myCall(ctx, ...preset, ...rest);          // ✅ returns the result
  }
  bound.prototype = Object.create(fn.prototype);    // instanceof keeps working
  return bound;
};
const c2 = { n: 7 };
function getN() { return this.n; }
getN.myCall(c2); getN.myApply(c2, []); getN.myBind(c2)();   // 7 7 7, and c2 keys stay ['n']
function P2(a, b) { this.s = a + b; }
const BP = P2.myBind(null, 1);
new BP(2).s;              // 3
new BP(2) instanceof P2;  // true
  • What happens: improved call/apply/bind: null → globalThis, primitives wrapped, a Symbol key avoids clashes, bind returns the result and supports new (instanceof still works).
  • Output: 7 7 7, 3, true.
  • ✅ Interview-ready versions.

6. once() Polyfill

Your Notes (oncePolyfill.js):
  1. It ensures that a function is executed only once.
  2. once limits a function's execution, i.e. the function is executed only once.
// once polyfill
function once(fun, context) {
  let run;
  return function (...args) {
    if (fun) {
      run = fun.apply(context || this, args);
      fun = null;   // Ensure the function is not called again
    }
    return run;     // Return the result of the first call
  };
}
const add = (num1) => {
  console.log(num1 * num1)
}
const called = once(add);
called(10);   // → 100
called(20)    // (nothing: already ran)
called(40)    // (nothing)
// ✅ correct (it's a closure + HOF; setting fun = null also lets the original be garbage-collected).
// (the helper is named "add" but it squares the number → name it square)
  • What happens: once runs the function the first time, stores the result, and sets fun = null so later calls just return the stored result.
  • Output: 100, then nothing.
  • ✅ Prevents double initialisation.
Note: once isn't a built-in, so strictly it's a utility (like lodash _.once), not a polyfill.

7. NEW: Object.assign() Polyfill

function myAssign(target, ...sources) {
  if (target == null) throw new TypeError("Cannot convert undefined or null to object");
  const to = Object(target);
  for (const src of sources) {
    if (src == null) continue;                            // null/undefined sources are skipped
    for (const key of Reflect.ownKeys(src)) {             // own string + Symbol keys
      if (Object.prototype.propertyIsEnumerable.call(src, key)) to[key] = src[key];
    }
  }
  return to;   // shallow copy; later sources win
}
myAssign({ a: 1 }, { b: 2 }, null, { a: 3 });   // { a: 3, b: 2 }
  • What happens: Object.assign polyfill: copies own enumerable string and Symbol keys from each source into the target; null sources are skipped; later sources win.
  • Output: { a: 3, b: 2 }.
  • ⚠ Shallow copy only.

8. NEW: Object.create() Polyfill

function myCreate(proto) {
  if (proto !== null && typeof proto !== "object" && typeof proto !== "function")
    throw new TypeError("Object prototype may only be an Object or null");
  function F() {}
  F.prototype = proto;          // the classic pre-ES5 trick
  const obj = new F();          // obj.__proto__ === proto
  if (proto === null) Object.setPrototypeOf(obj, null);
  return obj;
}
myCreate({ hi() { return "hi"; } }).hi();     // "hi"
Object.getPrototypeOf(myCreate(null));        // null
  • What happens: Object.create polyfill: a temporary constructor whose prototype is proto creates the linked object.
  • Output: "hi", null.

9. NEW: deepClone (a structuredClone-like helper)

function deepClone(value, seen = new WeakMap()) {
  if (value === null || typeof value !== "object") return value;   // primitives (and functions) as-is
  if (seen.has(value)) return seen.get(value);                      // circular references
  if (value instanceof Date) return new Date(value);
  const out = Array.isArray(value) ? [] : Object.create(Object.getPrototypeOf(value));
  seen.set(value, out);
  for (const key of Reflect.ownKeys(value)) out[key] = deepClone(value[key], seen);
  return out;
}
const src = { a: [1, { b: 2 }], d: new Date(0) };
src.self = src;
const copy = deepClone(src);
copy.a[1] !== src.a[1];      // true  (nested objects copied)
copy.self === copy;          // true  (the cycle is preserved)
copy.d instanceof Date;      // true
  • What happens: deep clone: recurse into arrays/objects, copy Dates, keep prototypes and handle circular references with a WeakMap.
  • Output: true, true, true.
(Modern built-in: structuredClone(obj); JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) loses Dates, undefined, functions, and breaks on cycles.)

10. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. Write call, apply and bind polyfills. What's the core trick?
  • Implicit binding: temporarily store the function on the context (under a Symbol key), call it as ctx[key](...args), delete it, and return the result. bind returns a closure that does this later and handles new.
Q2. What's wrong with using ctx.fn = this in a call polyfill?
  • It can overwrite an existing fn property, fails for primitive contexts, and leaves garbage if an exception is thrown before delete. Use Object(ctx) plus a Symbol key (and try/finally).
Q3. How does bind behave with new?
  • The bound this is ignored; new creates a fresh instance of the original function (with the preset args). The polyfill checks new.target and sets bound.prototype.
Q4. Shallow vs deep copy polyfills?
  • Object.assign / spread copy one level (nested objects are shared). deepClone recurses, handles cycles with a WeakMap and special types (Date, Map…); structuredClone is the built-in.
Q5. Output-based questions
function f() { return this.x; }
console.log(f.call({ x: 1 }), f.apply({ x: 2 }, []), f.bind({ x: 3 })());   // → 1 2 3
console.log(f.bind({ x: 3 }).bind({ x: 4 })());     // → 3 (bind can't be re-bound)
const once1 = once(() => Math.random());
console.log(once1() === once1());                   // → true
console.log(Object.assign({}, { a: { b: 1 } }).a === Object.assign({}, { a: { b: 1 } }).a);   // → false (two different literals)
  • What happens: four output questions: call/apply/bind, bind can't be re-bound, once returns the same value, assign is shallow.
  • Output: 1 2 3, 3, true, false.
PolyfillKey idea
call(ctx, ...args)ctx[Symbol] = fn; ctx[Symbol](...args); delete
apply(ctx, arr)call with ...arr
bind(ctx, ...pre)Return a function; return the value; support new
once(fn)Closure flag; cache the first result
Object.assignOwn enumerable keys, shallow, later sources win
Object.createfunction F(){}; F.prototype = proto; new F()
deepCloneRecursion + WeakMap for cycles
थोडक्यात: call/apply/bind polyfill मध्ये function ला context वर Symbol key ने ठेवून call करा आणि नंतर delete करा. bind ने नवीन function परत करा, त्याचा return विसरू नका, आणि new ला support द्या. once = closure flag. assign shallow copy करतो, deepClone recursion ने खोल copy करतो.

1. Polyfill of Promise: the Idea

Your Notes (33_polyfill/promisePolyfill.js): constructor myPromise
  1. executor: the executor function is passed when creating a new promise. It receives the resolve and reject functions as arguments.
  2. onResolved and onRejected: these are placeholders for the callbacks passed to .then() and .catch().
  3. isFulfilled and isRejected: flags that indicate whether the promise has been resolved or rejected.
  4. isCalled: ensures the callbacks are only called once.
  5. value and error: store the resolved value or the rejection error if the handlers are not registered yet.
  1. then method: registers a callback to handle the resolved value. If the promise is already resolved, it calls the handler immediately. It returns the same promise object to enable chaining.
  2. catch method: registers a callback to handle the rejection error. If the promise is already rejected, it calls the handler immediately. It returns the same promise object to enable chaining.
  3. resolve function: invokes the success callback if registered; otherwise, stores the value and marks the promise as fulfilled.
  4. reject function: invokes the failure callback if registered; otherwise, stores the error and marks the promise as rejected.
  5. executor call: immediately calls the executor with resolve and reject. It wraps the call in a try/catch to handle any synchronous errors.
Example usage:
  • creates a new myPromise and simulates an asynchronous operation using setTimeout
  • resolves the promise with a value after a delay
  • chains .then() and .catch() to handle the resolved value or errors.

The Promise constructor takes an executor function, and this executor function has 2 arguments: resolve and reject. To consume the promise, we use .then() for a resolved promise and .catch() for a rejected promise.
Promise polyfill ची कल्पना: executor ला resolve/reject functions द्या. then/catch ने दिलेले callbacks साठवून ठेवा. resolve/reject झाल्यावर, callback आधीच दिला असल्यास तो लगेच चालवा, नाहीतर value/error साठवून ठेवा आणि then/catch नंतर दिल्यावर तो चालवा.

2. Your myPromise (promisePolyfill.js)

// here we create new instances of myPromise
function myPromise(executer) {
  var onResolve;   // onResolve is a variable defined to hold the callback for the resolve case
  var onReject;    // onReject is a variable defined to hold the callback for the reject case

  // These variables track whether it is fulfilled or rejected (i.e. whether resolve or reject was called)
  let isFulField = false;
  let isRejected = false;
  // used to store the resolved value
  let value;
  // used to store the rejection value
  let error;
  // used to track whether the handlers (onResolve, onReject) were called or not.
  let isCalled = false;

  // # 1 this.then = function (callback): the then method of the function, which lets you register a callback
  //   function that will be executed when the promise is successfully resolved
  this.then = function (callback) {
    // 2. here we assign the callback to onResolve, so onResolve is now the callback function
    // 3. onResolve can be called later, when the promise is resolved.
    onResolve = callback;
    // if the promise is already resolved and the callback has not been called yet, call it immediately with the resolved value
    if (isFulField && !isCalled) {
      // isCalled = true; onResolve(value);: sets the flag isCalled to true and calls the onResolve callback with the resolved value (value).
      isCalled = true;
      onResolve(value);
    }
    // Allow chaining by returning the same promise object
    return this;
  };

  // # 1 this.catch = function (callback): the catch method, which lets you register a callback function to handle any errors or rejections from the promise.
  this.catch = function (callback) {
    // 2. here we assign the callback to onReject, so onReject is the callback function
    // 3. onReject is called later if the promise is rejected.
    onReject = callback;
    // If the promise was already rejected, call the handler immediately:
    // if the promise is rejected and the callback has not been called yet, it immediately calls the callback with the rejection error
    if (isRejected && !isCalled) {
      isCalled = true;
      // isCalled = true; onReject(error);: sets the flag isCalled to true and calls the onReject callback with the rejection error (error).
      onReject(error);
    }
    // Allow chaining by returning the same promise object
    return this;
  };

  // # so here we define the resolve function to handle a successful async operation with its resulting value.
  function resolve(value) {
    // (synchronous case) check whether onResolve is a function; if not, store the value and mark it as fulfilled
    if (typeof onResolve === "function" && !isCalled) {
      isCalled = true;
      onResolve(value);
    } else {
      isFulField = true;
      value = value;      // ⚠ BUG
    }
  }

  // # so here we define the reject function to handle a failed async operation with its error
  function reject(error) {
    // (synchronous case) check whether onReject is a function; if not, keep the error for the catch block.
    if (typeof onReject === "function" && !isCalled) {
      isCalled = true;
      onReject(error);
    } else {
      error = error;      // ⚠ BUG
      onReject = true;    // ⚠ BUG
    }
  }

  // so here we call the executor function with two arguments, resolve and reject;
  // for error-handling purposes we wrap it in a try/catch block
  try {
    // Immediately invoke the executor function with resolve and reject
    executer(resolve, reject);
  } catch (e) {
    // If an error occurs in the executor, reject the promise
    console.log(error);   // ⚠ BUG
  }
}

let promise = new myPromise((resolve, reject) => {
  setTimeout(() => {
    if (true) {
      resolve("success");
    } else {
      reject("failed");
    }
  });
});
promise
  .then((res) => { console.log(res); })     // → success
  .catch((error) => { console.log(error); });

  • ✅ Shows the core idea: store callbacks until the value arrives.
  • ⚠ No chaining, callbacks run synchronously, can settle more than once.
✔ (all verified in Node) . The demo works only because resolve runs LATER (in setTimeout). With a synchronous executor:
  1. resolve(value): the parameter is named value, so value = value assigns the parameter to ITSELF; the outer value is never stored → new myPromise(r => r(5)).then(console.log) prints undefined. Rename the parameter: function resolve(val) { … value = val; }.
  2. reject(error): same self-assignment, and onReject = true should be isRejected = true → a synchronous reject is silently LOST (the catch never runs).
  3. The executor's catch logs error (the outer, undefined variable) instead of e, and doesn't call reject(e) as its own comment says.
resolve(value) मध्ये parameter चे नाव value असल्यामुळे value = value स्वतःलाच assign होते आणि बाहेरची value साठवली जात नाही. reject मध्ये isRejected ऐवजी onReject = true लिहिले आहे, म्हणून synchronous reject हरवतो. executor च्या catch मध्ये reject(e) करायला हवे.

3. The "Previous Repo" Version (kept in your file as a comment)

// =======================================================================================================================================
// # polyfill of promise
// =======================================================================================================================================
function myPromise(executor) {
  // Variables to store the success and failure handlers
  let onResolved;           // Will hold the callback for the resolve case
  let onRejected;           // Will hold the callback for the reject case
  let isFulfilled = false;  // Tracks whether resolve has been called
  let isRejected = false;   // Tracks whether reject has been called
  let isCalled = false;     // Prevents multiple calls to the handlers
  let value;                // Stores the resolved value
  let error;                // Stores the rejection error

  // this.then = function(callback): the then method, which lets you register a function (callback) that will be executed when the promise is successfully resolved.
  // onResolve = callback;: the callback passed into then is stored in the variable onResolve so it can be called later when the promise is resolved.
  // if(isFulField && !isCalled): if the promise has already been resolved (isFulField is true) and the callback hasn't been called yet (isCalled is false), it immediately calls the callback with the resolved value.
  // isCalled = true; onResolve(value);: sets the flag isCalled to true, to prevent the callback from being invoked multiple times, and calls the onResolve callback with the resolved value (value).
  // - Method to register the resolve handler
  this.then = function (callback) {
    // Assign the callback to onResolved
    onResolved = callback;
    // If the promise was already fulfilled, call the handler immediately
    if (isFulfilled && !isCalled) {
      isCalled = true;
      onResolved(value);
    }
    // Allow chaining by returning the same promise object
    return this;
  };

  // this.catch = function(callback): the catch method, which lets you register a function (callback) to handle any errors or rejections from the promise.
  // onReject = callback;: the callback passed into catch is stored in the variable onReject, to be called later if the promise is rejected.
  // if(isNotFulField && !isCalled): if the promise has been rejected (isNotFulField is true) and the callback hasn't been called yet (isCalled is false), it immediately calls the callback with the rejection error.
  // isCalled = true; onReject(error);: sets the flag isCalled to true and calls the onReject callback with the rejection error (error).
  // - Method to register the reject handler
  this.catch = function (callback) {
    // Assign the callback to onRejected
    onRejected = callback;
    // If the promise was already rejected, call the handler immediately
    if (isRejected && !isCalled) {
      isCalled = true;
      onRejected(error);
    }
    // Allow chaining by returning the same promise object
    return this;
  };

  // function resolved(val): called when the promise is resolved; it takes a value (val) as an argument.
  // if(typeof onResolve === 'function' && !isCalled): if the onResolve callback is defined and hasn't been called yet, it calls onResolve(val) with the resolved value (val), and sets isCalled to true to avoid multiple calls.
  // else { value = val; isFulField = true; }: if the onResolve callback is not defined, it stores the resolved value in value and marks the promise as fulfilled by setting isFulField to true.
  // - Resolve function to handle a successful async operation
  function resolve(result) {
    // If there's a registered success handler and it hasn't been called yet
    if (typeof onResolved === "function" && !isCalled) {
      onResolved(result);
      isCalled = true;
    } else {
      // If no handler is registered yet, store the result
      value = result;
      isFulfilled = true;
    }
  }

  // - for the finally block
  // this.finally = function(callback): the finally method, which lets you register a function (callback) that will always be executed when the promise is settled, whether resolved or rejected.
  // onFinally = callback;: the callback passed into finally is stored in the variable onFinally, to be called later.
  // if(isCalled){ onFinally(); }: if the promise is already settled (isCalled is true), it immediately calls the onFinally callback.

  // function rejected(err): called when the promise is rejected; it takes an error (err) as an argument.
  // if(typeof onReject === 'function' && !isCalled): if the onReject callback is defined and hasn't been called yet, it calls onReject(err) with the rejection error (err), and sets isCalled to true.
  // else { error = err; isNotFulField = true; }: if the onReject callback is not defined, it stores the rejection error in error and marks the promise as rejected by setting isNotFulField to true.
  // Reject function to handle a failed async operation
  function reject(err) {
    // If there's a registered failure handler and it hasn't been called yet
    if (typeof onRejected === "function" && !isCalled) {
      onRejected(err);
      isCalled = true;
    } else {
      // If no handler is registered yet, store the error
      error = err;
      isRejected = true;
    }
  }

  // Immediately invoke the executor function with resolve and reject
  try {
    executor(resolve, reject);
  } catch (err) {
    // If an error occurs in the executor, reject the promise
    reject(err);
  }
}

    console.log("Resolved value:", res);   // Logs: Resolved value: 2
  })
  .catch((error) => {
    console.log("Error:", error);          // Handles any errors (not applicable in this example)
  });

4. Promise.all Polyfill (promiseAllPolyfill.js)

Your Notes: in promise polyfills like Promise.all, Promise.allSettled and Promise.any, I used the forEach method because we need to run code with side effects. forEach is used here because it's the most straightforward way to loop over an array when you're not using the return values, only doing work (side effects) inside the loop.
Loop TypePurposeSuitable?
forEachRunning code with side effects✅ Yes
mapTransforming array elements into a new array❌ No
for...ofClean and readable for looping (with index via entries())✅ Yes
for loopAlso works, but more verbose✅ Yes
What is Promise.all? 1. Promise.all(iterable) takes an array of promises. It returns a single promise that:
  1. resolves when all the promises resolve, with an array of results in order;
  2. rejects immediately when any one promise rejects, with that rejection reason.
Example 1
function myPromisePolyfill(executer) {
  let onResolve, onReject, isFulField = false, isReject = false, value, error;
  let isCalled = false;
  this.then = function (callback) {
    onResolve = callback;
    if (isFulField && !isCalled) {
      isCalled = true;
      onResolve(value);
    }
    return this;
  };
  this.catch = function (callback) {
    onReject = callback;
    // Allow chaining by returning the same promise object
    if (isReject && !isCalled) {
      isCalled = true;
      onReject(error);
    }
    return this;
  };
  function resolve(val) {
    if (typeof onResolve === "function" && !isCalled) {
      isCalled = true;
      onResolve(val);
    }
    value = val;
    isFulField = true;
  }
  function reject(err) {
    if (typeof onReject === "function" && !isCalled) {
      isCalled = true;
      onReject(err);
    } else {
      error = err;
      isReject = true;
    }
  }
  try {
    executer(resolve, reject);
  } catch (error) {
    console.log(error);
    reject(error);
  }
}

5. Promise.allSettled Polyfill (polyfillAllSettled.js)

Your Notes: 1. The allSettled polyfill takes an array as input and returns a single promise with an array that contains the result of every promise, whether resolved or rejected.
What is Promise.allSettled? Promise.allSettled(iterable) takes an array of promises. It returns a new promise that:
  1. always resolves, after all the input promises settle (fulfilled or rejected);
  2. the result is an array of objects describing the outcome of each promise.
function myPromise(executer) {
  // used to store (hold) the callback functions we need to call later
  let onRejected, onResolved;
  // used to check whether it is fulfilled or rejected
  let isFulfilled = false, isRejected = false;
  // we track whether it was called or not
  let isCalled = false;
  let onFinally;
  // used to store the resolved and rejected values
  let error, value;

  this.then = function (cb) {
    // so onResolved is now the callback (we need to call it later with the resolved value)
    onResolved = cb;
    if (isFulfilled && !isCalled) {
      isCalled = true;
      onResolved(value)
    }
    return this;
  };
  this.catch = function (cb) {
    // so onRejected is also a function; if the promise is rejected, call it
    onRejected = cb;
    if (isFulfilled && !isCalled) {   // ⚠ should be isRejected
      isCalled = true;
      onRejected(error);
    }
    // this allows chaining by returning the same object
    return this;
  };
  this.finally = function (cb) {
    onFinally = cb
    if (isFulfilled || isRejected) {
      onFinally();
    }
    return this
  }
  function resolve(val) {
    if (typeof onResolved === "function" && !isCalled) {
      isCalled = true;
      onResolved(val);
    } else {
      isFulfilled = true;
      value = val;
    }
  }
  function reject(err) {
    if (typeof onRejected === "function" && !isCalled) {
      isCalled = true;
      onRejected(err);
    }
    isRejected = true;
    error = err;
  }
  try {
    executer(resolve, reject);
  } catch (error) {
    console.log(error);
    reject(error);
  }
}

p3 = new myPromise((resolved, reject) => { setTimeout(() => { reject("failed to load...."); }, 5000); });

// Define the polyfill
myPromise.myAllSettled = function (promises) {
  return new myPromise((resolve, reject) => {
    let temp = [];
    let completedPromise = 0;
    promises.forEach((promise, index) => {
      promise
        .then((result) => {
          temp[index] = { status: 'fulfilled', value: result };
          completedPromise++;
          if (completedPromise === promises.length) resolve(temp);
        })
        .catch((error) => {
          temp[index] = { status: 'rejected', reason: error };
          completedPromise++;
          if (completedPromise === promises.length) resolve(temp);
        });
    });
  });
};

  console.log(result)
  return result
}).catch((error) => {
  console.error(error)
})

If a promise rejects before .catch is registered, the rejection is never delivered and myAllSettled hangs. Also finally can fire before or without a settled check, and reject() marks isRejected even after calling the handler (harmless here).this.catch मध्ये isRejected ऐवजी isFulfilled तपासले आहे. इथे timer मुळे चालते, पण .catch लावण्यापूर्वीच reject झाला तर तो कधीच पोहोचत नाही आणि myAllSettled अडकून राहतो.

What is Promise.any? 1. Promise.any(iterable) takes an array of promises. It returns a single promise that:
  1. resolves as soon as any one promise fulfills;
  2. rejects only if all promises reject, with an AggregateError.
function myPromise(executer) {

      isCalled = true;
      onReject(val);      // ⚠ BUG: should be onResolve(val)
    } else {
      value = val;
      isFulField = true;
    }
  }
  function reject(err) {
    if (typeof onReject === 'function' && !isCalled) {
      isCalled = true
      onReject(err)
    } else {
      error = err;
      isRejected = true
    }
  }
  try {
    executer(resolve, reject)
  } catch (error) {
    console.log(error);
  }
}
myPromise.myAny = function (promises) {

        resolve(result)
      }).catch((error) => {

        compleatPromise++;
        if (compleatPromise === promises.length) {

7. Promise.race Polyfill (promiseRacePolyfill.js)

Your Notes:
  1. Promise.race() is a method in JavaScript that takes an iterable (like an array, or any other object with an iterator) of promises and returns a promise that resolves or rejects as soon as one of the promises in the iterable resolves or rejects.

It doesn't wait for the others to complete. It is often used when you need the result of the first completed promise, whether it's fulfilled or rejected. What is Promise.race? 1. Promise.race(iterable) takes an array of promises. It returns a single promise that settles as soon as the first promise settles (fulfilled or rejected). The result or error of the first-settled promise is used.

p3 = new myPromisePolyfill((resolve, reject) => { setTimeout(() => { resolve(2); }, 1000); });

myPromisePolyfill.myRace = function (promises) {
  return new myPromisePolyfill((resolve, reject) => {
    promises.forEach((promise, index) => {
      promise
        .then((result) => { resolve(result); })
        .catch((error) => { reject(error); });
    });
  });
};
myPromisePolyfill
  .myRace([p1, p2, p3])
  .then((result) => { console.log(result); })   // → 2 (verified; all three use 1000 ms, so the first registered wins)
  .catch((error) => { console.log(error); });
// ✅ correct logic: the isCalled flag in the outer promise ignores the later settlements.
//    Tip: test it with DIFFERENT delays (and a fast rejection) to really see the "race".
  • What happens: Promise.race polyfill: the first promise to settle decides the result.
  • Output: 2 (the first resolved value).

8. fullExampleOfPolyfill.js

// # full example of polyfill
let p1 = new myPromise((resolved, reject) => { setTimeout(() => { reject("promise resolved 1"); }, 3000); });
let p2 = new myPromise((resolved, reject) => { setTimeout(() => { resolved("promise resolved 2"); }, 1000); });
let p3 = new myPromise((resolved, reject) => { setTimeout(() => { reject("promise resolved 3"); }, 5000); });
let p4 = new myPromise((resolved, reject) => { setTimeout(() => { reject("fetch data..."); }, 2000); });
// (the labels say "resolved" but p1, p3 and p4 REJECT)

function myPromise(executer) {
  let onResolve,
    onReject,
    // these check whether the promise is fulfilled, rejected or not
    isFulField = false,
    isReject = false,
    // store the resolve and reject values
    value,
    error,
    // used to track the function call.
    isCalled = false,
    // used to handle the finally block
    isFinally;
  // register the resolved promise
  this.then = function (callback) {
    onResolve = callback;   // so here onResolve is the callback function
    if (isFulField && !isCalled) {
      isCalled = true;
      onResolve(value);
    }
    return this;   // return the same object for chaining
  };
  // used to register the rejected promise
  this.catch = function (callback) {
    onReject = callback;
    if (isReject && !isCalled) {
      onReject(error);   // (isCalled = true is missing here)
    }
    return this;
  };
  // function used to handle a resolved promise
  function resolved(val) {
    if (typeof onResolve === "function" && !isCalled) {
      isCalled = true;
      onResolve(val);
    }
    value = val;
    isFulField = true;
  }
  // function defined to handle a rejected promise
  function reject(err) {
    if (typeof onReject === "function" && !isCalled) {
      isCalled = true;
      onReject(err);
    } else {
      error = err;
      isReject = true;
    }
  }
  try {
    executer(resolved, reject);
  } catch (err) {
    console.error(err);   // (should be reject(err))
  }
}
// p1.then((result) => { console.log(result); }).catch((error) => { console.error(error); });
  • What happens: full example combining the custom promise with all/race/allSettled/any on promises with different delays.

9. Why These Simple Versions Are Not Real Promises

  1. No real chaining: then returns THIS, so .then(v => v * 2).then(…) doesn't pass the new value; the second then just overwrites the single handler.
  2. Only one handler: calling p.then(a); p.then(b) keeps only b; native promises call both.
  3. Synchronous callbacks: handlers run immediately; native .then callbacks always run as microtasks (after the current sync code).
  4. Shared isCalled: one flag for then AND catch; state can change twice (resolve then reject).
  5. No adoption: resolving with another promise doesn't wait for it.
These are fine for explaining the idea; for a strong interview answer, use the version below.
ही सोपी versions खरे promises नाहीत: then नवीन promise देत नाही (chaining नाही), एकच handler ठेवतात, callbacks लगेच (synchronously) चालवतात, आणि resolve झालेला promise पुन्हा reject होऊ शकतो. खाली दिलेली class हे सगळे बरोबर करते.

10. NEW: A Spec-like MyPromise Class (verified in Node)

class MyPromise {
  #state = "pending"; #value; #handlers = [];
  constructor(executor) {
    const settle = (state, value) => {
      if (this.#state !== "pending") return;                        // settle only ONCE
      if (state === "fulfilled" && value && typeof value.then === "function")
        return value.then((v) => settle("fulfilled", v), (e) => settle("rejected", e));   // adopt thenables
      this.#state = state; this.#value = value;
      this.#handlers.forEach((h) => this.#run(h)); this.#handlers = [];
    };
    try { executor((v) => settle("fulfilled", v), (e) => settle("rejected", e)); }
    catch (e) { settle("rejected", e); }                           // executor throws → reject
  }
  #run({ onF, onR, resolve, reject }) {
    queueMicrotask(() => {                                          // callbacks are ALWAYS async
      const cb = this.#state === "fulfilled" ? onF : onR;
      if (typeof cb !== "function") return (this.#state === "fulfilled" ? resolve : reject)(this.#value);   // pass through
      try { resolve(cb(this.#value)); } catch (e) { reject(e); }   // return → next fulfils; throw → next rejects
    });
  }
  then(onF, onR) {                                                  // returns a NEW promise → real chaining
    return new MyPromise((resolve, reject) => {
      const h = { onF, onR, resolve, reject };
      this.#state === "pending" ? this.#handlers.push(h) : this.#run(h);
    });
  }
  catch(onR) { return this.then(undefined, onR); }
  finally(cb) {
    return this.then(
      (v) => MyPromise.resolve(cb()).then(() => v),
      (e) => MyPromise.resolve(cb()).then(() => { throw e; })
    );
  }
  static resolve(v) { return v instanceof MyPromise ? v : new MyPromise((r) => r(v)); }
  static reject(e) { return new MyPromise((_, j) => j(e)); }
  static all(ps) {
    return new MyPromise((res, rej) => {
      const out = []; let n = 0;
      if (!ps.length) return res(out);
      ps.forEach((p, i) => MyPromise.resolve(p).then((v) => { out[i] = v; if (++n === ps.length) res(out); }, rej));   // fail-fast
    });
  }
  static allSettled(ps) {
    return new MyPromise((res) => {
      const out = []; let n = 0;
      if (!ps.length) return res(out);
      ps.forEach((p, i) => MyPromise.resolve(p)
        .then((v) => ({ status: "fulfilled", value: v }), (r) => ({ status: "rejected", reason: r }))
        .then((o) => { out[i] = o; if (++n === ps.length) res(out); }));
    });
  }
  static any(ps) {
    return new MyPromise((res, rej) => {
      const errs = []; let n = 0;
      if (!ps.length) return rej(new AggregateError([], "All promises were rejected"));
      ps.forEach((p, i) => MyPromise.resolve(p).then(res, (e) => {
        errs[i] = e; if (++n === ps.length) rej(new AggregateError(errs, "All promises were rejected"));
      }));
    });
  }
  static race(ps) { return new MyPromise((res, rej) => ps.forEach((p) => MyPromise.resolve(p).then(res, rej))); }
}
  • What happens: a spec-like MyPromise class: private state, settles once, adopts thenables, runs handlers asynchronously as microtasks, and then() returns a NEW promise (real chaining), plus catch/finally and the static combinators.
  • Output: (implementation).
  • ✅ Complete interview answer for "write your own Promise".
Verified results (d(v, ms, fail) = a delayed MyPromise): 
MyPromise.resolve(1).then(v => log(v)); log("after")   → after, 1          (then is async)
new MyPromise(r => r(2)).then(v => v * 10).then(v => { throw v + 1 }).catch(e => e + 1).finally(…)
                                                       → finally, then 22  (real chaining)
MyPromise.all([d(1,30), d(2,10), 3])                   → [1, 2, 3]          (input order)
MyPromise.all([d(1,30), d("x",10,true)])               → rejects "x"        (fail-fast)
MyPromise.allSettled([d(1,10), d("e",20,true)])        → [{fulfilled,1},{rejected,"e"}]
MyPromise.any([d("e1",10,true), d("ok",40), d("ok2",20)])  → "ok2"
MyPromise.any([two rejections])                        → AggregateError ['e1', 'e2']
MyPromise.race([d("slow",50), d("fast-fail",15,true)]) → rejects "fast-fail"
MyPromise.all([])                                      → []
  • What happens: test results for the class: async then, chaining with throw/catch/finally, all/allSettled/any behaviour.
  • Output: (results).
Figure 153: A real promise: settle once, store handlers, run them as microtasks, and return a new promise from every then.

11. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. What must a Promise polyfill guarantee?
  • Settle only once; multiple then handlers; then returns a NEW promise (chaining via return/throw); async (microtask) callbacks; executor errors → rejection; adopt returned promises/thenables; catch = then(undefined, f); finally passes the value through.
Q2. Write Promise.all. What are the edge cases?
  • Keep results by index (input order), count completions, reject on the first error, resolve [] for an empty input, and wrap non-promise values with Promise.resolve.
Q3. Promise.any vs race in a polyfill?
  • race: every promise's then(res, rej) (the first settle wins). any: then(res, onError) where onError collects errors and rejects with an AggregateError only after ALL have failed.
Q4. Why use queueMicrotask in the polyfill?
  • The spec says handlers run asynchronously, after the current synchronous code, as microtasks; so p.then(f); console.log("x") must print "x" first even when p is already resolved.
Q5. Output-based questions
const p = MyPromise.resolve(1);
p.then((v) => console.log("a", v));
p.then((v) => console.log("b", v));
console.log("sync");                       // → sync, a 1, b 1   (async + multiple handlers)
MyPromise.reject("x").then(() => 1).catch((e) => e + "!").then(console.log);   // → x!
MyPromise.race([]).then(() => console.log("never"));   // (stays pending forever, like native)
  • What happens: then is async and one promise can have many handlers; catch can recover; race([]) never settles.
  • Output: sync, a 1, b 1, x!.
PolyfillCore logic
Promisestate + value + handlers; settle once; then → new promise; microtasks
allout[i] = v; count === length → resolve; first error → reject
allSettledMap each to {status, value/reason}; never rejects
anyFirst fulfil → resolve; all errors → AggregateError
raceFirst settle (either way) wins
finallyRun cb, then pass the original value/reason through
थोडक्यात: तुमच्या simple myPromise मध्ये (1) value = value self-assignment, (2) onReject = true typo, (3) any मध्ये onReject/onResolve उलटे, (4) all मध्ये reject न करणे, हे bugs होते. खऱ्या promise मध्ये state एकदाच बदलते, then नवीन promise देतो, callbacks microtask म्हणून चालतात, आणि अनेक handlers चालतात. combinators = loop + counter.

Chapter 89: Error Handlingtry · catch · finally · throw · Error types · custom errors · error.cause · async errors · best practices
CHAPTER 89 INDEX
  1. What is an error? Built-in error types
  2. try...catch
  3. finally
  4. throw & custom error classes
  5. error.cause (ES2022) & re-throwing
  6. Errors in async code
  7. Best practices
  8. Interview Questions & Revision

1. What is an error? Built-in error types

Definition: An error is an object that describes something that went wrong while the program runs. When an error is thrown and nobody catches it, the script stops. Error handling lets the program react (show a message, retry, log) instead of crashing.
Error typeWhen it happensExample
ReferenceErrorUsing a variable/function that doesn't existundefinedFn()
TypeErrorWrong type of value for the operationnull.x, (5)()
SyntaxErrorInvalid code or invalid JSON textJSON.parse("{bad}")
RangeErrorA number outside the allowed rangenew Array(-1), "a".repeat(-1)
URIError / EvalErrorBad decodeURI() input / legacy eval errorsdecodeURI("%")
AggregateErrorSeveral errors togetherPromise.any() when all reject
Error म्हणजे program चालताना काहीतरी चुकल्याची माहिती देणारा object. तो कोणी catch केला नाही तर script थांबते. try...catch वापरून आपण program crash होण्याऐवजी error हाताळू शकतो.

2. try...catch

Example 1: catching a TypeError
try {
  null.x;                                   // reading a property of null
} catch (e) {
  console.log(e.name, "|", e.message);
}
// → TypeError | Cannot read properties of null (reading 'x')
What happens: the code inside try runs. null.x throws a TypeError, so JavaScript jumps immediately to catch and gives it the error object e. The lines after the failing line inside try are skipped.
Output: e.name is the error type, e.message is the human-readable text.
✅ Advantage: the program keeps running after the catch block; you decide what to show the user.
⚠ Disadvantage: an empty catch {} hides bugs. Always log or handle the error.
Example 2: the built-in error names
try { JSON.parse("{bad}"); } catch (e) { console.log(e.name); }   // → SyntaxError
try { undefinedFn(); }       catch (e) { console.log(e.name); }   // → ReferenceError
try { new Array(-1); }       catch (e) { console.log(e.name); }   // → RangeError
What happens: each line fails in a different way, and JavaScript creates the matching error type.
Output: SyntaxError (invalid JSON text), ReferenceError (unknown name), RangeError (invalid length).
✅ Advantage: checking e.name (or e instanceof TypeError) lets you handle each kind differently.
⚠ Trap: a SyntaxError in YOUR source code can't be caught by try...catch in the same file, because the file fails while parsing, before anything runs. Only runtime SyntaxErrors (JSON.parse, eval, new Function) are catchable.
Example 3: optional catch binding (ES2019)
let config;
try {
  config = JSON.parse('{"theme":"dark"}');
} catch {                                   // no (e) needed
  config = {};
}
console.log(config.theme);                  // → dark
What happens: since ES2019 you can write catch without (e) when you don't need the error object.
Output: dark, because the JSON is valid.
✅ Advantage: cleaner code for "try it, else use a default".
⚠ Disadvantage: you lose the error details, so use it only when the reason doesn't matter.
Example 4: try...catch does NOT catch errors in a later callback
try {
  setTimeout(() => { throw new Error("late"); }, 0);
} catch (e) {
  console.log("never runs");
}
// → Uncaught Error: late   (the try block finished long before the callback ran)
What happens: try only protects code that runs synchronously inside it. setTimeout just registers the callback; the try block ends; later the event loop runs the callback, outside any try.
Fix: put try...catch INSIDE the callback, or use promises with .catch / async-await with try...catch.
⚠ Common interview trap: "why doesn't my catch work?" → because the error happens asynchronously.
Figure 154: try → (error? catch) → finally always runs.

3. finally

Example 5: finally runs even after return
function f() {
  try {
    return "try";
  } finally {
    console.log("finally runs");
  }
}
console.log(f());
// → finally runs
// → try
What happens: return "try" prepares the return value, but before the function really leaves, finally runs. Then the saved value "try" is returned.
Output: "finally runs" is printed first, then "try".
✅ Advantage: perfect for cleanup that must always happen: hide a loader, close a file/connection, release a lock.
Example 6: return inside finally overrides everything
function g() {
  try {
    return "try";
  } finally {
    return "finally";
  }
}
console.log(g());   // → finally
What happens: a return in finally replaces the return value from try (and even swallows a thrown error).
Output: finally.
⚠ Disadvantage: this hides results and errors, so never return from finally; use it only for cleanup.

4. throw & custom error classes

Example 7: throwing your own error
function divide(a, b) {
  if (b === 0) throw new Error("Cannot divide by zero");
  return a / b;
}
try {
  divide(10, 0);
} catch (e) {
  console.log(e.message);   // → Cannot divide by zero
}
What happens: throw stops the function at once and sends the error up the call stack to the nearest catch.
Output: Cannot divide by zero (without the check, 10 / 0 would silently give Infinity).
✅ Advantage: invalid input fails loudly and early, with a clear message.
Example 8: throw a string vs throw an Error
try {
  throw "plain string";
} catch (e) {
  console.log(typeof e, e.stack);   // → string undefined
}
What happens: you CAN throw any value, but a string has no name, no message property and no stack trace.
Output: string undefined.
⚠ Disadvantage: you lose the stack trace (where the error came from). Always throw new Error(...) or a subclass.
Example 9: a custom error class
class ValidationError extends Error {
  constructor(field, msg) {
    super(msg);                    // sets message (and stack)
    this.name = "ValidationError";
    this.field = field;            // extra info
  }
}
try {
  throw new ValidationError("age", "Age must be positive");
} catch (e) {
  console.log(e instanceof ValidationError, e instanceof Error);   // → true true
  console.log(e.name, e.field, e.message);   // → ValidationError age Age must be positive
}
What happens: the class extends Error, so it gets message and stack; we add a name and extra fields.
Output: it is both a ValidationError and an Error, with our custom field.
✅ Advantage: catch blocks can react by type: if (e instanceof ValidationError) show the form message, else report a bug.
⚠ Trap: forgetting super(msg) → ReferenceError in the constructor; forgetting this.name → it prints as "Error".

5. error.cause (ES2022) & re-throwing

Example 10: wrapping an error with cause
try {
  try {
    throw new Error("inner");
  } catch (e) {
    throw new Error("outer", { cause: e });   // re-throw with more context
  }
} catch (e) {
  console.log(e.message, e.cause.message);   // → outer inner
}
What happens: the inner catch can't fully handle the problem, so it throws a new, more meaningful error and keeps the original in cause.
Output: outer inner.
✅ Advantage: high-level message for the user ("Saving failed") plus the low-level reason ("timeout") for debugging.
⚠ Rule: only catch what you can handle; otherwise re-throw instead of silently swallowing.

6. Errors in async code

Example 11: async/await with try...catch
async function load() {
  throw new Error("network");
}
(async () => {
  try {
    await load();
  } catch (e) {
    console.log(e.message);   // → network
  }
})();
What happens: an error thrown in an async function rejects its promise; await turns that rejection back into a throw, so the normal try...catch works.
Output: network.
✅ Advantage: async code reads like sync code, with one familiar error style.
⚠ Trap: without await (just load()), the try finishes first and the rejection is NOT caught → "Unhandled promise rejection".
Example 12: .catch() on a promise
load().catch(e => console.log(e.message));   // → network
What happens: .catch registers a handler for the rejected promise.
✅ Advantage: good for promise chains; one .catch at the end handles a failure from any earlier .then.
⚠ Disadvantage: a rejection with no .catch/try anywhere triggers the global "unhandledrejection" event (in Node it can crash the process).

7. Best practices

Extra Details:
  • Throw Error objects (or subclasses), never strings.
  • Catch at the level that can actually do something (show a message, retry, fallback).
  • Never leave catch empty; at least console.error(e) or send it to a logging service.
  • Use finally for cleanup (loaders, connections), never return from it.
  • Validate input early (guard clauses) and throw with clear messages.
  • Global safety nets: window.onerror / window.addEventListener("unhandledrejection", …) in the browser; process.on("uncaughtException") in Node; for logging only, not as normal flow.
नेहमी new Error(...) throw करा, string नाही, कारण stack trace मिळतो. catch रिकामा ठेवू नका. finally cleanup साठी आहे, त्यात return लिहू नका. Async code मध्ये await + try/catch किंवा .catch() वापरा, नाहीतर unhandled rejection येतो.

8. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. Does finally run if try has a return statement?
  • Yes. finally runs before the function returns; a return inside finally even overrides the try's return value.
Q2. Why doesn't try...catch catch an error thrown inside setTimeout?
  • The callback runs later, after the try block has finished, so it isn't inside any try. Catch inside the callback, or use promises/async-await.
Q3. How do you create a custom error?
  • class MyError extends Error { constructor(msg) { super(msg); this.name = "MyError"; } }, then check with instanceof.
Q4. Difference between throw "x" and throw new Error("x")?
  • Both stop execution, but only an Error object has name, message and stack (for debugging and instanceof checks).
Q5. Output-based questions
try { console.log(1); throw 2; console.log(3); } catch (e) { console.log(e); } finally { console.log(4); }   // → 1 2 4
function t() { try { throw 1; } catch { return "c"; } finally { console.log("f"); } } console.log(t());   // → f c
try { JSON.parse(""); } catch (e) { console.log(e.name); }   // → SyntaxError
console.log(new TypeError("x") instanceof Error);           // → true
  • What happens: four output questions on try/catch/finally: code after throw never runs, finally runs before return, JSON.parse("") is a SyntaxError, error classes inherit from Error.
  • Output: 1 2 4, f c, SyntaxError, true.
KeywordJob
tryCode that may fail
catch (e)Runs only if try threw; e = the error
finallyAlways runs (cleanup)
throwRaise an error yourself
extends ErrorCustom error types
{ cause }Keep the original error when wrapping
थोडक्यात: try मध्ये धोकादायक code, catch मध्ये हाताळणी, finally मध्ये cleanup. Async errors साठी await + try/catch किंवा .catch(). Custom errors extends Error ने बनवा.

Chapter 90: Iterators & Generatorsiterator protocol · function* · yield · next() · return() · throw() · yield* · infinite sequences · custom iterables · async generators
CHAPTER 90 INDEX
  1. The iterator protocol
  2. Generator basics: function* and yield
  3. Passing values into next()
  4. yield*, return() and throw()
  5. Practical uses: infinite IDs, custom iterables, lazy take()
  6. Async generators & for await...of
  7. Interview Questions & Revision

1. The iterator protocol

Definition: An iterator is an object with a next() method that returns { value, done }. An iterable is an object with a [Symbol.iterator]() method that returns an iterator; for...of, spread [...x], Array.from and destructuring all use it. A generator (function*) is the easiest way to create iterators: it can pause at yield and resume later.
Example 1: a plain object is not iterable
const o = { a: 1 };
for (const v of o) {}   // → TypeError: o is not iterable
What happens: for...of looks for o[Symbol.iterator]; plain objects don't have it.
Fix: loop over Object.entries(o), or give the object its own [Symbol.iterator] (Example 9).

2. Generator basics: function* and yield

Example 2: next() step by step
function* gen() {
  yield 1;
  yield 2;
  return 3;
}
const it = gen();          // nothing runs yet!
console.log(it.next());    // → { value: 1, done: false }
console.log(it.next());    // → { value: 2, done: false }
console.log(it.next());    // → { value: 3, done: true }
console.log(it.next());    // → { value: undefined, done: true }
What happens: calling gen() does NOT run the body; it returns a generator object. Each next() runs the body until the next yield, pauses there, and hands out that value. return ends it with done: true.
Output: 1, 2 (done false), then 3 with done true, then undefined forever.
✅ Advantage: the function keeps its local state between calls, so there is no need for outer variables.
⚠ Trap: generators can't be arrow functions, and you can't restart one; call gen() again for a fresh run.
Figure 155: A generator pauses at every yield and resumes on the next next() call.
Example 3: spread / for...of read the values
console.log([...gen()]);   // → [1, 2]
What happens: spread calls next() until done: true.
Output: [1, 2]. The return value 3 is NOT included, because for...of/spread ignore the value of the done: true step.
⚠ Interview trap: "why is 3 missing?" → return values are skipped by for...of; use yield for every value you want to iterate.

3. Passing values into next()

Example 4: two-way communication
function* two() {
  const x = yield "first";   // pauses here; x gets the NEXT next(arg)
  console.log("got", x);
  yield x * 2;
}
const t = two();
console.log(t.next().value);    // → first
console.log(t.next(5).value);   // → got 5, then 10
What happens: the first next() runs up to yield "first". The second next(5) resumes, and the paused yield expression evaluates to 5, so x = 5 and the next yield gives 10.
Output: first, got 5, 10.
✅ Advantage: this pause/resume-with-a-value idea is exactly how async/await works internally (await ≈ yield a promise, resume with its result).
⚠ Trap: the argument of the FIRST next() is ignored (nothing is waiting yet).

4. yield*, return() and throw()

Example 5: yield* delegates to another generator
function* inner() { yield "a"; yield "b"; }
function* outer() {
  yield 1;
  yield* inner();   // yields all of inner's values here
  yield 2;
}
console.log([...outer()]);   // → [1, 'a', 'b', 2]
What happens: yield* iterates over any iterable (a generator, an array, a string) and yields each value.
✅ Advantage: compose small generators; recursive tree walks become very short.
Example 6: return() stops a generator early
const r = gen();
console.log(r.next());       // → { value: 1, done: false }
console.log(r.return(99));   // → { value: 99, done: true }
console.log(r.next());       // → { value: undefined, done: true }
What happens: return(v) finishes the generator immediately (any finally blocks inside still run). break inside a for...of calls it automatically.
✅ Advantage: lets the consumer stop early and clean up resources.
Example 7: throw() sends an error inside
function* safe() {
  try { yield 1; yield 2; }
  catch (e) { console.log("caught", e); yield "recovered"; }
}
const s = safe();
s.next();
console.log(s.throw("boom"));   // → caught boom, then { value: 'recovered', done: false }
What happens: throw(err) resumes the generator as if the paused yield had thrown err, so the generator's own try...catch can handle it.
⚠ If the generator doesn't catch it, the error comes out of s.throw() to the caller.

5. Practical uses

Example 8: an infinite ID generator
function* ids() {
  let id = 1;
  while (true) yield id++;   // infinite, but lazy
}
const idg = ids();
console.log(idg.next().value, idg.next().value, idg.next().value);   // → 1 2 3
What happens: while (true) is safe because the generator pauses at every yield; values are produced only when asked (lazy evaluation).
✅ Advantage: unique IDs, pagination cursors, endless sequences without memory cost.
⚠ Disadvantage: [...ids()] or for...of without break never ends and freezes the program.
Example 9: making an object iterable
const range = {
  from: 1,
  to: 4,
  *[Symbol.iterator]() {
    for (let i = this.from; i <= this.to; i++) yield i;
  }
};
console.log([...range]);   // → [1, 2, 3, 4]
What happens: a generator method as [Symbol.iterator] makes range work with for...of, spread, Array.from and destructuring.
✅ Advantage: far shorter than writing a manual { next() { … } } iterator object.
Example 10: lazy take() from an infinite sequence
function* take(n, iterable) {
  for (const v of iterable) {
    if (n-- <= 0) return;
    yield v;
  }
}
console.log([...take(3, ids())]);   // → [1, 2, 3]
What happens: take pulls only 3 values from the infinite ids(), then returns, which also stops ids().
✅ Advantage: lazy pipelines handle huge or endless data one item at a time.

6. Async generators & for await...of

Example 11: async function* + for await
async function* stream() {
  yield 1;
  await null;          // could be: await fetch(page)
  yield 2;
}
(async () => {
  const out = [];
  for await (const v of stream()) out.push(v);
  console.log(out);    // → [1, 2]
})();
What happens: each next() of an async generator returns a promise; for await...of waits for each one.
✅ Advantage: reading paginated APIs or streams chunk by chunk with simple loop syntax.
⚠ for await works only inside async functions (or at the top level of modules).
Generator (function*) yield वर थांबतो आणि next() ने पुढे चालू होतो; त्याचे local variables जपले जातात. त्यामुळे lazy/infinite sequences, custom iterables आणि async/await ची मूळ कल्पना समजते. return value for...of मध्ये येत नाही.

7. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. Iterable vs iterator?
  • An iterable has [Symbol.iterator]() that returns an iterator; an iterator has next() returning { value, done }.
Q2. What does calling a generator function return?
  • A generator object (both an iterator and an iterable); the body doesn't run until the first next().
Q3. Why doesn't [...gen()] include the returned value?
  • Spread/for...of stop at done: true and ignore that step's value.
Q4. How are generators related to async/await?
  • async/await is like a generator that yields promises and is resumed automatically with each result (libraries like co did this before ES2017).
Q5. Output-based questions
function* g() { const a = yield 1; yield a + 1; }
const x = g(); console.log(x.next(10).value, x.next(20).value, x.next().done);   // → 1 21 true
console.log([...(function* () { yield* "hi"; })()]);                          // → ['h', 'i']
const [p, q] = (function* () { yield "A"; yield "B"; yield "C"; })(); console.log(p, q);   // → A B
  • What happens: the first next() argument is ignored; the second becomes a = 20; yield* spreads a string; destructuring pulls values from a generator.
  • Output: 1 21 true, ['h', 'i'], A B.
PieceMeaning
function*Declares a generator
yield vPause and give out v
next(arg)Resume; arg becomes the yield's result
yield*Delegate to another iterable
return() / throw()Stop early / inject an error
async function* + for awaitAsync streams
थोडक्यात: iterator = next() असलेला object; iterable = [Symbol.iterator] असलेला object; generator दोन्ही एकत्र देतो. yield थांबवतो, next() पुढे नेतो, आणि infinite sequences सुद्धा lazy असल्यामुळे सुरक्षित असतात.

Chapter 91: Memory Management & Garbage Collectionstack vs heap · reachability · mark-and-sweep · common memory leaks · WeakMap · WeakSet · WeakRef · finding leaks in DevTools
CHAPTER 91 INDEX
  1. Stack, heap & reachability
  2. Mark-and-sweep garbage collection
  3. Common memory leaks
  4. WeakMap, WeakSet & WeakRef
  5. Finding leaks
  6. Interview Questions & Revision

1. Stack, heap & reachability

Definition: JavaScript manages memory automatically. Primitives and references live on the stack (fast, per function call); objects, arrays and functions live in the heap. The garbage collector (GC) frees heap objects that are no longer reachable, i.e. that can't be reached from the roots (global object, the current call stack, active closures) through any chain of references.
Example 1: an object becomes garbage
let user = { name: "Vishal" };   // reachable through the variable user
user = null;                      // no reference left → unreachable → GC may free it
What happens: the object itself isn't deleted by user = null; only the reference is removed. Once nothing points to the object, the GC frees it at some later moment (you can't control when).
⚠ Trap: if another variable still points to it (const copy = user before), it stays alive.
Example 2: circular references are fine
let a = {}, b = {};
a.other = b;
b.other = a;     // a ↔ b point to each other
a = b = null;    // the pair is unreachable from the roots → both are collected
What happens: modern GCs use reachability (mark-and-sweep), not reference counting, so cycles that are cut off from the roots are still freed.
✅ Interview point: "circular references cause leaks" was true for very old IE (reference counting), not for modern engines.

2. Mark-and-sweep garbage collection

Figure 156: Mark-and-sweep: mark everything reachable from the roots, then free the rest (even cycles).
Extra Details: V8 also uses a generational heap: new objects go to a small "young generation" that is collected often and quickly (most objects die young); survivors move to the "old generation", collected less often. Collection is incremental/concurrent to avoid long pauses.

3. Common memory leaks

Example 3: accidental global variable
function save() {
  cache = new Array(1e6).fill("x");   // no let/const → window.cache, lives forever
}
What happens: in sloppy mode an undeclared assignment creates a global, which is a root, so it is never collected.
Fix: "use strict" (→ ReferenceError) and always declare variables.
Example 4: forgotten timers
const bigData = new Array(1e6).fill("x");
const id = setInterval(() => console.log(bigData.length), 1000);
// … component removed, but the interval keeps running and keeps bigData alive
clearInterval(id);   // ✔ fix: always clear intervals/timeouts you no longer need
What happens: the active interval holds its callback, and the callback's closure holds bigData.
⚠ In React/Vue, clear timers in the cleanup/unmount hook.
Example 5: event listeners on removed elements
const btn = document.querySelector("#save");
function onClick() { /* uses a big closure */ }
btn.addEventListener("click", onClick);
// before removing the element or leaving the page section:
btn.removeEventListener("click", onClick);   // ✔ same function reference needed
// or: btn.addEventListener("click", onClick, { once: true }) / an AbortController signal
What happens: listeners keep their closures alive; listeners on long-lived targets (window, document) are the most dangerous.
✅ Event delegation (one listener on a parent, Chapter 77) avoids many per-element listeners.
Example 6: closures holding big data & detached DOM nodes
function makeHandler() {
  const huge = new Array(1e6).fill("x");
  return () => huge.length;           // the returned function keeps huge alive
}
const handlers = [];
handlers.push(makeHandler());          // stored forever → huge stays in memory

let detached = document.querySelector("#list");
detached.remove();                     // removed from the page …
// … but the variable still references it → the whole subtree stays in memory
detached = null;                       // ✔ fix
What happens: closures keep their outer variables; JS references keep removed DOM nodes ("detached DOM trees").
⚠ Also watch unbounded caches/arrays/Maps that only grow: give them a size limit or use WeakMap.

4. WeakMap, WeakSet & WeakRef

Example 7: WeakMap for metadata about objects
const meta = new WeakMap();
let key = {};
meta.set(key, "meta");
console.log(meta.get(key), meta.has(key));   // → meta true
meta.set("str", 1);                           // → TypeError: Invalid value used as weak map key
key = null;    // the entry disappears automatically once key is garbage collected
What happens: a WeakMap holds its KEYS weakly: if nothing else references the key object, both key and value can be collected. Keys must be objects (or non-registered symbols).
✅ Advantage: cache or private data per DOM node/object without leaks.
⚠ Disadvantage: not iterable, no size, no clear(), because entries can vanish at any time.
Example 8: WeakSet and WeakRef
const seen = new WeakSet();
const k2 = {};
seen.add(k2);
console.log(seen.has(k2));               // → true   ("have I processed this object?")

let big = { data: new Array(3).fill("x") };
const ref = new WeakRef(big);
console.log(ref.deref() === big);        // → true now; later deref() may return undefined
What happens: WeakSet = a set of objects held weakly. WeakRef holds one object weakly; deref() gives it back, or undefined after collection.
⚠ WeakRef/FinalizationRegistry timing is unpredictable; use them only for caches, never for program logic.

5. Finding leaks

Extra Details (Chrome DevTools):
  1. Performance monitor: watch "JS heap size" while repeating an action; a staircase that never goes down = leak.
  2. Memory tab → Heap snapshot: take one, repeat the action, take another, compare ("Objects allocated between snapshots"); search for "Detached" to find detached DOM trees.
  3. Allocation timeline shows which code allocates the memory that survives.

In Node: process.memoryUsage() and --inspect.
JS मध्ये memory आपोआप मोकळी होते: जे object roots (global, stack, closures) पासून पोहोचू शकत नाहीत ते GC काढून टाकतो. Leak म्हणजे नको असलेले object अजूनही कुठून तरी reachable राहणे: global variables, न थांबवलेले setInterval, न काढलेले event listeners, मोठे closures, detached DOM. WeakMap/WeakSet keys ना जिवंत ठेवत नाहीत.

6. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. How does garbage collection work in JavaScript?
  • Mark-and-sweep: starting from the roots, mark every reachable object; free everything unmarked (generational + incremental in V8).
Q2. Name 4 common memory leaks.
  • Accidental globals, uncleared timers/intervals, event listeners not removed, closures/caches/detached DOM nodes holding large data.
Q3. Map vs WeakMap?
  • Map keeps keys alive and is iterable (any key type); WeakMap keys must be objects, are held weakly, and it isn't iterable.
Q4. Does setting obj = null delete the object?
  • No, it removes one reference; the GC frees the object later only if no other references exist.
Q5. Output-based questions
const wm = new WeakMap(); const o = {}; wm.set(o, 1); console.log(wm.has(o), typeof wm.size);   // → true undefined
const m = new Map([[{}, 1]]); console.log(m.size);                                               // → 1 (Map keeps the key alive)
let x = { v: 1 }; const y = x; x = null; console.log(y.v);                                      // → 1 (still referenced by y)
  • What happens: WeakMap has no size; a Map keeps its object key alive; setting x = null doesn't free an object still referenced by y.
  • Output: true undefined, 1, 1.
Leak sourceFix
Undeclared variablelet/const + "use strict"
setIntervalclearInterval on cleanup
Event listenersremoveEventListener / { once } / AbortController
Detached DOMNull the references
Growing cacheSize limit or WeakMap
थोडक्यात: reachable = जिवंत, unreachable = GC. Timers आणि listeners साफ करा, global variables टाळा, आणि object-आधारित cache साठी WeakMap वापरा.
