1. Why the file doesn't run (read first)

Extra Details (verified in Node): mock-interview/interview.js is a collection of separate interview answers pasted into ONE file, so running it gives SyntaxError: Identifier 'a' has already been declared (line 504) and not a single line runs. A SyntaxError is found while parsing, before any code executes.
Names declared twice with let/const/class in the same file: students, result, data, a, b, c (let and var), str, person, arr, res, name (class and let), sum. Duplicate function declarations (allowed, the last one wins because of hoisting): myFunction, example, pendingPromise. The file also uses document (browser only), top-level await (ES modules only) and fetch to fake URLs.
How to practise: copy one question at a time into its own file (or wrap each answer in its own { … } block). This chapter shows every answer separately, with the real verified outputs.
ही file एकाच वेळी चालत नाही, कारण अनेक variables (a, b, students, data…) दोनदा let/const ने declare केले आहेत; SyntaxError मुळे एकही ओळ चालत नाही. प्रत्येक प्रश्न वेगळ्या file मध्ये किंवा वेगळ्या { } block मध्ये चालवा.

2. Students array: map & filter tasks

Your Notes:
1. return only the names of the students, capitalized
// # 1. return only the names of the students, capitalized
const students = [
    {
      id: 1,
      name: "Alice Johnson",
      age: 20,
      grade: "A",
      subjects: ["Math", "Science", "English"]
    },
    {
      id: 2,
      name: "Bob Smith",
      age: 22,
      grade: "B",
      subjects: ["History", "Geography", "Economics"]
    },
    {
      id: 3,
      name: "Charlie Brown",
      age: 21,
      grade: "A",
      subjects: ["Physics", "Chemistry", "Biology"]
    },
    {
      id: 4,
      name: "Diana Green",
      age: 19,
      grade: "C",
      subjects: ["Art", "Music", "Drama"]
    },
    {
      id: 5,
      name: "Ethan White",
      age: 23,
      grade: "B",
      subjects: ["Computer Science", "Math", "English"]
    }
  ];
  const studentsName = students.map((data)=>{
    return data.name.toUpperCase();
  })
  console.log(studentsName)   // → ['ALICE JOHNSON', 'BOB SMITH', 'CHARLIE BROWN', 'DIANA GREEN', 'ETHAN WHITE']
  • What happens: map returns a new array with each student's name in upper case.
  • Output: ['ALICE JOHNSON', …].
  • ✅ Interview tip: say "upper case", or capitalize only the first letters if asked.
2. return only the details of those whose age is more than 21
// # 2. return only the details of those whose age is more than 21
const result =students.filter((data)=>{
    return data.age > 21;
})
console.log(result)           // → Bob Smith (22) and Ethan White (23) objects
  • What happens: filter keeps students older than 21.
  • Output: Bob Smith and Ethan White.
3. return those whose age is less than 20 and id is greater than 3
// # 3. return those whose age is less than 20 and id is greater than 3
const data = students.filter((student)=>{
    return student.id > 3 && student.age < 20;
})
console.log(data)             // → [Diana Green] (id 4, age 19)
  • What happens: filter with two conditions joined by &&.
  • Output: [Diana Green].
✔ "capitalize" usually means only the first letter big ("Alice Johnson"); toUpperCase() makes the WHOLE name upper case ("ALICE JOHNSON"). Say "convert to upper case" in the answer, or capitalize with name.split(" ").map(w => w[0].toUpperCase() + w.slice(1)).join(" ")."Capitalize" म्हणजे फक्त पहिले अक्षर मोठे; toUpperCase() पूर्ण नाव मोठ्या अक्षरात करतो.
map() प्रत्येक element बदलून नवीन array देतो (इथे नावे upper case), तर filter() फक्त अट पूर्ण करणारे elements ठेवतो. दोन्ही मूळ array बदलत नाहीत.

3. Factorial & reverse a string

4. find the factorial of the number n using recursion
//# 4. find the factorial of the number n using recursion
let n = 5
function findFactorial(n){
    if(n === 0 ) return 1
return n * findFactorial(n -1)
}
console.log(findFactorial(n))   // → 120
// ✔ note: a negative n (or 2.5) never reaches 0 → "Maximum call stack size exceeded"; guard with if (n <= 1) return 1.
  • What happens: recursion: n × factorial(n − 1) until the base case 0.
  • Output: 120.
  • ⚠ Negative or decimal n never reaches 0 → stack overflow; use n <= 1.
5. reverse a string in JavaScript
// # 5. reverse a string in JavaScript
// 1
let str = 'vishal'
let reverseString = str.split("").reverse().join("");
console.log(reverseString)        // → lahsiv
// 2
function reverseString1(str) {
    if (str === '') {
        return '';
    } else {
// the recursion unfolds as follows:
// "ello" + "h"
// "llo" + "e"
// "lo" + "l"
// "o" + "l"
// "" + "o"
        return reverseString1(str.substr(1)) + str.charAt(0);
    }
}
console.log(reverseString1("hello"));   // output: "olleh"
  • What happens: two ways: split/reverse/join, and recursion (reverse the rest, then add the first character at the end).
  • Output: lahsiv, olleh.
  • ⚠ substr is deprecated; use slice(1).
✔ substr() is deprecated (legacy); use str.slice(1) or str.substring(1), same result here. For emoji-safe reversing use [...str].reverse().join("").substr() जुना (deprecated) आहे; slice(1) वापरा. Emoji असलेल्या string साठी [...str] वापरा.
Figure 157: Recursive string reverse: each call waits for the smaller string, then adds its first character at the end.
Recursion मध्ये function स्वतःला लहान input ने call करतो आणि base case ("" किंवा 0) ला थांबतो. Factorial मध्ये negative number दिला तर base case कधीच येत नाही आणि stack overflow होतो.

4. Function expression, spread & rest

what is a function expression in JavaScript?
// # what is a function expression in JavaScript?
// A function expression is when you define a function and assign it to a variable; it may be a named function or an
// anonymous function. When a function is stored inside a variable, it is called a function expression.
let functionExpress = function sum(a , b){
    return a + b;
}
console.log(functionExpress(10,20))   // → 30
  • What happens: a function stored in a variable; the inner name sum is visible only inside it.
  • Output: 30.
what is the spread operator?
//# what is the spread operator?
// The spread operator allows you to expand or unpack the elements of an array, object or iterable into individual elements.
let a = [1,2,3,4]
let b = [5,6,7,4]
let finalArray = [a, b];
console.log(finalArray);              // → [[1, 2, 3, 4], [5, 6, 7, 4]]  (nested, NOT spread)
let finalArray1 = [...a, ...b];
console.log(finalArray1)              // → [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 4]
  • What happens: [a, b] nests the arrays; [...a, ...b] spreads their items into one array.
  • Output: [[1,2,3,4],[5,6,7,4]], [1,2,3,4,5,6,7,4].
what is the rest parameter?
// # what is the rest parameter?
// It collects elements into an array: the rest parameter allows you to collect multiple arguments or the remaining
// elements into a single array. It is primarily used in function definitions to handle an indefinite number of arguments.
function sum1(...number){
    return number;
}
console.log(sum1(a,b));               // → [[1, 2, 3, 4], [5, 6, 7, 4]]
  • What happens: rest collects all arguments into one array (here two arrays).
  • Output: [[1,2,3,4],[5,6,7,4]].

7. Deep clone & structuredClone()

// # how to deep clone an object
const person = {
  name: 'John Doe',
  age: 30,
  address: {
    street: '123 Main St',
    city: 'New York',
    country: 'USA'
  },
  hobbies: ['reading', 'traveling', 'swimming'],
  education: {
    degree: 'Bachelor of Science',
    university: {
      name: 'Harvard University',
      location: {
        city: 'Cambridge',
        state: 'Massachusetts'
      }
    }
  }
};
console.log(person);
const deepCloneObject = structuredClone(person);
console.log(deepCloneObject);    // same content, but every nested object is a NEW object
  • What happens: structuredClone makes a fully independent deep copy of nested data.
  • Output: two equal-looking objects.
  • ⚠ Can't clone functions or DOM nodes.
What is the structuredClone() method in JavaScript? The structuredClone() method is used to create a deep clone of a given object. It creates a new object that is structurally identical to the original object, but completely independent from it, meaning that changes to the cloned object don't affect the original object. structuredClone() can also clone arrays, RegExp, Date, Set and Map. Return value: it returns a deep copy of the provided value. ✔ Added (verified): structuredClone can NOT clone functions, DOM nodes or class methods: structuredClone({ f() {} }) → DataCloneError, and class instances come back as plain objects. Full comparison: Chapter 55 (Shallow Copy vs Deep Copy).structuredClone functions आणि DOM nodes clone करू शकत नाही (DataCloneError).

8. Single thread, event loop & runtime

? JavaScript is single-threaded, but how does it achieve asynchronous behavior? It achieves this behavior using the event loop, Web APIs, promises, callbacks and async-await. ✔ the question said "synchronous behave"; it should be ASYNCHRONOUS behavior (synchronous is the default).प्रश्न asynchronous behavior बद्दल आहे.
  • JavaScript is single-threaded: it runs on a single thread, meaning it executes one task at a time in a sequential manner. This is called the "Call Stack" model.
  • How does JavaScript handle asynchronous tasks? JavaScript achieves asynchronous execution using Web APIs (like setTimeout, fetch, DOM events), the Callback Queue & Event Loop, and Promises & Async/Await.
// Why does this happen?
console.log("Start");
setTimeout(() => {
    console.log("Inside setTimeout");
}, 2000);
console.log("End");
// → Start, End, (after 2 s) Inside setTimeout
// setTimeout is handled by the Web API (not JavaScript itself).
// JavaScript does not wait for it to finish.
// After 2 seconds, the callback function moves to the Callback Queue.
// The Event Loop pushes it to the Call Stack once it's free.
  • What happens: setTimeout hands the callback to the browser's timer; JS continues; after 2 s the callback is queued and run when the stack is empty.
  • Output: Start, End, Inside setTimeout.
Event loop & callback queue (how it works):
  1. JavaScript executes synchronous code first (call stack).
  2. Asynchronous tasks (like setTimeout) are sent to the Web APIs.
  3. Once the delay is over, the Web API moves the task to the callback queue.
  4. The event loop checks whether the call stack is empty and then moves the task from the callback queue to the call stack.
  5. The task gets executed.

Asynchronous execution using promises: a Promise allows non-blocking execution and better handling of async operations.
Summary: how JavaScript handles asynchronous tasks.
  • ✔ JavaScript is single-threaded, but achieves async behavior using: Web APIs (setTimeout, fetch, event listeners, etc.)
  • the callback queue &
  • event loop
  • the microtask queue (for Promises &
  • async/await). ✔ The event loop makes sure async tasks run only when the call stack is empty. ✔ Promises &
  • async/await help you write better non-blocking code.


# Are the event loop, setTimeout and Promise part of JavaScript or not? No, the event loop is not part of JavaScript itself. It is part of the JavaScript runtime environment, which is provided by browsers (like Chrome, Firefox) or Node.js. JavaScript alone is single-threaded: JavaScript itself only has the call stack to execute code synchronously. It does not have timers (setTimeout), fetch(), or an event loop. ✔ Promise IS part of JavaScript (the ECMAScript language, since ES6), and so are the microtask "jobs" it uses. setTimeout, fetch and the event loop come from the host (browser / Node.js). Also "avaScript" → JavaScript.Promise हा JavaScript भाषेचा भाग आहे; setTimeout, fetch आणि event loop browser/Node देतात.
# Who provides the event loop?
  • Browsers (like Chrome, Firefox) have a JavaScript engine (e.g. V8 for Chrome) along with a runtime environment that includes: the call stack (executes JavaScript code)
  • Web APIs (setTimeout, fetch, DOM events)
  • the callback queue &
  • microtask queue
  • the event loop. Node.js also provides an event loop, but it is built on libuv (a C++ library) instead of Web APIs.
✔ libuv is written in C (not C++).libuv C भाषेत लिहिलेली library आहे.
# How the event loop works:
  • the event loop manages asynchronous operations and makes sure JavaScript runs efficiently. It executes synchronous code (call stack)
  • sends async tasks (like setTimeout, fetch) to the Web APIs
  • once the async task completes, the callback is moved to the callback queue or microtask queue
  • the event loop checks whether the call stack is empty and moves tasks from the queue back to the call stack for execution.

# Summary:
  • the event loop is not part of JavaScript but is provided by the browser or Node.js runtime. ✔ It helps manage asynchronous operations by handling callback queues &
  • microtasks. ✔ Microtasks (Promises) run before the callback queue (setTimeout, I/O tasks, etc.). Full details: Chapter 69 (The Event Loop, Microtasks &
  • Macrotasks).

9. Promise states without new Promise & typeof questions

1. how to create a pending promise without the new Promise constructor (it is possible usi
// 1. how to create a pending promise without the new Promise constructor (it is possible using async/await)
//  In JavaScript, an async function always returns a Promise. Let's explore how to create fulfilled, rejected, and
//  pending states using async/await without explicitly using new Promise()
async function resolvePromise() {
  return "promise resolve";
}
console.log(resolvePromise().then((res) => console.log(res)));
// → Promise { <pending> }  (the promise returned by .then()), and later: promise resolve

async function rejectPromise() {
  throw new Error("rejected value");
}
console.log(rejectPromise().catch((error) => console.error(error)));
// → Promise { <pending> }, and later: Error: rejected value

async function PendingPromise() {
  return new Promise(() => {});
}
console.log(PendingPromise());   // → Promise { <pending> } (stays pending forever)
// ✔ note: this one still uses new Promise inside; a version without it: async () => { await new Promise(() => {}) }
//   also uses one. A pending promise always needs something that never settles.
  • What happens: async functions always return promises: return → fulfilled, throw → rejected, awaiting a never-settling promise → pending.
  • Output: pending promises, then the values/errors.
2. what is the type of a class?

  constructor(name) {
    this.name = name;
  }
  getData() {
    return this.name;
  }
}
let p = new Home("vishal");
console.log(p.getData());        // → vishal
console.log(typeof Home);        // function
  • What happens: a class is a special kind of function.
  • Output: vishal, function.
3. what is the type of a function?
// 3. what is the type of a function?
function myFunction() {}
console.log("function type ", typeof myFunction);   // → function type  function
  • What happens: typeof a function is "function".
  • Output: function type function.
4. what is the type of an array?
// 4. what is the type of an array?
let arr4 = [];
console.log(typeof arr4);        // object
  • What happens: arrays are objects.
  • Output: object.
# What is a promise and its states? A promise is an object or placeholder where we store the result of an asynchronous operation, whether it is a failure or a success. It has 3 states:
  1. pending,
  2. fulfilled,
  3. rejected.
✔ "filefield" → fulfilled."filefield" नाही, "fulfilled".
Figure 158: An async function's promise: return → fulfilled, throw → rejected, never settling → pending.
async function नेहमी promise देतो: value return केली तर fulfilled, error throw केला तर rejected, आणि कधीच settle न होणाऱ्या promise ची वाट पाहिली तर pending. typeof class आणि typeof function दोन्ही "function" देतात, typeof [] "object" देतो.

10. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. Why does the whole interview.js file fail before printing anything?
  • Redeclaring a let/const/class name in the same scope is a SyntaxError, and SyntaxErrors are reported while parsing, so no line runs.
Q2. Which array methods mutate the original array?
  • fill, sort, splice, push/pop/shift/unshift, reverse, copyWithin. concat, slice, map, filter (and toSorted/toSpliced/toReversed) return new arrays.
Q3. Why does [1, 2, 10].sort() give [1, 10, 2]?
  • The default sort converts items to strings and compares UTF-16 code units ("10" < "2"). Use sort((a, b) => a - b).
Q4. Is Promise part of JavaScript? Is setTimeout?
  • Promise yes (ECMAScript ES6). setTimeout, fetch, DOM events and the event loop are provided by the host environment (browser / Node.js).
Q5. Output-based questions
console.log([1, 2, 3, 4].fill(0, 1, 3));                 // → [1, 0, 0, 4]
console.log(['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'].splice(1, 2));          // → ['b', 'c']
console.log([1, 3, 5].find(n => n % 2 === 0), [1, 3].findIndex(n => n > 5));   // → undefined -1
console.log('hello'.substring(4, 1), String.fromCharCode(97));   // → ell a
console.log(typeof class {}, typeof [], typeof null);     // → function object object
  • What happens: five output questions from the mock interview.
  • Output: [1, 0, 0, 4], ['b', 'c'], undefined -1, ell a, function object object.

// ? tell me the output

// Each time you use {}, it creates a new, unique object in memory.
// == checks for equality with type conversion (when comparing objects, it checks if they reference the same object in memory).
// Since {} creates a new object each time, two different {} objects do not reference the same object in memory.

Explanation: value vs reference. In JavaScript, primitive values (like numbers, strings, etc.) are compared by their value. Objects (including arrays and functions) are compared by their reference (memory location), not by their content or structure.
Loose equality (==): == performs type coercion for primitive values. For example, 2 == '2' is true, because the string '2' is coerced to the number 2. However, for objects, == still checks whether they reference the same object in memory. Even if two objects have the same structure or properties, if they are not the exact same object (i.e. the same reference), == returns false.
Strict equality (===): === checks both type and reference without type coercion. For objects, === checks whether both operands reference the exact same object in memory.

? separate the characters and numbers from the given array
// ? separate the characters and numbers from the given array
let array = [1, 'a', 'b', "c", 6, 7, 8, '5'];
function separationOfArray(array) {
  let numberArray = [];
  let charArray = [];
  for (let element of array) {
    if (typeof element === 'number') {
      numberArray.push(element);
    } else {
      charArray.push(element);
    }
  }
  return {
    numberArray,
    charArray
  };
}
const result = separationOfArray(array);
console.log("Numbers:", result.numberArray);     // → Numbers: [1, 6, 7, 8]
console.log("Characters:", result.charArray);    // → Characters: ['a', 'b', 'c', '5']   ('5' is a string)

? give an example of function currying
//? give an example of function currying
function currying(operator){
  return function(a){
      return function(b){
          return function(c){
              if(operator ==='add'){
                  return a+b+c;
              }else if(operator === 'mul'){
                  return a*b*c
              }else{
                  throw new Error ('unsupported operation')
              }
          }
      }
  }
}
const calculate = currying('mul');
console.log(calculate(1)(2)(3))   // → 6
  • What happens: currying: pick the operator first, then take a, b, c one call at a time.
  • Output: 6.

? What are the differences between the map function and the forEach function?
  • map: returns a new array with the transformed elements, based on the callback function; does not modify the array, it creates a new array; chaining methods (like filter, reduce) is allowed.
  • forEach(): doesn't return anything (undefined), it simply executes the function for each element; it modifies the original array if you change the elements inside the callback; chaining isn't possible.

? What do you mean by event bubbling? Event bubbling is a concept in the DOM (Document Object Model) where an event starts at the most specific element (the target element) and then "bubbles up" through its ancestors in the DOM hierarchy, triggering the same event handler on each ancestor. This process continues until it reaches the root element of the document.
How event bubbling works: event occurrence: when an event (like a click, keydown, etc.) occurs on a target element, the event is first received by that element. Propagation: the event then bubbles up from the target element to its parent element, then to its parent's parent, and so on, until it reaches the root element (usually the <html> or <body> element). Event handlers: as the event bubbles up, any event listeners attached to these ancestor elements are triggered, provided that they listen for that event type. ✔ it triggers the handlers REGISTERED on each ancestor for that event type (not "the same handler"), and bubbling continues past <html> to document and then window. Some events (focus, blur, mouseenter) don't bubble. See Chapter 77.Bubbling प्रत्येक ancestor वर लावलेले handlers चालवतो आणि document, window पर्यंत जातो; focus, blur सारखे events bubble होत नाहीत.

4. Pure/impure functions & transpiling

? What is a pure function in JavaScript, with an example? (Deterministic: given the same inputs, it always returns the same output. No side effects: it doesn't modify external state, e.g. global variables, the DOM, databases.) A pure function is a function that gives the same output when executed multiple times with the same arguments; it doesn't modify variables, the DOM or global variables, and it has a constant result for the same input; it doesn't rely on or modify any state; it doesn't perform any side effect. 
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
console.log(add(2, 3));   // 5
console.log(add(2, 3));   // 5 (same input, same output)
  • What happens: pure: same input → same output, no side effects.
  • Output: 5, 5.
? What is an impure function? It is not deterministic: the same input may not return the same output. It has side effects: it modifies external state (e.g. global variables, the DOM, API calls, databases). 
let total = 0;
function addToTotal(value) {
    total += value;   // modifies a global variable
    return total;
}
console.log(addToTotal(5));   // 5
console.log(addToTotal(5));   // 10 (same input, different output)
  • What happens: impure: changes outside state, so the same call gives different results.
  • Output: 5, 10.
? What is transpiling in coding? Transpiling is the process of converting modern JavaScript (ES6+) code into an older version (ES5 or earlier), so that it can run in older browsers that don't support the latest features. Tools: Babel (most popular), TypeScript (also compiles to JavaScript), SWC (a faster alternative to Babel).
When you want to convert one type of source code into another, you're typically using a transpiler or a compiler. These tools take source code written in one language or syntax and transform it into another format or language.
? Why is transpiling needed? New JavaScript features (e.g. let, const, arrow functions, classes, async/await) may not be supported in older browsers. Transpiling ensures backward compatibility.
  • Transpiling from TypeScript to JavaScript: TypeScript is a superset of JavaScript that adds type annotations and other features. A transpiler like tsc (the TypeScript compiler) is used to convert TypeScript code into regular JavaScript code.
  • ES6+ to ES5 (JavaScript transpiling): tools like Babel are used to convert modern JavaScript (ES6 or later) into an older version (ES5), for compatibility with older browsers that don't support newer syntax (like arrow functions, async/await, etc.).
  • SASS/SCSS to CSS: a CSS preprocessor like SASS is used to write styles in a more feature-rich syntax. These tools transpile SCSS into regular CSS that browsers can read.
  • JSX to JavaScript (React): in React, JSX is used to write UI components, but browsers can't directly interpret JSX. A tool like Babel, or a build tool like Webpack, is used to convert JSX into regular JavaScript.
Transpilers allow developers to write code in a more expressive, efficient, or higher-level way, and then transform it into a more widely supported or optimized version. If you're talking about converting one source-code language or format into another, transpilers are probably what you're looking for. ✔ Note: a transpiler only rewrites SYNTAX (arrow → function). New built-ins like Promise or Array.prototype.includes also need a polyfill (Chapters 82–84).Transpiler फक्त syntax बदलतो; Promise सारख्या नवीन built-ins साठी polyfill लागतो.
Pure function: same input → same output, आणि बाहेरचे काहीही बदलत नाही. Impure function global variable, DOM किंवा API बदलतो. Transpiling म्हणजे नवीन code (ES6+, TypeScript, JSX) जुन्या/browser ला समजणाऱ्या code मध्ये बदलणे (Babel, tsc).

5. ES6 features

? What are the new features in ES6? Please explain. ES6 features list with one-line descriptions 🚀 (this list appears twice in your file; both copies are merged here):
  1. let and const: block-scoped variable declarations (let is mutable, const is immutable).
  2. Arrow functions (=>): shorter function syntax that inherits this from the surrounding scope.
  3. Template literals: string interpolation using backticks (`Hello, ${name}!`).
  4. Default parameters: assign default values to function parameters (function greet(name = "User")).
  5. Destructuring assignment: extract values from arrays and objects into variables (const {name, age} = obj).
  6. Rest operator (...): collects multiple elements into an array (function sum(...nums)).
  7. Spread operator (...): expands an array or object (const arr2 = [...arr1, 4, 5]).
  8. Enhanced object literals: shorthand for defining object properties ({ name, age } instead of { name: name, age: age }).
  9. Promises: handle asynchronous operations (fetchData().then().catch()).
  10. Classes: ES6 class syntax for object-oriented programming (class Person { constructor(name) { this.name = name; } }).
  11. Modules (import/export): split code into reusable modules (import { func } from './module.js').
  12. Map and Set: new collection types (Map for key-value pairs, Set for unique values).
  13. for...of loop: iterates over iterable objects (for (let item of arr) {}).
  14. Object.entries() and Object.values(): retrieve keys and values from an object.
  15. find() and findIndex(): locate elements in an array based on a condition.
  16. includes() for arrays: checks whether an array contains a specific value (arr.includes(3)).
  17. startsWith() and endsWith(): check string prefixes and suffixes (str.startsWith("Hello")).
  18. Number.isFinite() and Number.isNaN(): improved number checking methods.
  19. Generators (function*): create iterators with the yield keyword (function* gen() { yield 1; yield 2; }).
  20. WeakMap and WeakSet: similar to Map and Set, but with weak references.
✔ (1) const is not "immutable": the BINDING can't be reassigned, but a const object/array can still be changed (const a = []; a.push(1) works). (2) Object.entries()/Object.values() are ES2017 and Array.prototype.includes() is ES2016, not ES6. Spread for OBJECTS ({...obj}) is ES2018; ES6 had array spread. (3) The second copy of the list was numbered 1–18 and then the last 2 items had no numbers. See Chapter 84 for features by version.const म्हणजे पुन्हा assign करता येत नाही, पण object आतून बदलता येतो. Object.entries/values ES2017, includes ES2016, object spread ES2018 मध्ये आले, ES6 मध्ये नाही.

6. Promises on button click & await outside async

? What is a promise and its states? Promises are objects or placeholders where we store the failure or success of an asynchronous operation. A promise has 3 states: the pending state, the fulfilled state, the rejected state. 
// 1. create a promise that is resolved or rejected when I click a button
let button = document.getElementById("btn1");
let button2 = document.getElementById("btn2");
const myPromise = new Promise((res, rej) => {
  button.addEventListener("click", () => {
    setTimeout(() => {
      res("promise are resolved");
    }, 1000);
  });
  button2.addEventListener("click", () => {
    setTimeout(() => {
      rej("promise are rejected");
    }, 1000);
  });
});
console.log(myPromise)   // → Promise {<pending>} (until a button is clicked)
// myPromise
//   .then((res) => {
//     console.log(res);
//   })
//   .catch((error) => {
//     console.log(error);
//   });
  console.log(myPromise)
  async function example(){
    const res = myPromise
    return 'vishal'
  }
  let res = await example()
  console.log("res", res)   // → res vishal
  console.log(example());   // → Promise {<fulfilled>: 'vishal'}… (an async function always returns a promise)
  • What happens: a promise settled by button clicks; top-level await works only in modules; an async function returns a promise.
  • Output: Promise {}, res vishal, a promise.
  • ⚠ A promise settles once; later clicks are ignored.
✔ (1) document exists only in the browser (in Node → ReferenceError: document is not defined). (2) let res = await example() at the top level works only in an ES module (<script type="module">); in a normal script it is a SyntaxError. (3) const res = myPromise without await does nothing: example() doesn't wait for the click. (4) A promise settles only ONCE: after the first click, later clicks on either button change nothing. (5) "promise are resolved" → "promise is resolved".document फक्त browser मध्ये असतो; top-level await फक्त module मध्ये चालतो; promise एकदाच settle होतो, म्हणून नंतरचे clicks काही बदलत नाहीत.

// In JavaScript, an async function always returns a Promise. Let's explore how to create fulfilled, rejected, and
// pending states using async/await without explicitly using new Promise():
// 1. fulfilled promise (resolved by default): an async function automatically returns a resolved promise when it returns a value.
async function fulfilledPromise() {
    return "Resolved Value";   // implicitly resolves
}
fulfilledPromise().then(console.log);   // output: Resolved Value
  • What happens: returning a value from an async function fulfils its promise.
  • Output: Resolved Value.
2. rejected promise: to create a rejected promise, simply throw an error inside an async f
// 2. rejected promise: to create a rejected promise, simply throw an error inside an async function.
async function rejectedPromise() {
    throw new Error("Rejected Value");   // implicitly rejects
}
rejectedPromise().catch(console.error);
// output: Error: Rejected Value
// pending promise (indirectly): a function's promise remains pending if it never reaches a resolution or rejection.
// One way to do this is to use await inside an async function on a promise that never resolves.
async function pendingPromise() {
    await new Promise(() => {});   // never resolves
}
console.log(pendingPromise());
// output: Promise { <pending> }
  • What happens: throwing rejects; awaiting a never-settling promise stays pending.
  • Output: Error: Rejected Value, Promise { }.
# Can we use await outside an async function? No, await can't be used outside an async function in regular JavaScript. It must always be inside an async function. However, there are two exceptions:
  1. using await at the top level in modern JavaScript environments (ES2022+, in modules);
  2. using immediately invoked async functions (IIFE) to wrap await.

If your JavaScript file is an ES module (i.e. using type="module" in HTML, or the .mjs extension), you can use await at the top level:
Example 1
// works in ES modules
const data = await fetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1").then(res => res.json());
console.log(data);   // → { userId: 1, id: 1, title: 'delectus aut autem', completed: false }
//  <script type="module" src="top-level-await.js"></script>
  • What happens: top-level await (ES modules only).
  • Output: the todo object.
2. Using an immediately invoked async function (IIFE): for environments where top-level aw
// 2. Using an immediately invoked async function (IIFE): for environments where top-level await is not supported,
//    you can wrap the code in an Immediately Invoked Function Expression (IIFE):
(async () => {
    const data = await fetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1").then(res => res.json());
    console.log(data);
})();
  • What happens: an async IIFE gives the same result in normal scripts.
  • Output: the todo object.

7. Students marks: map, filter, reduce chains

1. get only the names in capital letters
// # 1. get only the names in capital letters
const students = [
  { name: "Alice", rollNumber: 101, marks: 87 },
  { name: "Bob", rollNumber: 102, marks: 76 },
  { name: "Charlie", rollNumber: 103, marks: 35 },
  { name: "Diana", rollNumber: 104, marks: 68 },
];
let name = [];
for (let i = 0; i < students.length; i++) {
  name.push(students[i].name.toLocaleUpperCase());
}
console.log(name);    // → ['ALICE', 'BOB', 'CHARLIE', 'DIANA']
// solution using map
let data = students.map((ele, i, arr) => {
  return ele.name.toLocaleUpperCase();
});
console.log(data);    // → ['ALICE', 'BOB', 'CHARLIE', 'DIANA']
  • What happens: collect upper-case names with a loop, or with map.
  • Output: ['ALICE', 'BOB', 'CHARLIE', 'DIANA'] twice.
return only those students whose marks are greater than 75
// # return only those students whose marks are greater than 75
let marks = students.filter((ele, i, arr) => {
  return ele.marks > 75;
});
console.log(marks);   // → Alice (87), Bob (76)
  • What happens: filter marks > 75.
  • Output: Alice, Bob.
return only those records with more than 80 marks and roll number greater than 100
// # return only those records with more than 80 marks and roll number greater than 100
let mark = students.filter((ele, i, arr) => {
  return ele.marks > 80 && ele.rollNumber > 100;
});
console.log(mark);    // → Alice (87)
  • What happens: filter with two conditions.
  • Output: Alice.
give the sum of all the marks in the given array
// # give the sum of all the marks in the given array
let sum = students.reduce((acc, ele, i, arr) => {
  return (acc = acc + ele.marks);
}, 0);
console.log(sum);     // → 266
  • What happens: reduce sums the marks.
  • Output: 266.
return only the names of students who scored more than 80
//  # return only the names of students who scored more than 80
let output = students.filter((ele,i,arr)=>{
    return ele.marks > 80
}).map((ele)=>{
    return ele.name
})
console.log(output);  // → ['Alice']
  • What happens: filter then map to names.
  • Output: ['Alice'].
return the total marks of students with marks greater than 60, after 20 marks have been ad
// # return the total marks of students with marks greater than 60, after 20 marks have been added to those who scored less than 60
let totalMark = students.map((ele)=>{
    console.log(ele);
    if(ele.marks < 60){
      ele.marks = ele.marks + 20
    }
    return ele
}).filter((ele,i,arr)=>{
    return ele.marks > 60
}).reduce((acc,ele)=>{
    return acc = acc + ele.marks
},0)
console.log(totalMark)   // → 231 (87 + 76 + 68; Charlie 35 + 20 = 55 is still not > 60)
  • What happens: map (+20 if below 60), filter > 60, reduce sum; map mutates the original objects.
  • Output: 231.
  • ⚠ Copy the objects instead of changing them.
✔ (side effect, verified) ele.marks = ele.marks + 20 changes the ORIGINAL students array (Charlie's marks become 55 for the rest of the program), so this map is impure. Return a copy instead: .map(ele => ele.marks < 60 ? { ...ele, marks: ele.marks + 20 } : ele). Also return acc + ele.marks is enough; acc = … is not needed.map मध्ये ele.marks बदलल्यामुळे मूळ students array बदलतो; त्याऐवजी { ...ele } ची copy return करा.

// In JavaScript, an async function always returns a Promise. Let's explore how to create fulfilled, rejected, and
// pending states using async/await without explicitly using new Promise():
async function fulField(){
  return 'resolved value'

fulField().then((res)=> console.log(res))   // → resolved value

8. Multiple APIs & ways to handle async

# JS is single-threaded, so how does it handle multiple APIs? JavaScript + browser = asynchronous power. JavaScript runs in a single thread, but the browser or Node.js environment provides asynchronous APIs (e.g. fetch, setTimeout, XMLHttpRequest, etc.) that are non-blocking. These APIs are handled by the browser's Web APIs or Node's libuv system, outside the JavaScript engine. Once a task is complete, its callback or Promise reaction is queued, and the event loop pushes it onto the call stack. To make multiple API calls, use Promise.all, or async-await with Promise.all. ✔ "avaScript" → JavaScript; the callback is QUEUED, and the event loop moves it to the call stack (it is not "pushed into the event loop").Callback queue मध्ये जातो आणि event loop त्याला call stack वर आणतो. 
const api1 = fetch('https://api.example.com/data1');
const api2 = fetch('https://api.example.com/data2');
Promise.all([api1, api2])
  .then(([res1, res2]) => Promise.all([res1.json(), res2.json()]))
  .then(([data1, data2]) => {
    console.log('Data 1:', data1);
    console.log('Data 2:', data2);
  });
  // using async
  async function fetchData() {
  const [res1, res2] = await Promise.all([
    fetch('https://api.example.com/data1'),
    fetch('https://api.example.com/data2')
  ]);
  const data1 = await res1.json();
  const data2 = await res2.json();
  console.log(data1, data2);
}
// ✔ note: api.example.com is a placeholder (the fetch fails); add .catch() / try…catch, because Promise.all rejects
//   as soon as ONE request fails (use Promise.allSettled to keep the other results).
  • What happens: Promise.all runs both requests in parallel, then parses both bodies; the async version does the same with await.
  • Output: Data 1 / Data 2 (with real URLs).
  • ⚠ One failure rejects everything.
# How many ways are there to handle asynchronous operations in JS?
1: Callbacks
// 1: Callbacks
function fetchData(callback) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    callback("Data loaded");
  }, 1000);
}
fetchData((data) => console.log(data));
  • What happens: the result is passed to a callback after 1 s.
  • Output: Data loaded.
2: Promises
// 2: Promises: introduced in ES6, more readable, and avoids "callback hell".
const fetchData = () => {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => resolve("Data loaded"), 1000);
  });
};
fetchData().then((data) => console.log(data));
  • What happens: the function returns a promise; then reads the value.
  • Output: Data loaded.
3: Async/Await
// 3: Async/Await: built on top of Promises, introduced in ES2017; makes async code look like synchronous code.
const fetchData = async () => {
  return "Data loaded";
};
const showData = async () => {
  const data = await fetchData();
  console.log(data);
};
showData();
  • What happens: await reads the promise's value inside an async function.
  • Output: Data loaded.
  • ⚠ Each snippet redeclares fetchData; run them separately.
4. setTimeout / setInterval: useful for scheduling tasks, but not reliable for precise con
// 4. setTimeout / setInterval: useful for scheduling tasks, but not reliable for precise control.
setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("Executed after 1 second");
}, 1000);
  • What happens: a simple timer.
  • Output: Executed after 1 second.
(These 4 snippets were inside a /* */ comment in your file; each one redeclares fetchData, so run them separately.)

9. Single thread, DOM, ES5 vs ES6

# Why is JavaScript single-threaded? Single-threaded: JS runs one task at a time; there is only one call stack, so the whole JS code is executed line by line on a single call stack. JavaScript was designed to run in the browser, and to make DOM (Document Object Model) manipulation safe, it uses a single thread.
# What makes JavaScript asynchronous? Not JavaScript alone: it uses asynchronous features through the browser environment (or Node.js APIs). The runtime environment (browser or Node.js) provides:
  1. Web APIs, like setTimeout, fetch, DOM events, etc.;
  2. task queues, to hold the callbacks (callback queue / macrotask queue);
  3. the event loop, to coordinate and push those tasks onto the main thread when it's free.

It is responsible for managing async tasks and ensuring smooth execution.
# What is the DOM in JavaScript?
  1. DOM stands for Document Object Model.
  2. It is a programming interface for web documents.
  3. The DOM is a tree-like structure that represents the HTML elements of a webpage, so that JavaScript can interact with them.
  4. JavaScript and the DOM: JavaScript uses the DOM to read, change, create, or delete elements.
  5. The DOM is not part of JavaScript itself, but part of the Web APIs provided by the browser.

JavaScript interacts with the DOM to make dynamic changes to the webpage.
# What are the differences between ES5 and ES6?
1. ES5:
  1. variables are declared with var only;
  2. traditional function expressions (function + prototype);
  3. ES5 supports for...in and the for loop;
  4. callbacks for asynchronous purposes;
  5. default parameters are not supported, you handle them manually inside the function;
  6. destructuring is not available;
  7. for string concatenation in ES5 we have to use the + operator;
  8. spread and rest operators are not available;
  9. import/export is not supported.

2. ES6:
  1. let and const variable declarations are introduced;
  2. arrow functions and the class keyword are introduced;
  3. ES6 supports for...of, Map and Set;
  4. promises are introduced for asynchronous purposes (and later async/await);
  5. default parameters are supported in ES6;
  6. destructuring is introduced;
  7. template literals are used here (template strings with backticks);
  8. spread and rest operators are available;
  9. ES6 introduces import/export.
✔ the ES6 list had two items numbered "7" (the last one is 9); async/await came later, in ES2017.ES6 list मध्ये 7 क्रमांक दोनदा होता; async/await ES2017 मध्ये आले.

10. Interview Questions & Revision

Q1. What does a[b] = 600 store when b is an object?
  • The key "[object Object]" (objects are converted to strings as keys), so every plain object key hits the same slot. Use Map for object keys.
Q2. 10 === new Number(10) and 10 == new Number(10)?
  • false (number vs object) and true (== unwraps the object with valueOf()).
Q3. How do you make an async function reject?
  • throw inside it (or return Promise.reject(err)). Returning any value, even 'reject value', fulfills the promise.
Q4. Why can't await be used everywhere?
  • It is allowed only inside async functions and at the top level of ES modules (ES2022); otherwise wrap the code in an async IIFE.
Q5. Output-based questions
const x = {}, y = { k: 1 }, z = { k: 2 }; x[y] = 1; x[z] = 2; console.log(x[y]);   // → 2
console.log(false * 12, "5" * "2", true + true);          // → 0 10 2
console.log(typeof new Number(5), new Number(5) == 5);    // → object true
(async () => "v")().then(v => console.log("then", v));   // → then v
console.log([87, 35].map(m => m < 60 ? m + 20 : m).filter(m => m > 60).reduce((a, m) => a + m, 0));   // → 87
  • What happens: five output questions: object keys, coercion, Number objects, async functions return promises, map/filter/reduce chain.
  • Output: 2, 0 10 2, object true, then v, 87.
